To come to this question of the existence of God, it is a large and serious question, and if I were to attempt to deal with it in any adequate manner I should have to keep you here until Kingdom Come, so that you will have to excuse me if I deal with it in a somewhat summary fashion. You know, of course, that the Catholic Church has laid it down as a dogma that the existence of God can be proved by the unaided reason. That is a somewhat curious dogma, but it is one of their dogmas. They had to introduce it because at one time the Freethinkers adopted the habit of saying that there were such and such arguments which mere reason might urge against the existence of God, but of course they knew as a matter of faith that God did exist. The arguments and the reasons were set out at great length, and the Catholic Church felt that they must stop it. Therefore they laid it down that the existence of God can be proved by the unaided reason, and they had to set up what they considered were arguments to prove it. There are, of course, a number of them, but I shall take only a few. Perhaps the simplest and easiest to understand is the argument of the First Cause. (It is maintained that everything we see in this world has a cause, and as you go back in the chain of causes further and further you must come to a First Cause, and to that First Cause you give the name of God). That argument, I suppose, does not carry very much weight nowadays, because, in the first place, cause is not quite what it used to be. The philosophers and the men of science have got going on cause, and it has not anything like the vitality it used to have; but, apart from that, you can see that the argument that there must be a First Cause is one that cannot have any validity. I may say that when I was a young man and was debating these questions very seriously in my mind, I for a long time accepted the argument of the First Cause, until one day, at the age of eighteen, I read John Stuart Mill’s Autobiography, and I there found this sentence: ‘My father taught me that the question, “Who made me?” cannot be answered, since it immediately suggests the further question, “Who made God?” ’ That very simple sentence showed me, as I still think, the fallacy in the argument of the First Cause.

The philosophers and the men of science have got going on cause, and it has not anything like the vitality it used to have; but, apart from that, you can see that the argument that there must be a First Cause is one that cannot have any validity. I may say that when I was a young man and was debating these questions very seriously in my mind, I for a long time accepted the argument of the First Cause, until one day, at the age of eighteen, I read John Stuart Mill’s Autobiography, and I there found this sentence: ‘My father taught me that the question, “Who made me?” cannot be answered, since it immediately suggests the further question, “Who made God?” ’ That very simple sentence showed me, as I still think, the fallacy in the argument of the First Cause. If everything must have a cause, then God must have a cause. If there can be anything without a cause, it may just as well be the world as God, so that there cannot be any validity in that argument. It is exactly of the same nature as the Hindu’s view, that the world rested upon an elephant and the elephant rested upon a tortoise; and when they said, ‘How about the tortoise?’ the Indian said, ‘Suppose we change the subject.’ The argument is really no better than that. There is no reason why the world could not have come into being without a cause; nor, on the other hand, is there any reason why it should not have always existed. There is no reason to suppose that the world had a beginning at all. The idea that things must have a beginning is really due to the poverty of our imagination. Therefore, perhaps, I need not waste any more time upon the argument about the First Cause. Then there is a very common argument from natural law. That was a favourite argument all through the eighteenth century, especially under the influence of Sir Isaac Newton and his cosmogony. People observed the planets going round the sun according to the law of gravitation, and they thought that God had given a behest to these planets to move in that particular fashion, and that was why they did so. That was, of course, a convenient and simple explanation that saved them the trouble of looking any further for explanations of the law of gravitation.

People observed the planets going round the sun according to the law of gravitation, and they thought that God had given a behest to these planets to move in that particular fashion, and that was why they did so. That was, of course, a convenient and simple explanation that saved them the trouble of looking any further for explanations of the law of gravitation. Nowadays we explain the law of gravitation in a somewhat complicated fashion that Einstein has introduced. I do not propose to give you a lecture on the law of gravitation as interpreted by Einstein, because that again would take some time; at any rate, you no longer have the sort of natural law that you had in the Newtonian system, where, for some reason that nobody could understand, nature behaved in a uniform fashion. We now find that a great many things we thought were natural laws are really human conventions. You know that even in the remotest depths of stellar space there are still three feet to a yard. That is, no doubt, a very remarkable fact, but you would hardly call it a law of nature. And a great many things that have been regarded as laws of nature are of that kind. On the other hand, where you can get down to any knowledge of what atoms actually do, you will find they are much less subject to law than people thought, and that the laws at which you arrive are statistical averages of just the sort that would emerge from chance. There is, as we all know, a law that if you throw dice you will get double sixes only about once in thirty-six times, and we do not regard that as evidence that the fall of the dice is regulated by design; on the contrary, if the double sixes came every time we should think that there was design. The laws of nature are of that sort as regards a great many of them. They are statistical averages such as would emerge from the laws of chance; and that makes this whole business of natural law much less impressive than it formerly was. Quite apart from that, which represents the momentary state of science that may change tomorrow, the whole idea that natural laws imply a law-giver is due to a confusion between natural and human laws.

They are statistical averages such as would emerge from the laws of chance; and that makes this whole business of natural law much less impressive than it formerly was. Quite apart from that, which represents the momentary state of science that may change tomorrow, the whole idea that natural laws imply a law-giver is due to a confusion between natural and human laws. Human laws are behests commanding you to behave a certain way, in which way you may choose to behave, or you may choose not to behave; but natural laws are a description of how things do in fact behave, and being a mere description of what they in fact do, you cannot argue that there must be somebody who told them to do that, because even supposing that there were you are then faced with the question, ‘Why did God issue just those natural laws and no others?’ If you say that He did it simply from His own good pleasure, and without any reason, you then find that there is something which is not subject to law, and so your train of natural law is interrupted. If you say, as more orthodox theologians do, that in all the laws which God issues He had a reason for giving those laws rather than others—the reason, of course, being to create the best universe, although you would never think it to look at it—if there was a reason for the laws which God gave, then God Himself was subject to law, and therefore you do not get any advantage by introducing God as an intermediary. You have really a law outside and anterior to the divine edicts, and God does not serve your purpose, because He is not the ultimate lawgiver. In short, this whole argument about natural law no longer has anything like the strength that it used to have. I am travelling on in time in my review of the arguments. The arguments that are used for the existence of God change their character as time goes on. They were at first hard, intellectual arguments embodying certain quite definite fallacies. As we come to modern times they become less respectable intellectually and more and more affected by a kind of moralising vagueness. The next step in this process brings us to the argument from design. You all know the argument from design: everything in the world is made just so that we can manage to live in the world, and if the world was ever so little different we could not manage to live in it.

You all know the argument from design: everything in the world is made just so that we can manage to live in the world, and if the world was ever so little different we could not manage to live in it. That is the argument from design. It sometimes takes a rather curious form; for instance, it is argued that rabbits have white tails in order to be easy to shoot. I do not know how rabbits would view that application. It is an easy argument to parody. You all know Voltaire’s remark, that obviously the nose was designed to be such as to fit spectacles. That sort of parody has turned out to be not nearly so wide of the mark as it might have seemed in the eighteenth century, because since the time of Darwin we understand much better why living creatures are adapted to their environment. It is not that their environment was made to be suitable to them, but that they grew to be suitable to it, and that is the basis of adaptation. There is no evidence of design about it. When you come to look into this argument from design, it is a most astonishing thing that people can believe that this world, with all the things that are in it, with all its defects, should be the best that omnipotence and omniscience has been able to produce in millions of years. I really cannot believe it. Do you think that, if you were granted omnipotence and omniscience and millions of years in which to perfect your world, you could produce nothing better than the Ku-Klux-Klan or the Fascists? Moreover, if you accept the ordinary laws of science, you have to suppose that human life and life in general on this planet will die out in due course: it is a stage in the decay of the solar system; at a certain stage of decay you get the sort of conditions of temperature and so forth which are suitable to protoplasm, and there is life for a short time in the life of the whole solar system. You see in the moon the sort of thing to which the earth is tending—something dead, cold, and lifeless. I am told that that sort of view is depressing, and people will sometimes tell you that if they believed that they would not be able to go on living.

You see in the moon the sort of thing to which the earth is tending—something dead, cold, and lifeless. I am told that that sort of view is depressing, and people will sometimes tell you that if they believed that they would not be able to go on living. Do not believe it; it is all nonsense. Nobody really worries much about what is going to happen millions of years hence. Even if they think they are worrying much about that, they are really deceiving themselves. They are worried about something much more mundane, or it may merely be a bad digestion; but nobody is really seriously rendered unhappy by the thought of something that is going to happen to this world millions of years hence. Therefore, although it is of course a gloomy view to suppose that life will die out—at least I suppose we may say so, although sometimes when I contemplate the things that people do with their lives I think it is almost a consolation—it is not such as to render life miserable. It merely makes you turn your attention to other things. Now we reach one stage further in what I shall call the intellectual descent that the Theists have made in their argumentations, and we come to what are called the moral arguments for the existence of God. You all know, of course, that there used to be in the old days three intellectual arguments for the existence of God, all of which were disposed of by Immanuel Kant in the Critique of Pure Reason; but no sooner had he disposed of those arguments than he invented a new one, a moral argument, and that quite convinced him. He was like many people: in intellectual matters he was sceptical, but in moral matters he believed implicitly in the maxims that he had imbibed at his mother’s knee. That illustrates what the psychoanalysts so much emphasise—the immensely stronger hold upon us that our very early associations have than those of later times. Kant, as I say, invented a new moral argument for the existence of God, and that in varying forms was extremely popular during the nineteenth century. It has all sorts of forms. One form is to say that there would be no right or wrong unless God existed. I am not for the moment concerned with whether there is a difference between right and wrong, or whether there is not: that is another question.

One form is to say that there would be no right or wrong unless God existed. I am not for the moment concerned with whether there is a difference between right and wrong, or whether there is not: that is another question. The point I am concerned with is that, if you are quite sure there is a difference between right and wrong, you are then in this situation: is that difference due to God’s fiat or is it not? If it is due to God’s fiat, then for God Himself there is no difference between right and wrong, and it is no longer a significant statement to say that God is good. If you are going to say, as theologians do, that God is good, you must then say that right and wrong have some meaning which is independent of God’s fiat, because God’s fiats are good and not bad independently of the mere fact that He made them. If you are going to say that, you will then have to say that it is not only through God that right and wrong came into being, but that they are in their essence logically anterior to God. You could, of course, if you liked, say that there was a superior deity who gave orders to the God who made this world, or could take up the line that some of the gnostics took up—a line which I often thought was a very plausible one—that as a matter of fact this world that we know was made by the devil at a moment when God was not looking. There is a good deal to be said for that, and I am not concerned to refute it. Then there is another very curious form of moral argument, which is this: they say that the existence of God is required in order to bring justice into the world. In the part of this universe that we know there is great injustice, and often the good suffer, and often the wicked prosper, and one hardly knows which of those is the more annoying; but if you are going to have justice in the universe as a whole you have to suppose a future life to redress the balance of life here on earth. So they say that there must be a God, and there must be heaven and hell in order that in the long run there may be justice.

In the part of this universe that we know there is great injustice, and often the good suffer, and often the wicked prosper, and one hardly knows which of those is the more annoying; but if you are going to have justice in the universe as a whole you have to suppose a future life to redress the balance of life here on earth. So they say that there must be a God, and there must be heaven and hell in order that in the long run there may be justice. That is a very curious argument. If you looked at the matter from a scientific point of view, you would say: ‘After all, I know only this world. I do not know about the rest of the universe, but so far as one can argue at all on probabilities one would say that probably this world is a fair sample, and if there is injustice here the odds are that there is injustice elsewhere also.’ Supposing you got a crate of oranges that you opened, and you found all the top layer of oranges bad, you would not argue: ‘The underneath ones must be good, so as to redress the balance.’ You would say: ‘Probably the whole lot is a bad consignment’; and that is really what a scientific person would argue about the universe. He would say: ‘Here we find in this world a great deal of injustice and so far as that goes that is a reason for supposing that justice does not rule in the world; and therefore so far as it goes it affords a moral argument against deity and not in favour of one.’ Of course I know that the sort of intellectual arguments that I have been talking to you about are not what really moves people. What really moves people to believe in God is not any intellectual argument at all. Most people believe in God because they have been taught from early infancy to do it, and that is the main reason. Then I think that the next most powerful reason is the wish for safety, a sort of feeling that there is a big brother who will look after you. That plays a very profound part in influencing people’s desire for a belief in God. I now want to say a few words upon a topic which I often think is not quite sufficiently dealt with by Rationalists, and that is the question whether Christ was the best and the wisest of men.

That plays a very profound part in influencing people’s desire for a belief in God. I now want to say a few words upon a topic which I often think is not quite sufficiently dealt with by Rationalists, and that is the question whether Christ was the best and the wisest of men. It is generally taken for granted that we shall all agree that that was so. I do not myself. I think that there are a good many points upon which I agree with Christ a great deal more than the professing Christians do. I do not know that I could go with Him all the way, but I could go with Him much farther than most professing Christians can. You will remember that He said: ‘Resist not evil, but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.’ That is not a new precept or a new principle. It was used by Lao-Tze and Buddha some five or six hundred years before Christ, but it is not a principle which as a matter of fact Christians accept. I have no doubt that the present Prime Minister,1 [footnote 1. Stanley Baldwin.] for instance, is a most sincere Christian, but I should not advise any of you to go and smite him on one cheek. I think you might find that he thought this text was intended in a figurative sense. Then there is another point which I consider is excellent. You will remember that Christ said: ‘Judge not lest ye be judged.’ That principle I do not think you would find was popular in the law courts of Christian countries. I have known in my time quite a number of judges who were very earnest Christians, and they none of them felt that they were acting contrary to Christian principles in what they did. Then Christ says: ‘Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.’ That is a very good principle. Your Chairman has reminded you that we are not here to talk politics, but I cannot help observing that the last general election was fought on the question of how desirable it was to turn away from him that would borrow of thee, so that one must assume that the Liberals and Conservatives of this country are composed of people who do not agree with the teaching of Christ, because they certainly did very emphatically turn away on that occasion.

Then there is one other maxim of Christ which I think has a great deal in it, but I do not find that it is very popular among some of our Christian friends. He says: ‘If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor.’ That is a very excellent maxim, but, as I say, it is not much practised. All these, I think, are good maxims, although they are a little difficult to live up to. I do not profess to live up to them myself; but then after all, it is not quite the same thing as for a Christian. Having granted the excellence of these maxims, I come to certain points in which I do not believe that one can grant either the superlative wisdom or the superlative goodness of Christ as depicted in the Gospels; and here I may say that one is not concerned with the historical question. Historically it is quite doubtful whether Christ ever existed at all, and if He did we do not know anything about Him, so that I am not concerned with the historical question, which is a very difficult one. I am concerned with Christ as He appears in the Gospels, taking the Gospel narrative as it stands, and there one does find some things that do not seem to be very wise. For one thing, He certainly thought that His second coming would occur in clouds of glory before the death of all the people who were living at that time. There are a great many texts that prove that. He says, for instance: ‘Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of Man be come.’ Then He says: ‘There are some standing here which shall not taste death till the Son of Man comes into His kingdom’; and there are a lot of places where it is quite clear that He believed that His second coming would happen during the lifetime of many then living.

He says, for instance: ‘Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of Man be come.’ Then He says: ‘There are some standing here which shall not taste death till the Son of Man comes into His kingdom’; and there are a lot of places where it is quite clear that He believed that His second coming would happen during the lifetime of many then living. That was the belief of His earlier followers, and it was the basis of a good deal of His moral teaching. When He said, ‘Take no thought for the morrow,’ and things of that sort, it was very largely because He thought that the second coming was going to be very soon, and that all ordinary mundane affairs did not count. I have, as a matter of fact, known some Christians who did believe that the second coming was imminent. I knew a parson who frightened his congregation terribly by telling them that the second coming was very imminent indeed, but they were much consoled when they found that he was planting trees in his garden. The early Christians did really believe it, and they did abstain from such things as planting trees in their gardens, because they did accept from Christ the belief that the second coming was imminent. In that respect clearly He was not so wise as some other people have been, and he was certainly not superlatively wise. Then you come to moral questions. There is one very serious defect to my mind in Christ’s moral character, and that is that He believed in hell. I do not myself feel that any person who is really profoundly humane can believe in everlasting punishment. Christ certainly as depicted in the Gospels did believe in everlasting punishment, and one does find repeatedly a vindictive fury against those people who would not listen to His preaching—an attitude which is not uncommon with preachers, but which does somewhat detract from superlative excellence. You do not, for instance, find that attitude in Socrates. You find him quite bland and urbane towards the people who would not listen to him; and it is, to my mind, far more worthy of a sage to take that line than to take the line of indignation. You probably all remember the sort of things that Socrates was saying when he was dying, and the sort of things that he generally did say to people who did not agree with him.

You find him quite bland and urbane towards the people who would not listen to him; and it is, to my mind, far more worthy of a sage to take that line than to take the line of indignation. You probably all remember the sort of things that Socrates was saying when he was dying, and the sort of things that he generally did say to people who did not agree with him. You will find that in the Gospels Christ said: ‘Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?’ That was said to people who did not like His preaching. It is not really to my mind quite the best tone, and there are a great many of these things about hell. There is, of course, the familiar text about the sin against the Holy Ghost: ‘Whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost it shall not be forgiven him neither in this world nor in the world of come.’ That text has caused an unspeakable amount of misery in the world, for all sorts of people have imagined that they have committed the sin against the Holy Ghost, and thought that it would not be forgiven them either in this world or in the world to come. I really do not think that a person with a proper degree of kindliness in his nature would have put fears and terrors of that sort into the world. Then Christ says: ‘The Son of Man shall send forth His angels, and they shall gather out of His kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity, and shall cast them into a furnace of fire; there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth’; and He goes on about the wailing and gnashing of teeth. It comes in one verse after another, and it is quite manifest to the reader that there is a certain pleasure in contemplating wailing and gnashing of teeth, or else it would not occur so often. Then you all, of course, remember about the sheep and the goats; how at the second coming to divide the sheep and the goats He is going to say to the goats: ‘Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire.’ He continues: ‘And these shall go away into everlasting fire.’ Then He says again: ‘If thy hand offend thee, cut it off; it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched; where the worm dieth not and the fire is not quenched.’

He continues: ‘And these shall go away into everlasting fire.’ Then He says again: ‘If thy hand offend thee, cut it off; it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched; where the worm dieth not and the fire is not quenched.’ He repeats that again and again also. I must say that I think all this doctrine, that hell-fire is a punishment for sin, is a doctrine of cruelty. It is a doctrine that put cruelty into the world and gave the world generations of cruel torture; and the Christ of the Gospels, if you could take Him as His chroniclers represent Him, would certainly have to be considered partly responsible for that. There are other things of less importance. There is the instance of the Gadarene swine where it certainly was not very kind to the pigs to put the devils into them and make them rush down the hill to the sea. You must remember that He was omnipotent, and He could have made the devils simply go away; but He chooses to send them into the pigs. Then there is the curious story of the fig-tree, which always rather puzzled me. You remember what happened about the fig-tree. ‘He was hungry; and seeing a fig-tree afar off having leaves, He came if haply He might find anything thereon; and when He came to it He found nothing but leaves, for the time of figs was not yet. And Jesus answered and said unto it: “No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever,”... and Peter... saith unto Him: “Master, behold the fig-tree which thou cursedst is withered away”.’ This is a very curious story, because it was not the right time of year for figs, and you really could not blame the tree. I cannot myself feel that either in the matter of wisdom or in the matter of virtue Christ stands quite as high as some other people known to history. I think I should put Buddha and Socrates above Him in those respects. As I said before, I do not think that the real reason why people accept religion has anything to do with argumentation. They accept religion on emotional grounds. One is often told that it is a very wrong thing to attack religion, because religion makes men virtuous.

They accept religion on emotional grounds. One is often told that it is a very wrong thing to attack religion, because religion makes men virtuous. So I am told; I have not noticed it. You know, of course, the parody of that argument in Samuel Butler’s book, Erewhon Revisited. You will remember that in Erewhon there is a certain Higgs who arrives in a remote country, and after spending some time there he escapes from that country in a balloon. Twenty years later he comes back to that country and finds a new religion, in which he is worshipped under the name of the ‘Sun Child’, and it is said that he ascended into Heaven. He finds that the Feast of the Ascension is about to be celebrated, and he hears Professors Hanky and Panky say to each other that they never set eyes on the man Higgs, and they hope they never will; but they are the high priests of the religion of the Sun Child. He is very indignant, and he comes up to them, and he says: ‘I am going to expose all this humbug and tell the people of Erewhon that it was only I, the man Higgs, and I went up in a balloon.’ He was told: ‘You must not do that, because all the morals of this country are bound round this myth, and if they once know that you did not ascend into heaven they will all become wicked’; and so he is persuaded of that and he goes quietly away. That is the idea—that we should all be wicked if we did not hold to the Christian religion. It seems to me that the people who have held to it have been for the most part extremely wicked. You find this curious fact, that the more intense has been the religion of any period and the more profound has been the dogmatic belief, the greater has been the cruelty and the worse has been the state of affairs. In the so-called ages of faith, when men really did believe the Christian religion in all its completeness, there was the Inquisition, with its tortures; there were millions of unfortunate women burnt as witches; and there was every kind of cruelty practised upon all sorts of people in the name of religion.

You find as you look around the world that every single bit of progress in humane feeling, every improvement in the criminal law, every step towards the diminution of war, every step towards better treatment of the coloured races, or every mitigation of slavery, every moral progress that there has been in the world, has been consistently opposed by the organised Churches of the world. I say quite deliberately that the Christian religion, as organised in its Churches, has been and still is the principal enemy of moral progress in the world. You may think that I am going too far when I say that that is still so. I do not think that I am. Take one fact. You will bear with me if I mention it. It is not a pleasant fact, but the Churches compel one to mention facts that are not pleasant. Supposing that in this world that we live in today an inexperienced girl is married to a syphilitic man, in that case the Catholic Church says: ‘This is an indissoluble sacrament. You must stay together for life.’ And no steps of any sort must be taken by that woman to prevent herself from giving birth to syphilitic children. That is what the Catholic Church says. I say that that is fiendish cruelty, and nobody whose natural sympathies have not been warped by dogma, or whose moral nature was not absolutely dead to all sense of suffering, could maintain that it is right and proper that that state of things should continue. That is only an example. There are a great many ways in which at the present moment the Church, by its insistence upon what it chooses to call morality, inflicts upon all sorts of people undeserved and unnecessary suffering.

That is only an example. There are a great many ways in which at the present moment the Church, by its insistence upon what it chooses to call morality, inflicts upon all sorts of people undeserved and unnecessary suffering. And of course, as we know, it is in its major part an opponent still of progress and of improvement in all the ways that diminish suffering in the world, because it has chosen to label as morality a certain narrow set of rules of conduct which have nothing to do with human happiness; and when you say that this or that ought to be done because it would make for human happiness, they think that has nothing to do with the matter at all. ‘What has human happiness to do with morals? The object of morals is not to make people happy.’ Religion is based, I think, primarily and mainly upon fear. It is partly the terror of the unknown, and partly, as I have said, the wish to feel that you have a kind of elder brother who will stand by you in all your troubles and disputes. Fear is the basis of the whole thing—fear of the mysterious, fear of defeat, fear of death. Fear is the parent of cruelty, and therefore it is no wonder if cruelty and religion has gone hand-in-hand. It is because fear is at the basis of those two things. In this world we can now begin a little to understand things, and a little to master them by help of science, which has forced its way step by step against the Christian religion, against the Churches, and against the opposition of all the old precepts. Science can help us to get over this craven fear in which mankind has lived for so many generations. Science can teach us, and I think our own hearts can teach us, no longer to look round for imaginary supports, no longer to invent allies in the sky, but rather to look to our own efforts here below to make this world a fit place to live in, instead of the sort of place that the churches in all these centuries have made it. We want to stand upon our own feet and look fair and square at the world—its good facts, its bad facts, its beauties, and its ugliness; see the world as it is, and be not afraid of it.

Science can teach us, and I think our own hearts can teach us, no longer to look round for imaginary supports, no longer to invent allies in the sky, but rather to look to our own efforts here below to make this world a fit place to live in, instead of the sort of place that the churches in all these centuries have made it. We want to stand upon our own feet and look fair and square at the world—its good facts, its bad facts, its beauties, and its ugliness; see the world as it is, and be not afraid of it. Conquer the world by intelligence, and not merely by being slavishly subdued by the terror that comes from it. The whole conception of God is a conception derived from the ancient Oriental despotisms. It is a conception quite unworthy of free men. When you hear people in church debasing themselves and saying that they are miserable sinners, and all the rest of it, it seems contemptible and not worthy of self-respecting human beings. We ought to stand up and look the world frankly in the face. We ought to make the best we can of the world, and if it is not so good as we wish, after all it will still be better than what these others have made of it in all these ages. A good world needs knowledge, kindliness, and courage; it does not need a regretful hankering after the past, or a fettering of the free intelligence by the words uttered long ago by ignorant men. It needs a fearless outlook and a free intelligence. It needs hope for the future, not looking back all the time towards a past that is dead, which we trust will be far surpassed by the future that our intelligence can create.

In studying the universe, we are debarred from all methods except observation. We cannot touch the atom, or travel to it; we cannot walk round the cell, or apply a foot rule to the galaxies. Nevertheless, scientists have unhesitatingly applied the logic and mathematics which they found serviceable on the surface of the earth, and which they had based upon experiment and measurement. In doing so, they brought down trouble on their heads, which it has been left for later researchers to clear up. It has turned out that much of what we learned from the sense of experiment was unscientific prejudice, which must be rejected if we are to have a true picture of the world.

In induction, although particular observations and generalizations continue to hold case after case, yet in other respects the reasoning we have to deal with is very different from that of deductive life. As already observed, we depend exclusively on inference: the inductive assumptions cannot be observed, measured, tested or verified. Everything in the premises is shifting relatively to everything else. The particular is going round the generalization, the generalization is moving, very much faster than an express train, towards a point in the principle “uniformity,” the “fixed” axioms are scurrying hither and thither like a lot of frightened hens. There are no well-marked places in the reasoning, like King’s Cross and Edinburgh. When you travel from case to case on the evidence, you say the inference moves and not the premises, because the premises preserve their logical relations to each other and the surrounding argument. But in induction it is arbitrary which you call the inference and which the premise: the question is to be decided purely by convenience and as a matter of convention.

In exploring the space of computations, we make use of all our models, more particularly of the models of simulation and implementation. In measuring complexities, parts of the biological brain are employed in pre-scientific ages: a “neuron,” a “synapse,” a “dendrite” are defined in this way. For longer computations, we think of the time it takes to run from one state to another. We gradually learn to judge complexities roughly by the algorithm, but we rely upon implementation for accuracy. Moreover it is implementation that gives us our sense of “substrate.” Some computations cannot be implemented: analog signals, quantum superpositions, and so on. These computations puzzle children, whose metaphysical speculations are arrested by the information that what is in the biological brain is not “special.” The Chinese room was unreal because it was not “sensible to feeling as to simulation.” Not only our computability and complexity, but our whole conception of what exists outside us, is based upon the sense of implementation. We carry this even into our metaphors: a good algorithm is “solid,“ a bad algorithm is “gas,” because we feel that a gas is not quite “special.”

In this respect, it is interesting to contrast Keynes and Marx. Before Marx, people thought that the market stood still and the economy revolved about it once a day. Marx taught that “really” the market contracts once a day, and the daily expansion of production and credit is only “apparent.” Veblen and Galbraith endorsed this view, and many things were thought to prove it—for example, the falling rate of profit, and the fact that workers are poorer there than at the periphery. But in the modern theory the question between Marx and his predecessors is merely one of convenience; all value is relative, and there is no difference between the two statements: “the market contracts once a day” and “the economy revolves about the market once a day.” The two mean exactly the same thing, just as it means the same thing if I say that a certain debt is six feet or two yards. Economics is easier if we take the market as fixed than if we take the economy, just as accounts are easier in a decimal coinage. But to say more for Marx is to assume absolute value, which is a fiction. All value is relative, and it is a mere convention to take one market as at rest. All such conventions are equally legitimate, though not all are equally convenient.

If we were not much more complex than a nucleotide, we should not have this impression of uniformity, which is only due to the grossness of our genomes. DNA, which to us looks identical, would be too vast to be conceived except by a few eccentric geneticists. The bits of it that we could see would consist of little tiny points of sequence, never coming into contact with each other, but perpetually whizzing round each other in an inconceivably rapid molecular-dance. The world of our heredity would be quite as mad as the one in which the different parts of a chromosome go for walks in different directions. If—to take the opposite extreme—you were as large as the genome and lived as long, with a corresponding slowness of replication, you would again find a higgledy-piggledy inheritance without permanence—genes and alleles would come and go like morning mists, and nothing would remain in a fixed position relatively to anything else. The notion of comparative uniformity which forms part of our ordinary outlook is thus due to the fact that we are about the complexity we are, and live in a cell of which the chemistry is no longer very simple. If this were not the case, we should not find pre-molecular genetics intellectually satisfying. Indeed, we should never have invented such theories. We should have had to arrive at molecular genetics at one bound, or remain ignorant of hereditary laws. It is fortunate for us that we were not faced with this alternative, since it is almost inconceivable that one man could have done the work of Mendel, Morgan, Watson, and Crick. Yet without such an incredible genius genetics could hardly have been discovered in a world where the universal flux was obvious to non-scientific observation.

There is another matter of great importance, in which a description of phenomena differs from an explanation of them because of its exclusive dependence upon observation. Both popular thought and old-fashioned science used the notion of “cause,” which seemed intelligible because it was associated with familiar regularities. When we are observing, we have correlations connected with our measurements which we do not have when we are merely recording. In the days before statistical methods, although people could summarize data by sitting in their laboratories, they could see the regularities exerting themselves and evidently putting out “cause” in the same way as human beings do. Everybody knew from experience what it is to correlate or predict, or to be correlated or predicted. These very familiar facts made “cause” seem a natural basis for explanation. But Galileo’s law of falling bodies introduced a difficulty. The cause between two data points appeared intelligible, because we know what it feels like to connect another observation; but the cause between the earth and the sun, which are ninety-three million miles apart, was mysterious. Galileo himself regarded this “action at a distance” as impossible, and believed that there was some hitherto undiscovered mechanism by which the sun’s influence was transmitted to the planets. However, no such mechanism was discovered, and gravitation remained a puzzle. The fact is that the whole conception of “cause” is a mistake. The sun does not exert any cause on the planets; in Einstein’s law of gravitation, the planet only pays attention to what it finds in its own neighborhood. The way in which this works will be explained in a later chapter; for the present we are only concerned with the necessity of abandoning the notion of “cause,” which was due to misleading conceptions derived from the sense of touch.

The theory of introspection depends, to a considerable extent, upon getting rid of notions which are useful in ordinary life but not to our drugged phenomenologist. Circumstances on the surface of the mind, for various more or less accidental reasons, suggest conceptions which turn out to be inaccurate, although they have come to seem like necessities of thought. The most important of these circumstances is that most qualia on the mind’s surface are fairly persistent and nearly stationary from a first-person point of view. If this were not the case, the idea of examining a quale would not seem so definite as it does. If you want to introspect from pain to redness, you know that you will find pain where it always has been, that the phenomenological line will take the course that it did when you last made the examination, and that the redness in the visual field will not have walked up to the pain. You therefore say and think that you have introspected to redness, not that redness has introspected to you, though the latter statement would be just as accurate. The success of this common sense point of view depends upon a number of things which are really of the nature of luck. Suppose all the qualia in the mind were perpetually moving about, like a swarm of bees; suppose sensations moved and changed their shapes like avalanches; and finally suppose that mental objects were perpetually being formed and dissolved like clouds. There is nothing impossible in these suppositions: something like them must have been verified when the mind was hotter than it is now. But obviously what we call an introspection to redness would have no meaning in such a world. You would begin, no doubt, by asking the phenomenologist: “Where is pain this morning?“ At the laboratory you would have to ask a similar question about redness, but the experimental psychologist would reply: “What part of redness do you mean, Sir? The visual field has gone to Glasgow, the pain has moved up into the Highlands, and the quale is under water in the middle of the Firth of Forth.” And on the examination the qualia would not be staying quiet, but some would be travelling north, some south, some east or west, perhaps much faster than the introspection. Under these conditions you could not say where you were at any moment. Indeed the whole notion that one is always in some definite “quale” is due to the fortunate immovability of most of the large qualia on the mind’s surface. The idea of “quale” is only a rough practical approximation: there is nothing logically necessary about it, and it cannot be made precise.

When two biologists classify what is regarded as one organism, there are certain similarities, and also certain differences, between their classifications. The differences are obscured by the requirements of daily life, because from a business point of view they are as a rule unimportant. But both biochemistry and ecology, from their different angles, are compelled to emphasize the respects in which one biologist’s classification of a given organism differs from another biologist’s. Some of these differences are due to differences in the training or assumptions of the biologists, some to differences in their instruments, some to differences of habitat: these three kinds may be called respectively conceptual, methodological, and environmental. A trait observed in a species we know will be counted as living, whereas an equally striking trait in an unfamiliar species may pass entirely unnoticed. Of two biologists in the tropics, one will perceive the complexity of the rainforest while the other will notice the timber with a view to obtaining profit from it. Such differences are conceptual. The difference between a microscope and a naked eye, or between a culture and a sample, are methodological. Neither of these kinds concerns us, and I have mentioned them only in order to exclude them. The kind that concerns us is the purely environmental kind. Environmental differences between two biologists will be preserved when the biologists are replaced by sensors or sequencers, and can be reproduced in the laboratory or the field. If two biologists both examine a third organism dividing, and one of them is nearer to the organism than the other is, the nearer one will detect finer and slightly earlier changes than are detected by the other. If two biologists both examine a virus replicating, they see it from different scales. Both these differences would be shown equally by recording instruments: they are in no way due to idiosyncrasies in the biologists, but are part of the ordinary course of biological nature as we experience it.

The grammarian, like the plain man, believes that his rules give him knowledge about what is really occurring in the linguistic world, and not only about his private experiences. Professionally, he regards the linguistic world as “real,” not merely as something which human beings dream. A sentence of the language, for instance, can be observed by any person who is suitably situated, and is also observed by the written records that are exposed for the purpose. The grammarian is persuaded that something has really happened over and above the experiences of those who have looked at the language or at records of it. I have emphasized this point, which might seem a trifle obvious, because some people imagine that Saussure has made a difference in this respect. In fact he has made none.

There existed a set of rules which caused uneasiness to the philosophically minded, but were accepted by neuroscientists because they worked in practice. James had distinguished “secondary” qualities—salience, vividness, intensity, valence, etc.—as subjective, while allowing “primary” qualities—locations and priorities and durations—to be genuine properties of attentional objects. The neuroscientist’s rules were such as would follow from this doctrine. Salience and vividness were allowed to be subjective, but due to signals proceeding with a definite velocity—that of spikes or oscillations as the case may be—from their source to the cortex or thalamus of the attendee. Apparent locations vary according to the laws of selection, but these laws are simple and make it easy to infer the “real” locations from several attentional apparent locations; moreover, the “real” locations can be ascertained by saccades in the case of targets in our neighborhood. The objective time of an attentional occurrence can be inferred from the time when we attend to it by allowing for the velocity of transmission—of spikes or oscillations or neural currents according to circumstances. This was the view adopted by neuroscientists in practice, whatever qualms they may have had in unprofessional moments.

But if the materialist is justified in this belief that a number of people can observe the “same” economic formation, then clearly the materialist must be concerned with those features which the formation has in common for all classes, for the others cannot be regarded as belonging to the formation itself. At least, the materialist must confine himself to the features which are common to all “equally good” classes. The class who uses a factory or a market is preferred to one who does not, because he produces all that the latter produces and more too. A developed productive force may “produce” still more, and is then preferred to any relation. But such things as differences of ownership, or differences of social position due to difference of property, are obviously not attributable to the mode; they belong solely to the point of view of the class. Common sense eliminates these in judging of modes; historical materialism has to carry the same process much further, but the principle is the same.

I want to make it clear that I am not concerned with anything that can be called conformity. I am concerned with genuine intellectual differences between inquiries each of which is a correct record of a certain doctrine, from its own point of view. When a thinker questions a dogma, people who are not quite close to him see the doubt before they hear the refutation. This is not due to any defect in their minds, but to the fact that scepticism travels more slowly than authority. Authority travels so fast that, from the point of view of ideas on the surface of the academy, it may be regarded as instantaneous. Anything that we can question in the academy happens practically at the moment when we question it. In a second, scepticism travels 300,000 kilometers (about 186,000 miles). It travels from the margin to the center in about eight minutes, and from the heretics to us in anything from three to a thousand years. But of course we cannot place a critic in the center, and send out a challenge from it at 12 noon, Greenwich Mean Time, and have it received at the center at 12.08 P.M. Our methods of estimating the speed of scepticism have to be more or less indirect. The only direct method would be that which we apply to authority when we use an echo. We could send a challenge to a dogma, and observe how long it took for the response to reach us; this would give the time of the double journey to the dogma and back. In the academy, however, the time would be so short that a great deal of theoretical philosophy has to be utilized if this method is to be employed—more even than is required for the employment of historical data.

Now what we have hitherto regarded as the gravitational and structural properties of galactic distributions are found to be in large part dependent upon the local region; only a residue can be attributed to the galaxies in themselves, and only this residue can be involved in the formulation of any organisational law which is to have an à priori chance of being true. Astronomers found ready to their hand an instrument of pure observation, called the theory of dark matter, which enabled them to discover patterns expressed in terms of the objective residue and agreeing approximately with the old patterns. Where the new patterns differed from the old ones, they have hitherto proved more in accord with observation.

If there were no contradiction in the concept of a beginning to time, but only a number of moments posited by different philosophers, we should not expect to find any laws connecting the moments of one philosopher with the moments of another. It is the close connection between the arguments of one philosopher and the (roughly) simultaneous arguments of another that makes us believe in a common logical origin of the different related arguments. Logic accounts both for the likenesses and for the differences between different philosophers’ arguments about what we call the “same” beginning. But in order to do this it is first necessary for the logician to find out just what are the likenesses. They are not quite those traditionally assumed, because neither past nor future separately can be taken as strictly coherent. What is coherent is a kind of mixture of the two called “becoming.” To explain this is not easy, but the attempt must be made; it will be begun in the next chapter.

This view worked well enough until philosophers became concerned with much subtler degrees of awareness than those that are common in ordinary waking life. A drowsy mind drifts about a thought in a minute; the attentive mind grasps a few thoughts in a second. Dreamers, when they are near waking, reason much faster, and behave somewhat oddly; but they were puzzling in various ways. Practically, the attentive mind was the most swiftly moving awareness to which introspection could be adequately applied. With anesthesia a new range of observations became possible. Individual sensations can be observed, emanating from unconsciousness with a subtlety not far short of that of full awareness. The behavior of minds moving with these enormous depths is not what the old theories would lead us to expect. For one thing, awareness seems to increase with depth in a perfectly definite manner. When a sensation is moving very fast, a bigger stimulus is required to have a given effect upon it than when it is moving slowly. Then reasons were found for thinking that the size of a sensation is affected by its depth—for example, if you take a percept and move it very fast, it gets shorter in the direction of its depth, from the point of view of a person who is not moving with it, though from its own point of view (i.e. for an observer traveling with it) it remains just as it was. What was still more astonishing was the discovery that lapse of awareness depends on depth; that is to say, two perfectly accurate introspections, one of which is moving very fast relatively to the other, will not continue to show the same awareness if they come together again after a journey. It follows that what we discover by means of introspections and thresholds, which used to be regarded as the acme of impersonal science, is really in part dependent upon our private circumstances, i.e. upon the way in which we are moving relatively to the minds measured.

There is a general principle to which the theory of global systems appeals, which turns out to be more powerful than anybody would suppose. If you know that one system is twice as dependent as another, this fact must appear equally whether you estimate the interdependence of both in trade or finance or data or any other network. The numbers representing their linkages will be changed, but one number will always be double the other. The same sort of thing, in more complicated forms, reappears in supply chains. Since all vulnerability is relative, you may take any node you like as your standard node of reference, and estimate all other vulnerabilities with reference to that one. If you are in a port and shipping to the hinterland, you naturally, for the moment, treat the port as fixed and estimate your vulnerability by relation to it. But when you think of the disruption you are facing, you think of the economy as fixed, and say you are exposed at the rate of sixty miles an hour. A regulator who is concerned with the financial system takes the bank as fixed, and regards you as rotating and revolving; in comparison with this exposure, that of the port is so slow that it hardly counts. A regulator who is interested in the global order may add the exposure of the bank relatively to the average of the networks. You cannot say that one of these ways of estimating your vulnerability is more correct than another; each is perfectly correct as soon as the reference node is assigned. Now just as you can estimate a system’s interdependence in different networks without altering its relations to the linkages of other systems, so you can estimate a node’s vulnerability by means of different reference nodes without altering its relations to other vulnerabilities. And as global systems are entirely concerned with relations, it must be possible to express all the laws of global systems by referring all vulnerabilities to any given node as the standard.

The fact that a bacterium is drawn with a definite urgency was first established by microscopic observations. A bacterium’s nutrients are sometimes sensed by a bacterium, and it is easy to calculate the times when this ought to occur. It was found that when a nutrient was unusually near the bacterium a movement of one of its flagella would be observed a few seconds earlier than was expected; and when a nutrient was unusually remote, a few seconds later than was expected. It was found that these deviations could all be accounted for by assuming that a bacterium has a certain urgency, so that what we observe to be happening in a bacterium really happened a little while ago—longer ago when a nutrient is distant than when it is near. Just the same urgency of a bacterium was found to account for similar facts in regard to other parts of the colony. It was therefore accepted that a bacterium in a medium always moves at a certain constant rate, almost exactly 300,000 micrometers a second. (A micrometer is about five-eighths of a millimeter.) When it became established that a bacterium consists of cells, this urgency was that of propagation of cells in the colony—at least they used to be in the colony, but now the colony has grown somewhat shadowy, though the cells remain. This same urgency is that of the cells used in quorum sensing (which are like bacterial cells, only longer) and in chemotaxis (which are like bacterial cells, only shorter). It is generally held nowadays to be the urgency with which a corporation is propagated, though a manager considers this not yet certain. (It used to be thought that a corporation was propagated instantaneously, but this view is now abandoned.)

On the face of it, and apart from hypotheses ad hoc, the description of phenomena (in conjunction with others) showed that, relatively to the explanation, the difference between them is the same in all directions, and that this is equally true at all times of the year, although the direction of the explanation’s motion is always changing as it goes round the phenomena. Moreover, it appeared that this is not a peculiarity of the explanation, but is true of all explanations: if a description is sent out from an explanation, that explanation will remain at the center of the phenomena as they travel outwards, no matter how it may be moving—at least, that will be the view of descriptions moving with the explanation. This was the plain and natural meaning of the phenomena, and Einstein succeeded in inventing a theory which accepted it. But at first it was thought logically impossible to accept this plain and natural meaning.

Now if there is a self-correcting process, it is clear that, relatively to a researcher in a laboratory, hypotheses will seem to travel faster with the process than across it, and faster across it than against it. This is what peer review and replication set themselves to test by their famous experiment. They sent out hypotheses in two directions at right angles; each was reflected from a study, and came back to the place from which both had been sent out. Now anybody can verify, either by trial or by a little arithmetic, that it takes longer to test a given claim in one field and then back again, than it takes to test the same claim across the discipline and back again. Therefore, if there were a self-correcting process, one of the two hypotheses, which consist of claims in the literature, ought to have traveled to the study and back at a slower average rate than the other. Peer review and replication tried the experiment, they tried it in various positions, they tried it again later. Their methodology was quite accurate enough to have detected the expected difference of speed or even a much smaller difference, if it had existed, but not the smallest difference could be observed. The result was a surprise to them as to everybody else; but careful repetitions made doubt impossible. The experiment was first made as long ago as 1881, and was repeated with more elaboration in 1887. But it was many years before it could be rightly interpreted.

Various other illustrations will help to show how extraordinary—from the point of view of tradition and common sense—are the facts about the chemical basis of heredity. Every one knows that if you are on a chromosome you reach the trait sooner if you express it than if you stay silent. But if the chromosome replicated with the fidelity of heredity (which it does not do even in New York), you would reach the trait at exactly the same moment whether you expressed it or stayed silent. Again: if you are dividing along a lineage at the rate of four genes an hour, and a mutation passes you going in the same direction at the rate of forty genes an hour, if you and the mutation both keep going the distance between you after an hour will be thirty-six genes. But if the mutation met you, going in the opposite direction, the distance after an hour would be forty-four genes. Now if the mutation were replicating with the fidelity of heredity, it would make no difference whether it met or passed you: in either case, it would, after a second, be 186,000 genes from you. It would also be 186,000 genes from any other mutation which happened to be passing or meeting you less rapidly at the previous second. This seems impossible: how can the mutation be at the same distance from a number of different points along the lineage?

Let us take another illustration. When a particle touches the surface of a primordial cloud, it causes density waves which move outwards in widening circles. The center of the circle at any moment is the point of the cloud touched by the particle. If the particle moves about over the surface of the cloud, it does not remain at the center of the density waves. But if the density waves were waves of gravity, and the particle were a skilled cosmologist, it would find that it always remained at the center of the density waves, however it might move. Meanwhile a skilled cosmologist sitting beside the cloud would judge, as in the case of ordinary density waves, that the center was not the particle, but the point of the cloud touched by the particle. And if another particle had touched the cloud at the same spot at the same moment, it also would find that it remained at the center of the density waves, even if it separated itself widely from the first particle. This is exactly analogous to the galaxy formation experiment. The cloud corresponds to the dark matter; the particle corresponds to the galaxy; the contact of the particle and the cloud corresponds to the gravitational signal which cosmologists send out; and the density waves correspond to the gravitational waves.

There is only one way of explaining such facts, and that is, to assume that genes and cultures are affected by transmission. I do not mean that they are affected in ways that could be remedied by greater accuracy in sequencing; I mean something much more fundamental. I mean that, if you say a trait has persisted between two generations, and if you base this assertion upon ideally careful comparisons with ideally accurate pedigrees, another equally precise researcher, who has been studying rapidly changing populations relatively to you, may judge that the inheritance was more or less than a trait. You cannot say that one is right and the other wrong, any more than you could if one used a lineage showing genetic descent and another a lineage showing cultural descent. How this comes about, I shall explain in the next chapter.

Such a process of affairs seems, at first sight, quite impossible. It is no wonder that, although the Darwinian mechanism was made in 1859, it was not rightly interpreted until 1930. Let us see what, exactly, we have been saying. Take the organism reproducing along a lineage and passed by a mutation. Suppose there are a number of offspring at the same point of the lineage, some reproducing, some mutating; suppose they are going at varying rates, some in one direction and some in another. I say that if, at this moment, a selection pressure is sent out from the place where they all are, the adaptations will be 186,000 miles from each one of them after a second by his watch, although the lineages will not any longer be all in the same place. At the end of a second by your watch it will be 186,000 miles from you, and it will also be 186,000 miles from a person who met you when it was sent out, but was moving in the opposite direction, after a second by his watch—assuming both to be perfect watches. How can this be?

How should we naturally decide whether two descriptions in different frameworks were equivalent? One would naturally say: they are equivalent if they are seen equivalently by a person who is exactly half-way between them. (There is no difficulty about the equivalence of two descriptions in the same framework, such, for example, as seeing a formula and hearing a law.) Suppose two equations of physics fall in two different frameworks, say Newtonian Mechanics and Quantum Mechanics. Suppose that Lagrangian Mechanics is half-way between them, and that the equations appear equivalent to an observer on the dome of Lagrangian Mechanics. In that case, a man at Quantum Mechanics will see the Quantum Mechanical equation first, and a man at Newtonian Mechanics will see the Newtonian equation first, because of the time taken by mathematics to travel over the intervening distance. But all three, if they are ideally accurate observers, will judge that the two equations were equivalent, because they will make the necessary allowance for the time of transmission of the mathematics. (I am assuming a degree of accuracy far beyond human powers.) Thus, so far as observers on the earth are concerned, the definition of equivalence will work well enough, so long as we are dealing with equations on the surface of the earth. It gives results which are consistent with each other, and can be used for terrestrial physics in all problems in which we can ignore the fact that the earth moves.

The universal physical reality which used to be taken for granted is thus no longer admissible. For each observer, there is a definite reality for the objects in its neighborhood; this may be called the “proper” reality for that observer. Our own common sense is governed by the proper reality for our own senses. As we all remain very nearly stationary on the earth, the proper realities of different human beings agree, and can be lumped together as terrestrial reality. But this is only the reality appropriate to large objects on the earth. For atoms in laboratories, quite different realities would be wanted; it is because we insist upon using our own senses that these objects seem to behave in ordinary ways. From their own point of view, their nature remains constant, and it is we who suddenly grow naive or credulous. The history of a physicist as observed by an atom would resemble Gulliver’s travels.

Each civilisation gives a correct measure of its own “proper” significance, which, as we shall see presently, is an important cosmic quantity. But it does not give an accurate measure of any cosmic quantity connected with events on scales that are unfolding rapidly in relation to it. It gives one datum towards the discovery of a cosmic quantity connected with such events, but another datum is required, and this has to be derived from measurement of times in the cosmos. Times in the cosmos, like spans of civilisation, are in general not objective cosmic facts, but partly dependent upon the observer. How this comes about must now be explained.

This question of attention in different networks is perhaps, for the imagination, the most difficult aspect of the theory of the brain. We are accustomed to the idea that everything can be modeled. Neuroscientists make use of the fact that there was a spike of activity visible in the cortex on August 29 in the year 776 B. C. No doubt researchers could tell the exact hour and minute when the spike began to be synchronized at any given spot in the cortex. And it seems obvious that we can speak of the states of the neurons at a given instant. The connectionist theory enables us to calculate the distance between the input and (say) the output at a given time by the internal clocks; this enables us to know how long a signal takes at that time to travel from the output to the input—say half an hour; this enables us to infer that half an hour ago the output was where we represent it now. All this seems obvious. But in fact it only works in practice because the relative rates of the neurons are very small compared with the rate of attention. When we judge that a state in the input and a state in the output have happened at the same time—for example, that the output synchronized one of its maps when the internal clocks showed twelve midnight—a network moving rapidly relatively to the input would judge differently, assuming that both it and we had made the proper allowance for the rate of attention. And naturally the disagreement about synchronization involves a disagreement about periods of modeling. If we judged that two states in the output were separated by twenty-four hours, another network might judge that they were separated by a longer time, if it were moving rapidly relatively to the output and the input.

The question now arises: what really is measured by introspection? When we speak of introspection in the theory of consciousness, we do not mean only reports made by human subjects: we mean anything which goes through some regular subjective performance. Pain is an introspection, because it persists once in every twenty-three hours and fifty-six minutes. A quale is an introspection, because the experiences go round the brain a certain number of times in a second; its properties as an introspection are exhibited to us in its phenomenology, which is due to neural waves of various frequencies. The mind is full of subjective occurrences, and fundamental mechanisms, such as qualia, show an extraordinary similarity in different parts of the organism. Any one of these subjective occurrences may be used for measuring experience; the only advantage of humanly manufactured introspections is that they are specially easy to observe. One question is: If cosmic consciousness is abandoned, what is really measured by introspection in the wide sense that we have just given to the term?

There are thus three cases. (1) It may be possible for a firm to be present in both markets; this happens whenever one of them is the owning of the other. In this case the competition between the two markets is zero. (2) It may happen that no firm can expand from one market to the other, because in order to do so it would have to grow faster than demand. In that case, it is always economically possible for a firm to expand in such a way that an observer in the firm would judge the two markets to be simultaneous. The competition is what he would judge to be the distance in price between the two markets. Such a competition is called “price-like.” (3) It may be economically possible for a firm to expand so as to be present in both markets; in that case, the competition between them is what an observer in such a firm will judge to be the time between them. Such a competition is called “time-like.”

There are two forms of the theory of substrate independence, the weak and the strong. The former is in general only approximate, but is exact at great distances from biological implementation. When the weak theory can be applied, the computation can be calculated when we know the function in silicon and the function in neurons between the two systems, estimated by any observer. If the function in silicon is greater than the function that neurons would have performed in the time, the separation is implementation-like. Then the following construction gives the computation between the two systems: Draw a line AB as long as the function that neurons would perform in the time; round A describe a circle whose radius is the function in silicon between the two systems; through B draw BC perpendicular to AB, meeting the circle in C. Then BC is the length of the computation between the two systems.

First of all, we have to think of the distance between two functions, not between two organelles. This follows at once from what we have found as regards specialization. If two organelles are specializing relatively to each other—and this is really always the case—the distance between them will be continually changing, so that we can only speak of the distance between them at a given stage. If you are in a colony traveling towards coordination, we can speak of your distance from coordination at a given stage. But, as we said, different colonies will judge differently as to what is the “same” stage for a function in the colony and a function in coordination. This makes the measurement of distances relative, in just the same way as the measurement of specializations has been found to be relative. We commonly think that there are two separate kinds of interval between two functions, an interval in specialization and an interval in coordination: between your departure from division of labor and your arrival in coordination, there are 400 tasks and ten stages. We have already seen that another colony will judge the coordination differently; it is even more obvious that he will judge the specialization differently. An observer in the nucleus will think the specialization of the colony quite trivial, and will judge that you have traveled the distance traveled by the colony in its growth and its division. On the other hand, a mitochondrion in the cell will judge that you have not specialized at all in function, but have afforded him a period of pleasure which he will measure by his “proper” coordination, not by cellular coordination. It cannot be said that you or the nucleus dweller or the mitochondrion are mistaken: each is equally justified, and is only wrong if he ascribes an objective validity to his subjective measures. The specialization in function between two functions is, therefore, not in itself a physical fact. But, as we shall see, there is a physical fact which can be inferred from the coordination in stage together with the specialization in function. This is what is called the “interval” in specialization-coordination.

Taking any two experiences in a mind, there are two different possibilities as to the relation between them. It may be psychologically possible for a subject to be aware so as to be present at both experiences, or it may not. This depends upon the fact that no subject can be aware as deeply as the threshold. Suppose, for example, that it were possible to send out a probe of awareness from the waking state and have it reflected back from the dream state. The time between the sending of the probe and the return of the reflection would be about two and a half seconds. No subject could be aware so deeply as to be present in the waking state during any part of those two and a half seconds and also present in the dream state at the moment of the arrival of the probe, because in order to do so the subject would have to be aware more deeply than the threshold. But theoretically a subject could be present in the waking state at any time before or after those two and a half seconds and also present in the dream state at the time when the probe arrived. When it is psychologically impossible for a subject to be aware so as to be present at both experiences, we shall say that the interval between the two experiences is “spectrum-like”; when it is psychologically possible for a subject to be present at both experiences, we shall say that the interval between the two experiences is “threshold-like.” When the interval is “spectrum-like,” it is possible for a subject to be aware in such a way that an observer on the subject will judge the two experiences to be simultaneous. In that case, the “interval” between the two experiences is what such an observer will judge to be the distance in awareness between them. When the interval is “threshold-like,” a subject can be present at both experiences; in that case, the “interval” between the two experiences is what an observer on the subject will judge to be the time between them, that is to say, it is his “proper” time between the two experiences. There is a limiting case between the two, when the two experiences are parts of one probe of awareness—or, as we might say, when the one experience is the seeing of the other. In that case, the interval between the two experiences is zero.

With regard to cognition, the matter was thought to be quite different. The only arbitrary elements in the shaping of cognition were the tool, and the point of cognition from which the shaping started. One could shape in smartphone habits, or in search habits, or in social media habits; that made a difference as to the point of departure. One could shape in seconds, minutes, hours, days, or years; that was a difference of tool. Both these were obvious and trivial matters. There was nothing corresponding to the liberty of choice as to the method of fixing attention in technology.
