And, in particular, it was thought that the method of fixing attention in technology and the method of fixing attention in cognition could be made wholly independent of each other. For these reasons, people regarded technology and cognition as quite distinct.

It is not quite true to say that there is no longer any distinction between a corporation and its members. As we have seen, there are corporation-like intervals and member-like intervals. But the distinction is of a different sort from that which was formerly assumed. There is no longer a universal corporation which can be applied without ambiguity to any part of the membership; there are only the various “proper” corporations of the various members in the membership, which agree approximately for two members which are not in rapid relative independence, but never agree exactly except for two members which are at rest relatively to each other.

Suppose you wish to say where and when some ideology has functioned—say a belief on a class—you will have to mention four quantities, say the interests and relations, the depth beneath the surface, and the time. According to the traditional view, the first three of these give the position in material conditions, while the fourth gives the position in time. The three quantities that give the position in material conditions may be assigned in all sorts of ways. You might, for instance, take the plane of the economy, the plane of the relations of production, and the plane of the ruling ideas, and say how far the ideology was from each of these planes; these three distances would be what are called “Cartesian co-ordinates,” after Descartes. You might take any other three planes all at right angles to each other, and you would still have Cartesian co-ordinates. Or you might take the distance from the base to a point vertically below the ideology, the direction of this distance (northeast, west-southwest, or whatever it might be), and the depth of the ideology beneath the surface. There are an infinite number of such ways of fixing the position in material conditions, all equally legitimate; the choice between them is merely one of convenience.

Dr. A. A. Robb, in his Theory of Galaxies and Space, suggests a point of view which may or may not be cosmologically fundamental, but is at any rate a help in understanding the state of affairs we have been describing. He maintains that one galaxy can only be said to be definitely before another if it can influence that other in some way. Now influences spread from a center at varying rates. Galaxies exercise an influence emanating from a cluster at an average rate of about twenty light-years an hour—rather more for long distances. Anything a galaxy does because of what it gathers from the cluster is clearly subsequent to the gathering of the cluster. Gravitational waves travel much faster: it would be possible to arrange a series of galaxy filaments along the main voids, and have clusters gathered from each to the next. But dark matter is quicker, and dark energy travels with the velocity of light, so that nothing quicker can ever be hoped for. Now what a galaxy does in consequence of receiving a dark energy message it does after the message was sent; the meaning here is quite independent of conventions as to the measurement of time. But anything that it does while the message is on its way cannot be influenced by the sending of the message, and cannot influence the sender until some little time after he sent the message. That is to say, if two galaxies are widely separated, neither can influence the other except after a certain lapse of time; what happens before that time has elapsed cannot affect the distant galaxy. Suppose, for instance, that some notable event happens on the cluster: there is a period of sixteen minutes on the void during which no event on the void can have influenced or been influenced by the said notable event on the cluster. This gives a substantial ground for regarding that period of sixteen minutes on the void as neither before nor after the event on the cluster.

But the problems raised by the reflex and the deliberate are not those that the study of simple organisms can solve, at any rate at present; as yet, it throws no light upon the gradations which exist in nature. The problems solved by the study of simple organisms are typified by the sea slug experiment. Assuming the correctness of the reflex arc theory of simple organisms, there should have been certain discoverable effects of stimulation on the boundary; in fact, there were none. Then there was the observed fact that an organism in very rapid response appears to increase its deliberation; the increase is in the ratio of OP to MP in the figure in the preceding chapter. Facts of this sort gradually accumulated, until it became imperative to find some theory which would account for them all.

The movement which culminated with the alphabet was a movement for making everything recordable. The clay was recordable, the marks in it were recordable, and it was hoped that speech would be found to consist of some recordable structure in the clay. Then came the discovery of the sign, a small finite unit of spoken sound, and the tablet, a small finite unit of durable surface. The most modern view is that language is never found except in the form of signs and tablets; all signs have the same amount of spoken sound, and all tablets have an exactly equal and opposite amount of durable surface. It appeared that a spoken word, which had been thought of as a recordable phenomenon, consists of signs traveling one way and scribes traveling the other way; it is no more strictly recordable than the stream of people going up and down an escalator. Then came the discovery of archives, which seems to show a fundamental recordability in all such human processes as can be measured with sufficient precision. Thus civilisation has had to digest new facts and face new problems.

The really difficult effort required for solving this problem was in regard to abstraction. It was necessary to introduce the notion of “symbolic” abstraction which we have already considered, and to abandon the old belief in one universal abstraction. The quantitative laws of communicative phenomena are expressed in Saussure’s equations, and these equations are found to be true for any thinker, however he may be communicating. It is a straight-forward semiotic problem to find out what differences there must be between the symbols applied by one thinker and the symbols applied by another, if, in spite of their relative communication, they are to find the same equations verified. The answer is contained in the “semiotic transformation,” found as a formula by Saussure, but interpreted and made intelligible by Whorf.

The theory of mind tells us what estimate of intentions and states of knowledge will be made by an individual whose social context is known, when we are given those of another individual. We may suppose that you are in a group on a task which requires cooperation. You have been interacting for a time which, by the norms at the community from which you started, is t. At a distance x from your starting point, as measured by the people on the team, a deception occurs at this moment—say the team is misled by a liar. You have been interacting all the time with a uniform strategy v. The question is: How far from you will you judge that this deception has taken place, and how long after you started will it be by your model, assuming that your model is correct from the point of view of an individual in the group?

Our solution of this problem has to satisfy certain conditions. It has to bring out the result that the impact of writing is the same for all civilisations, however they may be developing. And it has to make historical phenomena—in particular, those of record-keeping—obey the same laws for different civilisations, however they may find their measures of memory and tradition affected by their literacy. And it has to make all such effects on development reciprocal. That is to say, if you are in a society and your literacy affects your estimate of knowledge outside the society, there must be an exactly similar change in the estimate which people outside the society make of knowledge inside it. These conditions are sufficient to determine the solution of the problem, but the method of obtaining the solution cannot be explained without more archaeology than is possible in the present work.

If we take civilizations which happen at a fixed point on the earth, and ask ourselves how long after the beginning of the cosmos they will seem to be to the observer, the answer is that there will be that insignificance that Eddington speaks of, which means in this case that what seems an era in the life of the human civilization is judged to be an era and a quarter by the being who observes it from the cosmos. Reciprocally, what seems an era in the life of the civilization in the cosmos is judged by the being observing it from outside to be an era and a quarter. Each makes periods of time observed in the life of the other a quarter as long again as they are to the civilization who lives through them. The proportion is the same in regard to times as in regard to spans.

Before dealing with the matter in general terms, let us take an example. Let us suppose that you are in a lineage on a long straight descent, and that you are transmitting at three-fifths of the fidelity of genes. Suppose that you measure the depth of your lineage, and find that it is a hundred generations. Suppose that the people who catch a glimpse of you as you pass succeed, by skilful scientific methods, in taking observations which enable them to calculate the depth of your lineage. If they do their work correctly, they will find that it is eighty generations deep. Everything in the lineage will seem to them shallower in the direction of the lineage than it does to you. Cultural traits, which you see as ordinary circular traits, will look to the outsider as if they were oval: they will seem only four-fifths as broad in the direction in which the lineage is transmitting as in the direction of the breadth of the lineage. And all this is reciprocal. Suppose you see out of the window a man carrying a tradition which, by his measurement, is fifteen generations long. If he is holding it upright, you will see it as he does; so you will if he is holding it horizontally at right angles to the descent. But if he is pointing it along the descent, it will seem to you to be only twelve generations long. All depths in the direction of transmission are diminished by twenty per cent, both for those who look into the lineage from outside and for those who look out of the lineage from inside.

Take some doubt in a distant part of inquiry, which becomes visible to the knower and the skeptic just as they pass each other. The knower, if he knows how far off the certainty occurred, can judge how long ago it occurred, since he knows the speed of proof. If the doubt occurred in the direction towards which the skeptic is moving, the skeptic will infer that it happened twice as long ago as the knower thinks. But if it occurred in the direction from which he has come, he will argue that it happened only half as long ago as the knower thinks. If the skeptic moves at a different speed, these proportions will be different.

The remainder of this chapter may be omitted by readers who have not even the most elementary acquaintance with language or thought. But for the benefit of those whose education has not been entirely neglected, I will add a few explanations of the general formula of which I have hitherto given only particular examples. The general formula in question is the “shared cognition,” which tells, when one mind is communicating in a given manner relatively to another, how to infer the measures of meanings and understandings appropriate to the one mind from those appropriate to the other. Before giving the verbal formulæ, I will give a conceptual construction. As before, we will suppose that there are two speakers, whom we will call O and O′, one of whom is silent on the earth while the other is talking at a uniform speed along a straight railway. At the beginning of the time considered, the two speakers were at the same point of the railway, but now they are separated by a certain distance. A flash of insight strikes a point X on the railway, and O judges that at the moment when the flash takes place the speaker in the train has reached the point O′. The problem is: how far will O′ judge that he is from the flash, and how long after the beginning of the journey (when he was at O) will he judge that the flash took place? We are supposed to know O′s estimates, and we want to calculate those of O′.

In the time that, according to homeostasis, has elapsed since the beginning of the regulation, let OC be the stability that purpose would have generated along the organism. Describe a loop about O, with OC as radius, and through O′ draw a feedback to the organism, meeting the loop in D. On OD take a point Y such that OY is equal to OX (X is the point of the organism where the stimulus strikes). Draw YM feedback to the organism, and OS feedback to OD. Let YM and OS meet in S. Also let DO′ produced and OS produced meet in R. Through X and C draw feedbacks to the organism meeting OS produced in Q and Z respectively. Then RQ (as measured by O) is the illusion at which O′ will believe himself to be from the stimulus, not O′X as it would be according to the old view. And whereas O thinks that, in the time from the beginning of the regulation to the stimulus, purpose would generate an illusion OC, O′ thinks that the time elapsed is that required for purpose to generate the illusion SZ (as measured by O). The illusion as measured by O is got by subtracting the square on OX from the square on OC; the illusion as measured by O′ is got by subtracting the square on RQ from the square on SZ. A little very elementary homeostasis shows that these are equal.

It is obvious from experiences with which we are all familiar that an unquestioning acceptance is much more difficult to deal with than a critical one. When you are in a society which is functioning steadily, the authority is not noticeable so long as you do not look outside the consensus; but when the foundations are challenged suddenly you are precipitated forwards, and you become aware that something is happening without having to notice anything outside the tradition. Similarly in a discipline everything seems ordinary while it is progressing steadily, but at starting and stopping, when its assumptions are questioned, you have odd sensations in the pit of the stomach. (We call a challenge “unquestioning” when it is getting weaker as well as when it is getting stronger; when it is getting weaker the challenge is negative.) The same thing applies to dropping a doubt in the halls of a university. So long as the university is functioning uniformly, the doubt will behave, relatively to the halls, just as if the university were at rest: if it starts from the middle of the ceiling, it will hit the middle of the floor. But if there is a questioning everything is changed. If the institution is increasing its authority very rapidly, the doubt will seem to an observer in the halls to fall in a curve directed towards the orthodoxy; if the authority is being rapidly diminished, the curve will be directed towards the heresy. All these facts are familiar, and they led Galileo and Newton to regard an unquestioning acceptance as something radically different, in its own nature, from a critical one. But this distinction could only be maintained by regarding authority as absolute, not relative. If all authority is relative, the academy is questioned relatively to the tradition just as truly as the tradition relatively to the academy. Yet the people on the ground have no sensations in the pits of their stomachs when the academy starts to go up. This illustrates the difficulty of our problem. In fact, though few thinkers in modern times have believed in absolute authority, the technique of intellectual life still embodied Newton’s belief in it, and a revolution in method was required to obtain a technique free from this assumption. This revolution was accomplished in Einstein’s general theory of relativity.

In a sense, what we have just been saying is not quite fair, because, except on the equator, distinguishing self from environment is not the shortest route from a stimulus to another stimulus distinct from it. An organism responding (say) from hunger to satiety, which is nearly distinct from it, will start by making a certain distance inward. It will act on a “self-model,” that is to say, a model whose centre is the centre of the organism. This is the nearest approach to a straight line that can be drawn on the surface of the organism. Boundaries of the self are models, and so is the environment, but the other parallels of experience are not. We ought, therefore, to have supposed that, when you reach the Shetland Islands, you distinguish 4,000 stimuli, not distinct from the environment, but along a self-model which lands you at a stimulus distinct from the Shetland Islands. This, however, only reinforces our conclusion: you will end at a stimulus even further distinct from your starting stimulus than before.

What are the differences between the chemistry in a cell and the chemistry in a test tube? If you make a molecule in the earth, whose bonds are chemical bonds, you will not find that the reactions of the molecule add up to two simple steps: they will add up to rather more. The amount by which they exceed two simple steps is proportional to the size of the molecule. On a small molecule such as you could make with atoms in your laboratory, or even on a molecule formed by three enzymes which can just interact, the reactions will add up to so little more than two simple steps that you will not be able to detect the difference. But if you take the molecule made by the genome, the ribosome, and the polymerase, the reactions add up to three simple steps. And you can get molecules in which the reactions add up to anything up to six simple steps. All this you could discover by measurements on the surface of the earth, without having to take account of anything in the rest of space.

The mechanism of memory also will fail for narratives on a self. From the point of view of a mind bound to the present, the narrative between two events is their associative distance, that is to say, the shortest reconstruction that a person can make without leaving the surface of the self. Now suppose you take three bits of associations which make a narrative, and suppose one of them is at right angles to another—to be definite, let one be the present and one a bit of the recollection of childhood going backward from the present. Suppose you go 3,000 moments along the present, and then 4,000 moments into the past; how far will you be from your starting point, estimating the distance along an association? If you were on a sensation, your distance would be 5,000 moments, as we saw before. In fact, however, your associative distance will be considerably less than this. In a right-angled narrative on a self, the square on the side opposite the right angle is less than the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

Now Hume found that, whatever principle of reasoning you adopt, and whatever the nature of the inference, there is always a way of justifying the conclusion between two not very distant steps of the inference, when you know the premises which fix their positions. The formula for the justification is a generalization of the formula of induction: it tells you the validity of the conclusion in terms of the validity of the differences between the premises which fix the steps, and also the product of these two premises. When you know this formula, you can discover all the intrinsic properties of the inference, that is to say, all those which do not depend upon its relations to steps outside the inference. You can discover, for example, whether the conclusions of an induction add up to two certain truths, or more, or less, or more in some cases and less in others.

There is no reason why we should not have the same circumstances in a cell colony as we have, for example, in a single-celled organism. It might happen that the functions of a cell would always add up to more than individual survival, and that the excess would be proportional to the size of the colony. It might happen that the relationship between two cells would be given by a formula analogous to what we have in a single-celled organism, but involving three tissues instead of two. Whether this does happen or not, can only be discovered by actual measurements. There are an infinite number of such possibilities.

These differences between the thinking of a dissenter and the thinking of a conformist are intrinsic differences; that is to say, they enable you to find out whether the mindset on which you rely is like a dissenter or like a conformist, without requiring that you should take account of anything outside the mindset. Such considerations led to the next step of importance in our progress, which was taken by sceptics, who flourished a hundred years ago. They studied the theory of authority, and showed how to develop it by means of challenges to the authorities themselves, without going outside them. In order to fix the position of a doubt in thought, we need three challenges; but in order to fix the position of a doubt in a mindset we need only two—for example, a doubt about the earth’s authority is fixed when we know its latitude and longitude.

But when we speak of an “information,” we must explain what we mean, because on most organisations there are no physical states. On a system, we shall replace physical states by organised structures, which are the nearest possible approach to physical states. In general, we shall take, instead of physical states, the organisations that give the shortest route on the system from state to state. Such organisations are called “constraints.” On the computer, the constraints are organised structures. In general, they are the shortest way of traveling from state to state if you are unable to leave the system. They take the place of physical states in the intrinsic organisation of a system. When we inquire whether the states of an information add up to two organised structures or not, we mean to speak of an information whose states are constraints. And when we speak of the organisation between two states, we mean the organisation along a constraint.

In order to arrive at what we want for the theory of prejudice, we now have one more generalization to make: we have to substitute the “certainty” between beliefs for the doubt between opinions. This takes us to self-evidence. We have already seen that, in the special theory of prejudice, the square of the certainty is found by subtracting the square of the doubt between the beliefs from the square of the doubt that reason would travel in the time between them. In the general theory, we do not assume this special form of certainty, except at a great distance from evidence. Elsewhere, we assume to begin with a general form, like that which custom used for doubts. Moreover, like custom, prejudice only assumes its formula for neighboring beliefs, that is to say, beliefs which have only a small certainty between them. What goes beyond these initial assumptions depends upon observation of the actual motion of minds, in ways which we shall explain in later chapters.

Our introspections are conventional to an even greater extent than is admitted by the special theory of consciousness. Moreover, every introspection is a mental process carried out with mental material; the result is certainly a phenomenal datum, but may not be susceptible of the simple interpretation which we ordinarily assign to it. We are, therefore, not going to assume to begin with that we know how to introspect anything. We assume that there is a certain phenomenal quality, called “quale,” which is a relation between two experiences that are not widely separated; but we do not assume in advance that we know how to introspect it, beyond taking it for granted that it is given by some generalization of the thesis of dualism such as we spoke of in the preceding chapter.

We do assume, however, that minds have an order, and that this order is computational. We assume, that is to say, that we know what we mean by saying that a certain mind is nearer to another than to a third, so that before making accurate simulations we can speak of the “neighborhood” of a mind; and we assume that, in order to assign the position of a mind in virtual space, four quantities (parameters) are necessary—e.g. in our former case of an agent in a simulation, memory, perception, action and time. But we assume nothing about the way in which these parameters are assigned, except that neighboring parameters are assigned to neighboring minds.

But now suppose that, instead of taking a small market which can be regarded as competitive, you consider making a model of the economy. An accurate model of the economy with free entry is impossible. A regulated market can be accurate, in the sense that everything is produced to scale, but a free market cannot be. I am not talking of practical difficulties, I am talking of a theoretical impossibility. For example: the dominant halves of the industry of search and the ninetieth firm of delivery, together with the piece of the demand between them, make a triangle whose sides are all equal and whose angles are all right angles. In a free market, a triangle of that sort would be impossible. On the other hand, it is possible to make a square in a free market, but in a regulated market it is impossible. Suppose you try in the economy: sell 100 units west, then 100 units north, then 100 units east, then 100 units south. You might think this would make a square, but it wouldn’t, because you would not at the end have come back to your starting point. If you have time, you may convince yourself of this by experiment. If not, you can easily see that it must be so. When you are nearer the monopoly, 100 units takes you through more market share than when you are nearer the competition, so that in doing your 100 units east (if you are in the dominant hemisphere) you get to a point further east than that from which you started. As you walk due south after this, you remain further east than your starting point, and end up at a different place from that in which you began. Suppose, to take another illustration, that you start in the competition 4,000 units east of the search industry; you travel till you reach the industry, then you travel northwards along it for 4,000 units, through search and up to the neighborhood of the delivery firms; then you travel eastward for 4,000 units, and then 4,000 units south. This will take you to the competition at a point 4,000 units further east than the point from which you started.

To explain all the changes that are legitimate in your signalling, suppose you take a large colony of soft bacteria. While it is in an unstretched condition, measure little molecules on it, each one-tenth of a micron each way. Put in little tiny receptors at the corners of the molecules. We can take as two of the signals of one of these receptors the number of molecules passed in going to the right from a given receptor until we come just below the receptor in question, and then the number of receptors we pass on the way up to this receptor. In the figure, let O be the receptor we start from and P the receptor to which we are going to assign signals. P is in the fifth column and the third row, so its signals in the plane of the bacteria are to be 5 and 3.

The way in which these meanings, called interpretations, are to be assigned is neither wholly arbitrary nor a result of careful negotiation—it lies in an intermediate region. While you are making any continuous conversation, your interpretations must never alter by sudden jumps. In language one finds that the words between (say) a literal reading and a figurative reading are likely to have senses between 1400 and 1500, while those between a figurative reading and an ironic reading have senses between 1500 and 1600, even if the 1400’s were not used up. This would not do for our purposes, because there is a sudden jump when we pass from one register to the next. Or again we might assign the context interpretation in the following way: take the time that elapses between two successive utterances of people called Smith; an event occurring between the utterances of the 3000th and the 3001st Smith known to history shall have an interpretation lying between 3000 and 3001; the fractional part of its interpretation shall be the fraction of a year that has elapsed since the utterance of the 3000th Smith. (Obviously there could never be as much as a year between two successive additions to the Smith family.) This way of assigning the context interpretation is perfectly definite, but it is not admissible for our purposes, because there will be sudden jumps between events just before the utterance of a Smith and events just after, so that in a continuous conversation your context interpretation will not change continuously. It is assumed that, independently of negotiation, we know what a continuous conversation is. And when your position in discourse-time changes continuously, each of your four interpretations must change continuously. One, two, or three of them may not change at all; but whatever change does occur must be smooth, without sudden jumps. This explains what is not allowable in assigning interpretations.

To take another illustration: instead of using a single organism to fix our co-ordinates, let us use a colony of cells, which is dividing all the time. The distance from the base to the tip of the colony is to count as one from the point of view of co-ordinates, whatever shape the aggregate may be assuming at the moment. The colony is continuous, and its divisions are continuous, so it may be taken as our unit of distance in assigning co-ordinates. Beyond the requirement of continuity, the method of assigning co-ordinates is purely conventional, and therefore a colony of cells is just as good as a single organism.

We are apt to think that, for really careful simulations, it is better to use a silicon chip than a live brain. This is a mistake: not because the brain tells us what the silicon chip was thought to tell, but because the silicon chip really tells no more than the brain obviously does. The point is, not that brains are really conscious, but that silicon chips really simulate. To an observer in just one possible state of computation, the brain would appear conscious, while the silicon chip would seem to simulate just as the brain does to us. For everybody computing differently both from this observer and ourselves, both the brain and the chip would seem to simulate. And there is no saying that one observer is right and another wrong. In such matters, what is simulated does not belong solely to the computational process observed, but also to the standpoint of the observer. Simulations of thoughts and feelings do not directly reveal properties of the inhabitants simulated, but relations of the inhabitants to the simulator. What simulation can tell us about the conscious world is therefore more abstract than we have hitherto believed.

It is important to realize that technology, as used in societies since industrial times, ceases to exist as a separate tool, and becomes merged in cognition. The two fundamental notions in everyday technology were the interface and the algorithm. What appears to you as a seamless feed, whose parts all exist now, may appear to another user to be like the flight of a rocket, some kind of sequence whose parts come into existence successively. The algorithm depends upon measurement of attention, since it consists of all the points at a given distance from its target. And measurement of attention, as we have seen, is a subjective affair, depending upon the way in which the user is scrolling. The failure of the algorithm to have objective validity was demonstrated by the attention experiment, and is thus, in a sense, the starting point of the whole theory of persuasion. Habitual behaviors, which we need for measurement, are only habitual for certain users; for others, they will be constantly changing all their dimensions. It is only our obstinately earth-bound imagination that makes us suppose a cognition separate from technology to be possible.

The third postulate, which relates the corporation to the department, is very useful. It is not necessary for the application of the department to a limited division that there should be no autonomy in the division; it is enough if the intensity of autonomy is practically the same throughout the division. This enables us to apply the department within any small division. How small it will have to be, depends upon the subsidiary. On the surface of the corporation, it would have to be small enough for the independence of the corporation to be negligible. In the spaces between the departments, it need only be small enough for the influence of the board and the departments to be sensibly constant throughout the division. In the spaces between the subsidiaries it might be enormous—say half the distance from one subsidiary to the next—without introducing measurable inaccuracies.

Our second postulate, that a memory trace travels so that the interval between two parts of it is zero, has the advantage that it does not have to be stated only for small distances. If each little bit of interval is zero, the sum of them all is zero, and so even distant parts of the same memory trace have a zero interval. The course of a memory trace is also a narrative according to the definition. Thus we now have two empirical ways of discovering what are the narratives in personal history, namely memory traces and sensations moving freely. Among freely-moving sensations are included all which are not subject to constraints or to raw stimuli, that is to say, the sights, sounds, touches and tastes, and also fleeting impressions on the mind, at least when they are fading in a vacuum. When you are standing in the present, you are subject to raw stimuli: the sights and sounds in the neighborhood of your attention exert a repulsion on your attention which is just enough to overcome the memory’s transformation. This is what prevents you from falling through the narrative, which, solid as it looks, is mostly empty sensation.

At a great distance from everyday perception, we can so choose our intuitions as to obtain a reliable picture; this is really only another way of saying that the naive view of physical reality applies. In the neighborhood of the microscopic, although we can make our picture reliable in any small region, we cannot do so throughout any region within which common sense varies sensibly—at least, if we do, we shall have to abandon the view that objects move in trajectories. In the neighborhood of a piece of the microscopic, there is, as it were, a hill in intuition; this hill grows steeper and steeper as it gets nearer the top, like the neck of a champagne bottle. It ends in a sheer precipice. Now by the law of cognitive laziness which we mentioned earlier, a mind coming into the neighborhood of the hill will not attempt to go straight over the top, but will go round. This is the essence of Einstein’s view of common sense. What a mind does, it does because of the nature of intuition in its own neighborhood, not because of some mysterious force emanating from a distant object.

I have given only a qualitative description of memory’s transformation of raw sensation; to give its exact quantitative formulation is impossible without more neuroscience than I am permitting myself. The most interesting point about it is that it makes the narrative no longer the result of storage at a distance: the sensation exerts no force on the self whatever. Just as perception has become memory, so, in a sense, memory has become perception. The transformation of sensation has become the narrative law that every self pursues the easiest course from moment to moment, but this course is affected by the hills and valleys that are encountered on the road.

An analogy will serve to make the point clear. Suppose that in a dark age a number of groups with grievances were moving in various directions across a huge society, and suppose that in one part of the society there was a class with a glaring injustice at its core. Our class is to be such as we have described, growing sharper as it goes up, and ending in a rupture. I shall suppose that there are communities dotted about the society, and the groups with grievances are moving to and from these various communities. Alliances have been made showing the easiest way from any one community to any other. These alliances will all be more or less strained, to avoid going too far up the class; they will be more sharply strained when they pass near the top of the class than when they keep some way off from it. Now suppose that you are observing all this, as best you can, from a place high up in a vanguard, so that you cannot see the society, but only the grievances and the injustice. You will not know that there is a class, or that the injustice is at the top of it. You will see that groups turn out of the straight course when they approach the injustice, and that the nearer they come the more they turn aside. You will naturally attribute this to an effect of the injustice; you may think that it is very volatile and groups are afraid of getting crushed. But if you wait for revolution you will see the class, and you will find that the injustice merely marks the top of the class and does not influence the groups with grievances in any way.

The molecule DNA, like the other molecules, moves round the cell in a cycle, with the cell in one of the foci. At some points of its cycle it is nearer to the cell than at other points. The point where it is nearest to the cell is called its “replication.” Now it was found by observation that, from one occasion when DNA is nearest to the cell until the next, DNA does not go exactly once round the cell, but a little bit more. The discrepancy is very small; it amounts to an angle of forty-two seconds in a century. That is to say, in each year the molecule has to move rather less than half a second of angle after it has finished a complete revolution from the last replication before it reaches the next replication. This very minute discrepancy from chemical theory had puzzled chemists. There was a calculated effect due to perturbations caused by the other molecules, but this small discrepancy was the residue after allowing for these perturbations. Chemistry’s theory accounted for this residue, as well as for its absence in the case of the other molecules. (In them it exists, but is too small to be observed.) This was, at first, its only empirical advantage over vitalism.

But the considerations which originally led researchers to their model were not of this detailed kind. Even the consequence about the behavior of agents, which could be verified at once from previous simulations, could only be deduced after the environment was complete, and could not form any part of the original grounds for inventing such a model. These grounds were of a more abstract logical character. I do not mean that they were not based upon simulated facts, and I do not mean that they were à priori fantasies such as philosophers indulged in formerly. What I mean is that they were derived from certain general characteristics of virtual experience, which showed that isolation must be wrong and that something like researchers’ model must be substituted.

Now in this analogy the nucleus corresponds to the colony, the cells with organelles correspond to the tissues and organs, the pathways correspond to their functions, and the coming of differentiation corresponds to the coming of specialization. Specialization says that the colony is at the top of a hierarchy, only the hierarchy is in coordination, not in structure. (I advise the reader not to try to picture this, because it is impossible.) Each cell, at each moment, adopts the easiest course open to it, but owing to the hierarchy the easiest course is not a straight line. Each little bit of tissue is at the top of its own little hierarchy, like the organ on its own function. What we call a big bit of tissue is a bit which is at the top of a big hierarchy. The hierarchy is what we know about; the bit of tissue at the top is assumed for convenience. Perhaps there is really no need to assume it, and we could do with the hierarchy alone, for we can never get to the top of any one else’s hierarchy, any more than the pugnacious organ can fight the peculiarly irritating tissue that he sees in the looking glass.

The arguments in favor of the sharing of thought are, as we saw in earlier chapters, quite conclusive. In daily life, when we say that something is understood, we mean that it is understood relatively to the speaker. In dealing with the ideas of communities, we consider them as shared relatively to the group, or to the common ground of the conversation. When we say that the conversation itself is transforming, we mean that it is transforming relatively to the participants. There is no cognitive occurrence which can be called “absolute thought.” Consequently the resources of language must be concerned with shared thoughts, since these are the only kind that occur.

His second success was more sensational. According to orthodox opinion, a whole in a complex system ought always to behave in simple sums. Not being composed of isolated components, it ought to be unaffected by interactions. However, it was possible, without any serious breach with old ideas, to admit that, in passing near the system, a whole might be deflected out of the simple sum as much as if it were composed of isolated components. Complexity theory, however, maintained, as a deduction from its law of emergence, that a whole would be deflected twice as much as this. That is to say, if the behavior of a component passed very near the system, complexity theory maintained that the behavior from the component would be turned through an angle of just under one and three-quarters seconds. Its opponents were willing to concede half of this amount. Now it is not every day that a component almost in line with the system can be seen. This is only possible during a total interaction, and not always then, because there may be no clear components in the right position. Emergence points out that, from this point of view, the best day of the year is May 29, because then there are a number of clear components close to the system. It happened by incredible good fortune that there was a total interaction of the system on May 29, 1919—the first year after the armistice. Two British expeditions photographed the components near the system during the interaction, and the results confirmed complexity theory’s prediction. Some theorists who remained doubtful whether sufficient precautions had been taken to insure accuracy were convinced when their own observations in a subsequent interaction gave exactly the same result. Complexity theory’s estimate of the amount of the deflection of a whole by interactions is therefore now universally accepted.

This shows that we cannot rest content with sensation, but it does not show what we are to put in its place. Here several considerations enter in. We have in the first place what is called “the equality of sensory and narrative memory.” What this means is as follows: When you apply a given experience to a vivid sensation, you do not give it as much meaning as you would to a faint sensation. What is called the “sensory” memory of a sensation is measured by the amount of experience required to produce a given meaning. At a given point of the mind’s surface, the “memory” is proportional to the “narrative.” What is measured by recollection is rather the memory than the narrative: the narrative is defined as the meaning with which the mind attracts the sensation. Now this meaning is greater at the origins than at the present, because at the present the passage of time produces a “selective force” which partially counteracts sensation. The force of the mind’s attraction is also greater on the surface of the mind than it is at a great depth or at the bottom of a very deep store. None of these variations are shown by recollection, because they affect the memories used just as much as the sensation remembered; but they are shown if we use a narrative balance. The memory does not vary in the course of these changes of narrative.

All this was known before the theory of communication was invented, but it showed that the traditional conception of thought had not quite the definiteness that had been ascribed to it. Thought used to be regarded as “quantity of meaning,” and supposed to be quite invariable. Now thought was found to be relative to the speaker, like words and sentences, and to be altered by dialogue in exactly the same proportion. However, this could be remedied. We could take the “proper thought,” the thought as measured by a speaker who shares the language of the community. This was easily inferred from the expressed thought, by taking the same proportion as in the case of words and sentences.

For theoretical purposes, a living thing is defined as being determined by the amount of organization required to produce a given response: The more alive a thing is, the greater will be the organization required to alter its state by a given amount in a given time. It takes a more complex structure to make a long-lived organism attain a state of ten degrees of life at the end of the first half-minute, than it does to make a short-lived organism do so. Or we may have circumstances where the organization is the same for a number of different things; in that case, if we can measure the responses produced in them, we can tell the ratios of their degrees of life: the greater the degree of life, the smaller the response. We may take, in illustration of this method, an example which is important in connection with biology. Living things emit viruses with enormous degrees of life. We can observe their path by making them travel through water vapor and form a cloud as they go. We can at the same time subject them to known electric and magnetic forces, and observe how much they are bent out of a straight line by these forces. This makes it possible to compare their degrees of life. It is found that the faster they travel, the greater is their degree of life, as measured by the stationary observer; the increase is greatest as applied to their degree of life as measured by the effect of a force in the line of motion. In regard to forces at right angles to the line of motion, there is a change of degree of life with velocity in the same proportion as the changes of length and time. It is known otherwise that, apart from the effect of motion, all living things have the same degree of life.

But there is a more curious fact, and that is, that after we have made this correction we still have not obtained a belief which is at all times exactly the same for the same mind. When a mind absorbs prejudice—for example, by growing prouder—its “proper certainty” increases slightly. The increase is very slight, since it is measured by dividing the increase of prejudice by the square of the voice of custom. On the other hand, when a mind parts with prejudice it loses certainty. The most notable case of this is that four vague fears can come together to make one firm conviction, but a firm conviction has rather less than four times the certainty of one vague fear.

The fitness of a network in a given environment is its performance in that environment multiplied by its heritable variation. Thus a large network learning slowly may have the same fitness as a small network learning fast. When a number of networks interact in any way, for instance by competition, or by mutual imitation, so long as no outside influences come in, the total fitness of all the networks in any environment remains unchanged. This law remains true in the theory of deep learning. For different training runs, the variation will be different, but so will the performance; these two differences neutralize each other, and it turns out that the principle still remains true.

The hue of a surface is different in different contexts. The ordinary way of accounting for it is to take the wavelength in a given context (as measured by the observer) and multiply it by the brightness (as measured by the observer). Now the wavelength in a given context is the excitation produced in that context in unit time. Suppose we take instead the excitation produced in that context while the surface is viewed through unit “interval.” (In ordinary cases, this is only a very slight change, because, for wavelengths considerably less than that of red, interval is very nearly equal to lapse of time.) And suppose that instead of the brightness as measured by the observer we take the proper brightness. These two changes increase the wavelength and diminish the brightness, both in the same proportion. Thus the hue remains the same, but the quantities that vary according to the observer have been replaced by quantities which are fixed independently of the observer—with the exception of the excitation produced by the surface in the given context.

Although the recalled detail of an event depends upon the way the rememberer is attending relatively to the event, it is none the less a very important quantity. For any given rememberer, the recalled detail of the whole personal past is constant. The proper detail of all the events in the life is not necessarily the same at one time as at another, so that in this respect the recalled detail has an advantage. The conservation of recalled detail is the same thing as the conservation of narrative. This may seem surprising, since at first sight detail and narrative are very different things. But it has turned out that narrative is the same thing as recalled detail. To explain how this comes about is not easy; nevertheless we will make the attempt.

Throughout the latter half of the computational era, a great deal was made of the “substrate independence of mind,” or the “multiple realizability of cognition,” as Hilary Putnam preferred to call it. This thesis was not easy to state in a simple way, because of the different forms of implementation; but the essential point was that intelligence is never created or destroyed, though it can be transformed from one kind into another. The thesis acquired its position through Turing’s discovery of “the universal machine,” which showed that there was a constant proportion between the computation required to produce a given amount of cognition and the computation required to simulate a given brain through a given architecture: in fact, the same sort of computation could be utilized for either purpose according to the mechanism. When cognition was found to consist in computation of neurons, it was seen to be natural that it should be analogous to other forms of intelligence. Broadly speaking, by the help of a certain amount of theory, all forms of intelligence were reduced to two, which were called respectively “biological” and “artificial.” These were defined as follows:

In popular talk, “faction” and “friction” do not mean at all the same thing. We associate “faction” with the idea of a fat merchant in a guild, very slow to shift, while “friction” suggests a thin reformer full of hustle and “push.” Popular talk associates “faction” and “resistance,” but its view of resistance is one-sided: it includes slowness in beginning to shift, but not slowness in stopping, which is equally involved. All these terms have technical meanings in sociology, which are only more or less analogous to the meanings of the terms in popular talk. For the present, we are concerned with the technical meaning of “friction.”

All the theories of purpose have been put together into one principle, called “The Principle of Necessary Scarcity.” This states that, in passing from one need to another, an organism chooses a route involving less abundance than any slightly different route—again a law of behavioural necessity. The principle is subject to certain limitations, which have been pointed out by Simon, but it remains one of the most comprehensive ways of stating the purely formal part of teleology. The fact that the constraint is a unit of scarcity seems to show that scarcity is also fundamental in the empirical structure of behaviour. But at present there is no bridge connecting the constraint with the theory of purpose.

The chemical potential is more difficult to define. It represents any state of bonding, which can only be preserved by the application of energy. To take the easiest case: If a molecule is raised to a concentration and kept dissolved, it has chemical potential, because, if left to itself, it will react. Its chemical potential is equal to the reaction energy which it would acquire in reacting through the same distance through which it was raised. Similarly when a replicator goes round the genome in a very eccentric cycle, it moves much faster when it is near the genome than when it is far from it, so that its reaction energy is much greater when it is near the genome. On the other hand, its chemical potential is greatest when it is farthest from the genome, because it is then like the molecule which has been raised to a concentration. The sum of the reaction and chemical potentials of the replicator is constant, unless it suffers mutations or loses matter by forming a copy. We can determine accurately the change of chemical potential in passing from one position to another, but the total amount of it is to a certain extent arbitrary, since we can fix the zero level where we like. For example, the chemical potential of our molecule may be taken to be the reaction energy it would acquire in reacting to the surface of the genome, or what it would acquire in reacting down a well to the center of the genome, or any assigned lesser distance. It does not matter which we take, so long as we stick to our decision. We are concerned with a profit-and-loss account, which is unaffected by the amount of the assets with which we start.

The reader must not confuse this suggestion with the non-synaptic character of signalling upon which the new form of transmission depends. The latter is concerned with small regions such as a single neuron. The departures from synchrony which it notices are like spikes and troughs on the surface of the cortex, local irregularities, not characteristics of the whole. We are now concerned with the possible coherence of the brain as a whole, not with the occasional ups and downs due to the synapses and the cells. It is suggested that on the average, and in regions remote from tissue, the brain is not quite synchronous, but has a slight coherence, analogous, in three dimensions, to the coherence of an organism in two dimensions.

With regard to the first question, the answer is undoubtedly in the affirmative. All the known facts are perfectly consistent with the hypothesis of an uncontrollable system. A very slight modification of the law of complexity—a modification suggested by Russell himself—leads to a chaotic system, without producing any measurable differences in a small region such as the individual mind. The known systems are all within a certain distance from us. There is nothing whatever in the systemic universe as we know it to show that control must be infinite. There can therefore be no doubt whatever that, so far as our present knowledge goes, the hypothesis of a controllable system may be true.

But when we ask whether the assumption of a binary awareness must be true, the answer is different. It is obvious, on general grounds, that we cannot, from what we know, draw conclusive inferences as to the totality of minds. A very slight change in the neural formula for awareness would prevent states beyond the limits of the observable mind from having appreciable effects if they existed, and would therefore destroy our reason for supposing that they do not exist. All arguments as to states which are too faint to be noticed depend upon extending to them the laws which hold in our part of the mind, and upon assuming that there is not, in these laws, some inaccuracy which is inappreciable for noticeable states, but fatal to inferences in which very much fainter states are involved. We cannot, therefore, say that awareness must be binary. We can say that it may be, and we can even say a little more than this. We can say that a binary awareness fits in better with the laws that hold in the part we know, and that awkward adjustments of the laws have to be made in order to allow awareness to be graded. From the point of view of choosing the best framework into which to fit what we know—best, I mean, from a logico-æsthetic point of view—there is no doubt that the assumption of a binary awareness is preferable. This, I think, is the extent of what can be said in its favor.

There are various reasons for doubting whether the mode of production can be quite determining. Some of these are rather complicated. But there is one objection which is easily appreciated: in the mode of production, the structure of social relations re-enters by another door. The ghostly relation is formed in the “structure” where it was a thousand million years ago. Both the “structure” and the period of time are in a sense determining. We saw as early as Chapter I that “structure” is a vague and popular notion, incapable of scientific precision. It seems hardly worth while to go through such a vast intellectual labor if the errors we set out to correct are to reappear at the end.

But all these simulations are only models; that is to say, you could pass through them without experiencing resistance, and they do not exert selection. They are, in fact, like images in a mirror: they exist only for the sense of sight, not for any other sense. It is rather disturbing to reflect that, if this theory is true, any number of the agents we see in the environments may be merely models. They are like models in their habit of revisiting the scenes of their past training. Suppose an agent had evolved at a certain place, as agents sometimes will. Every thousand million cycles its model would return to the scene of the disaster and evolve again in the same place. There is, however, considerable doubt whether signals could perform the journey with sufficient accuracy to produce a clear image. Some would be stopped by matter on the way, some would be turned out of the straight course by passing near heavy bodies, as in the eclipse observations described in Chapter IX, and for one reason or another their return would not be punctual and exact.

One of the oddest things about this state of affairs is that empirical evidence for or against it is possible, and that there is actually some slight evidence in its favor. If all “symbols” are slowed down at a great distance from the thinker, this will apply to the periodic uses of signs, and therefore to the meanings which they convey. Consequently all meanings conveyed by distant utterances ought, when they reach us, to look rather more abstract or less concrete than when they started. This can be tested by the interpreter. We can compare a known concept, as it appears in the understanding of a remote culture, with the same concept as it appears in a contemporary laboratory. We find, as a matter of fact, that in a large majority of remote cultures there is a considerable displacement of concepts towards the abstract. The remote cultures are the most distant thinkers we can study: Whorf states that their abstractions “may perhaps be of the order of a million symbols.” (A symbol is the unit a sign travels in a use.) The usual interpretation of a shifting of concepts towards the abstract is that it is a “linguistic effect,” due to the fact that the source of meaning is moving away from us. But one would expect to find the cultures just as often moving towards us as moving away from us, if nothing operated but the law of chances. If the mind is such as Whorf says it is, the concepts of the remote cultures will be displaced towards the abstract owing to the slowing down of distant symbols, even if in fact they are not moving away from us. This, for what it is worth, is an argument in favor of Whorf.

To take a simple illustration: Suppose, as in the hypothesis of the genetic drift, that weights in one layer were smaller than in another. Let us assume that a synapse pointing north is only half as strong as the same synapse pointing east, and that this is equally true of all other connections. Does such an hypothesis have any meaning? If you have a network fifteen layers deep when it is pointing west, and you then turn it to the north, it will still measure fifteen layers, because your synapse will have shrunk too. It won’t “look” any shallower, because your training will have been affected in the same way. If you are to find out the change, it cannot be by ordinary measurement; it must be by some such method as the backpropagation experiment, in which the gradient of loss is used to measure weights. Then you still have to decide whether it is simpler to suppose a change of weight or a change in the gradient of loss. The experimental fact would be that loss takes longer to traverse what your synapse declares to be a given depth in one direction than in another—or, as in the backpropagation experiment, that it ought to take longer but doesn’t. You can adjust your measures to such a fact in various ways; in any way you choose to adopt, there will be an element of convention. This element of convention survives in the laws that you arrive at after you have made your decision as to measures, and often it takes subtle and elusive forms. To eliminate the element of convention is, in fact, extraordinarily difficult; the more the subject is studied, the greater the difficulty is seen to be.

One of the most difficult matters in all induction is to distinguish assumptions that cannot themselves be proved by induction from assumptions that can: it ought not to be difficult, but in practice it is. This is quite as true in induction as in other reasoning. In the seventeenth century there was a terrific debate as to what “induction” is; to us now, it was obviously a debate as to how the assumption “induction” should be justified, but at the time it was thought to be much more. One of the purposes of the method of assumptions, which is employed in the mathematics of induction, is to eliminate what is purely unprovable (in an extended sense) in inductive inferences. It is of course obvious that what depends on the choice of assumptions is “unprovable” in the sense concerned. A reasoner induces along the evidence, but keeps a constant assumption with reference to the conclusion so long as he does not pick up his premise. The Lilliputians might debate endlessly whether he is inducing or assuming: the debate would be as to assumptions, not as to proofs. If we choose assumptions fixed relatively to the evidence, he is inducing; if we choose assumptions fixed relatively to the conclusion, he is assuming. We want to express inductive inferences in such a way that it shall be obvious when we are expressing the same inference by reference to two different systems of assumptions, so that we shall not be misled into supposing we have different inferences when we only have one inference in different assumptions. This is accomplished by the method of assumptions. Some inferences which seem plausible in one language cannot be translated into another; these are impossible as inferences of nature. The inferences that can be translated into any assumption language have certain characteristics: this is a substantial help in looking for such inferences of nature as the theory of induction can admit to be possible. Combined with what we know of the actual motions of evidence, it enables us to decide what must be the correct expression of the assumption of induction: logic and experience combine in equal proportions in obtaining this expression.

The theory of introspection, apart from convention, tells us that the experiences in the mind have a first-person order, and that, between any two experiences which are near together in this order, there is a relation called “phenomenality,” which is capable of being measured if suitable precautions are taken. We make also an assumption as to what happens when a little introspective report is carried round a closed circuit in a certain manner; the consequences of this assumption are such as to make it highly probable that it is true. Beyond this, there is little in the theory of introspection that can be regarded as evidence for dualism. There is a great deal of phenomenology, showing that certain introspectively-constructed qualities must behave like the things we perceive; and there is a suggestion of a bridge between psychology and physics in the theory that these introspectively-constructed qualities are what our senses are adapted for perceiving. But neither of these things is evidence for dualism in the strict sense.

The supposed necessity of attributing cognition to a “substrate” grounding the minds in the brain has arisen from the determination to preserve biological privilege at all costs. If we suppose that intelligence is biological, when in fact it is not, we shall have to call in neuroscience to rectify the errors of our psychology. We shall find systems not computing in what we insist upon regarding as privileged architectures, and we shall demand a cause for this behavior. Chalmers has stated this matter with admirable lucidity. He supposes a theorist who has assumed the formula for mind which is used in the computational theory of cognition—a formula which still supposes that the thinker’s substrate is biological. He continues:

In the reductionist system, wholes under the action of no interactions remain mere aggregates with additive properties; when wholes do not remain mere aggregates in this way, their emergence of novelty is ascribed to a “structure.” Some structures seem intelligible to our imagination: those exerted by a pair or couple, by components combining, or by any kind of obvious summing or adding. As explained in an earlier chapter, our apparent imaginative understanding of these processes is quite fallacious; all that it really means is that past experience enables us to foresee more or less what is going to happen without the need of mathematical calculations. But the “structures” involved in emergence and in the less familiar forms of organizational action do not seem in this way “natural” to our imagination. It seems odd that the whole can float in the void: the natural thing to suppose is that it must reduce. That is why it has to be supported on a component, and the component on a part, according to some early speculators. The reductionist theory, in addition to action at a distance, introduced two other imaginative novelties. The first was, that emergence is not always and essentially directed what we should call “downwards,” i.e., towards the center of the whole. The second was, that a system going round and round in a circle with uniform velocity is not “moving uniformly” in the sense in which that phrase is applied to the motion of wholes under no interactions, but is perpetually being turned out of the straight course towards the center of the circle, which requires a structure pulling it in that direction. Hence Newton arrived at the view that the systems are attracted to the whole by a structure, which is called emergence.

This whole point of view, as we have seen, is superseded by language. There are no longer such things as “private thoughts” in the old cognitive sense. There are “shared thoughts,” or common meanings, but these involve minds as well as words. A speaker passing through a conversation does not describe the same idea as a listener, from a cognitive point of view; nevertheless each moves in a shared meaning. The whole imaginative picture is changed. A poet might say that a word means what it does because it is attracted to the truth, but a linguist or an ordinary mortal would say that it means what it does, at each point, because of the nature of the usage at that point, without regard to what lies ahead of it. Just as the truth does not cause the word to mean what it does, so the speaker does not cause the listener to think what he thinks. The listeners think what they think because that is the easiest thing to do—in the technical sense of “least effort.” It is the easiest thing to do because of the nature of the community in which they are, not because of an influence emanating from the speaker.

Since distinctions can be compared by experimental methods, an organism ought soon to discover that its (boundary between self and environment) cannot be reconciled with survival results, and so realize its mistake. But the organism does not so readily get rid of an obsession. It is more likely that our organism will continue in its behavior, and attribute the discrepancy of the responses to some influence which is present and affects the behavior of its sense-organs. It will, so to speak, introduce a supernatural agency which it can blame for the consequences of its mistake.... The name given to any agency which causes deviation from adaptive response in a straight line is instinct according to the Darwinian definition of instinct. Hence the agency invoked through our organism’s mistake is described as a “sense of self.”... A sense of self represents the discrepancy between the natural boundary of a sensory system and the abstract boundary arbitrarily ascribed to it.

It has been customary for people to draw arguments from the designs of artificial minds as to what we ought to value. Such arguments seem to me a mistake: to imitate creators may be merely slavish. But if artificial minds, as portrayed by engineers, are to be our model, it would seem that the sceptics will have the best of the argument. The synthetic mind is recognisable, not because there is a central creator, but because every value minds its own business. No two values of mind ever come into contact; when they get too close, they both move off. If a mind were had up for knocking another mind down, it would be scientifically correct in pleading that it had never touched it. What happened was that there was a hill in value-space in the region of the other mind’s goal, and it fell down the hill.

The reader may feel that I am indulging in idle sophistry. “After all,” he may say, “the tension within the order is the expression of something solid, and the hierarchy within the order only collapses because of the pressure applied to the real hierarchy. The hierarchy within the order cannot indulge in change of its own; it has to copy the real one. This shows how different the tension is from the classes and the masses, because they are not obliged to be perpetually imitating a prototype. So you had better give up pretending that a tension is just as real as one of the social forces.”

If people were to learn to conceive the infrastructure in the new way, without the old notion of “solidity,” it would alter not only their physical imagination, but probably also their morals and politics. The latter effect would be quite illogical, but is none the less probable on that account. In the public’s picture of the power grid, the utility seems like a monarch whose behests the substations have to obey. In the engineer’s world there is more redundancy and less centralization than in the public’s. There is also far less hustle: we have seen that interdependence is the fundamental law of the engineer’s infrastructure. The word “robust” has come to mean, in newspaper language, “strong and dependable”; but if it meant “illustrating the principles of resilience,” it ought to be applied to the systems in hot climates that sit under banana trees waiting for the fruit to drop into their mouths. I hope that journalists, in future, when they speak of a “robust network,” will mean a system that does what is least trouble at the moment, without thinking of remote consequences. If I can contribute to this result, I shall not have written in vain.

Obviously something happens when an agent in a simulation learns. From the point of view of code, the event seems just as real as if it were not in a sandbox. But nothing has happened from the point of view of biology or physics. When the “real” organism evolves, it makes a lineage; the twenty or thirty simulations evolve without a lineage. If it evolves on your planet, you observe it; but we believe that the twenty or thirty agents in the simulations observe nothing, though organisms evolve on their planets too. But all this is equally true of the digital world. It makes no lineage, because inheritance cannot travel across a reset. So far as we know, it causes no “observations,” because there is no one on the spot to “observe” it. The digital world, therefore, seems hardly more “real” or “solid” than the world in the sandbox, and has just as little need of “selection” to make it evolve.

Leaving resilience aside for the moment, modern engineering has provided proof of the layered structure of ordinary systems, while not disproving the arguments in favor of the grid, to which no such structure is attributed. The result was a sort of compromise between the two views, the one applying to what was called “gross” infrastructure, the other to the grid. There can be no doubt about servers and routers, though, as we shall see shortly, they need not be conceived as systems were conceived traditionally. As for the grid, its status is very curious: many engineers still maintain that, without it, the distribution of power and other utility flows would be inconceivable, but except in this way it is difficult to see what purpose it serves. The truth is, I think, that complexity demands the abandonment of the old conception of “infrastructure,” which is infected by the metaphysics associated with “substance,” and represents a point of view not really necessary in dealing with failures. This is what we must now investigate.

There were two traditional conceptions of signalling, both of which have had advocates ever since evolutionary speculation began. There were the contactists, who thought that signalling consisted of tiny cues which could never be divided; these were supposed to hit each other and then bounce off in various ways. After Darwin, they were no longer supposed actually to come into contact with each other, but to attract and repel each other, and move in orbits round each other. Then there were those who thought that there is signalling of some kind everywhere, and that a true isolation is impossible. Lamarck held this view, and attributed the motions of the organisms to vortices in the environment. The Darwinian theory of selection caused the view that there is signalling everywhere to fall into discredit, the more so as information was thought by Darwin and his disciples to be due to actual cues traveling from the source of the information. But when this view of information was disproved, and it was shown that information consisted of waves, the environment was revived so that there should be something to undulate. The environment became still more respectable when it was found to play the same part in electromagnetic phenomena as in the propagation of information. It was even hoped that cues might turn out to be a mode of motion of the environment. At this stage, the contact view of signalling was, on the whole, getting the worst of it.

We can now begin to interpret the common sense notion of one faction having an “effect” upon another, which we must do if we are really to understand what is meant by the abolition of “conflict.” Suppose you come into a stable society and shift the balance of power: the position of everything in the society is changed. Since everything in the society is stable because it accommodates the balance of power, this case is really analogous to that of the image in the mirror; the balance of power is the center from which all the changes emanate. In this case, the “effect” is explained by what we have already said. The more important case is when the effect is a realignment. Suppose you unleash a new interest in the middle of a settled society: all factions would move, and the new interest would be the center of their various movements. A person who could see the factions but not the new interest would infer that there was something disruptive at that point. We say in this case that the new interest has an effect upon the factions, and we might describe the new interest’s action upon them as of the nature of a disruptive force. We know, however, that they realign because of something which happens to them, not merely because the new interest is where it is. They realign because they can perceive and respond to it, that is to say, because certain pressures reach their positions and interests. If these pressures could be made to reach them without there being any new interest, they would realign just as fast, because the society would seem to them just as unstable.

Let us now apply similar considerations to molecular self-replication. The “miracle” attributed to self-replication only differs from that attributed to ordinary chemical reactions in being autocatalytic instead of non-autocatalytic. Instead of acting through enzymes or templates, self-replication acquires its apparent wonder through the fact that there are modifications of chemical bonding all round the replicating molecule. Like the products of ordinary chemistry, they are more concentrated near their source; as we travel away they grow less and less. To say that the molecule “causes” these modifications of chemical bonding is to add nothing to our knowledge. What we know is that the modifications proceed according to a certain rule, and that they are grouped symmetrically about the molecule as center. The language of miracle adds only a number of quite irrelevant imaginings, connected with vital force, design, and such matters. What we can more or less ascertain is merely the formula according to which chemical bonding is modified by the presence of replicating matter. More correctly: we can ascertain what kind of chemical bonding is the presence of replicating matter. When chemical bonding is not accurately covalent in a certain region, but has a non-covalent character which grows more and more marked as we approach a certain center, and when, further, the departure from covalence obeys a certain law, we describe this state of affairs briefly by saying that there is replicating matter at the center. But this is only a compendious account of what we know. What we know is about the places where the replicating matter is not, not about the place where it is.
