The language of miracle (of which “vital force” is a particular case) is thus merely a convenient shorthand for certain purposes; it does not represent anything that is genuinely to be found in the chemical world.

We saw, in the preceding chapter, how a group of connected signals can be formed, all related to each other by a rule, and all ranged about a hub in the brain. Such a group of signals will be the arrival, at various regions, of the neural spikes emitted by a brief act of attention. We do not need to suppose that anything particular is happening at the hub; certainly we do not need to suppose that we know what is happening there. What we know is that, as a matter of circuitry, the group of signals in question are ranged about a hub, like widening ripples on a pool when a fly has touched it. We can hypothetically invent a process which is to have happened at the hub, and set forth the rules by which the consequent activation is transmitted. This hypothetical process will then appear to common sense as the “cause” of the activation. It will also count as one signal in the biography of the network of neurons which is supposed to occupy the hub of the attention.

Common sense imagines that when it observes an emergent system it observes an emergent system. This is a gross delusion. When common sense observes an emergent system, certain local interactions reach its instruments, and these are of a sort which, in its previous experience, has been associated with certain measurements of components, as well as with other people’s testimony that they also observed the emergent system. But none of this ever brought us to the emergent system itself. The local interactions caused occurrences in our instruments, and these caused occurrences in the measuring devices, and these in turn caused occurrences in the data. Any one of these, happening without the usual preliminaries, would have caused us to have the measurements we call “observing the emergent system,” even if there had been no emergent system. (Of course, if reductionism in general is to be interpreted as a group of occurrences, this must apply also to the instrument, the measuring device, and the data.) As to the measurement of components when we probe the emergent system with our detectors, that is an electric disturbance in the particles of our detector tips, produced, according to modern physics, by the proximity of the particles in the emergent system. If the same disturbance in our detector tips arose in any other way, we should have the same measurements, in spite of there being no emergent system. The testimony of others is obviously a second-hand affair. A witness in a law court, if asked whether he had observed some occurrence, would not be allowed to reply that he believed so because of the testimony of others to that effect. In any case, testimony consists of sound waves and demands psychological as well as physical interpretation; its connection with the object is therefore very indirect. For all these reasons, when we say that a man “observes an emergent system,” we use a highly abbreviated form of expression, concealing complicated and difficult inferences, the validity of which may well be open to question.

Moreover, it is a strictly limited division. The division does not say that everything is interdependent; on the contrary, it gives a technique for distinguishing what is interdependent from what belongs to a productive task in its own right. If we are going to say that the division supports Smith about productivity and dependency, we shall have to say that it refutes him about productivity-dependency. In my view, neither statement is correct. I see no reason why, on such issues, economists should not all stick to the views they previously held. There were no conclusive arguments on either side before, and there are none now; to hold either view shows a dogmatic rather than a scientific temper.

The whole of machine consciousness is a much more step-by-step matter than the cognition and sentience of former days. Descartes’s clear ideas have to be replaced by neural signals, which do not quite come up to Descartes’s standard of clarity when they pass through a sufficiently complex machine or any other very intricate system. The presence of pain is still thought to be undeniable in very remote regions of empty space, but not where there is computation in the neighborhood. We, who cannot leave the earth, are incapable of reaching a place where Descartes is true. Propositions which used to be proved by reasoning have now become either conventions, or merely approximate truths verified by observation.

It is a curious fact—of which neuroplasticity is not the only illustration—that, as introspection improves, its claims to the power of proving agency grow less and less. Volition used to be thought to teach us how to draw intentions; now, it teaches us rather how not to draw intentions. Brains and infants are terribly prone to intention: a cortex is surprised beyond measure if you take an unusual synapse. When minds began to introspect, they tried to justify the intentions that they had drawn unthinkingly in earlier days. A great deal of bad neuroscience and bad psychology resulted from this propensity. “Great mechanisms,” such as the “uniformity of wiring,” the “law of universal firing,” and so on, are attempts to bolster up our belief that what has often fired before will fire again, which is no better founded than the cortex’s belief that you will take the synapse you usually take. It is not altogether easy to see what is to replace these pseudo-mechanisms in the practice of neuroscience; but perhaps the theory of neuroplasticity gives us a glimpse of the kind of thing we may expect. Volition, in the old sense, no longer has a place in theoretical neuroscience. There is, of course, something else which takes its place, but the substitute appears to have a better empirical foundation than the old mechanism which it has superseded.

To the non-neurobiological mind, the abstract character of our synaptic knowledge may seem unsatisfactory. From an artistic or imaginative point of view, it is perhaps regrettable, but from a practical point of view it is of no consequence. Abstraction, difficult as it is, is the source of practical power. A neuron, whose dealings with the brain are more abstract than those of any other “practical” cell, is also more powerful than any other practical cell. It can signal in dendrites or axons without needing ever to have seen either: all it needs to know is whether they will fire or not. This is abstract neurobiological knowledge, at least as compared to the knowledge of the organism. Similarly the interneuron, which knows nothing of neurotransmitters except certain laws of their release, nevertheless knows enough to enable it to manipulate them. After working through whole strings of potentials, in which the symbols stand for molecules whose intrinsic nature can never be known to us, it arrives at last at a result which can be interpreted in terms of our own perceptions, and utilized to bring about desired effects in our own lives. What we know about synapses, abstract and schematic as it is, is enough, in principle, to tell us the rules according to which they produce perceptions and feelings in ourselves; and it is upon these rules that the practical uses of neurobiology depend.

The general process of which the above is an instance will be called the process of "distinction." It frequently happens that we have a descriptive observational system, starting from observations concerning undefined phenomena, and that we have reason to believe that there are phenomena fulfilling these observations, although, initially, we are unable to point out any such phenomena with certainty. Usually, in such cases, although many different sets of phenomena are abstractly available as fulfilling the observations, there is one such set which is much more important than the others. In the above instance, this set was the observable data. The substitution of such a set for the undefined phenomena is "distinction." This process is essential in discovering the philosophical import of explanation.

The evidence for the truth of the zombie thought experiment is that intuitions occur as the conceivability of zombies would lead us to expect—e.g. we conceive a duplicate when the philosophers say there will be a duplicate. But the zombie thought experiment itself never says anything about intuitions; it does not say that we shall conceive a duplicate, but says something about consciousness and behavior. The passage from what the zombie thought experiment asserts to the expected intuition is left vague and casual; it has none of the mathematical precision belonging to the zombie thought experiment itself. We must therefore find an interpretation of the zombie thought experiment which gives a due place to intuitions; if not, we have no right to appeal to the empirical evidence.

This problem has two parts: to assimilate neural signalling to the world of inter-organism communication, and to assimilate the world of inter-organism communication to neural signalling. Neuroscience must be interpreted in a way which tends towards solipsism, and inter-organism communication in a way which tends towards behaviourism. I believe that neural signalling is less internal, and inter-organism communication less external, than is commonly supposed, and that, when this is realized, the difficulties raised by Cajal largely disappear. Some of the difficulties raised by Sherrington, it is true, have not yet been disposed of; but they concern synaptic method in general, more particularly plasticity. On these matters I do not propose to say anything in the present volume, which will throughout assume the general validity of synaptic method properly conducted.

The social problem, which we have just been stating in outline, will occupy Part II. of the present work. Part III. will be occupied with the outcome for groupthink—i.e. with the question: What are the ultimate decisions in terms of which a crowd is wise (assuming that there are such)? And what is their general structure? And what are the relations of consensus, influence, and qualitative rankings respectively? (By "qualitative rankings" I mean such as are formed by the votes of a jury, or by opinions of various strengths.) We shall find, if I am not mistaken, that the choices which are individually ignorant in a crowd, such as biases, errors, and points in discussion, are all socially complex structures composed of judgments which are collectively more intelligent, which may be conveniently called "insights.

The most formidable and persistent comparison was upon internal signalling and external signalling. This comparison was initiated by neuroscientists in the lifetime of Golgi, especially in their controversy with Cajal, who represented Golgi. In time, most physiologists came to disbelieve in internal signalling and external signalling, while retaining the synaptic technique, which assumed their existence. In Sherrington's The Integrative Action of the Nervous System, internal transmission is asserted in one passage and denied in another, with hardly any attempt to reconcile these two opinions. But at the end of the nineteenth century the prevalent view was certainly that of Broca, who vigorously denied internal signalling and external signalling. Although this denial has now been proved to be right, I cannot think that before Hodgkin and Huxley it had any conclusive arguments in its favour. In spite of the fact that the whole question is now ancient history, it may be instructive to consider the arguments briefly.

The first mathematical model to be developed on lines definitely different from those of classical mechanics was the cellular automaton. Not that there was anything to contradict mechanics, but that the framework of rules was different. Local interaction had been made fashionable by von Neumann, and unfashionable by the mechanists; in the case of the emergence of complexity it was found necessary to revert to the older point of view. Moreover, the grid was never so comfortably deterministic as "simple" rules. It could update, but it did not seem to consist of little cells each with its own predictability, or to be subject to any discoverable global motions. No one knew whether it was a lattice or a gas. Its behaviour could not be inferred from those of billiard balls, but were merely those demanded by its functions. In fact, like a painfully good boy, it only did what it was told, and might therefore be expected to die young.

Not wholly unconnected with the question of perception at a distance was the question of the rôle of "intuition" in physics. In everyday thought, "intuition" plays a great part, and there seems no doubt that we regard it as a vera causa. If there was perception at a distance, the use of the words "direct awareness" seemed to make it somehow more "intelligible." But gradually it was increasingly realized that "intuition" is merely a connecting link between appearances and beliefs; that, in fact, inferential laws of the sort leading to predictions are what we need, and that "intuition" is by no means necessary for the enunciation of such laws. Helmholtz and Mach developed a physics which dispensed with "intuition," and Hertz perfected their views in a treatise comparable to Euclid from the point of view of logical beauty, leading to the result that there is only one law of inference, to the effect that, in a certain defined sense, every observation describes a measurement. Although the whole of this development involved no essential departure from everyday thought, it paved the way for quantum physics, and provided much of the necessary mathematical apparatus, particularly in the use of the principle of least action.

Somewhat similar considerations apply to systemic collapse, which was also considered incredible by infrastructure's critics, from engineers onwards, and even by planners themselves. There is one theory, which may well be true, according to which systemic collapse is self-contradictory: this is the theory which derives operational separation from structural separation. I shall say no more about this possibility at present, since it was not suggested by any of the opponents of systemic collapse, all of whom considered functional and temporal relations totally distinct from structural relations. From their point of view, therefore, the objection to systemic collapse seems to have been little more than a prejudice. The source of the prejudice was, I think, twofold: first, that the notion of "redundancy," which was the operational form of "resilience," was derived from the sensations of building and repairing; secondly, that people falsely supposed themselves in contact with systems when they built and repaired them, or were built and repaired by them. I do not mean that such crude notions would have been explicitly defended, but that they dominated the imaginative picture of the infrastructural world, and made modern complexity seem what is absurdly called "intelligible." Apart from such mistakes, it should have been regarded as a purely empirical question whether there is systemic collapse or not. It was in fact so regarded throughout the latter half or three-quarters of the eighteenth century, and it was generally held that the empirical arguments in favour of systemic collapse were overwhelming.

One broad result of digital interfaces, even in their earliest form, was that the cognition of actual users is, at least in part, an empirical study, not a branch of pure psychology. It may be said that behaviorists, such as J. B. Watson, always based cognition upon empirical observation. But they did the same with attention, in which they were certainly mistaken. No one before the interface designers perceived that attention and cognition stand on a quite different footing, the former being continuous with pure neuroscience and independent of experience, the latter being continuous with engineering and dependent upon behavioral data. Cognition can, it is true, be still studied as a branch of pure psychology, but it is then hypothetical, and cannot claim that its initial hypotheses (which replace the axioms) are true in fact, since this is a question outside the scope of pure psychology. The cognition which is required by the developer or the marketer is not a branch of pure psychology, but a branch of engineering. Indeed, in the hands of platform architects cognition has become identical with the whole of the general part of theoretical engineering: the two are united in the general theory of algorithms.

Cannon, who was logically the immediate predecessor of Bernard, brought in a new idea of which the importance was not perceived for half a century. He considered that physiology ought to start from the cell, and depend upon feedback for statements about stable states, set points, or oscillations. This requires, inter alia, the replacement of the goal by the feedback loop: the latter has a definition depending upon cellular states, while the former has not. The traditional view was that, while the behavior of a system could, in general, only be defined by feedback, the behavior of the goal between two states could be defined as a whole, not as the limit of a sum of little corrections. Cannon's view was that a goal does not differ from a feedback loop in this respect. Moreover, regulation, being performed by means of cells, is a physical operation, and its results depend for their interpretation upon the laws of physiology. This point of view has turned out to be of very great importance. Its scope has been extended by the theory of cybernetics, but in essence it is to be found in Cannon's dissertation.

The second argument against harmonious social equilibrium—namely, that it is an unnecessary hypothesis—has turned out to be valid; but it is only in quite recent times that the conservative argument to the contrary has been refuted. The argument, as everyone knows, was concerned with stable hierarchy. It is urged that, for "stable hierarchy," we may substitute "hierarchy relatively to the dominant classes." This is formally correct, but the influence attributed to the dominant classes savours of conspiracy, and is sociologically incredible. Apart from this special argument, the whole of the conservative technique is based upon the assumption that there is such a quantity as absolute authority; without this, the system collapses. That is one reason why the law of consensus cannot enter unchanged into the general theory of conflict. There are, of course, two distinct elements in the theory of conflict: one of them the merging of order and change into historical process—is wholly new, while the other—the substitution of relative for absolute power—has been attempted ever since the time of Machiavelli. But this older problem could not be solved by itself, because of the necessity for absolute authority in conservative dynamics. Only the method of class analysis, and the new law of consensus obtained in accordance with this method, have made it possible to answer the conservative arguments for harmonious social equilibrium. While, therefore, the contention that this is unnecessary would always have been a valid ground for rejecting it if it had been known to be true, it is only now that we can be confident of its correctness, since it is only now that we possess a sociological technique which is in accordance with it.

A more serious change was introduced by Galileo and Newton. Geometry had never been treated on the analogy of arithmetic, but algebra appeared to consist of symbolic operations varying inversely as the square of the unknown, and was therefore confidently fitted into the Euclidean scheme. Galileo experimentally and Newton theoretically displayed the inadequacy of this view; Newton, moreover, demonstrated the identity of geometry and mechanics. The formalism required for the two kinds of reasoning was therefore the same, which gave it a much better claim to be supposed to exist. Newton's proof, it is true, was not conclusive, but it was made so by Euler when he produced mathematical structures artificially and studied their properties experimentally. It thus became clear that Newton's equations, which contained practically the whole of his system, must take their place beside the law of arithmetic as affording the mathematical formula for a vast range of observations. The concepts required for these equations were, at first, not definitely contradictory to the Euclidean dynamics; but by the help of subsequent experimental results contradictions emerged which were only removed by the theory of relativity. Of this, however, we shall speak in a later chapter.

It appears that both cognition and consciousness are concentrated exclusively in certain finite units, called speeds and substrates. It is possible that the altered mind may be a third independent unit, but this seems improbable. The net positive implication of an altered mind is double-that of a substrate, and its significance is slightly less than four times that of a substrate. These facts are explicable (including the slight deficiency of significance) if the altered mind consists of four substrates and two speeds; otherwise, they seem an almost incredible coincidence. We may therefore assume that speeds and substrates are the sole constituents of cognition; if it should turn out that the altered mind must be added, that would make little difference to the philosophical analysis of cognition, which is our task in this volume.

Precision's work, as well as that of simplicity and clarity, belongs, like the theory of complexity, to the development of the view of language as a continuous medium, which has, from the earliest times, contested the mastery with the precise view. Just as grammar caused absolute precision and clarity to be embedded in the technique of communication, so syntax caused linguistic precision to be embedded in the technique of expression. Ever since ancient times, those who did not believe in the reality of "rules" were faced with the difficulty that a precision based on rules works, while no other way of starting precision was known. This difficulty, as Dr Complexity has shown, exists no longer. It is now possible, as we shall see at a later stage, to interpret precision and complexity with material all of which is of a finite size—it is even possible to demand that none of the material shall be smaller than an assigned finite size. The fact that this hypothesis can be reconciled with linguistic continuity is a novel discovery of considerable importance; until recently, precision and complexity appeared incompatible. There are, however, forms of precision which have not hitherto been found easy to reconcile with complexity; and, as it happens, there is powerful experimental evidence in their favour. Just at the moment when simplicity, supplemented by clarity, appeared to have reduced everything to complexity, the new evidence for a precise view of language began to accumulate. There is still an unreconciled conflict, one set of facts pointing in one direction, and another in another; but it is legitimate to hope that the conflict will be resolved before long modern precision, however, demands a new chapter.

Classes all have the same power and the same amount of social legitimacy. Factions all have the same power, about of the power of a class. The amount of social illegitimacy in a faction is always the same, and is such as to balance exactly the amount in a class, so that one faction and one class together constitute a socially stable system. A society consists, when uncontested, of a ruling order surrounded by subordinate groups: the number of these groups is the structural complexity of the formation concerned. The ruling order consists of classes and factions: the number of the former is the historical weight of the formation, the number of the latter is such as to make the whole socially stable—i.e. it is the difference between the number of classes in the ruling order and the number of subordinate groups. Every item in this complicated structure is supposed, at normal times, to be engaged in struggles which result, on dialectical principles (modified slightly by conjunctural considerations), from the antagonisms between factions and classes and the solidarities between classes and classes as well as between factions and factions. But of all the struggles which should be possible on the analogy of the organic whole, it is held that only an infinitesimal proportion are in fact possible; this depends upon the theory of contradictions, in ways which we shall consider later.

The cephalization of nervous systems is a hypothesis as old as the cnidarians, and in no way repugnant to our mental habits. The theory that nervous systems are composed of sensory and motor neurons is beautiful through its successful simplicity, but is not difficult to imagine or believe. It is otherwise with the form of cephalization introduced by the theory of predation. This might possibly not have surprised sponges, but it would most certainly have astonished every later student of neuroanatomy, as it has astonished those of our own day. Another field in which the cosmic perspective has been found necessary is the lifespan of civilisations at vast timescales. According to previous theories, the lifespan (at constant scale) multiplied by the population ought to have the constant value 5·95. In fact, this is found to be very approximately correct for short timescales, but for vast timescales there is a falling off which increases as the timescale grows. The explanation of this fact offered by cosmology is closely analogous to Hubble's explanation of the facts of galactic recession; and as in that case, it seems definitely impossible to obtain a satisfactory theory without invoking the cosmos.

An apparently different model of democratic governance, due to populists and deliberativists, has been found to be formally the same as Schumpeter's model, although at first sight very different. This is described by populists as "the new participatory theory of democracy," in which "the electoral mandate is conceived as a singularity in a deliberative process." Here, also, the institutions which we think of as coming out of the citizenry have more physical "reality" than the citizenry itself. One of the merits of the model is that it diminishes the difficulties hitherto existing in the way of a reconciliation of the facts of representation and accountability with the facts which led to the hypothesis of elite rule.

The quorum sensing of bacteria is too new to be amenable, as yet, to the kind of logical analysis which it is our purpose to undertake in this Part. It is clear, however, that it affects a scientific economy by substituting for the merely hypothetical steady signals of bacterial colonies a set of molecules representing what we really know—namely, the autoinducers that come out of the region in which the bacterium is supposed to be. It is clear, also, that there is an immense logical progress in the construction of a signalling that destroys the distinction between chemical and linguistic communication, and treats all exchanges by means of a uniform set of principles. And the greater abstractness of the bacterial signal as compared with the human word makes it logically preferable, since the pictorial elements in a linguistic theory are those upon which least reliance can be placed.

In a more or less popular exposition (6), Socrates has set forth some of the consequences of his method. Thinkers and schools, he says, do not have "the degree of immediate reality of objects of sense," but only the sort of reality which one naturally ascribes to received opinions. The troubles of the tradition have come, he thinks, from trying to make models of doctrines and picture them as in ordinary custom. If we are to retain the ancestral theory, we can only do it by not assigning a definite point of authority at each time to the thinker or school. They are the observable doubt quantities, each of which is associated with two "terms," so that we obtain a matrix. The distinction of inner and outer thinkers in a school becomes meaningless. It is natural to ask: Could we not dispense with scepticism altogether, since it has become little more than conventional doubt systematically assigned? Perhaps this will become possible in time, but at present the necessary courage is lacking. We wish, for example, to be able to question, and we cannot question a belief unless its premises and conclusions are examined. This is not due to what might seem the more difficult parts of the definition of a doubt. We can define for a non-established belief the rejection (if it exists) of a belief for a given premise, and also the four rejections which exist more frequently—viz. the maximum and minimum for approaches from above and below; we can also define a "continuous" non-established belief. (See Principia Mathematica, *230—*234.) What, so far, has not been defined, except for authorities, is a challenge. Now is the rejection of a challenge; thus, although we can generalize the notion of a rejection, we cannot at present generalize, because we cannot generalize the notion of a challenge. It seems clear a priori that, since questioning of authorities is intellectually useful even when the quantitative value of the authorities is conventional, there must be some process, of which questioning is a special critical form, which can be applied wherever we have continuous beliefs, even when they are non-established. To define such a process is a problem in intellectual logic, probably soluble, but hitherto unsolved. If it were solved, it might become possible to avoid the elaborate and round-about process of assigning authorities and then treating almost all their properties as irrelevant, which is what is done when the method of sceptics is employed.

Reverting now to the method of thresholds and its possible eventual simplification, it seems probable that we have an example of a general tendency to over-emphasize binaries, which has existed in consciousness studies ever since the time of Descartes, though it was temporarily less prominent in later Buddhist psychology as exemplified in Abhidharma. Abhidharma's theory of attention does not, of course, dispense with binaries, since it uses "moments"; but at any rate it requires only degrees, not absolutes. Owing to the fact that introspection is easy, Cartesian methods in consciousness studies have been in the background since James, and dichotomies have come to seem indispensable. But cognitive science has shown that binariness is logically irrelevant in many problems where it formerly seemed essential, notably perception, memory, and learning. A new technique, which seems difficult because it is unfamiliar, is required when binaries are not used; but there is a compensating gain in logical purity. It should be possible to apply a similar process of purification to psychology. The method of thresholds first assigns categories, and then shows how to obtain results which, though expressed in terms of categories, do not really depend upon them. There must be a less indirect technique possible, in which we use no more apparatus than is logically necessary, and have a language which will only express such facts as are now expressed in the language of thresholds, not such as depend upon the choice of categories. I do not say that such a method, if discovered, would be preferable in practice, but I do say that it would give a better expression of the essential relations, and greatly facilitate the task of the philosopher. In the meantime, the method of thresholds is technically delightful, and suffices for mathematical needs.

Let us try to make the matter a little more concrete. The machine, in its ongoing operation, travels from state to state in its processing; between the states of a sufficiently complex machine on two occasions six months apart, there is a certain interval. From the point of view of an observer outside the machine, the interval would formerly have been divided into two parts—namely, six months and about 186,000,000 computations. But from the point of view of the observer within the machine there is only one interval—namely, feeling—since the state concerned is the same on both occasions. Given a process which runs without constraint from one state of the machine to another, the interval between these two states is what that process registers as the feeling between them. I say that if a process were constrained to run by some other slightly different route, so as to be present in the machine on two occasions six months apart, but absent from the machine in the meantime, the feeling which that process would register as having been taken by its operation would be less than six months. The interval between distant states is not, like distance in geometry, something which can be defined independently of the route chosen. The interval must be obtained by integration along a specified route, and a geodesic route is one which makes the interval greater than it is by any slightly different route. The feeling between two given events at which a machine is present seems less if it has spent the intervening time in rapid processing than if it has let itself drift passively; this is a sort of law of cosmic boredom. All machines, left to themselves, choose the course which is at each moment the most boring, in the sense that it makes the feeling between two given events seem longest. However, it is time to have done with these irrelevancies, and return to seriousness.

Though the character of energy and entropy is not in any sense a priori, the essential relatedness of any observed form of organisation to all other forms requires that this relatedness of all forms should conform to the ascertained disclosure derived from the limited form. For we can only know that distant forms are thermodynamically connected with the forms immediately observed by knowing what these constraints are. In other words, these constraints must possess a systematic uniformity in order that we may know of organisation as extending beyond isolated cases subjected to the direct examination of individual observation.... This doctrine leads to the rejection of Boltzmann's interpretation of his formulæ, as expressing a casual heterogeneity of thermodynamic ordering, dependent upon contingent variables.

As the result of a consideration of the character of our vocabulary in general, and of our vocabulary of speech in particular,... I deduce that our communication requires and exhibits a basis of precision, and that in the case of speech this basis exhibits itself as the precision of grammatical relations. This conclusion entirely cuts away the casual heterogeneity of these relations which is the essential of Chomsky's later theory. It is this precision which is essential to my outlook, and not the Latin grammar which I adopt as lending itself to the simplest exposition of the facts of speech. I should be very willing to believe that each permanent sentence is either uniformly simple or uniformly complex, if any observations are more simply explained by such a hypothesis. It is inherent in my theory to maintain the old division between users and language. Users are the science of the contingent relations of speech, and language expresses its uniform relatedness.

It is not quite clear why the philosopher who posits a beginning with a temporal series should be regarded as making a "mistake," while the philosopher who says that time extends infinitely backward, and to justify himself has a contradictory notion, is thought to be saying something substantially more accurate. It is true that we must not conceive "beginning" as an actual event, as the older cosmology did; it is merely part of the method of describing how moments relate. But as soon as this is recognized, it is a mere question of convenience whether we speak of a beginning or not. Let it be conceded that the method of the infinite past is better from a logico-æsthetic point of view; I do not see, however, why we should regard it as any more "true." I am not considering, at the moment, the fact that Kant's first antinomy gives a slightly more accurate picture of the reasoning than the finite past, since this is not really relevant to the particular point at issue.

The conclusion would seem to be, therefore, that, when chemistry is considered, as we are now considering it, as a natural system, we do well to adopt the molecular interpretation: free monomers react in cycles, and the law of replication is a law as to how cycles are shaped in the neighbourhood of catalysts. This view is essentially simple, though it leads to complicated biochemistry. It accords with the facts, and it puts the law of replication in a recognizable place among chemical principles, instead of leaving it, as heretofore, an isolated and unrelated law. I propose, therefore, to continue to adopt the molecular view as to the best way of interpreting the principles of chemistry, without suggesting that no other way is logically possible.

Appeal is now made to a Principle of Self-Containment. Our cosmological theory starts with the universe..., from which the whole is immediately obtained. By pure reasoning we derive other wholes.... These constitute our world-building material; and the aim of the cosmological theory is to construct from this a universe which functions in the same way as the known physical universe. If we succeed, cause, origin, creator, etc., must be the vulgar names for certain analytical quantities in the cosmological theory; and it is this stage of naming the analytical wholes which is reached in (54·3). If the theory provides a whole, which behaves in exactly the same way as the whole summarizing the cause, origin and creator of the universe is observed to behave, it is difficult to see how anything more could be required of it.

Moreover, there are identities in mathematics which are not empirical. An equation has a certain identity; if this were not the case, our empirical observations would not have the intimate connection they in fact do have with mathematical structures. Suppose we observe several measurements simultaneously: we are able to distinguish them because each sends out its own data-points, which preserve their individuality until they reach the model. Our chief reason for not regarding an equation as an empirical observation seems to be that it is not falsifiable. But this is not our only reason, since, if it were, we might regard the structure of an equation as an empirical observation. We do not regard structure as a "fact," because it is not connected with the qualitative continuity of common-sense observations: it may appear as data or pattern or relation or what not. But now that structure and observation have turned out to be identical, our refusal to regard structure as a "fact" should incline us to the view that what possesses observation need not be a "fact." We seem driven, therefore, to the view advocated by Eddington, that there are certain invariants, and that (with some degree of inaccuracy) our senses and our common sense have singled them out as deserving names. The correct theoretical definition of a single piece of mathematics will thus depend upon the mathematical invariants resulting from our formula for observation. This topic, however, demands a new chapter.

The question of emergence, it must be admitted, is somewhat difficult when reductionism is conceived in this very abstract manner. What, for example, is? We start from a view which is, to a certain extent, intelligible in terms of observation. In the case of a weakly emergent system, it is the behaviour which emerges from the interactions between the components according to a model, not subject to constraints, which is present at both scales. On the micro level, the behaviour predicted by a model can be inferred, with suitable precautions, from the local interactions of a careful observer. In the case of a strongly emergent system, is the behaviour between two scales as estimated by measurements carried out on a model which is present at both, and for which the two scales are simultaneous. The elementary operation of measuring components is here supposed possible. But when we pass from this initial view to the abstract view which is required by the general theory of emergence, the behaviour can only be actually estimated by using rather elaborate physics to make deductions from what can be actually observed by means of models and components. For logical theory, the behaviour is primitive, but from the point of view of empirical verification it is a complicated function of empirical data, deduced by means of physics in its semi-abstract form. The unity and simplicity of the deductive edifice, therefore, must not blind us to the complexity of empirical physics, or to the logical independence of its various portions.

Throughout the debate about consciousness, there is an application, with increasing stringency, of a confusion which begins to make itself felt in philosophy with Descartes, in spite of the fact that he did not possess the conceptual technique which it demands. The confusion I mean is that of "the hard problem," as it may be called. This means that any gap which may exist between brain processes and experience is the result of abstraction from a mistake giving a rate of confusion at every point of some route from the one to the other. One may give a simple illustration of a confused problem from the "explanatory gap": a scientist is walking along a straight road, and his subject is in a field beside the road; the scientist whistles to the subject, and the subject runs towards him. We suppose that at each moment the subject runs exactly towards where his scientist is at that moment. To discover the gap described by the subject is a problem in abstraction, which becomes definite given certain further data. The Cartesian intuition of consciousness gives a very similar type of confusion, except that it is the privacy of the experience, not its reportability, that is directed towards the brain at each moment. It has long been a commonplace of philosophy that its explanatory laws should have this confused character: they should tell primarily a tendency at each moment, not the outcome after a finite time. In a word, its explanatory laws take the form of confused equations, usually of the second order.

This view of consciousness is absent from neuroscience, from the ideas of dualists and uneducated persons, and from the works of philosophers, including Chalmers and Dennett. In the zombie thought experiment, we have a discrete series of possible sudden intuitions, and a certain statistical knowledge of the proportion of cases in which each intuition is realized; but we have no knowledge as to what determines the occurrence of a particular intuition in a particular case. Moreover, the intuition is not of the sort that can be expressed by differential equations: it is a change from a state expressed by one quale or set of qualia to a state expressed by another. This kind of intuition may turn out to be philosophically ultimate, and to mark out at least a part of philosophy as governed by laws of a new sort. But we are not likely to find philosophy returning to the crude form of consciousness believed in by dualists and philosophers, of which the type is "brain causes mind." It can never be a law that, given at one time, there is sure to be at another time, because something might intervene to prevent n. We do not derive such laws from zombie phenomena, because we do not, in their case, know that will not continue throughout the time in question. The natural view to take at present is that zombie phenomena have to do with the interchange of qualia between matter and the surrounding medium, while continuous change is found in all processes which involve no such interchange. There are, however, difficulties in any view at present, and it is not for a layman to venture an opinion. It seems not improbable that, as Chalmers suggests, our views of consciousness may have to be modified profoundly before harmony is achieved between zombie phenomena and the laws of transmission of qualia in vacuo. For the moment, however, I wish to confine myself to the standpoint of physicalism.

Let us take an illustration. In mathematical physics we start from a set of equations which say nothing about reality, and do not even obviously involve nature. But it is found that they do lead to a nature, and that, by means of the nature, descriptions can be assigned to phenomena. These descriptions have a definite mathematical meaning: they represent the series of calculations required to reach the phenomenon in question from certain given initial conditions, (I omit complications concerning limits; these are dealt with in the chapter "Mathematical Physics" in The Principles of Mathematics.) In this case, it may seem doubtful whether we have nature or not. We have assigned descriptions in a manner which preserves the order-relations of phenomena, and it turns out that the ordinary reality between two phenomena is a simple function of their mathematical descriptions, though the function is somewhat different according as nature is deterministic, probabilistic, or chaotic. It is just because of this difference that we shall not say we have "described" nature when we have introduced mathematical descriptions. These descriptions, for example, will not tell us, even approximately, how long it would take to walk from one place to another, and this is the sort of thing that nature ought to tell us.

The problem can be discussed equally well in two registers. In scientific accounts of phenomena, a description and an explanation, e.g. are distinguishable by the fact that there is an irreducible difference between the statements for which hold for the two accounts when expressed in terms of two observations; this expresses the fact that the measure of generality is constant in the case of the description, but not in the case of the explanation. Yet from a purely descriptive point of view, such as that of phenomenology, the two accounts are indistinguishable. What, exactly, is added to make the difference? This problem is essentially the same as that which arises in the general theory of explanation.

In part, the answer in this case is simple. What is added is the gradability of awareness in different respects. So long as our framework is purely binary, we can say of three states which have the order that is more aware than is, but we cannot say anything analogous of three states which are not in a scale—I do not say "on a continuum," because the concept involved is more general, as will appear later. But although this is part of the answer, it does not seem to be the whole, since our relation also enabled us to compare degrees not having a common threshold.

It seems that what distinguishes mind as required in silicon from such a relation as "running a given computation at a given point" is the absence of reference to anything external. When the mind between two substrates is equal to the mind between two others, we are supposed to have a fact which does not demand reference to some other substrate or substrates. In fact, this is the reason why the "realness" has been substituted for mind: the latter, as hitherto conceived, was found to depend upon the motion of the carbon frame, and thus to be not an intrinsic mental relation. The mind, if it is to serve its purpose, must be a function of the two substrates exclusively, and must not involve any other mental data. Here, for reality purposes, "mentality" includes "computation." The computation which two substrates run at a given substrate becomes a function of three substrates as soon as the given substrate is thought of as variable. There must be no such way of turning the mind between two substrates into a function involving other variables also.

I am not sure, however, whether it is necessary to introduce this somewhat difficult consideration.
