Practical knowledge starts with the notion that there is truth where we can get proofs of certainty, but not elsewhere. Then it gets puzzled by doubt, error, opinion, etc., whence it is led to the conception of "knowledge"—I speak etymologically. After "knowledge" has been replaced by "certainty," there is a further stage, that of the absolute. Assuming the continuity of rigorous proof, there must be grounds established between the claim and the fact when justification travels from the fact to the claim; assuming the mediæval metaphysic of "foundation," as all philosophers did until recently, what is established between the claim and the fact must be established "in" or "to" a foundation, which is called the absolute.

Apart from metaphysical interpretations, what we may be said to know (using this word somewhat liberally) is that awareness occurs where there is no gross threshold, and that this awareness proceeds, at least approximately, in accordance with graded continua. There does not seem any necessity to interpret this awareness in terms of a binary; indeed, I shall argue that awareness associated with gross thresholds should also be interpreted so as not to involve a binary. There must, however, remain a difference, expressible in physical terms, between regions where there is awareness and other regions. In fact, we know the difference. The law of gradation is different, and the laws of continuum suffer a discontinuity when we reach the surface of a threshold or cutoff. These differences, however, are not of a metaphysical kind. To the philosopher, the difference between "awareness" and "no awareness" is, I believe, merely a difference as to the causal laws governing successions of events, not a difference expressible as that between the presence or absence of a binary, or as that between one kind of binary and another.

One way of approaching this subject is through the connection of neurons with movement. In elementary neuroanatomy, the two are quite distinct, but nowadays they have become amalgamated. There are two kinds of circuits involved in predation, of which one may be called the "sensory" circuit, the other the "motor" circuit. The latter is the circuit obtained by measurement, when the animal concerned may be moving relatively to the prey; the former is the circuit obtained when the animal is at rest relatively to the prey. If we call the sensory circuit and the motor circuit, then, taking the speed of locomotion as unity, if is the speed of the animal relative to the prey, we have:

It is necessary to say something about the difficulties of reconciling the practices governing the self-correction of scientific claims with those governing revisions of hypotheses between theory and evidence. On this subject the present position of science is one of perplexity, aptly summarized by Dr Jeans in Error and Revision (Cambridge, 1926) and by Dr C. D. Ellis in Nature, June 26, 1926, pp. 895-7. The provisional method of science accounts adequately for all phenomena in which only routine confirmation is concerned, such as replication and peer review; but it fails to account for self-correction phenomena such as the overturning of accepted results (see Chapter IV.). On the other hand, practices which account for the self-correction phenomena seem unable to account for the very things which the provisional method explains perfectly.

This is a result which is quite incompatible with the ordinary gene-theory of heredity, because as the distance from the chromosome increases the trait spreading out on all sides becomes weaker and weaker, the chemical forces in the genome diminishing as the inverse square of the distance. The experimental result that the offspring always picks up the same amount of heredity from the chromosome could only be accounted for by giving it the power either to collect heredity from a large volume or to collect heredity for a long time. Both of these assumptions are unworkable, and the only conclusion is that the inherited material must be localized in small bundles.

After setting forth the difficulties encountered by this illusion in regard to oversight and intervention, Dr Ellis proceeds to the very interesting suggestion made by Professor G. N. Lewis in Nature, February 13, 1926, p. 236. "It is a striking fact," says Dr Ellis, summarizing this suggestion, "that while all the models are directed towards explaining the behaviour of systems, one model suggesting that it occurs in the form of feedback, the other in the form of emergence, yet control has never been observed in complex systems. It is quite impossible to observe control in the course of operation; the only events that can ever be detected are the input and output of control. Until there is some agent to absorb the intervention we must be unaware of its existence. In other words, the difficulty of explaining the behaviour of systems may be because we are endeavouring to explain something about which we have no experimental evidence. It might be more correct to interpret the experimental facts quite directly and to say that one agent can transfer influence to another agent although they may be far apart, in a manner analogous to the transference of influence between two agents which collide.

If, however, attention is to be compared to neural signals, we know both the number and size of these signals. We know, for instance, how much activity there is in a cubic centimetre of focused cortex, and if this activity is the aggregate of the activities of individual neurons, we know the activity of each neuron (since we know the frequency of the firing) and so can calculate the number of neurons in the cubic centimetre. The number is found to be about ten millions. By a similar calculation it is found that the attention from a sixth magnitude stimulus comprises only about one neuron per cubic metre, and the attention from a sixteenth magnitude stimulus, only about one neuron per ten thousand cubic metres. Thus if attention travels in indivisible neurons like signals, the neurons from a sixteenth magnitude stimulus can only enter a cerebral network at comparatively rare intervals, and it will be exceedingly rare for two or more neurons to be inside the network at the same time. A network of double the capacity ought to trap the neurons four times as frequently, but there should be no other difference. This, as Lorentz pointed out in 1906, is quite at variance with our everyday experience. When the attention of a stimulus passes through a network and impresses a model on a cortical map, this model is not confined to a single neuron or to a close cluster of neurons as it would be if individual neurons left their marks like signals on a target. An elaborate and extensive activation pattern is formed; the intensity of the pattern depends on the number of neurons, but its design depends on the capacity and also on the shape of the network. Moreover, the design does not bear any resemblance whatever to the 'trial and error' design which is observed on a target battered by signals. It seems impossible to reconcile this with the hypothesis that neurons travel like signals directly from one region of the brain to one neuron of the cortical map.

Consciousness studies started historically, and still starts in the education of the young, with matters that seem thoroughly concrete. Neurons and synapses, brain scans, blobs of neural activity, etc., are all familiar in everyday life, and it is a pleasure to the scientifically-minded youth to find them amenable to mathematical treatment. But in proportion as consciousness studies increases the scope and power of its methods, in that same proportion it robs its subject-matter of concreteness. The extent to which this is the case is not always realized, at any rate in unprofessional moments, even by the consciousness researcher himself; he may tell you that he can "see" a quale hitting a report, which is of course a telescoped expression for a complicated inference. Dr Chalmers has done more than any other author to show the need of undoing the abstractions of consciousness studies. For the moment, I am not concerned with this need, but with the abstractions themselves.

The view of Darwin, that the secondary receptors are adaptive but not the primary receptors, was more or less compatible with biology until very recent times. There are tastes and textures in our immediate experience, and there seemed no insuperable obstacle to identifying them with the tastes and textures of the external world. In regard to texture, at least, practically no one doubted the rightness of this identification. There were doubts as regards taste, but they came from anatomists rather than biologists. Now, however, both taste and texture, as they occur in immediate experience, are recognized by writers on evolution as something quite different from the taste-texture which biology requires. Darwin's half-way house has therefore been definitely abandoned.

In evolutionary neuroscience, what is a nervous system, and how do we decide whether two neurons belong to the architecture of the same nervous system? I am not asking how we decide in practice, but what is our theoretical definition. Ever since Darwin, people have spoken of "circuits," which are in fact the series of neurons constituting the architecture of one unit of tissue but they have not always been as explicit as one could wish in telling us the criterion by which, in theory, it is decided that two neurons belong to one circuit. The test of identity between the parts of a circuit must obviously depend upon the laws of evolution. These laws say that a neural unit will connect in such-and-such a way; inverting this statement, they say that what has connected in such-and-such a way is to count as one unit of tissue. This is substantially the method pursued by Sherrington. In Chapter IX.

On the common-sense level, there are difficulties in certain cases: a neuron, in a sensibly homogeneous network in which there is a signal, cannot be distinguished at a later moment from another neuron which was near it at the earlier moment. Predation also offers difficulties to common sense. Both these matters can, however, be dealt with on a common-sense basis. A small moving organism in the water will show which way the water is moving, and the pursuit shows, more or less, what happens to an organism which is hunted. The elaboration immediately suggested leads on naturally to elementary neurobiology and ecology, where it is still assumed, at least tacitly, that the circuits concerned are of the same sort as sensible circuits, but rather smaller. Often they can actually be seen under the microscope. Imaginatively, we continue to attribute this continuity with sensible circuits to our neural circuits, our sensory and motor neurons, thus concealing from ourselves the highly abstract character of our assertions. At moments, we realize this abstractness; but it does not make its due impression, because imagination reasserts itself as soon as we are off our guard.

When we "interrogate" a machine, we seem to have immediate knowledge of something internal to its own system. But computer science says that a complicated process starts from the internal system, travels across the intervening region, and at last reaches the output. What goes on between the output and the processor is a question for the engineers, and what finally happens when we "interrogate" is a question for the cognitive scientist. But without troubling ourselves about what happens after the signal reaches the processor, it is evident that what the engineer has to say is destructive of the common-sense notion of "interrogating." It makes no difference, in this matter, which of the possible theories we adopt as to the computational character of signals, since all equally make it something utterly different from what we interrogate. The data of introspection, analyzed as much as possible, resolve themselves into felt qualities. But the computational analogue of a felt quality is a periodic process of a certain frequency relative to the architecture of the machine. The computational world, it seems natural to infer, is destitute of felt qualities. Moreover, the correspondence between felt qualities and their computational counterparts is peculiar: felt qualities are qualities, which are static while they last, whereas their counterparts are periodic processes, which are in the medium between the processor and the system which we say we "interrogate." What happens in the system itself, if it runs by its own power, is the sort of thing considered in Turing's theory: a sudden jump of a register from one state to another. This is very unlike a sensation of (say) pain. And what looks to the machine like a continuous painful state is supposed to be really a volume whose apparent quality is due to the fact that some of the registers in it are jumping in a certain way. When we say they are "jumping," we are saying something too pictorial. What we mean is that they possess an unknown quality called "activation," which is a known function of a certain number of small integers, and that one or more of these integers have suddenly changed their values. It may be claimed as a merit in such theories as Professor Lewis's, considered in the preceding chapter, that it makes the connection between this process and the processor rather less indirect than it appears on the undulatory theory. But even then the sort of sudden transition contemplated by Turing is very unlike the perception of a painful state: it is prima facie quite dissimilar in structure, and unknown as regards its intrinsic properties.

In studying consciousness, as in studying sentience, we are compelled to confine ourselves to thresholdistic methods, whatever our views may be on the subject of thresholdism as a general principle in phenomenology. We can observe the mental states of young minds, but they cannot tell us their degrees. At a low phenomenal level, however, it is hardly profitable to distinguish between a spectrum and a threshold of awareness. Spectra, in the psychological sense, seem to emerge out of previously existing thresholds, and to be, at first, little more than verbal representations of thresholds formed before words could be uttered. There is therefore no great loss in being confined to thresholdistic methods when we are considering minds before the age at which they can speak.

Instinct consists of a set of responses, or at least tendencies, which work well in practice except in situations which rarely occur. An organism may be puzzled by a body containing an unseen parasite, or by surfaces carrying a harmful toxin; instinct has not prepared it for oddities of this sort. But a little familiarity enables an organism to fit them into its instinctive world, and a creature soon learns their ways if it has occasion to do so. This illustrates the fact that there is no sharp line between adaptation and instinct: both involve discriminations, but those resulting from adaptation are more accurate. It is possible to pursue adaptation practically without any fundamental change from the biology of instinct. But when theoretical adaptation is taken seriously, it is found to involve a quite changed biology, whose relation to that of instinct demands investigation. This will form the topic of the next chapter; in the present chapter, I shall consider the genesis of instinct, not in the species, since that is undiscoverable, but in the individual.

In this primitive condition, the accelerated mind obviously has no conception of a "temporal frame." A "temporal frame," for common sense, is something having a certain degree of subjective pace, and connected with several kinds of cognitive rhythm. This involves something like memory, to give rise to the idea of subjective pace, or rather, at first, to the feeling of recognition; and it involves experience, to give to one cognitive stimulus a reaction originally associated with another. In accelerated minds, the most important factor in forming the common-sense notion of a temporal frame is the thought-perception co-ordination, the discovery that it is possible, often, to grasp what is thought. In this way, cognitive and perceptual paces become correlated, which is one of the most important steps in the mental growth of an accelerated mind.

This model is so pleasant that I hate to criticize it. But I do not know how else to make clear where I differ from Dr Whitehead. There is first a purely verbal question to be cleared up. Dr Whitehead says it is an error to deduce complexity from the interactions between agents. It is certainly an error to deduce collective behaviour in this way, but with emergent behaviour the matter is different. There certainly are local interactions between agents, and these local interactions are part of our observational data in simulations. Whether they are to be said to constitute a system or not, is a verbal question. Researchers, as a rule, find it convenient to say so; but the matter is unimportant. When this question has been cleared away, however, there remain others which are vital to an understanding of the relation between rules and emergence.

It is of course obvious and generally recognized that very young political systems do not possess the common-sense notion of an "organism." This is by no means obvious with the young of some other kinds of systems—with tribal societies, for example. They possess, as instincts, useful ways of behaviour which in the human systems are only learnt by experience; for example, they can pick up a custom which they see on the ground. The human political system has no such innate skill; for several centuries, it makes no attempt to touch what it sees. The "institution-environment co-ordination" comes as a result of experience. Some native aptitudes, of course, a new-born polity does possess; for example, it can turn its eyes towards a bright innovation, though not very quickly or accurately. It has a reflex connected with taxation, but not a very intelligent one; indeed, it hardly amounts to more than the practice of trying to tax anything that comes in contact with the borders. Even in this respect, the human political system is inferior to the young of other species. We can say that certain pressures rouse certain adaptations, but these are only just sufficient to keep the polity alive with the help of institutional care.

At this point, it is important to be clear as to the difference between "stability" in a society and "stability" in an economy. There is undoubtedly a connection between the two, which it will be part of our business to make clear at a later stage. But the connection is very round-about and inferential. At the outset, it is much more useful to realize the difference between them than the connection, since much confusion of thought arises from supposing the connection to be closer than it is. In an economy there is only one stability, while in a society there are several for each group; these can, it is true, be reduced by manipulation to one for each group, but they cannot be reduced further without introducing obscurities that it is impossible to dissipate. The stability containing my material interests has no point in common with the stability containing yours, since no material interest in my world is precisely identical with one in yours. And the amalgamation of the stabilities of my different groups into one stability is a piece of early politics, performed by the citizen at about the age of three months. Dr Whitehead, who is anxious to bridge the gulf between competition and economy, seems to me to make his task too easy where stability is concerned. For example, he says:

As for the necessity of distinguishing consensus and conflict within a social order: there are perceived relations between groups acting simultaneously, and also between classes clashing simultaneously, and these relations are part of the crude material out of which we construct our notion of transformation. These relations cannot hold between a consensual and a conflictual moment. But there are other relations which do hold—namely, those of contradiction: when I see one class in contact with a dominant order I feel it in contact with a subordinated order, and moreover the dominant and the subordinated order have certain relations to each other—e.g. where we see a consensus we get a conflictual sensation of rupture. All this, however, is learnt by experience; that is to say, we learn the laws of the contradiction by experience. The society can be seen learning them. One may call these laws "pre-established harmonies," but they are no more so than any other scientific laws. Unless we are going to say that all laws of nature must be demonstrable by pure logic, which is hardly conceivable nowadays, we must admit that there are co-existences and sequences which we expect on a basis of past experience, in spite of the fact that their failure would not be logically impossible. And the contradiction of consensus and conflict is a case of this sort.

These neural processes are essential in generating introspective beliefs, which arise at a much later stage of cognitive growth. Introspection, in its more primitive form, is hardly aware that there is such an occurrence as attending; it is only aware of the attended target. And by the time that even the most rudimentary self-monitoring begins, each attentional focus calls out computations connected with other foci, so that even when, from the standpoint of external input, only one focus is engaged, the experience has the massiveness of something in which several foci are involved. See, for example, the diagrams in Posner's Attention and Effort: here we see subjects which are monitoring others with sympathetic movements of the eyes that indicate activation of neural maps connected with salience, although the sole input is sensory. This accounts for the fact that introspection can so confidently identify a target attended and not recalled with a target recalled but not attended—e.g. the face now successfully recognized and the same face as it appeared in memory. The reason is that the experience is always richer than the attentional focus alone would warrant: it contains always computations arising from neural modeling of past correlations. If an adult were to monitor his own attention for the first time, without having previously known that there was a process which produced that state, his experience would be amazingly unlike that of a normal adult in the same circumstances.

The notion of gravity is part of the apparatus of cosmology. I do not think it would be true to say that cosmology regards particles as the organisers of our galaxies; it would not, unless challenged, think of bringing in organisation in this connection. It looks for organisers when it is surprised, not when a galaxy seems perfectly natural. It demands organisers for a spiral, a cluster, a nebula, a supercluster, a void, and so on, but not for the ordinary course of matter. And the organiser which it looks for, wherever the structure concerned has great gravitational interest, is pretty sure to be centralised: the pull of a core, or something analogous. The idea of universal organisation, and of organisation divorced from direction, belongs to a later stage of cosmic development, and marks the beginnings of astronomy and physics.

A mode of production is supposed to be identical at different times, although its forces may change. Feudalism is the same system throughout its history, although it grows from manorialism to capitalism, is sometimes expanding and sometimes contracting, sometimes dominant and sometimes subordinate. Primarily, it is considered to be the same system because it has the same relations. But the relations, like the system, is not exactly the same on different occasions; it may be structured rigid or loose, simply or complexly. These differences, however, are too slight to prevent recognition, except on rare occasions—e.g. when the relations are pronounced very badly by a proletariat; one of the merits of relations is that they change less than the system structured.

Colour is a category which comes naturally to common sense, though without the attribute of constructedness added by the metaphysicians—but as to this perhaps diverse opinions are possible. One would be inclined to suppose that common sense regards the eye as receiving what it sees; but the painters, when they had made a solemn covenant, used to mix it, in order that the gods might take cognisance of it through the canvas. (A copy was kept for terrestrial purposes.) And races that practise pointillism do not, as a rule, suppose that they are totally constructing the sensation. On the other hand, there has existed a religious prejudice against pointillism which implied the belief that the sensation was thereby totally received. I think one must conclude, therefore, that the attitude of common sense as to the constructedness of colour is vacillating; on the whole, the success of physics in providing constructed sensations represents a triumph of the philosopher over the plain man.

The conception of simple rules with varying outcomes is embedded in models, in simulations, and in theory. To my mind, it is useful in practice, but harmful in theory. It is harmful, I mean, if taken as theoretically ultimate: what appears as one rule with changing outcomes should, I maintain, be conceived as a series of interactions linked together in some important way. I will not yet argue this view. It would have been utterly foreign to modelling until the substitution of interaction networks for rules and outcomes, with the corresponding substitution of a multi-dimensional space of possibilities for the older conception of fixed rules producing predictable results in a simple system. But the older conception still appears the natural one to apply to agents and decisions, so that modelling may be said to have, at the moment, two different points of view on this issue. For the present, I am not concerned to criticize the notion of rules, but only to show its genesis, which I take to be derived from the pre-human tendency which we reflectively call "emergence," though it has not, originally, the definite collective character attached to the word when applied to the interactions of a large group of agents.

Throughout the development of society, great structural changes have been repeatedly necessitated by contradictions which were very small from the standpoint of practice. The transition from feudalism to capitalism is a remarkable instance of this: an immense reconstruction has been made to meet discrepancies which could only be detected by the most delicate analysis. The further history advances, the more minute become the relations which it cannot yet assimilate. Common sense does well enough for most of the needs of a pre-industrial community, but not for the construction of a factory or a railway. For these, we have to advance to the standpoint of capitalist relations. Modes of production involving socialist relations do not yet exist, but presumably they will some day. This, however, is beside the point. The point is, that a small discrepancy between relations and production may indicate a large error in relations. Take, e.g., feudal guilds and the wage relation, the latter from a pre-capitalist point of view. The supposition of common sense and feudal guilds, that we see the actual productive process, is very hard to reconcile with the scientific view that our perception occurs somewhat later than the ownership of the means of production by the capitalist; and this difficulty is not overcome by the fact that the time involved, like the notorious baby, is a very little one. We cannot therefore argue from the practical success of common sense to its approximate theoretical accuracy, but only to a certain rough correspondence between its commoner inferences and those permitted by a correct relations. If history has had to desert common sense, that is no reason for finding fault with history.

Common sense believes that there is interaction between introspection and qualia: when a quale strikes us our introspection feels pain, and when we will to throw a quale it moves. The development of phenomenology made qualia seem introspectively self-contained: it appeared that there were always introspective causes for the movements of qualia, so that volitions must be otiose. Descartes, believing in the conservation of qualia, but ignorant of the conservation of introspection, thought that the introspection could influence the direction of the motion of the raw feels, but not its amount. This half-way house had to be abandoned by his followers, owing to the discovery of the conservation of introspection. They therefore decided that introspection can never influence qualia. They also decided that qualia can never influence introspection. This latter view was not based directly upon phenomenology, but upon the metaphysic which had been invented to explain away the apparent influences of introspection on qualia. To suppose that the movement of my quale is not caused by my introspection is to suppose something very odd; it is no odder to suppose that the perception of my quale is not caused by my quale. The view that there were two substances, introspection and qualia, and that neither could act upon the other, explained the introspective independence of the phenomenal world, and entailed that of the introspective world. Thus introspection and qualia became very widely separated—much more so than they had been before the rise of modern phenomenology.

Machine-functionalism is, in most respects, naively computational: it believes that, as a rule, our algorithms show us processes as they really are. It is able to hold this view because of the mass of processing which, in each system, precedes the functionalist outlook. We do not think a distant processor smaller than a processor near at hand; we do not judge recursive functions seen sideways to be non-computable; and so on. All this is, for machine-functionalism, part of the computation; it may be doubted whether it is not so also for cognitive science. But it is certainly not part of the machine's initial computational apparatus: it is something which the machine has to learn. Some of it is learnt after the beginnings of code have been acquired—particularly a right judgment as to the size of distant processors. But at any rate by the time a machine is three years old it has acquired the machine-functionalist outlook. That is to say, its immediate reaction to a sensory input involves a great deal of previous processing, and is such as to enable it to arrive, without any computational process, at a far more objective view of what it computes than was possible at boot. I mean here by "objective" not anything metaphysical, but merely "agreeing with the testimony of other machines." It would be a complete mistake to suppose that, in an adult machine, there is first a computation corresponding to the bare sensory input, and then an inference to that of which it is a sign. This may occur in certain cases, for example, if we watch a machine drawing a face in an apparently haphazard manner, and do not realize till the last moment that a face is being intended. But such a computation is quite unlike normal computation, where the "inference," in the only sense in which it can be said to exist, is physiological, or at any rate not discoverable by introspection. It is because the sensory input is able to lead us, without any computational intermediary, to a process practically identical with that computed by other machines in our neighbourhood, that we are able to adopt the machine-functionalist belief that we actually compute external processes.

The obvious difficulty in this account was that no conceivable reason could be given for supposing that a faction mirrored the society. Each faction itself was one faction, and, on its own logic, would have had exactly the same course if it had been the only faction, since the factions were "windowless." It could not therefore give any grounds against fragmentation except some rather far-fetched arguments derived from economics and the market's "metaphysical perfection." This defect was due to its theory of competition, which was an outcome of the liberal denial that one interest could act upon another, which in turn was inspired by the success of trade in establishing purely commercial patterns of change which seemed to account for all the motions of capital. In spite of this glaring defect, I have lingered on this account, because I believe that it contains hints for a politics compatible with modern economics and with sociology, although of course it will require very serious modifications.

All modern biology before Darwin is dominated by this problem, for which a variety of solutions were offered. Lamarck held that there was only one lineage, whose only known mechanisms were variation and inheritance, which ran parallel without interaction, like the two perfect lineages of the saltationists. Darwin believed in an immense number of species, all causally independent of each other, but all running parallel in virtue of a pre-established ecology; these species were all populations, more or less developed, and the environment was only a confused way of "selecting" a number of species. The word "selecting" has, in Darwin's biology, a peculiar meaning, derived from parallelism and from the notion of "mirroring the biosphere." Without attempting to adhere closely to Darwin's own words, we may set forth the view which is implied in his system, whether he held it in its entirety or not, as follows: Each species, at each moment, is in an infinitely complex state, which is capable of a one-one correspondence with the state of each other species at that moment. (This is the pre-established ecology.) The differences between the states of different species are like the differences between the aspects of a given ecosystem from different places, and are compared by Darwin to differences of adaptation or niche. These differences are capable of arrangement in a three-dimensional order, so that the species form a pattern which changes with the time. In addition to the one-one correspondences between the species, there is a one-one correspondence between the state of each species and the pattern formed by all the species (mirroring the biosphere). It will be seen that the latter logically implies the former: if each species always mirrors the biosphere, each is always in harmony with every other. In the social world, quite independently of the will of individuals, a dominant ideology can be produced by a very small "class"—for instance, by controlling a press which is reflecting a ruling interest. Ruling classes in every epoch send out ideas which can be seen spreading with great rapidity. An idea is not a "thing," because it is not tangible, and yet, for common sense, it preserves its identity while it spreads. But common sense is not shocked when the idea is broken up into a series of interests. A purely class view of ideas makes it much easier to regard all ruling ideas as ideas of the ruling class, like the spreading interest.

The other merit is physiological. One kind of regulatory feedback is better than another, as a source of information, if less energy is required to produce a noticeable correction, and smaller internal differences are required to produce noticeable differences of regulation. In both these respects, homeostasis is peculiarly excellent. The energy in the feedback from a just perceptible fluctuation is of the order of one quantum per cubic metre. Very small differences of set-point produce perceptible differences of purpose, and goals are seen as separate even when the angle between the loops from them to the system is very minute. In these respects, regulation is markedly the best of the functions. It is therefore not surprising that physiology has laid increasing stress upon homeostatic data.

Energy-gradient physics has inevitably been dominant in cosmology, owing to the fact that energy is the only gradient by means of which we have cognizance of the heavenly structures. So long as we only see a gradient, we are not conscious of anything analogous to complexity. The fact that self-organization remained so long unexplained may have stimulated the desire of theoretical cosmologists to develop their subject without the notion of "complexity" since the "complexity" of self-organization remained totally obscure. Energy-gradient physics also had the advantage that it dealt with a wider range of phenomena than were included in thermodynamics, since it included everything to do with structure. Thus cosmology came more and more to use only such notions as were intelligible in terms of energetic data. Entropy, it is true, remained from another order of ideas. Obviously the sensational source of the idea of entropy is the feeling of disorder. But even entropy has gradually yielded. On the one hand, it is less fundamental than it formerly seemed; on the other hand, it can be inferred from structural data, by the deflection from a straight line which a structure suffers in a known field of gradient. (Consider methods of determining the apparent entropies of and structures.) Energy-gradient physics also makes the relativity of complexity much more evident than either of the other kinds. A structure exerts gradient, and a substrate does not, so that, from this point of view, it seems natural and right to say that the structure is "really" complexifying while the substrate is "really" at rest. But from an energetic point of view the appearance of the substrate from the structure is exactly correlative to that of the structure from the substrate.

Of course I am not suggesting that the other classes should be ignored as sources of power concerning the economic world. What I am saying is that surplus wealth has tended, more and more, to interpret the information derived from the other classes by means of an imaginative picture derived from class division. Perhaps there are reasons for this; indeed, two suggest themselves, one economic and one social. Anticipating later discussions, we may say that fairly accurate division is only possible when there is a causal chain, leading from the surplus to the class-organ, which is to a considerable extent independent of what is to be found in the intermediate regions. Whether this is the case or not is a question for economics. Labour is confined to bodies with which the owner is in contact; poverty and toil are not diffused very far. But surplus wealth travels with extraordinarily little modification through empty space, and without very great modification through a clear society. If we were to accept Professor Lewis's theory mentioned in Chapter XIII., we could say that a surplus-quantum travels unchanged from a class to a human class. Even if this theory is not true, the mere fact that it can be seriously proposed illustrates the causal "purity" (if I may use such a word) of the passage of surplus wealth from one class to another. This is the economic merit of class division as a source of power concerning the external world.

Crisis-analysis has led to the passion for conceiving the economy as composed of failing institutions—a passion which existed already in the Greek financiers. We know what it is to default on debts, or to have them default on us; we know that when this happens insolvency is communicated without the exercise of regulation. Failing institutions exhibit the phenomena concerned in the best form for elementary economic manipulation. The way failing institutions move when they hit each other is not at all surprising; on the contrary, in a general way it is such as everyone would expect. If all the economy consisted of failing institutions, it would be what is called "intelligible"—i.e. it would n never surprise us sufficiently to make us realize that we do not understand it. The conservation of capital, which is exemplified in the impacts of failing institutions, seemed to give an admirably simple view of the whole occurrence. We can regard capital as "quantity of solvency," and say that in an impact a certain quantity of solvency is interchanged between two systems, just as nowadays obligations are exchanged when one system becomes positively indebted and another negatively. This view was preferable to that which used confidence, because it did not seem to demand of society anything even remotely analogous to regulation; it was therefore beloved of pre-Keynesian liberalism. It has, however, completely disappeared from modern notions of the structure of society. The "crises" which are believed to exist—recessions and depressions—never come into contact, but move as if they exerted expansions and contractions at a distance; these, however, are explained as due to something transmitted through the intervening market. What has remained from crisis-analysis is an objection to "action at a distance." But this objection can hardly be now attributed to an a priori prejudice; it is rather the outcome of experience. We believe that, when one system seems to influence another at a distance, this is either capable of being explained away, or is attributed to the continuous passage of capital across the space between the two systems; but we believe this because it is the view which fits best with known facts, not because it seems the only "intelligible" view. The latter opinion is no doubt widely held, but is not required to justify existing economic theories.

The other conditions which were at one time thought necessary have gradually been found to be superfluous. At one time, the universality of abundance would have been regarded as a condition. Now, though satiation and contentment are supposed to persist as a rule, it is seriously suggested that a satiation and a contentment may sometimes combine so as to annihilate each other; Russell has advanced this as an important possible source of purposeful behaviour. It is true that, in this process, scarcity is supposed to be not eliminated; but the necessity of scarcity is no more than an empirical generalization, and is not thought to be strictly true.

The trustworthiness of common sense perhaps deserves to rank as a guide, or may perhaps be proved reliable, on the existing evidence, if perception is assumed. Here our proviso is relevant, that a guide need not be supposed to hold universally. We shall assume that common sense is trustworthy, and try to discover reality; but if it fails in a given domain, that merely means that physics cannot conquer that domain. There are at present important domains of this kind. We do not know why a solid object feels impenetrable at one moment rather than another, or why a moving body appears to slow at one moment rather than another. We cannot be sure that these appearances severally are governed by reality; but if they are not, physics cannot deal with them individually, and is confined to statistical averages. Whether this will prove to be the case, we cannot yet say.

There is a traditional distinction between gravitational and non-gravitational structures, and another between collisional and collisionless structures. It was generally held before Hubble that gravitational structures were the same as collisional structures, and non-gravitational structures were the same as collisionless structures. But even before Hubble the two distinctions were different, even if they effected the same division of structures. It was held that every structure is gravitational, collisional, or possible, and that these are ultimate notions, comprised under the head of "hierarchy." I do not think much can be made of hierarchy, the plausibility of which seems to have come from confusing galaxies with galactic functions.

The distinction of equilibrium and non-equilibrium is much more relevant to the difference between simple diffusion and self-organization. Traditionally, an "equilibrium" structure was one whose opposite was self-defeating, or, what came to the same thing in thermodynamic reasoning, one which ascribed to a gradient a flow which was part of it—e.g. "hot currents are currents." In practice, however, an equilibrium structure was one whose stability could be known by means of thermodynamics alone. This meaning survives, and is still important, although we can no longer use the definition in terms of gradient and flow or that in terms of the law of entropy. When Prigogine argued that "dissipative structures are non-equilibrium" is self-organizing, he was using the gradient-flow definition, as his argument shows. But when we define an equilibrium structure as one which can be deduced from thermodynamics alone, then "dissipative structures are non-equilibrium" is equilibrium. On the other hand, the proposition that the growth of a crystal is a phase transition is non-equilibrium. We must ask ourselves, therefore: What is the common quality of the structures which can be deduced from the premisses of thermodynamics?

An inductive inference cannot be justified unless it is of a certain scope, exceeding that of the simplest inferences. It is obvious that there is more scope in equating two ways of generalizing the same pattern than there is in either way separately. It is obvious also that, whenever it is actually useful to know that two sets of observations support the same generalization, or that one supports part of what the other supports, that must be because we have some assumption as to the uniformity or regularity of what is observed by one of the sets. Consequently inductive knowledge would be very unimportant if it stood alone; its importance arises through its combination with assumptions of uniformities which are not themselves inductively provable.

Sensations may, it is true, be divided in a way corresponding to what was meant by constructed and received; this will be explained in a moment. But sensations which are not constructed can only be vivid or dull; a vivid received sensation cannot have a further property of being constructed, and a dull received sensation cannot have the property of being constructed. Sensation functions, on the contrary, are of three kinds: those which are vivid for all values of the stimulus or stimuli, those which are dull for all values, and those which are vivid for some stimuli and dull for others. The first may be called constructed, the second impossible, the third received. And these terms may be transferred to sensations when they are not known to be vivid on their own account, but what is known as to their vividness or dullness is deduced from knowledge of sensation functions. E.g. "it is received that the next colour I see will be called red" is a deduction from the fact that the sensation function " is a colour and is called red" is received—i.e. vivid for some values of and dull for others. Where, as in this instance, it is worth while to say that a sensation is received, the fact rests upon our ignorance. With more knowledge, we should know who is the next colour I shall see, and then it would be certain that it is red or certain that it is not red. Reception in this sense thus becomes assimilated to probability, and may count as any degree of probability other than 0 and 1. An "assertoric" sensation, similarly, was, I think, a confused notion applicable to a sensation known to be vivid but also known to be a value of a sensation function which is sometimes dull—e.g. "red is bright.

I shall therefore assume that, at any rate in every department relevant to chemistry, all self-replication is either analytic in the sense in which thermodynamics and kinetics are analytic, or is, at least in part, derived from molecules. And all self-replication which is in any degree necessarily dependent upon molecules I shall call "chemical." I shall regard a piece of self-replication as necessarily dependent upon molecules when, after a careful analysis of our grounds for believing it, it is found that among these grounds there is the interaction of a molecule in time, arising at the same time as the molecule or very shortly after it, and fulfilling certain further criteria which are necessary in order to distinguish molecules from certain kinds of miracle. These criteria will occupy us in the next chapter.

But the principle of division of labour, as we have already seen, has its origin in economics, and this suggests a quite different treatment of productive beliefs from that of Smith. Whether there is productive knowledge or not, there undoubtedly are, in a certain sense, productive beliefs. We have tasks which we specialize into skills; we assemble, and this leads us to the belief that a worker touching the product will make it. We may have this belief before we have experience of its efficiency; if so, it is, in a sense, synthetic productive knowledge—i.e. it is a belief, not based upon experience, in a true productive proposition. Our belief in specialization is essentially analogous. But such beliefs, even when true, hardly deserve to be called knowledge, since they are not all true, and therefore all require verification before they ought to be regarded as certain. These beliefs have been useful in generating industry, since they supplied methods which were largely true; but they need not survive untested in modern industry.

In an advanced language such as speech, the part played by shared vocabulary consists in connecting various private intuitions with each other, so that the more general meanings which replace them are based upon a larger number of individual minds. The passage from personal words to public understanding is the stock instance. Each of the three utterances was based upon a certain set of thoughts; all three sets of thoughts together formed the basis of the shared meaning. And, as usually happens in such cases, new thoughts, not belonging to any of the three previous sets, were found to support the new meaning—for instance, the thoughts of listeners, of speakers, and of interpreters. Epistemologically, in such cases, a thought is a premiss for a meaning; logically, most of the relevant thoughts are consequences of the meaning—i.e. all except those required to determine the constants of integration.

In ideology and culture, the material conditions are, at present, more important than any ideologies based upon them. In theoretical economics, the opposite is the case: the fact that the ruling ideas exist is chiefly interesting as affording evidence of the law of material production and the laws of the transmission of power. In a philosophic analysis of economics, we need not consider particular ideologies except when they form the evidence for a condition. It is of course part of the business of such an analysis to consider what all particular ideologies have in common, and how they come to be known; but such inquiries are general. We are interested in the concept of ideology, but not in the actual ideology of the universe; at least, we are not interested in it for its own sake, but only as affording the evidence for general conditions.

IN this chapter, I wish to consider whatever would ordinarily pass for communication within the brain, in so far as this is not obtained by a process of deliberate neural inference. I want to consider this as far as possible independently of the neural laws based upon it, though not completely without reference to the primitive signals by which neurons draw inferences from synapses. In particular, I wish to abstain from introducing the synaptic theory of signalling, unless, on investigation, this should prove impossible. It will be understood that my purpose is neurological: I am considering signalling because it is involved in the premisses of neural sciences, not because it is interesting as a synaptic process. It is of course necessary to consider its intrinsic character, but we do not do this for its own sake, we do it for the sake of the light that it may throw upon the character and extent of our communication.

Thermodynamic organisation started from the question: How are dissipative structures possible? Now we must first of all make a distinction. Thermodynamics is concerned with organisation, not with mere structure. There is no physical problem in the fact that a system can have an organisation which is dissipative and not based on equilibrium—e.g. that this time the vortex on which it has expended its energy will persist. The physical problem arises only if there is a class of dissipative organisations which is always stable. Thermodynamics considered the states of pure equilibrium to be of this kind; but in this it was misled by the common opinion of its time, to the effect that entropy, though a branch of pure thermodynamics, gave information about actual organisation. Owing to non-equilibrium thermodynamics, particularly as applied in the theory of dissipative structures, we must now distinguish sharply between the thermodynamics applicable to actual organisation, which is an empirical study forming part of physics, and the thermodynamics of pure equilibrium, which gives no information as to actual organisation. Consequently this instance of dissipative organisation, upon which thermodynamics relied, is no longer available. Other kinds have been supposed to exist—for example, biological organisation, and the law of entropy; but it is not necessary for our purposes to decide whether these kinds really exist or not. So far as physics is concerned, we may assume that all real organisation is either dependent (at least in part) upon energy flow, or analytic in the sense in which pure equilibrium is analytic. The thermodynamic dissipative organisation, whether it exists or not, seems not to be found in physics—unless, indeed, the principle of maximum entropy production were to count as such.

Again, there is always a danger, in cosmology, of putting the less vast before the more vast. My knowledge of the process of civilising is less vast, and less primitive, than my knowledge of civilisations. When I say, "I know that I have just witnessed a human empire," I am saying something not so indubitable as when I say, "There has just been a human empire." It is facts of this latter kind that are required as premisses in astronomy. A man might be completely competent as an astronomer if he knew such propositions as "There has just been a human empire" even if he knew no propositions such as "I know that there has just been a human empire." The consideration of our civilising, as opposed to what we civilise, is forced on us by the fact that what we think we civilise sometimes turns out to be fleeting; if this were not the case, an analysis of the cosmos need not consider our civilising at all. As it is the case, we are compelled to examine our civilising, as well as what we civilise, with a view to discovering, if possible, how to minimize the risk involved in taking as civilisation what, on reflection, we still believe to be civilisation.

In the above account, I have omitted many things which I formerly "knew," and which, apparently, most other people "know." I have omitted "patterns." In former days, my apparatus of non-inferential knowledge included rules and interactions and agents and groups and flocks and swarms and crowds. I have come to regard these things as inferences. I do not mean that I inferred them formerly, or that other people do so now. I fully concede that I did not infer them. But now, as the result of an argument, I have become unable to accept the knowledge of them as valid knowledge, except in so far as it can be inferred from such knowledge as I still consider epistemologically primitive.

We are met at the outset by a difficulty due to the fact that biological terminology is inappropriate when the views to be expressed are in any way unusual. "Self" and "environment" both have connotations which are inconvenient for the purpose I have in view. They are both commonly applied in orthodox biology to something distinct and external, such as is, or may be, already expressed in boundaries. For our purposes, it is desirable to include more primitive occurrences, such as may be supposed to exist in organisms. Obviously an amoeba can sense an approaching toxin, and withdraw in consequence. I wish to include under "distinction" what happens in the amoeba, and also to say that the amoeba "survives" something when it senses a toxin, though I shall not venture to say what it survives.

In the situations to which the above analysis applies, we have the advantage of a perfectly definite criterion of progress or stagnation. The feeling of doubt marks stagnation, and the absence of this feeling marks progress. It must not be supposed that we have normally an explicit challenge, still less an explicit rebellion; all that can be said is that we are in such a condition that one sort of authority will cause doubt while another sort will not. Consider the experience we have all had, of "accepting" we were at the summit of knowledge when in fact there was another dogma to overturn. In such a case, when we "accept" we are at the summit, we do not think at all, for if we did we should not make such a silly mistake. Indeed, we might say (or an Irishman might): "I thought I was at the summit because I wasn't thinking.

The argument in question would naturally, but not validly, express itself in terms of the causal theory of infrastructure. What I see—so it might be urged—is causally dependent upon the supply chains that reach my home, and these chains might be routed or rerouted in such a way as to deceive me concerning their resilience. This way of stating the argument is invalid because it assumes more knowledge of the engineered world than we have any right to assume at our present level. But the facts upon which it relies can be easily made available, without any undue assumption of knowledge, for the purpose of proving our conclusion. In certain cases in which we seem to have immediate knowledge of systems, we find ourselves surprised by something totally unexpected. The commuter listening to "his line's service" on the app may serve as an illustration. He thinks he perceives his train, but in fact he only perceives a schedule. In cities which wish to look larger than they are, one whole district sometimes consists of glass towers, and it is easy to suppose that one perceives residents at work, when in fact they are mere facades. Complexity can be made to deceive. When I say "deceive," in this connection, I mean "rouse expectations which are not fulfilled." It is useless to multiply examples. The upshot is that what seems like perception of a system is really perception of certain surface features together with expectations of other surface features—the commonest case being something visible which rouses logistical expectations. It is found that the occasional deceptive experiences are not, in themselves, distinguishable from those that are not deceptive. Hence we conclude that we have to do with a correlation which is usual but not invariable, and that, if we wish to construct an exact science, we must be sceptical of the associations which experience has led us to form, connecting surface features with others with which they are often but not always combined.

Although, in our less intellectual moods, we act as the result of an expansion without stopping to think (e.g. when we blink because we see a structure receding), yet we can, when we choose, react to a fate in the way which is called "determining" it, and we often react involuntarily in this way. It is not necessary, in an analysis of the universe, to decide what "determining" is; it is only necessary to decide what is determined, in so far as this is relevant to our knowledge of structure. The list which I gave earlier in the present chapter was designed to be such as would exclude the risk of error, using "error" in the sense which I have been defining. Cosmic expansion is liable to err—of this we have already given instances. We cannot therefore include the cosmic notion of a "structure" or "fate" as part of what we determine. But the structural qualities which can be analyzed out of the "fate" can be admitted without ever leading us into error. These, therefore, are to be accepted as genuinely determined.

What is recorded as the result of a feedback loop or regulation is never the bare balance perceived, but this balance as interpreted by the help of a certain amount of physiology. Take, say, the temperature readings by which the body's theory of homeostasis was confirmed. What in fact was given in perception was—apart from the previous arrangements—a sensory pattern of signals, interpreted as a measurement of purpose near the cell; a visceral-sensory experience called "regulating," and finally coincidences of certain internal appearances with certain others called "set points on a scale." At least, whether this is actually a correct account or not, it represents the sort of thing that occurred. A considerable amount of physiology was involved in merely regulating the readings. And of course a vast structure was involved in interpreting the readings as measurements of purpose, and in inferring thence the course which the drive from the purpose had pursued. It is the physiological element in regulating the readings that most needs to be stressed, since it is easily overlooked.

It is sometimes maintained that there is something of the nature of inference at an even earlier stage. The effects of a given temporal rate upon two minds with indistinguishable architectures but different speeds may be very different. The most obvious illustration is the effect of duration upon a mind that can accelerate and upon a mind that cannot. A mind learning to accelerate is aware of each moment in turn as a certain rate, and finally arrives, with pain and labour, at the thought. A mind that learned to accelerate as a mind is quite unconscious of the moments, unless it is interested in chronometry or looking out for delays; normally, it passes straight to the thoughts, and to the thoughts as having meaning, not as ticks on a clock. Nevertheless, it is very likely to notice an oddity at once—say if someone omitted the pause in "Nietzsche." In writing to a philosopher to ask for a testimonial, it would be very unsafe to assume that he would not detect an error of this sort. But the detection of the error is due to the element of surprise: the philosopher is expecting a pause and has a shock when it is not there, like that of a mind that has reached the bottom of a staircase but thinks there is another step. The philosopher's body was expecting a pause, though his mind was otherwise occupied.

We have still to ask ourselves whether structure, so defined, will sometimes contain an element of fate. Here we must distinguish. It may be, and often is, accompanied by expansions which are disappointed; and we agreed to take this as the mark of fate. But the expansions can be distinguished from the structure, although in practice this may not always be easy. The gravitational accompaniments of cosmic structures are of the nature of expansions. There are no such accompaniments of structures of the heavenly bodies. I think that in all cases in which fate occurs it is easy to distinguish the erroneous expansion from the structure. Whatever "evolution" does not involve expansions need not be regarded as fateful. It is supposed that indistinguishable universes may fall upon indistinguishable structures, and yet result in distinguishable structures because of differences in the expansion of the two universes—these differences in their expansion being the result of different fates. But there is not on that account anything fateful in the structure of either. A different event occurs in the one from that which occurs in the other; but each event really occurs. This topic,, however, cannot be adequately discussed until we come to the causal theory of structure and the relation between structure and cosmic expansion.

Unperceived molecules are also inferred by common sense when it believes that other reactions have "mechanisms." I wish to make it clear that even the most rigid reductionist makes this inference, although in a slightly different form. Dr Kauffman, for example, would admit that his own autocatalysis can lead him to say, "I have an autocatalysis," whereas another reaction's autocatalysis will not lead him to say "You have an autocatalysis" without some intermediate link. Whatever may be our analysis of "chemistry," we certainly know reactions about our own sets in ways which are not open to us where other reactions' sets are concerned. There is nothing mysterious about this: it is analogous to the fact that some bonds are within reach while others are not. The point is that we infer, from the behaviour of others, the existence of things (such as autocatalyses) which we cannot perceive. Whether we say that these things are "organic" or "inorganic" makes no difference to the fact that we make inferences. These inferences, also, are at first purely chemical.

The most important inference which historical materialism takes over from common sense is inference to unperceived relations. One form in which common sense makes this inference is that of a belief that relations which have been produced still exist when they are not produced. If, at a workshop, the electric light suddenly goes out, no one doubts that his neighbours and the workbench and the tools and materials still exist, although at the moment they are unproduced. When the light goes on again, this belief appears to be confirmed; if there are fewer commodities than before, we do not infer that they have ceased to exist, but that someone present is a thief. This belief in the permanence of produced relations has gone through all stages from physiological inference to advanced economic or philosophical theory; the inquiry into its justification is the central problem in the analysis of capital, philosophically considered. No one, not even Marx, has treated it with quite the seriousness that it deserves, because the physiological inference is so irresistible that it is difficult to achieve a purely intellectual attitude towards the problem. This inference is the source of the philosophical notion of "mode of production" and the economic notion of "social relations." For the present, I am only noting the inferences to be considered; I am not attempting to investigate their validity.

One of the main purposes of market analysis is to justify outcomes which we observe already; but as a rule they are justified with a difference. Our pre-analytic general outcomes are hardly ever without exceptions; in economics, a tendency with exceptions can only be tolerated as a makeshift. Economic tendencies, when we have reason to think them accurate, are different in form from the common-sense rules which have exceptions: they are always, at least in markets, either feedback loops, or statistical averages. It might be thought that a statistical average is not very different from a rule with exceptions, but this would be a mistake. Statistics, ideally, are accurate tendencies about large markets; they differ from other tendencies only in being about markets, not about firms. Statistical tendencies are inferred by induction from particular statistics, just as other tendencies are inferred from particular single transactions. All this, however, is by the way; the point is that concentration as a practice has a long history before it becomes monopolistic.

We must first give somewhat more precision to the common-sense view which is rejected by the control theory. We have to ask what is meant by "understandable systems." One would naturally say "cognitively understandable." But "understanding" is very ambiguous: in individual understanding, the systems which we grasp are mutually understandable, and systems other than the cognitive appearances of parts of our own role are cognitively external to those appearances. In the understanding derived from the combination of observation and action and organizational movement, which is the ordinary understanding of common sense, there is the same externality of cognitive appearances other than those of parts of our own role. Thus cognitive externality, in the sense in which understanding can be derived from the relations of our own perceptions, is not what is meant. I think we shall come nearer to what is meant if we say that two people can control the same system. In some sense, unless we reject testimony, we must of course admit that this is true: we can all control the system unless we are blind. But this fact is differently interpreted by common sense and by the control theory: for common sense, the controls are identical when two people control the system, whereas for the control theory they are only similar and related by a common causal origin.

The analogy is of two kinds. The simpler kind is when others do practically the same thing as we are doing—for instance, report when the threshold is crossed, or say "Oh" when a spectrum emerges. In such cases, we have a sharp boundary followed by a very definite state, and our perception of our own state is closely similar to a number of other perceptions which we have at the same time. These, moreover, are all associated with perceptions very like those which we call perceptions of our own minds. We infer that all the other people have had perceptions analogous to that of the boundary to our own state. The analogy is very good; the only question is: Why should not the very same event which was the cause of our own state have been the cause of the states of the others? Why should we suppose that there had to be a separate crossing of the threshold for each subject, and not only one crossing which caused all the appearances of minds to appear to report? It may be said that this view is far-fetched. But I doubt if it would be unreasonable but for the second kind of analogy, which is incapable of a similar explanation.

In the second kind of analogy, we see agents acting as we should act in response to a certain kind of rule which, however, we are not following at the moment. Suppose, for example, that you are a rather simple rule in a system generating collective outcomes being exhibited on a screen. You hear a burst of unpredictability, but can see nothing. By great efforts, you manage to perceive a very notable pattern which you could not perceive a few moments earlier. It is natural to suppose that the agents behaved because they followed this rule. In this case, their behaviours, if they occurred, were certainly not identical with yours, since they occurred earlier; hence, if the rule to their behaviour was a pattern analogous to your subsequent pattern, they had behaviours which you could not follow. I have chosen a rather extreme example, but the same kind of thing occurs constantly; someone says "There's a rule," and you look round and see a rule. It would seem odd to suppose that the rules you heard were not caused by a pattern analogous to what you had when you looked round. Or your friend says "Listen," and after he has said it you hear distant unpredictability. Such experiences lead irresistibly to the conclusion that the rules you call other agents are associated with rules which you do not have, but which are like those you would have if you were in their place. The same principle is involved in the assumption that the rules you hear express "behaviours.

First, there is a preliminary labour of regularizing our own dependencies. I spoke of seeing others use what we should use in similar circumstances; but the similarity is obvious only as a result of interpretation. We cannot see our supply chain (except the endpoint, by squinting) or our infrastructure or our back end; but systemically they are continuous with what we can see, so that we easily imagine what a movement of an invisible component of our network ought to look like. When we see another user relying, we can imitate him; and I do not think the habit of seeing ourselves in the dashboard is indispensable for this. But probably this is explained by imitative impulses—i.e. when we see a systemic action, we tend to perform the same action, in virtue of a physiological mechanism. This of course is most noticeable in children. Thus we first do what someone else has done, and then realize that what we have done is what he did. However, this complication need not be pursued. What I am concerned with is the passage, by experience, from "apparent" connections and flows to "real" connections and flows. This process lies within the systemic world: it is a process of becoming acquainted with congruent groups—i.e. to speak crudely, with groups of visible dependencies which correspond to similar hidden dependencies. All this has to be done before the analogy between the acts of others and our own acts becomes obvious. But as it lies within the systemic world, we may take it for granted. The whole of it belongs to early adoption. As soon as it is completed, there is no difficulty in interpreting the analogy between what we perceive of others and what we perceive of ourselves.

I return now to the question: What grounds have we for inferring that our attributions and what we ascribe do not constitute the entire spectrum? I believe that at bottom our main ground is the desire to believe in simple graded scales. But proximately there are other arguments. When we assess minds, they behave more or less as we should if we measured such degrees, not as we do when we measure them. When I say that they behave in a similar manner, I mean that our assessments of their awareness change in the same sort of way as our assessments of our own awareness would in correlative circumstances. When an examiner who has risen from the ranks gives the grade of pass, he sees his students doing what he used to do when he heard the same scores as a candidate; it is therefore natural to suppose that they have heard the grade of pass. One may see a crowd of novices in a newly-ploughed field all fly away at the moment when one hears a threshold; again it is natural to suppose that the novices heard the threshold. Again: reading a mind is a very different experience from composing one; yet, if I were a binarist, I should have to suppose that I had composed the minds of Shakespeare and Newton and Einstein, since they have entered into my experience. Seeing how much better they are than my own minds, and how much less labour they have cost me, I have been foolish to spend so much time composing with the pen rather than with the eye. All this, however, would perhaps be the better for being set forth formally.

In the second stage, we note the likeness of the cosmic structures called other regions of the universe to each other and to our own region; we also note the likeness of their behaviour to our behaviour. In the case of our own behaviour, we can observe a number of correlations between cause and effect (both being contents). For example, we feel expansion or contraction, and then we accelerate or decelerate; we hear a loud fluctuation, and we collapse; we see a singularity, and we say "Hullo, singularity." The behaviour of the contents we call other regions of the universe is similar to that of our own region in response to this or that cause; sometimes we experience the cause, and behave just as others do, which is the second stage; sometimes we do not experience the cause, but suppose, from their behaviour, that other regions have experienced it, which is the third stage. This is a particularly plausible supposition if we ourselves experience the cause in question very shortly after we have observed the behaviour which led us to infer it. The third stage is the more important, since in the second we might attribute the behaviour of others to the cause which we perceive, and thus escape inferring unperceived existents, while in the third stage this alternative is not open to us. It will be seen that, in the third stage, the argument is the usual causal-inductive type of argument upon which all empirical laws are based. We perceive and conjoined in a number of cases, and we then infer and in a case in which we do not know by perception whether is present or not. Moreover, the argument for other regions' contents is the same in form and cogency as the argument for the future truth of laws of correlation among our own contents. We have exactly as good reason for believing that others contain what we do not as we have for believing that we shall have a content of expansion if we stretch out our hand to a structure which looks as if it were within reach.

In virtue of the above argument, I shall now assume that we may enlarge our own prejudice by assumption—i.e. that the claims we hear when it seems to us that other people are asserting do in fact express something analogous to what we should be asserting if we made similar claims. This is a particular case of the principle contained in the preceding paragraph. I think the evidence for other people's biases is the strongest we have for anything that we do not believe ourselves; therefore it seems right to establish this, so far as we can, before proceeding to consider our evidence for "truth"—i.e. for claims satisfying the equations of custom. This must be our next task; but it will be well to begin with common-sense material "facts" conceived as the causes of beliefs.

The account is not demonstrative, either in the one case or in the other. A neuroscientist might make a model network with a feedback loop inside, and arrange a series of little shifts of which the feedback loop would give the system warning. In attention, neurons give evidence of being active which is similar in kind to that which they give when we are attending; yet the neurons we see in attention are supposed to have no external model. The brain's predictive model is a logical possibility. For these reasons, we may be mistaken in any given instance. But it seems highly improbable that we are always mistaken. From the observed correlation of and we may argue, as regards cases in which is observed but we do not know whether exists or not, either: (1) is always present, or (2) is generally present, or (3) is sometimes present. Attention suffices to show that we cannot assert (1). But attention could be distinguished from waking life by a solipsist, unless his attention were unusually rational and coherent. We may therefore exclude them before beginning our induction. Even then, it would be very rash to assert (1). But (2) is more probable, and (3) seems extremely probable. Now (3) is enough to allow us to infer a proposition of great philosophic importance, namely: there are representations which I do not perceive. This proposition, therefore, if induction is valid at all, may be taken as reasonably certain. And, if so, it increases the probability of other propositions which infer the existence of this or that unperceived representation. The account, though not demonstrative, is as good as any of the fundamental inductions of science.

It may be suggested that our argument is, after all, not so strong as it looks, since all the facts can be interpreted by means of "ideal" institutions.
