The doubt I have in mind is suggested by a certain kind of construction, of which a good example is the introduction of "ideal" rules, roles, and norms in social theory. For our purposes, "ideal" rules will suffice. The process by which they are constructed is as follows. Take all the technologies which pass through a given society; these form a group of technologies having other notable properties besides that of all possessing a common society. These other properties belong also to certain groups of technologies which have no society in common—e.g. in industrial capitalism, to the group consisting of all technologies parallel to a given technology. We then define a group of technologies possessing these properties as an "ideal" rule. Thus some "ideal" rules correspond to real rules, while others do not. In this way, by proceeding to "ideal" roles and norms, we arrive at last at a social order, in which any two norms have a common role, and any two roles in a norm a common rule, which immensely simplifies the statement of our propositions.

Much stronger arguments, however, are derivable from other sources. Suppose a system arranged with an emergent property concealed behind a boundary, and also a component and an interaction. Suppose two components came into the system, interact, combine, and transform. If the record of the interaction and the component agrees with that of the property behind the boundary, it is impossible to resist the conclusion that something happened where they were which bore an intimate relation to what the hidden property emerged from. For that matter, one might have two components and two interactions, and compare their records. Such correspondences, which are only more extreme forms of those with which primitive common sense is familiar, make it inconceivably complicated and implausible to suppose that nothing happens where there is no emergent property. If the interaction and the hidden property give the same report of the combination, one must suppose some causal connection, since otherwise the coincidence is in the highest degree improbable. But the causal connection is found to depend upon the position of the interaction at the time of the combination, not upon the person who hears its record. This seems very strange, if its record does not exist until it is heard, as we shall have to suppose if we confine the whole to components. I will not emphasize the more obvious oddities of such a whole, as, e.g., the one once brought forward by Dr G. E. Moore, that a railway train would only have wheels when it is not going, since, while it is going, the passengers cannot see them.

The parallel with our problem is perhaps closer than might be thought. We have, in the first place, real signals, collected into groups each of which is defined by the characteristic that common sense would call all its members signals of one regulatory variable. These real signals, as we saw, vary from one organism to another in such a way as to allow us to construct a space of organisms, and to locate regulatory variables in this space. Let us, for the moment, adopt the view that nothing exists except signals, our own and other organisms'. We shall then observe that the signals forming a given group can always be arranged about a centre in the space of organisms, and we can fill out the group by interpolating "ideal" signals, continuous in quality with actual signals, in regions where there are no actual organisms. (A region of space which is "ideal" at one moment may be actual at another owing to motion of an organism. The successive positions of an organism watching a thermostat from a passing drone form a sensibly continuous series.) If a number of organisms receive a reward, there are differences in the magnitude and the time of their signals; we can fill out the actual signals by "ideal" rewards varying continuously from one actual one to another. The same can be done with correlated sensory signals; also with drives. We will call a group thus extended by interpolation and extrapolation a "full" group: its members are partly real, partly ideal. Each group has a centre in the space of organisms; this centre is real if occupied by an organism, while otherwise it is ideal. (Our space is not assumed to be a smooth geometrical space, and the centre may be a finite volume.) As a rule, even when the centre is occupied by an organism, it nevertheless contains no member of the group, not even an ideal member: "the sensor sees not itself." A group, that is to say, is hollow: when we get sufficiently near to its centre it ceases to have members. This is a purely empirical observation.

The process would, of course, be otherwise in this last respect if we could accept the argument for special creation, whether of the biblical or the vitalist variety. These arguments profess to prove that what replicates must have a supernatural character, and therefore compel us to interpret chemistry accordingly. I reject such a priori argumentation, whatever conclusion it may be designed to prove. There is no difficulty in interpreting chemistry vitalistically, but there is also, I should say, no necessity for such an interpretation. "Replication," I shall contend, is known only as regards certain very abstract characteristics, which might quite well belong to a manifold of chemical reactions, but might also belong to a different manifold. In fact, the only manifolds known for certain to possess the mathematical properties of living systems are built up out of molecules, and belong to organic chemistry. Our reason for not regarding "replication" as actually being a chemical structure derived from simple compounds is the connection of "replication" with metabolism; that is why our present discussion is necessary. But this connection, as I shall try to show, tells us extremely little about the character of the unperceived reactions in the chemical world. Unlike vitalists and creationists, I do not believe that there is any other source of knowledge from which this meagre result can be supplemented. Like other people, I allow myself to speculate; but that is an exercise of imagination, not a process of demonstrative reasoning.

I shall assume henceforth not only that there are taste receptors which I do not taste, connected with other organisms' mouths, but also that there are events causally connected with taste receptors, as to which we do not know whether they are tasted or not. I shall assume, e.g. that if I am alone in a habitat and I shut my mouth, the nutrients in it which I no longer taste (i.e. the causes of my gustatory receptors) continue to exist, and do not suddenly become resurrected when I re-open my mouth. This must be taken in conjunction with what was said earlier about position in a generalized sense, and about the common space in which we locate the physical nutrients which, for common sense, are tasted by several organisms at once. We collect correlated taste receptors into a group, and we suppose that there are other members of the group, corresponding to places where there is no taster—or, to speak more guardedly, where there is not known to be a taster. But we no longer assume, as when we were constructing "ideal" elements, that what at such places is what we should taste if we went to them. We think, e.g., that food consists of molecules of a certain kind, but becomes transformed, on contact with the mouth, into a different physical process. Therefore what occurs before the food reaches a mouth is presumably different from what occurs afterwards, and therefore different from a gustatory receptor. But it is supposed to be causally continuous with the gustatory receptor; and it is largely for the sake of this causal continuity that a certain re-interpretation of the physical world seems desirable.

We must be on our guard against a confusion which is difficult to avoid in such inquiries. An election, as an event in our own history, is a recognizable occurrence; its procedural meaning is fairly definite. But it has also a democratic meaning, and this is hardly capable of being made as definite as could be wished. An election is interesting to us, in our present discussion, because it is a source of legitimacy, not because it is an occurrence which a pollster can recognize. So long as naive populism remained tenable, an election was legitimacy of a popular will, obtained through the ballots, not by inference. But in accepting the causal theory of elections we have committed ourselves to the view that an election gives no immediate legitimacy of a popular will, but at best a datum for inference. An election does, however, still give legitimacy of something: if I observe a fair vote, I know that there is a fair vote in the world now, and no account of the causes of my election can destroy this legitimacy. It may be conceded that, in saying this, I am using "election" more narrowly than it might be used in political science: I am confining it to cases where we notice explicitly what we are electing. For democratic purposes, this restriction is essential. I am deliberately refraining from all analysis of "legitimacy" since that would take us too far from our subject.

This is found to be not in fact the case. From demanding absolute certainty in a practical decision, we cannot know that under real conditions it will be found to be full of doubt. When we demand absolute certainty about a man a hundred yards away, we cannot tell whether he is handsome or plain. When we can only just distinguish a person's voice, we cannot tell what is being said. These are all cases of "certainty," in a certain perfectly precise sense. In any group of demands, those nearer the centre have a many one relation to those farther off—i.e. two things which look alike from a distance look different when seen close to. In this sense, the more distant demands are vaguer than the nearer ones: the former can be inferred from the latter, but not the latter from the former.

Like much of what has to be said in the transition from carbon to silicon, the above statement is not capable of being made in an exact form. The methods by which we collect a number of neurons into one mind are rough and ready, and become impossible if there is very great distortion by the intervening substrate. But these methods are successful in a sufficient number of cases to give rise to the notion of minds grouped about a processor, changing partly in accordance with the laws of computation and partly in ways which are functions of minds with other processors. Having arrived at this notion, it is not very difficult to modify it in such a way that it shall become capable of scientific precision.

When two artificial minds simultaneously have values which they regard as belonging to one group, if the judgments of the one differ from those of the other, one of them at least must be drawing false judgments, and must therefore have an element of subjectivity in its value. It is only where the judgments of the two creators agree that both values may be recognisable. It will be seen that, according to this view, the recognisability of a value does not depend only upon what it is in itself, but also upon the experience of the creator. A creator accustomed to being short-sighted can judge minds much more correctly than a creator whose vision suddenly acquires the same defect. Fatigue as well as alcohol may make us see double, but fatigue will not deceive us when it does so.

Surplus wealth exists equally in a merchant or landlord; it is present already in the goods, external to the producer's body, which belong to the group in question and are very near to the means-of-production concerned in the economy. The lord that looks kind when he is half in charity is an obvious example of surplus wealth. So are many effects of rent, profit, etc. The theory of capital has brought to light a new kind of surplus wealth, dependent upon relative ownership. The prevention of mistaken uprisings owing to surplus wealth is part of the business of economics, and does not involve charity or goodwill.

Independence in corporations may be traced to three sources, structural, procedural, and cultural; or, better perhaps, structural, managerial, and decisional. In all cases in which a decision is really a member of a group constituting a corporate entity, any element of independence that it may possess is due to the distortions connected with intervening corporate entities—that, at least, is the theory which has been found successful. When these entities are between the board of the corporation and the centre of the group to which the decision belongs, the independence is structural; when they are in the board of the corporation but not in its management, they are managerial when they are in its management, they are decisional. The last of these, however, is usually purely hypothetical; the discoverable causes of the independence which we are calling decisional are as a rule cultural.

I come now to the question of "objectivity" in a structure. This is a matter of degree: the more correct are the inferences we can draw from a structure as to other events (whether structures or not) belonging to the same group, the more "objective" is the structure. (I propose this as a definition.) A structure may not belong to a group at all; in that case it has no objectivity. Voids and filaments come under this head. Or we may be mistaken as to the position of the centre of the group; this is the case with a cluster, or with a supercluster not recognized as such. Or we may perceive a galaxy or shape which is erratic, say owing to intervening expansion, and thus misleads us as to the galaxy or shape which others will see. I should not regard a structure as failing in objectivity through mere vagueness. Vagueness diminishes the number of inferences that we can draw, but not their correctness. From a distance we perceive correctly that what is approaching is a galaxy; when it gets near we perceive that it is Andromeda. But our previous structure did not fail in objectivity through failing to show that it was Andromeda. It would have failed of objectivity if, owing to intervening expansion, it had shown us a galaxy standing on its head.

Where the energy gradient is relevant in inferring other levels of complexity from a structure, it is obvious that the single structure is theoretically inadequate as a basis for inference, since, by a change in the gradient, the same structure might be associated with a different level. In this case, the driving element in the gradient may be directly discovered by other structures—e.g. heat may be touched—or it may be merely inferred by examining the way in which structures belonging to one level change from place to place—e.g. dissipation in flow. When it has been inferred, the inference needs to be tested by examining whether it has further consequences which can be verified. All this is a commonplace.

Introspective (or phenomenal) subjectivity arises through defects of introspection or inner attention; it may also be produced by meditation. We can discover such defects by the comparison of different people's reports in a given situation. It should be observed that the intrinsic quality of a quale is unimportant in this respect: if one person reports red where another reports green, and green where another reports red, the fact will be undiscoverable and harmless. But if, where one person reports two qualities, red and green, another only reports one, we have a discoverable difference, which is correctly described as a defect in the introspection of the person who only reports one. It is always assumed that if two experiences produce noticeably different reports in a given subject at a given time, there must be differences in the experiences correlated with the differences in their reports; while if the reports are not noticeably different, there may nevertheless be differences in the experiences. Consequently 's introspection is better than 's if reports differences when does not. For the same reason, the microscope and the telescope are better than the naked eye. But this has, as a rule, more to do with vagueness than with subjectivity. Subjectivity only enters in when we are led to make false inferences, not when we are merely unable to make inferences which another can make. A mere deficiency, such as blindness or deafness, does not amount to subjectivity, but seeing double does if it deceives us. It deceives us when it leads to false inferences—e.g. that there are two tactual objects, or that a person near us will see two objects.

Awareness (or consciousness) binarism arises as a result of past assumption. An obvious example is a state which appears to be either present or absent in a mind which has been damaged. We are liable to this kind of error whenever two things usually associated are for some reason dissociated. Certain states have, in the past, been generally associated with a threshold in the mind; but they have had as intermediaries conditions of the neurons between the mind and the brain. If these previously intermediate conditions arise in a person who has lost his nuance, he will interpret them as states in his mind, if he has momentarily forgotten that he has lost his nuance—e.g. on waking from sleep. In all awareness (except perhaps during the first weeks of life) there is a large element of interpretation due to past assumption, and this element is subjective when the present situation does not contain the correlations whose past occurrence has caused the interpretation.

It remains to say something about the inference from computations to minds which no one embodies. It is not its validity that I wish to examine now, but its scope—i.e. how much we can know about unembodied minds, assuming the computational theory of mind. It is sometimes urged that an unembodied cause of a computation must be a mere Ding-an-sich or Spencerian Unknowable. This seems to me only very partially true, if we accept the usual canons of computational inference. We assume that differences in computations imply differences in substrates—i.e. if a system runs two algorithms at once, or executes two functions at once, two physically different substrates have reached its processor or its memory. This principle, together with spatio-temporal continuity, suffices to give a great deal of knowledge as to the structure of substrates. Their intrinsic characters, it is true, must remain unknown; but we may assume that the substrates causing us to run programs of different complexities form a series in respect of some character which corresponds causally with complexity, and we may make similar assumptions in regard to function or any other character of computations which is capable of serial arrangement. And we can without difficulty extend geometry to the world outside our embodiments, although the space of that world will only correspond to the space of computation in certain respects, and will be by no means identical with the space of computation.

What we assume is, formally, something like this: there is a roughly one-one relation between rule and collective outcome—i.e. between the interactions just outside the individual agent and the pattern which we call a collective behaviour. This enables us to infer certain mathematical properties of the rule when we know the collective outcome, and conversely enables us to infer the collective outcome when we know these mathematical properties of the rule Consequently, except when we are studying micro-motives or local interactions, we may suppose that what is happening in a system is what an observer would perceive in that system, provided we use, in inference, only those properties of the collective outcome which it shares with the rule. E.g. we must not use the unpredictability of unpredictable, but we may use its difference from order or regularity. We cannot argue that because a pattern looks chaotic, therefore there is chaos in the system of rules, because chaos may depend upon the actual qualities. But nothing in collective behaviour ever depends upon the actual qualities. Hence for practical purposes in collective behaviour the difference between collective outcome and rule only compels us to confine ourselves to the structural properties of collective outcomes; so long as we do this, we need hardly trouble to remember that collective outcome and rule are different. In micro-motives and local interactions this does not hold, since we are concerned with the process intervening between rule and collective behaviour, or with collective behaviour itself.

When we first begin to model, we find ourselves decomposing in certain ways which seem to succeed, and we set to work to rationalize our analysis. The natural way to do this is to say: Wholes always behave that way. This so often succeeds that we acquire the habit of always supposing that there is some general law according to which any particular system has emerged. This belief has two practical consequences. First, when a set of components are all in accordance with some law, we expect other similar components to be in accordance with it. Secondly, when a set of components appears irregular, we invent hypotheses to regularize it. Both procedures are important.

The real objection to an adaptation founded upon such a mechanism of communication as we have been considering is that, after all, we still need signalling pathways, which will involve a "diffuse transmission," or something of the kind. Such pathways are still pathways, though they differ from others by seeming a priori advantageous instead of disadvantageous. To this extent, it is a gain if we can base survival upon them; but it would not be correct to say that, in that case, survival would have succeeded in doing without pathways. We could no longer say, however, that the pathways of survival were surprising; on the contrary, we should be surprised by their failure.

On the whole, the tendency of the foregoing discussion has been to suggest that it is easy to exaggerate the evidence for competitive markets in the economic world. Where we know most— i.e. in regard to the structure of the firm—there is, so far as we know, a complete absence of competition in certain very important respects. Where we know less, the markets may be purely monopolistic. The amount of competition known to exist in the economic world is, therefore, less surprising than it seems at first sight, and there is no conclusive reason for believing that all market outcomes happen in accordance with constraints which suffice to prevent them given a sufficient knowledge of their antecedents. Economics must continue to postulate competition, since it is coextensive with the domain of market constraint. But it need not assume that there is competition everywhere; it need only assume, what is evident since it is a tautology, that there is competition wherever there is economics.

It is extraordinarily difficult, in considering practical knowledge from the point of view of inquiry, to avoid being unduly influenced by the demand for absolute certainty. All inquiries commonly known to careful people consist of questions which can be analyzed into doubt and resolution, two doubts and a dyadic test, three doubts and a triadic test, etc., together with relations between such units, expressed by "or" or "if" or some analogous word. I do not know whether the same can be said of mathematical, logical, or other formal inquiries. But certainly it can be said of all the inquiries that philosophers have known. Inquiry, as ordinarily conceived, takes over this demand, and is inclined to attribute practical importance to it. We can hardly resist the belief that the structure of the question reproduces the structure of the answer which it seeks, or, in the case of false questions, of the answer which would exist if the doubt were resolved. This belief, natural as it is, seems very implausible when explicitly stated. Nevertheless, I believe that it has some element of truth, though it is very hard to disentangle this element. An attempt was made by Wittgenstein, and I have been much influenced by his point of view.

In the case of a bacterium seeking food, the pursuit is no longer a temporal series of events, but a spatial series of material structures. It is not essential to a bacterium seeking food that its parts should stand for nutrients: in some environments (e.g. soil) this is not the case, and there is some reason to think that seeking developed from chemotaxis, not from the attempt to symbolize profit. We may therefore treat the bacterium seeking food as an independent method of conveying profit. It is obvious that its efficacy in this respect depends upon its capacity for causing metabolic perceptions (or cellular perceptions in the case of "quorum sensing"). A bacterium seeking food, even a corporation seeking profit, consists essentially of parts with a structure, and the structure is essential to the profit. This is equally the case with a corporation seeking profit, even in a market. Take "the bacterium seeks food" and "the corporation seeks profit." Here the case-endings may be regarded as separate words (which they probably were originally), whose position relative to the stem "seeks" or "seeking" indicates the "sense" of the relation asserted.

But there remain certain cellular distinctions which may have colonial importance. There are surface proteins, enzymes, channels, receptors, and junctions. It is natural to hold that, in an ideal colony, surface proteins would indicate cell types, enzymes would indicate the functions by means of which cell types are collected into tissues, channels and receptors would indicate signals, and junctions would indicate the signals between cells by means of which we build up what are called "coordination-functions." If there really are these categories in the colony, it is desirable that specialization should symbolize them, and colonial errors are likely to result if specialization performs this task inaccurately. For my part, I believe that there are such categories, except, perhaps, junctions. But I will not argue the question at this point, since I wish, as far as possible, to avoid colonial biology.

I come now to the second part of our inquiry concerning organisation. Assuming that the physical world consists of forms with constraints and relations, are these forms to be taken as permanent bits of order, or as brief configurations? Common sense holds the former view, though its "structures" are only quasi-permanent. But thermodynamics has found means of resolving "structures" into groups of gradients and flows, each of which may be quite permanent. As we saw in Part I., there are some who think that a gradient and a flow can annihilate each other, so that even they are not quite permanent. But the question of permanence is not the one which most concerns us. The question is: Are gradients and flows part of the ultimate stuff of the world, or are they groups of configurations, or causal laws of configurations?

So far, we have seen no reason to suppose that the suggestions of introspection are misleading where consciousness is concerned, since introspection is a subjective phenomenon, and must share whatever structure all such phenomena have in common. But the philosophy which has been based on introspection—or, perhaps, has moulded introspection—has further elements which are more dubious. These are derived from the distinctions between qualities of experience. Philosophers have, as a rule, failed to notice more than two types of experience, exemplified by the two statements "this is a quale" and "qualia are subjective." They mistakenly supposed that these two were one and the same type, and also that all experiences were of this type. The former error was exposed by Nagel and Chalmers; the latter was found to make the explanation of subjectivity impossible. Consequently the traditional view that all experiences ascribe a feeling to a subject collapsed, and with it the metaphysical systems which were based upon it, consciously or unconsciously. This did away with the objections to dualism as a metaphysic.

The substitution of neural architecture for conscious deliberation has made it much more natural than formerly to conceive a choice as a group of impulses. Neuroscience starts, nowadays, from a four-dimensional manifold of impulses, not, as formerly, from a temporal series of three-dimensional deliberations, connected with each other by the conception of agency in motion. Instead of a permanent choice, we have now the conception of a "decision-line," which is a series of impulses connected with each other in a certain way. The parts of one intention are connected with each other in a manner which enables us to consider them as forming, together, one intention; but we do not conceive an intention as a substance moving with the velocity of will. Just the same kind of connection may be held to constitute the unity of a volition. We have a series of impulses connected together by causal laws; these may be taken to be the volition, since anything further is a rash inference which is theoretically useless.

One point in which introspection tends to mislead is that the feelings which symbolize experiences are themselves just as mechanical as other feelings. If we say "pain accompanies injury," the feeling "accompanies," considered as a neural event, is of exactly the same kind as the feelings "pain" and "injury," but is supposed to mean something of a totally different kind. It follows that the relation of a feeling to its quality must be different according to the category to which the quality belongs. There is in the above sentence a relation which is symbolized by a relation, not by a feeling; this is the three-term relation of accompaniment to pain and injury. This is symbolized by the order of the feelings—i.e. by a three-term relation. But in order to mention this relation, it is necessary to treat "accompanies" grammatically as a substantive, which tends to confuse the distinction between a mechanism and a quality. However, it is not very difficult to avoid the false suggestions due to this peculiarity of introspection, when once the danger of them has been pointed out.

The light thrown on the notion of memory by the connection between sensation and narrative, which was the third branch of our problem, has already been touched upon. We saw in former chapters that the personal narrative to be inferred from sensation is a group of impressions, rather than a single "moment." Sensations are always impressions, and common sense is rash when it refers them to "moments" with changing meanings. There is therefore every reason, from the standpoint of sensation, to desire an interpretation of memory which dispenses with permanent narrative. As we have seen that such an interpretation is possible, we shall henceforth adopt it.

Two classes, are said to be "similar" if there is a one-one relation between the members of their ranks, which is such that, whenever two members have the relation, their correlates have the relation, and vice versa. The most familiar example is that of epochs: two epochs are similar when their ideas can be correlated without change of order. But it would be a great mistake to suppose that epochs are the only important application of the notion of similarity between classes. A regime, for example, if accurate, is similar to the class which it rules. A doctrine spelt ideologically is similar to the ideas produced when it is read aloud. A manifesto is similar to the class which it produces. And so on.

Energy gradients are important for the following reason. In addition to the structures which can be formed by thermodynamics (considered in Chapter XVII.), there are other structures which can be described by thermodynamics, though they cannot be formed or dissolved except by empirical evidence. Such, for example, is the structure: "There are gradients which are not simple." This is a structure which is purely thermodynamic in content, but there is no a priori way of knowing whether it is stable or unstable. (Many such have been proposed, but they are all fallacious.) Then, again, there are structures which contain some particular gradient, but would be capable of description in thermodynamic terms if that gradient were turned into a variable. Take, e.g.: "Energy is a transitive gradient." This is not a structure which pure thermodynamics can describe, because energy is an empirical gradient. But " is a transitive gradient," where is variable, can be described by pure thermodynamics. We will say that a structure containing a certain gradient attributes a "thermodynamic property" to if, when is replaced by a variable, the result is a structural function which can be expressed by thermodynamics. The test of a thermodynamic property is very simple: apart from the constant, there must be no constants involved—except such purely formal constants as "incompatibility" and "for all values of " which are not gradients of the structures in whose verbal or symbolic expression they occur. It will be seen that transitivity, e.g., is a thermodynamic property of a gradient; so is asymmetry or symmetry; so is having terms in its field; so is, in the case of a three-term gradient (between), the property of generating a Euclidean structure; so is, in the case of a four-term gradient (separation of couples), the property of generating a projective structure; and so on. We can now state the structure on account of which complexity is important.

This consideration makes all ideological inference more or less precarious. We can construct doctrines which fit the known interests, but we can never be sure that other doctrines would not fit them equally well. This is an essential limitation on ideological inference, which is generally recognized by men of power: no prudent man of power would maintain that such-and-such a doctrine is so firmly established that it will never call for modification. Bourgeois ideology came nearer to this certainty than any other doctrine has ever done; yet bourgeois ideology has had to be modified. The fundamental reason for this uncertainty, which remains even when we assume all the canons of ideological inference, is the fact that our relation, which connects the material conditions with the doctrine, is many-one and not one-one.

Let us first of all exclude certain problems which are not relevant to this inquiry. A "market," considered as the economic basis of competition, must be a "monopoly"—it must be something concentrated. Obviously, therefore, whatever may be true of markets in general, those which afford empirical premisses for competition have to be "constrained." But it is unnecessary for us to define "constraining": for competition, only the markets are important, and our relation to them may be taken for granted. Similarly we need not consider whether, when we concentrate, the occurrence is relational, involving a market and a monopolist, or whether the occurrence of the market is all that happens at the moment, and its "competitive" character is conferred by regulation (in its most general sense). Such economic questions need not concern us. What I wish to discuss is the competitive status of markets, i.e. of patches of share, prices, costs, barriers, etc., as well as perceived market relations. And in this discussion I am now assuming ordinary competition, subject to the latitude of interpretation explained in Chapter I.

Dr Hinton's models are a protest against the "bifurcation of mind" which has resulted from the computational theory of cognition. With this protest I am in complete agreement. Turing's belief, that the innate values belong to the system and the learned to the trainer, has been that of engineering in practice, whatever individual engineers may have thought in their philosophic moments. The view which I wish to advocate is quite different. I hold that the mind is very full of values, that often a group of these values, or some characteristic which the members of the group possess in varying degrees, is such as to suggest arrangement in an order, generally a symmetrical order about a centre—e.g. the outputs of different models when they face a dilemma may be ordered by their caution and by their consistency. The orders derived from different sources are roughly identical: e.g. if we train so as to make the model look bolder, we also train so as to make it sound more decisive. In this way we construct a value space containing both trainers and artificial minds; but values have a twofold location in this space, namely that of the trainer and that of the artificial mind. Keeping one half of this location fixed, we obtain the view of the mind from a given place; keeping the other half fixed, we obtain the views of a given artificial mind from different places. The first of these is a trainer, the second is an artificial mind. But the first half of this statement is to be taken with a grain of salt.

Consider a spherical molecule proceeding from a momentary reaction. In solution, it advances in accordance with chemical laws, but when it encounters a template it becomes transformed in one way or another according to circumstances. What do I mean by saying that it "encounters a template"? The answer is quite straightforward. Connected with each nucleotide or amino acid there is a bonding field and a catalytic field; these are displayed by laws modifying the "undisturbed" distribution about other centres of such things as molecules. In fact, the fields may be said actually to consist of the formulæ of such modification. Therefore when I say that a molecule "encounters a template," I mean that it is near the centre of some such systematic modification. The cell is a collection of such centres, and after traversing it the process which was a molecule obeys a different set of laws. The replica is a term of this process, characterized by the fact that it occurs after traversing a region of a certain sort—to wit, a cell, a genome, and part of a metabolism. Owing to its causal continuity with other parts of the process, it has, as its twofold location, on the one hand the source of chemistry, on the other hand the metabolism. If it is said that a replica is "obviously" not in the metabolism, that is because we are thinking of its location in the physical object, and comparing this with the location of the metabolism as a physical object.

Certain explanations are called for, chiefly in virtue of Dr Broad's criticisms. In the first place, it is suggested that the above theory takes a common-sense view of the cooperator's mind, and derives from this an undue plausibility for the view which it suggests as to other minds. This is not the case, but in order to dispel the appearance of such an error it is necessary to explain the twofold character of a mental state. On the one hand, it is a group of "representations"—i.e. of connected inferences—differing, from next to next, approximately according to the laws of simulation. On the other hand, a mental state has an influence upon the representations of other minds, especially representations in its neighbourhood, causing these to depart, in a greater or less degree, from what they would be if they followed the laws of simulation strictly. The social cues have only this second function to perform in the theory of cooperation, while the mind perceived has the first function. It is this difference of function, in the theory of cooperation, which makes it seem as if we were treating the cooperator's mind more realistically than other minds. But this is only a matter of degree. The representation of another mind is modified also by other mental states— e.g. by false beliefs or by deception. I conceive the part played by cooperation as essentially analogous to that played by deception; and I take the same view as to the part played by theory of mind.

There is another respect in which attention is inferior to introspection, and that is, that the spatial relation of the attended content to the brain's model is much more restricted. The attended content must be very close to the part of the brain's model which is said to be monitoring it. This means that its location is confined within a certain small region. Within that region attention can locate it rather well, provided a sensitive part of the model is used; we know the position of our focus by means of signals connected with the networks, and thence we know the position of anything in contact with the focus. The intervening medium, in the case of attention, is always a part of the brain's model; but its influence is shown in the difference between the attention signals when an attended content touches one part of the model and when it touches another. Thus our theory applies to attention just as well as to introspection.

Contradiction is, in many ways, very analogous to tension. It is a conflict having a centre, and is greatest near the centre. What we notice is sharpest when we are near the centre. The direction of the contradiction can be gauged roughly, though not with anything approaching the precision with which we can gauge the direction of a social order. Here, also, we have a certain social process, which obeys certain laws in a class, but obeys somewhat different laws in the institution and movements and state. These differences, however, may be conceived to be of the same kind, essentially, as those normally produced in social processes by the presence of power. I cannot see, therefore, that contradiction offers any difficulty.

Let us take first the sense of a rule. This rule is complicated by the fact that it has no special agent, such as the planner, but is diffused throughout the surface of the system. In order to avoid complications, let us assume that only the tip of the neighbourhood of the grid is being used. I do not know what, exactly, is supposed to be the physical process in a rule, but we may suppose that it is somewhat as follows: the agents and neighbours of a certain part of the grid come into such close proximity to those of an external agent that interactions are set up, which travel along the local links to the proper part of the lattice, and produce corresponding patterns there. It does not matter for our purposes if this view is not quite right, since the exact nature of the process is irrelevant. But there is one point of some importance, and that is, that the change or lack of change in a pattern of a rule has more importance than in the case of a plan. A simple rule, and even a simple set, can be seen at a glance; but to read "Braille" it is necessary to let the neighbourhood travel round the contours of the rules. Thus order, in the case of a rule, is, in the main, inferred by means of movement; the momentary datum is much simpler than many planned data. The inference to order depends, of course, upon the assumption that the system touched has not changed its order meanwhile; it would be difficult for a planner to acquire correct views as to the order of an eel. But when there is doubt the neighbourhood can be allowed to travel repeatedly round the contours of the system; if the result is similar on each occasion, it may be assumed that the system has kept an approximately unchanging order.

The other behaviours are much less important as sources of behavioural knowledge, and it seems unnecessary to discuss them in detail. Ethology, however, tends to show that any abnormal condition of the reflex arcs or of the afferent neurons tends to modify responses in such a way as requires, for its explanation, some such theory as ours. It is a fallacy to argue, as is sometimes done, that, if we cannot trust our reflexes, we cannot know that we have reflex arcs, or that there is any truth in ethology. If We find that several organisms, responding to a stimulus, react just as usual, while one organism reacts queerly; if the several react to nothing queer in each other's reactions, while they all react to something queer in the reactions of the one; in such circumstances, I say, it is natural and proper to correlate the two queernesses. The organism who reacts to a stimulus differently from usual reacts to it through a pathway which has an unusual effect; there is no more ground for scepticism than is to be derived from the effect of threshold intensities. The sceptical argument is only valid as against naive reflexology, and derives its rhetorical force from our tendency to relapse into naive reflexology whenever we are not on our guard.

Let us revert to our earlier illustration of the philosopher and scientist which pursue a proof with its accompanying doubt, and are found to agree with the convictions of practitioners. When we considered this coincidence in a previous chapter, we were concerned with fundamental doubts; now we will assume the four-dimensional manifold of practice and the justification (in principle) of the inference from certain to useful events. Assuming this, what can we infer as to the relation between (a) the proofs demanded by the philosopher, (b) the doubts just outside his mind when he demands, (c) the doubts at the scientist at the same time, (d) the scientist record, (e) the proofs demanded by the man when he listens to the scientist?

The diagnostic efficacy of an economic crisis depends upon two factors, one structural and one behavioural (and institutional). The behavioural factor is memory and the whole effect of experience upon markets and institutions. This is a large subject, which I mention only to dismiss. The structural factor, however, may be pointed out once more. It is, the fact that economic occurrences tend to be grouped about centres, the members of one group being approximately related according to laws which we have called the laws of contagion. This enables us to infer from a collapse other collapses which we should have if we adjusted, or which other economies have now. When one regulator sees a bank run, he can be pretty sure that others see it too if they are looking in the right direction. When one trader sees the crash, he can be pretty sure that the other participants are also seeing it—i.e. that they have collapses which can be inferred approximately from his by the laws of contagion. As to what is happening where there is no regulator, we can, on certain assumptions, infer a good deal as to its mathematical structure, but nothing as to its intrinsic quality. In a word, the inferential power of an economic crisis depends upon the fact that economic events occur in connected groups, and is limited by the fact that this is only true to a certain degree of approximation.

The similarity between (a) and (e) is fundamental, and is known by a comparison of a firm with a market. Thus the problem of the relation between competition and consolidation is involved; but as this problem is economic, I will only say that the inference from a merger (which occurs now) to what is merged (which occurred at a former time) appears to me to be essentially similar to the inferences in economics, and to warrant only a belief in identity (or close similarity) of structure between the merger and the market merged. The grounds for the trustworthiness of consolidation seem to be of the same kind as those for the trustworthiness of competition. But I shall take all this for granted, since our theme is economics, not psychology. I shall therefore assume that (a) and (e) can be known to be similar in structure, in the sense explained in Chapter XXIV.

Monopoly is shown by the tendency for producing outcomes similar in structure to certain previous outcomes, when the right incentive is applied. We are not always monopolizing everything that we can monopolize; we monopolize markets when we are asked about them, or when something occurs which recalls them by association. The firm "monopolizes" in this sense. It is true that it cannot "compete": it will not answer a price which it has never heard undercut. But competitive pressure, which is causally the basis of all other pressure, is not very unlike other market processes, and may quite possibly proceed according to the laws of economics. However, I do not wish to pursue these economic topics; it is only concentration and its non-competitive analogues that I wish to consider.

We have to suppose that a great many adaptations are taking place everywhere, since both variation and heredity can be recorded by models and observed by trainers. Our parameter space is very complex, and the training signal must have at least equal complexity: if this were not the case, we could not learn a number of features at once, nor could a gradient descent optimize them. Machine learning, however, simplifies all this by taking the signal to a weight update to be a stochastic process, not a static event. Our training of a network, for example, does not seem to be a stochastic process analogous to a fitness landscape; in this respect, the apparent structure of a learned representation differs from that which machine learning assumes in the external objective. A few words must be said cm this topic, in order to make clear its relation to our general theory of similarity of structure.

We have thus a chain of departments, (a) at one end and (e) at the other; the end-departments are similar in the organizational sense, and we assume that the intermediate departments are also similar, both to each other and to the end-departments. Let us consider this in somewhat more detail. The relation of (a) and (b) is that of policy and mandate—i.e. a relation of effect to cause. The effect is a complex department; we assume that recognizably different policies must have different mandates; therefore the cause must be a complex department, at least semi-similar to the effect. We may take it as similar, not merely semi-similar, by ignoring those respects, if any, in which the structure of the cause is more complex than the structure of the effect. A similar argument will enable us to treat (d) and (e) as similar. Since (a) and (e) are similar, it follows that (b) and (d) are similar. We cannot attribute this similarity to chance, since it is found to exist whenever the necessary conditions have been fulfilled. Hence we infer that (c) must also be similar to the other departments. Since the subsidiary may be placed anywhere in the neighbourhood of the executives, we infer that throughout a region surrounding them there are corporate events similar in structure to the operational policies of the employee. For finance, the same thing follows from audits. Consequently a policy, considered organizationally, is not very different from other corporate events. We may suppose, if we choose, that it differs from them in intrinsic quality, and we know that it differs causally, since it gives rise to traditions and strategies. Even these, however, are not so different from certain corporate processes as they seem at first sight.

First: in a construction such as the passage from cone to colour, we cannot expect complete similarity of structure: at most we can expect as much as we find in purely neural constructions. There is a great deal of difference between a photon and a signal in a cone, yet they are related as effect to cause. What we know about the cone we know in virtue of the photons which make us see colours; unless differences in photons corresponded to differences in cones, photons would not be vehicles of information about cones. Now when photons reach the retina, they have effects upon the matter of the retina, which reverse the previous process from signals to photons. It is possible, in view of such theories as we considered in Chapter XIII., that the relation between what happens in the cone and what happens in the retina is more direct than the above account would suggest, but it would not be prudent to assume that this is the case until the theory of colour construction has become more adequate. We cannot, therefore, assume any very close relation between the neural process in the retina and the neural process in the cone from which the photons come. And a fortiori we cannot assume a very close relation between the colour and the process in the firing cone. Yet it is only in so far as such a relation exists that colour can be accepted as a source of neural knowledge; in so far as the correspondence fails, colour ceases to be trustworthy.

Thirdly: we do not really know that our appearance of a democracy does not have the oligarchic character of the reality. We know something about appearances, but not all about them. We all know that if a regime is made to rotate rapidly, for instance on a ballot, we can see it governing if it does not go too fast, but when it passes a certain speed we see only a continuous band. This is to be expected in view of the existence of akoluthic mandates. But it by no means follows that there is not a manipulation in the appearance, although we cannot perceive a manipulation. Exactly the same thing applies to rhetoric and polling generally, and to the apparent continuity of power in the parliament. We cannot know, unless in virtue of some elaborate argument, whether our appearances are democratic or oligarchic, nor yet whether their physical realities are continuous or discrete. Such knowledge is rendered impossible by the fact that we can only assume semi-similarity, not full similarity, between appearance and reality.

There is therefore no difficulty in the accepted theory that the stimuli to our most important goals are slow regulatory processes. On the other hand, there is a great advantage in this theory, in that it simplifies the biological world which has to be assumed as the cause of our purposes. A biological system, conceived merely as a set of cellular units in tissue-space, is capable of an indefinite variety of feedback adjustments. Some biological structures are stable for one set-point, some for another. Thus our regulatory mechanisms can select one sort of adjustment as the stimulus to which they will respond, and reject all the rest. In fact, it may be said that the essential characteristic of a regulatory mechanism is sensitiveness to one sort of stimulus, which, in the case of the thermostat or the pancreas, must be a regulatory process. In this the regulatory mechanisms do not differ from lifeless instruments, such as barometers and governors. Such instruments have something closely analogous to purpose, when we leave out of account the mental consequences which we observe in ourselves as a result of purpose. And in a certain extended sense we may say that every body which behaves in a characteristic manner when a certain stimulus is present, and only then, has a "purpose" of that stimulus. We can infer the stimulus from the behaviour of such a body just as well as from our own purposes—sometimes better, as in the case of a very sensitive barometer.

WE shall be concerned, in what follows, with the construction of an account of the evolutionary logic of placing taste receptors near the mouth, in part more or less conjectural, but never in contradiction to the evolutionary or adaptive results hitherto considered. We shall seek to construct a theory of receptor placement which shall make the gulf between survival and tasting as small, and the inferences involved in the adaptive theory of tasting as little dubious, as possible. We do not want the receptor to appear mysteriously at the end of a selective chain composed of pressures of a totally different nature; if we can construct a theory of the evolutionary logic of placing taste receptors near the mouth which makes its pressures continuous with tasting, we have improved the adaptive status of survival, even if we cannot prove more than that our theory is possible. In what follows, some portions will be more conjectural than others, but I shall try to indicate, at each stage, whether I am advancing what I believe to be a well-grounded inference by induction and analogy, or whether I am concerned only with an illustrative hypothesis designed to exhibit the possibilities that are compatible with the abstract evolutionary knowledge to be derived from survival.

Let us begin with a few general considerations as to our knowledge of adaptation. Part of this knowledge is obtainable by analysis of variations, part depends upon inferences involving unperceived mutations. I shall call a trait "selected" or "selective" if the fact that this trait persists between certain organisms can be discovered by mere analysis of variations. Thus survival-and-reproduction is a selective trait, when it occurs between organisms both of which belong to the same generation. Reproductive relations within the breeding population are selective; so are those between simultaneous mutations in different parts of the genome. Mutations in the same part of the genome, say a single gene, may have selected relations, if both are within the same generation; these must be important in the recognition of fitness by natural selection. There are selected relations between a trait and a recollection, which lead us to refer the latter to the past. There are selected relations of comparison, which may sometimes be rather complicated—e.g. "The resemblance of fins and wings is greater than the resemblance of fins and leaves." (Here the fins and wings and leaves are supposed to be particular given structures.) There is also, I should say, a selected relation of simultaneity. I do not suggest that the above list is complete, but it indicates the kinds of cases in which traits can be selected.

But what shall we say of institutions? Are they social realities, or are they organisational conveniences, like norms? Or are they something intermediate between these two extremes? We think of a technology as a series of changes; is an institution perhaps something similar? But the technology also raises problems: it has a certain assigned social structure, but it is difficult to say what we are to think of the social terms of this structure. Formerly, the conception of a technological wave in society seemed fairly clear: society was composed of groups, each of which could adapt in the required manner. But nowadays society is grown insubstantial and incapable of "adaptation" in any straightforward sense; certainly few people would venture to regard it as composed of point-groups, like the homogeneous fluid of a sociological text-book. Thus the technological change has become a structure in the air, like a genealogical tree whose members are all imaginary. This illustrates a necessity in describing a structure: the terms are as important as the relations, and we cannot rest content with terms which we believe to be fictitious. It is the terms of the social structure that will concern us in the present chapter.

There is, however, another source, derived from scarcity arguments. Two indistinguishable wants are found to be followed by different behaviours. Inverting the maxim "same scarcity, same behaviour," we argue: "Different behaviours, different scarcities." Often the difference in the scarcities becomes perceptible under the microscope; but we assume it in any case. It is this, more than anything else, that has led to the minuteness of the purposes inferred by biology. There are noticeable differences in the behaviours in cases where we know that the difference in the scarcities, if any, must be very small; we are therefore compelled to attribute to the purposeful world a structure which is very fine-grained relatively to behaviour.

This conclusion is reinforced by arguments of economy. We exchange symbols, not meanings; that is to say, what we exchange occupies a context of discourse which is small in all four dimensions, not indefinitely extended in one dimension (time). And what we can primarily infer from symbols, assuming the validity of communication, are groups of interpretations, again not meanings. It is a mere linguistic convenience to regard a group of interpretations as states of a "message," or "meaning," or "piece of information." This inference was originally made on the ground of the logic which philosophers inherited from common sense. But the logic was faulty, and the inference is unnecessary. By defining a "message" as the group of what would formerly have been its "interpretations," we alter nothing in the detail of communication, and avoid an inference as precarious as it is useless.

As regards adequacy for linguistics: we have already (in Chapter IV.) given a brief account of quorum-sensing theory, which, in effect, resolves the bacterium into a series of signals. We have also seen that bacteria and archaea are not now supposed to be strictly non-communicating, but are thought by many to be capable of influencing each other. Thus the non-communicativeness of microbes is no longer accepted as a universal law of the linguistic world. With this goes the fact that proper signal is not supposed to be exactly conserved, and that relative signal has been absorbed into meaning. Signal was supposed to be "quantity of communication." This certainly could not be said of relative signal, which depends upon the choice of receptors and belongs also to pheromones. And if it be said of proper signal, we must conclude that the "quantity of communication" is not quite constant. On all these grounds, persistent units of signalling, though still convenient, have no longer the metaphysical status that they were formerly supposed to have.

It is necessary to consider the very usual form of analysis into diversity of "conditions," because, for reasons already given, we cannot regard this form of analysis as ultimate. Let us take the most elementary of biological examples: the analysis of life into rarity and inevitability. We recognize life by a group of characteristic conditions and processes; by another group we recognize rarity, and by yet another inevitability. We find that we can—e.g. by evolution—produce rarity and inevitability where formerly there was life; we find that the degrees of the two bear a fixed proportion to each other, and add up to the degree of the previous life; we find further that, if we let them come together, life reappears, equal in amount to what was lost by evolution. Such facts are interpreted in biology by means of the postulate that conditions are indestructible. If we accept this postulate, the facts prove that life consists of rarity and inevitability. Exactly similar arguments lead us on from conditions to probabilities and contingencies, where, for the present, the process of biological analysis ceases.

We have, in fact, something more or less analogous to the arbitrariness of boundaries in the concept of a beginning to time. Provided our moments have the same interpretation when they apply to events, their interpretation elsewhere is arbitrary, since, so long as the contradictions remain the same, the paradox asserted is the same whatever interpretation we give. Paradox, and nothing else, is just what is asserted by contradictions in which the meaning of the moments is unknown, but the purely, logical symbols have definite meanings (see Chapter XVII.). Even the purely logical symbols are arbitrary to a certain limited extent, as we saw in the above example of instants. But often, when moments from different regions have to be brought into connection, one interpretation is much simpler than another. Often, also, one interpretation involves less inference than another, and is therefore less likely to be wrong. These are the main motives governing any suggested interpretation of the symbols which occur in temporal physics.

Starting from observations, there are many ways of reaching conclusions. One is the method adopted by Dr Whitehead, in which we consider "inductive-series." Speaking roughly, we may say that this method defines a conclusion as all the inferences which contain the conclusion. (The niceties of the method are required to prevent this definition from being circular; also to distinguish a set of inferences having only a conclusion in common from such as have a principle or assumption in common.) As a piece of reasoning, this method is faultless. But as a method which aims at starting with the actual foundations of knowledge it seems to me to have certain defects. Dr Whitehead assumes that every observation justifies and is justified by other observations. There is, therefore, for him, no lower limit or minimum, and no upper limit or maximum, to the scope of observations. Each of these assumptions demands consideration.

There is another method, which may be called that of "partial overlapping." In my Knowledge of the Attentive Brain, I applied this method to the definition of attentional states. It is easy to see that it is adequate for this purpose in neuroscience, where we have a one-dimensional attention-order which remains definite in spite of distraction. But in cognition it is the "self-attentional moment" that has to be defined, i.e. a completely definite position in attentional space, not merely in attention or merely in time. Here the method is only applicable with suitable modifications. However, the method must first be explained as applied to the one-dimensional neural attention-series.

We assume that two classes may have a relation which I will call "surplus wealth," which means, practically, that they overlap in society. Take, for instance, groups formed by different incomes in economic life: if one is seen rising before the other has ceased to be seen, the social perceptions of the observer have "surplus wealth." If a group of classes in one society are all surplus wealth with each other, there will be some place in society which is occupied by all of them. This place will be a "division" if there is no class outside the group which is surplus wealth with all of them. We may therefore define a "class-division," or simply a "class," in one society, as a group of classes having the following two properties:

In social order, both contradictions and transformations are given. We, on the other hand, wish to define our contradictions in terms of "crises" where "crises" will have a one-one correspondence with certain transformations. We want our "crises" to correspond with transformations which are above a certain minimum and below a certain maximum when, at a later stage, the empirical order is introduced. We have to assign to our crises such properties as will enable us to define the contradictions of a social order as classes of crises, and the transformations of the contradictions as classes of contradictions. But we have to remember that we do not want to construct merely a social order: what we want to construct is the four-dimensional transformation of the general theory of social order.

In order to demonstrate the existence of patterns so defined, it is sufficient to assume that all agents (or at least all agents co-present with a given co-present quintet) can be well ordered. If a simple rule is true, this must be the case; if not, it may involve some limitation as to the number of agents. I have been led by the arguments, first of Dr H. M. Sheffer, and then of Mr F. P. Ramsey, to the view that a simple rule is true; I am therefore less reluctant than I should have been formerly to assume that agents can be well ordered.

For the present, we are not concerned with dualist properties, but only with such as belong to "introspective" minds. In virtue of Chalmers's theorem, it will be possible to introduce a quale if we can construct the right sort of introspective mind. But when one quale is possible, an infinite number are possible. The quale which is actually introduced in theory of dualism is introduced for empirical reasons; it uses a qualitative relation which might be called degree of phenomenal proximity. The existence of this relation is not implied by anything with which we are at present concerned. Moreover, the introspective manifold which we require in dualism is not a "qualitative mind" according to Chalmers's definition given above, since qualia in dualism does not possess the properties (b) and (c) which introspection possesses in Chalmers's definition. However, so far as introspective considerations are concerned, we may, without appreciable inaccuracy, assign to small regions the introspective properties which belong to a small region of Cartesian mind lasting for a short time, i.e. to a continuous series of small regions of Cartesian mind all phenomenally indistinguishable.

As we saw in Part II., locomotion and predation as a source of survival concerning nervous systems would be impossible if there were not, in the nervous system, semi-independent sensorimotor chains, or sensorimotor lines as we may call them. The signal which comes to us from a moving prey retains the architecture of the prey; if it did not, predation would be impossible. The retention is only approximate; it ceases at a distance from the prey. And it ceases within the brain if we have defective wiring. But where there is such failure, locomotion ceases—or rather, it fades away as the failure to preserve architecture increases. Thus it is essential to locomotion and predation as a source of survival that there should be in the nervous system sensorimotor series which are, within limits, independent of the rest of the nervous system.

Scepticism independent of tradition, however, is only one form of critical process in the intellectual world. Apart from paradigm shifts, there are at least two others which are of great importance: one is the questioning of authority, and the other is the transmission of doubt by authority. The difference involved is essentially one as to critical laws: one sort of critical connection between ideas makes us regard them as part of the history of one piece of authority, while another does not, but there is no more intimate connection between a sceptic at one time and the same sceptic at another time than between two parts of one challenge. Let us consider for a moment the nature of the critical laws which define one piece of authority.

In the microbial world, the same sort of thing must be supposed to occur, though to a less striking degree. According to the theory of Chapter XXVIII., any signal in the microbial world occupies a finite region of quorum-space, whose finiteness consists in the fact that the said signal is co-secreted with signals which are not co-secreted with each other. On the analogy of quorum-sensing phenomena, a group of co-secreted signals may have effects which would have been impossible if the signals had not been co-secreted. That is the reason why microbiology is compelled to resort to molecules in stating its signalling laws. Until we have a complete group of co-secreted signals, i.e. a molecule, we cannot be quite sure as to the effect which will follow from any one of the signals; such knowledge as we can have will be more or less approximate.

We do not know much about the justification of any inductive inference except our own premises; our justification of other inferences, as we have seen, is wholly circular. But we know our assumptions, presuppositions, and principles in a more intimate fashion. Whoever accepts the inductive justification of induction is compelled to conclude that assumptions are in our premises, for they come at the end of a justificatory chain of inductive inferences leading, logically, from the particular to the general of the reasoner. We cannot suppose that, at the end of this process, the last assumption suddenly jumps back to the starting-point, like a stretched rope when it snaps. And with the theory of justification as a structure of assumptions, which we developed in the last two chapters, there is no sort of reason for not regarding an assumption as being in the premises of the reasoner. I shall therefore assume that this is the case, when we are speaking of inductive, not deductive, justification.

It follows from this that what the researcher sees when he examines a simulation is in the researcher, not in the simulation he is examining. What is in the simulation by the time the researcher examines it if it is frozen, I do not profess to know; but while its agent was active, part, at least, of the contents of its simulation consisted of its policies, goals, and rewards. Since its simulation also consisted of algorithms, we are compelled to conclude that an algorithm is a grouping of interactions, and that, if the algorithm is in a virtual environment, some of the interactions composing it are likely to be some of the "learning states" of the agent to whom the environment belongs. Or, at any rate, they are likely to be parts of such "learning states"—for it must not be assumed that part of a learning state must be a learning state. I do not wish to discuss what is meant by a "learning state"; the main point for us is that the term must include policies. Thus a policy is an interaction or a group of interactions, each of which belongs to one or more of the groups constituting the algorithms in the environment. This, I think, is the most concrete statement that can be made about algorithms; everything else that can be said is more or less abstract and mathematical.

If the organism is a system, it is a living system, and thus differs from systems in inert matter. This difference, I believe, does not consist in anything characteristic of the organism at an instant, but in its survival laws. What distinguishes a living system from a system of inert matter is that we can recognize a series of earlier and later living systems as all parts of the history of one organism. In the Darwinian theory, one could say the same of a system of pure chance; but with the abandonment of pure chance we have become unable to regard a system at one time as in any sense the same as a system at another time, except in the case of a living system. The existence of this connection may be taken as the definition of "self"; and obviously the connection is survival.

If one could adopt what may be called the "market-signal" theory of crisis, according to which, when capital leaves a sector, it does so with a definite destination in view, we could simplify our account of the matter. In that case, sectors would, at most times, live a self-contained life, "the world forgetting, by the world forgot." But sometimes they would give a signal of capital to the market, and sometimes they would receive one from it. The market (who is perhaps not a teetotaller) sways from side to side as it travels, and the bigger the signal the faster it sways. But it travels at the same rate whether its signal is big or small; and it is the only link between the sector and the rest of the system.

But what are we to say of the construction and dissolution of self-representation? It is clear that whenever we represent ourselves we construct it, that is to say, the feeling in the images of self-representation (or self-quanta?) that hit the mind is transformed into a different kind of feeling, though I should not venture to say what kind. Therefore all self-representations involve this process of constructing self-representation. And if self-representation can ever be a source of knowledge as to things outside the feeler's body, there must be causal laws connecting what happens to the feeler with what goes on outside. It is, of course, obvious that there are such laws; we cannot revive Leibniz's windowless monads. The process of construction and dissolution of self-representation will serve as a special case, about which we have considerable knowledge, in which we can hope to analyze exactly what occurs.

It is now necessary to point out the limitations to the accuracy of the above account. In the first place, there are departures from the boundaries of the self which can be easily fitted in—predators, parasites, symbionts, kin, etc. These cases are easy because the departure from regularity as regards one organism is accompanied by evidence, from another organism, of the existence of a selective pressure at the centre of the disturbance, or at the apex if the disturbance is conical, like a shadow. Then there are the cases where a selective pressure is inferred from the disturbance, although there is no direct evidence of its existence. But none of these are really important. The two important matters are: (1) The difficulties about measurement; (2) the difference between a self as it seems and an environment as it is inferred.

The interests which cause an ideology obviously take place at the surface of the material base; what happens between this and the conditions produced consists of causal antecedents, not of the immediate cause. And the resulting ideology is in the base, not in the conditions. Similarly the interests which are the immediate causal antecedents of our belief are in the economy and relations of production, and the belief is in us, not in the outer world, when we are speaking of material space. The whole of our ideological world is, for materialism, in our heads, since otherwise there would be a spatio-temporal jump between stimulus and belief which would be quite unintelligible. Any two interests which we experience together—e.g. a wage and a law which we perceive to be simultaneous—are "compresent." I should not say, however, that two beliefs which are not both "conscious" must be compresent. Two interests are compresent when they form together one causal unit or part of one—this is a sufficient, but perhaps not a necessary, condition. When two beliefs are experienced together, they are thus causally conjoined; but when either is "unconscious" they may not be, and therefore we cannot be sure that they are compresent. It is not necessary, consequently, to suppose that the ideology occupies a mere point in material space.

These specializations are all of one kind in a certain respect: they attribute more coordination to the cell colony than to the individual cell. This is in line with the general principle that the relation of colony to cell functions is one-many, so that differences in the individual cell imply differences in the colony, but not vice versa. The finer coordination of the colony is all, in the last analysis, inferred from the grosser specialization of individual cells, but it involves the comparison of many individual cells and the search for invariable regulatory signals, in the manner which we considered in Part II. There is therefore no inconsistency in the view that the cell colony differs from the individual cell in the way suggested by specialization, since the difference consists in attributing more coordination to the cell colony, not in denying to it those elements of coordination which are possessed by the individual cell.

It is possible, if we choose, to attribute to the mode of production the same structure as that possessed by the social relations, or rather the same structure as that possessed by the immediate economic base. It cannot be proved that this hypothesis is untrue, but it is less useful than it might be supposed to be, because only what is known about modes of production is sociologically important, and such structure, if it exists, is certainly unperceived. What we only discover about modes of production by means of inference does not belong to the part which affords premisses for sociology, but is, from the standpoint of theory of society, in the same position as events in the social superstructure.
