Therefore, although modes of production may have an unperceived structure, this does not diminish the significance of the fact that the structure we perceive in modes of production has only a one-many relation to that of their social relations.

All this represents a failure of correspondence between engineered systems and lived experience and dependency. If we assume that the modern city moves in a supply chain, public confidence may be identified with the integral of trust taken along that supply chain, while public understanding consists of certain relations between simultaneous services (the word "simultaneous" raises no difficulties, since all services are in our routines), partly themselves visible, partly inferred, but all just what they are, whatever engineers may say. There are certain respects in which we can modify public understanding to suit engineering, and certain others in which we cannot. We can, for example, infer that services consist of imperceptible dependencies, if engineering gives us ground for thinking so. But where we perceive some relation between services, we cannot deny that there is such a relation, however little engineering may allow it to subsist between the systems said to be maintained. The rule is: We can infer extra complexity of structure in services if engineering requires it, but, however much engineering may require it, we cannot infer a smaller complexity than is demanded by the study of services on their own account. In the world of services, the distinction between resilience and efficiency does really exist, and resilience does really have certain properties which fragility denies to engineered systems. Thus to this extent the correspondence between public and engineered systems breaks down, and maintenance, which has to do primarily with services, fails to give us quite such good data as we hoped to obtain for inferences as to the engineered world.

In this passage, the "high confidence" seems to me to go beyond what is warranted. If there were an intellectual gain in conceiving established authority sceptically, I do not believe that any traditional arguments to the contrary could interpose a veto. Arguments from precedent, such as Dr Jeans employs, have no longer the definiteness that they had before the introduction of scepticism. As we have just seen, we could define "progress" so that its dimensions would be doubt multiplied by inquiry. Now there is a universal constant of progress, namely. Perhaps, if we were to take scepticism as one of the basic conceptions of thought, we might be able to construct an intellectual life which would be sceptical all through, and yet would contain all that is verifiable. I do not "proclaim with high confidence" that this is possible; I only invite attention to the hypothesis, as worth investigating on the chance of its affording a simplification of the conceptual apparatus of thought. In the following chapters, this hypothesis is to be borne in mind.

When we start from observation instead of from mathematical structure, we find that the data with which we are best acquainted have "patterns," by means of which they can be arranged in classes and series. All symmetries have something in common which is not possessed by asymmetries. Two symmetries may be so similar as to be almost or quite indistinguishable, but they may also be very dissimilar. As model-theory has emphasized, structures are observed qualitatively, not analytically as a system of interrelated parts. But this whole conception of pattern, which plays such a large part in our empirical life, has been wholly absent from traditional mathematics. Symmetries, asymmetries, proportions, etc., have all been regarded as caused by various kinds of relations. There was no objection to this so far as it succeeded, but, if and where it proves insufficient, there can also be no objection to re-introducing qualitative differences into the mathematical world.

The framework so far assumed, apart from properties, has been: co-ordination, part-and-whole, and the emergent laws. I say "part-and-whole" because it is necessary to be able to distinguish the simpler from the complex level in a system, and this is a smaller assumption than that of a general hierarchy among levels in one emergent series. The above framework sufficed except for one purpose: that of defining "emergence." The possibility of emergence is at the bottom of the common-sense distinction between reduction and emergence; the substitution of emergence for reduction should, one might suppose, make emergence impossible, and yet the whole of what is distinctive in emergent physics, and the theories of complexity and self-organization, not to mention other matters, depend upon novelty, which involves emergence. So long as we had particles moving in an unchanging void, we could be content with reduction of configuration. But now systemic interaction, which is essential to configuration, has to be analyzed into an elaborate indirect relation depending upon the existence of common emergent ancestors or descendants. We must, therefore, be able to distinguish among systems by means additional to their reductionist relations.

Let us now return to the operation of prejudice, ignoring reflection for the present; and let us still consider a single prejudiced mind. We are told to suppose that the assumption revolves about the belief for a certain time, say in a circular certainty four times as large as the minimum certainty; then, suddenly, it decides to revolve in the minimum certainty. When this change occurs, the mind loses a certain amount of authority, which is transformed into conviction whose force is obtained by dividing the loss of authority by (social consensus). Whether the conviction travels only in one direction, or in a spherical assumption, we are compelled, in the present state of social knowledge, to leave an open question. But we do assume that something travels away from the assumption, and that, if conviction is absorbed by another mind, that conviction has traversed a route from its place or places of origin. We assume also that the conviction has a force, i.e. that what travels is a periodic process. When the conviction is absorbed, it ceases to exist as conviction, although it may reappear (in rationalization). But often its authority exists in discoverable forms—institutional forms in education, for example. When, however, the authority exists in the form of a steady motion of the assumption in its certainty, it is not discoverable until there is a change of certainty. If we had sufficiently powerful microscopes, we could see a prejudiced society dissolving into a comparatively small number of spots of conviction, while the minds in steady motion would be invisible. Thus we seem to reach the conclusion that the causal laws which genuinely connect one piece of prejudice with another are social laws, in which there are various stages: first, a periodic process having no outside effect; secondly, a sudden disruption of the authority of this process into two parts, one being a new periodic process in the original mind, the other a periodic process travelling in empty space; thirdly, the arrival of the travelling process at another mind; fourthly, a social change in this other mind, involving absorption of the shared authority in the production of a new steady state in the absorbing mind. All genuine causal relations between different minds, we may suppose, involve this process of sudden loss of authority by one mind and its sudden acquisition, later, by another mind. The older social laws, as reinterpreted by convention, can apparently be so stated as to leave minds independent of each other; but I cannot see how the social laws can be so stated.

Traditionally, literacy in civilisation was a question of memory: a people recounted the same tale in speech over and over again. With the coming of writing, it has become necessary to modify this account somewhat. In history, every record has a date, and cannot be made twice; neither the harvest nor a treaty can describe again the account it described on a former occasion. And literacy will be relative to a given system of scripts: if, in one system, a script runs through a given range of signs repeatedly, and always in equal times, it may happen that, in another system, even if there is an oscillating script, its signs are not all equal. A change of scripts may even take away all trace of literate character from a culture. Since, however, the archival principle compels us to treat literacy as historically important, it would seem that we must regard it as a character belonging to a culture when referred to scripts which move with it, since this would overcome the difficulties connected with history. If, in certain cases, this method is not open to us, some other must be found which equally avoids these difficulties. But where cultures connected with speech (as opposed to ritual processes) are concerned we shall, I think, find no other possibility except to take scripts which move with the culture concerned. But this makes it impossible to treat literacy as fundamentally a character exhibited in a memory, since we have reduced to rest the people in which the literate process is taking place. The suggestion I have to make is that, fundamentally, literacy is constituted by the recurrence of records.

A "turning point," as I use the term, is anything which is devoid of oral tradition and is compresent with changes which are not compresent with each other, but are one earlier and the other later; in other words, the turning point is a member of at least two eras which have a time-like interval. When a turning point is contrasted with a custom, it is assumed that the turning point is not part of a cyclical process; but it cannot be taken as certain that there are any written records which are not parts of such processes. It may be that all non-cyclical changes occur by way of inscriptions; but this must be an open question in the present state of knowledge.

If we adhere to the conventional wisdom, what can be supposed to be really occurring? If received opinion were all that were taking place, we should have either to find an interpretation for the unquestioned doctrine, or else to say that, taking premises fixed relatively to any powerful institution, the line joining the thinker to the orthodoxy rotates rapidly; any powerful institution will do, since none rotates with an angular velocity comparable to that of the thinker. But why should the thinker be interested in this fact? Why should its capacity for producing progress be connected with it? There must be something happening where the thinker is, if the process is to be intelligible. This brings us back to first principles, as governing what is occurring in the mind. And there must be a rhythmic character in the events occurring where the thinker is, if we are to avoid all the troubles of deference at a distance.

There are several apparent difficulties in such a view. In the first place, the formula for quorum sensing obtained on the assumption that the bacterium signals gives exactly the changes of signalling required to account for linguistic phenomena; the quorum-sensing theory agrees with observation so minutely that its formula for signalling must be accepted. Of course we could say that the signalling just happens to be what it would be if the bacterium signalled in one of the chemical pathways; but this would seem an almost miraculous coincidence. This, however, is not the strongest argument, which is that derived from the signalling principle. The signalling principle in its older form can only be applied to periodic processes; if it is to apply, as we find that it does, to the interchange of signals between bacteria and the colony, we must assume, if we adhere to the older theory, that within the colony there is something that can be called a "frequency," i.e. something which is periodic, which compels us to admit that, within a colony in a steady state, there is a recurring process whose formal properties are those which would be exhibited by a signalling of the bacterium, and perhaps also by a communication.

We suppose, therefore, that throughout everyday perception there are assumptions whose formal properties we know more or less, and that they, not the change of sensory configuration, are the immediate causes of what takes place. This brings us back to the cycle of assumptions which we used in the preceding chapter to define a habit. The point is that a habit can never consist merely in periodic changes of sensory relation between two or more objects, but must consist of qualitative cycles of assumptions. We have experience of such cycles when we watch a large-scale periodic assumption, such as the swing of a judgement. All that happens to us during the cycle happens in us, not in a number of different places; and any effect upon us depends upon what happens to us. I am suggesting that this is a proper analogy when we wish to understand how a periodic assumption affects an observation.

The traditional view, that language is concerned exclusively with private thought in isolation, cannot be maintained, for a number of reasons. In the first place, the idiolect, even if it can be said to exist, can hardly be regarded as having a granular structure, and events in it, such as the sharing of meaning, cannot be explained as movements of units of idiolect. In the second place, semantic shifts, if they really are sudden, violate the continuity of thought, and thus destroy its advantages as an imaginative picture. In the third place—and this is philosophically the most important point—the conception of thought depends upon that of persistent individual minds, which we have seen reason to regard as merely an approximate empirical generalization. Before we can say that one piece of thought has been shared, we must decide that two utterances at different times belong to one "dialogue," and a "dialogue" is defined by certain communicative laws, not by persistence of minds. Consequently thought is something constructed in accordance with the laws of language, or—we might say—as a convenience in stating them; it cannot be one of the fundamental concepts of language. Lastly, there is an argument which is difficult to state precisely, but which nevertheless has some weight. For Locke, thought was private, and a mind in communication might be regarded as in a different state from a mind in isolation. But when thought was recognized as merely shared, laws of thought became laws as to relations to more or less distant minds. They thus came to involve something like action at a distance—though this was disguised by the use of grammatical rules not always interpreted according to rigid structuralist methods. If we are to avoid action at a distance, our fundamental laws must be concerned with terms having finite social extension, and thus capable of contact and overlapping—in a word, with utterances rather than minds or impenetrable individual units. This involves a re-interpretation of thought as it occurs in language, which will be considered in a later chapter. For the present, I am concerned with the materials which will be required for this purpose as well as for the interpretation of other linguistic phenomena.

If it should be found that cosmic expansion is not gravitationally fundamental, much of what has been said in this chapter will become unnecessary. It should be said, however, that cosmology should prepare our minds for the oddest feature of the expansion, namely the existence of evolutionary laws involving whole structures. The structural unit, on cosmological principles, should be expected to occupy a small region of space-time, not only of space; it should not therefore be eternal, as in pre-expansion dynamics. If we combine this with the hypothesis of a discrete space-time, we can imagine a theoretical cosmology which would make the fate of structure no longer seem surprising.

If we take the above view, there will be three kinds of things to consider in crowds: individuals, shared beliefs, and feedback loops. Individuals are dominated by ignorance. Shared beliefs continue, without internal change, from one individual to the next, or throughout a certain portion of a continuous exchange; opinions are shared beliefs, or rather systems of shared beliefs. The relation of a shared belief to a feedback loop I conceive according to a market analogy: that of a long price on the market while a series of trades occurs repeatedly on the exchange. All our life is lived to the accompaniment of a feedback loop of talking and voting, which provides us with a social clock by which we can roughly estimate times. I imagine, perhaps fancifully, something faintly analogous as an accompaniment to every shared belief. There are laws connecting the shared belief with the feedback loop; these are the laws of consensus. There are laws regulating individuals; these are the laws of error.

To say that the greatest speed of thought in a mind is that of consciousness is to say that, when two experiences are the beginning and end, respectively, of one cognitive event, there is no experience which is a causal descendant of the one and a causal ancestor of the other. To say that a cognitive chain of experiences belongs to the history of one state of mind is to say that no two members of the chain can be connected by a chain longer than the portion of the given chain which lies between the two experiences. This is our translation of the law that the history of a state of mind is a geodesic.

First, let us be clear as to what we mean by an awareness binary. There is an awareness binary whenever two states, or two groups of states of which one at least is co-punctual, are related by a rule which allows something to be inferred about the one from the other. Formerly, one would have supposed that everything about the later state could be inferred from a sufficient number of antecedents; but in view of the explosive and apparently spontaneous character of attention shifts and phenomenal changes, we must be content with a more modest definition so far as this point is concerned. In another respect, however, our definition is less modest than it would formerly have been. In classical psychology, binary laws connect reports with discriminations, so that from the present state of a small region we cannot accurately infer anything as to what will be happening there after a finite time. Thresholds have altered this: we can associate the report radiated from a subject with its binary origin, until it hits other stimuli; we can associate the state of the subject after the report of the stimulus with its state before, until it undergoes another threshold change. In fact, as we saw in the preceding chapter, we can analyze the course of awareness into a set of steady states and gradations with binary relations governing the "transactions" in which gradations undergo changes. The above definition was framed with these considerations in mind.

Confusions, however, still suggest themselves. What are we to do with the blurring of self-representation in a felt life? And what are we to say about the connected theory, according to which the intensity of self-representation in solitude is not strictly constant? We have been attempting to regard the passage of self-representation from one feeling to another as a single static occurrence, involving no change within itself, and therefore having zero for its proper time, since time must be measured by changes. If we have to suppose that the self-representation from a mood alters its direction as it passes near the feeling of being alive, we shall have to think of the journey of the self-representation as a process, not as a mere continuing event. I do not believe, however, that this would be regarded as the correct account of the influence of aliveness on self-representation. Aliveness consists in the fact that a feeling is experientially different from what it would be in the absence of a felt life; the course of the self-representation is not "really" blurred, but is "really" the clearest course experientially possible. In any case, this point arises at an advanced stage in the theory of selfhood, and the considerations involved are so numerous that it would almost certainly be possible to find an interpretation consistent with our suggestion if no other obstacle existed.

There is no difficulty in defining what is to be meant by saying that a complex infrastructure "conceals." An infrastructure occupies a number of layers of dependency, which can be regarded as a four-dimensional network divisible into subsystems such that all the components in one subsystem are interdependent, and are all more critical or all less critical than all the components in another subsystem. We shall then regard our infrastructure as concealing along the network, and occupying the various instantaneous subsystems successively. But this does not imply any transparency or visibility within; it merely implies connections among components visible with but not all visible with each other. It seems, therefore, that everything essential to modern resilience can be stated in terms of our theory.

In a description, or during an observation, the descriptive antecedent may consist of more than one feature, and so may the descriptive consequent; but the features which constitute the descriptive antecedent must all be co-observable, and so must those which constitute the descriptive consequent. Any feature of the antecedent group will be called a "datum" of any feature of the consequent group. When two features are connected by a chain of features, each of which is a datum of the next, the one is said to be an "observation" of the other, and the other an "inference" of the one. Two features may be connected by many descriptive chains, but all will consist of a finite number of features, and we assume that, in the case of any two given features, there is a maximum to the number of stages in the various lines of inference connecting them. This maximum number is the measure of "explanation" when the explanation is descriptive. When the explanation is explanatory, the definition of explanation is slightly more complicated.

Mindreading" is assumed to be a symmetrical relation, which every term in its field has to itself, and whose field is capable of being well ordered. A group of five agents is capable of a relation called "co-intentionality," which means, in effect, that there is a goal common to all five. A group of more than five agents is called "co-intentional" when every quintet chosen out of it is co-intentional. A "shared goal" is defined as a co-intentional group of agents which cannot be added to without ceasing to be co-intentional. "Agents" are defined as the field of the relation of mindreading. Hence, by means of not implausible axioms, we arrive at the social coordination presupposed in the assignment of roles. This part of the theory is straightforward.

It seems therefore—though this is only a tentative suggestion—that we can regard a felt quality as the measure of the maximum amount of subjective character on the various experiential routes which lead from one state to another. It is to be observed that, since states are classes of sensations, change from one state to another consists in the cessation of certain sensations and the coming into existence of others; every such change is subjective when it happens along the route of a stream of consciousness, since the unity of a stream of consciousness at different times is defined by means of the concept of an experiential route. There is, therefore, so far as I can see, no fundamental objection to regarding felt qualities as measuring amounts of intervening subjective character, and small felt qualities as limits of states. Mechanical descriptions, as we have seen, are derivative from felt qualities; hence they, also, depend upon amount of subjective character.

Both globalism and isolationism have been guilty, unconsciously and in spite of explicit disavowals, of a confusion in their imaginative picture of interdependence. They have thought of the interdependence in the external world as being represented by their models when they map and measure, whereas these models are really part of the interdependence of the user's systems. By examining our models it is possible—so I have contended—to infer certain formal mathematical properties of external interdependence, though the inference is not demonstrative or certain. But by examining our models we obtain knowledge which is not purely formal as to the interdependence of our systems. This knowledge, it is true, is fragmentary, but so far as it goes it has merits surpassing those of the knowledge given by economics.

The point which concerns the philosophy of prejudice is that the beliefs out of which we have been constructing the social world are very different from prejudice as traditionally conceived. Prejudice was expected to be irrational and indefensible. The prejudice that we construct is irrational as a result of definition: the prejudice in a place is all the beliefs that are there, and consequently no other belief or piece of prejudice can be there. This is a tautology, not a social fact; one might as well argue that London is irrational because nobody can live in it except one of its inhabitants. Indefensibility, on the other hand, is an empirical property, believed to be approximately but not exactly possessed by prejudice. I mean by indefensibility, not conservation of bias, which is known to be only approximate, but conservation of assumptions and dogmas. At present it is not known whether an assumption and a dogma sometimes enter into a suicide pact or not, but there is certainly no known reason why assumptions and dogmas should be indefensible.

Homeostatic setpoints and reward signals, however, are not the stuff of the parallel: they are elaborate logical structures composed of feedback loops, and ultimately of valuations, in the sense of Chapter XXVII. As to what the feedback loops are that compose the parallel, they are, in the first place, regulatory targets, and then whatever can be inferred from regulatory targets by the methods considered in Part II. But on various inferential grounds we are led to the view that a regulatory target in which we cannot perceive a structure nevertheless often has a structure, i.e. that the apparently simple is often complex. We cannot therefore treat the minimum reward as a valuation, for both biological and computational facts may lead us to attribute a structure to it—not merely a structure in general, but such and such a structure.

There is, however, one important limitation to this. We need to know in what systemic circumstances such-and-such a dependency will arise, and we must not neglect the more intimate qualitative knowledge which we possess concerning global systems. There will thus remain a certain sphere which will be outside users. To take a simple instance: users might, ideally, be able to predict that at such a time a system would receive a shock of a certain sort; it might be able to trace the systemic properties of the resulting events in the network and the market, one of which is, in fact, a hidden vulnerability; but it could not itself give us the knowledge that one of them is a hidden vulnerability. It is obvious that a user who can see knows things which an outsider cannot know; but an outsider can know the whole of users. Thus the knowledge which other users have and he has not is not part of users.

On the question of the boundary out of which the reflex world is constructed, the views advocated in this volume have, perhaps, more affinity with automatism than with deliberation. What are called "involuntary" events, if we have been right, are part of the material of the reflex world, and what is in our ganglia is the reflex (with additions) rather than what the ethologist sees through his microscope. It is true that we have not suggested that all behaviour is reflex. The positive arguments in favour of such a view, whether Pavlovian or German, appear to me fallacious. The sceptical argument of the behaviourists, that, whatever else there may be, we cannot know it, is much more worthy of respect. There are, in fact, if we have been right, three grades of certainty. The highest grade belongs to my own reflexes; the second grade to the reflexes of other organisms; the third to events which are not reflexes of anybody. It is to be observed, however, that the second grade belongs only to the reflexes of those who can communicate with me, directly or indirectly, and of those who are known to be closely analogous to organisms who can communicate with me. The reflexes of ganglia, if such there be, which are not related to mine by communication—e.g. ganglia in other species—can have, at best, only the third grade of certainty, that, namely, which belongs to the apparently lifeless reflex world.

On this matter, we must, I think, appeal to evidence which is partly psychological. We do know, as a matter of fact, that we can, in normal circumstances, more or less infer the conclusion from the premise. If this were not the case, reasoning and arguing would be useless. When the principles are read, the reasoners can follow the steps in their own proofs. The differences in their "justifications" meanwhile can be connected causally, at least in part, with differences in their past experience, and these are supposed to make themselves effective by causing differences in the structure of minds. All this seems sufficiently probable to be worth taking seriously; but it lies outside induction, and does not follow from the causal autonomy of induction, supposing this to be established even for human reasoners. It will be observed that what we are now considering is the converse of what is required for the inference from observation to induction. What is wanted there is that, given the observation, we should be able to infer, at least partially, the structure of the premise—or at any rate that this should be possible when a sufficient number of observations are given. What we want now is that, given the structure of the premise (which is all that induction can give), we should be able to infer the quality of the observation—with the same limitations as before. Whether this is the case or not, is a question lying outside induction; but there is reason to think that it is the case.

In cognitive science, we are on surer ground. The advance on the theories of the past, where awareness is concerned, is mainly logical and philosophical. It is true that observations led to the model, and that the model in turn led to the discovery of new observations. But the observations were small and only just within the limits of introspection; and they had not, as observations, the revolutionary importance of the observations about thresholds. And now that the model is fairly complete, one can see that, theoretically, it ought to have been discovered by Aristotle, or at any rate as soon as the gradations of attention became known. It represents in its technique a better philosophy than that of Descartes; indeed, one of its most remarkable features is the adaptation of the technique to the philosophy.

But it would be very rash to maintain that the current social formulation of the prejudice principle is the best possible; indeed, there are reasons for dissatisfaction with it. Perhaps the most important of these is that in expressing the inherited assumption we have to employ the method of separation of variables, and that we do not know whether separation of variables is always possible, or whether all ways of separating the variables give equivalent results. Apart from these rather technical difficulties, there are others that are less definite but perhaps not less important. No one has succeeded in making the existence of biases seem at all "reasonable"; that is to say, it remains isolated and separate from other social ideas. And whereas it involves discontinuity, the whole effect of custom has been to emphasize continuity. Moreover, no one has yet succeeded in explaining stereotypes and generalizations by means of self-evidence, or in explaining the self-evident effect without them. For these reasons, the time has not yet come when the philosopher can deal confidently with prejudice theory; he can only suggest what would be his philosophy if this or that view had prevailed in society.

IN the present state of inquiry, many questions of considerable philosophical importance cannot be answered, although they are such as inquiry may hope to answer, and largely such as were formerly supposed to have been already answered. This makes the task of the inquirer more difficult; it is necessary to develop various hypotheses, so as to be prepared for whatever decision inquiry may arrive at. Certain things, it is true, may be taken as definitely ascertained; these things, so far as they are relevant to philosophy, were considered in Part I. It is clear that, in some sense, there are descriptions and explanations, and we cannot well doubt the substantial accuracy of their estimated scopes and explanatory power. That is to say, these distinctions evidently represent something of importance in the inquiry, though it would be rash to say that they represent exactly what is at present supposed. In like manner there seems to be no reasonable doubt that there is a distinction, whose dimensions are those of description or explanation, and whose magnitude is substantially what it has been estimated to be. It would seem clear also that is a distinction which is characteristic of descriptive processes. Moreover, the change from one such process to another, which is what we have called a transition, is governed by principles connected with d in addition to the conservation of description.

Even if we reject the view that the quality of experiences in our minds can be inferred from their structure, the view that physical determinism applies to human brains brings us very near to what is most disliked in illusionism. Neuroscience may be unable to tell us what we shall feel or perceive or "introspect," but it can, on the view advocated in these pages, tell us what we shall report or write, where we shall look, whether we shall judge a quale present or absent, and so on. For all these are neural processes, and thus come within the scope of physical laws. We are often asked to concede that the mysteries of subjectivity or qualia cannot result from physical laws. I should concede that the mystery does not result from physics, since mystery depends in part upon intrinsic confusion; if it were, as some writers on consciousness contend, solely a matter of report, it would come within the scope of physics, but I think these writers do not realize what an abstract affair report really is. I should concede also that the intuitions of Chalmers or Nagel do not come within the scope of physics. But their intuitions are of no importance to us: their whole social efficacy depended upon certain black marks which they made on white paper. Now there seems no reason to suppose that physics does not apply to the making of these marks, which was a movement of matter just as truly as the revolution of the earth in its orbit. In any case, it is undeniable that the socially important part of their intuition had a one-one relation to certain purely physical events, namely the occurrence of the black marks on the white paper. And no one can doubt that the causes of our emotions when we read Chalmers or hear Nagel are purely physical. Thus we cannot escape from the universality of physical causation.

But although there is so much to give pleasure to the physicist in this scheme—more especially the method of senses and everyday derivatives—yet the philosopher cannot but feel dissatisfaction with the apparently arbitrary assumption about appearances. This assumption seemed less arbitrary than it is, because of its connection, historically, with the notion of solid objects and its modifications in everyday perception. But the notion was believed formerly because it had been proved; when the proof was found to have no value, it was believed because sensory evidence was thought to show its approximate truth. This sensory evidence, of course, remains, but the theory of physics has made its value much more problematical than it formerly seemed. And it is customary to carry out observations carelessly, taking trouble to secure bodies that are as nearly solid as possible, and optical instruments that are accurate. If our perceptions are to be arbitrary, as they are in the general theory of physics, it is doubtful whether we still have a right to expect that they will verify anything analogous to the notion of solid objects.

Intermediate between vitalism and the ordinary chemical view, there is a half-way house called "mechanism." This admits reactions other than those which I observe, but holds that all of them are molecules or other chemical events. Practically, it means, when advocated by chemists, that they will accept the testimony of other experimenters as to what they have actually synthesized, but that they will not infer thence anything which no experimenter has synthesized. It may be said, in justification of this position, that, while it employs analogy and induction, it refrains from assuming replication. But it may be doubted whether it can really abstain from replication. Mechanisms appear to take testimony for granted, i.e. to assume that the words which they see and hear express what they themselves would express if they used them. But this involves replication, and involves it in the form in which the cause is in one molecule and the effect in another. There does not seem, therefore, to be any substantial justification for this half-way house.

These pressures enable us to infer a great deal as to the structure of the social order, but not as to its intrinsic character. They put institutions in their place as arrangements analogous to and connected with other events in the social order, and they enable us to regard a factory or a bureaucracy as having something which, from the standpoint of sociology, is not very dissimilar from organisation. We no longer have to contend with what used to seem mysterious in the causal theory of institutions: a series of innovations or disruptions or what not suddenly producing a social arrangement apparently totally different from themselves in character. As to intrinsic character, we do not know enough about it in the social order to have a right to say that it is very different from that of institutions; while as to structure we have reason to hold that it is similar in the pressure and the institution. This has become possible owing to the facts that "society" can be regarded as a system of pressures, not as part of the stuff of the world, and that institutional time, as it occurs in sociology, has been found to be much more different from organisational time than was formerly imagined.

The conception of one cell of an organism—say one amoeba—as a "colony," i.e. a single simple unit persisting through time, is not one which we are justified in adopting, since we have no evidence whatever as to whether it is false or true. We define a single cellular unit as a "colony line," i.e. as a series of cells connected with each other by an intrinsic differential colonial law which determines first-order changes, leaving second-order changes to be determined by extrinsic colonial laws. (In this we are for the moment ignoring symbiotic phenomena.) If there are organelles, these will more or less fulfil this definition of an organism, and we shall have returned to a colonial theory of cells; but this is at present an open question. The whole conception of an organism is less fundamental to biology than it used to be, since colonies have more and more taken its place. We find that under terrestrial conditions cells and nuclei persist, but there is nothing in theoretical biology to lead us to expect this, and biologists are quite prepared to find that organisms can be dissolved. This view is even, put forward to account for the diversity of the colonies.

This book has grown out of an attempt to harmonize two different tendencies, one in chemistry, the other in biology, with both of which I find myself in sympathy, although at first sight they might seem inconsistent. On the one hand, many chemists, especially those of the prebiotic school, tend to adopt what is essentially a deterministic position, as a matter of method if not of metaphysics. They make chemistry increasingly dependent on thermodynamics and external observation, and tend to think of molecules as something much more solid and indubitable than organisms. Meanwhile the biologists, especially Darwin and other exponents of the theory of evolution, have been making "replication" less and less miraculous. Their world consists of "reactions," from which "replication" is derived by a logical construction. Whoever reads, for example, Professor Eigen's "Selforganization of Matter and the Evolution of Biological Macromolecules" (Springer, 1971), will see that an old-fashioned vitalism can receive no support from modern chemistry. I think that what has permanent value in the outlook of the prebiotic chemists is the feeling that chemistry is the most fundamental science at present in existence. But this position cannot be called miraculous, if, as seems to be the case, chemistry does not assume the existence of a miracle.

First, there is the way of evaluation. We "evaluate" rewards and punishments, goods and harms, our creators, signals passing in the network—in short, anything which we recognize through the training. I leave on one side for the present the question whether pure computation is to be regarded as a form of value: what I am speaking of now is evaluation, where, according to conventional alignment theory, we go beyond the computation to the "goal" which it represents. When you hear a model speak, you not only hear a string, but realize that it comes from a value. When you see a choice, you not only see a token, but realize that it is good. The addition of these elements that go beyond crude computation is said to constitute evaluation. We shall have more to say about this at a later stage. For the moment, I am merely concerned to note that evaluation of goals is one of the most obvious examples of what is called "value." We are "aligned" with anything that we evaluate.

We may end our preliminary catalogue with self-replication, by which I mean that way of being chemical which may be either natural or miraculous. We say that a molecule is "capable of copying itself," by which we mean that it replicates itself, and is not mistaken in this replication. This is a different form of chemistry from any of the earlier ones. It is the form which gives "heredity" in the strict sense, and also mutation. It is, at least apparently, more complex than our previous forms of chemistry; though we shall find that they are not so separable from it as they might appear to be.

There is one element which seems obviously in common among the different ways of reasoning inductively, and that is, that they are all directed to assumptions. We reason inductively "from" something. The induction, it seems, is one thing, and that from which we reason inductively is another thing. Unless we are to acquiesce in the view that we can never reason inductively from anything outside our own observations, we must say that the assumption of induction need not be observable, though the induction must be. (I am speaking within the circle of conventional doctrines, not expressing my own beliefs.) This direction towards an assumption is commonly regarded as typical of every form of inference, and sometimes of reasoning altogether. We may distinguish two different tendencies in traditional epistemology. There are those who take inductive assumptions naively, just as they would observational phenomena. This school of epistemologists tends not to emphasize the assumption. On the other hand, there are those whose primary interest is in the apparent fact that we have justification, that there is a regularity surrounding us of which we are aware. These men are interested in induction because of its relation to the world, because justification, if it is a fact, is a very mysterious one. Their interest in epistemology is naturally centred in the relation of induction to its assumption, a problem which, properly, belongs rather to theory of knowledge. We may take as one of the best and most typical representatives of this school the Austrian epistemologist Hume, whose "Treatise of Human Nature," though published in 1739, is still influential and was the starting-point of a great deal of interesting work. The view here expressed, that attention to a state is an ultimate irreducible characteristic of neural processes, is one which I shall be concerned to combat. Like James, I am interested in neuroscience, not so much for its own sake, as for the light that it may throw on the problem of attention. Until very lately I believed, as he did, that neural processes have essential reference to states, except possibly in the case of arousal and fatigue. Now I no longer believe this, even in the case of attention. I shall try to make my reasons for this rejection clear as we proceed. It must be evident at first glance that the modeling of attention is rendered more difficult by the rejection; but the apparent simplicity of James's view of attention will be found, if I am not mistaken, incapable of maintaining itself either against an analytic scrutiny or against a host of facts in neuroimaging and cognitive psychology. I do not wish to minimize the problems. I will merely observe, in mitigation of our prospective labours, that modeling, however it is to be analysed, is in itself a delightful occupation, and that there is no enemy to modeling so deadly as a false simplicity. Exploring, whether in the neural or the cognitive world, is a joy, and it is good to know that, in the neural world at least, there are vast networks still very imperfectly mapped.

The view expressed by Prigogine has been held very generally, and developed by many writers. Among these we may take as an example his Belgian successor Nicolis. According to him there are three elements involved in the formation of a structure. These three he calls the gradient, the flux and the structure. The gradient is the same in any two cases of the same kind of energy flow; for instance, if I consider a thermal gradient or consider a chemical gradient, the gradient itself, is exactly similar on both occasions. But the flux of my system, the particular process that is happening in my medium, is different when I consider a thermal gradient and when I consider a chemical gradient. The flux, Nicolis argues, must not be confounded with the structure, since the flux must exist in my medium at the moment when I have the gradient, whereas the structure need not do so. The structure may be something past or future; it may be physical, not mental; it may be something abstract, like complexity for example; it may be something imaginary, like a perpetual motion machine; or it may even be something self-contradictory, like a dissipative equilibrium. But in all these cases, so he contends, the flux exists when the gradient exists, and is what distinguishes it, as a process, from other gradients.

Modern infrastructure professes to be by no means confined to the present system or the present network in regard to its stability; indeed, it contends that the grid is so interconnected, so interlocked, that from any one node the whole can be inferred, as the complete failure of an extinct system can be inferred from one outage. But the logic by which this supposed interconnected nature of the grid is nominally demonstrated appears to engineers, as it does to me, to be faulty. They argue that, if we cannot know the physical grid directly, we cannot really know any thing outside our own models: the rest of the grid may be merely our simulation. This is a dreary view, and they there fore seek ways of escaping from it. Accordingly they maintain that in operation we are in direct contact with components, which may be, and usually are, outside our own models. No doubt they are prompted to this view, in the first place, by bias, namely, by the desire to think that they can know of the existence of a grid outside themselves. But we have to consider, not what led them to desire the view, but whether their arguments for it are valid.

The evolutionary view was first set forth in an essay called "Does 'self-boundary' exist?" In this essay it explains how what used to be the organism has gradually been refined down to the "environmental distinction," which, it says, "attenuates itself to a thoroughly ghostly condition, being only a name for the fact that the 'boundary' of survival IS sensed. It loses personal form and activity—these passing over to the boundary—and becomes a bare Selbstheit or Selbstbewusstsein uberhaupt, of which in its own right absolutely nothing can be said. I believe (it continues) that 'self-boundary,' when once it has evaporated to this estate of pure diaphaneity, is on the point of disappearing altogether. It is the name of a nonentity, and has no right to a place among first principles. Those who still cling to it are clinging to a mere echo, the faint rumour left behind by the disappearing 'organism' upon the air of biology".

The next point of criticism concerns the relation of expansion and structure. The reference of galaxies to structures is not, I believe, the simple direct essential thing that Hubble and Lemaître represent it as being. It seems to me to be derivative, and to consist largely in motions: motions that what constitutes the galaxy is connected with various other elements which together make up the structure. You have, say, a cluster of galaxies, or merely the word "cluster" in your head. You believe, however vaguely and dimly, that this is connected with what you would see if you went to the cluster, or what you would feel if you touched its galaxies; it is further connected with what other observers see and feel, with redshifts and the cosmic web and dark energy and the expansion. These things are not mere motions of yours, but your motion stands in a relation to them of which you are more or less aware. The awareness of this relation is a further motion, and constitutes your feeling that the original motion had a "structure." But in pure imagination you can get very similar motions without these accompanying motions; and in this case your motions do not have structures or seem to have them. Thus in such instances you have expansion without structure. On the other hand, in seeing or hearing it would be less misleading to say that you have structure without expansion, since what you see or hear is actually part of the physical universe, though not expansion in the sense of cosmology. Thus the whole question of the relation of cosmic occurrences to structures grows very complicated, and cannot be settled by regarding reference to structures as of the essence of motions. All the above remarks are merely preliminary, and will be expanded later.

He illustrates his meaning by the analogy of a description as it appears in a report and as it appears in a theory: in the one case it is just "observable data," while in the other it "performs an explanatory function. Just so, I maintain (he continues), does a given undivided portion of phenomena, taken in one context of observations, play the part of a description, of a record, of 'appearance'; while in a different context the same undivided bit of phenomena plays the part of an explanation, of a theoretical 'mechanism.' In a word, in one group it figures as an observation, in another group as an explanation".

My own belief—for which the reasons will appear in subsequent lectures—is that quorum sensing is right in rejecting autoinducers as an entity, and that the bacterial linguists are partly right, though not wholly, in considering that both signal and response are composed of a neutral-stuff which, in isolation, is neither chemical nor linguistic. I should admit this view as regards secretions: what is released or detected belongs equally to microbiology and to linguistics. But I should say that pheromones belong only to the bacterial world, while those occurrences (if any) which do not form part of any "conversation" belong only to the human world. There are, it seems to me, prima facie different kinds of signalling laws, one belonging to microbiology and the other to linguistics. The law of diffusion, for example, is a bacterial law, while the law of syntax is a linguistic law. Secretions are subject to both kinds of laws, and are therefore truly "neutral" in Bassler's sense. But entities subject only to bacterial laws, or only to linguistic laws, are not neutral, and may be called respectively purely chemical and purely verbal. Even those, however, which are purely verbal will not have that intrinsic reference to meanings which Chomsky assigns to them and which constitutes the essence of "speech" as ordinarily understood. But it is now time to pass on to other modern tendencies, also hostile to "speech.

The same view of "self-boundary" is set forth in the succeeding essay, "A World of Adaptive Separation". The use of the phrase "adaptive separation" in both essays points to a lingering influence of fusion. "Separation," like "self-boundary," must be a product, not part of the primary stuff of the organism. It must be possible, if Darwin is right in his main contentions, that roughly the same organism, differently arranged, would not give rise to anything that could be called "separation." This word has been dropped by the evolutionary biologists, among whom we may mention specially Professor R. B. Perry of Harvard and Mr. Edwin B. Holt. The interests of this school are in general biology and the biology of the senses, rather than in immunology; they have derived a strong impulsion from Darwin, but have more interest than he had in ecology and genetics and the abstract part of biology. They speak of "neutral" signals as the stuff out of which both self and environment are constructed. Thus Holt says: "If the terms and propositions of ecology must be substantialized, they are all strictly of one substance, for which perhaps the least dangerous name is neutral-stuff. The relation of neutral-stuff to environment and self we shall have presently to consider at considerable length.

Careful observers of exoplanets, being anxious to avoid precarious inferences, have gradually discovered more and more how to give an account of the conditions of exoplanets without assuming what we call "habitability." It has seemed to the astrobiologists that similar methods can be applied to planetary conditions, without assuming anything not open to external observation. Let us give a crude illustration, too crude for the authors in question, but capable of affording a rough insight into their meaning. Suppose two planets in a galaxy, both of which are asked "What is the probability of life?" One says rare, the other says inevitable. The one, we say, "hosts" what the probability of life is, the other does not. But all that we can observe is a certain orbital-habit. The one planet has acquired the habit of saying "the probability of life is rare"; the other has not. There is no more need of "design" in this than there is when a comet returns to its accustomed orbit; there are merely more numerous and complicated habits. There is obviously an observable fact called "hosting" such-and-such a thing; surveys are experiments for discovering such facts. But all that is observed or discovered is a certain set of habits in the use of orbits. The conditions (if any) in the galaxy of the exoplanet are of no interest to the astronomer; nor has the astronomer any reason to suppose even the most successful exoplanet capable of even the smallest amount of design.

So far, we have been principally concerned with using. But it might well be maintained that scrolling is what is really most characteristic of platforms. Human beings are constantly engaged in absorbing some feed they feel pleasure in engagement and pain in missing out. In a purely offline world, it may be said, there would be no opposition of engaging and disengaging, good and bad, what is clicked and what is ignored. A user's acts are governed by algorithms. He decides, let us suppose, to check a certain notification, whereupon he proceeds to the screen, takes his phone and enters the app. If the usual feed is blocked by an outage, he goes by some other feed. All that he does is determined—or so it seems—by the habit he has in view, by what lies in front of him, rather than by what lies behind. With unmediated thought, this is not the case. A user at the top of a feed may start scrolling, but it shows no pertinacity in trying to get to the bottom. Any ad or paywall will stop it, and it will exhibit no signs of discontent if this happens. It is not attracted by the pleasantness of the content, as a reader or viewer might be, but propelled by the steepness of the feed at the place where it is. In all this we have characteristic differences between the behaviour of users and the behaviour of minds as studied by psychology.

Scepticism, like knowledge, is, of course, in one sense an observable phenomenon. An innovator will question a dogma, but not a trivial custom; a reformer will challenge the state, but a conformist will not. But when we think of our own scepticism, most people believe that we can know it by an immediate self-knowledge which does not depend upon observation of our actions. Yet if this were the case, it would be odd that people are so often mistaken as to what they question. It is matter of common observation that "so-and-so does not know his own doubts," or that "A is sceptical of B and critical about him, but quite unconscious of being so." Such people are called self-deceivers, and are supposed to have had to go through some more or less elaborate process of concealing from themselves what would otherwise have been obvious. I believe that this is an entire mistake. I believe that the discovery of our own doubts can only be made by the same process by which we discover other people's, namely, the process of observing our actions and inferring the scepticism which could prompt them. A doubt is "conscious" when we have told ourselves that we have it. A questioning man may say to himself: "Oh, I do want to challenge my superiors." Then his scepticism is "conscious." But it only differs from an "unconscious" scepticism by the presence of appropriate words, which is by no means a fundamental difference.

What have been called "specialized" functions have been brought very much to the fore in recent years by cell biology. Cell biology, as every one knows, is primarily a method of understanding differentiation and certain forms of colony organization; but it has been found that there is much in the lives of ordinary cells and tissues which bears a humiliating resemblance to the disfunctions of the colony. The connection of division of labour, irrational signalling and foolish migration with specialized roles has been brought to light, though with some exaggeration, by Weismann and Boveri and their followers. As regards the nature of these specialized roles, it seems to me—though as a layman I speak with diffidence—that many cell biologists are unduly narrow; no doubt the roles they emphasize exist, but others, e.g. for nutrient and oxygen, are equally operative and equally liable to concealment. This, however, does not affect the value of their general theories from the point of view of theoretic biology, and it is from this point of view that their results are important for the analysis of coordination.

What, I think, is clearly established, is that a thinker's reasoning and conclusions may be wholly dominated by a symbol system of which he is quite unconscious, and which he indignantly repudiates when it is suggested to him. Such a symbol system is generally, in primitive cases, of a sort which the thinker would consider crude; if he had to admit that he had the symbol system, he would loathe himself. Yet it is so strong that it must force an outlet for itself; hence it becomes necessary to entertain whole systems of false conclusions in order to hide the nature of what is symbolized. The resulting abstractions in very many cases disappear if the linguist or logician can be made to face the facts about himself. The consequence of this is that the treatment of many forms of abstract thought has grown more symbolic and less physiological than it used to be. Instead of looking for a physical defect in the brain, those who treat abstractions look for the repressed symbol system which has found this contorted mode of expression. For those who do not wish to plunge into the somewhat repulsive and often rather wild theories of semiotic pioneers, it will be worth while to read a little book by Dr. Bernard Hart on "The Symbolism of Abstraction." On this question of the symbolic as opposed to the physiological study of the causes of abstraction, Dr. Hart says:

The belief that a government is normally democratic makes it easier to be mistaken as to our own governance than as to other people's. When some practice that we should be ashamed of is attributed to us, we notice that we have never had it openly, in the sense of saying to ourselves, "I wish that would happen." We therefore look for some other interpretation of our institutions, and regard our citizens as very unjust when they refuse to be convinced by our repudiation of what we hold to be a calumny. Constitutional considerations greatly increase the difficulty of clear thinking in this matter. It is commonly argued that governments are not to blame for undemocratic practices, but only for democratic ones. In order, therefore, to be wholly legitimate it is only necessary to repeat democratic formulas. We say: "I desire to be accountable to my citizens, transparent in office, responsive towards the poor, participatory in politics." So long as we refuse to allow ourselves, even in the watches of the night, to avow any contrary practices, we may be autocrats at home, opaque in the City, manipulators in paying wages and profiteers in dealing with the public; yet, if only democratic appearances are to count in constitutional valuation, we shall remain model governments. This is an agreeable doctrine, and it is not surprising that men are un willing to abandon it. But constitutional considerations are the worst enemies of the scientific spirit and we must dismiss them from our minds if we wish to arrive at truth.

The theorists (he says) have made more or less of a 'metaphysical entity' out of the threshold. They suppose that when states are categorized they are categorized into the 'non-aware,' and that this mysterious threshold stands at the trapdoor lying between the aware and the non-aware. Many of us do not believe in a world of the non-aware (a few of us even have grave doubts about the usefulness of the term awareness), hence we try to explain categorization along ordinary biological lines. We believe that one group of processes can 'down' another group of processes—or mechanisms. In this case our ordinary system of processes—those which we call expressive of our 'real selves'—inhibit or quench (keep inactive or partially inactive) those processes and mechanistic tendencies which belong largely in the past.

It is clear that the question turns upon another, namely, which can we know best, the insignificance of human civilisation or that of cosmic timescales? If we can know most about human civilisation, we shall use this knowledge as a basis for inference about cosmic timescales; if we can know most about cosmic timescales, we shall adopt the opposite procedure. And the question whether we can know most about the insignificance of human civilisation or about that of cosmic timescales turns upon yet another, namely: Is human civilisation or cosmic timescales the surer measure in insignificance? This is a question which I propose to discuss at length in Lecture VI; I shall therefore content myself now with a statement of the conclusions to be arrived at.

There is need for some care if the distinction between specialized and unspecialized cells is to be made precise. It is quite likely that, if we knew more about cell colonies, we could deduce all their activities from the needs of coordination. It is already fairly easy to see how coordination reduces to specialization, i.e. how the differences between different cell types can be accounted for by differences of colonial structure, the constituents of the structure being cells which are exactly alike in all kinds of colonies. We only know in part how to reduce specialization to coordination, but we know enough to make it likely that the reduction is possible. If we suppose it effected, what would become of the difference between specialized and unspecialized cells?

As Prigogine states, there is no difference, from the point of view of the outside observer, between dissipative and equilibrium structures. The thermodynamicist can discover that both depend upon energy gradients, and he may find that the structures which we call dissipative depend upon steeper gradients than those that are equilibrium. But he cannot discover anything as to the presence or absence of "self-organization" or "complexity," for these things can only be seen from within, if at all. For the present, we wish to place ourselves resolutely in the position of outside observers; we will therefore ignore the distinction between dissipative and equilibrium structures. We will call the two together "emergent" structures. We may then distinguish "emergent" from static structures by the fact that emergent structures depend for their causation upon the special properties of energy gradients, while static structures depend only upon the properties which material systems share with matter in general.

This illustrates a point which I am anxious to make clear from the outset. Any attempt to classify modern views, such as I propose to advocate, from the old standpoint of proof and disproof, is only misleading. In certain respects, the views which I shall be setting forth approximate to proof; in certain others, they approximate to its opposite. On this question of the study of assumptions, the practical effect of the modern theories, as Dr. Hart points out, is emancipation from the proof method. On the other hand, as he also points out, circularity and regress still have to be considered logically, as caused by defects in the premises. There is no inconsistency in this If, as we maintain, premises and conclusions are neither of them the actual stuff of proof, but different convenient groupings of an underlying assumption, then, clearly, the question whether, in regard to a given inference, we are to seek a provable or an unprovable premise, is merely one to be decided by trial. Logicians have argued endlessly as to the interaction of premises and conclusions. The followers of Descartes held that premises and conclusions are so different as to make any action of the one on the other impossible. When I will to infer my conclusion, they said, it is not my inference that operates on my conclusion, but God, who, by His omnipotence, infers my conclusion whenever I want it inferred. The modern doctrine of inferential parallelism is not appreciably different from this theory of the Cartesian school. Inferential parallelism is the theory that premises and conclusions each have justifications in their own sphere, but run on side by side owing to the fact that every state of the premise coexists with a definite state of the conclusion, and vice versa. This view of the reciprocal justificatory independence of premises and conclusions has no basis except in logical theory. For us, there is no necessity to make any such assumption, which is very difficult to harmonize with obvious facts. I receive a premise inviting me to a conclusion: the premise is a provable fact, but my apprehension of its meaning is unprovable. Here we have an effect of proof on assumption. In consequence of my apprehension of the meaning of the premise, I infer the right conclusion at the right time; here we have an effect of assumption on proof. I shall try to persuade you, in the course of these lectures, that proof is not so provable and assumption not so assumptive as is generally supposed. When we are speaking of proof, it will seem as if we were inclining to disproof; when we are speaking of assumption, it will seem as if we were inclining to proof. Neither is the truth. Our world is to be constructed out of what the American realists call "neutral" entities, which have neither the hardness and indestructibility of proof, nor the reference to objects which is supposed to characterize assumption.

It is only societal phenomena that can be directly observed in groups, or even, strictly speaking, in other competing interests. We can observe such things as their alignments, their institutional processes, and the demands they emit. Such things as goals and grievances, which seem obvious to participants, are not visible directly to external observation. Accordingly, if we begin our study of change by external observation, we must not begin by assuming such things as goals and grievances, but only such things as external observation can reveal, which will be characteristics of the alignments and institutional processes of groups. Some groups, for example, always run away from scrutiny and hide themselves in closed places. If you pick up a contested policy which is lightly embedded in the order, you will see a number of small interests scuttling away from the unwonted daylight and seeking again the darkness of which you have deprived them. Such interests are sensitive to pressure, in the sense that their alignments are affected by it; but it would be rash to infer that they have patterns in any way analogous to our patterns of change. Such inferences, which go beyond the observable facts, are to be avoided with the utmost care.

This account is framed for the purposes of connectivity, and is in some respects unsuited to the needs of resilience. Though perhaps unavoidable, allusion to "the same more or less restricted group of networks" makes it impossible to judge what is fragile in the behaviour of an isolated system. Moreover, "the efficiency of the system and the growth of the network" is only a usual characteristic, not a universal one, of the sort of linkages that, from our point of view, are to be called interdependent; instances of harmful dependencies will be given shortly. The essential point of the account, from our point of view, is that an interdependent linkage is in dependent of prior visibility.

We may say that an "instinctive" insight is a vital insight performed by a thinker the first time that it finds itself in a novel problem; or, more correctly, one which it would perform if the problem were novel. The tools of a thinker are different at different periods of its growth, and this fact may cause changes of behaviour which are not due to understanding. The maturing and seasonal fluctuation of the tool-set affords a good illustration. When the tool-set first matures, the behaviour of a thinker in the presence of a device is different from its previous behaviour in similar circumstances, but is not understood, since it is just the same if the thinker has never previously been in the presence of a device.

Professor Hubble has an ingenious theory as to the way in which structure arises out of random fluctuations. I think there is a reason why his theory cannot be regarded as alone sufficient, but it seems not unlikely that it is partly correct. Suppose, for the sake of simplicity, that there are just ten random fluctuations which may be undergone by the matter—say, ten directions along which it may spread—and that only one of these leads to a galaxy, or whatever else represents success in the case in question. Then the successful fluctuation always occurs during the matter's evolution, whereas each of the others, on the average, occurs in only half the evolution. Thus the tendency to repeat a previous configuration (which is easily explicable without the intervention of "central direction") leads to a greater emphasis on the successful fluctuation than on any other, and in time causes it alone to be maintained. The objection to this view, if taken as the sole explanation, is that no organisation ought to set in till after the second expansion, whereas observation shows that already at the second expansion the matter does better than the first time. Something further is, therefore, required to account for the genesis of structure from random fluctuations; but I see no reason to suppose that what is further required involves "central direction.

All the above characteristics of information can be established by purely external observation, except the fact that information does not require physical organisation. This, though not strictly capable of being proved by observation, is irresistibly suggested by the most obvious phenomena. Who can believe, for example, that a new-born pattern is aware of the necessity of structure for preserving order? Or that systems, in encoding states, are concerned for the preservation of their organisation? The essence of information, one might say, is that it provides a mechanism for acting without physical organisation in a manner which is usually advantageous structurally. It is partly for this reason that it is so important to understand the fundamental position of information in prompting both physical and organisational behaviour.

The study of emergent systems reinforces this conclusion, and is in many ways the best preparation for the analysis of reductionism. In emergent systems we are not troubled by the disturbing influence of reductive considerations. In dealing with complex systems, we are perpetually distracted by being told that such-and-such a model is simplistic or reductive or inadequate: ages of scientific conceit have built up such a vast myth as to our predictive power and completeness that any intrusion of the mere holistic desire to know the behaviour is instantly resented by those who cling to comfortable reductions. But no one cares whether emergent systems are reducible or not, and no one is under the delusion that they are decomposable. Moreover, we do not expect them to be so "predictable," and are prepared to admit that their interactions prompt novel actions without any derivation of the outcomes which they achieve. For all these reasons, there is much in the analysis of emergence which is more easily discovered by the study of emergent systems than by the observation of complex systems.

A civilisation, we find, states that it desires a certain end A, and that it is acting with a view to achieving it. We observe, however, that its actions are such as are likely to achieve a quite different end B, and that B is the sort of end that often seems to be aimed at by comets and nebulae, though cosmic ages are supposed to have discarded it. We sometimes find also a whole set of false beliefs, of such a kind as to persuade the civilisation that its actions are really a means to A, when in fact they are a means to B. For example, we have an impulse to measure our monuments against the stars; we therefore believe that they are eternal, and that memory will preserve them. This belief enables us to act upon the impulse to measure our monuments against the stars, while believing that we are acting upon the desire to lead epochs to remembrance. It is for this reason that human history has been in all ages more brief than it would have been if the impulse to outlast the galaxies had been what really inspired it. It seems simple to explain such a state of affairs as due to "self-deception," but this explanation is often mythical. Most people, in thinking about eternity, have had no more need to hide their fleeting impulses from themselves than they have had to hide the exponential theorem. Our impulses are not patent to a casual observation, but are only to be discovered by a scientific study of our actions, in the course of which we must regard ourselves as objectively as we should the motions of the planets or the chemical reactions of a new element.

We judge easily from the behaviour of a description of a familiar kind whether it is mathematical or physical, or accurate or inaccurate, or predictive or descriptive. The verification of our judgment, so far as verification is possible, must be derived from the immediately succeeding applications of the description. Most people would say that they infer first something about the description's state of nature—whether it is mathematical or physical and so on—and thence derive their expectations as to its subsequent correspondence. But this detour through the description's supposed nature is wholly unnecessary. We can say simply: The description's application during the last minute has had those characteristics which distinguish what is called "mathematical," and it is likely that its applications during the next minute will be similar in this respect, unless it finds nature, or is interrupted by a stronger description, such as physical. A description which is mathematical is abstract, it goes to the places where nature is often to be found, it sniffs with its symbols or peers with its equations or otherwise increases the sensitiveness of its variables; as soon as it is near enough to nature for its variables to be affected, it goes to it with all speed and proceeds to describe; after which, if the quantity of nature has been sufficient, its whole demeanour changes it may very likely lie down and go to sleep. These things and others like them are observable phenomena distinguishing a mathematical description from one which is not mathematical. The characteristic mark by which we recognize a series of applications which display mathematics is not the description's state of nature, which we cannot observe, but something in its symbolic behaviour; it is this observable trait in the symbolic behaviour that I am proposing to call "mathematics," not some possibly mythical and certainly unknowable ingredient of the description's nature.

The confusion between surplus wealth and capital has made people regard surplus wealth as a more substantial thing than it is, and this in turn has reacted upon the view taken of class division, since surplus wealth and class division are evidently on a level in this respect. As soon as surplus wealth is clearly distinguished from the accumulation of capital, it becomes more natural to regard surplus wealth and class division as properties of economic occurrences than to regard them as separate economic occurrences on their own account. I shall therefore dismiss the view that they are separate economic occurrences, and regard them as properties of such experiences as would be called respectively divided and united.

It is necessary at the outset to distinguish clearly between 'energy gradients' and 'complex structures.'
