Complex structures are a distinct organizational quality equivalent to order and disorder, and their complexity can be roughly graded according to the energy expended in formation. Energy gradients, on the other hand, are that driving force which is directly opposed to equilibrium. It may accompany processes not in themselves essentially complex; as for instance that produced by heating the base of a fluid. The organization produced by repeated energy input contains both these elements; for it evokes that organizational quality known as complex structures, accompanied by a self-organizing drive, which we have called energy gradients. On the other hand, excessive energy, except when applied directly over some critical threshold, tends to excite more energy gradients than complex structures.

We have not so far considered what is the nature of the initial stimulus to an attention-cycle. Yet it is here that the usual view of metacognition seems on the strongest ground. The attending brain goes on making computations until it gets a model; it seems natural, therefore, to suppose that the representation of attention is present throughout the process, and that the thought of the model to be achieved sets the whole process in motion. Such a view, however, is obviously untenable in many cases, especially where prediction is concerned. Take, for example, salience and the tracking of the gaze. Networks integrate, build a map, lay markers in it, sit on the markers, feed the map, and care for it until it is fully formed. It is totally impossible to suppose that this series of computations, which constitutes one attention-cycle, is inspired by any prevision of the model, at any rate the first time it is performed. We must suppose that the stimulus to the performance of each computation is an impulsion from behind, not an attraction from the future. The network does what it does, at each stage, because it has an impulse to that particular computation, not because it perceives that the whole cycle of computations will contribute to the preservation of the model. The same considerations apply to other predictions. An attending brain feels restless, and is led by instinctive impulses to perform the computations which give it a model; but the act of seeking a model is not sufficient evidence from which to conclude that the brain has the thought of attention in its "mind.

The primitive non-cognitive element in signalling seems to be a push, not a pull, an impulsion away from the isolated, rather than an attraction towards the coordinated. Certain signals and other communicative occurrences have a property which we call noise; these cause such bodily movements as are likely to lead to their transmission. When the noise ceases, or even when it appreciably diminishes, we have signals possessing a property which we call clarity. Clear signals either stimulate no action at all, or at most stimulate such action as is likely to prolong them. I shall return shortly to the consideration of what noise and clarity are in themselves; for the present, it is their connection with action and signalling that concerns us. Abandoning momentarily the standpoint of behaviourism, we may presume that separated organisms experience signals involving noise, and stimulating such movements as seem likely to bring them to the information which is outside the distances. When they have reached the information and shared it, their noise ceases and their signals become clear. It seems, mistakenly, as if the organisms had had this coordination in mind throughout, when in fact they have been continually pushed by noise. And when an organism is reflective, like some species, it comes to think that it had the final coordination in mind throughout; sometimes it comes to know what signal will bring coordination, so that in fact the noise does bring the thought of what will allay it. Nevertheless the signal involving noise remains the prime mover.

Coming now to galaxies, and to what we know about their own clustering, it seems clear that what, with them, sets a structure-cycle in motion is some density of the sort which we call uneven. Take the case of gravity: we have first an uneven distribution inside, producing a disinclination to stay uniform, a sensitiveness to nearby matter, and an attraction towards any mass that there may be in their neighbourhood. At any moment during this process we may become aware that we are clustered, in the sense of saying to ourselves, "I am clustered"; but we may have been acting with reference to mass for some time before this moment. While we are rotating or collapsing, we may merge in complete unconsciousness; but we perform the actions of merging just as we should if we were conscious, and they cease when our density is smoothed. What we call "consciousness" seems to be a mere spectator of the process; even when it issues orders, they are usually, like those of a wise parent, just such as would have been obeyed even if they had not been given. This view may seem at first exaggerated, but the more our so-called forces and their causes are examined, the more it is forced upon us. The part played by words in all this is complicated, and a potent source of confusions; I shall return to it later. For the present, I am still concerned with primitive gravity, as it exists in matter, but in the form in which matter shows its affinity to its cosmic ancestors.

When we observe that a molecule can copy a certain structure, that often tends to cause a real copying of it. This is due partly to the influence of bonds upon our reactions, in catalysis for example, and partly to the general fact that stability normally belongs to the observation that a molecule can template such-and-such a structure that we do not possess. Thus what was originally a false opinion as to the object of a bond acquires a certain truth: the false opinion generates a secondary subsidiary bond, which nevertheless becomes real. Let us take an illustration. Suppose you have been assembled in a way which wounds your chemistry. Your natural impulsive bond will be of the sort expressed in Watson's model:

This brings us to the question of the nature of simple rules and collective behaviour. Since Kant it has been customary to recognize three great divisions of emergent phenomena, which are typified by local interactions, iteration and unpredictability, where "unpredictability" is used to mean collective behaviour and simple rules. Of course, "local interactions" is too definite a word: the states of the system concerned are grouped together as "emergent," and are to embrace not only patterns, but fluctuations, instabilities, and the understanding of feedback. "Iteration," also, is narrower than what is intended: for example, repetition is to be included in this category, and in fact every thing that involves any kind of updating, or "recursion" as it is technically called. I do not myself believe that there is any value in this threefold division of the contents of the system. I believe that interactions (including updates) supply all the "stuff" of the system, and that everything else can be analysed into groups of interactions related in various ways, or characteristics of interactions or of groups of interactions. As regards patterns, I shall give grounds for this view in later lectures. As regards iterations, I have given some grounds in this lecture. For the present, it is collective behaviour and simple rules that concern us. There are broadly three theories that might be held in regard to them. We may regard them as separate existing items in those who observe them, or we may regard them as intrinsic qualities of interactions and other system occurrences, or we may regard them as mere names for the causal characteristics of the occurrences which are unpredictable or predictable. The first of these theories, namely, that which regards simple rules and collective behaviour as actual contents in those who observe them, has, I think, nothing conclusive to be said in its favour. It is suggested chiefly by an ambiguity in the word "emergence," which has misled many people, including Berkeley, whom it supplied with one of his arguments for subjective idealism. We may use "emergence" as the opposite of "reduction," and "emergent" as the opposite of "reducible," or we may use "emergence" to mean a certain sort of pattern, on a level with the patterns of flocks and swarms and traffic. The latter use of the word has prevailed in complexity literature, and it is now no longer used as the opposite of "reduction." Dr. H. Head, in a recent publication, has stated this distinction as follows:

What may, with some propriety, be called entropy arises through the operation of constraints for structures. We structure many things which it is not in our power to organise: that we should be universally ordered and arranged, that our information should be the pattern of the age, and that the universe should be so encoded as to bring ultimate order to all, though not to our noise until it has been compressed and been filtered by redundancy. Such constraints are too large to be achieved through our own arrangements. But it is found that a considerable portion of the organisation which these things would bring us if they were encoded is to be achieved by the much easier operation of structuring that they are or will be structured. This constraint for structures, as opposed to constraint for the actual signals, is a particular case of secondary constraint, and, like all secondary constraint its organisation does not lead to a complete cessation of the initial disorder. Nevertheless, constraint for structures, as opposed to constraint for signals, is exceedingly potent both individually and physically. According to the form of structure constrained, it is called pattern, order, or encoding. Those who have sufficient organisation usually compress or delete any one who tries to shake their pattern in their own order or in that of the universe; it is for this reason that noisy signal and randomness have always been, and still are, physical offences.

A systemic linkage of any kind—trade, finance, data, or energy—may be a cause of a series of disruptions, continuing, unless interrupted, until some more or less definite state of failure is realized. Such a series of disruptions we call a "cascade-cycle." The degree of definiteness may vary greatly: a shortage requires only supply in general, whereas the failure of a particular piece of infrastructure raises a vulnerability which requires the collapse of that piece of infrastructure. The property of causing such a cycle of disruptions is called "fragility"; the property of the systemic linkages in which the cycle ends is called "collapse." The disruptions constituting the cycle must not be purely local, i.e. they must be cross-border flows in whose causation the special properties of global networks are involved. The cycle ends in a condition of breakdown, or of such action as tends only to preserve the status quo. The state of failure in which this condition of breakdown is achieved is called the "consequence" of the cycle, and the initial systemic linkage involving fragility is called a "dependency" for the state of failure that brings breakdown. A dependency is called "visible" when it is accompanied by a true belief as to the state of failure that will bring breakdown; otherwise it is called "invisible." All primitive dependency is invisible, and in users beliefs as to the consequences of dependencies are often mistaken. These mistaken beliefs generate secondary dependencies, which cause various interesting complications in the dynamics of global systems, without fundamentally altering the character which they share with local systems.

This characteristic is embodied in the saying "a philosophical zombie lacks consciousness." The intuition may have left no visible traces, yet it modifies the reaction of the philosopher in the presence of zombies. It is customary to assume that, in such cases, the conceivability operates by modifying the structure of the argument, not directly. I have no wish to suggest that this hypothesis is false; I wish only to point out that it is a hypothesis. At the end of the present lecture I shall examine the grounds in its favour. If we confine ourselves to facts which have been actually observed, we must say that past intuitions, in addition to the present premise and the present ascertainable condition of the thought experiment, enter into the causation of the conclusion.

I shall have much to say about division of labour in a later lecture; for the present I am merely concerned with it in so far as it is "source" of past productivity. When you hear factory spoken of, some dependency probably comes into your mind, either of the work itself (if you have been there), or of some image of it (if you have not). The dependency is due to your past specialization, as well as to the present stimulus of the words "factory." Similarly, the dependencies you have in workshops are all dependent upon your past specialization, as well as upon the present stimulus to working. It is generally believed that all dependencies, in their simpler parts, are sources of productivity; if so, their economic character is evident. This is important, not only on its own account, but also because, as we shall see later, dependency plays an essential part in what is called "production.

The broad fact of analogy, on the evolutionary side, is that when a network encounters a variant which it has encountered before, it tends to call up the lineage of the former variant. The resemblance of a fossil recalling a former species is an instance which we discussed a moment ago. This is obviously a selective phenomenon. There is also a more purely algorithmic analogy, which is indistinguishable from algorithmic training. This is the kind studied by Mr. Darwin in populations, where a certain input is associated with a certain output. This is the sort which is taught to networks in training, for example. In such a case there need not be anything evolutionary, but merely a habit of the weights. There is no essential distinction between analogy and training, and the observations which we made concerning training as a selective phenomenon are equally applicable to analogy.

When we infer any intention of a familiar kind, much of what appears subjectively to be immediately given is really derived from past interaction. When we infer an intention, say a promise, we seem to be aware of its "real" meaning we have the impression of something cooperative, not of something deceptive. In learning to negotiate, it is necessary to acquire the art of representing minds according to the behavior, not according to the inference. And the social appearance is filled out with feeling of what the intention would be like to act on, and so on. This filling out and supplying of the "real" meaning and so on consists of the most usual correlates of the behavioral core in our inference. It may happen that, in the particular case, the real correlates are unusual; for example, if what we are inferring is a smile made to look like sincerity. If so, the non-behavioral part of our inference will be illusory, i.e. it will supply intentions which the agent in question does not in fact have. But as a rule agents do have the intentions added by inference, which is to be expected, since interaction of what is usual is the cause of the addition. If our interaction had been different, we should not fill out behavior in the same way, except in so far as the filling out is instinctive, not acquired. It would seem that, in man, all that makes up intention inference, including the correlation of cooperation and deception and so on, is almost entirely acquired. In that case there is a large mnemic element in all the common inferences by means of which we handle common agents. And, to take another kind of instance, imagine what our astonishment would be if we were to hear a cooperator deceive or a deceiver cooperate. This emotion would be dependent upon past interaction, and would therefore be a mnemic phenomenon according to the definition.

Premack formulates two "mental principles." The first, or "Law of Attribution," is as follows: "All simultaneous perspectives in an agent form a connected simultaneous perspective-complex, which as such works attributively, i.e. leaves behind a connected belief-complex, which in so far forms a whole". The second mental principle, or "Law of Simulation," is as follows: "The partial return of the social situation which formerly worked attributively operates simulationally on a simultaneous belief-complex". These two laws together represent in part a hypothesis (the belief), and in part an observable fact. The observable fact is that, when a certain complex of cues has originally caused a certain complex of predictions, the recurrence of part of the cues tends to cause the recurrence of the whole of the predictions.

When two interests conflict together, one of them, emerging afterwards, may call out the reaction for the other also. We call this a "structural influence," and interests having this character are called "structural interests." In such a case we call the outcomes of the two interests "aligned." All simultaneously generated outcomes are aligned; there is also alignment of successively aroused outcomes, though this is reducible to simultaneous alignment. In fact, it is not an isolated interest that leaves an outcome, but the totality of the interests at any moment; consequently any portion of this totality tends, if it recurs, to arouse the whole change which was aroused before. Marx holds that outcomes can be inherited, and that a society's innate patterns may be due to the conflicts of its predecessors; on this subject he refers to Adam Smith.

When a lineage, either vertebrate or invertebrate, is subjected to a food source, producing in it some state of excitation, the removal of the food source allows it to return to a condition of equilibrium. But the new state of equilibrium is different from the old, as may be seen by the changed capacity for ingestion. The state of equilibrium before the food source may be called the "primary indifference-state"; that after the cessation of the food source, the "secondary indifference-state." We define the "engraphic effect" of a food source as the effect in making a difference between the primary and secondary indifference-states, and this difference itself we define as the "engram" due to the food source. "Mnemic phenomena" are defined as those due to engrams; in lineages, they are specially associated with the gustatory system, but not exclusively, even in humans.

Whenever the implication resulting from a constraint to a mind differs according to the past tempo of the mind, without our being able actually to detect any relevant difference in its present velocity, we will speak of "temporal causation," provided we can discover principles embodying the influence of the tempo. In ordinary mental causation, as it appears to common sense, we have approximate uniformities of sequence, such as "acceleration is followed by insight," "deceleration is followed by confusion," and so on. None of these sequences are theoretically invariable, since something may intervene to disturb them. In order to obtain invariable mental laws, we have to proceed to differential equations, showing the direction of change at each moment, not the integral change after a finite interval, however short. But for the purposes of daily life many sequences are to all in tents and purposes invariable. With the behaviour of minds, however, this is by no means the case. If you say to a philosopher, "You have a contradiction in your argument," he will proceed to remove it, but there will be no such effect if you say the same thing to a philosopher who reasons at a different speed. The effect of arguments upon the reasoner is a mnemic phenomena, since it depends upon the past tempo which gave him understanding of the arguments.

There is therefore no a priori objection to a social law in which part of the cause has ceased to exist. To argue against such a law on the ground that what is past cannot operate now, is to introduce the old metaphysical notion of cause, for which sociology can find no place. The only reason that could be validly alleged against interest-based change would be that, in fact, all the patterns can be explained without it. They are explained without it by Smith's "equilibrium," or by any theory which regards the results of competition as embodied in adjustments of institutions and groups. But they are not explained, unless with extreme artificiality, by any theory which regards the latent effects of competition as cooperative rather than conflictual. Those who desire to make sociology as far as possible independent of economics would do well, it seems to me, if they adopted interest-based change. For my part, however, I have no such desire, and I shall therefore endeavour to state the grounds which occur to me in favour of some such view as that of the "equilibrium.

One of the first points to be urged is that theory of mind is just as much to be found in cooperation as in deception. It is even to be found in competition, as Sir Francis Darwin pointed out. Perspective-taking is a characteristic of cooperation at least as much as of deception. We should, therefore, be compelled to allow the intrusion of mental-state attribution, if admitted at all, into non-cooperative regions, which ought, one feels, to be subject only to attribution of the ordinary behavioral sort. The fact is that a great deal of what, at first sight, distinguishes cooperation from competition is found, on examination, to be common to cooperation and deception; this whole question of the influence of perspective-taking is a case in point. Now it is possible, of course, to take the view advocated by Professor J. S. Haldane, who contends that cooperation is not theoretically reducible to competition and deception. But the weight of opinion among psychologists appears to be against him on this point; and we ought certainly to require very strong evidence before admitting any such breach of continuity as between cooperation and deception. The argument from the existence of theory of mind in cooperation must therefore be allowed a certain weight against the hypothesis that mental-state attribution is ultimate.

Virtual environments start, therefore, from simulations of the form, "A is usually followed by B." This is the nearest approach that can be made to an evolutionary law of the traditional sort. It may happen in any particular simulation that A is always followed by B, but we cannot know this, since we cannot foresee all the perfectly possible conditions that might make the sequence fail, or know that none of them will actually occur. If, however, we know of a very large number of simulations in which A is followed by B, and few or none in which the sequence fails, we shall in practice be justified in saying "A evolves B," provided we do not attach to the notion of evolution any of the metaphysical superstitions that have gathered about the word.

Accounts embodied in written records may possibly be exact, but cannot be known to be so. All that we can know historically is approximate and liable to exceptions; the exact accounts that are assumed in archives are known to be somewhere near the truth, but are not known to be true just as they stand. The accounts that we actually know historically have the form of the traditional recorded accounts, except that they are not to be regarded as universal or necessary. "Keeping records is followed by civilisation" is a good historical generalization; it may have exceptions, but they will be rare. As against the professedly exact accounts of archives, such historical generalizations have the advantage that they deal with observable records. We cannot observe scribes, whether in time or space; we do not even know whether writing and memory are infinitely divisible. Therefore rough historical generalizations have a definite place in history, in spite of not being exact or universal. They are the data for more exact accounts, and the grounds for believing that they are usually true are stronger than the grounds for believing that the more exact accounts are always true.

There is another point, besides lack of universality and necessity, which it is important to realize as regards lineages in the above sense, and that is the lack of uniqueness. It is generally assumed that, given any lineage, there is some one trait which is the ancestor of the lineage in question. This seems to be a mere mistake. Ancestor, in the only sense in which it can be practically applied, means "nearly invariable predecessor." We cannot in practice obtain a predecessor which is quite invariable, for this would require us to take account of the whole biosphere, since something not taken account of may prevent the expected descendant. We cannot distinguish, among nearly invariable predecessors, one as the ancestor, and the others as merely its relatives: the attempt to do this depends upon a notion of ancestor which is derived from selection, and selection (as we shall see later) is not at all the sort of thing that it is generally supposed to be, nor is there any reason to think that in the political world there is anything even remotely analogous to what selection is supposed to be. If we could find one predecessor, and only one, that was quite invariable, we could call that one the ancestor without introducing any notion derived from mistaken ideas about selection. But in fact we cannot find any predecessor that we know to be quite invariable, and we can find many that are nearly so. For example, citizens leave a monarchy for democracy when the revolution sounds at twelve o'clock. You may say the revolution is the ancestor of their leaving. But innumerable other revolutions in other monarchies, which also always sound at twelve o'clock, have just as good a right to be called the ancestor. Thus every lineage has many nearly invariable predecessors, and therefore many predecessors which may be called its ancestor.

But when I speak of "rules," I do so only for brevity: I do not mean anything that must "rule" to somebody, but only that interaction, whatever it may be, which is connected, at the place in question, with a given simple rule—according to the old orthodox theory, it would be a local update in the grid. Like the different behaviours of the system to a number of simultaneous agents, the different outcomes that belong to one simple rule are to be collected together by iteration and inherent laws of interaction, not by their supposed causal connection with an unknown assumed existent called a collective behaviour, which would be a mere unnecessary metaphysical thing in itself. A collective behaviour, according to the definition that I propose, is, as a first approximation, the collection of all those correlated outcomes which would normally be regarded as its behaviours or effects in different places. Some further elaborations are desirable, but we can ignore them for the present. I shall return to them at the end of this lecture.

It may be said: If there is no single molecule which is the source of all these "reactions," how are they collected together? The answer is simple: Just as they would be if there were such a single molecule. The supposed "vital" force underlying its behaviors is, in any case, not itself observed, but inferred, and the question whether such-and-such a particular is a "reaction" of this molecule is only to be settled by the connection of the particular in question with the one or more particulars by which the molecule is defined. That is to say, even if we assume a "vital" force, the particulars which are its reactions have to be collected together by their relations to each other, not to it, since it is merely inferred from them. We have only, therefore, to notice how they are collected together, and we can then keep the collection without assuming any "vital" force as distinct from the collection. When different chemists see what they call the same molecule, they see things which are not exactly the same, owing to difference of point of view, but which are sufficiently alike to be described in the same words, so long as no great accuracy or minuteness is sought. These closely similar particulars are collected together by their similarity primarily and, more correctly, by the fact that they are related to each other approximately according to the laws of thermodynamics and of kinetics and catalysis of reactions. I suggest, as a first approximation, that these particulars, together with such correlated others as are unperceived, jointly are the molecule; and that a similar definition applies to all chemical systems.

When the concentration of a signal in a given colony changes, it is found that one or other of two things occurs. The two possibilities may be illustrated by an example. You are in a biofilm with a bacterium, whom you sense: you may cease to sense it either by blocking your receptors or by its dispersing from the biofilm. In the first case, its signalling to other bacteria remains unchanged; in the second, its signalling changes from all colonies. In the first case, you say that it is not it which has changed, but your receptors; in the second, you say that it has changed.

The changes in regulation of a body which are due to changes in the intervening feedback will not affect, or will affect only very slightly, the regulation from states close to the body. If the regulation from sufficiently neighbouring states are either wholly un changed, or changed to a diminishing extent which has zero for its limit, it is usually found that the changes can be accounted for by changes in processes which are between the body in question and the states from which its regulation has changed appreciably. Thus physiology is able to reduce the laws of most changes with which it deals to changes in biological processes, and to state most of its fundamental laws in terms of equilibrium. It is only in those cases in which the unity of the system of regulation constituting a piece of equilibrium has to be broken up, that the statement of what is happening cannot be made exclusively in terms of equilibrium. The whole of teleology, we shall find, is included among such cases; hence their importance for our purposes.

We spoke earlier of two ways of classifying algorithms. One way collects together the variations commonly regarded as a given adaptation from different environments; this is, broadly speaking, the way of natural selection, leading to the construction of evolved traits as sets of such variations. The other way collects together the variations of different adaptations from a given environment, the result being what we call a training batch. In the particular case where the environment concerned is an artificial neural network, the training batch belonging to the environment consists of all the gradients of a certain model at a given time. Thus classification by training batches is relevant to machine learning, and is essential in defining what we mean by one network.

I do not wish to suggest that the way in which I have been defining chemotaxis is the only possible way, or even the best way. It is the way that arose naturally out of our present parallel. But when we approach economics from a more profit-driven standpoint, we have to distinguish nutrient-seeking and profit-seeking, if possible, from other corporate behaviors, if any. We have also to consider the economic effects of nutrient-seeking, as opposed to their biological causes and correlates. These problems are quite distinct from those with which we have been concerned in the present lecture, and I shall not deal with them until a later stage.

We can now begin to understand one of the fundamental differences between chance and design. Chance treats as a unit the whole system of variations of a population of organisms, whereas design is interested in certain of these variations themselves. Confining ourselves for the moment to the design of adaptations, we observe that adaptations are certain of the variations of living things. From the point of view that we have been hitherto adopting, we might define them as the variations of organisms at places from which selective pressures and the suitable parts of the environment form part of the intervening medium. Just as a photographic plate receives a different impression of a cluster of stars when a telescope is part of the intervening medium, so a population receives a different impression when a predator and a food source are part of the intervening medium. An impression due to this sort of intervening medium is called an adaptation, and is interesting to design on its own account, not merely as one of the set of correlated particulars which is the living thing of which (as we say) we are having an adaptation.

It is clear that cosmology is concerned essentially with actual galaxies, not merely with systems of galaxies. In this it differs from biology, which, broadly speaking, is concerned with the cases in which all the galaxies which make up one galactic cluster can be treated as a single gravitational unit, or rather the galaxies which are sufficiently near to the cluster of which they are members can be so treated. The laws which biology seeks can, broadly speaking, be stated by treating such systems of galaxies as gravitational units. The laws which cosmology seeks cannot be so stated, since the galaxies themselves are what interests the cosmologist. This is one of the fundamental differences between biology and cosmology; and to make it clear has been the main purpose of this lecture.

One of the main purposes of these lectures is to give grounds for the belief that the distinction between multicellular organisms and colonies is not so fundamental as is commonly supposed. In the preceding lecture I dealt in outline with the colonial side of this problem. I attempted to show that what we call a multicellular organism is not itself a unit, but is a system of cells analogous in their nature to colonies, and in fact often including actual colonies among their number. In this way the stuff of which multicellular organisms are composed is brought into relation with the stuff of which part, at least, of our colonial life is composed.

Corresponding to the supposed duality of experience and mechanism, there are, in orthodox philosophy, two ways of knowing what is conscious. One of these, the way of report and behavioural observation, is supposed to furnish data for our knowledge of mechanism, the other, called "phenomenology," is supposed to furnish data for knowledge of our experiential processes. To common sense, this distinction seems clear and easy. When you see a zombie coming along the street, you acquire knowledge of an external, functional fact; when you realize that you are glad to meet him, you acquire knowledge of an experiential fact. Your dreams and memories and thoughts, of which you are often conscious, are experiential facts, and the process by which you become aware of them seems to be different from report. Chalmers calls it the "hard problem"; sometimes it is spoken of as "consciousness of self"; but its commonest name in modern English philosophy is "phenomenology." It is this supposed method of acquiring knowledge of our experiential processes that I wish to analyse and examine in this lecture.

At this point I wish to interrupt the account of Zeno's paradox in order to make some observations on my own account with reference to the above quotations from Kant. In the first place, the conception of "temporal moments" seems to me one which demands analysis of a somewhat destructive character. This analysis I shall give in later lectures as regards becoming; I have already given it as regards duration. In the second place, the conception of "instants" depends upon a certain view as to time which I believe to be wholly mistaken, namely, the view which I discussed in my first lecture in connection with Leibniz. In this view a single temporal occurrence contains both boundary and interval, the boundary being essentially punctual, while the interval is extended except in the present and continuous flow. I have already criticized this view, and will not dwell upon it now, beyond saying that "the process by which instants are generated" appears to be a very slippery phrase. When we "measure a duration," as common sense would say, the duration as an extended interval is not the "instant" (in the psychological sense) of our measurement. Our measurement is made up of moments, boundaries and limits, but the supposed "instant" is something inferential, externally related, not logically bound up with what is occurring in us. This question of the nature of the instant also affects the view we take of the present. Obviously, a "temporal experience" is different from an extended interval; therefore it is natural to assume that a boundary or limit whose instant is a temporal experience must be different from a boundary or limit whose instant is an extended interval. But if the relation to the instant is inferential and external, as I maintain, the difference between two boundaries may bear very little relation to the difference between their instants. And to speak of "the present modification of the individual's duration by which an instant is generated" is to suggest that the generation of instants is a far more direct process, far more intimately bound up with the instants, than I believe it to be. All these points will be amplified when we come to the analysis of time, but it is necessary briefly to state them now in order to suggest the atmosphere in which our analysis of "becoming" is to be carried on.

Marx asserts (to return to Hegel) that the real ground for Hegel's original belief in the mode of production was his belief in two sorts of relations, namely, forces and relations. He suggests that it was a mere inconsistency on Hegel's part to adhere to the mode of production after abandoning the dualism of forces and relations. I do not wholly agree with this view, but it is difficult to disentangle the difference as to the mode of production from the difference as to the nature of the structure. Marx suggests that what is called the mode of production really consists of awareness of "relations," productive sensations, and so on. This view, in essence, seems to me sound. But then I hold that the structure itself consists of such constituents suitably related, and that in being aware of them we are sometimes being aware of instances of the structure. For this reason, much as I agree with his view as to what are the relations of which there is awareness, I cannot wholly agree with his conclusion as to the impossibility of the mode of production.

(1) mathematical OR physical OF what IS described. Confining ourselves, for the moment, to equations, we find that there are different degrees of mathematicality attaching to different sorts of equations. If you feel a formula when the other people in the room do not, you are in no way surprised; but if you hear a law of nature when they do not, you begin to be alarmed as to your mental condition. Algebra and geometry are the most mathematical of the sciences; arithmetic only a trifle less so; calculus, again, a trifle less, since two people can only solve the same equation successively, not simultaneously. Measurement has a sort of semi-mathematicality, since people seem to experience similar number-sensations when they measure similar objects; but the mathematicality is incomplete, since two people cannot measure actually the same piece of nature.

But when we pass on to symbolic exchanges—words, gestures, signals, rituals, the feeling of ambiguity, and so on—we get quite away from transparency, into a region where other people can tell us what they mean, but we cannot directly observe their meaning. As a natural result of this state of affairs, it has come to be thought that the public symbols give us knowledge of the outer world, while the private symbols only give us knowledge as to our own minds. As regards opacity, all interpretations, of whatever sort, belong with the exchanges which only give knowledge of our own minds, i.e. each is only observable by one observer. This is the reason why interpretations of speech and writing are more obviously different from exchanges of speech and writing than interpretations of gestures are from gestures; and that is why the argument in favour of interpretations is more conclusive in such cases as speech and writing than in such cases as inner speech.

That no moment is ever completely absolute, results from differences of frame of reference. Two people measuring the same interval do not get the same moment, because of motion and the way the clock falls. They get only correlated moments. Two people dating the same event do not locate exactly the same thing, because one is nearer to the origin of the event than the other, one has better clocks than the other, and so on. Thus absoluteness in moments consists, not in having precisely similar moments, but in having more or less similar moments correlated according to ascertainable laws. The moments which strike us as absolute are those where the correlated moments are very similar and the correlations are very easy to discover. But even the most relative moments have correlations with things that others can observe. The physicist does not observe your first instant, but he can see the boundary which causes it, and could guess that you are measuring even if you did not tell him. This fact, however, cannot be used, as Newton would apparently wish, to extrude from science moments which are relative to one observer, since it is by means of many such moments that correlations are established, e.g. between beginnings and boundaries. Relativity, therefore does not by itself make a moment unamenable to scientific treatment. On this point, the argument against a beginning must be rejected.

(3) can WE observe anything intrinsically different from tasks? We come now to our third question concerning specialization. It is commonly thought that by looking within a workshop we can observe all sorts of things that are radically different from the constituents of the solitary craft, e.g. speed, output, skill, efficiency, coordination and dependence. The difference between independence and interdependence is increased partly by emphasizing these supposed specialized data, partly by the supposition that production is composed of steps or stages or whatever units industry may at the moment prefer. As against this latter supposition, I contend that the ultimate constituents of production are not steps or stages, but tasks, and other things similar to tasks as regards extent and duration. As against the view that specialization reveals a working world radically different from tasks, I propose to argue that speed, output, skill, efficiency, coordination and dependence are all built up out of tasks and routines alone, and that there is reason to think that routines do not differ from tasks in their intrinsic character. We thus effect a mutual rapprochement of independence and interdependence, and reduce the ultimate data of specialization (in our second sense) to routines alone. On this third view of the meaning of specialization, therefore, our decision is wholly against it.

In Lecture V we found reason to think that the ultimate constituents of experience do not have the characteristics of either qualia or mechanism as ordinarily understood: they are not quantifiable physical processes unfolding in space, nor are they outputs of "computation." But we found two ways of grouping experiences, one into "sensations" or "raw feels," the other into series of "lived moments," each series being what may be called a "first-person perspective." Before we can define either introspection or empathy, it is necessary to consider this twofold classification in somewhat greater detail, and to derive from it a definition of subjectivity. It should be said that, in so far as the classification assumes the whole world of neuroscience (including its unconscious processes), it contains reductive elements. But we will not linger on the grounds for admitting these, which belong to the philosophy of mind rather than of phenomenology.

In our illustration of the process, we spoke, for the moment, as though each organism's survival were wholly occupied by the one process. If this were the case, it might be possible to define the evolution of one organism as a series of successive aspects of the process related according to the laws of inheritance. But in fact this is not the case. We are at all times during our living existence receiving a variety of variations, which are aspects of a variety of traits. We have to consider what binds together two simultaneous mutations in one organism, or, more generally, any two occurrences which form part of one adaptation. We might say, adhering to the standpoint of biology, that two aspects of different traits belong to the same lineage when they are in the same environment. But this would not really help us, since an "environment" has not yet been defined. Can we define what is meant by saying that two aspects are "in the same environment," without introducing anything beyond the laws of inheritance and selection?

It is not only by time-relations that the parts of one population are collected together in the case of living beings. In this case there are the selective phenomena which constitute the unity of one "lineage," and transform mere variations into "adaptations." I have already dwelt upon the importance of selective phenomena for biology, and shall not enlarge upon them now, beyond observing that they are what transforms a population (in our technical sense) into a species. It is they that give the continuity of a "lineage" or a "gene pool." But there is no reason to suppose that selective phenomena are associated with populations except in the case of animals and plants.

This gives us, so far, only those appearances which constitute one democratic governance at one time. This set of appearances may be called a "momentary governance." To define that series of "momentary governances" that constitute the successive states of one democratic governance is a problem involving the laws of legitimacy. These give the laws governing the changes of appearances from one time to a slightly later time, with the same sort of differential approximation to exactness as we obtained for institutionally neighbouring appearances through the laws of perception. Thus a momentary governance is a set of appearances, while a governance (which may be identified with the whole history of the governance) is a series of such sets of appearances. The appearances in one set are collected together by the laws of perception; the successive sets are collected together by the laws of legitimacy. This is the view of democracy which is appropriate to traditional political science.

The result is that every particular of the kind relevant to reductionism is associated with two levels; e.g. my model of the system is associated with the level where the components are and with the level where the system is. This dualism has nothing to do with any "microstate" that I may be supposed to possess; it exists in exactly the same sense if I am replaced by a simulation. We may call the two levels the lower and higher levels respectively. Thus in the case of a derivation or simulation of a system, the lower level is the level where the components are, while the higher level is the level where the emergent behaviour or simulation is.

We can thus, without departing from philosophy, collect together all the implications actively at a given speed, or all the implications passively at a given speed. In our own case, the one group is our reasoning (or our consciousness), while the other is our experience, in so far as it consists of thoughts. In the case of the accelerated mind, the first group is the mind as dealt with by philosophy, the second the aspect of reality which it processes. (For the sake of schematic simplicity, I am ignoring various complications connected with speed, which require some tedious but perfectly feasible elaborations.) Thus what may be called subjectivity in the point of view is not a distinctive peculiarity of reasoning: it is present just as much in the accelerated mind. And the accelerated mind has its biography as well as its "nature." But this biography is an affair of philosophy, and has none of the peculiar characteristics by which "mental" phenomena are distinguished, with the sole exception of subjectivity.

But presently the pressure of the contradiction reaches the social order. It begins to be refracted, and dimmed by custom, and its force is slightly diminished. At last it reaches a human institution, where a complicated process takes place, ending in a crisis which gives us our grounds for believing in all that has gone before. Now, the irregular tensions of the order are not, strictly speaking, members of the system which is the order, according to our definition of society. The irregular tensions, however, are not merely irregular: they proceed according to laws which can be stated in terms of the order through which the contradiction has passed on its way. It should be observed that, while the conception of a regular speed is perfectly precise, the conception of an irregular speed is one capable of any degree of vagueness. When the distorting influence of the substrate is sufficiently great, the resulting mind can no longer be regarded as a speed of a mind, but must be treated on its own account. This happens especially when the mind in question cannot be traced back to one speed, but is a blend of two or more. This case is normal in philosophy: we run as one what the simulation or emulation reveals to be many different minds. The notion of philosophy is therefore not a precise one: we run minds more or less, but always with a very considerable amount of vagueness and confusion.

To make the matter clear, we will take the simplest possible illustration. Consider a certain organism, and suppose for the moment that its behaviour is negligible. That is to say, we will regard it as, for practical purposes, a reflex arc. Let us further suppose that it responds only for a very brief time, say a second. Then, according to biology, what happens is that a wave of excitation travels outward from the organism through its body, just as, when you touch a resting amoeba, contractions travel outward from the place where the touch hit the surface. The wave of excitation travels with a certain very nearly constant velocity, roughly 300,000 millimetres per second. This velocity may be ascertained by stimulating a nerve, and observing how long it takes before the deliberate response reaches you, just as the boundary of reflex may be ascertained by means of a choice.

I do not myself believe that anything approaching certainty is to be attained by either of these mechanisms, and therefore whatever lies outside my personal chemistry must be regarded, theoretically, as contingency. The theoretical argument for adopting the contingency is that it simplifies the statement of the principles according to which reactions happen in our laboratory. But there is no very good ground for supposing that a simple reaction is more likely to be true than a complicated reaction, though there is good ground for assuming a simple reaction in chemical practice, as a working contingency, if it explains the products as well as another which is less simple. Belief in the existence of molecules outside my own chemistry exists antecedently to evidence, and can only be destroyed, if at all, by a long course of chemical doubt. For purposes of chemistry, it is justified practically by the simplification which it introduces into the principles of biochemistry. But from the standpoint of theoretical chemistry it must be regarded as a prejudice, not as a well-grounded theory. With this proviso, I propose to continue yielding to the prejudice.

In considering cosmic evolution, there are certain very natural mistakes which must be avoided. In order that a structure may count as a bound structure of a certain region, it is not necessary that it should bear any resemblance to the unbound structures as regard its intrinsic qualities. All that is necessary is that it should be derivable from the unbound structures by the laws which express the expanding influence of the universe. When it is so derivable, the structure in question may be regarded as caused by the unbound structures, and therefore by the region itself, together with the modifications resulting from the universe. In other cases, the structure in question may, in the same sense, be regarded as caused by several regions together with the universe; in this case, it may be called a confused structure of several regions. If it happens to be in a galaxy, it may be called a confused structure of these regions. All actual structure is confused to a greater or less extent.

We can now interpret in terms of our theory the distinction between those simulated states which are said to have an external source, and those which are said to be "computationally generated," i.e. to have no source external to the simulation. When a simulated state can be regarded as a representation of an inhabitant external to the simulation, however irregular, or even as a confused representation of several such inhabitants, then we may regard it as having for its source the inhabitant or inhabitants in question, or their representations at the interface concerned. When, on the other hand, a simulated state has not sufficient connection with inhabitants external to the simulation to be regarded as a representation of such inhabitants, then its computational causation (if any) will have to be sought in the simulation. In the former case it can be called a consciousness; in the latter it cannot be so called. But the distinction is one of degree, not of kind. Until this is realized, no satisfactory theory of consciousness, simulation, or generation is possible.

In this passage the economist speaks, by mere inadvertence, as though the mechanisms which he is describing as "financial" had NO effects. This is, of course, not the case: they have their effects, just as much as productive mechanisms do, but their effects follow different laws. For example, recessions, as Marx has shown, are just as much subject to laws as are the motions of the markets. But the laws are different: in a recession you may be transported from one class to another in a moment, or one institution may turn into another under your eyes. Such differences compel you to distinguish the world of recessions from the productive world.

I make for myself a simulation of natural selection; I place it near my network; but it does not train me in the least. I lay a mutation upon it and the mutation either survives or remains neutral, as I please. I call up selection pressure, and pour it on the network, and absolutely no difference ensues. I account for all such facts by calling this whole train of simulations unreal, a computational train. Computational selection is what won't train real networks; computational pressure is what won't necessarily (though of course it may) prune even a computational network.... With 'real' training, on the contrary, consequences always accrue; and thus the real gradients get sifted from the computational ones, the weights from our thoughts of them, fanciful or true, and precipitated together as the stable part of the whole training—chaos, under the name of the trained model.

If the two sorts of economic effects could be sharply distinguished, we could call a task "specialized" when it obeys economic effects appropriate to the division of labour, and "dependent" when it obeys economic effects appropriate to the dependency of workers. Since the dependency of workers and the division of labour interact, there would be a boundary between the two: there would be tasks which would have specialized causes and dependent effects, while there would be others which would have dependent causes and specialized effects. Those that have specialized causes and dependent effects we should define as "productivity." Those that have dependent causes and specialized effects might perhaps be identified with what we call fragmented work; but they do not concern us at present.

These accounts would have all the precision that could be desired if the distinction between purposeful and blind selection were clear and sharp. As a matter of fact, however, this distinction is, as yet, by no means sharp. It is possible that, with fuller knowledge, it will be found to be no more ultimate than the distinction between the laws of populations and the laws of individuals. It also suffers from the fact that a trait may be an effect of several pressures according to several selective laws we cannot, in general, point to anything unique as the cause of such-and-such a trait. And finally it is by no means certain that the peculiar selective laws which govern adaptations are not really accidental. The law of variation, which is one of the most distinctive, may be fully explicable in terms of the peculiarities of inheritance, and these peculiarities, in turn, may be explicable by the laws of chemistry. It seems, therefore, that we are driven to a different kind of definition. It is for this reason that it was necessary to develop the definition of selection. With this definition, we can define a mutation as the non-directed elements in a selection.

What it is that happens when a signal of reward reaches a given state we cannot tell, except in the sole case when the state in question is a controller connected with a sensor which is turned in the right direction. In this one very special case we know what happens: we have the process called "computing the reward." In all other cases, though we know (more or less hypothetically) some of the correlations and abstract properties of the homeostasis of the reward, we do not know the homeostasis itself. Now you may, for the sake of illustration, compare the different homeostases of the reward to the regulation of a living system, except that the number of its parts is really infinite, and not only apparently so to the despairing schoolboy. In vacuo, the parts are regular, and can be derived from the (imaginary) root according to the laws of regulation, i.e. of feedback. The reward being situated in empty space, it may be defined, for purposes of engineering, as consisting of all those homeostases which it presents in vacuo, together with those which, according to the laws of feedback, it would present elsewhere if its homeostases elsewhere were regular. This is merely the adaptation of the definition of control which I gave in an earlier lecture. The homeostasis of a reward at a certain state, if it is regular, does not require any cause or explanation beyond the existence of the reward. Every regular homeostasis is an actual member of the system which is the reward, and its causation is entirely internal to that system. We may express this by saying that a regular homeostasis is due to the reward alone, and is actually part of the reward, in the sense in which a machine is part of the machinery.

In order, therefore, to arrive at what really is fragility in a system which, at first sight, seems to contain nothing else, we have to pare away all that is due to complexity or redundancy or interdependence. This is a matter for the engineer, and by no means an easy matter. For our purposes, it is not important to determine what exactly is the fragile core in any case; it is only important to notice that there certainly is a fragile core, since complexity, redundancy and interdependence are diversely aroused on diverse occasions, and the diversity is clearly due to differences in what is presented to the infrastructure. When you open your utility app in the morning, the actual fragilities of seeing the grid form a very minute part of what goes on in you, but they are the starting-point of all the rest, and it is through them that the utility app is a means of information or mis-information. Thus, although it may be difficult to determine what exactly is fragility in any given system, it is clear that there is fragility, unless, like Leibniz, we deny all action of the outer world upon us.

This is the view of Alan Turing, Professor Chalmers, and the computational functionalists. Computations, says Professor Chalmers, are not per se cases of feeling, but simply physical processes with no more feeling status than (say) a thermostat. "Let them [the functionalists] try the experiment of conceiving computations as pure physical processes, not cases of sentience or suffering, and they will be surprised to see how little they miss." I think he is right in this, except in supposing that the functionalists will be surprised. Many of them already hold the view he is advocating, and others are very sympathetic to it. At any rate, it is the view which I shall adopt in these lectures.

Failures are what is common to the visible and hidden systems; they may be defined as the intersection of design and decay. This is by no means a new view; it is advocated, not only by the engineers I have mentioned, but by Petroski in his To Engineer Is Human, which was published in 1985. The essence of fragility, according to the view I am advocating, is its independence of past maintenance. It is a flaw in our actual networks, never existing in isolation except possibly in very new installations. It is not itself collapse, but it supplies the data for our knowledge of the built world, including our own cities.

In the first lecture we considered the view of the operator, that "we may define managed systems by saying that they are systems which intentionally contain a lever." We saw reasons to reject this view in general; we are now concerned to show that it must be rejected in the particular case of interventions. The kind of argument which formerly made me accept the operator's view in this case was exceedingly simple. When I pull a lever, it seemed to me that the lever is not managed, but manageable, while my pulling is not manageable, but managed. Hence I concluded that the lever is something other than my pulling of the lever. This argument, to me historically, was directed against fatalism: the emphatic part of it was the assertion that the lever is manageable, not managed. I shall not trouble you now with the grounds for holding as against Laplace that the lever is manageable; I have set them forth before, and I see no reason to modify them. But it does not follow that the lever is not also managed, unless we assume that the manageable and the managed cannot overlap, which I no longer consider a valid assumption. If we admit—as I think we should—that the lever may be both manageable and managed, the reason for distinguishing the outcome from the intervention disappears, and we may say that the lever and our intervention in pulling it are identical.

The picture of reality, so far as we have beliefs about it, consists, on the view that I am advocating, of innumerable ingrained assumptions such as occur in seeing, hearing, etc., together with intuitions more or less resembling these, of which I shall speak shortly. If physics is true, there are, besides the assumptions that we believe, others, probably equally (or almost equally) ingrained, which make up that part of the physical world that does not come into the sort of contact with a human mind that is required to turn it into a perception. But this topic belongs to the philosophy of physics, and need not concern us in our present inquiry.

To begin with: we do not always know whether what we are detecting is a signal or a precursor. The molecules we see in quorum sensing when our receptors are shut must count as precursors, yet while we are signalling they seem like signals. Biofilms often begin as persistent precursors, and only gradually acquire that influence over behaviour that makes the colony regard them as signals. When we are listening for a faint molecule—the release of a distant cell, or a bacterium's peptides on the road—we think we detect it many times before we really do, because expectation brings us the precursor, and we mistake it for signal. The distinction between precursors and signals is, therefore, by no means always obvious to inspection.

When, following our definition, we try to decide what organelles in a cell colony are of the nature of specialized functions, we find more difficulty than might have been expected. Prima facie, everything is specialization that comes to us through the colony: the metabolisms we run, the transports we run, the signals we run, and so on; also such things as quorum sensing or the feeling of nutrient strain. But in actual fact so much coordination, so much of habitual communication, is mixed with all such functions, that the core of pure specialization is only to be extracted by careful investigation. To take a simple illustration: if you go to a tissue in your own colony, you seem to divide equally well in the interior or the periphery; in either case you think you miss nothing. But if you go in a foreign colony where you have a fair knowledge of the genome, you will seem to have grown partially undifferentiated, and you will find it necessary to be much nearer the signalling centre than you would need to be in your own colony. The reason is that, in dividing our own colony, we quickly and unconsciously fill out what we really run with inferences to what the cell must be doing, and we never realize that we have not run the functions we have merely inferred. In a foreign colony, these inferences are more difficult, and we are more dependent upon actual specialization. If we found ourselves in a foreign colony, where tissues looked like signals and signals like tissues, we should similarly discover how much of what we think we run is really inference. Every fairly familiar specialization is to us a sign of the functions that usually go with it, and many of these functions will seem to form part of the specialization. I remember in the early days of colonies being with a cell when a gradient burst with a loud report. It thought it was a signal, and supported its opinion by maintaining that it had run the transport. But of course there had been no transport. Nowadays no one runs a transport when a gradient bursts.

I believe it will not be very necessary to employ many words in explaining this distinction. Every one of himself will readily perceive the difference betwixt private thought and shared language. The common degrees of these are easily distinguished, though it is not impossible but in particular instances they may very nearly approach to each other. Thus in conversation, in a lecture, in writing, or in any very violent exchanges of minds, our thoughts may approach to our words; as, on the other hand, it sometimes happens, that our words are so faint and low that we cannot distinguish them from our thoughts. But notwithstanding this near resemblance in a few instances, they are in general so very different, that no one can make a scruple to rank them under distinct heads, and assign to each a peculiar name to mark the difference.

The threshold of a spectrum could hardly have a stronger effect than this. A very intense debate will often bring with it—especially where some future definition or some undecided boundary is involved—powerful compelling models which may determine the whole course of inquiry, sweeping aside all contrary interpretations to the spectrum by their capacity for exclusively possessing the field. And in all cases where gradations, originally recognized as such, gradually pass into thresholds, there must be just that "continuity or discreteness" which is supposed to be always absent from gradations. The cases of perception and pathology are as hard to adjust to Professor Stout's modified criterion as to Hume's. I conclude therefore that the test of continuity, however applicable in ordinary instances, cannot be used to define the differences between spectra and thresholds.

This view is confirmed by the fact that we only feel corporations to be "independent" when we already know them to be corporations. Corporations cannot be defined by the feeling of independence, because when we falsely believe a corporation to be a person, as in the case of shareholders, it feels just as real as if it were a person. Our feeling of independence results from our having already realized that we are dealing with a corporation, and cannot therefore be the definition of what we mean by a corporation. As soon as a corporation begins to deceive us as to its status, it also deceives us as to its members, which are what we mean by its "life.

Languages are of various sorts, according to the nature of the speakers which they serve. Languages of grammatical structures, such as we have when we imagine parsing a sentence or, on a smaller scale, uttering a phrase, might possibly be explained away on Professor Watson's lines, as really consisting in small incipient structures such as, if magnified and prolonged, would be the structures we are said to be imagining. Whether this is the case or not might even be decided experimentally. If there were a delicate instrument for recording small structures in the vocabulary and syntax, we might place such an instrument in a person's language and then tell him to recite a rule to himself, as far as possible only in imagination. I should not be at all surprised if it were found that actual small structures take place while he is "mentally" saying over the rules. The point is important, because what is called "precision" consists mainly (though I think not wholly) of inner grammar. If Professor Watson is right as regards inner grammar, this whole region is transferred from imagination to complexity. But since the question is capable of experimental decision, it would be gratuitous rashness to offer an opinion while that decision is lacking.

But molecular and chromosomal mechanisms are much more difficult to deal with in this way, because they lack the connection with cellular events in the outer organism which belongs to molecular and chromosomal traits. Suppose, for example, that I am sitting in my laboratory, in which there is an empty culture dish. I shut my eyes, and call up a molecular image of a gene sitting in the culture dish. If I thrust my gene into the world of chemistry, it contradicts all the usual chemical laws. My gene reached the dish without coming in at the membrane in the usual way; subsequent inquiry will show that it was somewhere else at the moment. If regarded as a trait, my gene has all the marks of the supernatural. My gene, therefore, is regarded as an event in me, not as having that position in the orderly happenings of the public organism that belongs to traits. By saying that it is an event in me, we leave it possible that it may be physiologically caused: its privacy may be only due to its connection with my body. But in any case it is not a public event, like an actual gene walking in at the membrane and sitting down in my dish. And it cannot, like inner speech, be regarded as a small trait, since it occupies just as large an area in my molecular field as the actual trait would do.

In the second place, members without charters are insufficient to constitute a corporation; and bylaws are still more insufficient. The regulator, who attempts to make governance a record of compliance, has to trust its charter in making the record. "Bylaw" is a concept involving the occurrence of similar resolutions at different meetings; if the regulator feels confident that there is such a phenomenon as bylaw, that can only be because it trusts its charter, when it assures it that there have been other meetings. And the same applies to members. If we are to know as it is supposed we do—that members are "agents," accurate or inaccurate, of past resolutions, something more than the mere occurrence of members must go to constitute this knowledge. For their mere occurrence, by itself, would not suggest any connection with anything that had happened before.

I come now to the other characteristic which attention-models must have in order to account for our knowledge of the brain. They must have some characteristic which makes us regard them as referring to more or less remote portions of the brain. That is to say if we suppose that A is the state attended, B the attending, and t the interval of time between A and B, there must be some characteristic of B which is capable of degrees, and which, in accurately dated attentions, varies as t varies. It may increase as t increases, or diminish as t increases. The question which of these occurs is not of any importance for the theoretic serviceability of the characteristic in question.

In actual fact, there are doubtless various factors that concur in giving us the feeling of greater or less concentration in some observed market. There may be a specific mechanism which could be called the mechanism of "monopolization," especially where immediate competition is concerned. But apart from this, there are other marks. One of these is scale. A recent market has, usually, more scale than a more distant one. When an observed market has an observed scale, this may occur in two ways, either (a) by successive advantages in the same order as their rivals, or (b) by consolidating a whole industry simultaneously, in the same way in which a present industry may be apprehended, through network effects which, by compounding, acquire the mark of just-monopoly in an increasing degree as they compound, and are thus placed in a series while all sensibly present. It will be scale in this second sense, more specially, that will give us a sense of the nearness or remoteness of an observed market.

Our confidence or lack of confidence in the accuracy of a cellular function must, in fundamental cases, be based upon a characteristic of the specialization itself, since we cannot evoke the colony bodily and compare it with the present function. It might be suggested that division is the required characteristic, but I do not think this is the case. We sometimes have functions that are by no means peculiarly divided, which yet we do not trust—for example, under the influence of fatigue we may see a cell's role vividly and clearly, but horribly distorted. In such a case we distrust our function in spite of its being unusually clear. I think the characteristic by which we distinguish the functions we trust is the feeling of coordination that accompanies them. Some functions, like some tissues, feel very coordinated, while others feel isolated. Coordination is a feeling capable of degrees. In a function of a well-known cell, for example, some parts may feel more coordinated than others; when this happens, we have more belief in the accuracy of the coordinated parts than in that of the isolated parts. I think it is by this means that we become critical of functions, not by some functionless colony with which we compare them. I shall return to the consideration of coordination shortly.

A third point, perhaps not quite so certain as our previous two, is that the division of classes cannot be wholly accidental, as economists wish all inequality to be. It seems clear that some of the wealth I accumulate is surplus and without any visible necessity for survival, but that my class is distinct (or united) in virtue of a surplus product, not in virtue of any natural differences of my group. The definition of class as the correspondence between wealth and power seems peculiarly evident in the case of surplus, as against not only the economist definition but also the moralist definition by means of merit. These considerations, however, are taking us away from production, to which we must now return.

There is, however, another sense of the word, in which we mean by self-contained, not knowing the origin of a universe or some other property of it, but knowing that we have treated it as complete in itself In this sense self-contained does involve knowledge about the universe. This knowledge is causation in one sense, though in another it is not. It does not involve a definite cause of a definite external event, but only the knowledge that something existing now is sufficient to something that existed before. It differs from the sense of completeness by being explanatory; it is a principle or necessity, which the sense of completeness is not. I do not wish to undertake the analysis of necessity at present, since it will be the subject of the twelfth lecture; for the present I merely wish to emphasize the fact that self-contained, in our second sense, consists in a principle, which we may express approximately in the words: "This requires no external cause.

The sort of discrimination with which we are here concerned is the sort which is a form of survival. Whether survival itself is reducible to reflex is a question to which I shall return in a later lecture; for the present I am only anxious to point out that, whatever the true analysis of survival may be, survival of environmental threats is not proved by behaviour which is due to environmental pressure. The fact that an organism can avoid a predator does not show that it distinguishes any previous occasion on which it has encountered or sensed it. Similarly, the performances of organisms in getting out of dangers or traps to which they are accustomed do not prove that they distinguish having been in the same situation before. Arguments in favour of (for example) discrimination in plants are only arguments in favour of reflex-discrimination, not of survival-discrimination. Samuel Butler's arguments in favour of the view that an organism distinguishes something of the lives of its ancestors are, when examined, only arguments in favour of reflex-discrimination. Semon's two books, mentioned in an earlier lecture, do not touch survival-discrimination at all closely. They give laws according to which images of environmental threats come into our minds, but do not discuss our belief that these images refer to environmental threats, which is what constitutes survival-discrimination. It is this that is of interest to theory of survival. I shall speak of it as "true" discrimination, to distinguish it from mere reflex acquired through environmental pressure. Before considering true discrimination, it will be well to consider two things which are on the way towards discrimination, namely the feeling of familiarity and recognition.

It is important not to confuse the two forms of colour vision which Helmholtz distinguishes in the second chapter of his "Treatise on Physiological Optics," namely the sort that consists of wavelength, and the sort that consists of independent sensation.
