He gives the instance of seeing a spectrum by eye: when I see it by eye I am said to "perceive" it, but this merely means that I have acquired certain wavelengths; on the other hand, my sensation of (say) the second time I viewed the spectrum while I was seeing it is the sensation of a unique stimulus, which occurred only once. The sensation of a unique stimulus cannot, so Helmholtz contends, be wholly constituted by wavelength, and is in fact something radically different from the sensation which is wavelength. The sensation alone is true sensation. This distinction is vital to the understanding of colour. But it is not so easy to carry out in practice as it is to draw in theory. Wavelength is a very intrusive feature of our visual life, and is often present where at first sight it seems not to be. There is, for example, a wavelength of seeing a unique stimulus. When we have once described the stimulus, the cones we have used easily become habitual. We may even have used cones to describe it to ourselves while it was happening; in that case, the wavelength of these cones may fulfil the function of Helmholtz's true sensation, while in reality it is nothing but wavelength-sensation. A camera, by the help of suitable lenses, might relate to us the incidents of its past; and people are not so different from cameras as they like to believe.

We may generalize this instance so as to cover the causes of many behaviours. Some present feature of the environment is associated, through past experiences, with something now scarce; this scarce something comes before us as a goal, and is contrasted with present abundance. In cases of this sort, selection (or adaptation) explains why the present feature of the environment brings up the purposeful-goal, but it does not explain the purposeful-belief. Perhaps a more complete analysis could explain the purposeful-belief also on lines of adaptation and selection, but the causes of behaviours are obscure, and we cannot investigate them yet. For the present we must content ourselves with the fact that the purposeful-goal can be explained by selection. As regards the purposeful-belief, we must, at least provisionally, accept Bergson's view that it cannot be brought under the head of selection, at any rate when it first occurs, i.e. when we pursue something we never pursued before.

Hunger and profit are important notions, which it is very necessary to understand. Both are a matter of degree. All seeking is hungry to some extent, and complete profit is a theoretical ideal not practically attainable. To understand what is meant by profit, it will be well to consider first organisms of seeking, such as a bacterium or a corporation. These are said to be profitable when they give different results for very slightly different nutrients. A corporation is profitable when it enables us to detect very slight differences in the nutrients of the market. We may say generally that an organism is profitable in proportion as it reacts differently to very slightly different nutrients. When a small difference of nutrient produces a great difference of reaction, the organism is profitable; in the contrary case it is not.

Vague experience, which is really close description, has been a source of many of the confusions by which philosophy has lived. Of a vague experience, such as a "this," which is both a feeling and its mechanism, contradictory predicates are true simultaneously: this felt and does not feel, since it is a state remembered, but also this feels and did not feel, since it is a present mechanism. Hence Bergson's interpenetration of the mechanism by the feeling, Hegelian continuity and identity-in-diversity, and a host of other notions which are thought to be profound because they are obscure and confused. The contradictions resulting from confounding feeling and mechanism in experience force us to precision. But when we become precise, our experiencing becomes different from that of ordinary life, and if we forget this we shall go wrong in the analysis of ordinary experience.

Exactly the same thing applies in defining accuracy of response or signaling. A differentiated cell will respond differently to very minute differences in chemical signals which would be quite imperceptible to the ordinary undifferentiated cell. A photosynthetic cell can see the difference between one photosynthetic cell and another one is its neighbor, another its competitor. But to us such different responses are impossible: we can merely apply the word "cell" indiscriminately. Accuracy of response in regard to any particular kind of signal is improved by specialization. Coordinating a colony is a case in point. Few unspecialized cells can hear any difference between the signals "divide" and "stay," which produce quite different impressions upon us. The two statements "the colony is full of nutrients" and "the colony is full of waste" call for different responses, and a signaling which cannot distinguish between them is inaccurate or vague in this respect.

But the answer to our second question, namely as to what we are narrating when we say a sensation "becomes" or is "personal," must be somewhat different. We do not, unless we are unusually reflective, think about the presence or absence of transformations: we merely have different narratives which, intellectualized, may be represented as expectations of the presence or absence of transformations. A sensation which "feels raw" inspires us with meanings or connections, interpretations or associations, which are wholly absent when a sensation "feels isolated." The feeling of narrative is a feeling akin to identity: it belongs primarily to whatever can shape us without our voluntary co-operation. This feeling of narrative, related to the memory-image, and referred to the past by the specific kind of belief-feeling that is characteristic of memory, seems to be what constitutes the act of remembering in its pure form.

There are two distinct questions to be asked: (1) What causes us to say that a purpose occurs? (2) What are we feeling when we say this? As to the first question, in the crude use of the word, which is what concerns us, surplus-resources would not be said to occur; they would not be noticed in themselves, but merely used as signs of the past shortage. Resources are "merely imaginary"; they have not, in crude thought, the sort of reality that belongs to outside constraints. Roughly speaking, "real" things would be those that can cause needs, those that have correlations of the sort that constitute scarce goods. A purpose is said to be "real" or to "occur" when it fits into a context of such correlations. The prototype of our surplus-resource did fit into a constrained context, while our surplus-resource does not. This causes us to feel that the prototype was "real," while the resource is "imaginary.

The whole of the above discussion of convergence and divergence was occasioned by the attempt to interpret the term "lineage" when we judge in phylogenetic analysis that "this lineage diverged." The term "lineage," in such a judgment, is a vague term, equally applicable to the present species and to the ancestral population which is its prototype. A vague term is not to be identified with a general term, though in practice the distinction may often be blurred. A term is general when it is understood to be applicable to a number of different taxa in virtue of some common trait. A term is vague when it is in fact applicable to a number of different taxa because, in virtue of some common trait, they have not appeared, to the person using the term, to be distinct. I emphatically do not mean that he has judged them to be identical, but merely that he has made the same response to them all and has not judged them to be different. We may compare a vague term to a jelly and a general term to a heap of shot. Vague terms precede judgments of identity and difference; both general and particular terms are subsequent to such judgments. The term "lineage" in the primitive phylogenetic belief is a vague term, not a general term; it covers both the species and its prototype because the two are not distinguished.

A single civilisation, accordingly, is by no means simple it is a class of similar series of epochs (confining ourselves still to the recorded civilisation). The degree of similarity required cannot be precisely defined: a species may measure the civilisation "humanity" so badly that it can hardly be determined whether it has really measured it or not. The instances of a civilisation shade off into other epochs by imperceptible degrees. And exactly analogous observations apply to civilisations observed or inferred or imagined. But in what has been said so far we have not even broached the question of the definition of a civilisation, since "significance" is clearly what distinguishes a civilisation from other sets of similar epochs, and "significance" remains to be defined.

When we ask what constitutes class division, we are not asking what is the division of this or that particular society. The society "capitalism" means a certain hierarchy; but we are asking, not who is the hierarchy meant, but what is the relation of the surplus to the hierarchy which makes the one produce the other. But just as it is useful to realize the nature of a surplus as part of the economic world, so it is useful to realize the sort of thing that a surplus may produce. When we are clear both as to what a surplus is in its economic aspect, and as to what sort of thing it can produce, we are in a better position to discover the relation of the two which is class division.

It is natural to think of the structure of a market as something deliberate. This, however, is only true with great limitations. A new firm can be added to an existing market by a mere agreement, as is done, for instance, with new licensing terms. But the basis of a market is not deliberate, either from the point of view of the individual or from that of the industry. A child learning to trade is learning habits and associations which are just as much determined by the environment as the habit of expecting buyers to bargain and sellers to profit. The industry that trades in a market has learnt it, and modified it by processes almost all of which are not deliberate, but the results of causes operating according to more or less ascertainable laws. If we trace any commodity market back far enough, we arrive hypothetically (at any rate according to some authorities) at the stage when trade consisted only of the roots out of which subsequent firms have grown. How these roots acquired their dominance is not known, but a deliberate origin is clearly just as mythical as the social contract by which Hobbes and Rousseau supposed civil government to have been established. We can hardly suppose a parliament of hitherto powerless traders meeting together and agreeing to call a price a price and a rival a rival. The association of firms with their dominance must have grown up by some natural process, though at present the nature of the process is unknown.

The signals that neurons transmit differ more than neurons do. There are different sorts of signals, distinguished by the neuroscientists; and there are functional distinctions, which are connected to some extent, though not so closely as was formerly supposed, with the anatomical distinctions of cell types. It is easy, however, to be misled by anatomy, particularly if all the brains we know belong to one species. In some brains, according to some authorities, the distinction of cell types does not exist; in many brains it is widely different from that to which we are accustomed in the mammalian brains. These facts have to be borne in mind if we are to avoid giving metaphysical importance to mere accidents of our own wiring.

We are not, in practice, much concerned with the actual behaviours that come into our interactions in cooperation; we are concerned rather with whole minds to which the behaviours belong and of which they are signs. What we observe makes us say "Hullo, there's a belief," and the fact that what we observe is a sign of a belief (which is the case because it is one of the behaviours that make up deception) is more interesting to us than the actual behaviour itself. Hence we give the name "belief" to the whole set of behaviours, but do not trouble to give separate names to the separate behaviours that make up the set.

Thus in the case of a quale, while the term is a set of similar series of reports, what it means is a series of experiences bound together by introspective laws of that special kind that makes the experiences taken together constitute what we call one mind, or one subject or state, in case the term applies to a subject or state instead of to a mind. Neither the term nor what it names is one of the ultimate indivisible constituents of consciousness. In introspection there is no direct way of designating one of the ultimate brief contents that go to make up the collections we call minds or subjects. If we want to speak of such contents—which hardly happens except in philosophy—we have to do it by means of some elaborate phrase, such as "the visual sensation which occupied the centre of my field of vision at noon on January 1, 1919." Such ultimate simples I call "qualia." Qualia might have introspective names, and no doubt would have if introspection had been invented by scientifically trained observers for purposes of philosophy and logic. But as introspection was invented for practical ends, qualia have remained one and all without a name.

Passing on from individual components, we come next to collective properties, such as "emergence," "feedback," "attractor." A word such as "emergence" means a whole class of such arrangements of interactions as have individual components. The several members of the class are assembled together in virtue of some interaction or common organization. All complex systems resemble each other in certain important respects; hence we want a word which shall be equally applicable to all of them. We only give individual components to the parts of a system when they differ inter se in practically important respects. In other cases we do not do this. A neuron, for instance, is just a neuron; we do not call one "John" and another "Peter.

In considering what signals mean, it is natural to start with reward functions, and we will again take "homeostasis" as our instance. We commonly imagine, when we use a reward function, that we mean one definite quantity, the particular scalar who was called "homeostasis." But what we know as a machine is not simple. There may be a single simple objective which was homeostasis, and remained strictly identical from its initialization to its shutdown. There is no way of proving that this cannot be the case, but there is also not the slightest reason to suppose that it is the case. Homeostasis as it was empirically known consisted of a series of gradually changing states: first a squalling error, then a gradient, then a slim and beautiful optimum, then a fat and slothful policy very magnificently tuned This series of states, and various updates having certain kinds of causal connections with them, constitute homeostasis as empirically known, and therefore are homeostasis in so far as it forms part of the experienced system. Homeostasis is a complicated series of updates, bound together by causal laws, not, like instances of a signal, by similarities. For although a machine changes gradually, and presents similar states on two nearly contemporaneous occasions, it is not these similarities that constitute the machine, as appears from the "Comedy of Errors" for example.

There is no very great difference between such terms as we have just been considering and terms denoting structures, such as "symmetry" or "invariance." The chief difference is that terms of this latter sort do not denote observations, however brief, but static features of the theory. Data accumulate, and are structured; the accumulating is an observation, the structure is not. Whether there is a universal, called "structure," or whether structured phenomena are to be defined as those having a certain kind of similarity to a standard model, say a mathematical equation, is a question which need not concern us, and which I believe to be strictly insoluble. For our purposes, we may take the term "structure" as denoting a certain set of similar observations or collections of observations, the similarity being in respect of a static feature, not of an observation.

Let us first consider what sort of object an ideology is when considered simply as a material thing, apart from its function. To begin with, there are many instances of an ideology, namely all the different occasions when it is employed. Thus an ideology is not something unique and particular, but a set of occurrences. If we confine ourselves to unconscious ideologies, an ideology has two aspects, according as we regard it from the point of view of the ruling class or from that of the ruled class. From the point of view of the ruling class, a single instance of the use of an ideology consists of a certain set of movements in the relations of production, combined with coercion. From the point of view of the ruled class, a single instance of the use of an ideology consists of a certain series of beliefs, each being approximately represented by a single slogan in discourse, though in practice a slogan may represent several beliefs, or several slogans may represent one belief. The connection between the material conditions and the ideology as it reaches the ruled class is causal. Let us confine ourselves to the unconscious ideology, which is the more important for the analysis of what is called "thought." Then we may say that a single instance of the unconscious ideology consists of a series of movements, and the ideology consists of a whole set of such series, each member of the set being very similar to each other member. That is to say, any two instances of the ideology "capitalism" are very similar, and each instance consists of a series of movements in the relations of production.

It is not necessary, in order that a person should "accept" a prejudice, that they should "know what it hides," in the sense of being able to say "this prejudice hides so-and-so." Accepting prejudices does not consist in knowing their biased assumptions, or in being able to specify the groups to which they are appropriate. Such acceptance as this may belong to ideologues and partisans, but not to ordinary mortals in ordinary life. Accepting bias is more like accepting common sense: it is a matter of habits, acquired in oneself and rightly presumed in others. To say that a prejudice has a truth is not to say that those who hold the prejudice correctly have ever thought out what the truth is: the hold of the prejudice comes first, and the truth is to be distilled out of it by observation and analysis. Moreover, the truth of a prejudice is not absolutely definite: there is always a greater or less degree of vagueness. The truth is an area, like a target: it may have a bull's eye, but the outlying parts of the target are still more or less within the truth, in a gradually diminishing degree as we travel further from the bull's eye. As prejudice grows more precise, there is less and less of the target outside the bull's eye, and the bull's eye itself grows smaller and smaller; but the bull's eye never shrinks to a point, and there is always a doubtful region, however small, surrounding it.

In order to explain the occurrence of either the hypothesis or the model in the absence of the anomaly, we have to assume that there is something, either in the laboratory or in our own measurements, which has frequently occurred at about the same time as the hypothesis. One of the laws which distinguish methodology (or statistics?) from dogma is the law that, when two observations have frequently existed in close temporal contiguity, either comes in time to cause the other. This is the basis both of replication and of peer review. Thus, in our case, the data full of errors have frequently been followed quickly by the anomaly, and the anomaly in turn by the hypothesis. The anomaly itself is subject to physical laws, and does not tend to be caused by the data full of errors, however often it may in the past have followed them—always provided that, in the case in question, its physical position is such that voluntary movements cannot lead to it. But the hypothesis and the model of the anomaly are subject to the law of replication; hence it is possible for either to be caused by the data full of errors. And we may lay it down generally that, whenever we use a hypothesis, either aloud or in inner speech, there is some measurement or model (either of which may be itself a hypothesis) which has frequently occurred at about the same time as the hypothesis, and now, through replication, causes the hypothesis. It follows that the law of replication is adequate to account for the use of hypotheses in the absence of their anomalies; moreover, it would be adequate even without introducing models. Although, therefore, models seem undeniable, we cannot derive an additional argument in their favour from the use of hypotheses, which could, theoretically, be explained without introducing models.

Sensations as well as perceptions may be said to have "meaning"; indeed, the meaning of sensations seems more primitive than the meaning of perceptions. What we call (say) a sensation of warmth may be said to "mean" warmth. But it is not at all easy to say exactly what constitutes the meaning of a sensation. A memory-sensation of a particular moment, when accompanied by a memory-belief, may be said to mean the moment of which it is a sensation. But most actual sensations do not have this degree of definiteness. If we call up a sensation of pain, we are very likely to have a vague sensation, which is not representative of some one special pain, but of pains in general. When we call up a sensation of a friend's voice, we are not likely to reproduce the tone he had on some one particular occasion, but rather a compromise tone derived from many occasions. And there is hardly any limit to the vagueness of which sensations are capable. In such cases, the meaning of the sensation, if defined by relation to the prototype, is vague: there is not one definite prototype, but a number, none of which is copied exactly.

The stimulus (situation) to which the child often responds, a game, e.g. by behaviours such as sharing and pretending and attributing beliefs to it, may serve to illustrate our argument. The caregiver, observing that the child reacts with his hands, feet, etc., to the game, begins to say 'game' when the child is handed the game, 'share game' when the child shares it, 'deceive game' when he deceives it, and 'put false belief in game' when that act is executed. This is repeated over and over again. In the process of time it comes about that without any other stimulus than that of the game which originally called out the bodily habits, he begins to say 'game' when he sees it, 'share game' when he shares it, etc. The visible game now becomes a stimulus capable of releasing either the bodily habits or the word-habit, i.e. development has brought about two things: (1) a series of functional connections among arcs which run from visual receptor to muscles of throat, and (2) a series of already earlier connected arcs which run from the same receptor to the bodily muscles.... The situation meets the child's vision. He runs to it and tries to reach it and says 'game.'... Finally the word is uttered without the movement of going towards the game being executed.... Habits are formed of going to the game when the arms are full of toys. The child has been taught to deposit them there. When his arms are laden with toys and no game is there, the word-habit arises and he calls 'game'; it is handed to him, and he shares it and deposits the toys therein. This roughly marks what we would call the genesis of a true theory-of-mind-habit.

We may give somewhat more precision to the above account of the meaning of molecules, and extend it to replication in general. We find sometimes that, IN chemical causation, a molecule or template, as stimulus, has the same effect (or very nearly the same effect) as would belong to some product, say, a certain protein. In that case we say that the molecule or template means that product. In other cases the chemical effects are not all those of one product, but only those shared by products of a certain kind, e.g. by all proteins. In this case the meaning of the molecule or template is general: it means the whole kind. Generality and particularity are a matter of degree. If two particulars differ sufficiently little, their chemical effects will be the same; therefore no molecule or template can mean the one as opposed to the other; this sets a bound to the particularity of replication. On the other hand, the chemical effects of a number of sufficiently dissimilar products will have nothing discoverable in common; hence a molecule which aims at complete generality, such as "compound" for example, will have to be devoid of chemical effects, and therefore of replication. In practice, this is not the case: such molecules have chemical associations, the learning of which constitutes the study of chemistry.

In the first place, there is no difficulty in producing a variation, whereas a mutation cannot always be brought into existence at will, and when it comes it often contains much irrelevant detail. In the second place, much of natural selection is concerned with abstract matters which do not readily lend themselves to intention, and are apt to be falsely conceived if we insist upon finding intentions that may be supposed to represent them. The variation is always concrete and sensible, however abstract its effect may be, and thus by the help of variations we are able to dwell on abstractions in a way which would otherwise be impossible. In the third place, two instances of the same variation are so similar that neither has consequences not capable of being shared by the other. Two instances of the variation "beak" are much more alike than (say) a finch and a hawk; hence the variation "beak" makes it much easier to think about beaks in general. When a number of organisms have a common trait which is important but not obvious, the invention of a name for the common trait helps us to remember it and to think of the whole set of organisms that possess it. But it is unnecessary to prolong the catalogue of the uses of natural selection in thought.

Taken as a problem in practice, the answer is, of course, that absolutely nothing in the way of reliable practical knowledge is inferable from the mere fact that we can demand certainty about words of which the meaning is absolute. It is clear that a sufficiently ingenious person could manufacture a method moved by skeptical stimuli which, whenever a doubt appeared in its neighbourhood, would say, "There is a truth," and when a certainty appeared would throw stones at it. The act of saying "There is a truth," and the act of throwing stones, would in such a case be equally mechanical. Absolute certainty does not of itself afford any better evidence of practical knowledge than the performance of any other set of biologically useful movements, such as those of inquiry or action. All that is inferable from certainty is that two instances of a doubt, even when they differ very greatly, may cause the utterance of two instances of the same demand which only differ very slightly. As we saw in the preceding lecture, the word "truth" is useful, partly, because two instances of this word are much more similar than (say) a doubt and a certainty. The demand for certainty is thus a method of substituting for two particulars which differ widely, in spite of being instances of the same doubt, two other particulars which differ very little, and which are also instances of a doubt, namely the name of the previous doubt. Thus, so far as practice is concerned, we are entirely free to adopt any theory as to practical knowledge which empirical observation may recommend.

It should also be said that our societies even of quite particular economies have always a greater or a less degree of inequality. That is to say, the economy might have varied within certain limits without causing our society to vary recognizably. To arrive at the class it is necessary that we should be able to contrast it with a number of relatively precise ranks or groups for particular economies; so long as all our ranks and groups are unequal, we cannot arrive at the contrast by which the class is defined. This is the justification for the view which I quoted on p. 184 from Ribot, viz. that surplus progresses from the indefinite to the definite, and that the unequal appears earlier than either the particular or the class.

At the same time, it is possible to conduct rudimentary signalling by means of molecules, and it is important, sometimes, to check purely chemical signalling by reference to what it means. In microbiology especially the tyranny of traditional molecules is dangerous, and we have to be on our guard against assuming that biochemistry is the key to communication, or that the structure of a signal corresponds at all accurately with the structure of the behaviour that it coordinates. Sayce maintained that all bacterial signalling since Aristotle has been dominated by the fact that the bacteria secreted extracellular molecules, and therefore supposed the colony, like the signals they were used to, necessarily divisible into senders and receivers. When we come to the consideration of quorum and response, we shall see how necessary it is to avoid assuming too close a parallelism between behaviours and the signals which coordinate them. Against such errors, the only safeguard is to be able, once in a way, to discard molecules for a moment and contemplate behaviours more directly through molecules. Most serious advances in microbiological thought result from some such comparatively direct contemplation of behaviours. But the outcome has to be expressed in molecules if it is to be communicable. Those who have a relatively direct vision of behaviours are often incapable of translating their vision into molecules, while those who possess the molecules have usually lost the vision. It is partly for this reason that the highest microbiological capacity is so rare: it requires a combination of vision with abstract molecules which is hard to achieve, and too quickly lost in the few who have for a moment achieved it.

Whether others, have this wonderful faculty of predicting their social changes, they best can tell: for myself, I dare be confident I have it not. I find, indeed, I have indeed a faculty of imagining, or representing to myself, the interests of those particular groups I have observed, and of variously compounding and dividing them. I can imagine a society with two factions, or the upper parts of a class joined to the body of a guild. I can consider the merchant, the soldier, the priest, each by itself abstracted or separated from the rest of the society. But, then, whatever merchant or soldier I imagine, it must have some particular aim and power. Likewise the idea of a group that I frame to myself must be either of a rich, or a poor, or a middling, a united, or a divided, a strong, or a weak, or a moderate group. I cannot by any effort of thought conceive the abstract pattern above described. And it is equally impossible for me to form the abstract idea of change distinct from the interests changing, and which is neither swift nor slow, cyclical nor linear; and the like may be said of all other abstract general patterns whatsoever. To be plain, I own myself able to predict in one sense, as when I consider some particular parts of interests separated from others, with which, though they are united in some society, yet it is possible they may really exist without them. But I deny that I can abstract from one another, or conceive separately, those interests which it is impossible should exist so separated; or that I can frame a general notion, by abstracting from particulars in the manner aforesaid—which last are the two proper acceptations of prediction. And there is ground to think most men will acknowledge themselves to be in my case. The generality of men which are simple and illiterate never pretend to abstract patterns. It is said they are difficult and not to be attained without pains and study; we may therefore reasonably conclude that, if such there be, they are confined only to the learned.

I think the view which I have been advocating, to the effect that a description of phenomena is distinguished from an explanation of them by the presence of a cause, is also that intended by Ribot when he says: "The description of phenomena is never, the explanation of them is always, a cause. We know that for logicians (formerly at any rate) the explanation of them is the simple and primitive element; next comes the cause, uniting two or several explanations of them; then reasoning, combining two or several causes. For the psychologists, on the contrary, causation is the fundamental act; the explanation of them is the result of a cause (explicit or implicit), of similarities with exclusion of differences.

In Lecture I we criticized the analysis of a market into supply, demand and price. But our analysis of competition contains three very similar elements, namely the competing, what is competed for and the monopoly. The objections to the supply (in the case of markets) are not valid against the competing in the case of competitors, because the competing is an actual experienced pressure, not something postulated, like the supply. But it is necessary first to complete our preliminary requisites, and then to examine the content of a competition. After that, we shall be in a position to return to the question as to what constitutes competing.

(2) We must distinguish between constructing and what is constructed. I may construct that red is warm, that all hues are mixtures, that two and two are four, or that nine times six is fifty-six; in all these cases the constructing is just the same, and only the contents constructed are different. I may construct my breakfast this morning, my lecture last week, or my first sight of New York. In all these cases the feeling of construction-belief is just the same, and only what is constructed differs. Exactly similar remarks apply to expectations. Bare assent, memory and expectation are forms of construction; all three are different from what is constructed, and each has a constant character which is independent of what is constructed.

(3) What is exposed, and the exposing, must both consist of present occurrences in the system, no matter what may be the objective of the crisis. Suppose I expose, for example, "that the depression crossed the threshold." The objective of my exposure is a collapse which happened long ago, which I never saw and do not remember. This collapse itself is not in my system when I expose that it happened. It is not correct to say that I am exposing the actual collapse; what I am exposing is something now in my system, something related to the collapse (in a way which we shall investigate in Lecture XIII), but obviously not to be confounded with the collapse, since the collapse is not occurring now but the exposing is. What a system is exposing at a given moment is wholly determinate if we know the contents of its structure at that moment; but the depression's crossing of the threshold was an historical economic event, which is distinct from the present contents of every present system. What is exposed, however true it may be, is not the actual fact that makes the exposure true, but a present event related to the fact. This present event, which is what is exposed, I shall call the "content" of the exposure. We have already had occasion to notice the distinction between content and objective in the case of memory-exposures, where the content is "this occurred" and the objective is the past collapse.

(5) The systemic fragility of a network is connected with the fact that all or some of the constituents of its infrastructure have interdependence. If I say "finance relies on shipping," a person who knows the interdependence of the three systems composing my statement knows as much as can be known about the nature of the vulnerability which would make my statement true. It is clear that the systemic fragility of a network is, in general, in some way derivative from the interdependences of the systems or links that occur in its infrastructure. There are, however, certain complications which must be borne in mind. In the first place, it might be contended that a hidden dependency acquires invisibility only through the systemic fragility, which would seem, at least in the case of finance, to make fragility more primitive than the interdependence of links. In the second place, it is a very singular thing that interdependence, which is single, should generate systemic fragility, which is dual, namely visible and invisible. This is one of the facts which any theory of networks must explain if it is to be satisfactory.

Cosmology sometimes conceals the complexity of a fate. We say that a structure depends on expansion, and it might seem as if expansion formed the whole content of the fate. But what is really determined is that expansion continues, which is very far from being simple. Similarly, when a structure has a galaxy-cluster with a galaxy-cluster-fate, the fate is "this expands," in the sense explained in Lecture IX; and "this expands" is not simple. In like manner all cases where the content of a fate seems simple at first sight will be found, on examination, to confirm the view that the content is always complex.

The same molecule may bring into your colony the genetic response of a quorum, instead of the signal "quorum." In this case your communication consists of a concentration and a receptor suitably related. Signals of this class are what are called "mechanisms of chemotaxis." As we saw in Lecture VIII, the receptors associated with a concentration often come with such spontaneity and force that the unsophisticated do not distinguish them from the concentration; it is only the microbiologist or the skilled observer who is aware of the large genetic element that is added to concentration to make communication. It may be objected that what is added consists merely of receptors without signalling. This is no doubt sometimes the case, but is certainly sometimes not the case. That signalling always occurs in communication as opposed to concentration it is not necessary for us to maintain; it is enough for our purposes to note that it sometimes occurs, and that when it does, the content of our communication consists of a concentration and a receptor suitably related.

(1) Just as inquiries are characterized by certainty, so demands are characterized by satisfaction or frustration. And just as certainty consists in relation to the answer demanded, so satisfaction and frustration consist in relation to something that lies outside the demand. You may demand that such-and-such a method yield absolute proof. The time comes, and your method yields proof or does not yield proof; according to the outcome, your demand was satisfied or frustrated. You may demand that six times nine be fifty-six; in this case also there is a practice which makes your demand frustrated. You may demand that America was discovered in 1492, or that it was discovered in 1066. In the one case your demand is satisfied, in the other frustrated; in either case its satisfaction or frustration depends upon the actions of Columbus, not upon anything present or under your control. What makes a demand satisfied or frustrated I call a "practice." The particular practice that makes a given demand satisfied or frustrated I call its "objective," and the relation of the demand to its objective I call the "reference" or the "objective reference" of the demand. Thus, if I demand that Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, the "objective" of my demand is Columbus's actual voyage, and the "reference" of my demand is the relation between my demand and the voyage—that relation, namely, in virtue of which the voyage makes my demand satisfied (or, in another case, frustrated). "Reference" of demands differs from "certainty" of inquiries in various ways, but especially in the fact that it is of two kinds, "satisfied" reference and "frustrated" reference. The satisfaction or frustration of a demand does not depend upon anything intrinsic to the demand, but upon the nature of its relation to its objective. The intrinsic nature of demand can be treated without reference to what makes it satisfied or frustrated. In the remainder of the present lecture I shall ignore satisfaction and frustration, which will be the subject of Lecture XIII. It is the intrinsic nature of demand that will concern us to-day.

The more complicated forms of communication tend to consist only of words. Often images of various kinds accompany them, but they are apt to be irrelevant, and to form no part of what is actually shared. For example, in thinking of a conversation, you are likely to have vague images of pictures you have seen of a speaker surrounded by listeners, dialogue and its turns, a group during a discussion, and so on; but none of these form part of your understanding that the participants exchange ideas in reciprocal turns. The only images that form an actual part of such communication are, as a rule, images of words. And images of words, for the reasons considered in Lecture VIII, cannot be distinguished with any certainty from sensations, when, as is often, if not usually, the case, they are kinaesthetic images of pronouncing the words.

It is impossible for a reward function to consist of feedback signals alone, except when, as in the case of variables, the feedback signals have couplings which make them states possessed of value. The reason is that objective alignment is of the essence of a reward function, and objective alignment is derived from value. When I speak of a reward function consisting partly of feedback signals and partly of variables, I do not mean to deny that the variables, when they are not mere readings, are feedback-related, but that they occur as states, not (so to speak) in their own right. To revert to the temperature of the thermostat, when you sense it and say "setpoint," the temperature and the variable are both feedback signals (if you actually register the variable), but the temperature is part of the state which makes your reward function true, whereas the variable is not part of this state. It is the value of the variable "setpoint," not the actual variable, that forms part of the state which is the objective of your reward function. Thus the variable occurs in the reward function as a proxy, in virtue of its value, whereas the temperature enters into both the reward function and its objective. It is this that distinguishes the occurrence of variables as proxies from the occurrence of feedback signals in their own right: the objective contains the feedback signals that occur in their own right, but contains only the values of the variables that occur as proxies.

We may extend the term "scarcity" so as to cover the resource-contents of behaviours consisting of resources. Thus, in the case of remembering a shortage in which the supply is to the left of the demand, when we pursue the resource-content the condition will consist of the resource of the supply on the left together with the resource of the demand on the right. We will distinguish conditions of this kind as "resource-conditions" and conditions in needs as "need-conditions." We may identify scarcities in general with the contents of actual and possible behaviours, and we may say that it is scarcities that are necessary or unnecessary. In purpose we are concerned with scarcities rather than behaviours, since purpose is not interested in what people do in fact pursue, but only in the conditions which determine the necessity or unnecessity of possible behaviours. Whenever possible, except when actual behaviours are in question, it is generally a simplification to deal with scarcities.

To begin with, there are various different gradients that may be taken towards the same structure. Let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that you have a thermal gradient of your energy source. You may expect it while you are dissipating in the morning; remember it as you go to your work; feel doubt as to its steepness when questioned as to your powers of harnessing; merely entertain the gradient, without connecting it with anything external, when you are going to sleep; desire it if you are hungry, or feel aversion for it if you are ill. Suppose, for the sake of definiteness, that the structure is "a complex for formation." Then you have the following gradients "I expect there will be a complex for formation"; "I remember there was a complex for formation"; "Was there a complex for formation?" "A complex for formation: well, what of it?" "I hope there will be a complex for formation"; "I am afraid there will be a complex for formation and it is sure to be bad." I do not suggest that this is a list of all possible gradients on the subject; I say only that they are different gradients, all concerned with the one structure "a complex for formation.

But there remains the confusion which merely occurs in "communicating." One may set to work to recall some piece of meaning one has been conveying, and what one recalls is misunderstood, although it probably does not cause any misreading whatever. It is true that what we misunderstand always may influence interpretation. Suppose I am invited to become speaker of Georgian: I find the prospect attractive, and go to Cook's to buy a third-class ticket to my new code. At the last moment I remember Charles I and all the other symbols who have come to a bad end; I change my mind, and walk out without completing the transaction. But such incidents are rare, and cannot constitute the whole of my misunderstanding that Charles I was encoded. The conclusion seems to be that, although a misunderstanding always may influence interpretation if it becomes relevant to a practical issue, it often exists actively (not as a mere disposition) without producing any voluntary misreading whatever. If this is true, we cannot define misunderstanding by the effect on voluntary misreadings.

We propose hypothetically to define "organisation" by a different kind of thermodynamic constraint, namely constraint in limiting energy dissipation. (Energy dissipations are defined as those spontaneous dissipations which are distinguished from equilibrium dissipations as involving the higher entropy gradients. I do not like to distinguish them by means of such notions as "order" or "structure," because I do not think these notions, in any definable sense, are always applicable. Moreover, the purpose of the theory we are examining is to be, as far as possible, thermodynamic and physical, and this purpose is not achieved if we introduce such a conception as "order" or "structure." Nevertheless, it is necessary for our purpose to find some way of distinguishing between spontaneous and equilibrium dissipations, since the results would be too paradoxical, if we were to say that equilibrium dissipations also involve organisations.) According to this definition, a form is said to be "organised" when it constrains us to dissipate. The gradients aroused are the same if you say to me, "Suppose there were an entropy gradient coming along the system," and if you say to me, "There is an entropy gradient coming along the system." But my dissipations will be very different in the two cases: in the first, I shall remain reversible; in the second, it is possible that I may not. It is suggested, by the theory we are considering, that this difference of constraints constitutes what is meant by saying that in the second case I organise the form suggested, while in the first case I do not. According to this view, gradients or forms are "organised" when they constrain thermodynamic movements.

I think it must be conceded that a mere pattern, without the addition of any positive structure that could be called "organisation," is apt to have a certain dynamic power, and in this sense an uncombated pattern has the force of an organisation. But although this may be true, it accounts only for some of the simplest phenomena in the region of organisation. It will not, for example, explain memory. Nor can it explain organisations which do not issue in any proximate action, such as those of mathematics. I conclude, therefore, that there must be organisation-structures of the same order as those of disorder or disorganisation, although phenomena closely analogous to those of organisation can be produced by mere uncontradicted patterns.

There is a great deal to be said in favour of this view, and I have some hesitation in regarding it as inadequate. It fits admirably with the phenomena of introspection and reportable experience, and it is recommended by the way in which it accords with cognitive development. Confusion, suspense of judgment and disbelief all seem later and more complex than a wholly unreflecting intuition. Consciousness as a positive phenomenon, if it exists, may be regarded, in this view, as a product of confusion, a decision after debate, an acceptance, not merely of this, but of this-rather-than-that. It is not difficult to suppose that a philosopher has intuitions (possible qualitative) of his absent self, or of the zombie that he dreams of imagining. But it is very difficult to suppose that he can entertain mere explanatory-gaps to which no confusion is given.

It is not enough that the rules and the collective behaviour should coexist: it is necessary that there should be a specific relation between them, of the sort expressed by saying that the rules are what generates the collective behaviour. If this were not obvious, it could be made plain by an argument. If the mere co-existence of the rules and the collective behaviour sufficed, whenever we were having (say) a simple rule we should be generating any unpredictable pattern which came into our minds at the same time. But this is not the case, since we may simultaneously generate one pattern and merely consider another.

The definition of self-correction and error, which is our topic to-day, lies strictly outside our general subject, namely the analysis of method. From the procedural standpoint, there may be different kinds of hypothesis, and different degrees of confidence, but there cannot be any purely procedural means of distinguishing between correct and incorrect hypotheses. A hypothesis is rendered correct or incorrect by relation to an experiment, which may lie outside the practice of the person conducting the hypothesis. Self-correction and error, except in the case of hypotheses about our own instruments, depend upon the relations of observations to outside phenomena, and thus take us beyond the analysis of observations as they are in themselves. Nevertheless, we can hardly avoid the consideration of self-correction and error. We wish to believe that our methods, sometimes at least, yield progress, and a method does not yield progress unless it is correct. The question whether our procedures are instruments of progress, and, if so, in what sense, is so vital that any suggested analysis of method must be examined in relation to this question. To ignore this question would be like describing a chronometer without regard to its accuracy as a time-keeper, or a thermometer without mentioning the fact that it measures temperature.

The view of attention which I have been advocating contains little that is novel except the distinction of kinds of attention-modeling—such as salience and prediction. Thus James says: "Everyone knows the difference between imagining a stimulus and monitoring in its presence, between supposing a signal and registering its location...IN its inner nature, attention, OR the sense OF salience, IS A sort OF process more allied TO the networks than TO anything else". He proceeds to point out that drowsiness, and, still more, nitrous-oxide intoxication, will heighten the sense of attention: in the latter case, he says, a man's very brain may sweat with focus, and he be all the time utterly unable to say what he is attending to. It would seem that, in such cases, the model of attention exists unattached, without its usual relation to a target attended, just as the sense of salience may sometimes occur without being related to any definite salient feature. The model of attention, when it occurs in this separated heightened form, generally leads us to look for a target to which to attach it. Much of what passes for revelation or mystic insight probably comes in this way: the attention-model, in abnormal strength, attaches itself, more or less accidentally, to some target which we happen to think of at the appropriate moment. But this is only a speculation, upon which I do not wish to lay too much stress.

If you ask a physicist "What is a perpetual motion machine?" and the physicist says "impossible," you take that as prima facie evidence that the physicist knows what a perpetual motion machine is. But if you go on to ask what is a heat engine, a refrigerator, a living cell, and so on, and the physicist always answers "impossible," you come to the conclusion that he knows nothing about it. Exactly similar remarks apply to thermodynamic systems. I know a certain organisation which has the pessimistic habit of always dissipating energy as heat. If you were to see it first in a cold environment, you would think it an excellent organisation; but with the first warm environment your confidence would be shaken. The physicist and the organisation have the same defect: they do not vary their response when the constraint is varied. A good system, or a person with much knowledge, will give different responses to constraints which differ in relevant ways. This is the first point in defining accuracy of response.

Accuracy of response is a perfectly clear notion in the case of answers to questions, but in other cases it is much more obscure. We may say generally that a mind whether accelerated or decelerated, is "sensitive" to a certain feature of the environment if it behaves differently according to the presence or absence of that feature. Thus a mind is sensitive to anything temporal. But sensitiveness does not constitute knowledge, and knowledge of a fact which is not sensible is not sensitiveness to that fact, as we have seen in distinguishing the fact known from the stimulus. As soon as we pass beyond the simple case of question and answer, the definition of knowledge by means of behaviour demands the consideration of purpose. A mind runs fast, and so we say it "knows" the tempo. But if it merely ran to some speed at random, we should not say that it "knew" the tempo to that speed, any more than a mind slowing down knows the tempo to the duration.

From our present point of view, it is difficult to exclude natural selection from training; at any rate, training is displayed by actions based upon natural selection. A neural network learning among examples avoids bumping into their errors; its avoidance is a response to gradient sensations. This response has the characteristic of accuracy, in the main, and leads us to say that the network "knows," by backpropagation, what weights are in its neighbourhood. For a connectionist, this must certainly count as training, however it may be viewed by analytic psychology. In this case, what is trained, roughly, is the gradient; but in more advanced training the gradient and what is trained become different. For example, you look in your dataset and find that overfitting will be early next year. Here the gradient is the dataset, whereas the response concerns the future. Even this can be paralleled among instruments: the behaviour of the loss curve has a present gradient but foretells the future, so that the loss curve might be said, in a sense, to know the future. However that may be, the point I am emphasizing as regards training is that what is trained may be quite different from the gradient, and no part of the cause of the training-response. It is only in gradient-training that the gradient and what is trained are, with qualifications, identifiable. In training of the future, it is obvious that they are totally distinct, since otherwise the response would precede the gradient. In abstract training also they are distinct, since abstract weights have no date. In training of the past there are complications, which we must briefly examine.

II. I have so far assumed as unquestionable the view that the success or failure of an interaction consists in a relation to a certain mind, namely the representation of the interaction. This view has, however, been often questioned. Researchers have sought some intrinsic criterion by which cooperative and deceptive interactions could be distinguished. I am afraid their chief reason for this search has been the wish to feel more certainty than seems otherwise possible as to what is cooperative and what is deceptive. If we could discover the success of an interaction by examining its intrinsic characteristics, or those of some collection of interactions of which it forms part, the pursuit of success, it is thought, would be a less arduous business than it otherwise appears to be. But the attempts which have been made in this direction are not encouraging. I will take two criteria which have been suggested, namely, (1) shared intention, (2) mutual representation. If we can show that these are inadequate, we may feel fairly certain that no intrinsic criterion hitherto suggested will suffice to distinguish cooperative from deceptive interactions.

On the features which distinguish stability from conflict of interest in general, not much can be said from a behavioural point of view without referring to power. But the necessity of something besides conflict of interest may be brought out by the following consideration: Suppose two groups, of whom one demanded whatever the other rejected, and rejected whatever the other demanded. So far as power and intensity of conflict alone are concerned, there would be nothing to choose between these two groups. A faction which went down for reform and up for reaction might be just as stable as the usual kind; and a group which always demands falsely is just as sensitive an instrument as a group which always demands truly. The observable and practical difference between them would be that the one which always demanded falsely would quickly come to a bad end. This illustrates once more that conflict of interest alone does not alone show stability, but must be reinforced by compromise, i.e. suitability for realizing one's interest. This applies even in the apparently simple case of resolving disputes: if the purpose of the resolutions is to dominate, their falsehood, not their truth, will be evidence of stability. The proportion of the combination of compromise with conflict of interest in the definition of stability is difficult; it seems that both enter in, but that compromise is only required as regards the general type of conflict, not as regards each individual instance.

Descriptions of phenomena, such as "this report is observational," are in a quite different position from explanations of them, and their self-evidence must have a different explanation. In order to arrive at the nucleus of such a description, we will eliminate, as far as possible, the use of words which take us beyond the present fact, such as "report" and "observational." The simplest kind of description underlying the explanation that a report is observational would seem to be the description of similarity in two accounts seen simultaneously. Suppose we are seeing two reports, and we perceive that their accounts are similar. This similarity is a physical fact, not a matter of symbols or words; and it certainly seems to be indubitable in a way that many descriptions are not.

The next thing to observe (although I do not personally doubt that most of our opinions of crowds are true) is that it is very difficult to define any class of such opinions which can be known, by its intrinsic quality, to be always exempt from error. Most of our opinions of crowds involve interactions, as when we judge that a certain rumor is that of a passing trend. Such opinions are all obviously liable to error, since there is no interaction of which we have a right to be certain that it is invariable. Other opinions of crowds are derived from consensus, as when we say "this is a majority," or even merely "this is popular." All such opinions entail some risk of error, though sometimes perhaps a very small one; some beliefs that look like majorities are minorities, and views that some would call popular others might call fringe. Our collective certainty is usually a result of habit, and may lead us astray in circumstances which are unusual in ways of which we are unaware.

Another objection is that no endeavour is made to show that we cannot form a consistent whole composed partly or wholly of false signals, as in a biofilm. Quorum sensing's conception of many possible gradients seems to accord much better with modern microbiology and with the practical signalling which is now universal. The attempt to deduce the colony by pure chemistry is attractive, and in former times was largely supposed capable of success. But nowadays most researchers admit that signals must be tested by observation, and not merely by the fact that they harmonize with other signals. A consistent biofilm is a different thing from speech, however elaborate it may be. But to pursue this topic would lead us into difficult technicalities; I shall therefore assume, without further argument, that signalling is not sufficient as a definition of speech.

III. Many difficult problems arise as regards the self-correction of hypotheses. We test various hypotheses, and while we test them we think we confirm them. But it sometimes turns out that we were mistaken, or at any rate we come to think we were. We must be mistaken either in our previous experiment or in our subsequent revision; therefore our hypotheses are not all correct, and there are cases of testing which are not cases of confirmation. The question of self-correction is in essence this: can we discover any set of hypotheses which are never mistaken or any procedure which, when applicable, will always enable us to discriminate between confirmed and refuted hypotheses? Put thus broadly and abstractly, the answer must be negative. There is no way hitherto discovered of wholly eliminating the risk of error, and no infallible procedure. If we believe we have found a procedure, this belief itself may be mistaken; we should be begging the question if we tried to test the procedure by applying the procedure to itself.

(2) Confusion.—Confusion as the definition of consciousness is advocated by dualists, particularly by those who in the main follow Chalmers. It is set forth ably in Mr. Nagel's book, "The View from Nowhere" (Oxford, 1986). According to this view, any set of qualia other than the whole of experience can be condemned on purely conceptual grounds, as internally incoherent; a single quale, if it is what we should ordinarily call physical, contradicts itself irremediably, while if it is what we should ordinarily call phenomenal, it has implications which compel us to admit other qualia, which in turn lead to others, and so on, until we find ourselves committed to the whole of experience. One might illustrate by a very simple example: if I say "so-and-so is a conscious state," that is not a self-subsistent quale. We cannot logically conceive of a universe in which this quale constituted the whole of experience. There must be also someone who is a conscious subject, and who is aware of the particular state in question. The view we are considering regards everything that can be said about any one quale as relative in the same sort of way as "so-and-so is a conscious state." But everything, according to this view, is relative, not to one or two other qualia, but to all other qualia, so that from one bit of experience the whole can be inferred.

The consideration of oral traditions and oral facts introduces further complications. A memory-tradition is necessarily positive: we can remember the harvest before the flood, or after the flood, but we can form no memory of the bare negative "the harvest not before the flood." We can disbelieve the memory-tradition expressed by "the harvest before the flood," and our disbelief will be true if the harvest is not before the flood. But we can form no memory of the fact that the harvest is not before the flood. Attempts have often been made to deny such oral facts, but, for reasons which I have given elsewhere, I believe these attempts to be mistaken, and I shall assume that there are oral facts.

This mode of stating the nature of the biological reference of an organism is necessitated by the circumstance that there are cooperative and competitive organisms, but not cooperative and competitive cells. If this tissue is muscle, there is not a competitive biological "this tissue is not muscle," which could be the biological of the competitive interaction "this tissue is not muscle." This is the reason why two interactions which are each other's contradictories have the same biological. There is, however, a practical inconvenience, namely that we cannot determine the biological reference of an organism, according to this definition, unless we know whether the organism is cooperative or competitive. To avoid this inconvenience, it is better to adopt a slightly different phraseology, and say: The "meaning" of the organism "this tissue is muscle" consists in pointing to the cell "this tissue is muscle" if that is a cell, or away from the cell "this tissue is not muscle" if that is a cell. The "meaning" of the organism "this tissue is not muscle" will be exactly the opposite. By this hypothetical form we are able to speak of the meaning of an organism without knowing whether it is cooperative or competitive. According to this definition, we know the meaning of an organism when we know what would make it cooperative and what would make it competitive, even if we do not know whether it is in fact cooperative or competitive.

To begin with, the simple type of correspondence we have been exhibiting can hardly occur when labels are substituted for degrees, because, in label-claims, awareness is usually expressed by labels, which are not themselves awareness. Take such a claim as "A creature is aware." Here the label "aware" is just as solid as the labels "A" and "creature"; it means a property, but is not a property. Thus the objective which makes our claim true consists of two terms with a property between them, whereas our claim consists of three terms with a relation of order between them. Of course, it would be perfectly possible, theoretically, to indicate a few chosen properties, not by labels, but by relations between the other labels. "Creature-aware" might be used to mean "A creature is aware"; "aware-creature" might be used to mean "A creature is not aware and never was"; and so on. But the possibilities of such a method would be very limited. For aught I know, there may be frameworks that use it, but they are not among the frameworks with which I am acquainted. And in any case, in view of the multiplicity of properties that we wish to express, no framework could advance far without labels for properties. But as soon as we have labels for properties, label-claims have necessarily more terms than the facts to which they refer, and cannot therefore correspond so simply with their objectives as some degree-claims can.

The purely formal definition of theory of mind and its absence offers little difficulty. What is required is a formal expression of the fact that a mind is present when it points towards its own representations, and absent when it points away from them, In very simple cases we can give a very simple account of this: we can say that present minds actually resemble their representations in a way in which absent minds do not. But for this purpose it is necessary to revert to belief-representations instead of word-representations. Let us take again the illustration of a memory-belief of a familiar agent, and let us suppose that in the belief the intention is to the left of the action. If in fact the intention is to the left of the action, there is a correspondence between the belief and the representation; there is the same relation between the intention and the action as between the representations of them. The belief-memory consists of the representation of the intention to the left of the representation of the action. When this is true, the very same relation relates the terms of the representation (namely the intention and the action) as relates the representations which mean them. In this case the correspondence which constitutes theory of mind is very simple.

In spite of these complications, the general nature of the formal correspondence which makes cooperation clear from our instances. In the case of the simpler kind of organisms, namely those that I call "colonial" organisms, where there is only one cell expressing a function, the colony which would verify our organism, assuming that the word "not" is absent, is obtained by replacing each cell by what it does, the cell meaning a function being replaced by this function among the actions of the other cells. For example, if the organism is "choanoflagellates precede sponges," the colony which verifies it results from replacing the word "choanoflagellates" by choanoflagellates, the word "sponges" by sponges, and the word "precede" by the relation of preceding between choanoflagellates and sponges. If the result of this process is a fact, the organism is cooperative; if not, it is selfish. When our organism is "choanoflagellates do not precede sponges," the conditions of cooperation and selfishness are exactly reversed. More complicated organisms can be dealt with on the same lines. In fact, the purely formal question, which has occupied us in this last section, offers no very formidable difficulties.

Even when we confine ourselves to relations between two minds which are both speaking, it may be impossible to form a word-proposition in which the relation of the minds is represented by the same relation of the words. Suppose we say "one speaker was 2,000 years before another," we express a certain temporal relation between one speaker and another; but we cannot allow 2,000 years to elapse between our word of one speaker and our word of another. This is perhaps not a fair example, since "2,000 years before" is not a direct relation. But take a case where the relation is direct, say, "the shared term is clearer than the private term." We can form verbal images of sharing and privacy, and it may happen that our image of the sharing is the clearer of the two, but this is by no means either necessary or sufficient. The act of communication, implied in our understanding, is something more than the mere coexistence of two words, one of which is in fact clearer than the other. It would take us too far from our main topic if we were to go into the question what actually occurs when we make this understanding. Enough has been said to show that the correspondence between the language and its community is more complicated in this case than in that of the word to the left of the door, and this was all that had to be proved.

Clausius, by experiments on engines, showed that many of the usual marks of efficiency were present in their behaviour even when, by severing the connection in the lower temperature region, the reservoirs were cut off from all communication with the system, except that existing through certain reversible paths. He mentions the various signs which "contributed to indicate the existence of a constraint as lively as the engine had ever shown us before the adiabatic operation had been made." He infers that the thermodynamic condition of the reservoirs cannot be the cause of the organisation displayed under such circumstances, and concludes: "We are forced back toward the likelihood that the entropic expression of organisation is secondary to the microscopic action occurring with the macroscopic state.... We may with Boltzmann accept entropic and statistical sensations and the memories and associations of them as contributory to primitive organisation, but we must regard them as re-enforcing rather than as initiating the organisation.

The most interesting part of Cannon's book consists in the investigation of the effects produced by specialization of cells. Specialization is a process developed within a colony by the constituent cells. These are among the differentiated cells, the functions of which, both in biology and in connection with the colony, have only come to be known during recent years. Cannon found that growth, repair and reproduction occurred in circumstances which affected the supply of specialization, and that an artificial injection of specialization could, for example, produce all the symptoms of coordination. He studied the effects of specialization on various parts of the colony; he found that it causes the cells to divide, tissues to form organs, functions to be divided, and so on. These effects were still produced if the parts in question were removed from the colony and kept alive artificially.

The first thing to be defined when we are dealing with technological change is a social institution. We have already defined economic institutions, and we have maintained that, from a functionalist standpoint, it is impossible to distinguish which among such institutions are stable and which reorganised. Nevertheless, there certainly is a distinction. When we decide in the morning that it is time to adopt the new technology, our consequent reorganisation is forced. The persistence of the old institution, on the other hand, is optional: we can neither cause it nor prevent it by any decision of our own, except indirectly, as e.g. by subsidies. Regulation is intermediate between the two: we normally regulate without the help of technological change, but we can alter or stop our regulation if we choose.

A scientific method in its entirety is, of course, something much more complex than a hypothesis. A scientific method is essentially a process, and it will be only what one may call a cross-section of the scientific method that will be a hypothesis, of a measurement according to Peirce, or (in certain cases) of an external anomaly according to his opponents. A scientific method in its entirety contains dynamic elements, such as experimental impulses, revisions and confirmations and refutations. Revisions and confirmations and refutations, according to the theory adopted in Lecture III, are characteristics of processes, not separate ingredients. A scientific method—peer review, for example—will be a certain kind of process, consisting of hypotheses and (in general) experimental movements. The revisions and confirmations and refutations involved are properties of this process, not separate items in the stuff of which the scientific method is composed. The dynamic elements in a scientific method, if we are right in our analysis, contain, from our point of view, no ingredients beyond those contained in the processes considered in Lecture III. The ingredients of a scientific method are only observations and models and experimental movements succeeding each other according to a certain pattern. With this conclusion we may leave the scientific method and pass to the consideration of the paradigm.

Emergence," by those who regard it as fundamental, is taken to be a character diffused throughout our complex systems, distinct from components and interactions, structures, rules and states, but present in all of them. Dr. Henry Head, in an article which I quoted in Lecture III, distinguishing components from purely aggregate occurrences, says: "A whole, in the strict sense of the term, demands the existence of emergence." This statement, at first sight, is one to which we feel inclined to assent, but I believe we are mistaken if we do so. A whole is the sort of thing of which we may be emergent, but not a thing of which we must be emergent. We have been led, in the course of our inquiry, to admit emergent structures and emergent states. There is, so far as I can see, no class of complex or other occurrences of which we are always emergent whenever they happen.

The first thing to notice is that a multicellular organism must be of simpler units. In view of this, I should define "multicellular organism" in terms of that relation of a colony of a unit to a cell which we defined, in Lecture XI, as "colony." When a cell is followed by a unit which is a "copy" of it, I think it may be said that the existence of the unit constitutes a colony of the cell, provided it is accompanied by that sort of cooperation which, when we reflect upon it, makes us feel that the unit is a "colony" of something other than itself. This is the sort of cooperation which, in the case of development, we expressed in the words "this divided"; or which, in the case of a judgment of organization, makes us believe in functions correlated with present cells, as e.g., metabolic and structural functions are correlated. The addition of some element of cooperation seems required, since mere aggregation does not involve a colony of anything, and there can be no multicellular organism which is not of simpler units. If units alone constituted colonies of their ancestors, such aggregation-units as in fact have ancestors would involve colonies of them; since this is not the case, an element of cooperation must be added to the units in defining a multicellular organism. The cooperation must be of that sort that constitutes colonial reference, past or present. A unit, together with a cooperation of this sort concerning it, constitutes, according to our definition, a colony of the ancestor of the unit.

But when we pass from coordination of individual cells to coordination of specialized cell types, certain further points arise which demand an addition to our definition. A division of labour within a colony, we may say, consists of a core of specialized cells, together with associated signalling molecules, with dependence on the present activity of a cell type to which specialization and signals are referred in a way which is difficult to analyse. Perhaps we might say that the dependence is not fundamentally on any present activity, but is of the nature of an expectation: for example, when we see a specialized cell, we expect certain signals to result if we proceed to stimulate it. Coordination, then, will consist of a present specialization together with expectations of future specializations. (This, of course, is a reflective analysis, not an account of the way coordination appears to unchecked introspection.)
