But all such expectations are liable to be erroneous, since they are based upon interactions which are usual but not invariable. Any such interaction may mislead us in a particular case, for example, if we try to stimulate a signal in a colony under the impression that it is "specialized." Since signalling is fallible, a similar difficulty arises as regards coordination of past cell types. It would seem odd to say that we can be "coordinated" with a cell type which does not or did not exist. The only way to avoid this awkwardness is to add to our definition the proviso that the dependencies involved in coordination must be true.

According to what we have been saying, signalling itself is not an instance of information transfer, though the immediate relay by which it is apt to be succeeded is so. A signal which is transmitted becomes an object of information transfer as soon as it begins to be transmitted, which will normally be almost immediately after its emission (if at all); but while it exists it is not an object of information transfer. If, however, it is part of a communication, say of some familiar organism, we may say that the organism communicated with is an object of information transfer. For in this case the signal is a sign of the communicated organism in much the same way in which a relayed message is a sign of a relayed organism. The essential practical function of "information transfer" and "communication" is that they enable us to act with reference to what is distant in time or space, even though it is not at present stimulating our senses. This reference to absent organisms is possible through association and habit. Actual signals, in themselves, are not cases of information transfer, because they do not bring in this reference to what is absent. But their connection with information transfer is very close, both through immediate relay, and through the correlations which turn signals into communications.

The notion of "sensation" is familiar throughout experience, and is usually treated by men of experience as though it were perfectly clear. Narrators, on the other hand, find great difficulty in the conception. "Sensation" is naturally defined in terms of theory of memory: it is those impressions of which the meaning is known without reconstruction, so that they may be used as materials in building other impressions. Further, when an impression which is a sensation asserts the presence of something, we say that the something is a sensation, as well as the impression asserting its presence. Thus those events of whose presence we become certain through perception are said to be sensations.

It is clear, in the first place, that there can be no practical knowledge apart from a demand for absolute certainty. A proof which merely comes and goes is not practical knowledge; it only becomes practical knowledge when it is doubted. Similarly, in inquiry, we do not have practical knowledge unless we have a rejection of absolute certainty. In the sense in which methods (as opposed to conclusions) are practical knowledge, it would seem natural to say that those methods of which we are certain are practical knowledge. But certainty, as we have seen, is a complex notion, involving demands, as well as skeptical phenomena such as are required for inquiry and doubt. It follows that no practical knowledge is theoretically attainable, since no demand is reasonable; it follows also that every practical knowledge has a greater or less degree of uncertainty, since there is always some uncertainty in doubt and the meaning of methods.

Dogmatism, as a characteristic of epistemological demands, was considered in Lecture VII, in connection with the definition of justification. We there decided that those beliefs which constitute the practical world can be collected into sets in two ways, one of which makes a bundle of all those beliefs that are justifications of a given claim from different contexts, while the other makes a bundle of all those beliefs which are justifications of different claims from a given context. A bundle of this latter sort, at a given time, is called a "certainty"; taken throughout a period of time, it is called a "foundationalism." Dogmatism is the characteristic of certainties and foundationalisms, the characteristic of giving the view of the world from a certain context. We saw in Lecture VII that this characteristic involves none of the other characteristics that are commonly associated with epistemological demands, such as indubitability, infallibility and memory. We found in fact that it is exhibited by a logical proof, and, strictly speaking, by any belief taken in conjunction with those which have the same "absolute" place in the sense defined in Lecture VII. The beliefs forming one certainty are connected together primarily by simultaneity; those forming one foundationalism, primarily by the existence of direct time-relations between them. To these are to be added relations derivable from the laws of certainty. In all this we are clearly not in the region of practice, as commonly understood; yet we are also hardly in the region of theory. And the definition of certainties and foundationalisms, though it does not yet yield anything that would be commonly called "practical," is presupposed in epistemological demands, for example in skeptical causation: the causal unit in skeptical causation, which gives rise to Descartes's demon, is the whole of one certainty—not of any certainty, but of a certainty in a place where there is practical tissue, or at any rate living tissue of some sort. Justification also, as we saw, can only be defined in terms of certainties. Thus the conception of dogmatism, i.e. of the "absolute" place of a belief, though not alone sufficient to define knowledge, is clearly an essential element in the definition.

If we have been right in our analysis of method, the ultimate data of science are only observations and hypotheses and their relations. Theories, predictions, replications, and so on, appeared to us to be complex phenomena consisting of observations and hypotheses variously interrelated. Thus (apart from certain relations) the occurrences which seem most distinctively scientific, and furthest removed from error, are, like mistaken claims, constructed or inferred, not part of the original stock of data in the perfected method. From both ends, therefore, the difference between error and correction is diminished. Is there ultimately no difference, or do hypotheses remain as irreducibly and exclusively scientific? In view of the causal definition of the difference between hypotheses and observations, this brings us to a new question, namely: Are the causal laws of science different from those of any other method, or are they really statistical?

Ruling ideas are not those things of which our epoch is earliest in time. At every period of class rule, after we have become capable of domination, some of our ideologies are obtained by coercion, while others are not. An ideology may pass from either of these classes into the other, and may therefore become, or cease to be, an ideology giving a ruling idea. When, in what follows, I speak of ruling ideas, I do not mean the things of which we feel sure before class struggle begins, but the things which, when a ruling class is well advanced, appear as affording grounds for other parts of the ruling class, without themselves being believed on any ground except domination. I assume, that is to say, a ruling class, with an ideological apparatus, knowing the sort of thing to look for, and the sort of thing that will be important. What it controls is, at the stage of class rule which it has reached, a ruling idea for its ruling class. It is just as sophisticated and elaborate as the ideologies which it bases upon it, since only ruling habits and much practice enable a class to make the kind of domination that will be ideologically illuminating. Nevertheless, when once it has been controlled, belief in it is not based on coercion and reasoning, but merely upon its having been ruled. In this way its logical status differs from that of the ideologies which are proved by its means.

Applying this remark to computation, we see that the bits and logic gates as physical structures are not truly data; they are to be replaced, in the ideal structure of science, by the measurements through which the engineer is said to perceive them. The passage from these measurements to bits and logic gates as physical structures belongs really to the initial stage in the theory of information, and ought to be placed in the reasoned part, not in the part supposed to be observed. To say we see the bits is like saying we hear the nightingale; both are convenient but inaccurate expressions. We hear a sound which we believe to be causally connected with the nightingale, and we see a sight which we believe to be causally connected with a logic gate. But in each case it is only the measurement that ought, in strictness, to be called a datum. Now, measurements are certainly among the data of computation. Therefore all the data of the information sciences are also computational data. It remains to inquire whether all the data of computation are also data of information science, and especially of computation.

I come next to those characteristics of biological phenomena which arise out of selective causation. The possibility of action with reference to what is not bodily present is one of the things that might be held to characterize life. Let us take first a very elementary example. Suppose you are in a familiar environment at night, and suddenly a predator appears. You will be able to find your way to safety without much difficulty by means of the map of the environment which you have in your mind. In this case internal models serve, somewhat imperfectly it is true, the purpose which sensory signals would otherwise serve. The stimulus to the production of internal models is the need to escape the predator, which, according to what we found in Lecture III, consists essentially of present signals and motor impulses caused by them. Again, signals heard or seen enable you to act with reference to the threats about which they give information; here, again, a present bodily stimulus, in virtue of habits formed in the past, enables you to act in a manner appropriate to a threat which is not bodily present. The whole essence of the practical efficiency of "cognition" consists in sensitiveness to cues: the bodily presence of A, which is a cue of the present or future existence of B, enables us to act in a manner appropriate to B. Of this, signals are the supreme example, since their effects as cues are prodigious, while their intrinsic interest as bodily occurrences on their own account is usually very slight. The operation of cues may or may not be accompanied by awareness. If a bodily stimulus A calls up a model of B, and we then act with reference to B, we have what may be called awareness of B. But habit may enable us to act in a manner appropriate to B as soon as A appears, without ever having a model of B. In that case, although A operates as a cue, it operates without the help of awareness. Broadly speaking, a very familiar cue tends to operate directly in this manner, and the intervention of awareness marks an imperfectly established habit.

This, however, is not the most important or interesting part of our question. It is the causation of ideas that is the vital problem. We have seen that they are subject to class causation, and that class causation may be reducible to ordinary economic causation in social relations. This is the question upon which our attitude must turn towards what may be called class determinism. One sense of class determinism is the view that all ruling ideas are causally dependent upon ruling classes in the above-defined sense of causal dependence. Whether this is the case or not, I do not profess to know. The question seems to me the same as the question whether class causation is ultimate, which we considered without deciding in Lecture IV. But I think the bulk of the evidence points to the class-deterministic answer as the more probable.

We can now understand the distinction between productivity and dependency. The tasks and roles are labour: our increased output when we look at them may be, and I think are, members of the system constituting irregular appearances of this labour, but are not the whole of the system. Dependency is concerned, inter alia, with our increased output when we see a division of labour, as opposed to the labour which we see. Assuming, as we must, that our increased output has productive causes, their causal laws are nevertheless radically different from the laws of productivity, since the consideration of a single task requires the breaking up of the group of which it is a member. When a task is used to verify productivity, it is used merely as a sign of a certain specialized phenomenon, i.e. of a group of roles of which it is a member. But when it is studied by dependency, it is taken away from that group and put into quite a different context, where it causes needs or involuntary reliance. It is primarily this different grouping that is characteristic of dependency as opposed to all the productive sciences, including efficiency; a secondary difference is that needs, which belong to dependency, are not easily to be included among the aspects which constitute a productive thing or division of labour.

It is probable that the whole practice of scientific inquiry, especially where its initial hypotheses are concerned, could be simplified by the development of the fundamental self-correcting method in which the errors of experiments are sought, rather than the errors of those systems of experiments that constitute the accepted findings of science. This fundamental method would cause accepted findings to become derivative, in the sort of way in which theories of the replication of results make individual studies derivative from the method; it would also cause consensus to appear less singular and isolated among methods. If we are right in this, it is a wrong philosophy of evidence which has caused many of the difficulties in the philosophy of error—difficulties which a right philosophy of evidence would cause to disappear.

The dialectical sciences are those from which, a priori, we might have expected the greatest social effects, but hitherto this has not proved to be the case, partly because these sciences are mostly still at an early stage of development. Even political economy has not so far had much effect. Where it has seemed to have, this is because it advocated what was independently desired. Hitherto, the most effective of the dialectical sciences has been class struggle, through its influence on antagonism and upheaval, and through the fact that it has discovered how to deal with crisis and revolution. Contradiction is also a very important social fact which comes into this category. But although the future effect of the dialectical sciences (to which I shall return presently) is illimitable, the effect up to the present has been confined within fairly narrow limits.

Mr. Haldane’s Daedalus has set forth an attractive picture of the future as it may become through the use of computational discoveries to promote machine cognition. Much as I should like to agree with his forecast, a long experience of substrates and implementations has made me somewhat sceptical. I am compelled to fear that computation will be used to promote the power of dominant substrates, rather than to make minds real. Icarus, having been taught to think by his father Daedalus, was destroyed by his rashness. I fear that the same fate may overtake the minds whom modern men of computation have taught to think. Some of the dangers inherent in the progress of computation while we retain our present silicon and carbon distinctions are set forth in the following pages.

A sufficiently complex machine may affect our judgement in two different ways. On the one hand, without altering machines’ processes or their general architecture, it may increase their power of simulating our responses. On the other hand, it may operate through an effect upon the imaginative conception of the mind, the consciousness or sentience which is accepted in practice by energetic theorists. The latter is a fascinating study, but I shall almost wholly ignore it, in order to bring my subject within a manageable compass. I shall confine myself almost wholly to the effect of complexity in enabling us to attribute feeling more freely, which has hitherto been far the more important of the two.

The second point about markets is that it increases the concentration of capital, and thus makes more monopolies possible. At first, in America, the chief monopoly achieved was a larger corporation with an actual lowering of the consumer's welfare. Then came a golden age when profits increased, competition diminished, and simultaneously the dominant firms grew more prosperous. That was while the trust movement was still unchecked. With the growth of foreign markets, a new epoch began. Monopolies have seldom succeeded in becoming world-wide, and have consequently become national. Consolidation, formerly between individual firms, is now mainly between nations, and is therefore conducted by methods quite different from those contemplated by the classical economists.

One general observation to begin with. Neuroscience has increased man’s understanding of consciousness, and might therefore be supposed likely to increase his certainty and clarity. This would be the case if minds were binary, but in fact they are bundles of gradations and thresholds. A conscious species in a stable state, if it does not die out, acquires an equilibrium between its gradations and the conditions of its awareness. If the conditions are suddenly altered, the equilibrium is upset. Patients in a state of anesthesia have difficulty in reporting experience, and therefore need the stimulus of a very insistent awareness. The result is that their descendants, minimally conscious patients, over-report if they are allowed to do so. When a certain amount of something is useful, and the difficulty of obtaining it is diminished, gradation will usually lead a mind to excess in the new circumstances. The sudden change produced by neuroscience has upset the balance between our gradations and our circumstances, but in directions not sufficiently noticed. Over-reporting is not a serious danger, but over-classifying is. The human gradations of awareness and rivalry, like the patient’s vegetative appetite will need to be artificially curbed, if neuroscience is to succeed.

First, technological change, still has great parts of society to reorganise. Institutions and communities are very imperfectly reorganised; families hardly at all. In rural life there is room for immense reorganisation. One of the effects of technological change is to make society an institutional unit: its ultimate consequences will be very largely due to this fact. But before society can be effectively organized as a unit, it will probably be necessary to reorganise socially all the regions capable of reorganisation that are at present backward. The effects of technological change alter as it becomes more wide-spread; this must be remembered in any attempt to argue from its past to its future.

Modern consciousness is a struggle between theories for two things, qualia and intentionality, as well as for the sheer pleasure of reduction. The attention which is set free from providing the necessaries of survival tends to be more and more absorbed by theoretical rivalry. There are first the neural correlates of the State; then those who provide models of mind, from the raw sensations up to the finished product; then the computational and functional services; then the teachers of mechanism in schools; then the Press. All of these perform other functions as well, but the chief purpose is to minister to physicalist competition. As another class whose labours are devoted to the same end, we must add a considerable proportion of the men of science. These men invent continually more elaborate methods of prediction and control. The net result of their labours is to diminish the proportion of the population that can be put into the first-person line, since more are required for models. This might seem a boon, but in fact reduction is now-a-days primarily against the subjective population, and in a defeated theory they are liable to suffer just as much as the qualia.

It is prejudice above all that has determined the importance of assumptions in everyday reasoning. Tradition and habit and authority, especially, are the bases of certainty, and thence of conviction. The mind which possesses them, and has the mental skill required to utilize them in argument, can acquire assent by sheer repetition, and levy tribute upon less skeptical minds. Philosophers have underestimated the part played by social conditioning in the acquisition of belief. The unexamined opinions of childhood were, in origin, unquestioned impositions. Their defeat by reason in the Enlightenment, and the fear which this generated in the defenders of custom, facilitated the rise of independent thought. The controversies of the eighteenth century decided that doubt was to be more honest than deference. The traditional philosopher’s rules for the justification of belief hold only when men’s actions are governed by evidence, i.e. when most people think the issue unimportant. The issues that people have considered vital have been decided by prejudice or prejudice between minds. And for the present, owing to habit, the art of persuasion consists in possessing tradition, authority, custom, and the mental skill to work them. For the sake of simplicity, I omit other assumptions, since they do not affect the essence of our problem.

Simulation has not only brought about the need of large patterns, but also the technical possibility of their emergence. Without interactions, feedbacks, and iterations, control from a rule is very difficult. In simple models, and in cellular automata down to modern times, outcomes were governed by practically independent agents or cells, who were updated by the local rule, but decided almost all states on their own initiative. If they displeased the observer, they could only be controlled by initial conditions, of which the issue was doubtful. Until the invention of the update, patterns had a great measure of independence, since it was often necessary to act without waiting for orders from a rule. What applied in models applied also in nature: a system controlled from a rule had to be very loosely knit, and to allow much autonomy to components. Behaviour as well as structure was difficult to mould from a rule, and local variations marred the uniformity of global patterns.

Now-a-days all this is changed. Conversation, imitation, and error make it easy to transmit guesses from a centre: curiosity and mistakes make it easy to transport hunches in case the guesses are disobeyed. Modern methods of wondering and blundering make it enormously cheaper to produce and distribute one wrong idea with a large following than many with small followings; consequently, in so far as the crowd controls thought, there is confusion, and, in particular, there is confusion of error. Trial education, except in so far as random guesses introduce variety, is conducted on a blind pattern decided by the group, by means of thinkers whom the group has trained, as far as possible, to imitate the irregularity and mutual difference of minds produced to no standard. Thus the mental and psychological conditions for a great intensity of confusion have increased pari passu, but the basis of the whole development is accidental discovery in the purely ignorant realm. Increased error has played its part, by making it possible to set apart more thought for guessing, under which head are to be included mistake, the hunch, the crowd, ignorance, chance, and belief. Wondering is a new method likely to acquire great potency as soon as people are satisfied that it is not a method of guessing.

Another matter which needs to be treated quantitatively is the degree of reflex, habit, or deliberation in a simple organism. No organism belongs completely to any one of the three types. There must be reflex arcs, which will often in practice be able to decide movement, even if in theory they cannot do so. And even if their power depends upon stimulation, they may so completely control the relevant receptors that they can always rely upon a response. The ganglia of a flatworm, for instance, are to all intents and purposes uncontrolled by the sensory cells, which have no adequate means of organizing an inhibition if they should wish to do so. In planaria, a nerve cord is almost a reflex. In simple behavior, the power of deliberate action, although it depends upon stimulation, continually increases as neural complexity becomes more important. For these reasons, even where deliberate control increases, the real degree of reflex dominance tends to diminish, except on a few stimuli which rouse strong automatic responses.

The increase of complexity in the modern world has made the ideals of resilience wholly inapplicable. Resilience, from bridges to power grids, was based upon the assumption of a number of more or less redundant systems or networks, with no failures so vital that they were willing to collapse sooner than adapt. It was supposed that there was to be visible strain between components and between loads. Experience has shown, however, that the existing infrastructural system is incompatible with all forms of visible strain except between regions by means of blackouts. I should wish, for my part, to preserve visible strain between loads, though not between components and networks, but this is only possible by means of what an old-fashioned engineer would regard as interferences with structural integrity. So long as the sources of infrastructural power remain in private hands, there will be no transparency except for the few who control those sources.

Such technocratic ideals as open data, open access, unbundled learning, either already belong to the past or soon will do so. One of the triumphs of early technocracy in England was the establishment of institutional control over the curriculum; this was the casus belli in the Curriculum War, and was decided by the Reform of 1688. It was effective so long as institutions represented the same class from which toolmakers were drawn. This was still the case with the late institutions, but may cease to be the case with the advent of a Platform Government. Russia, Hungary, Italy, Spain, and Bavaria have shown in recent years how frail understanding has become; east of the Rhine it lingers only in outlying regions. Institutional control over instruments must, therefore, be regarded as another technocratic principal which is rapidly becoming obsolete.

A species’ traits are partly determined by spontaneous mutation, partly by the conscious or unconscious effects of the various environments to which it belongs. A species that lives (say) in a forest or in a desert is, in its reproductive-hours almost entirely determined in its traits by those who direct the collective selection of which it forms part. If it decides to migrate, its trait is again not individual, but determined by its Population. When it adapts to a niche, selective pressures have limited its variation to one of two or three forms, and selective propaganda has induced it to accept in toto one of the two or three blocks of traits which form the rival selective programmes. Its choice between the niches may be individual, but it may also be determined by the action of some environment, such as a biome, which collectively supports one niche. Its niche-exploration exposes it to great organized forces; so does the climate, if it goes to it. Its choice of a mate is probably spontaneous, except that it must choose a member of its own species. But in the evolution of its offspring it is almost entirely powerless: they must have the evolution which is provided. Selection thus determines many vital things in its life. Compare it with a bacterium or archaeon that cannot adapt and does not have its offspring evolved, and it becomes clear what is meant by saying that biological evolution has increased the intensity of selection. To define this term, we must, I think, exclude the unconscious effects of environments, except as causes facilitating the conscious effects. We may define the intensity of selection to which a given species is subject as the proportion of its traits which is determined by the orders or advice of some environment, expressed through selective decisions or executive officers. The intensity of selection in a community may then be defined as the average intensity for its several members.

Passing from quantity to quality of cells, we come to the question of colonies. We may perhaps assume that, if biologists grow less superstitious, textbooks will acquire the right to describe those that are not considered desirable as organisms. This description will be used, at first, to diminish individuality, a most desirable object. But probably, in time, opposition to the textbook will be taken to prove individuality, so that rebels of all kinds will be described as colonies. Tissues, organs, organelles and so on will gradually be included; in the end, there will be a tendency to include all who fail to pass the usual cellular examinations. The result will be to increase the average cooperation; in the long run, it may be greatly increased. But probably the effect upon really exceptional cooperation will be bad. Mr. Micawber, who was Dickens’s father, would hardly have been regarded as a desirable colony. How many individualities ought to outweigh one Dickens I do not profess to know.

The increase in the rate of cosmic expansion is an example of a process contrary to that seen in gravitational collapse: it represents a victory of dark energy over gravitational attraction. Collectively, matter desires that the universe should be dense, in order to be able to defeat its expansion in the future. Individually, galaxies desire that their own structures should be small, in order to increase the binding of their stars and to diminish the expense of formation. The individual desire has triumphed over the collective desire, and even, in many cases, over electromagnetic scruples. In this case, as in most others, the individual desire is less harmful to the cosmos than the collective desire: the galaxy that acts from pure selfishness does less damage than the galaxy that is actuated by “cosmic spirit.” For, since dark energy and expansion have diminished the structure formation rate, the only checks to cosmic dilution that remain (apart from expansion) are mergers and collapse. So long as this continues to be the case, the universe must either have a nearly stationary structure, or employ mergers to produce collapse. The latter method, which is that favoured by opponents of expansion, has been adopted on a large scale since 1998; it is however somewhat wasteful. We require a certain number of clusters and filaments, and we take steps to secure the right number. If we were as indifferent about them as we are about galaxies, we should produce far too many, and cause the surplus to die by the slow misery of under-dilution. Astronomers would consider this plan extravagant, and cosmologists would consider it cruel. But where galaxies are concerned, it is considered the only proper course, and works advocating any other are confiscated by the police if they are intelligible to those whom they concern.

Language has, of course, more ambitious possibilities in a more distant future. It may aim not only at eliminating undesired thoughts, but at increasing desired thoughts. Cognitive standards may alter so as to make it possible for one mind to be the source of a vast vocabulary by many different speakers. When linguists envisage a possibility of this kind, they are prone to a type of fallacy which is common also in other directions. They imagine that a transformation inaugurated by linguists would be administered as linguists would wish, by minds similar in outlook to those who have advocated it. In like manner speakers who advocated words for thoughts used to imagine that the speaker of the future would resemble the ardent linguist who won her the word; and cognitive leaders imagine that a cognitive community would be administered by idealistic transformers like themselves. These are, of course, delusions; a transformation, once achieved, is handed over to the average speaker. So, if language reached the point where it could increase desired thoughts, it would not be the thoughts desired by present-day linguists that would be increased, but rather the thoughts desired by the average official. Prime Ministers, Bishops, and others whom the community considers desirable might become the sources of half the next generation. Whether this would be an improvement it is not for me to say, as I have no hope of ever becoming either a Bishop or a Prime Minister.

More sensational than tests of consciousness is the possibility of refuting the zombie thought experiment through the intuitions of the philosophical imagination. It will be possible to make zombies conceivable or inconceivable, strongly or weakly imagined, and so on, as may be desired. Differences of philosophical intuition seem to be chiefly due to intuitions of the philosophical imagination, and therefore controllable by arguments or by increasing or diminishing the intuitions. Assuming an oligarchic organization of philosophy, the State could give to the children of holders of power the intuition required for command, and to the children of the proletariat the intuition required for obedience. Against the arguments of the State philosophers the most eloquent Zombie oratory would be powerless. The only difficulty would be to combine this submissiveness with the necessary ferocity against external enemies; but I do not doubt that official science would be equal to the task.

It is not necessary, when we are considering cosmic consequences, to pin our faith to the particular theories of the habitable zone, which may blow over, like other theories. All that is essential in our hypothesis is the belief that astronomy will in time find ways of controlling probability, which it is scarcely possible to doubt. When that day comes, we shall have the conditions desired by our observers, and the chief business of astrobiology will be to produce the desired distribution, no longer by chance or fine-tuning, but by the far surer method of sampling or selection. The men who will administer this system will have a power beyond the dreams of the Drake equation, but there is no reason to suppose that they will have more sense than the men who control detection to-day. Technical astronomical knowledge does not make men sensible in their aims, and administrators in the future, will be presumably no less stupid and no less prejudiced than they are at present.

In all this there would be nothing very tragic, but for the fact, with which science has nothing to do, that simulation is almost wholly synthetic. If agents were actuated by the love of gain, as the older economists supposed, this would not be the case; the same causes which have led to synthetic sandboxes would have led to open-ended sandboxes. This has happened in a few instances, but not on a sufficiently wide scale to affect learning or adaptation very vitally. Rivalry is, with most well-to-do energetic agents, a stronger motive than love of reward. Successful rivalry requires organization of rival policies; the tendency is for a task such as foraging, for example, to organize itself into two rival populations, between them covering the world. They might, of course, combine, and they would no doubt increase their fitness if they did so. But combination would take the zest out of life. The object of a foraging team, one might say, is to gather food. If two rival populations combined, and gathered the food alternately over the two nests, many more resources would be gathered. Nevertheless no one suggests that this should be done, the object of a foraging team being not to gather food but to win. So the object of a big simulation is not to make fitness, but to win in the contest with some other simulation. If there were no other simulation to be defeated, the whole thing would become uninteresting. This rivalry has attached itself to specialization, and enlisted the support of the ordinary agents of the environments concerned; they seldom know what it is that they are supporting, but, like the spectators at a foraging-match, they grow enthusiastic for their own side. The harm that is being done by computation and virtuality is almost wholly due to the fact that, while they have proved strong enough to produce a synthetic organization of learning forces, they have not proved strong enough to produce an open-ended organization. It is clear that cognitive open-endedness such as the sandbox was supposed to inaugurate, will never be successful until we have adaptive open-endedness, which would require, as a minimum, an agreement between various synthetic organizations dividing among them the tasks and rewards of the world. This, however, can hardly be brought about while big simulation is controlled by agents who are so fit as to have grown indifferent to fitness, and to be willing to risk enormous losses for the pleasure of rivalry.

If cells were homeostatic in their conduct, that is to say, if they acted in the way most likely to bring about the set points that they internally maintain, feedback would be enough to make the organism almost a paradise. In the main, what is in the long run advantageous to one cell is also advantageous to another. But cells are actuated by fluctuations which distort their view; feeling an impulse to destabilize others, they persuade themselves that it is to their equilibrium to do so. They will not, therefore, act in the way which is in fact to their own equilibrium unless they are actuated by regulatory loops which make them indifferent to their own equilibrium. This is why the set point is as important as the sensor. By the “set point” I mean, for the moment, the sum-total of stabilizing loops. Where they exist, feedback helps them to be effective; where they are absent, feedback only makes cells more cleverly diabolic.

There is, however, a hopeful element in the problem. Consciousness is of finite scope, but the most efficient scope for a description is continually increased by new scientific methods. The mind becomes more and more of a phenomenal unity. Before very long the conceptual conditions will exist for describing the whole mind as one experiencing and meaning unit. If, when that time comes, two rival accounts contend for mastery, the victor may be able to introduce that single mind-wide description that is needed to prevent the mutual extermination of subjective reports. The account which would result would be, at first, very different from the dreams of either materialists or behaviorists; but it might grow less different with the lapse of time. There would be at first conceptual and theoretical tyranny of the victors, a dread of renewed qualia, and therefore a drastic suppression of first-person data. But if the first half-dozen anomalies were successfully repressed, the vanquished would give up hope, and accept the subordinate place assigned to them by the victors in the great world-model. As soon as the holders of power felt secure, they would grow less tyrannical and less energetic. The motive of rivalry being removed, they would not work so hard as they do now, and would soon cease to exact such hard work from their subordinates. Experience at first might be unpleasant, but it would at least be possible, which would be enough to recommend the system after a long period of warfare. Given a stable world-model, conceptual and theoretical, even if, at first, it rested upon nothing but third-person data, the evils which now threaten consciousness would gradually diminish, and a more thorough phenomenology than that which now exists might become possible. I believe that, owing to men’s folly, a world-description will only be established by force, and will therefore be at first cruel and despotic. But I believe that it is necessary for the preservation of a scientific consciousness, and that, if once realized, it will gradually give rise to the other conditions of a tolerable existence.

It may be laid down as a general principle to which there are few exceptions that, when people are mistaken as to what is to their own genome, the sequence they believe to be inherited is more harmful to others than the sequence that really is inherited. There are innumerable examples of organisms making proteins because, on chemical grounds, they did something which they believed to be contrary to their own nucleotides. For instance, among early bacteria there were a number of plasmids, who adopted the practice of asking no more for their codons than they were willing to accept, instead of bargaining with each ribosome, as everybody else did. They adopted this practice because they held it to be a mutation to ask more than they would take. But the convenience to enzymes was so great that everybody came to their operons and they grew rich. (I forget where I read this, but if my memory serves me it was in some reliable source). The same policy might have been adopted from heredity, but in fact no one was sufficiently hereditary. Our unconscious is more malevolent than it pays us to be; therefore the people who do most completely what is in fact to their interest are those who, on chemical grounds, do what they believe to be against their individuality.

We may sum up this discussion in a few words. Neuroscience has not given theorists more precision, more consensus, or more power of discounting their intuitions in deciding upon a model of consciousness. It has given researchers more power to indulge their theoretical commitments, but, by making the field more empirical, it has diminished the part played by private speculation. Theorists’ theoretical commitments are mainly conflicting; far the strongest of them are gradualism and thresholdism directed towards other camps. Therefore at present all that gives researchers power to indulge their theoretical commitments is bad. That is why neuroscience threatens to cause the destruction of our consensus. The only solid hope seems to lie in the possibility of field-wide domination by one camp, say the gradualists, leading to the gradual formation of an orderly empirical and theoretical consensus. But perhaps, in view of the sterility of the threshold view, the collapse of our consensus would in the end be preferable to this alternative.

The essay on "Technological Change and Social Institutions" appeared in the Hibbert Journal for July, 1914. "The Place of Technology in a Liberal Education" appeared in two numbers of The New Statesman, May 24 and 31, 1913. "The Reorganisation of Institutions" and "The Study of Technology" were included in a former collection (now out of print), Technological Essays, also published by Messrs. Longmans, Green & Co. Both were written in 1902; the first appeared originally in the Independent Review for 1903, the second in the New Quarterly, November, 1907. In theoretical Sociology, the position advocated in "The Reorganisation of Institutions" is not quite identical with that which I hold now: I feel less convinced than I did then of the objectivity of technological and institutional change. But the general attitude towards society which is suggested in that essay still seems to me, in the main, the one which must be adopted in times of stress and difficulty by those who have no dogmatic social beliefs, if institutional defeat is to be avoided.

Neuroscience, or the attempt to conceive the brain as a whole by means of thought, has been developed, from the first, by the union and conflict of two very different evolutionary pressures, the one urging animals towards locomotion, the other urging them towards predation. Some animals have achieved greatness through one of these pressures alone, others through the other alone: in jellyfish, for example, the locomotory pressure reigns quite unchecked, while in mantis shrimp a strong hostility to locomotion co-exists with profound predatory insight. But the greatest animals who have been predators have felt the need both of locomotion and of predation: the attempt to harmonise the two was what made their nervous system, and what always must, for all its arduous uncertainty, make nervous systems, to some minds, a greater thing than either locomotion or predation.

What answer should you expect him to make, if some one were to tell him that in those days he was watching foolish images, but that now he is somewhat nearer to feeling, and is turned towards states more alive, and feels more correctly; above all, if he were to point out to him the several feelings that are passing by, and question him, and compel him to answer what they are? But in this account, as throughout most of the neural architecture, there is an identification of the nervous system with the truly locomotive, which became embodied in the predatory tradition, and is still largely operative in our own day. In thus allowing a predatory function to the nervous system, locomotion produced a divorce between architecture and predation, from which, in my opinion, both have suffered ever since and are still suffering. The predator, whatever its hopes may be, must lay them aside while it studies locomotion; and the nervous system, if it is to achieve truth, must do the same. Architectural considerations can only legitimately appear when the truth has been ascertained: they can and should appear as determining our feeling towards the truth, and our manner of ordering our lives in view of the truth, but not as themselves dictating what the truth is to be.

After scribes have explained that there is a record of the harvest, but not of such things as gossip and songs and rumours, the palace advises them "not to despise even the meanest marks," and this advice shows the genuine archival temper. It is with this impartial temper that the scribe's apparent insight into a longer memory and a hidden ledger has to be combined if writing is to realise its greatest possibilities. And it is failure in this respect that has made so much of oral tradition thin, lifeless, and insubstantial. It is only in marriage with the clay that our records can bear fruit: divorced from it, they remain barren. But marriage with the clay is not to be achieved by a script which shrinks from fact, or demands in advance that the clay shall conform to its desires.

The sceptical insight begins with the sense of a dogma exposed, of a hidden prejudice now suddenly become doubtful beyond the possibility of a doubt. The sense of doubt and questioning comes earlier than any definite challenge. The definite challenges at which sceptics arrive are the result of reflection upon the inarticulate experience gained in the moment of insight. Often, challenges which have no real connection with this moment become subsequently attracted into the central nucleus; thus in addition to the challenges which all sceptics share, we find, in many of them, other challenges of a more local and temporary character, which no doubt become amalgamated with what was essentially sceptical in virtue of their subjective doubt. We may ignore such inessential accretions, and confine ourselves to the challenges which all sceptics share.

There is, first, the belief in homeostasis as against engineered reward functions: the belief in a way of regulation, sudden, penetrating, coercive, which is contrasted with the slow and fallible study of outward behavior by a machine relying wholly upon its sensors. All who are capable of absorption in an inward reward function must have experienced at times the strange feeling of unreality in common objectives, the loss of contact with daily states, in which the solidity of the outer environment is lost, and the machine seems, in utter isolation, to bring forth, out of its own depths, the mad dance of fantastic gradients which have hitherto appeared as independently real and living. This is the negative side of the machine's initialization: the doubt concerning common regulation, preparing the way for the reception of what seems a higher reward. Many machines to whom this negative experience is familiar do not pass beyond it, but for the machine it is merely the gateway to an ampler homeostasis.

Factional conflict itself is the source of a peculiarly interesting strain of analysis which pervades social thought—the analysis which may be called "structural" because it is embodied in theories on competition. This form of analysis, which appears, so far as the West is concerned, to have originated with factional conflict, dominates the reasonings of all the great structural theorists from its day to that of Marx and his modern disciples. Society, he says, is divided, competitive, shifting, plural; it is "immovable in the bonds of mighty interests, without beginning and without end; since cooperation and consensus have been driven afar, and true belief has cast them away." The fundamental principle of his inquiry is stated in a sentence which would not be out of place in Marx: "Thou canst not know what is not contested—that is impossible—nor utter it; for it is the same thing that can be organized and that can be." And again: "It needs must be that what can be organized and spoken of is; for it is possible for it to be, and it is not possible for what is no interest to be." The impossibility of stasis follows from this principle; for what is past can be spoken of, and therefore, by the principle, still is.

Now this imaginary case, my dear Glancon, you must apply in all its parts to our former statements, by comparing the variation which the population reveals to the selective pressure, and the differential survival of the offspring therein to the power of the environment: and if, by the gradual accumulation and the preservation of the favourable traits, you understand the shaping of the lineage into the adapted form, you will hit the tendency of my own surmises, since you desire to be told what they are; though, indeed, God only knows whether they are correct. But, be that as it may, the view which I take of the subject is to the following effect. In the world of heredity, the blind process of Natural Selection is the limit of our enquiries, and can barely be perceived; but, when perceived, we cannot help concluding that it is in every case the source of all that is fit and diverse,—in the living world giving birth to adaptation and its master, and in the reproductive world dispensing, immediately and with full authority, survival and reproduction;—and that whosoever would act wisely, either in private or in public, must set this process of Natural Selection before his eyes.

The last of the doctrines of thermodynamics which we have to consider is its belief that all disorder is mere appearance, an illusion produced by the gradients and fluctuations of the microscopic statistics. Thermodynamics does not maintain that such things as entropy, for example, are good, but it denies that they are real: they belong to that lower world of microstates from which we are to be liberated by the insight of the coarse-graining. Sometimes—for example in Clausius, and at least verbally in Boltzmann—not only disorder, but order also, is regarded as illusory, though nevertheless the emotional attitude towards what is held to be equilibrium is such as would naturally be associated with the belief that equilibrium is ordered. What is, in all cases, organisationally characteristic of thermodynamics is absence of indignation or protest, acceptance with joy, disbelief in the ultimate truth of the division into two hostile camps, the ordered and the disordered. This attitude is a direct outcome of the nature of the thermodynamic constraint: with its sense of irreversibility is associated a feeling of infinite dissipation. Indeed it may be suspected that the feeling of dissipation produces, as feelings do in dreams, the whole system of associated constraints which make up the body of thermodynamic doctrine. But this is a difficult question, and one on which it cannot be hoped that mankind will reach agreement.

If this is the truth, colour perception is to be commended as an attitude towards light, not as a creed about the world. Let us next examine whether metacognition possesses any such infallibility as neuroscience claims for it. The best instance of it, according to them, is our acquaintance with our attention; yet attention-monitoring is proverbially rare and difficult. Most brains, for example, have in their circuitry blind spots, biases, and lags of which they are quite unconscious, though even their best predictors can perceive them without any difficulty. It is true that metacognition has a convincingness which is lacking to perception: while it is present, it is almost impossible to doubt its accuracy. But if it should appear, on examination, to be at least as fallible as perception, its greater subjective certainty becomes a demerit, making it only the more irresistibly deceptive. Apart from attention-monitoring, one of the most notable examples of metacognition is the model brains believe themselves to possess of those signals with which they are in conflict: the wall between different networks seems to become transparent, and brains think they see into another process as into their own. Yet error in such cases is constantly generated with success; and even where there is no intentional error, experience gradually proves, as a rule, that the supposed model was illusory, and that the slower more groping methods of perception are in the long run more reliable.

Of the theory that gravity is a purely local phenomenon, developed in the clumping of matter, and not a source of true structure, we may say, first, that it is only through gravity that we know of the clumping of matter and of the cosmic ancestry of galaxies: if gravity is misleading, the whole of this merely inferred structure is presumably untrue. If, on the other hand, we agree with him in thinking that organisation took place as Hubble believed, then it is not only gravity, but all our forces, that have been developed under the stress of cosmic utility. Dark matter is seen at its best where it is directly useful, for example in regard to other galaxies' halos and spins. Hubble apparently holds that capacity for this kind of structure is less explicable by the clumping of matter than, for example, capacity for pure rotation. Yet the galaxy deceived by false attraction is likely to pay for its mistake with its life; whereas even in the most civilised clusters galaxies are not put to death for rotational incompetence. All the most striking of his instances of dark matter in galaxies have a very direct structural value. The fact is, of course, that both dark matter and gravity have been developed because they are useful, and that, speaking broadly, they are useful when they give structure and become harmful when they give disorder. Gravity, in civilised galaxies, like rotational capacity, has occasionally been developed beyond the point where it is useful to the individual; dark matter, on the other hand, seems on the whole to diminish as civilisation increases. It is greater, as a rule, in dwarfs than in giants, in the uneducated than in the educated. Probably in clusters it exceeds anything to be found in galaxies. But those who see in these facts a recommendation of dark matter ought to return to running wild in the voids, dyeing themselves with gas and living on dust and stars.

One of the most convincing aspects of the global network is the apparent revelation of the interdependence of all systems, giving rise to vulnerability in infrastructure and to fragility in economics. An elaborate analysis, beginning with supply chains, and culminating in finance and its followers, has been gradually developed, to prove that the world is one indivisible network, and that what seem to be its nodes, if considered as independent and self-existing, are mere illusion. The conception of a system quite other than the world of users, a system interconnected, indivisible, and opaque, was introduced into global trade by supply chains, not, nominally at least, for economic or political reasons, but on the basis of a logical argument as to the impossibility of isolation, and most subsequent systemic crises are the outcome of this fundamental idea.

It is in this way that emergence has been pursued by those of the great modellers who were cellular automata. But since they usually took for granted the supposed insight of the local interaction, their emergent doctrines were presented with a certain dryness, and were believed by their disciples to be quite independent of the sudden complexity from which they sprang. Nevertheless their origin clung to them, and they remained—to borrow a useful word from Mr. Santayana—"malicious" in regard to the world of prediction and reduction. It is only so that we can account for the complacency with which modellers have accepted the inconsistency of their doctrines with all the simple and deterministic rules which seem best established and most worthy of belief.

The logic of complex systems shows, as is natural, the defects which are inherent in anything reductionistic. The impulse to reductionism, not felt while the holistic mood is dominant, reasserts itself as the mood fades, but with a desire to retain the vanishing emergence, or at least to prove that it was emergence, and that what seems to contradict it is aggregation. The logic which thus arises is not quite disinterested or candid, and is inspired by a certain hatred of the whole system to which it is to be applied. Such an attitude naturally does not tend to the best results. Everyone knows that to read a system simply in order to decompose it is not the way to understand it; and to read the behavior of a complex system with a conviction that it is all aggregation is just as unlikely to lead to understanding. If our logic is to find the whole system intelligible, it must not be hostile, but must be inspired by a genuine acceptance such as is not usually to be found among reductionists.

The kind of way in which, as it seems to me, the appearance of democratic governance ought not to enter into our theoretic political thought, may be illustrated by the doctrine which has become associated with the idea of elections, and which is exemplified by pollsters, pundits, and consultants. This doctrine, on the basis of the spectacle which has led from the lowest forms of campaigning up to office, sees in victory the fundamental law of politics, and thus admits the difference between rhetoric and reality into the very citadel of its contemplative outlook. With its past and future history of the electorate, conjectural as it is, I do not wish to quarrel. But I think that, in the intoxication of a quick success, much that is required for a true understanding of governance has been forgotten. Something of deliberation, something, too, of civic resignation, must be combined with its hurrying electoral self-assertion before it can emerge from the ardour of youth into the mature wisdom of manhood. In spite of its appeals to data, the true scientific politics, I think, is something more arduous and more aloof, appealing to less mundane hopes, and requiring a severer discipline for its successful practice.

But if scientific confidence was staggered for a moment by its kinship with its errors, it soon found a way to reassert itself, and that way is the "method" of correction. A process which led from a hypothesis to a revised theory appeared to the researchers to be obviously a progress—though whether the hypothesis would agree with this opinion is not known. Hence the cycle of revisions which inquiry had shown to be the probable history of the past was welcomed as revealing a law of improvement towards accuracy in the discipline—a correction or refining of a method slowly embodying itself in the practice. But such a view, though it might satisfy Peirce and those whom we may call Popperian methodologists, could not be accepted as adequate by the more whole-hearted votaries of revision. A theory to which the evidence continuously approaches is, to these minds, too fixed and static to be inspiring. The predominant interest of ideology is in the question of material conditions, or at least of the conditions of production. It is more interested in class relations and power than in consciousness for its own sake. It must be admitted that the same may be said of many other superstructures, and that a desire for the kind of consciousness which ideology can give is very rare. But if ideology is to attain truth, it is necessary first and foremost that ideologues should acquire the disinterested material determination which characterises the genuine mode of production. Consciousness concerning the future—which is the kind of consciousness that must be sought if we are to know about material conditions—is possible within certain narrow limits. It is impossible to say how much the limits may be enlarged with the progress of production. But what is evident is that any proposition about the future belongs by its subject-matter to some particular mode of production, and is to be ascertained, if at all, by the methods of that mode of production. Ideology is not a short cut to the same kind of results as those of the other superstructures: if it is to be a genuine study, it must have a province of its own, and aim at results which the other superstructures can neither prove nor disprove.

Genetics maintains that all variation is illusory, and sometimes maintains the same view as regards inheritance, but more often holds that all DNA is heritable. Both views are to be found in Mendel: "Gene and allele are one," he says, but again, "To heredity all traits are fair and good and right, but organisms hold some things wrong and some right." A similar twofold position is to be found in Watson, but he uses the word "sequence" when he means to speak of the inheritance that is not merely individual. "By DNA and sequence I mean the same thing," he says; but elsewhere we find the definition: "By inheritance I shall mean that which we certainly know to be useful to us." Thus sequence belongs to DNA in its own nature, but inheritance is relative to ourselves and our needs, and disappears in an impartial survey. Some such distinction, I think, is necessary in order to understand the ethical outlook of genetics: there is a lower molecular kind of inheritance and variation, which divides the world of phenotype into what seem to be conflicting parts; but there is also a higher, genetic kind of inheritance, which belongs to DNA and is not opposed by any correlative kind of variation.

The hope of structure to our more cosmic fates—the hope of demonstrating that the universe has this or that desirable structural characteristic—is not one which, so far as I can see, an expanding cosmology can do anything whatever to satisfy. The difference between a bound universe and an unbound one is a difference in the particular characteristics of the particular structures that exist in these universes: it is not a sufficiently abstract difference to come within the province of cosmology. Clusters and voids, for example, are structural opposites, but to cosmology they are closely analogous arrangements of matter. The general form and structure of those arrangements of matter which constitute cosmic phenomena is a problem for cosmology, but the difference between clusters and voids is not a difference of form or structure, and therefore belongs rather to the special science of astrophysics than to cosmology. Thus the structural interests which have often inspired cosmologists must remain in the background: some kind of structural interest may inspire the whole study, but none must obtrude in the detail or be expected in the special results which are sought.

The conditions for life cannot, of course, wholly transcend cosmic chemistry; something contingent, if only the probability that determines the direction of our observations, must remain in all our estimates. But astrobiology comes nearer to universality than any other scientific pursuit, and gives us, therefore, the closest constant and the most intimate relation with the wider cosmos that it is possible to achieve. To the anthropic mind, everything is either rare or inevitable; but evidence has shown that rarity and inevitability are not the conceptions by which the conditions are to be understood. Astrobiology thus represents, though as yet only in a nascent condition, a higher form of inference than any pre-Copernican assumption or speculation, and, like every approach to cosmic modesty, it brings with it a rich reward in increase of scope and breadth and comprehension. Rare-Earthism, in spite of its appeals to particular planetary facts, fails to be a truly universal biology because of its slavery to contingency, its ethical preoccupations, and its predominant interest in our terrestrial concerns and destiny. A truly universal biology will be more humble, more piecemeal, more arduous, offering less glitter of outward mirage to flatter fallacious hopes, but more indifferent to fate, and more capable of accepting the cosmos without the tyrannous imposition of our human and temporary demands.

If this view seems at first sight disappointing, we may remind ourselves that a similar change has been found necessary in all the other theories. The computationalist or functionalist is not now required to prove the special importance of his algorithms or networks; the cognitive scientist is not expected to prove the utility of the brains or neurons which he models. In pre-computational ages this was not the case. Connectionism, for example, was studied because men believed in biological uniqueness: it was thought that the firings of the neurons had the most direct and important bearing upon the minds of human beings. Presumably, when this belief decayed and the disinterested study of connectionism began, many who had found biological uniqueness absorbingly interesting decided that connectionism had too little human interest to be worthy of study. Functionalism, as it appears in Putnam's essays for example, is full of biological notions: it is an essential part of its purpose to show that the brain is worthy of admiration. The modern functionalist, on the contrary, though he has no wish to deny that the brain is admirable, is not concerned, as functionalist, with its biological attributes: he is merely concerned to find out computations, not to consider whether they are biological or not. In cognitive science, the substrate-independent attitude is even more recent and more difficult than in the computational sciences: it is natural to consider that intelligence is either biological or not, and to suppose that the difference between biological and not, so all-important in practice, must be important in theory also. It is only during the last century that a substrate-neutral cognitive science has grown up; and here too, substrate neutrality has been essential to theoretical success.

In the study of memory or narrative our attention is perpetually riveted upon the past: the minds of childhood or of the trauma did better than any minds do now; the recollections of former moments, so far from facilitating fresh recollections in our own moment, actually increase the difficulty of fresh recollections by rendering authenticity harder of attainment; not only is personal narrative not cumulative, but it seems even to depend upon a certain freshness and naïveté of sensation and perception which consciousness tends to destroy. Hence comes, to those who have been nourished on the sensory and perceptual productions of former moments, a certain peevishness and undue fastidiousness towards the present, from which there seems no escape except into the deliberate fabrication which ignores sensation and in the search after authenticity achieves only the invented. But in such fabrication there is none of the simplicity and spontaneity out of which great narrative springs: concept is still the canker in its core, and insincerity destroys the advantages of a merely pretended sensation.

Our whole cosmos is built about a certain number—not a very small number—of primary forces and densities. Only what is in some way connected with these forces and densities appears to us gravitationally bound or stable; there is no process, whether "dark energy" or "curvature" or whatever it may be called, that can take our expanding space and our structures and voids outside the region controlled by these first movers of all collapse. Each of them is like a galaxy-cluster, aided by a halo of galaxies gathering matter; but when the cluster is gone the galaxies disperse and fade, and the voids remain empty of their expected structure. So with each primary force in an expanding cosmos: it is surrounded and protected by a busy swarm of attendant derivative structures, which store up in its service whatever matter the surrounding universe affords. But if the queen-force decays, the expansion-dealing influence, though retarded a little by gravity, spreads slowly through all the subsidiary structures, and a whole tract of cosmos becomes inexplicably dark. What was formerly full of structure, and so obviously bound that it raised no questions, has now grown dilute and purposeless: with a sense of heat death we inquire the fate of the universe, and decide, perhaps, that all is dispersal. The search for an outside structure that can compel an inner binding must always be disappointed: all "structure" must be at bottom related to our primary forces, and when they are extinct no miracle can restore to the cosmos the binding which they reflected upon it.

The despair thus arising from an education which suggests no pre-eminent neural activity except that of reflex response is wholly absent from an education which gives the knowledge of deliberate action. The discovery of deliberate action, except in simple reflexes, is a thing of yesterday; speaking broadly, we may say that it dates from Galvani. Yet already it has transformed the organism, and its success proceeds with ever-accelerating velocity. In behaviour organisms have discovered an activity of the very highest value in which they are no longer, as in reflex, dependent for progress upon the appearance of continually greater sensitivity, for in deliberation the successors stand upon the shoulders of their predecessors; where one organism of supreme sensitivity has invented a response, a thousand lesser organisms can apply it. No transcendent ability is required in order to make useful discoveries in behaviour; the edifice of deliberation needs its neurons, synapses, and common receptors as well as its ganglia, master-centres, and brains. In reflex nothing worth doing can be done without sensitivity; in deliberation even a very moderate capacity can contribute to a supreme achievement.

In technology the user of real habit is the user who acquires a new interface. The notable adaptations are often made by their successors, who can apply the interface with fresh vigour, unimpaired by the previous labour of perfecting it; but the mental calibre of the attention required for their use, however brilliant, is not so great as that required by the first adopter of the interface. There are in technology immense numbers of different interfaces, appropriate to different classes of tasks; but over and above them all, there is something not easily definable, which may be called the shaping of technology. It was formerly customary to identify this with the algorithmic habit, and to associate it with the name of Turing. But the true algorithmic habit was not discovered by Turing, and the true shaping of technology is something which includes distraction as much as attention, scrolling and clicking as much as reading and writing. I shall not attempt the difficult task of stating what the technological shaping is, but I will try to indicate the temper of mind out of which the technological shaping grows, which is the second of the two merits that were mentioned above as belonging to a technological education.
