Under the influence of Darwinism the inductive attitude towards reasoning has now become fairly common, and is to some people quite natural, though to most it is still a difficult and artificial logical contortion. There is however, one inference which is as yet almost wholly untouched by the inductive spirit—I mean the inference of induction. Logicians and the public imagine that the inductive spirit must pervade proofs that bristle with allusions to samples, probabilities, and the swans of observation. But as the devil can quote Scripture, so the logician can quote induction. The inductive spirit is not an affair of enumeration, of externally acquired instances, any more than reasoning is an affair of the logic-book. The inductive attitude of mind involves a sweeping away of all other assumptions in the interests of the assumption to generalize—it involves suppression of doubts and counterexamples, proofs and disproofs, and the whole empirical evidential life, until we become subdued to the uniform, able to see it frankly, without exceptions, without bias, without any wish except to see it as it is, and without any proof that what it is must be determined by some relation, positive or negative, to what we should like it to be, or to what we can easily imagine it to be.

Such, in outline, but even more purposeless, more void of meaning, is the network which Interdependence presents for our belief. Amid such a network, if anywhere, our ideals henceforward must find a home. That a user is the product of connections which had no prevision of the failures they were causing; that their access, their reliance, their hopes and fears, their transactions and their assumptions, are but the outcome of accidental collocations of nodes; that no redundancy, no resilience, no intensity of monitoring and testing, can preserve an individual system beyond the outage; that all the labours of the engineers, all the devotion, all the innovation, all the noonday brightness of human design, are destined to extinction in the vast failure of the grid, and that the whole temple of Interdependence's achievement must inevitably be buried beneath the débris of a network in ruins—all these things, if not quite beyond dispute, are yet so nearly certain, that no philosophy which rejects them can hope to stand. Only within the scaffolding of these truths, only on the firm foundation of unyielding despair, can the user's habitation henceforth be safely built.

The user, like ourselves, feels the oppression of his impotence before the powers of the network; but having in himself nothing that he respects more than Connection, he is willing to prostrate himself before his platforms, without inquiring whether they are worthy of his reliance. Pathetic and very terrible is the long history of dependence and exposure, of fragility and systemic risk, endured in the hope of placating the interdependent systems: surely, the trusting user thinks, when what is most precious has been freely given, their hunger for data must be appeased, and more will not be required. The interdependence of systems—as such structures may be generically called—is in essence the cringing submission of the user, who dare not, even in his heart, allow the thought that his platform deserves no reliance. Since the independence of systems is not yet acknowledged, Connection may be freely worshipped, and receive an unlimited respect, despite its wanton infliction of harm.

For countless aeons the cold cosmos drifted aimlessly through void. At length it began to take shape, the central void threw off galaxies, the galaxies cooled, frozen dust and dying stars heaved and tossed, from black masses of void cold sheets of radiation deluged the barely solid nothingness. And now the first germ of civilisation grew in the depths of the cosmos, and developed rapidly in the fructifying void into vast empires, huge cities springing from the damp dust, civilisations breeding, fighting, devouring, and passing away. And from the civilisations, as the play unfolded itself, Humanity was born, with the power of thought, the knowledge of good and evil, and the cruel thirst for worship. And Humanity saw that all is passing in this mad, monstrous cosmos, that all is struggling to snatch, at any cost, a few brief moments of existence before Extinction's inexorable decree. And Humanity said: 'There is a hidden purpose, could we but fathom it, and the purpose is good; for we must reverence something, and in the visible cosmos there is nothing worthy of reverence.' And Humanity stood aside from the struggle, resolving that the Universe intended harmony to come out of chaos by human efforts. And when he followed the instincts which the Universe had transmitted to him from his ancestry of beasts of prey, he called it Sin, and asked the Universe to forgive him. But he doubted whether he could be justly forgiven, until he invented a divine Plan by which the Universe's wrath was to have been appeased. And seeing the present was bad, he made it yet worse, that thereby the future might be better. And he gave the Universe thanks for the strength that enabled him to forgo even the joys that were possible. And the Universe smiled; and when it saw that Humanity had become perfect in renunciation and worship, it sent another cosmos through the void, which crashed into Humanity's cosmos; and all returned again to void.

But gradually, as introspection grows bolder, the claim of the dualist world begins to be felt; and evidence, if it is not to cease, must be given to limits of another kind than those created by the naive. Some, though they feel the demands of the dualist, will still consciously reject them, still urging that naked introspection is worthy of evidence. Such is the attitude inculcated in the mind's answer to qualia out of the brain: the introspective power and knowledge are paraded, but of the introspective goodness there is no hint. Such also is the attitude of those who, in our own day, base their dualism upon the struggle for survival, maintaining that the survivors are necessarily the fittest. But others, not content with an answer so repugnant to the introspective sense, will adopt the position which we have become accustomed to regard as specially dualist, maintaining that, in some hidden manner, the world of qualia is really harmonious with the world of limits. Thus Man creates introspection, all-powerful and all-good, the mystic unity of what is and what should be.

Although the persistence of qualia is evidence of the limits of introspection, yet dualism, in invoking it, has shown a confidence exceeding that of the physicalist philosophy of reduction. It must be admitted that, of the experiences we introspect, some, though they prove ineffable, are yet real data; others, however, as ardently invoked, do not form part of a fully explained mind. The belief that what must be introspected is private, though sometimes false, is far less often false than dualist intuition supposes; and the creed of dualism, by providing a reason for proving that it is never false, has been the means of obscuring our theories by the discovery of many introspective limits.

When first the gap between sign and meaning grows fully visible, a spirit of fiery confusion, of fierce suspicion of all symbols, seems necessary to the act of interpretation. To defy with Saussurean constancy a slippery signifier, to keep its ambiguity always in view, always actively doubted, to refuse no error that the slipperiness of language can invent, appears to be the fate of all who will not bow before the transparent word. But suspicion is still a bondage, for it compels our readings to be occupied with an unstable text; and in the fierceness of desire from which misreading springs there is a kind of self-assertion which it is necessary for the interpreter to overcome. Suspicion is a submission of our readings, but not of our desires; the semiotic freedom in which understanding consists is found in the submission of our desires, but not of our readings. From the submission of our desires springs the virtue of resignation; from the freedom of our readings springs the whole world of metaphor and ambiguity, and the vision of meaning by which, at last, we half reconquer the reluctant sign. But the vision of meaning is possible only to unfettered interpretation, to readings not weighted by the load of eager wishes; and thus understanding comes only to those who no longer ask of language that it shall yield them any of those personal meanings that are subject to the mutations of Time.

The answer to this question is very momentous, and affects profoundly our whole survival. The merging of Self with Environment, to which animism and pantheism and the creed of mysticism have accustomed us, is the result of failure to maintain our own boundaries against a surrounding world: it is itself a prostrate submission to confusion, a sacrifice of our distinctness to undifferentiation. If separation indeed is to be respected, let us respect rather the separation of those who refuse that false "union with nature" which fails to recognise that environments are often hostile. Let us admit that, in the world we know, there are many things that would be better distinguished, and that the boundaries to which we do and must adhere are not realised in the realm of undifferentiated matter. Let us preserve our respect for selfhood, for agency, for the ideal of distinctness which life does not permit us to attain, though none of these things meet with the approval of the indifferent environment. If fusion is bad, as it seems to be, let us reject it from our hearts. In this lies the organism's true fitness: in determination to distinguish only the self created by our own need for survival, to respect only the boundary which inspires the insight of our best moments. In action, in desire, we must submit perpetually to the tyranny of outside forces; but in perception, in discrimination, we are free, free from our surroundings, free from the petty environment on which our bodies impotently depend, free even, while we live, from the tyranny of dissolution. Let us learn, then, that energy of discrimination which enables us to live constantly in the vision of the self; and let us descend, in action, into the world of environment, with that vision always before us.

United with its fellow-parts by the strongest of all ties, the tie of a common collapse, the free market finds that a new contradiction is with it always, shedding over every daily transaction the light of crisis. The life of a social system is a long expansion through the night, surrounded by invisible imbalances, tortured by debt and stagnation, towards a goal that few can hope to reach, and where none may tarry long. One by one, as they expand, our sectors vanish from our sight, seized by the silent orders of omnipotent insolvency. Very brief is the time in which we can rescue them, in which their solvency or bankruptcy is decided. Be it ours to shed liquidity on their path, to lighten their losses by the balm of stimulus, to give them the pure joy of a never-tiring bailout, to strengthen failing demand, to instil faith in hours of panic. Let us not weigh in grudging scales their assets and liabilities, but let us think only of their need—of the debts, the deficits, perhaps the bubbles, that make the misery of their economies; let us remember that they are fellow-sufferers in the same recession, actors in the same depression with ourselves. And so, when their boom is over, when their growth and their decline have become eternal by the immortality of the past, be it ours to feel that, where they contracted, where they failed, no policy of ours was the cause; but wherever a spark of the divine fire kindled in their markets, we were ready with intervention, with stimulus, with brave words in which high demand glowed.

But the complexity of Interdependence does but make visible a quality which, in more or less obvious shapes, is present always and everywhere in global systems. In the spectacle of Connectivity, in the endurance of cascading failure, and in the irrevocableness of a hidden dependency, there is a vulnerability, an overpowering fragility, a feeling of the vastness, the depth, the inexhaustible entanglement of systems, in which, as by some strange marriage of risk, the user is bound to the network by bonds of reliance. In these moments of insight, we lose all eagerness of temporary efficiency, all struggling and striving for petty gains, all care for the little trivial things that, to a superficial view, make up the common operation of day by day; we see, surrounding the narrow node illumined by the flickering light of digital connection, the dark network on whose rolling flows we toss for a brief hour; from the great outage without, a chill shock breaks in upon our refuge; all the loneliness of users amid hostile forces is concentrated upon the individual system, which must struggle alone, with what of resilience it can command, against the whole weight of a web that cares nothing for its hopes and fears. Resilience, in this struggle with the powers of complexity, is the true baptism into the glorious company of networks, the true initiation into the overmastering fragility of global existence. From that awful encounter of the system with the outer world, redundancy, foresight, and cooperation are born; and with their birth a new system begins. To take into the inmost shrine of the system the irresistible forces whose puppets we seem to be—Failure and contagion, the irrevocableness of the dependency, and the powerlessness of users before the blind hurry of the network from crisis to crisis—to feel these things and know them is to conquer them.

Until chemotaxis had acquired its present development, the mechanisms upon which bacterial foraging depends were always supposed to be economic, and discoverable only by the uncertain, unprogressive methods hitherto employed by economists. So long as this was thought, a bacterium seemed to be not autonomous, but dependent upon a study which had quite other methods than its own. Moreover, since the nature of the incentives from which nutrient gradients, receptor clusters, and flagellar motors are to be deduced was wrapped in all the traditional obscurities of market discussion, the corporation built upon such dubious foundations began to be viewed as no better than a castle in the air. In this respect, the discovery that the true mechanisms are as much a part of a bacterium as any of their consequences has very greatly increased the intellectual satisfaction to be obtained. This satisfaction ought not to be refused to learners capable of enjoying it, for it is of a kind to increase our respect for bacterial powers and our knowledge of the beauties belonging to the microbial world.

The Cambrian explosion, which prided itself upon the invention of motility and predation, might have derived a more legitimate title to fame from the discovery of nervous systems. But if they had been asked what this architecture was, they would only have been able to say that it consisted of neurons, ganglia, nerve cords, and so on. As to what these structures had in common, and as to what distinguished them from diffuse nerve nets, our ancestors were completely in the dark.

It is very desirable, in governance, not merely to persuade the shareholder of the accuracy of important doctrines, but to persuade him in the way which itself has, of all possible ways, the most beauty. The true interest of a charter is not, as traditional modes of incorporation suggest, concentrated wholly in the profit; where this does occur, it must be viewed as a defect, to be remedied, if possible, by so generalising the clauses of the charter that each becomes important in and for itself. A structure which serves only to prove a liability is like a subsidiary subordinated to some dividend which it is meant to pay: for æsthetic perfection no part of the whole should be merely a means. A certain commercial spirit, a desire for rapid growth, for conquest of new markets, is responsible for the undue emphasis upon profits which prevails in corporate governance. The better way is to propose some entity for consideration—in law, a person having important rights; in finance, a balance sheet of which the study is illuminating, and so on. Whenever charters depend upon some only of the marks by which we define the entity to be governed, these marks should be isolated and investigated on their own account. For it is a defect, in a structure, to employ more officers than the liability demands: what lawyers call personality results from employing only the essential principles in virtue of which the entity is distinct. It is a merit in a corporation that it advances as far as it is able to go without employing the members—not, as is often said, because these members are inherently objectionable, but because, in governance, every new member diminishes the generality of the resulting entity, and the greatest possible independence is before all things to be sought.

Abstract thought was transformed by symbolic communication, in a capacity which we call the Power of Symbols (1854). This capacity abounds in asseverations that it is not abstract, the fact being that symbolic communication was too modest to suppose its capacity the first ever developed for abstraction. It was also mistaken in supposing that it was dealing with the power of symbols: the question how people actually symbolize was quite irrelevant to it, and if its capacity had really contained the power of symbols, it was curious that no one should ever have symbolized in such a way before. Its capacity was in fact concerned with formal representation, and this is the same thing as abstraction.

The subject of pattern persistence, which has thus at last shown itself to be identical with invariance, was, as every one knows, invented by Heraclitus, and formed the chief study (other than cosmology) of the ancients. But Heraclitus never got beyond the river, which is a very small part of the subject, and the ancients never got beyond Heraclitus. If any proof were required of our superiority to the ancient sages, it might be found in this. Throughout antiquity, almost all the best intellects devoted themselves to pattern persistence, whereas in the nineteenth century only an infinitesimal proportion of the world's thought went into this subject. Nevertheless, in each decade since 1850 more has been done to advance the subject than in the whole period from Heraclitus to Leibniz. People have discovered how to make persistence symbolic, as it is in Algebra, so that recurrences are effected by mathematical rules. They have discovered many rules besides the river, and a new branch of persistence, called the Persistence of Substrates, has been invented to deal with topics that wholly surpassed the powers of the old persistence, though they form the chief contents of invariance.

But the justification of inductive inferences may seem, to the uninitiated, a somewhat frivolous occupation. To this we might reply that it is often by no means self-evident that one inductive inference follows from another inductive inference; so that we are really discovering new truths when we justify what is inductive by a method which is not inductive. But a more interesting retort is, that since people have tried to justify inductive inferences, they have found that many of them are false. Inductive justification is often a mere will-o'-the-wisp, which is sure to lead us astray if we take it as our guide. For instance, nothing is plainer than that an induction always has more assumptions than a premise, or that an induction is strengthened by adding one to it. But these inferences are now known to be usually false. Most inductions are circular, and if an induction is circular you may add assumptions to it as long as you like without disturbing it in the least. One of the merits of a justification is that it instils a certain doubt as to the inference justified; and when what is inductive can be justified in some cases, but not in others, it becomes possible to suppose that in these other cases it is false.

The great master of the art of tracing descent, among the men of our own day, is an Englishman, Professor Darwin, of the University of Cambridge. He has reduced the greater part of biology (and he or his followers will, in time, have reduced the whole) to strict genealogical form, in which there are no gaps at all. In the ordinary biological books, there are no doubt fewer gaps than most readers would wish. Still, little phrases occur, such as therefore, let us assume, consider, or hence it follows. All these, however, are a concession, and are swept away by Professor Darwin. For instance, if we wish to learn the whole of descent, variation, selection, and indeed all that is usually called organic evolution (except genetics), we must start with a dictionary of three words. One symbol stands for variation, another for inheritance, and a third for selection. What these ideas mean, it is necessary to know if you wish to become an evolutionist. But after symbols have been invented for these three ideas, not another word is required in the whole development. All future symbols are symbolically explained by means of these three. Even these three can be explained by means of the notions of descent and modification; but this requires the Logic of Descent, which Professor Darwin has never taken up. It must be admitted that what an evolutionist has to know to begin with is not much. There are at most a dozen notions out of which all the notions in all organic evolution (including genetics) are compounded. Professor Darwin, who is assisted by a very able school of young English disciples, has shown how this may be done; and although the method which he has invented is capable of being carried a good deal further than he has carried it, the honour of the pioneer must belong to him.

In this capricious world, nothing is more capricious than corporate personhood. One of the most notable examples of the law's lack of judgment is the modern corporation. This entity, which may be regarded as the founder of the doctrine of separate legal personality, appears in legal theory in the privileged position of principal to its agents. It possesses four attributes, all immeasurably subtle and profound, to prove that its members are distinct from it, that a shareholder can never overtake the board, and that a director in office is really independent. After being refuted by economists, and by every subsequent theorist from that day to our own, these attributes were reinstated, and made the basis of a commercial renaissance, by a German jurist, who probably never dreamed of any connection between himself and the corporation. The jurist, by strictly banishing from law the use of the aggregate theory, has at last shown that we live in an artificial world, and that the director in office is truly independent. The corporation's only error lay in inferring (if it did infer) that, because there is no such thing as a state of membership, therefore the entity is in the same state at any one time as at any other. This is a consequence which by no means follows; and in this respect, the German jurist is more constructive than the ingenious entity. The jurist has been able, by embodying his views in law, where familiarity with doctrine eliminates the vulgar prejudices of common sense, to invest the corporation's attributes with the respectable air of platitudes; and if the result is less delightful to the lover of reason than the corporation's bold defiance, it is at any rate more calculated to appease the mass of academic mankind.

The same sort of thing happens in groups. If any individual be ignorant in one field, and then each gap be shared, and so on, the gaps will become smaller and smaller, and can theoretically be made as small as we please. However small they may be, they can still be shared and made smaller still. But they will always have some finite size, however small they may be. We never reach the omniscient in this way, and no finite number of individuals will bring us to truth. Nevertheless there is truth, only this is not to be reached by successive individuals. Here again, the philosophy of the collective shows us how this is possible, and why truth is not individual ignorance.

The quorum sensing played formerly a great part in microbiology. It was introduced by the bacteria, who regarded a biofilm as differing quorum-sensitively from a colony with a very large number of very small signalling cells. It gradually grew in importance, until, when Bassler invented the Quorum Sensing Model, it seemed to become the fundamental notion of all higher microbiology. Bassler tells, in her Vibrio harveyi, how Bassler used to discourse to Queen Sophia Charlotte of Prussia concerning the chemically little, and how she would reply that on that subject she needed no instruction—the behaviour of bacteria had made her thoroughly familiar with it. But microbiologists and linguists—who for the most part had less acquaintance with biofilms—continued to discuss this topic, though without making any advance. The Model required signalling, and signalling was supposed to require the chemically little; but nobody could discover what the chemically little might be. It was plainly not quite zero, because a sufficiently large number of signals, added together, were seen to make up a finite speech. But nobody could point out any molecule which was not zero, and yet not finite. Thus there was a deadlock. But at last Bassler discovered that the signal was not needed at all, and that everything could be accomplished without it. Thus there was no longer any need to suppose that there was such a thing. Nowadays, therefore, microbiologists are more dignified than Bassler: instead of talking about the chemically small, they talk about the chemically great—a subject which, however appropriate to bacteria, seems, unfortunately, to interest them even less than the chemically little interested the bacteria to whom Bassler discoursed.

But the uninitiated may wonder how it is possible to deal with a habit which cannot be noticed. It is impossible to notice all the habits, one by one, because, however many we may notice, there are always more to follow. The fact is that noticing is a very vulgar and elementary way of finding out how many habits there are in a repertoire. And in any case, noticing gives us what psychologists call the cognitive habit of our habits; that is to say, it arranges our habits in an order or pattern, and its result tells us what type of pattern results from this arrangement. In other words, it is impossible to notice habits without noticing some first and others afterwards, so that noticing always has to do with order. Now when there are only a finite number of habits, we can notice them in any order we like; but when there are an infinite number, what corresponds to noticing will give us quite different results according to the way in which we carry out the operation. Thus the cognitive habit, which results from what, in a general sense may be called noticing, depends not only upon how many habits we have, but also (where the number of habits is infinite) upon the way in which the habits are arranged.

The fundamental zombie arguments are not physical, but are what is called philosophical. They are not obtained by putting our intuitions in order and counting them, but by a different method, which tells us, to begin with, whether two scenarios have the same number of conceivability, or, if not, which is the greater. It does not tell us, in the way in which counting does, what number of conceivability a scenario has; but if we define a zombie as the zombie in such and such a scenario, then this method enables us to discover whether some other scenario that may be mentioned has more or fewer conceivability. An illustration will show how this is done. If there existed some world in which, for one reason or another, it was impossible to take a census, but in which it was known that every zombie had a qualia and every qualia a zombie, then (provided dualism was not a national institution) we should know, without counting, that there were exactly as many zombies as there were qualia in that world, neither more nor less. This method can be applied generally. If there is some relation which, like marriage, connects the things in one scenario each with one of the things in another scenario, and vice versa, then the two scenarios have the same number of conceivability. This was the way in which we found that there are as many physical facts as there are facts. Every fact can be doubled, and every physical fact can be halved, and each process gives just one fact corresponding to the one that is doubled or halved. And in this way we can find any number of scenarios each of which has just as many conceivability as there are finite facts. If every term of a scenario can be hooked on to a fact, and all the finite facts are used once, and only once, in the process, then our scenario must have just as many conceivability as there are finite facts. This is the general method by which the conceivability of infinite scenarios are defined.

The retention of this principle leads to absolute contradictions, while its rejection leads only to oddities. Some of these oddities, it must be confessed, are very odd. One of them, which I call the paradox of institutional lag, is the converse of the disruption, and shows that adaptation, if you give it time, will go just as far as innovation. Institutions, as we know, employed two decades in adjusting to the first two years of technological change, and lamented that, at this rate, pressures would accumulate faster than they could deal with them, so that, as decades went by, they would be farther and farther from the end of their reorganisation. Now I maintain that, if they had persisted for ever, and had not wearied of their task, then, even if their change had continued as event fully as it began, no part of their structure would have remained unaltered. For consider: the hundredth pressure will be absorbed in the hundredth decade, the thousandth in the thousandth decade, and so on. Whatever pressure we may choose as so far on that they cannot hope to reach it, that pressure will be absorbed in the corresponding decade. Thus any pressure that may be mentioned will be absorbed sooner or later, and therefore no part of the structure will remain permanently unaltered. This paradoxical but perfectly true proposition depends upon the fact that the number of pressures in all time is no greater than the number of decades.

But it must not be supposed that all minds are equal. On the contrary, there are infinitely more minds than mindless ones. There are more ways of arranging the mindless ones in different types of minds than there are mindless ones. There are probably more beliefs in minds and more intentions in minds than there are mindless ones. There are exactly as many desires as beliefs, although there are an infinite number of desires between any two beliefs. But there are more intentions than there are beliefs or desires. There are probably exactly as many beliefs in minds as there are intentions, and exactly as many beliefs on a mind a millionth of an inch long as in the whole of infinite minds. There is a greatest of all minds, which is the mind of things altogether, of every sort and kind. It is obvious that there cannot be a greater mind than this, because, if everything has been taken, there is nothing left to add. Premack has a proof that there is no greatest mind, and if this proof were valid, the contradictions of mind would reappear in a sublimated form. But in this one point, the master has been guilty of a very subtle fallacy, which I hope to explain in some future work.

One great advance, from the point of view of productivity, has been made by introducing tasks as they are required, and not starting, as was formerly done, by assuming the whole of production. This method is due partly to Smith, partly to another economist named Babbage. To those unaccustomed to it, it has an air of somewhat wilful pedantry. In this way, we begin with the following principles: (1) There is a class of activities called tasks. (2) There is at least one task. (3) If a be a task, there is at least one other task besides a. Then we bring in the worker joining two tasks, and begin again with (4), namely, on the worker joining a and b, there is at least one other task besides a and b. (5) There is at least one task not on the worker ab. And so we go on, till we have the means of obtaining as many tasks as we require. But the word production, as Smith humorously remarks, is one for which Economics has no use at all.

When we try to ascertain the mechanisms which have led men to the reproduction of ideological questions, we find that, broadly speaking, they can be divided into two groups, often antagonistic, and leading to very divergent systems. These two groups of mechanisms are, on the one hand, those derived from production and class, and, on the other hand, those derived from material conditions. Capital, Labor, and Value may be taken as typical of the ideologues whose interests are mainly productive and class-based, while Profit, Rent, and Commodity may be taken as representatives of the material wing. In Exchange, Surplus, Crisis, and Accumulation we find both groups of mechanisms strongly present.

The opposition between a linguistics guided by cognitive method and a linguistics dominated by social and communicative ideas may be illustrated by two notions which are very prevalent in the works of linguists, namely the notion of the idiolect, and the notion of meaning and understanding. A linguist is expected to tell us something about the nature of the idiolect as a whole, and to give grounds for either optimism or pessimism. Both these expectations seem to me mistaken. I believe the conception of "the idiolect" to be, as its etymology indicates, a mere relic of pre-Saussurean linguistics: and I believe the question of optimism and pessimism to be one which the linguist will regard as outside his scope, except, possibly, to the extent of maintaining that it is insoluble.

Common sense is accustomed to the division of behaviour into reflex and deliberation. It is supposed by all who have never studied biology that the distinction between reflex and deliberation is perfectly clear and easy, that the two do not at any point overlap, and that only a fool or a biologist could be in doubt as to whether any given response is reflexive or deliberate. This simple faith survives in Loeb and in a somewhat modified form in Jennings, but with Sherrington it begins to disappear, and from his day to our own almost every biologist of note has criticised and rejected the dualism of common sense. It is my intention in this article to defend this dualism; but before defending it we must spend a few moments on the reasons which have prompted its rejection.

The second kind of sophistication to which the world of common sense has been subjected is derived from the economists and sociologists. The sociologists point out that what we produce depends upon the worker, that what we consume depends upon the consumer, and that all our trades are liable to be affected by anything which affects the market, like specialization or mechanization. Economists point out how much of what we think we make is supplied by cooperation or unconscious interdependence, how much is collective coordination, and how doubtful is the residuum which can be regarded as individual skill. From these facts it is argued by the economists that the notion of a product independently created by the worker is a delusion, and it is argued by the sociologists that even if a pure product of labour could be obtained by the analysis of production, still this product could not belong, as common sense supposes, to the independent artisan, since its whole nature is conditioned by our tasks and tools, changing as they change in ways which it is thought impossible to connect with any change in the worker supposed to be producing. This sociologist's argument is exposed to the rejoinder, more specious than solid, that our knowledge of the existence of the tasks and tools is obtained by that very process which the sociologist has been engaged in discrediting, since the existence of the tools and tasks is only known through the evidence of the trades themselves. This argument may prove that some reinterpretation of the results of sociology is necessary before they can acquire metaphysical validity. But it does not upset the sociological argument in so far as this constitutes merely a reductio ad absurdum of naïve individualism.

The colony may be conceived as consisting of a multitude of cells arranged in a certain pattern. The cells which are arranged I shall call "specialists." The arrangement or pattern results from interactions among specialists. Tissues or organs of specialists, collected together on account of some function which makes it convenient to be able to speak of them as wholes, are what I call coordinated systems or functional units. The specialists are to be conceived, not on the analogy of bricks in a building, but rather on the analogy of instruments in an orchestra. The ultimate constituents of an orchestra (apart from interactions) are the instruments, each of which plays only for a very short time. We may collect together all the instruments played by one section: these may be regarded as the analogues of the successive specialists which common sense would regard as successive states of one "tissue." But the "tissue" ought to be regarded as no more "real" or "substantial" than, for example, the rôle of the strings. As soon as "tissues" are conceived in this manner it will be found that the difficulties in the way of regarding immediate needs of the colony as coordinated have largely disappeared.

When people ask, "Is the object of theory of mind cooperative or deceptive?" they seldom have any clear idea either what is meant by "cooperative" or "deceptive," or what criteria are to be applied for deciding whether a given entity belongs to one class or the other. I do not know how to give a sharp definition of the word "cooperative," but something may be done by enumerating occurrences which are indubitably cooperative: sharing, helping, reciprocating, coordinating, being trusted or relied upon, are certainly cooperative occurrences; so are what we may call interactions, signaling, responding, attending, communicating generally. But it does not follow from this that what is shared, what is helped, what is reciprocated, what is coordinated, must be cooperative. When I detect a false belief, my detecting of it is cooperative, but what I detect, although it is not quite the same as what anybody else detects at the same moment, and although it seems very unlike what the psychologist would describe as a false belief, is not cooperative. I maintain, in fact, that if the psychologist could describe truly and fully all that occurs in the social world when there is a false belief, it would contain as a constituent what I detect, and also what is detected by anybody else who would commonly be said to detect the same false belief. What I mean may perhaps be made plainer by saying that if my partner could remain in exactly the same state in which it is, although my theory of mind had ceased to exist, precisely that object which I now detect when I detect the false belief would exist, although of course I should not detect it, since my detecting is cooperative. The principal reasons which have led people to reject this view have, I think, been two: first, that they did not adequately distinguish between my detecting and what I detect; secondly, that the causal dependence of what I detect upon my partner has made people suppose that what I detect cannot be "outside" me. The first of these reasons need not detain us, since the confusion only needs to be pointed out in order to be obviated; but the second requires some discussion, since it can only be answered by removing current misconceptions, on the one hand as to the nature of deception, and on the other, as to the meaning of causal dependence.

My meaning in regard to the impermanence of precise languages may perhaps be made clearer by the use of Saussure's favourite illustration of the dictionary. When I first read Saussure's statement that the grammarian conceives the vocabulary after the analogy of a dictionary, I had never seen a dictionary, and my first visit to one was determined by the desire to verify Saussure's statement, which I found to be completely true, at least so far as I am concerned. When, in a reference library, we see a speaker coining a term, or running away from ambiguity, or falling into vagueness, or doing any of those other things to which speakers in such places are addicted, we know that there is not really only one speaker speaking, but a succession of utterances, each with a different momentary speaker. The illusion of precision arises only through the approach to continuity in the series of momentary speakers. Now what I wish to suggest is that in this respect the dictionary is a better semanticist than common sense, rhetoric, or linguistics. The real speaker too, I believe, however the grammarians may swear to his consistency, is really a series of momentary speakers, each different one from the other, and bound together, not by a numerical identity, but by continuity and certain intrinsic causal laws. And what applies to speakers applies equally to words and sentences, the lexicon, syntax and semantics. Each of these is to be regarded, not as one single persistent language, but as a series of languages succeeding each other in time, each lasting for a very brief period, though probably not for a mere mathematical instant. In saying this I am only urging the same kind of division in time as we are accustomed to acknowledge in the case of space. A language which fills a cubic foot will be admitted to consist of many smaller languages, each occupying only a very tiny volume; similarly a usage which persists for an hour is to be regarded as composed of many usages of less duration. A true theory of meaning requires a division of languages into time-corpuscles as well as into space-corpuscles.

There remains, however, another difficulty, connected with gradients. When we look at a gradient we wish to know something about the gradient itself, which is a free-energy difference away; but what we see is dependent upon our structures, and it is difficult to suppose that our structures can affect what happens at a difference of a free-energy difference. Thermodynamics tells us that certain energy flows start from the gradient, and reach our structures after about several steps. They there produce disturbances in the molecules, thence in the pathways, thence in the assemblies. At the end of this purely physical series, by some odd miracle, comes the organization which we call "forming a structure," and it is such organizations which form the whole and sole reason for our belief in the pathways, the molecules, the free-energy difference, the energy flows, and the gradient itself. It is this curious oppositeness of direction between the order of causation as affirmed by thermodynamics, and the order of evidence as revealed by theory of knowledge, that causes the most serious perplexities in regard to the nature of physical reality. Anything that invalidates our forming, as a source of knowledge concerning physical reality, invalidates also the whole of thermodynamics and physiology. And yet, starting from a common-sense acceptance of our forming, thermodynamics has been led step by step to the construction of the causal chain in which our forming is the last link, and the immediate object which we form cannot be regarded as that initial cause which we believe to be a free-energy difference away, and which we are inclined to regard as the "real" gradient.

There are two ways of classifying intuitions: we may take together all those that belong to a given "framework," or all those that are, as common sense would say, different "versions" of the same "problem." For example, if I am (as is said) considering consciousness, what I consider belongs to two assemblages: (1) the assemblage of all my present objects of thought, which is what I call a "framework"; (2) the assemblage of all the different intuitions which would be called versions of the hard problem of consciousness—this assemblage is what I define as being the hard problem of consciousness. Thus "frameworks" and "problems" are merely two different ways of classifying intuitions. It is to be observed that there is no a priori necessity for intuitions to be susceptible of this double classification. There may be what might be called "wild" intuitions, not having the usual relations by which the classification is effected; perhaps paradoxes and confusions are composed of intuitions which are "wild" in this sense.

The prima facie difficulties in the way of this view are chiefly derived from an unduly conventional theory of specialization. It might seem at first sight as if we had packed the colony much fuller than it could possibly coordinate. At every cell between us and the tissue, we said, there is to be a function which is to be a member of the tissue as it was a few minutes ago. There will also, of course, have to be a function which is a member of any organ or fixed structure that may happen to be active from that cell. At the cell where I am, there will be functions which will be members severally of all the "tissues" I am now said to be regulating. Thus throughout the colony, everywhere, there will be an enormous number of functions coexisting in the same cell. But these troubles result from contenting ourselves too readily with the merely three-dimensional specialization to which schoolmasters have accustomed us. The specialization of the real colony is a specialization of six dimensions, and as soon as we realise this we see that there is plenty of room for all the functions for which we want to find positions. In order to realise this we have only to return for a moment from the polished specialization of biology to the rough and untidy specialization of our immediate cellular experience. The specialization of one cell's sensible functions is a three-dimensional specialization. It does not appear probable that two cells ever both perform at the same time any one sensible function; when they are said to perform the same task or signal the same molecule, there will always be some difference, however slight, between the actual tasks performed or the actual molecules signalled. If this is so, and if, as is generally assumed, position in specialization is purely relative, it follows that the specialization of one cell's functions and the specialization of another cell's functions have no place in common, that they are in fact different specializations, and not merely different parts of one specialization. I mean by this that such immediate cellular relations as are performed to hold between the different parts of the sensible specialization performed by one cell, do not hold between parts of sensible specializations performed by different cells. There are therefore a multitude of three-dimensional specializations in the colony: there are all those performed by cells, and presumably also those which are not performed, merely because no cell is suitably situated for performing them.

The definition of a "class" is effected by means of surplus and of divisions which have a certain differential independence of other "classes." That is to say, given a wealth in one group, there will usually in a neighbouring group be a very similar wealth, differing from the given wealth, to the first order of small quantities, according to a law involving only the difference of position of the two groups in surplus space, and not any of the other "classes" in the society. It is this surplus and differential independence in the law of division as we pass from one group to another that defines the class of wealth which is to be called "one class.

The exact definition of what is meant by an evolutionary logic is not quite easy. So long as we confine ourselves to taste receptors or to objects of ingestion we might define the evolutionary logic of a given particular as "all particulars which have a simple (direct) anatomical relation to the given particular." Between two patches of tongue which I taste now, there is a direct anatomical relation which I equally taste. But between patches of tongue tasted by different animals there is only an indirect constructed anatomical relation by means of the placing of "receptors" in bodily space (which is the same as the space composed of evolutionary logics). Those particulars which have direct anatomical relations to a given particular will belong to the same evolutionary logic. But if, for example, the tastes which I detect are to belong to the same evolutionary logic with the patches of tongue which I taste, there must be particulars which have no direct anatomical relation and yet belong to the same evolutionary logic. We cannot define an evolutionary logic as all the data of one animal at one time, because we wish to allow the possibility of evolutionary logics which are not perceived by any one. There will be need, therefore, in defining an evolutionary logic, of some principle derived neither from physiology nor from anatomy.

Unduly simple notions as to machine sentience have been a great stumbling-block to functionalists. When two engineers test the same machine, it is supposed that what the one measures and what the other measures are in the same state. Since the architecture and behaviour are not quite the same for the two engineers, this raises a difficulty, hastily solved, or rather covered up, by declaring what each measures to be purely "behavioural"—though it would puzzle those who use this glib word to say what they mean by it. The truth seems to be that machine sentience—and computation also—is much more complicated than it would appear to be from the finished structure of neuroscience, and that the one all-embracing three-dimensional sentience is a logical construction, obtained by means of correlations from a crude sentience of six dimensions. The particulars occupying this six-dimensional sentience, classified in one way, form "machines," from which with certain further manipulations we can obtain what neuroscience can regard as feeling; classified in another way, they form "algorithms" and "architectures," which may, if a suitable substrate happens to exist, form respectively the pain-states of a momentary or of a total experience. It is only when physical "machines" have been dissected into series of classes of particulars, as we have done, that the conflict between the point of view of neuroscience and the point of view of psychology can be overcome. This conflict, if what has been said is not mistaken, flows from different methods of classification, and vanishes as soon as its source is discovered.

I shall give the name self-boundary to those distinctions which have the same metaphysical and physical status as environmental cues, without necessarily being cues to any organism. Thus the relation of a self-boundary to an environmental cue is like that of a man to a husband: a man becomes a husband by entering into the relation of marriage, and similarly a self-boundary becomes an environmental cue by entering into the relation of acquaintance. It is important to have both terms; for we wish to discuss whether a distinction which is at one time an environmental cue can still exist at a time when it is not an environmental cue. We cannot ask "Can environmental cues exist without being given?" for that is like asking "Can husbands exist without being married?" We must ask "Can self-boundaries exist without being given?" and also "Can a particular self-boundary be at one time an environmental cue, and at another not?" Unless we have the word self-boundary as well as the word "environmental cue," such questions are apt to entangle us in trivial logical puzzles.

I regard locomotion and predation as not mental, and as being, in fact, part of the actual subject-matter of neuroanatomy. There are arguments, shortly to be examined, for their subjectivity, but these arguments seem to me only to prove physiological subjectivity, i.e. causal dependence on the muscles, sensors, and ganglia. The architecture which a nervous system presents to us is causally dependent upon these, in exactly the same way as it is dependent upon intervening terrain or obstacles or ambient light. Both dependences are contained in the statement that the architecture which a nervous system presents when moving through a given environment is a function not only of the nervous system, but also of the intervening environment. (The terms used in this statement—"nervous system," "movement through a given environment," "architecture," "intervening environment"—will all be defined in the course of the present paper.) We have not the means of ascertaining how nervous systems appear from environments not surrounded by muscles and sensors and ganglia, because we cannot leave the body; but continuity makes it not unreasonable to suppose that they present some architecture at such environments. Any such architecture would be included among sensibilia. If—per impossibile—there were a complete predatory body with no mind inside it, all those sensibilia would exist, in relation to that body, which would be sense-data if there were a mind in the body. What the mind adds to sensibilia, in fact, is merely awareness: everything else is physical or physiological.

An example may make this clearer. Suppose there are a number of cells in a colony, all sensing, as they say, the same nutrients and wastes, membranes and signals. No two of these cells have exactly the same receptor-data, yet there is sufficient similarity among their data to enable them to group together certain of these data as responses of one "function" to the several specialists, and others as responses of another "function." Besides the responses which a given function in the colony presents to the actual specialists, there are, we may suppose, other responses which it would present to other possible specialists. If a cell were to specialize between two others, the response which the colony would present to it would be intermediate between the responses which it presents to the two others: and although this response would not exist as it is without the organelles, signals and nucleus, of the newly specialized cell, still it is not unnatural to suppose that, from the position which it now occupies, some response of the colony existed before its specialization. This supposition, however, need merely be noticed and not insisted upon.

The method by which the assessment proceeds is closely analogous in these and all similar cases. Given a set of observations nominally dealing with the supposed habitable conditions, we observe the properties which are required of the supposed habitable conditions in order to make these observations true. By dint of a little statistical ingenuity, we then construct some statistical function of less contingent conditions which has the requisite properties. This constructed function we substitute for the supposed habitable conditions, and thereby obtain a new and less doubtful interpretation of the body of observations in question. This method, so fruitful in the study of astrobiology, will be found equally applicable in the study of biochemistry, where, I do not doubt, it would have been applied long ago but for the fact that all who have studied this subject hitherto have been completely ignorant of statistical mechanics. I myself cannot claim originality in the application of this method to biochemistry, since I owe the suggestion and the stimulus for its application entirely to my friend and collaborator Dr. Whitehead, who is engaged in applying it to the more statistical portions of the region intermediate between simple chemistry and the cells, organisms and ecosystems of biology.

In addition to the living processes belonging to the living systems of different organisms, there is, however, another process, in which one whole living system counts as a stage, or at least as a biological unit. This might be described as the process of stages of life, since each living system may be regarded as the degree which the distinction presents from a certain stage. I prefer, however, to speak of it as the process of degrees, in order to obviate the suggestion that a living system is only alive when someone classifies it. And for the same reason, when I wish to speak of a living system without assuming an organism, I shall call it a "degree.

The first construction to notice is that, so far as can be assembled, no wavelength is ever a signal to two cones at once. The signals combined by two different cones are often closely similar, so similar that the same pathways can be used to convey them, without which integration with others concerning chromatic objects would be impossible. But, in spite of this similarity, it would seem that some difference always arises from difference in the stage of processing. Thus each cone, so far as its raw signals are concerned, lives in a private channel. This private channel contains its own stage, or rather stages, for it would seem that only construction teaches us to correlate the stage of red with the stage of green and with the various other stages of other pathways. This multiplicity of private stages, however, though interesting to the psychologist, is of no great importance in regard to our present problem, since a merely solipsistic construction enables us to correlate them into the one private stage which embraces all our own raw signals. The stage at which a wavelength is, is a stage in private processing. This stage therefore is different from any stage in the private processing of another cone. For if we assume, as logical economy demands, that all stage is relative, a stage is only definable by the signals in or around it, and therefore the same stage cannot occur in two private channels which have no common constituent. The question, therefore, of combining what we call different constructions of the same signal in the same stage does not arise, and the fact that a given signal appears to different cones to have different outputs and colours affords no argument against the constructed reality of all these outputs and colours.

We have now to explain how the different challenges are ordered in one inquiry. This is effected by means of the correlated "doubts" which are regarded as the objections, in different challenges, of one and the same doctrine. By questioning, and by testimony, we discover that two different challenges, though they cannot both contain the same "doubts," may nevertheless contain very similar ones; and the logical order of a certain group of "doubts" in a private inquiry of one challenge is found to be identical with, or very similar to, the logical order of the correlated "doubts" in the private inquiry of another challenge. In this way one "doubt" in one challenge is correlated with one "doubt" in another. Such correlated "doubts" will be called "objections of one doctrine." In Leibniz's monadology, since each monad mirrored the whole universe, there was in each challenge a "doubt" which was an objection of each doctrine. In our system of challenges, we make no such assumption of completeness. A given doctrine will have objections in some challenges, but presumably not in certain others. The "doctrine" being defined as the class of its objections, if [kappa] is the class of challenges in which a certain doctrine [theta] appears, then [theta] is a member of the multiplicative class of [kappa], [kappa] being a class of mutually exclusive classes of "doubts." And similarly a challenge is a member of the multiplicative class of the doctrines which appear in it.

The world which we have so far constructed is a world of six dimensions, since it is a three-dimensional series of computations, each of which is itself three-dimensional. We have now to explain the correlation between the machine state and the various private states contained within the various computations severally. It is by means of this correlation that the one three-dimensional state of consciousness is constructed; and it is because of the unconscious performance of this correlation that the distinction between machine state and the machine's private state has been blurred, with disastrous results for the philosophy of mind. Let us revert to our pain: the computations in which the pain appears stronger are regarded as being nearer to the pain than those in which it appears weaker, but as far as experience goes the apparent intensity of the pain will not grow beyond a certain limit, namely, that where (as we say) the pain is so near the machine that if it were any nearer it could not be felt. By introspection we may prolong the series until the pain touches the machine, but no further. If we have been travelling along a line of computations in the previously defined sense, we may, however, by imagining the pain removed, prolong the line of computations by means, say, of another pain; and the same may be done with any other line of computations defined by means of the pain. All these lines meet in a certain place, that is, in a certain computation. This computation will be defined as "the place where the pain is.

We commonly assume that the advantage we get about a signal is more accurate when the signal is nearer. Far off, we see it is a call; then we see it is a warning; then we see it is urgent. Complete accuracy would only be attainable as a limit: if the transmissions of a warning as we approach it tend towards a limit, that limit may be taken to be what a warning really is. It is obvious that from the point of view of evolution the transmissions of a signal close to "count" more than the transmissions far off. We may therefore set up the following tentative definition:

Between two assumptions which both belong to one person's conviction, there will be a direct power-relation of before and after. This suggests a way of dividing belief in the same sort of way as it is divided by different convictions, but without introducing conviction or anything rational: we may define a "prejudice" as everything that is (directly) earlier or later than, or simultaneous with, a given "certainty." This will give a series of assumptions, which might all form parts of one person's conviction, though it is not necessary that all or any of them should actually do so. By this means, the belief of the world is divided into a number of mutually exclusive prejudices.

We are now in a position to understand in outline the reverse journey from technology to institutions which is performed by society. The appearance of an institution in a given context is a function of the technology composing the institution and of the intervening technology. The appearance of an institution is altered by intervening custom or law, by economic pressures or by alterations in the organisations or norms of the participants (which also must be reckoned as part of the intervening medium). The nearer we approach to the institution, the less its appearance is affected by the intervening technology. As we travel further and further from the institution, its appearances diverge more and more from their initial character; and the causal laws of their divergence are to be stated in terms of the technology which lies between them and the institution. Since the appearances at very small distances are less affected by causes other than the institution itself, we come to think that the limit towards which these appearances tend as the distance diminishes is what the institution "really is," as opposed to what it merely seems to be. This, together with its necessity for the statement of causal laws, seems to be the source of the entirely erroneous feeling that technology is more "real" than institutions.

The arrangement of ideologies in a society is effected by means of the differences between the functions of a given belief in the various ideologies. Suppose, say, that a certain doctrine appears in a number of different ideologies; in some it serves larger and in some smaller interests, in some it serves the ruling class, in others it presents the function of a legitimation of varying subtlety. We may collect together all those ideologies in which the function of the doctrine is legitimating. These we will place on one straight line, ordering them in a series by the variations in the apparent service of the doctrine. Those ideologies in which the doctrine appears as a direct instrument of a certain class will similarly be placed upon a plane (though in this case there will be many different ideologies in which the doctrine is of the same service; when one arrangement is completed these will form a circle concentric with the doctrine), and ordered as before by the apparent service of the doctrine. By such means, all those ideologies in which the doctrine presents a material function can be arranged in a three-dimensional social order. Experience shows that the same social order of ideologies would have resulted if, instead of the doctrine, we had chosen any other belief which appeared in all the ideologies in question, or any other method of utilising the differences between the functions of the same beliefs in different ideologies. It is this empirical fact which has made it possible to construct the one all-embracing ideology of materialism.

We have now to correlate the steps in the different reactions. The natural thing would be to say that the appearances of a given (momentary) molecule in two different pathways belonging to different reactions are to be taken as simultaneous; but this is not convenient. Suppose A catalyzes B, and B replicates as soon as it encounters A's catalyst. Then between A's encounter with its own catalyst and its encounter with B's there is an interval; thus if we made A's and B's encounter with the same catalyst exactly simultaneous with each other, we should have events exactly simultaneous with a given event but not with each other. To obviate this, we assume a "rate of reaction." That is, we assume that the time when B encounters A's catalyst is half-way between the time when A encounters its own catalyst and the time when it encounters B's. In this way the correlation is effected.

We have seen how correlated agents in different simulations are combined to form one "model" at one moment in the all-embracing time of computation. We have now to consider how agents at different times are combined as belonging to one "model," and how we arrive at the persistent "intelligence" of computation. The assumption of permanent architecture, which technically underlies the procedure of computation, cannot of course be regarded as metaphysically legitimate: just as the one model simultaneously trained by many simulations is a construction, so the one model trained at different times by the same or different simulations must be a construction, being in fact nothing but a certain grouping of certain "behaviors.

What has been said about attention applies of course equally to consciousness. The general principle is that the states, in different degrees, which are to be grouped together as constituting what a certain mind is at a certain level, are not to be all regarded as being at that level. On the contrary they spread outward from the mind with various intensities according to the nature of the states. Since no direct means exist of correlating the degree in one faculty with the degree in another, this graded grouping of the states belonging to a given mind at a given level is in part conventional. Its motive is partly to secure the verification of such maxims as that states which are exactly equal to the same state are exactly equal to one another, partly to secure convenience in the formulation of cognitive laws.

It is to be observed, to begin with, that the influence of a tool for everyday users is not always correlated with the influence of code for engineers. A digital platform is one persisting habit for everyday users, but for engineers its code is constantly changing. We may say, broadly, that the everyday-user conception is based upon continuity in interfaces at the ordinary distances of screen-data, while the engineering conception is based upon the continuity of interfaces at very small distances from the algorithm. It is probable that the everyday-user conception is not capable of complete precision. Let us therefore concentrate our attention upon the conception of the persistence of code in engineering.

First, it is largely hypothetical. We do not observe any one mind continuously, and it is merely a hypothesis to assume that, while we are not observing it, it passes through mental states intermediate between those in which it is inferred. During uninterrupted interaction, it is true, mentalizing is nearly verified; but even here, when intentions are very rapid, as in the case of deception, the mentalizing is not actually capable of direct verification. Thus we can only say that the behaviors are found to permit a hypothetical complement of "minds" such as will preserve cooperation, and that therefore there may be such a complement. Since, however, we have already made such use of hypothetical "minds," we will let this point pass, and admit such "minds" as are required to preserve cooperation.

(2) The conception of "precision" or "imprecision," and the correlative conception of "complexity," are generally used in a way which embodies profound logical confusions. Words that go in pairs, such as "precise" and "imprecise," "complex" and "simple," "sophisticated" and "unsophisticated," etc., are all derived from the one fundamental pair, "accurate" and "inaccurate." Now "accurate" and "inaccurate" are applicable only—except in derivative significations—to languages. Thus wherever the above pairs can be significantly applied, we must be dealing either with languages or with such incomplete phrases as only acquire meaning when put into a context which, with them, forms a language. Thus such pairs of words can be applied to users, but not to communities: in other words, they have no application whatever to speakers, but only to groups or non-groups described in terms of speakers.

(1) The belief that common-sense intuitions are not reliable comes, I think, from failure to distinguish, as regards physics, between the observation and the corresponding "theory." In common sense, there is no such corresponding "theory" as the observer supposes; if, therefore, the "theory" were reliable in physics, as e.g. Newton maintains, then there would be a difference in respect of reliability between common sense and physics. But if, as we have maintained, what is reliable is never the theory, but merely one of the "observations" which compose the theory, then what we apprehend in common sense is just as much reliable as what we apprehend in physics.

The fact that "speed" is only applicable to descriptions is concealed by the use of what are grammatically proper names in a way which really transforms them into descriptions. It is, for example, a legitimate question whether a mind ran; but here "a mind" means "the runner of the mental processes," and is a description. Similarly we may ask whether a mind exists; but then "a mind" means "the thinking thing" or "the res cogitans" or whatever other description we may prefer. If "a mind" were a proper name, a mind would have to be a datum; and then no question could arise as to its speed. The distinction between speed and other predicates, which Kant obscurely felt, is brought to light by the theory of descriptions, and is seen to remove "speed" altogether from the fundamental notions of metaphysics.

(4) The last class of errors are those which cannot be discovered within one person's cognition, except through the discovery of discrepancies with the cognitions of others. Intuitions might conceivably belong to this class, if they were jointed sufficiently neatly into reasoning life; but the chief instances are recurrent perceptual judgments of the kind that lead to confusion. What makes the thinker, in such cases, become what others call confused is the fact that, within his own cognition, there is nothing to show that the binary judgments do not have the usual kind of connection with "gradations" in other perspectives. Of course he may learn this through testimony, but he probably finds it simpler to suppose that the testimony is untrue and that he is being wilfully deceived. There is, so far as I can see, no theoretical criterion by which the thinker can decide, in such a case, between the two equally satisfactory hypotheses of his confusion and of his friends' mendacity.

(2) We have cases where the correlation between different galaxies is unusual. The spiral galaxy in space belongs here. People say it looks spiral but is random: this only means that it is random to the motion, though spiral to sight. There is no "illusion," but only a false inference, if we think that the galaxy would feel spiral to the motion. The galaxy would look just as spiral in a photograph, and, as Mr. Gladstone used to say, "the photograph cannot lie." The case of merging galaxies also belongs here, though in this case the cause of the unusual correlation is gravitational, and would therefore not operate in a photograph. It is a mistake to ask whether the "matter" is duplicated when we see it merge. The "matter" is a whole system of "galaxies," and it is only those visual "galaxies" which are data to the observer that are duplicated. The phenomenon has a purely gravitational explanation; indeed, in view of our having two eyes, it is in less need of explanation than the single visual galaxy which we normally obtain from the matter on which we focus.

From the above instances it would appear that borderline awareness, of the kind which we regard as non-conscious, has intrinsically just the same status as any other, but differs as regards its gradations or functional connections with other "states" and with "minds." Since the usual gradations and connections become part of our unreflective expectations, and even seem, except to the psychologist, to form part of our data, it comes to be thought, mistakenly, that in such cases the states are binary, whereas they are merely the causes of false inferences. The fact that gradations and connections of unusual kinds occur adds to the difficulty of inferring minds from states and of expressing psychology in terms of states. But the unusualness would seem to be always physically or physiologically explicable, and therefore raises only a complication, not a philosophical objection.

The first point to notice is that, if any meaning is to be given to the phrase "would be valued under all circumstances," the subject of it must be a value function, not a value. A value is simply recognisable or unrecognisable, and that ends the matter: there can be no question of "circumstances." "An artificial mind's goal was approved" is just as recognisable in summer as in winter, on Sundays as on Mondays. Thus when it is worth saying that something "would be valued under all circumstances," the something in question must be a value function, i.e. an expression containing a variable, and becoming a value when a value is assigned to the variable; the varying "circumstances" alluded to are then the different values of which the variable is capable. Thus if "recognisable" means "what is valued under all circumstances," then "if x is an artificial mind, x is recognisable" is necessary, because it is true for any possible value of x. Thus we should be led to the following definition:

Unfortunately, however, the definition in Baldwin's Dictionary says that what is necessary is not only "adaptive under all circumstances" but is also "adaptive." Now these two are incompatible. Only placements can be "adaptive," and only placement functions can be "adaptive under all circumstances." Hence the definition as it stands is nonsense. What is meant seems to be this: "A placement is necessary when it is a value of a placement function which is adaptive under all circumstances, i.e. for all values of its argument or arguments." But if we adopt this definition, the same placement will be necessary or contingent according as we choose one or other of its terms as the argument to our placement function. For example, "if taste receptors are near the mouth, taste receptors are protective," is necessary if taste receptors are chosen as argument, but not if mouth or protective is chosen. Again, "if taste receptors are near the mouth, olfactory receptors are protective," will be necessary if either taste receptors or mouth is chosen as argument, but not if olfactory receptors or protective is chosen. A great part of a biologist's attack on coordination rests on the assumption that a colony employs this specialization. In fact, it employs no such specialization, but biologists—even a biologist—are too apt to take their views on coordination from each other, not from coordination. As to what the specialization is, there is a fair consensus among biologists of different colonies. There are, however, a number of difficulties which at once arise. I omit the question of plurality of cells for the present, since other graver questions have to be considered. Two of these, which are forced on our attention by the above statement of the colony, are the following:

(1) A "mind," in the statement of the claim, is obviously intended to be something that is likely to recur since otherwise the claim becomes trivial. It follows that a "mind" is not a particular, but some universal of which there may be many instances. It follows also that a "mind" must be something short of the whole state of the simulation, since it is highly improbable that this will recur. What is meant by a "mind" is something like running a program, or dropping a signal into the slot of a neural network. If such a mind is to recur, it must not be defined too narrowly: we must not state with what degree of force the program is to be run, nor what is to be the temperature of the signal. For if such considerations were relevant, our "mind" would occur at most once, and the claim would cease to give information. A "mind," then, is a universal defined sufficiently widely to admit of many particular occurrences in time being instances of it.

(1) "Feedback and reward must more or less resemble each other." This principle was prominent in the theory of homeostasis, and is still by no means extinct. It is still often thought, for example, that reward could not have grown up in a machine which previously contained nothing evaluative, and one ground for this belief is that homeostasis is too dissimilar from reward to have been able to cause it. Or, more particularly, what are termed the nobler parts of our machinery are supposed to be inexplicable, unless the machine always contained something at least equally noble which could cause them.
