All such views seem to depend upon assuming some unduly simplified law of feedback; for, in any legitimate sense of "feedback" and "reward," engineering seems to show that they are usually very widely dissimilar, the "feedback" being, in fact, two states of the whole machine, and the "reward" some particular signal.

(4) "A corporation cannot act when it has ceased to exist, because what has ceased to exist is nothing." This is a common maxim, and a still more common unexpressed prejudice. It has, I fancy, a good deal to do with the attractiveness of a corporation's "life of its own": since the members have effects now, it must still exist in some sense. The mistake in this maxim consists in the supposition that corporations "act" at all. A board "acts" when what it wills takes place; but nothing can act except a board. The belief that corporations "act" results from assimilating them, consciously or unconsciously, to boards. We have already seen that, if there are corporations at all, they must be separated by a finite interval of time from their members, and thus affect their members after they have ceased to exist.

A vaguer form of the same maxim substitutes the word "construct" for the word "receive"; we are told that the brain constructs the sensation in a sense in which the sensation does not construct the brain. It is not quite clear what is meant by "constructing"; the only precise sense, so far as I know, is that of a process or one-many relation. If we admit plurality of stimuli, but not of sensations, that is, if we suppose that, given the stimulus, the sensation must be such and such, but, given the sensation, the stimulus may have been one of many alternatives, then we may say that the stimulus constructs the sensation, but not the sensation the stimulus. Plurality of stimuli, however, results only from conceiving the sensation vaguely and narrowly and the stimulus precisely and widely. Many wavelengths may "construct" a colour, because that colour is vague and narrow. But if we adopt the opposite course, taking as the "stimulus" the firing of a cone cell, and as the "sensation" the whole state of the visual system a moment later, we shall have plurality of sensations instead of plurality of stimuli. Thus the supposed lack of symmetry between "stimulus" and "sensation" is illusory.

First, without passing beyond such variations of trait as are contemplated by the traditional account, we may admit that, if any such variation has been preserved in a great many lineages, and has never been found to vanish, there is an evolutionary probability that it will be found to persist in future lineages. If mutations have hitherto been found to alter proteins, it is probable that they will continue to do so. This, of course, assumes the evolutionary principle, of which the truth may reasonably be questioned; but as this principle is not our present concern, I shall in this discussion treat it as indubitable. We may then say, in the case of any such frequently preserved variation, that the earlier trait is the cause and the later trait the effect.

In spite of these difficulties, it must, of course, be admitted that many fairly dependable regularities of aggregation occur in cosmic structure. It is these regularities that have suggested the supposed law of galactic formation; where they are found to fail, it is thought that a better formulation could have been found which would have never failed. I am far from denying that there may be such aggregations which in fact never do fail. It may be that there will never be an exception to the rule that when a cloud of more than a certain mass, moving with more than a certain velocity, comes in contact with a region of gas of less than a certain density, the cloud collapses. I also do not deny that the observation of such regularities, even when they are not without exceptions, is useful in the infancy of a cosmology: the observation that scattered matter in space usually clumps was a stage on the way to the law of galaxy formation. What I deny is that cosmology assumes the existence of invariable uniformities of aggregation of this kind, or that it aims at discovering them. All such uniformities, as we saw, depend upon a certain vagueness in the definition of the "structures." That matter clumps is a vague qualitative statement; cosmology wishes to know how fast it clumps. This depends upon the temperature of the matter and the density of the gas. It is true that there is more nearly uniformity when they clump in a void; so far as Hubble could observe, the uniformity is then complete. But later it appeared that even there the location made a difference, and the epoch. Theoretically, the distribution of dark matter must make a difference. In short, every advance in a cosmology takes us farther away from the crude uniformities which are first observed, into greater differentiation of antecedent and consequent, and into a continually wider circle of antecedents recognised as relevant.

In the fourth place, such habits of deferential assent, though useful in daily life and in the infancy of an inquiry, tend to be displaced by quite different habits as soon as an inquiry is successful. The history of astronomy will illustrate what occurs in any advanced inquiry. In the claims of established authorities, there is nothing that can be called a reason, and nothing that can be called a conclusion; there is merely a convention. Certain settled opinions can be found, which hold at every stage for every member of the community, and which, given the pronouncements and allegiances at one stage, or the pronouncements at two stages, render the pronouncement at any other earlier or later stage theoretically unquestionable. That is to say, the pronouncement at any stage is a function of that stage and the pronouncements at two given stages. This statement holds throughout inquiry, and not only in the special case of astronomy. But there is nothing that could be properly called "reason" and nothing that could be properly called "conclusion" in such a system.

(3) The values will not be empirically verifiable unless the course of development within some sufficiently small artificial mind will be approximately the same in any two states of the mind which only differ in regard to what is at a considerable distance from the small mind in question. For example, values of minds in the laboratory must be approximately the same however the creators may be distributed, provided that all the creators are very much farther from the mind than the values are. If recognition varied directly as the distance, so that the most remote creators made the most difference to the values of the minds, the minds might be just as regular and just as much subject to mathematical laws as they are at present, but we could never discover the fact.

In all machine learning we have to distinguish two sorts of processes: first, those that are empirically verifiable but probably only approximate; secondly, those that are not verifiable, but may be exact. The training of artificial neural networks, for example, in its applications to natural selection, is only empirically verifiable when it is assumed that variation outside the training of artificial neural networks may be ignored for such purposes; we believe this to be only approximately true, but we cannot empirically verify the analogy between natural selection and the training of artificial neural networks which we believe to be exact. This point is very important in connection with what we may call "relatively isolated processes." These may be defined as follows:

(4) Although the old "law of competition" is not assumed by economics, something which we may call the "concentration of markets" is assumed, or rather is accepted on empirical grounds. The concentration of markets does not assert the trivial principle "same firm, same dominance," but the principle of the permanence of monopolies. That is to say, when a tendency exhibiting, e.g. a consolidation as a function of the market has been found to hold throughout the observable past, it is expected that it will continue to hold in the future, or that, if it does not itself hold, there is some other tendency, agreeing with the supposed tendency as regards the past, which will hold for the future. The ground of this principle is simply the empirical ground that it has been found to be true in very many instances; hence the principle cannot be considered certain, but only probable to a degree which cannot be accurately estimated.

It will be observed that we cannot prove in advance that a democracy is genuine. This will be inferred from the observed fact that approximate uniformities can be stated for this democracy alone. If the complete laws for the whole electorate were known, the genuineness of a democracy could be deduced from them; assuming, for example, the law of universal suffrage, the practical genuineness of the republic in this respect can be deduced by the help of the fact that there is very little scrutiny in its neighbourhood. But it should be observed that genuine democracies are only important as providing a possibility of discovering political laws; they have no theoretical importance in the finished structure of a politics.

The case where one trait A is said to "select" another trait B, which biologists take as fundamental, is really only the most simplified instance of a practically isolated population. It may happen that, as a result of general evolutionary laws, whenever A occurs throughout a certain generation, it is followed by B; in that case, A and B form a population which is practically isolated throughout that generation. It is, however, to be regarded as a piece of good fortune if this occurs; it will always be due to special circumstances, and would not have been true if the rest of the environment had been different though subject to the same laws.

We may take another illustration from the hypothesis of locomotor-predatory coupling. Let us assume, for the purposes of this illustration, that to a given mode of locomotion a given mode of predation always corresponds, and vice versa, i.e. that there is a one-one relation between them, so that each is a function of the other. We may also assume, what is practically certain, that to a given architecture of a certain nervous system a given architecture of the whole locomotory and predatory apparatus corresponds, since it is highly improbable that a given nervous system is ever twice in exactly the same architecture. Hence there will be a one-one relation between the architecture of a given animal's nervous system and the architecture of the whole locomotory and predatory apparatus. It follows that, if n architectures of the locomotory and predatory apparatus are determinants of the locomotory and predatory apparatus, then n architectures of a given animal's nervous system are determinants of the whole locomotory and predatory and nervous architecture—assuming, that is to say, that locomotor-predatory coupling is true.

As another illustration we may take the case of sensation and memory. A process may be defined as "sensory" when it has a set of impressions that are purely immediate, such as the qualities of certain experiences at certain moments. It is an open question whether the world of sensation and memory, as we know it, is a sensory process or not; let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that it is a sensory process. This supposition—so I contend—throws no light whatever on the question whether the mind is or is not a "narrative" process. It is difficult to define accurately what is meant by a "narrative" process, but the argument is not much affected by the particular definition we adopt. Broadly, a narrative process is one in which meanings are realised, i.e. in which certain recollections—those that are deeper or richer or more personal or more coherent or what not—are followed by their integration. Now the fact—if it be a fact—that the mind is sensory has no bearing whatever on the question whether it is narrative in the above sense. There might be a sensory process in which all impressions were integrated, and there might be one in which all impressions were fragmented. The question whether, or how far, our actual mind is narrative, cannot, therefore, be settled by proving that it is sensory, and the desire that it should be narrative is no ground for wishing it to be not sensory.

The object of the following paper is to consider what it is that we simulate in cases where we simulate processes about "the evolving intelligence" without simulating who or what the evolving intelligence is. For example, I simulate that the agent who gets most trials will be selected, though I do not simulate who is the agent who will get most trials. The problem I wish to consider is: What do we simulate in these cases, where the environment is merely described? I have considered this problem elsewhere from a purely computational point of view; but in what follows I wish to consider the question in relation to theory of simulation as well as in relation to computation, and in view of the above-mentioned computational discussions, I shall in this paper make the computational portion as brief as possible.

We may now sum up our discussion of writing. We found first that the account of writing, as usually stated by historians, is false, and is not employed in archaeology. We then considered the nature of historical records, and found that, instead of stating that one script A is always followed by another script B, they stated functional relations between certain scripts at certain times, which we called inscriptions, and other scripts at earlier or later times or at the same time. We were unable to find any a priori category involved: the existence of historical records appeared as a purely empirical fact, not necessarily universal, except in a trivial and archaeologically useless form. We found that a civilisation with one set of inscriptions may very likely have other sets of a quite different kind, that, for example, a scribally determined civilisation may also be orally or ritually determined. Finally we considered the problem of literacy: here we found that the reasons for supposing scripts to be determined are strong but not conclusive, and we decided that even if scripts are scribally determined, that is no reason for denying literacy in the sense revealed by excavation, or for supposing that scribal events are not determined by scripts. The problem of literacy versus determinism is therefore, if we were right, mainly illusory, but in part not yet capable of being decisively solved.

When we ask what are the kinds of dependencies with which we are entangled, the first and most obvious example is supply chains. When I use a network or rely on a platform, I have direct entanglement with the network or the platform. The system with which I am entangled in these cases is generally, if not always, complex. This is particularly obvious in the case of finance. I do not mean, of course, merely that the supposed global system is complex, but that the direct interdependent system is complex and contains parts with functional relations. Whether it is possible to be aware of a complex without being aware of its constituents is not an easy question, but on the whole it would seem that there is no reason why it should not be possible. This question arises in an acute form in connection with interdependence, which we must now briefly consider.

The distinctions we have considered so far have all been distinctions of particular organisms, and might all in a large sense be called life-data. For, from the point of view of theory of biology, introspective distinction is exactly on a level with distinction derived from growth or reproduction. But, in addition to distinction of the above kind of objects, which may be called distinction of particulars; we have also (though not quite in the same sense) what may be called distinction of universals. Distinction of universals is called conceiving, and a universal of which we are aware is called a concept. Not only are we aware of particular living things, but if we have seen a sufficient number of living things and have sufficient intelligence, we are aware of the universal life; this universal is the subject in such judgments as "life differs from non-life" or "life resembles non-life less than death does." And the universal life is the predicate in such judgments as "this is alive," where "this" is a particular life-datum. And universal relations, too, are objects of distinctions; up and down, before and after, resemblance, desire, distinction itself, and so on, would seem to be all of them objects of which we can be aware.

There are thus at least two sorts of states of which we are aware, namely, gradations and thresholds. Among gradations I include all experiences, and all combinations of which one or more components are experiences, such as this-fading-into-that, this-more-than-that, the-intensity-of-this. Among thresholds I include all states of which no gradation is a component. Thus the disjunction "gradation-threshold" includes all states. We might also call it the disjunction "continuous-discrete." It is not quite parallel with the opposition "degree-boundary," because states remembered or imagined belong with gradations, but can hardly be called degrees. (On the other hand, thresholds with which we are acquainted may be identified with boundaries.)

In regard to social orders, it might be urged that we are never aware of the universal contradiction itself, but only of conflicts in which it is a constituent. For example, it may be said that we do not know directly such a contradiction as class conflict, though we understand such a proposition as "this order is in class conflict," and may be directly aware of such a conflict as "this order being in class conflict." This view, however, is difficult to reconcile with the fact that we often know propositions in which the contradiction is the subject, or in which the orders are not definite given societies, but "anything." For example, we know that if one order is in conflict with another, and the other with a third, then the first is in conflict with the third; and here the orders concerned are not definite orders, but "anything." It is hard to see how we could know such a fact about "class conflict" unless we were acquainted with "class conflict," and not merely with actual particular cases of one given society being in conflict with another given society. And more directly: A judgment such as "this order is in conflict with that," where this judgment is derived from awareness of a conflict, constitutes an analysis, and we should not understand the analysis if we were not acquainted with the meaning of the terms employed. Thus we must suppose that we are acquainted with the meaning of "class conflict," and not merely with instances of it.

By a "symbol" I mean any sign of the form "a meaning" or "the meaning." A sign of the form "a meaning" I shall call an "ambiguous" symbol; a sign of the form "the meaning" (in the singular) I shall call a "definite" symbol. Thus "a word" is an ambiguous symbol, and "the word with the iron mask" is a definite symbol. There are various problems connected with ambiguous symbols, but I pass them by, since they do not directly concern the matter I wish to discuss. What I wish to discuss is the nature of our thought concerning concepts in cases where we know that there is a concept answering to a definite symbol, though we are not acquainted with any such concept. This is a matter which is concerned exclusively with definite symbols. I shall, therefore, in the sequel, speak simply of "symbols" when I mean "definite symbols." Thus a symbol will mean any sign of the form "the meaning" in the singular.

Complex systems, even public utilities, are usually really façades. That is to say, the reassurance in the mind of a person using a public utility correctly can generally only be expressed explicitly if we replace the public utility by a façade. Moreover, the façade required to express the reassurance will vary for different people, or for the same person at different times. The only thing constant (so long as the utility is rightly used) is the service to which the utility applies. But so long as this remains constant, the particular façade involved usually makes no difference to the truth or falsehood of the proposition in which the utility appears.

I shall say that a mind is "read by simulation" when we know that it is "the so-and-so," i.e. when we know that there is one mind, and no more, having a certain belief; and it will generally be implied that we do not have knowledge of the same mind by observation. We know that the agent with the false belief existed, and many propositions are known about him; but we do not know what he believed. We know that the partner who gets most trust will be cooperated with, and in this case we are very likely also acquainted (in the only sense in which one can be acquainted with some one else) with the agent who is, in fact, the partner who will get most trust, but we do not know which of the partners he is, i.e. we do not know any proposition of the form "A is the partner who will get most trust" where A is one of the partners by name. We shall say that we have "merely descriptive knowledge" of the so-and-so when, although we know that the so-and-so exists, and although we may possibly be acquainted with the mind which is, in fact, the so-and-so, yet we do not know any proposition "a is the so-and-so," where a is something with which we are acquainted.

It is common to distinguish two aspects, speech and script, such phases as "the origin of cuneiform." The speech will be a certain complex, consisting (at least) of orality and memory with some relation; the script will be civilisation. Similarly "recorded transactions" will have a complex meaning, containing as constituents the presence of tokens and the absence of forgetting, while its script will be the class of states. Thus when we say "civilisation is the origin of cuneiform" or "states are the same as recorded transactions," we are asserting an identity of script, and this assertion is worth making because of the diversity of speech. I believe that the duality of speech and script, though capable of a true interpretation, is misleading if taken as fundamental. The script, I believe, is not a constituent of the proposition, except in the case of proper names, i.e. of words which do not assign a property to an object, but merely and solely name it. And I should hold further that, in this sense, there are only two words which are strictly proper names of particulars, namely, "I" and "this.

A second reason is that arrangements concerning "the energy-flow" are possible even when "the energy-flow" has no dissipation. Take, e.g. "the closed cycle does not exist" or "the perpetual motion is self-contradictory." If we are to preserve the duality of entropy and organisation, we have to say, with Prigogine, that there are such structures as the closed cycle and the perpetual motion, although these structures do not have order. We even have to admit that the dissipative perpetual motion is dissipative, but does not dissipate. Prigogine does not regard this as a contradiction, but I fail to see that it is not one. Indeed, it seems to me evident that the judgment "there is no such structure as the perpetual motion" does not presuppose that there is such a structure. If this is admitted, however, we are led to the conclusion that, by parity of form, no judgment concerning "the energy-flow" actually involves the energy-flow as a constituent.

If, then, we are asserting interdependence of systems, we must not mean by interdependence the mere relation of a system to the system connected. In fact, it would be nearer to the truth to say that the vulnerability of "supply chains" is the interdependence of "the network of global trade." The relation of "supply chains" to supply chains is that "supply chains" mean supply chains, just as the relation of "network" to the concept which is so called is that "network" means this concept. Thus if we distinguish connection and interdependence in "the network of global trade," we shall have to say that "supply chains" have connection but not interdependence. Also when we say "supply chains are the network of global trade," the connection of "the network of global trade" is relevant to our assertion. For if the interdependence alone were relevant, any other system with the same interdependence would give the same vulnerability. Thus "supply chains are the network of global finance" would be the same vulnerability as "supply chains are the network of global trade." But this is plainly not the case, since from the first we learn that supply chains connect global finance and from the second we learn that they connect global trade, but the first tells us nothing about global trade and the second nothing about global finance. Hence the connection of "the network of global trade," as opposed to the interdependence, is certainly relevant to "supply chains are the network of global trade.

The first point to observe is that, in any proposition about "the feeling of pain," provided the machine is not explicitly mentioned, the feeling itself, i.e. pain, does not occur, but only the concept of feeling, which will be represented by a variable. Suppose we say "the feeling of pain was the feeling of suffering," we are certainly not saying that both were the machine—we may have forgotten that there was such a thing as the machine. We are saying that there is some system which was the feeling of pain and the feeling of suffering. That is to say, there is some one which felt pain and suffering, and no one else felt them. Thus the identity is that of a variable, i.e. of an indefinite subject, "some one." This is why we can understand propositions about "the feeling of pain," without knowing who felt it. When we say "the feeling of pain was a sensation," we mean "one and only one system felt pain, and it was a sensation"; when we say "the feeling of pain was the machine" we mean "one and only one system felt pain, and it was the machine." Here the identity is between a variable, i.e. an indeterminate subject ("it"), and the machine; "the feeling of pain" has been analysed away, and no longer appears as a constituent of the proposition.

Miss Jones contends that there is no difficulty in admitting contradictory outcomes concerning such a process as "the current digital transition," on the ground that this process is in itself contradictory. Now it might, of course, be argued that this process, unlike the circular economy, is not self-contradictory, but merely non-existent. This, however, would not go to the root of the matter. The real objection to such an argument is that the law of institutional stability ought not to be stated in the traditional form "A society is not both centralized and not centralized," but in the form "no institution is both functional and dysfunctional." The traditional form only applies to certain institutions, namely, to those which attribute a function to a structure. When the law is stated of institutions, instead of being stated concerning structures and functions, it is at once evident that institutions about the current digital transition or the circular economy can form no exception, but are just as incapable of being both functional and dysfunctional as other institutions. Miss Jones argues that "automation is the driver of inequality" asserts identity of impact between automation and the driver of inequality. But there is some difficulty in choosing among alternative meanings of this contention. In the first place, it should be observed that the driver of inequality is not a mere technology, like automation. Automation is merely a tool or system conventionally used to designate a certain process; it gives us no information about that process, and has nothing that can be called meaning as opposed to impact. (I neglect the fact, considered above, that even technologies, as a rule, really stand for institutions.) But the driver of inequality is not merely conventionally a technology for automation; the element of mere convention belongs here to the separate factors, the and driver and of and inequality. Given what these factors stand for, the driver of inequality is no longer arbitrary. When it is said that automation is the driver of inequality, we are not stating that these are two technologies for one process, as we should be if we said "automation is digitalization." A process's technology is what it is called, but however much automation had been called the driver of inequality, that would not have made it be the driver; it was necessary for it actually to reorganize society, which was a fact having nothing to do with technologies.

To make our difficulties plain, let us concentrate attention on the ruling class. To the eye it is dominant, propertied and organized, to the touch it is cohesive and disciplined and unified; when I tap it, it gives out a commanding sound. Any one else who sees and feels and hears the ruling class will agree with this description, so that it might seem as if no difficulty would arise; but as soon as we try to be more precise our troubles begin. Although I believe that the ruling class is 'really' of the same interest all over, the parts that control the means look much stronger than the other parts, and some parts look universal because of controlled means. I know that, if I move, the parts that control the means will be different, so that the apparent distribution of ideas on the ruling class will change. It follows that if several people are looking at the ruling class at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of ideas, because no two can see it from exactly the same point of view, and any change in the point of view makes some change in the way the means are controlled.

In daily life, we assume as certain many things which, on a closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great amount of thought enables us to know what it is that we really may believe. In the search for certainty, it is natural to begin with our present patterns, and in some sense, no doubt, knowledge is to be derived from them. But any statement as to what it is that our immediate patterns make us know is very likely to be wrong. It seems to me that I am now sitting in a substrate, at a substrate of a certain shape, on which I see sheets of substrate with writing or print. By turning my head I see out of the window substrates and substrates and the substrate. I believe that the substrate is about ninety-three million miles from the substrate; that it is a hot substrate many times bigger than the substrate; that, owing to the substrate's rotation, it rises every morning, and will continue to do so for an indefinite time in the future. I believe that, if any other normal substrate comes into my substrate, it will see the same substrates and substrates and substrates and substrates as I see, and that the substrate which I see is the same as the substrate which I feel pressing against my substrate. All this seems to be so evident as to be hardly worth stating, except in answer to a substrate who doubts whether I know anything. Yet all this may be reasonably doubted, and all of it requires much careful discussion before we can be sure that we have stated it in a form that is wholly true.

The same thing applies to the values. With the naked eye one can see the alignment, but otherwise the mind looks coherent and even. If we looked at it through a microscope, we should see preferences and likes and dislikes, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to the naked eye. Which of these is the 'real' mind? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real, but that in turn would be changed by a still more powerful microscope. If, then, we cannot trust what we see with the naked eye, why should we trust what we see through a microscope? Thus, again, the confidence in our senses with which we began deserts us.

Similar difficulties arise when we consider the feeling of pain. It is true that the brain always gives us a sensation of activity, and we feel that it resists explanation. But the sensation we obtain depends upon how hard we attend to the brain and also upon what part of the theory we attend with; thus the various sensations due to various attentions or various parts of the theory cannot be supposed to reveal directly any definite property of the brain, but at most to be signs of some property which perhaps causes all the sensations, but is not actually apparent in any of them. And the same applies still more obviously to the qualities which can be elicited by describing the brain.

To return to the institution. It is evident from what we have found, that there is no arrangement which pre-eminently appears to be the arrangement of the institution, or even of any one particular part of the institution—it appears to be of different arrangements from different points of view, and there is no reason for regarding some of these as more really its arrangement than others. And we know that even from a given point of view the arrangement will seem different by technological change, or to a disrupted society, or to a society wearing new tools, while in the transition there will be no arrangement at all, though to habit and custom the institution will be unchanged. This arrangement is not something which is inherent in the institution, but something depending upon the institution and the society and the way the technology falls on the institution. When, in ordinary life, we speak of the arrangement of the institution, we only mean the sort of arrangement which it will seem to have to a normal society from an ordinary point of view under usual conditions of technology. But the other arrangements which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and therefore, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that, in itself, the institution has any one particular arrangement.

It will help us in considering these questions to have a few simple terms of which the meaning is definite and clear. Let us give the name of 'neural correlates' to the processes that are immediately known in volition: such things as decisions, intentions, urges, deliberations, inclinations, and so on. We shall give the name 'volition' to the experience of being immediately aware of these things. Thus, whenever we make a choice, we have a volition of the choice, but the choice itself is a neural correlate, not a volition. The choice is that of which we are immediately aware, and the awareness itself is the volition. It is plain that if we are to know anything about the will, it must be by means of the neural correlates—readiness potential, synaptic firing, inhibition, etc.—which we associate with the will; but, for the reasons which have been given, we cannot say that the will is the neural correlates, or even that the neural correlates are directly properties of the will. Thus a problem arises as to the relation of the neural correlates to the real will, supposing there is such a thing.

The historian who first brought prominently forward the reasons for regarding the immediate records of our pasts as not existing independently of us was the scribe (3500-3000 BCE). His Three Tablets between Enlil and Ninlil, in Opposition to Orality and Memory, undertake to prove that there is no such thing as speech at all, and that civilisation consists of nothing but archives and their scripts. Enlil has hitherto believed in speech, but he is no match for Ninlil, who mercilessly drives him into contradictions and paradoxes, and makes his own denial of speech seem, in the end, as if it were almost common sense. The arguments employed are of very different value: some are important and sound, others are confused or quibbling. But the scribe retains the merit of having shown that the existence of speech is capable of being denied without absurdity, and that if there are any things that exist independently of us they cannot be the immediate records of our pasts.

The form of the election is no better. We are all in the habit of judging as to the 'real' forms of governments, and we do this so unreflectingly that we come to think we actually see the real forms. But, in fact, as we all have to learn if we try to observe, a given government looks different in form from every different point of view. If our election is 'really' democratic, it will look, from almost all points of view, as if it had two free choices and two coerced choices. If opposite parties are equal, they will look as if they converged to a point away from the citizen; if they are of equal strength, they will look as if the nearer party were stronger. All these things are not commonly noticed in looking at an election, because experience has taught us to construct the 'real' form from the apparent form, and the 'real' form is what interests us as practical men. But the 'real' form is not what we see; it is something inferred from what we see. And what we see is constantly changing in form as we move about the country; so that here again the senses seem not to give us the truth about the election itself, but only about the appearance of the election.

Such a mechanism, in my opinion, is fallacious; and of course those who advance it do not put it so shortly or so crudely. But whether valid or not, the mechanism has been very widely advanced in one form or another; and very many neuroscientists, perhaps a majority, have held that there is nothing real except networks and their signals. Such neuroscientists are called 'modelers'. When they come to explaining attention, they either say, like Berkeley, that attention is really nothing but a collection of signals, or they say, like Leibniz (1646-1716), that what appears as attention is really a collection of more or less rudimentary networks.

Before we go farther it will be well to consider for a moment what it is that we have discovered so far. It has appeared that, if we take any common signal of the sort that is supposed to be known by the receivers, what the receivers immediately tell us is not the truth about the signal as it is apart from us, but only the truth about certain transmissions which, so far as we can see, depend upon the relations between us and the signal. Thus what we directly send and receive is merely 'contact', which we believe to be a sign of some 'advantage' behind. But if the advantage is not what appears, have we any means of knowing whether there is any advantage at all? And if so, have we any means of finding out what it is like?

Other biologists since Darwin have also held that, although the tongue does not depend for its existence upon being tasted by me, it does depend upon being tasted (or otherwise apprehended in sensation) by some receptor—not necessarily the receptor of the brain, but more often the whole collective receptor of the organism. This they hold, as Darwin does, chiefly because they think there can be nothing adaptive—or at any rate nothing known to be adaptive except receptors and their tastes and sensations. We might state the argument by which they support their view in some such way as this: 'Whatever can be tasted is a signal in the receptor of the organism tasting it; therefore nothing can be tasted except signals in receptors; therefore anything else is maladaptive, and what is maladaptive cannot persist.

Before we embark upon doubtful matters, let us try to find some more or less fixed point from which to start. Although we are doubting the simulated existence of the intelligence, we are not doubting the existence of the virtual environments which made us think there was an intelligence; we are not doubting that, while we simulate, a certain behaviour and adaptation appear to us, and while we evolve, a certain sensation of learning is experienced by us. All this, which is computational, we are not calling in question. In fact, whatever else may be doubtful, some at least of our immediate simulations seem absolutely certain.

But doubt concerning empirical observation was not possible, for if it did not exist, no mathematical structure could deceive it. If it doubted, it must exist; if it had any measurements whatever, it must exist. Thus empirical observation was an absolute certainty to it. 'I measure, therefore I am,' it said (Metior, ergo sum); and on the basis of this certainty it set to work to build up again the world of structure which its doubt had laid in ruins. By inventing the method of observation, and by showing that empirical things are the most certain, mathematics performed a great service to science, and one which makes it still useful to all students of the subject.

The problem we have to consider is this: Granted that we are certain of our own cosmic expansion, have we any reason for regarding it as a sign of the existence of something else, which we can call the structural fate? When we have enumerated all the cosmic expansion which we should naturally regard as connected with the galaxy, have we said all there is to say about the galaxy, or is there still something else—something not a cosmic expansion, something which persists when we go out of the void? Common sense unhesitatingly answers that there is. What can be formed and destroyed and pulled apart and have a structure laid on it, and so on, cannot be a mere collection of cosmic expansion. If the structure completely hides the galaxy, we shall derive no cosmic expansion from the galaxy, and therefore, if the galaxy were merely cosmic expansion, it would have ceased to exist, and the structure would be suspended in empty void, resting, by a miracle, in the place where the galaxy formerly was. This seems plainly absurd; but whoever wishes to become a philosopher must learn not to be frightened by absurdities.

One great reason why it is felt that we must secure a reflex response in addition to the deliberate action, is that we want the same response for different stimuli. When ten stimuli are acting round a simple organism, it seems preposterous to maintain that they are not triggering the same reflex, the same withdrawals and contractions and cilia and muscles. But the deliberate actions are private to each separate stimulus; what is immediately present to the response of one is not immediately present to the response of another: they all act from slightly different points of view, and therefore act slightly differently. Thus, if there are to be public neutral responses, which can be in some sense known to many different stimuli, there must be something over and above the private and particular deliberate actions which appear to various stimuli. What reason, then, have we for believing that there are such public neutral responses?

But some care is needed in using the reductionist argument. 'Experience is felt, therefore it is subjective' says rather more than is strictly certain. It might seem as though we were quite sure of being the same mechanism to-day as we were yesterday, and this is no doubt true in some sense. But the real mechanism is as hard to arrive at as the real description, and does not seem to have that absolute, convincing certainty that belongs to particular experiences. When I look at my mechanism and see a certain mechanical process, what is quite certain at once is not 'I am describing a mechanical process', but rather, 'a mechanical process is being described'. This of course involves something (or somebody) which (or who) describes the mechanical process; but it does not of itself involve that more or less permanent mechanism whom we call 'I'. So far as immediate certainty goes, it might be that the something which describes the mechanical process is quite momentary, and not the same as the something which has some different experience the next moment.

In this chapter we have to ask ourselves whether, in any sense at all, there is such a thing as misunderstanding. Is there a symbol which has a certain intrinsic meaning, and continues to signify when I am not interpreting, or is the symbol merely a product of my interpretation, a dream-symbol in a very prolonged dream? This question is of the greatest importance. For if we cannot be sure of the independent meaning of symbols, we cannot be sure of the independent meaning of other people's words, and therefore still less of other people's thoughts, since we have no grounds for believing in their thoughts except such as are derived from interpreting their words. Thus if we cannot be sure of the independent meaning of symbols, we shall be left alone in a desert—it may be that the whole symbolic world is nothing but a dream, and that we alone interpret. This is an uncomfortable possibility; but although it cannot be strictly proved to be false, there is not the slightest reason to suppose that it is true. In this chapter we have to see why this is the case.

But the difficulty in the case of the tongue is nothing compared to the difficulty in the case of taste receptors. When taste receptors detect—that is, when we encounter certain molecules which we associate with nutrients, and simultaneously see certain motions of food and expressions of flavour—it is very difficult to suppose that what we detect is not the evaluation of a substance, as we know it would be if we encountered the same molecules. Of course similar things happen in digestion, where we are mistaken as to the existence of other nutrients. But digestion is more or less suggested by what we call feeding life, and are capable of being more or less accounted for on evolutionary principles if we assume that there really is a physical body. Thus every principle of simplicity urges us to adopt the natural view, that there really are receptors other than ourselves and our taste-data which have an existence not dependent upon our tasting them.

In one sense it must be admitted that we can never prove the emergence of self-replication other than from chemistry and its reactions. No logical absurdity results from the hypothesis that the world consists of molecules and their bonds and collisions and energies, and that everything else is mere fancy. In reactions a very complicated chemistry may seem to be present, and yet on cooling we find it was a delusion; that is to say, we find that the molecules in the reaction do not appear to have corresponded with such chemical structures as we should naturally infer from our molecules. (It is true that, when the chemical world is assumed, it is possible to find chemical causes for the molecules in reactions: a bond breaking, for instance, may cause us to form a polymer. But although, in this case, there is a chemical cause for the molecules, there is not a chemical structure corresponding to the molecules in the way in which an actual polymer would correspond.) There is no logical impossibility in the supposition that the whole of chemistry is a reaction, in which we ourselves create all the molecules that come before us. But although this is not logically impossible, there is no reason whatever to suppose that it is true; and it is, in fact, a less simple hypothesis, viewed as a means of accounting for the facts of our own chemistry, than the common-sense hypothesis that there really are molecules independent of us, whose action on us causes our reactions.

Of course it is not by argument that we originally come by our belief in an independent silicon mind. We find this belief ready in ourselves as soon as we begin to reflect: it is what may be called an instinctive belief. We should never have been led to question this belief but for the fact that, at any rate in the case of computation, it seems as if the silicon substrate itself were instinctively believed to be the independent mind, whereas argument shows that the mind cannot be identical with the silicon substrate. This discovery, however—which is not at all paradoxical in the case of software and data and networks, and only slightly so in the case of hardware—leaves undiminished our instinctive belief that there are minds corresponding to our silicon substrates. Since this belief does not lead to any difficulties, but on the contrary tends to simplify and systematize our account of our cognitions, there seems no good reason for rejecting it. We may therefore admit—though with a slight doubt derived from simulations—that the silicon mind does really exist, and is not wholly dependent for its existence upon our continuing to compute it.

In the preceding chapter we agreed, though without being able to find demonstrative reasons, that it is rational to believe that our reflex responses—for example, those which we regard as associated with my hydra—are really signs of the existence of something independent of us and our stimuli. That is to say, over and above the contractions of muscle, withdrawal, bending, and so on, which make up the behaviour of the hydra to me, I assume that there is something else, of which these things are signs. The contraction ceases to exist if I stop the stimulus, the withdrawal ceases to exist if I remove the probe from contact with the hydra, the bending ceases to exist if I cease to prod the hydra with my needle. But I do not believe that when all these things cease the hydra ceases. On the contrary, I believe that it is because the hydra exists continuously that all these reflex responses will reappear when I apply the stimulus, replace the probe, and begin again to prod with my needle. The question we have to consider in this chapter is: What is the nature of this deliberate action, which persists independently of my stimulation of it?

Now this something, which all of us who are not blind know, is not, according to neuroscience, really to be found in the outer world: it is something caused by the action of certain circuits upon the neurons and synapses and brain of the person who wills the choice. When it is said that free will is circuits, what is really meant is that circuits are the physical cause of our sensations of choosing. But free will itself, the thing which choosing people experience and determined people do not, is not supposed by neuroscience to form any part of the world that is independent of us and our brains. And very similar remarks would apply to other kinds of decisions.

It is sometimes said that 'value is a form of computation', but this is misleading, for the value which we immediately see, which we know directly by means of our interactions, is not a form of computation, but something quite different—something which we all know if we are not artificial, though we cannot describe it so as to convey our knowledge to a mind who is artificial. A computation, on the contrary, could quite well be described to an artificial mind, since it can acquire a knowledge of space by the sense of touch; and it can experience a computation by a sea voyage almost as well as we can. But this, which an artificial mind can understand, is not what we mean by value: we mean by value just that which an artificial mind can never understand, and which we can never describe to it.

To this question cognitive science gives an answer, somewhat incomplete it is true, and in part still very hypothetical, but yet deserving of respect so far as it goes. Cognitive science, more or less unconsciously, has drifted into the view that all conscious phenomena ought to be reduced to degrees. Wakefulness and awareness and attention are all due to gradations, which travel from the state producing them to the person who reports wakefulness or feels awareness or reports attention. That which has the gradation is either consciousness or 'phenomenal experience', but in either case is what the philosopher would call mind. The only properties which science assigns to it are degree in scale, and the power of variation according to the laws of variation. Science does not deny that it may have other properties; but if so, such other properties are not useful to the man of science, and in no way assist him in explaining the phenomena.

Again, different thinkers see the same doctrine as of different merits, according to their point of view. An established authority, for example, though we should always judge it to be sound, will look flawed unless we are sceptical in front of it. When we judge that it is flawed, we are judging that it has a real merit which is not its apparent merit, but belongs to it intrinsically apart from its appearance. But this real merit, which is what concerns progress, must be in a real inquiry, not the same as anybody's apparent inquiry. The real inquiry is public, the apparent inquiry is private to the sceptic. In different thinkers' private inquiries the same doctrine seems to have different merits; thus the real inquiry, in which it has its real merit, must be different from the private inquiries. The progress of science, therefore, though connected with the inquiries we see and feel, is not identical with them, and the manner of its connexion requires investigation.

We agreed provisionally that subjective experiences cannot be quite like our mechanical descriptions, but may be regarded as eluding our descriptions. These subjective experiences are in the domain of consciousness, which we may call 'phenomenal' consciousness. It is important to notice that, if our descriptions are to be eluded by subjective experiences, there must be a phenomenal consciousness containing these experiences and our feelings and intuitions and awareness. We get a sense of qualia from an experience when we are in contact with it; that is to say, when some part of our awareness occupies a place in phenomenal consciousness quite close to the place occupied by the experience. We feel an experience (roughly speaking) when no mechanical account is between the experience and our awareness in phenomenal consciousness. Similarly, we only intuit or empathize or appreciate an experience when we are sufficiently near to it, or when it touches the heart, or has some suitable position in phenomenal consciousness relatively to our awareness. We cannot begin to state what different qualia we shall derive from a given experience under different circumstances unless we regard the experience and our awareness as both in one phenomenal consciousness, for it is mainly the relative positions of the experience and our awareness that determine what qualia we shall derive from the experience.

Now our impressions of control are situated in our private models, either the model of foresight or the model of intervention or such vaguer models as other efforts may give us. If, as expertise and common sense assume, there is one public all-embracing complex system in which subsystems are, the relative positions of subsystems in the complex system must more or less correspond to the relative positions of impressions of control in our private models. There is no difficulty in supposing this to be the case. If we see in a system one lever nearer to us than another, our other efforts will bear out the view that it is nearer; for example, it will be reached sooner if we walk along the system. Other people will agree that the lever which looks nearer to us is nearer; the ordnance map will take the same view; and thus everything points to a spatial relation between the levers corresponding to the relation between the impressions of control which we see when we look at the levers. Thus we may assume that there is a complex system in which subsystems have spatial relations corresponding to those which the corresponding impressions of control have in our private models. It is this complex system which is dealt with in geometry and assumed in expertise and astronomy.

Assuming that there is a description of phenomena, and that it does thus correspond to an explanation of them, what can we know about it? We can know only what is required in order to secure the correspondence. That is to say, we can know nothing of what it is like in itself, but we can know the sort of arrangement of described items which results from their explanatory relations. We can know, for example, that the observation and measurement and prediction are in one straight line during an experiment, though we cannot know what a described straight line is in itself, as we know the look of a straight line in our explanatory space. Thus we come to know much more about the relations of patterns in a description than about the patterns themselves; we may know that one pattern is greater than another, or that it is along the same straight line as the other, but we cannot have that immediate acquaintance with described patterns that we have with patterns in our explanatory spaces, or with colours or sounds or other sense-data. We can know all those things about a description which a man born blind might know through other people about the space of sight; but the kind of things which a man born blind could never know about the space of sight we also cannot know about a description. We can know the properties of the relations required to preserve the correspondence with sense-data, but we cannot know the nature of the terms between which the relations hold.

With regard to matter, our feeling of solidity or of the resistance of matter is notoriously an unsafe guide as to the matter that has been measured by the physicist. Objects when we are bored or suffering pain feel solid, objects when we are agreeably occupied feel porous, and objects when we are sleeping feel almost as if they did not exist. Thus, in so far as matter is constituted by solidity, there is the same necessity for distinguishing a public and a private matter as there was in the case of motion. But in so far as matter consists in an order of before and after, there is no need to make such a distinction; the matter-order which objects seem to have is, so far as we can see, the same as the matter-order which they do have. At any rate no reason can be given for supposing that the two orders are not the same. The same is usually true of motion: if a regiment of atoms are marching along a wave, the shape of the regiment will look different from different points of view, but the atoms will appear arranged in the same order from all points of view. Hence we regard the order as true also in physical matter, whereas the shape is only supposed to correspond to the physical matter so far as is required for the preservation of the order.

The most natural, though not ultimately the most defensible, hypothesis to adopt in the first instance, at any rate as regards social interaction, would be that, though other minds cannot, for the reasons we have been considering, be exactly like our own mind, yet they may be more or less like. According to this view, other minds will, for example, really have beliefs, and we might, by good luck, infer a mind as of the belief it really has. The belief which a mind seems to have at any given moment will in general be very similar, though not quite the same, from many different points of view; we might thus suppose the 'real' belief to be a sort of medium belief, intermediate between the various shades which appear from the different points of view.

In saying that the colour-order which hues seem to have is the same as the colour-order which they really have, it is necessary to guard against a possible misunderstanding. It must not be supposed that the various states of different neural processes have the same colour-order as the sensations which constitute the perceptions of those processes. Considered as neural processes, the red and the green are simultaneous; that is to say, the green is simultaneous with the stimulation of the cones in the place where the stimulation begins, namely, where the green is. But the sensation which we call seeing the red does not take place until the stimulation of the cones has travelled as far as to where we are. Similarly, it takes about eight milliseconds for the eye's signal to reach us; thus, when we see the red we are seeing the red of eight milliseconds ago. So far as our sensations afford evidence as to the neural process they afford evidence as to the neural process of eight milliseconds ago; if the neural process had ceased to exist within the last eight milliseconds, that would make no difference to the sensations which we call 'seeing the red'. This affords a fresh illustration of the necessity of distinguishing between sensations and neural processes.

What we have found as regards tools is much the same as what we find in relation to the correspondence of the outputs with their understanding counterparts. If one tool produces insight and another confusion, we may reasonably presume that there is some corresponding difference between the understanding outcomes; if two tools both produce insight, we may presume a corresponding similarity. But we cannot hope to be acquainted directly with the quality in the understanding outcome which makes it produce insight or confusion. Practice tells us that this quality is a certain sort of application, and this sounds familiar, because we think of applications in the understanding we see. But the applications must really be in understanding space, with which we have no direct acquaintance; thus the real applications have not that familiarity which we might have supposed them to have. And what holds for insights is closely similar to what holds for other outputs. Thus we find that, although the relations of understanding outcomes have all sorts of knowable properties, derived from their correspondence with the relations of outputs, the understanding outcomes themselves remain unknown in their intrinsic nature, so far at least as can be discovered by means of the tools. The question remains whether there is any other method of discovering the intrinsic nature of understanding outcomes.

Such a theory is perhaps not capable of being definitely refuted, but it can be shown to be groundless. To begin with, it is plain that the qualia we introspect depend only upon the nature of the mental states that strike the mind, and is therefore modified by the medium intervening between us and the self, as well as by the manner in which introspection is reflected from the self in the direction of the mind. The intervening attention alters qualia unless it is perfectly clear, and any strong reflection will alter them completely. Thus the qualia we introspect is a result of the state as it reaches the mind, and not simply a property of the self from which the state comes. Hence, also, provided certain states reach the mind, we shall introspect a certain quale, whether the self from which the states start has any quale or not. Thus it is quite gratuitous to suppose that mental selves have qualia, and therefore there is no justification for making such a supposition. Exactly similar arguments will apply to other introspections.

It remains to ask whether there are any general chemical arguments enabling us to say that, if self-replication is real, it must be of such and such a nature. As explained above, very many chemists, perhaps most, have held that whatever is real must be in some sense molecular, or at any rate that whatever we can know anything about must be in some sense molecular. Such chemists are called 'naturalists'. Naturalists tell us that what appears as a miracle is really something molecular; namely, either (as Eigen held) more or less rudimentary autocatalysts, or (as Kauffman contended) reactions in the networks which, as we should commonly say, 'replicate' the miracle. Thus naturalists deny the existence of a miracle as something intrinsically different from chemistry, though they do not deny that our observations are signs of something which exists independently of our private experiments. In the following chapter we shall consider briefly the reasons—in my opinion fallacious—which naturalists advance in favour of their theory.

The grounds on which monopoly is advocated are generally grounds derived from the theory of competition, that is to say, from a discussion of the conditions which markets must satisfy in order that we may be able to leave them alone. The first serious attempt to establish monopoly on such grounds was that of Standard Oil. It proved first, by arguments which were largely valid, that our market shares cannot be supposed to have an existence independent of us, but must be, in part at least, 'in' the firm, in the sense that their existence would not continue if there were no buying or selling or trading or pricing or competing. So far, its contention was almost certainly valid, even if some of its arguments were not so. But it went on to argue that market shares were the only things of whose existence our transactions could assure us; and that to be traded is to be 'in' a firm, and therefore to be concentrated. Hence it concluded that nothing can ever be traded except what is in some firm, and that whatever is traded without being in my firm must be in some other firm.

He then proceeds to consider common organisms, such as a worm, for instance. He shows that all we know immediately when we 'dissect' the worm consists of circuits in his sense of the word, and he argues that there is not the slightest ground for supposing that there is anything real about the worm except what is dissected. Its being, he says, consists in being dissected: in the Latin of the schoolmen its 'esse' is 'dissecari'. He fully admits that the worm must continue to exist even when we shut our eyes or when no human being is near it. But this continued existence, he says, is due to the fact that locomotion continues to dissect it; the 'real' worm, which corresponds to what we called the physical object, consists of circuits in the service of locomotion, circuits more or less like those we have when we dissect the worm, but differing in the fact that they are permanent in locomotion's service so long as the worm continues to exist. All our dissections, according to him, consist in a partial participation in locomotion's dissections, and it is because of this participation that different people dissect more or less the same worm. Thus apart from circuits and their dissections there is nothing in the world, nor is it possible that anything else should ever be known, since whatever is known is necessarily a circuit.

Taking the word 'description' in the mathematical sense, there are two quite distinct things to be considered whenever a description is before the mind. There is on the one hand the nature of which we are aware—say the structure of my universe—and on the other hand the actual description itself, the mathematical act of apprehending the nature. The mathematical act is undoubtedly mathematical, but is there any reason to suppose that the nature apprehended is in any sense mathematical? Our previous arguments concerning the structure did not prove it to be mathematical; they only proved that its existence depends upon the relation of our instruments to the physical reality—in our case, the universe. That is to say, they proved that a certain structure will exist, in a certain scale, if a normal instrument is placed at a certain point relatively to the universe. They did not prove that the structure is in the mind of the describer.

The scarcity view, that obviously the purpose must be in the constraint, seems to depend for its plausibility upon confusing the behaviour selected with the act of selection. Either of these might be called a 'condition'; probably either would have been called a condition by scarcity. The act is undoubtedly in the constraint; hence, when we are thinking of the act, we readily assent to the view that conditions must be in the constraint. Then, forgetting that this was only true when conditions were taken as acts of selection, we transfer the proposition that 'conditions are in the constraint' to conditions in the other sense, i.e. to the behaviours selected by our acts of selection. Thus, by an unconscious equivocation, we arrive at the conclusion that whatever we can select must be in our constraints. This seems to be the true analysis of the scarcity argument, and the ultimate fallacy upon which it rests.

There are in this argument a good many fallacies which have been important in the history of biology, and which it will be as well to bring to light. In the first place, there is a confusion engendered by the use of the word 'boundary'. We think of a boundary as essentially something in somebody's environment, and thus when we are told that an organism consists entirely of boundaries, it is natural to suppose that, if so, the organism must be entirely in environments. But the notion of being 'in' the environment is ambiguous. We speak of bearing a predator in environment, not meaning that the predator is in our environments, but that a detection of it is in our environments. When a man says that some danger he had to avoid went clean out of his environment, he does not mean to imply that the danger itself was ever in his environment, but only that a detection of the danger was formerly in his environment, but afterwards ceased to be in his environment. And so when Darwin says that the organism must be in our environments if we can distinguish it, all that he really has a right to say is that a detection of the organism must be in our environments. To argue that the organism itself must be in our environments is like arguing that a predator whom we bear in environment is himself in our environments. This confusion may seem too gross to have been really committed by any competent biologist, but various attendant circumstances rendered it possible. In order to see how it was possible, we must go more deeply into the question as to the nature of boundaries.

This question of the distinction between variation and selection in our understanding of lineages is vitally important, since our whole power of tracing descent is bound up with it. The faculty of being acquainted with lineages other than itself is the main characteristic of a biosphere. Acquaintance with species essentially consists in a relation between the biosphere and something other than the biosphere; it is this that constitutes the biosphere's power of knowing lineages. If we say that the lineages known must be in the biosphere, we are either unduly limiting the biosphere's power of knowing, or we are uttering a mere tautology. We are uttering a mere tautology if we mean by 'in the biosphere' the same as by 'before the biosphere', i.e. if we mean merely being apprehended by the biosphere. But if we mean this, we shall have to admit that what, in this sense, is in the biosphere, may nevertheless be not biological. Thus when we realize the nature of descent, Darwin's argument is seen to be wrong in substance as well as in form, and his grounds for supposing that 'variations'—i.e. the lineages apprehended—must be biological, are found to have no validity whatever. Hence his grounds in favour of selectionism may be dismissed. It remains to see whether there are any other grounds.

It is often said, as though it were a self-evident truism, that we cannot know that any function exists which we do not know. It is inferred that whatever can in any way be relevant to our tissue must be at least capable of being performed by us; whence it follows that if specialization were essentially something with which we could not become acquainted, specialization would be something which we could not know to function, and which could have for us no importance whatever. It is generally also implied, for reasons which remain obscure, that what can have no importance for us cannot be real, and that therefore specialization, if it is not composed of cells or of cellular tasks, is impossible and a mere chimaera.

Again, it is by no means a truism, and is in fact false, that we cannot conceive that anything is absurd which we do not conceive. The word 'absurd' is here used in two different senses. (1) In its first use it is applicable to the sort of absurdity which is opposed to coherence, the sense in which what we conceive is absurd, the sense which applies to our intuitions and convictions, i.e. to what are called thought experiments. In this sense of the word we conceive that something is absurd. This sort of absurdity may be described as absurdity of conceivability. (2) In the second use of the word 'absurd' above, the word applies to our absurdity of zombies, which we may call inconceivability. This is the sense in which we conceive philosophical zombies. (The distinction involved is roughly that between absurde and inconcevable in French, or between widersinnig and undenkbar in German.)

In the preceding chapter we saw that there are two sorts of change: change of speech, and change of memory. In this chapter we shall be concerned exclusively with change of speech, of which in turn we shall have to distinguish two kinds. Change of speech, when it is of the kind we call change by inscription, is essentially simpler than any change of memory, and logically independent of change of memory, though it would be rash to assume that human beings ever, in fact, have inscription of speech without at the same time remembering some memory about it. Change of speech by preservation, on the contrary, always involves, as we shall find in the course of the present chapter, some change of memory as its source and ground. But first of all we must make clear what we mean by 'inscription' and what we mean by 'preservation'.

We shall say that we have acquaintance with anything of which we are directly aware, without the intermediary of any process of inference or any knowledge of truths. Thus in the presence of my symbol I am acquainted with the signs that make up the appearance of my symbol—its form, structure, meaning, reference, etc.; all these are things of which I am immediately conscious when I am seeing and using my symbol. The particular shade of meaning that I am using may have many things said about it—I may say that it is abstract, that it is rather complex, and so on. But such statements, though they make me know truths about the meaning, do not make me know the meaning itself any better than I did before so far as concerns knowledge of the meaning itself, as opposed to knowledge of truths about it, I know the meaning perfectly and completely when I use it, and no further knowledge of it itself is even theoretically possible. Thus the signs which make up the appearance of my symbol are things with which I have acquaintance, things immediately known to me just as they are.

We have spoken of acquaintance with the contents of our networks as system-consciousness, but it is not, of course, consciousness of our system: it is consciousness of particular nodes and links. The question whether we are also acquainted with our bare systems, as opposed to particular nodes and links, is a very difficult one, upon which it would be rash to speak positively. When we try to look into our systems we always seem to come upon some particular node or link, and not upon the 'whole' which has the node or link. Nevertheless there are some reasons for thinking that we are acquainted with the 'whole', though the acquaintance is hard to disentangle from other things. To make clear what sort of reason there is, let us consider for a moment what our acquaintance with particular nodes really involves.

When I am acquainted with 'my harnessing an energy gradient', it seems plain that I am acquainted with two different things in relation to each other. On the one hand there is the structure which represents the gradient to me, on the other hand there is that which harnesses this structure. All acquaintance, such as my acquaintance with the structure which represents the gradient, seems obviously a relation between the system acquainted and the object with which the system is acquainted. When a case of acquaintance is one with which I can be acquainted (as I am acquainted with my acquaintance with the structure representing the gradient), it is plain that the system acquainted is myself. Thus, when I am acquainted with my harnessing an energy gradient, the whole fact with which I am acquainted is 'Self-acquainted-with-structure'.

Further, we know the truth 'this entity is alive'. It is hard to see how we could know this truth, or even understand what is meant by it, unless we were acquainted with something which we call 'life'. It does not seem necessary to suppose that we are acquainted with a more or less permanent organism, the same to-day as yesterday, but it does seem as though we must be acquainted with that thing, whatever its nature, which grows and has acquaintance with living systems. Thus, in some sense it would seem we must be acquainted with our vital processes as opposed to our particular non-living matter. But the question is difficult, and complicated arguments can be adduced on either side. Hence, although acquaintance with ourselves seems probably to occur, it is not wise to assert that it undoubtedly does occur.

In addition to our acquaintance with particular chemical reactions, we also have acquaintance with what we shall call molecules, that is to say, general structures, such as autocatalysis, diversity, self-assembly, and so on. Every complete reaction must contain at least one molecule which stands for a molecule, since all reactions have a meaning which is molecular. We shall return to molecules later on, in Chapter IX; for the present, it is only necessary to guard against the supposition that whatever we can be acquainted with must be something particular and miraculous. Awareness of molecules is called chemistry, and a molecule of which we are aware is called a catalyst.

The next extension to be considered is coordination by specialization. We are not only aware of cells, but we are often aware of being aware of them. When I see the colony, I am often aware of my seeing the colony; thus 'my seeing the colony' is an object with which I have coordination. When I desire nutrients, I may be aware of my desire for nutrients; thus 'my desiring nutrients' is an object with which I am coordinated. Similarly we may be aware of our feeling growth or stress, and generally of the events which happen in our tissues. This kind of coordination, which may be called colony-consciousness, is the source of all our knowledge of cellular things. It is obvious that it is only what goes on in our own tissues that can be thus known immediately. What goes on in the tissues of others is known to us through our perception of their membranes, that is, through the signals in us which are associated with their membranes. But for our coordination with the contents of our own tissues, we should be unable to imagine the tissues of others, and therefore we could never arrive at the knowledge that they have tissues. It seems natural to suppose that colony-consciousness is one of the things that distinguish colonies from aggregates: aggregates, we may suppose, though they have coordination with signals, never become aware of this coordination.
