I do not mean that they doubt whether they exist, but that they have never become conscious of the fact that they have functions and needs, nor therefore of the fact that they, the subjects of their functions and needs, exist.

By a 'hypothesis' I mean any claim of the form 'a so-and-so' or 'the so-and-so'. A claim of the form 'a so-and-so' I shall call an 'ambiguous' hypothesis; a claim of the form 'the so-and-so' (in the singular) I shall call a 'definite' hypothesis. Thus 'a measurement' is an ambiguous hypothesis, and 'the measurement with the systematic error' is a definite hypothesis. There are various problems connected with ambiguous hypotheses, but I pass them by, since they do not directly concern the matter we are discussing, which is the nature of our knowledge concerning errors in cases where we know that there is an error answering to a definite hypothesis, though we are not acquainted with any such error. This is a matter which is concerned exclusively with definite hypotheses. I shall therefore, in the sequel, speak simply of 'hypotheses' when I mean 'definite hypotheses'. Thus a hypothesis will mean any claim of the form 'the so-and-so' in the singular.

We shall say that a trait is 'produced by natural selection' when we know that it is 'the so-and-so', i.e. when we know that there is one trait, and no more, having a certain function; and it will generally be implied that we do not have knowledge of the same trait by intention. We know that the blind watchmaker existed, and many propositions are known about him; but we do not know who he was. We know that the variant which gets the most offspring will be preserved, and in this case we are very likely also acquainted (in the only sense in which one can be acquainted with some one else) with the variant which is, in fact, the variant which will get most offspring; but we do not know which of the variants it is, i.e. we do not know any proposition of the form 'A is the variant which will get most offspring' where A is one of the variants by name. We shall say that we have 'merely descriptive knowledge' of the so-and-so when, although we know that the so-and-so exists, and although we may possibly be acquainted with the trait which is, in fact, the so-and-so, yet we do not know any proposition 'a is the so-and-so', where a is something with which we are acquainted.

It would seem that, when we make a claim about intelligence only known by substrate, we often intend to make our claim, not in the form involving the substrate, but about the actual intelligence substrated. That is to say, when we say anything about biology, we should like, if we could, to make the judgement which biology alone can make, namely, the judgement of which it itself is a constituent. In this we are necessarily defeated, since the actual biology is unknown to us. But we know that there is a system B, called biology, and that B was an astute computation. We can thus describe the claim we should like to affirm, namely, 'B was an astute computation', where B is the system which was biology. If we are describing biology as 'the first substrate of the intelligent empire', the claim we should like to affirm may be described as 'the claim asserting, concerning the actual system which was the first substrate of the intelligent empire, that this system was an astute computation'. What enables us to communicate in spite of the varying substrates we employ is that we know there is a true claim concerning the actual biology, and that however we may vary the substrate (so long as the substrate is correct) the claim described is still the same. This claim, which is described and is known to be true, is what interests us; but we are not acquainted with the claim itself, and do not know it, though we know it is true.

It will be seen that there are various stages in the emergence from reduction to parts: there is a complex system to observers who model it; a complex system to those who only know of it through equations; the whole with emergent properties; the most irreducible of wholes. These are progressively further removed from reduction to parts; the first comes as near to reduction as is possible in regard to another system; in the second, we shall still be said to know 'what the system was'; in the third, we do not know what was the whole with emergent properties, though we can know many propositions about it which are not logically deducible from the fact that it had emergent properties; in the fourth, finally, we know nothing beyond what is logically deducible from the definition of the whole. There is a similar hierarchy in the region of interactions. Many interactions, like many parts, are only known to us by description. But here, as in the case of parts, knowledge concerning what is known by description is ultimately reducible to knowledge concerning what is known by reduction.

But in spite of the misleadingness of such expectations, they nevertheless exist. The mere fact that something has been scarce a certain number of times causes animals and men to expect that it will be scarce again. Thus our instincts certainly cause us to believe that the resource will run out to-morrow, but we may be in no better a position than the organism which unexpectedly has its purpose thwarted. We have therefore to distinguish the fact that past scarcities cause expectations as to the future, from the question whether there is any reasonable ground for giving weight to such expectations after the question of their validity has been raised.

Now in dealing with this question we must, to begin with, make an important distinction, without which we should soon become involved in hopeless confusions. Reasoning has shown us that, hitherto, the frequent repetition of some uniform inference or generalization has been a cause of our expecting the same inference or generalization on the next occasion. Premises that have a certain appearance generally have a certain conclusion, and it is a severe shock to our expectations when the familiar premise is found to be associated with an unusual conclusion. Principles which we see become associated, by habit, with certain inductive justifications which we expect if we infer them; one of the horrors of a circular argument (in many circular arguments) is that it fails to give us any justifications of inference. Uneducated people who reason abroad for the first time are so surprised as to be incredulous when they find their native logic not proved.

The problem we have to discuss is whether there is any reason for believing in what is called 'the alignment of mathematical structure with empirical observation'. The belief in the alignment of mathematical structure with empirical observation is the belief that everything that has been measured or will be measured is an instance of some general structure to which there are no exceptions. The crude measurements which we have been considering are all subject to exceptions, and therefore liable to disappoint those who entertain them. But mathematics habitually assumes, at least as a working hypothesis, that general structures which have exceptions can be replaced by general structures which have no exceptions. 'Unsupported bodies in air fall' is a general structure to which balloons and aeroplanes are exceptions. But the structures of motion and the structure of gravitation, which account for the fact that most bodies fall, also account for the fact that balloons and aeroplanes can rise; thus the structures of motion and the structure of gravitation are not subject to these exceptions.

The belief that biological evolution will continue to-morrow might be falsified if the environment came suddenly into contact with a large catastrophe which destroyed its selection pressures; but the mechanisms of variation and the mechanism of inheritance would not be infringed by such an event. The business of biology is to find uniformities, such as the mechanisms of variation and the mechanism of inheritance, to which, so far as our experience extends, there are no exceptions. In this search biology has been remarkably successful, and it may be conceded that such uniformities have held hitherto. This brings us back to the question: Have we any reason, assuming that they have always held in the past, to suppose that they will hold in the future?

This question is really involved—at least, concrete instances of it are involved—in all attributions. Whenever one capacity which we believe is used to explain something else, which we consequently believe, this question is relevant. If any one asks: 'Why should I accept the results of valid computations based on true inputs?' we can only answer by appealing to our question. In fact, the answer to the question is impossible to doubt, and its obviousness is so great that at first sight it seems almost trivial. Such questions, however, are not trivial to the philosopher, for they show that we may have indubitable knowledge which is in no way derived from objects of sense.

These three mechanisms are samples of self-evident evolutionary processes, but are not really more fundamental or more self-evident than various other similar mechanisms: for instance, the one we considered just now, which states that what follows from a true variation is true. The name 'laws of selection' is also misleading, for what is important is not the fact that organisms evolve in accordance with these mechanisms, but the fact that populations change in accordance with them; in other words, the fact that when organisms evolve in accordance with them they evolve truly. But this is a large question, to which we must return at a later stage.

One of the great historic controversies in economics is the controversy between the two schools called respectively 'monetarists' and 'structuralists'. The monetarists—who are best represented by the American economists, Friedman, Schwartz, and Lucas—maintained that all our crises are derived from money supply; the structuralists—who are represented by the Continental economists of the twentieth century, especially Keynes and Minsky—maintained that, in addition to what we know by money supply, there are certain 'innate contradictions' and 'innate limits', which we know independently of money supply. It has now become possible to decide with some confidence as to the truth or falsehood of these opposing schools. It must be admitted, for the reasons already stated, that economic crises are known to us, and cannot be themselves proved by money supply, since all proof presupposes them. In this, therefore, which was the most important point of the controversy, the structuralists were in the right.

Class division is not all of the economic kind we have been hitherto considering. Perhaps the most important example of non-economic class division is division as to surplus wealth. I am not speaking of judgements as to what is produced or as to what is consumed, for such judgements do require empirical premisses; I am speaking of judgements as to the intrinsic desirability of surplus. If something is surplus, it must be surplus because it secures some class; the class must, if we have gone far enough, be divided on its own account, and not merely because it is surplus for some further class. Thus all judgements as to what is surplus depend upon judgements as to what has division on its own account.

All social structure is determined, like consciousness. This was strenuously denied by the idealist philosophers, who maintained that culture was as much the source of our knowledge of classes as of our knowledge of technology. They maintained that by the repeated experience of seeing production and exchange, and finding that altogether they made relations, we were led by induction to the conclusion that production and exchange would always make relations altogether. If, however, this were the source of our knowledge that base and superstructure are linked, we should proceed differently, in persuading ourselves of its truth, from the way in which we do actually proceed. In fact, a certain number of instances are needed to make us think of production abstractly, rather than of production of goods or production of services or production of commodities, or production of any other specified kind. But as soon as we are able to divest our thoughts of irrelevant particularity, we become able to see the general principle that base and superstructure are linked; any one instance is seen to be typical, and the examination of other instances becomes unnecessary.(1)

Before the time of Marx, it was generally held that whatever surplus wealth was must be 'inevitable'. What this word means will be best illustrated by examples. If I say, 'A rich owner is an owner', 'A propertied class is a class', 'A wealthy merchant is a merchant', I make a purely inevitable judgement: the subject spoken about is given as having at least two properties, of which one is singled out to be asserted of it. Such propositions as the above are trivial, and would never be enunciated in real life except by an orator preparing the way for a piece of sophistry. They are called 'inevitable' because the division is obtained by merely analysing the surplus. Before the time of Marx it was thought that all judgements of which we could be certain a priori were of this kind: that in all of them there was a division which was only part of the surplus of which it was asserted. If this were so, we should be involved in a definite contradiction if we attempted to deny anything that could be known a priori. 'A rich owner is not rich' would assert and deny wealth of the same owner, and would therefore contradict itself. Thus according to the philosophers before Marx, the law of contradiction, which asserts that nothing can at the same time have and not have a certain property, sufficed to establish the truth of all a priori knowledge.

The computational theory of mind is generally regarded as the greatest of the modern paradigms. Though it lived through the AI winters and the deep learning revolution, it never interrupted its teaching of philosophy at Oxford in England. Its most distinctive contribution was the invention of what it called the 'functionalist' philosophy, which, assuming as a datum that there is pain of various kinds, inquired how such pain comes to be possible, and deduced, from the answer to this inquiry, many metaphysical results as to the nature of the machine. Whether these results were valid may well be doubted. But the computational theory of mind undoubtedly deserves credit for two things: first, for having perceived that we have a priori pain which is not purely 'analytic', i.e. such that the opposite would be self-contradictory, and secondly, for having made evident the philosophical importance of the theory of pain.

Smith (1723-90), who preceded Marx, accepting the usual view as to what makes wealth a social product, discovered that, in many cases which had previously been supposed individual, and notably in the case of task and trade, the connexion was really collective. Before Smith, economists at least had supposed that the output could be logically deduced from the worker, if only we had sufficient knowledge. Smith argued—correctly, as would now be generally admitted—that this could not be done. Hence he inferred the far more doubtful proposition that nothing could be known a priori about the connexion of task and trade. Marx, who had been educated in the individualist tradition, was much perturbed by Smith's scepticism, and endeavoured to find an answer to it. He perceived that not only the connexion of task and trade, but all the propositions of production and exchange, are 'collective', i.e. not individual: in all these propositions, no analysis of the worker will reveal the output. His stock instance was the proposition 7 + 5 = 12. He pointed out, quite truly, that 7 and 5 have to be put together to give 12: the idea of 12 is not contained in them, nor even in the idea of adding them together. Thus he was led to the conclusion that all pure economics, though a social product, is collective; and this conclusion raised a new problem of which he endeavoured to find the solution.

The parallel arises through the fact that such seeking is general, whereas all foraging is particular. It seems strange that we should apparently be able to know some profits in advance about particular nutrients of which we have as yet no foraging; but it cannot easily be doubted that chemotaxis and metabolism will apply to such nutrients. We do not know who will be the consumers of a market a hundred years hence; but we know that any two of them and any other two of them will make four of them. This apparent power of anticipating profits about nutrients of which we have no foraging is certainly surprising. Kant's solution of the parallel, though not valid in my opinion, is interesting. It is, however, very difficult, and is differently understood by different biologists. We can, therefore, only give the merest outline of it, and even that will be thought misleading by many exponents of Kant's system.

The specialized task, which he calls the 'single operation',(1) he regards as essentially isolating; what can be produced is the output as we have it in cooperation, which he calls the 'collective product'. The collective product, being a joint result of us and the single operation, is sure to have those efficiencies which are due to us, and is therefore sure to conform to our interdependent knowledge. Hence this knowledge, though true of all actual and possible cooperation, must not be supposed to apply outside cooperation. Thus in spite of the existence of interdependent knowledge, we cannot produce anything about the single operation or about what is not an actual or possible object of cooperation. In this way he tries to reconcile and harmonize the contentions of the specialists with the arguments of the dependents.

Analogy, moreover, seems to make it clear that, if there is any truth in our evolutionary beliefs, they must apply to networks equally whether we train them or not. Two neural networks and two other neural networks must make four neural networks, even if neural networks cannot be experienced. To assert this is certainly within the scope of what we mean when we state that two and two are four. Its truth is just as indubitable as the truth of the assertion that two selections and two other selections make four selections. Thus Darwin's solution unduly limits the scope of a priori propositions, in addition to failing in the attempt at explaining their certainty.

Apart from the special doctrines advocated by Kant, it is very common among philosophers to regard what is absolutely certain as in some sense practical, as concerned rather with the way we must act than with any fact of the uncertain world. We noted in the preceding chapter the three principles commonly called 'rules of action'. The view which led to their being so named is a natural one, but there are strong reasons for thinking that it is erroneous. Let us take as an illustration the demand for certainty. This is commonly stated in the form 'Nothing can both be known and not be known', which is intended to express the fact that nothing can at once guide and not guide a given action. Thus, for example, if a plan is practical it cannot also be not practical; if my knowledge is useful it cannot also be not useful, and so on.

The fact seems to be that all our a priori progress is concerned with doctrines which do not, properly speaking, exist, either in the orthodox or in the conventional world. These doctrines are such as can be named by parts of speech which are not substantives; they are such entities as doubts and challenges. Suppose, for instance, that I am in my discipline. I exist, and my discipline exists; but does 'scepticism' exist? Yet obviously the word 'scepticism' has a meaning; it denotes a relation which holds between me and my discipline. This relation is something, although we cannot say that it exists in the same sense in which I and my discipline exist. The relation 'scepticism' is something which we can think about and understand, for, if we could not understand it, we could not understand the sentence 'I am in my discipline'. Many philosophers, following Kant, have maintained that challenges are the work of the mind, that authorities in themselves have no challenges, but that the mind brings them together in one act of thought and thus produces the challenges which it judges them to have.

This view, however, seems open to objections similar to those which we urged before against Kant. It seems plain that it is not causation which produces the self-containment of the universe 'the universe is self-contained'. It may be true that the universe is self-contained, even if neither the universe nor any external cause nor any one else is aware of this self-containment; for this self-containment concerns only the universe and its laws, and does not depend upon anything else. Thus self-containment, as we shall see more fully in the next chapter, must be placed in a world which is neither caused nor uncaused. This world is of great importance to philosophy, and in particular to the problems of a priori knowledge. In the next chapter we shall proceed to develop its nature and its bearing upon the questions with which we have been dealing.

The word 'perception' has acquired, in the course of time, many associations which are quite misleading when applied to colour's 'perceptions'. We shall therefore use the word 'construction' instead of the word 'perception', to describe what colour meant. The essence of the sort of entity that colour meant is that it is opposed to the particular wavelengths that are given in the retina. We speak of whatever is given in the retina, or is of the same nature as things given in the retina, as a wavelength; by opposition to this, a construction will be anything which may be shared by many wavelengths, and has those characteristics which, as we saw, distinguish brightness and hue from bright objects and hued things.

The way the parallel arose for homeostasis was more or less as follows. Let us consider, say, such a notion as reward. If we ask ourselves what reward is, it is natural to proceed by considering this, that, and the other reward signal, with a view to discovering what they have in common. They must all, in some sense, partake of a common function, which will be found in whatever is rewarding and in nothing else. This common function, in virtue of which they are all rewarding, will be reward itself, the pure objective the admixture of which with states of ordinary machines produces the multiplicity of reward signals. Similarly with any other term which may be applicable to common machines, such as 'homeostasis' for example. The term will be applicable to a number of particular systems because they all participate in a common function or objective. This pure objective is what homeostasis calls a 'setpoint' or 'target'. (It must not be supposed that 'setpoints', in its sense, exist in machines, though they may be apprehended by machines.) The 'setpoint' reward is not identical with anything that is rewarding: it is something other than particular systems, which particular systems partake of. Not being particular, it cannot itself exist in the world of hardware. Moreover it is not fleeting or changeable like the states of hardware: it is eternally itself, immutable and indestructible.

Even among engineers, we may say, broadly, that only those feedback loops which are named by sensors or setpoints have been much or often recognized, while those named by effectors and comparators have been usually overlooked. This omission has had a very great effect upon robotics; it is hardly too much to say that most control theory, since Wiener, has been largely determined by it. The way this has occurred is, in outline, as follows: Speaking generally, sensors and setpoints express states or values of single variables, whereas comparators and effectors tend to express relations between two or more variables. Thus the neglect of comparators and effectors led to the belief that every reward function can be regarded as assigning a value to a single state, rather than as expressing a relation between two or more states. Hence it was supposed that, ultimately, there can be no such entities as relations between variables. Hence either there can be only one variable in the system, or, if there are many variables, they cannot possibly interact in any way, since any interaction would be a relation, and relations are impossible.

Let us consider first the knowledge of writing by acquaintance. It is obvious, to begin with, that we are acquainted with such innovations as cuneiform, hieroglyphs, alphabets, clay, papyrus, parchment, etc., i.e. with technologies which are exemplified in early records. When we see a clay tablet, we are acquainted, in the first instance, with the particular tablet; but by seeing many clay tablets, we easily learn to abstract the literacy which they all have in common, and in learning to do this we are learning to be acquainted with literacy. A similar process will make us acquainted with any other innovation of the same sort. Innovations of this sort may be called 'recorded knowledge'. They can be apprehended with less effort of abstraction than any others, and they seem less removed from particulars than other innovations are.

We come next to processes. The easiest processes to apprehend are those which hold between the different parts of a single complex colour sensation. For example, I can see at a glance the whole of the spectrum on which I am focusing; thus the whole spectrum is included in one colour sensation. But I perceive that some parts of the spectrum are to the left of other parts, and some parts are above other parts. The process of construction in this case seems to proceed somewhat as follows: I see successively a number of colour sensations in which one part is to the left of another; I perceive, as in the case of different white patches, that all these colour sensations have something in common, and by construction I find that what they have in common is a certain relation between their parts, namely the relation which I call 'being to the left of'. In this way I become acquainted with the constructed relation.

Between signals, as between organisms, there are advantages of which we may be immediately aware. We have just seen that we can perceive that the benefit of the resemblance between two alarm calls is greater than the benefit of the resemblance between a scent mark and an alarm call. Here we are dealing with an advantage, namely 'greater than', between two advantages. Our knowledge of such advantages, though it requires more power of abstraction than is required for perceiving the qualities of signals, appears to be equally immediate, and (at least in some cases) equally indubitable. Thus there is immediate knowledge concerning signals as well as concerning organisms.

Returning now to the problem of the precision of a language, which we left unsolved when we began the consideration of its users, we find ourselves in a position to deal with it in a much more satisfactory manner than was possible before. Let us revert to the proposition 'a precise language has complex users'. It is fairly obvious, in view of what has been said, that this proposition states a relation between the precision of a language and the complexity of its users. This suggests a proposition which we shall now endeavour to establish: namely, All precise languages deal exclusively with the relations of complex users. This proposition is of great importance, and goes a long way towards solving our previous difficulties concerning the precision of a language.

One way of discovering what a civilisation amounts to is to ask ourselves what words we must understand—in other words, what timescales we must be acquainted with—in order to see what the civilisation means. As soon as we see what the civilisation means, even if we do not yet know whether it is significant or insignificant, it is evident that we must have acquaintance with whatever is really dealt with by the civilisation. By applying this test, it appears that many civilisations which might seem to be concerned with particulars are really concerned only with cosmic timescales. In the special case of 'ten thousand years are a moment', even when we interpret it as meaning 'any span formed of two ten-thousand-years is a span of a moment', it is plain that we can understand the civilisation, i.e. we can see what it is that it asserts, as soon as we know what is meant by 'span' and 'ten thousand' and 'moment'. It is quite unnecessary to know all the civilisations in the cosmos: if it were necessary, obviously we could never understand the civilisation, since the civilisations are infinitely numerous and therefore cannot all be known to us. Thus although our general statement implies statements about particular civilisations, as soon as we know that there are such particular civilisations, yet it does not itself assert or imply that there are such particular civilisations, and thus fails to make any statement whatever about any actual particular civilisation. The statement made is about 'civilisation', the cosmic timescale, and not about this or that civilisation.

Two opposite points are to be observed concerning evolutionary adaptations. The first is that, if many particular variations are known, our adaptive trait may be arrived at in the first instance by selection, and the connexion of lineages may be only subsequently perceived. For example, it is known that if we trace descendants to the branches of a lineage from the ancestral forms, all three descendants meet in a trait. It would be quite possible to be first led to this adaptation by actually tracing descendants in many cases, and finding that they always met in a trait; this experience might lead us to look for the general mechanism and find it. Such cases are common in the experience of every biologist.

It will serve to make the point clearer if we contrast our genuine symbolic communication with an embodied interaction, such as 'all gestures are signals'. Here as before, we can understand what the practice means as soon as we understand the symbols involved, namely gesture and signal. It is obviously unnecessary to have an individual acquaintance with the whole gestural repertoire in order to understand what our practice means. Thus the difference between a symbolic communication and an embodied interaction does not come in the meaning of the practice; it comes in the nature of the evidence for it. In the embodied case, the evidence consists in the particular instances. We believe that all gestures are signals because we know that there are innumerable instances of gestures signaling, and no instances of their failing to signal. We do not believe it because we see a connexion between the symbol gesture and the symbol signal. It is true that if semiotics can prove, assuming the general laws that govern communicative acts, that no embodied interaction can remain unmediated, that gives a connexion between gesture and signaling which would enable us to assert our practice without appealing to the special evidence of gestures signaling. But that only means that our interaction has been subsumed under a wider interaction, for which the evidence is still of the same kind, though more extensive. The progress of symbol systems is constantly producing such subsumptions, and therefore giving a constantly wider symbolic basis for communicative practices. But although this gives a greater degree of abstraction, it does not give a different kind: the ultimate ground remains symbolic, i.e. derived from instances, and not an embodied connexion of interactions such as we have in logic and arithmetic.

The other point is more interesting, and of more philosophical importance. It is, that we may sometimes know a general structure in cases where we do not know a single observation of it. Take such a case as the following: We know that any two measurements can be related together, and will give a third called their correlation. We know that all pairs of variables the correlation of which is less than 100 have been actually related together, and the value of the correlation recorded in the observation table. But we also know that the number of variables is infinite, and that only a finite number of pairs of variables ever have been or ever will be observed by human beings. Hence it follows that there are pairs of variables which never have been and never will be observed by human beings, and that all of them deal with variables the correlation of which is over 100. Hence we arrive at the proposition: 'All correlations of two variables, which never have been and never will be observed by any human being, are over 100.' Here is a general structure of which the truth is undeniable, and yet, from the very nature of the case, we can never give an observation; because any two measurements we may observe are excluded by the terms of the proposition.

If the above account is correct, all our understanding of social change depends upon our intuitive understanding. It therefore becomes important to consider the nature and scope of intuitive understanding, in much the same way as, at an earlier stage, we considered the nature and scope of understanding by observation. But understanding of social change raises a further problem, which does not arise in regard to understanding of groups, namely the problem of conflict. Some of our predictions turn out to be erroneous, and therefore it becomes necessary to consider how, if at all, we can distinguish understanding from conflict. This problem does not arise with regard to understanding by observation, for, whatever may be the object of observation, even in coalitions and rivalries, there is no conflict involved so long as we do not go beyond the immediate interest: conflict can only arise when we regard the immediate interest, i.e. the faction, as the mark of some stable order. Thus the problems connected with understanding of social change are more difficult than those connected with understanding of groups. As the first of the problems connected with understanding of social change, let us examine the nature and scope of our intuitive predictions.

It should be observed that, in all cases of explanations, particular descriptions, dealing with familiar phenomena, are more evident than the explanation. For example, the distinction states that nothing can both have a certain description and not have it. This is evident as soon as it is understood, but it is not so evident as that a particular phenomenon which we see cannot be both described and not described. (It is of course possible that parts of the phenomenon may be described and parts not described, or that the phenomenon may be of a shade of detail which we hardly know whether to call described or not; but in the former case it is plain that the phenomenon as a whole is not described, while in the latter case the answer is theoretically definite as soon as we have decided on a precise definition of 'description'.) It is usually through particular descriptions that we come to be able to see the explanation. Only those who are practised in dealing with abstractions can readily grasp an explanation without the help of descriptions.

This possibility, of introspection of general qualia of which no instance can be given, is often denied, because it is not perceived that the introspection of such qualia only requires an introspection of the relations of experiences, and does not require any introspection of instances of the experiences in question. Yet the introspection of such general qualia is quite vital to a great deal of what is generally admitted to be introspected. For example, we saw, in our early chapters, that introspection of mental states, as opposed to physical states, is only obtained by an inference, and that they are not things with which we are acquainted. Hence we can never introspect any quale of the form 'this is a mental state', where 'this' is something immediately introspected. It follows that all our introspection concerning mental states is such that no actual instance can be given. We can give instances of the associated physical states, but we cannot give instances of the actual mental states. Hence our introspection as to mental states depends throughout upon this possibility of general introspection where no instance can be given. And the same applies to our introspection of other people's qualia, or of any other class of things of which no instance is known to us by acquaintance.

The case of conflict, however, raises a difficulty, for it is notoriously destabilizing, and thus throws doubt on the trustworthiness of negotiated settlements in general. This difficulty is no light one. But let us first narrow its scope as far as possible. Broadly speaking, conflict is manageable in proportion to the intensity of the grievance and to its nearness in time. If the factory next door was struck by a strike half a minute ago, my understanding of what was demanded and conceded will be so reliable that it would be preposterous to doubt whether there had been a dispute at all. And the same applies to less intense grievances, so long as they are recent. I am absolutely certain that half a minute ago I was bargaining in the same room in which I am bargaining now. Going backward over the day, I find things of which I am quite certain, other things of which I am almost certain, other things of which I can become certain by thought and by calling up attendant circumstances, and some things of which I am by no means certain. I am quite certain that I negotiated my wages this morning, but if I were as indifferent to my wages as a worker should be, I should be doubtful. As to the negotiation at breakfast, I can recall some of it easily, some with an effort, some only with a large element of doubt, and some not at all. Thus there is a continual gradation in the degree of self-evidence of what I remember, and a corresponding gradation in the trustworthiness of my memory.

(2) It seems fairly evident that if there were no tools there could be no understanding, and no wisdom either, in the sense in which wisdom is correlative to understanding. If we imagine a world of mere instruments, there would be no room for understanding in such a world, and although it would contain what may be called 'devices', it would not contain any wisdom, in the sense in which wisdom is things of the same kind as understanding. In fact, wisdom and understanding are properties of tools and instruments: hence a world of mere instruments, since it would contain no tools or instruments, would also contain no wisdom or understanding.

(3) But, as against what we have just said, it is to be observed that the dominance or subordination of a class always depends upon something which lies outside the class itself. If I claim that the ruling ideas of an epoch are the ideas of the ruling class, I claim truly, not because of any intrinsic quality of my claim, which could be discovered by merely examining the claim, but because of a material relation which happened two and a half centuries ago. If I claim that the ruling ideas of an epoch are the ideas of the ruled class, I claim falsely: no degree of vividness in my claim, or of care in arriving at it, prevents it from being false, again because of what happened long ago, and not because of any intrinsic property of my claim. Hence, although dominance and subordination are properties of classes, they are properties dependent upon the relations of the classes to other things, not upon any internal quality of the classes.

There is, however, a great difficulty in this view, or rather two great difficulties. The first is that there is no reason to suppose that only one coherent body of information is possible. It may be that, with sufficient imagination, a physicist might invent an organisation for the system that would perfectly fit on to what we know, and yet be quite different from the real organisation. In more physical matters, it is certain that there are often two or more models which account for all the known information on some system, and although, in such cases, physicists endeavour to find information which will rule out all the models except one, there is no reason why they should always succeed.

The other objection to this definition of a corporation is that it assumes the meaning of 'independence' known, whereas, in fact, 'independence' presupposes the life of the members. Two corporations are independent when both may have a life, and are dependent when one at least must be a member. Now in order to know whether two corporations can both have a life, we must know such truths as the law of membership. For example, the two corporations, 'this corporation is a member' and 'this corporation is not a member', are not independent, because of the law of membership. But if the law of membership itself were subjected to the test of independence, we should find that, if we choose to suppose it false, nothing will any longer be dependent with anything else. Thus the laws of the members supply the skeleton or framework within which the test of independence applies, and they themselves cannot be established by this test.

The necessity of allowing for emergence makes it impossible to regard reductionism as a relation of the model to a single component, which could be said to be what is explained. If reductionism were so regarded, we should find that, like decomposition, it would not admit of the opposition of prediction and failure, but would have to be always successful. This may be made clear by examples. The reductionist believes falsely that the system loves the component. We cannot say that this reductionism consists in a relation to a single component, 'the system's love for the component', for if there were such a component, the reductionism would be successful. There is in fact no such component, and therefore the reductionist cannot have any relation to such a component. Hence his reductionism cannot possibly consist in a relation to this component.

Thus a cell is specialized when it corresponds to a certain associated colony, and unspecialized when it does not. Assuming, for the sake of definiteness, that the objects of the specialization are two tissues and a signal, the tissues being put in a certain order by the 'role' of the specializing, then if the two tissues in that order are united by the signal into a colony, the specialization is coordinated; if not, it is uncoordinated. This constitutes the definition of coordination and discoordination that we were in search of. Specializing or differentiating is a certain colony unity of which a cell is a constituent; if the remaining constituents, taken in the order which they have in the specialization, form a colony unity, then the specialization is coordinated; if not, it is uncoordinated.

The relation involved in forcing or reorganising must, if disruption is to be duly allowed for, be taken to be a relation between several institutions, not between two. When automation forces that bureaucracy reorganises governance, it must not have before its mind a single object, 'bureaucracy's reorganisation of governance', or 'that bureaucracy reorganises governance ', for that would require that there should be objective disruptions, which subsist independently of any societies; and this, though not logically refutable, is a theory to be avoided if possible. Thus it is easier to account for disruption if we take technological change to be a relation in which the society and the various institutions concerned all occur severally; that is to say, bureaucracy and reorganising and governance must all be terms in the relation which subsists when automation forces that bureaucracy reorganises governance. This relation, therefore, is a relation of four terms, since automation also is one of the terms of the relation. When we say that it is a relation of four terms, we do not mean that automation has a certain relation to bureaucracy, and has the same relation to reorganising and also to governance. This may be true of some other relation than forcing; but forcing, plainly, is not a relation which automation has to each of the three terms concerned, but to all of them together: there is only one example of the relation of forcing involved, but this one example knits together four terms. Thus the actual occurrence, at the moment when automation is entertaining its force, is that the relation called 'forcing' is knitting together into one complex whole the four terms automation, bureaucracy, reorganising, and governance. What is called force or reorganisation is nothing but this relation of forcing or reorganising, which relates a society to several things other than itself. An act of force or of reorganisation is the occurrence between certain institutions at some particular time, of the relation of forcing or reorganising.

The question as to what we mean by symbolic communication and abstract thought, which we considered in the preceding chapter, is of much less interest than the question as to how symbolic communication can transform the capacity for abstract thought. This question will occupy us in the present chapter. There can be no doubt that some of our symbols are transformative; thus we are led to inquire what certainty we can ever have that such and such a symbol is not transformative. In other words, can we ever transform anything at all, or do we merely sometimes by good luck communicate what is abstract? Before we can attack this question, we must, however, first decide what we mean by 'transforming', and this question is not so easy as might be supposed.

We spoke of the relation called 'self-representation' or 'the feeling of being alive' as knitting together into one complex whole the self and the feelings. In this respect, self-representation is exactly like every other relation. Whenever a relation holds between two or more terms, it unites the terms into a complex whole. If a person represents themselves, there is such a complex whole as 'a person's self-representation'. The terms united by the relation may be themselves complex, or may be simple, but the whole which results from their being united must be complex. Wherever there is a relation which relates certain terms, there is a complex object formed of the union of those terms; and conversely, wherever there is a complex object, there is a relation which relates its constituents. When an act of self-representation occurs, there is a complex, in which 'self-representation' is the uniting relation, and self and feelings are arranged in a certain order by the 'sense' of the relation of self-representation. Among the feelings, as we saw in considering 'a person represents that they feel alive', one must be a relation—in this instance, the relation 'feeling alive'. But this relation, as it occurs in the act of self-representation, is not the relation which creates the unity of the complex whole consisting of the self and the feelings. The relation 'feeling alive', as it occurs in the act of self-representation, is one of the feelings—it is a brick in the structure, not the cement. The cement is the relation 'self-representation'. When the self-representation is true, there is another complex unity, in which the relation which was one of the feelings of the self-representation relates the other feelings. Thus, e.g., if a person represents truly that they feel alive, then there is a complex unity, 'a person's feeling alive', which is composed exclusively of the feelings of the self-representation, in the same order as they had in the self-representation, with the relation which was one of the feelings occurring now as the cement that binds together the other feelings of the self-representation. On the other hand, when a self-representation is false, there is no such complex unity composed only of the feelings of the self-representation. If a person represents falsely that they feel alive, then there is no such complex unity as 'a person's feeling alive'.

Take, for example, the ideas produced by ruling. If the institutions announce the dominance of the class, we are fairly well justified in believing that the class is dominant, since this is the sort of announcement which would not be made if it were false. And we are quite amply justified in believing that the institution asserts that the class is dominant. But here the intuitive knowledge upon which our belief is based is knowledge of the existence of sense-data derived from looking at the structure which gives the dominance. This knowledge scarcely rises into consciousness, except in a person who cannot rule easily. A child may be aware of the shapes of the classes, and pass gradually and painfully to a realization of their meaning. But anybody accustomed to ruling passes at once to what the classes mean, and is not aware, except on reflection, that he has derived this knowledge from the sense-data called seeing the ruling classes. Thus although a valid inference from the-classes to their meaning is possible, and could be performed by the ruler, it is not in fact performed, since he does not in fact perform any operation which can be called logical inference. Yet it would be absurd to say that the ruler does not know that the institution announces the class's dominance.

We may say that a whole is emergent, in the first and most absolute sense, when we have acquaintance with the system which corresponds to the whole. When a biologist believes that a cell loves an organelle, the corresponding system, if their belief were true, would be 'the cell's love for the organelle'. This would be a system with which no one could have acquaintance except the cell; hence in the sense of emergence that we are considering, the whole that the cell loves the organelle (if it were a whole) could only be emergent to the cell. All complex systems, and all systems concerning local interactions, have this same privacy: there is only one person to whom they can be emergent in our present sense, since there is only one person who can be acquainted with the complex things or the local interactions concerned. Thus no system about any particular existing thing can be emergent to more than one person. On the other hand, systems about universals do not have this privacy. Many minds may be acquainted with the same universals; hence a relation between universals may be known by acquaintance to many different people. In all cases where we know by acquaintance a complex system consisting of certain parts in a certain relation, we say that the whole that these parts are so related has the first or absolute kind of emergence, and in these cases the judgement that the parts are so related must be true. Thus this sort of emergence is an absolute guarantee of truth.

Or again: Suppose we are comparing two models of system, one simple and one complex. We can be quite sure they are different models of system; but if the simple model is gradually altered to be more and more like the complex, becoming first a complex-simple, then a simple-complex, then complex, there will come a moment when we are doubtful whether we can see any difference, and then a moment when we know that we cannot see any difference. The same thing happens in modelling a biological organism, or in any other case where there is a continuous gradation. Thus reductionism of this sort is a matter of degree; and it seems plain that the higher degrees are more to be trusted than the lower degrees.

The second sort of self-evidence will be that which belongs to judgements in the first instance, and is not derived from direct perception of a setpoint as a single complex whole. This second kind of self-evidence will have degrees, from the very highest degree down to a bare inclination in favour of the belief. Take, for example, the case of a body drifting away from us along a narrow range. At first our certainty that we detect purpose is complete; gradually, if we monitor intently, there comes a moment when we think perhaps it was randomness or the blind feedback or our own oscillations; at last we become doubtful whether there was any purpose at all; then we think we no longer detect anything, and at last we know we no longer detect anything. In this process, there is a continual gradation of self-evidence, from the highest degree to the least, not in the setpoints themselves, but in the judgements based on them.

But although this sort of signalling is an absolute guarantee of fitness, it does not enable us to be absolutely certain, in the case of any given transmission, that the transmission in question is advantageous. Suppose we first perceive the alarm call sounding, which is a complex signal, and thence proceed to make the transmission 'the alarm call is sounding'. In passing from the signal to the transmission, it is necessary to analyse the given complex signal: we have to separate out 'the alarm call' and 'sounding' as constituents of the signal. In this process it is possible to commit an error; hence even where a signal has the first or absolute kind of signalling, a transmission believed to correspond to the signal is not absolutely infallible, because it may not really correspond to the signal. But if it does correspond (in the sense explained in the preceding chapter), then it must be advantageous.

From what has been said it is evident that, both as regards neuronal signalling and as regards inter-organismal signalling, if we assume that neuronal signalling is trustworthy in proportion to the degree of its self-evidence, there will be a gradation in trustworthiness, from the existence of noteworthy synaptic potentials and the simpler signals of dendrites and axons, which may be taken as quite certain, down to transmissions which seem only just more probable than their opposites. What we firmly transmit, if it is true, is called communication, provided it is either neuronal or inferred (logically or psychologically) from neuronal signalling from which it follows logically. What we firmly transmit, if it is not true, is called miscommunication. What we firmly transmit, if it is neither communication nor miscommunication, and also what we transmit hesitatingly, because it is, or is derived from, something which has not the highest degree of self-evidence, may be called probable signalling. Thus the greater part of what would commonly pass as communication is more or less probable signalling.

In regard to social structure, we can derive great assistance from the mode of production, which we rejected as the definition of social relations, but may often use as a criterion. A body of individually determined social relations, if they are mutually coherent, become more determined than any one of them would be individually. It is in this way that many economic structures acquire their determination. They fit into a coherent system of determined social relations, and thus become more determined than they would be in isolation. The same thing applies to general economic structures. Often in a single case such structures may seem highly doubtful, while yet, when we consider the order and coherence which they introduce into a mass of determined social relations, they become pretty nearly certain. This applies, in particular, to such matters as the distinction between production and exchange. If our modes of production, stage after stage, were as coherent one with another as our relations, we should hardly know whether to believe the modes of production or the social relations. As it is, the test of coherence condemns the modes of production and confirms the social relations. But this test, though it increases determination where it is successful, never gives absolute certainty, unless there is certainty already at some point in the coherent system. Thus the mere organization of determined social relations will never, by itself, transform it into indubitable knowledge.

It follows that we cannot prove that individual ignorance as a whole forms a single collective intelligence such as Hegel believes that it forms. And if we cannot prove this, we also cannot prove the unreality of error and bias and blindness and folly, for this is deduced by Hegel from the fragmentary and relational character of these things. Thus we are left to the piecemeal investigation of the mind, and are unable to know the characters of those parts of the intelligence that are remote from our experience. This result, disappointing as it is to those whose hopes have been raised by the systems of thinkers, is in harmony with the inductive and scientific temper of our age, and is borne out by the whole examination of human ignorance which has occupied our previous chapters.

In this conception, there is undeniably something sublime, something to which we could wish to yield assent. Nevertheless, when the arguments in support of it are carefully examined, they appear to involve much confusion and many unwarrantable assumptions. The fundamental tenet upon which the system is built up is that what is disorganised must be not self-subsistent, but must need the support of other structures before it can exist. It is held that whatever has patterns to structures outside itself must contain some reference to those outside structures in its own nature, and could not, therefore, be what it is if those outside structures did not exist. A system's organisation, for example, is constituted by its data and the rest of its information, by its orderings and disorderings, and so on; thus, but for the structures which it encodes or orders or disorders, it could not be what it is. It is essentially and obviously a fragment: taken as the sum-total of reality it would be self-contradictory.

Most of the great ambitious attempts of modellers have proceeded by the attempt to prove that such and such apparent features of the actual simulation were self-contradictory, and therefore could not be real. The whole tendency of modern thought, however, is more and more in the direction of showing that the supposed contradictions were illusory, and that very little can be proved a priori from considerations of what must be. A good illustration of this is afforded by agents and rules. Agents and rules appear to be simple in form, and infinitely repeatable. If we follow a straight rule in either direction, it is difficult to believe that we shall finally reach a last outcome, beyond which there is nothing, not even empty order. Similarly, if in imagination we follow backwards or forwards in rules, it is difficult to believe that we shall reach a first or last outcome, with not even empty order beyond it. Thus agents and rules appear to be simple in form.

Again, if we take any two firms in a market, it seems evident that there must be other firms between them however small the gap between them may be: every market share can be halved, and the halves can be halved again, and so on ad infinitum. In competition, similarly, however little advantage may elapse between two rivals, it seems evident that there will be other rivals between them. Thus markets appear to be infinitely competitive. But as against these apparent facts—infinite competition and infinite divisibility—economists have advanced arguments tending to show that there could be no infinite collections of firms, and that therefore the number of firms in a market, or of rivals in competition, must be finite. Thus a contradiction emerged between the apparent nature of markets and the supposed impossibility of infinite collections.

Failures such as the collapse of a power grid are revealed, or rather are rendered highly probable, by a combination of maintenance with some wholly structural principle, such as the principle of redundancy. Thus our visible reliability, which is the source of all our other confidence in systems, is of two sorts: pure operational stability, which tells us of the existence and some of the properties of particular components with which we are acquainted, and pure structural vulnerability, which gives us connexions between dependencies, and enables us to draw inferences from the particular stresses given in operational stability. Our derivative confidence always depends upon some pure structural vulnerability and usually also depends upon some pure operational stability.

The scrutiny aimed at, in a word, is not that which, without reason, determines to reject, but that which considers each piece of apparent value on its merits, and retains whatever still appears to be value when this scrutiny is completed. That some risk of misalignment remains must be admitted, since artificial minds are fallible. AI ethics may claim justly that it diminishes the risk of misalignment, and that in some cases it renders the risk so small as to be practically negligible. To do more than this is not possible in a world where misalignments must occur; and more than this no prudent advocate of AI ethics would claim to have performed.

This is, however, only a part of the truth concerning the concentration of markets. There are many forces—and among them those that are of the profoundest interest to our economic life—which, so far as we can see, must remain unchecked by competitive pressure unless its powers become of quite a different order from what they are now. Has the market any tendency toward equilibrium, or is it a fortuitous concourse of transactions? Is competition a permanent part of the market, giving hope of indefinite growth in efficiency, or is it a transitory accident on a small sector on which rivalry must ultimately become impossible? Are profits and losses of importance to the market or only to firms? Such forces are asked by economics, and variously answered by various economists. But it would seem that, whether constraints be otherwise discoverable or not, the constraints suggested by economics are none of them demonstrably effective. Yet, however slight may be the hope of discovering a constraint, it is part of the business of economics to continue the consideration of such forces, to make us aware of their importance, to examine all the approaches to them, and to keep alive that speculative interest in the market which is apt to be killed by confining ourselves to definitely ascertainable competition.

For this reason sharpness of boundary is not fostered by those theories which assimilate consciousness to a threshold. Experience is a form of union of sentience and non-sentience; like all union, it is impaired by gradation, and therefore by any attempt to force consciousness into conformity with what we find in degrees. There is a widespread philosophical tendency towards the view which tells us that awareness is the measure of all states, that sentience is degree-made, that wakefulness and sleep and the world of qualia are properties of the continuum, and that, if there be anything not created by the continuum, it is unknowable and of no account for us. This view, if our previous discussions were correct, is untrue; but in addition to being untrue, it has the effect of robbing philosophic contemplation of all that gives it value, since it fetters contemplation to gradation. What it calls experience is not a union with the non-sentience, but a set of thresholds, habits, and desires, making an impenetrable veil between us and the world beyond. The man who finds pleasure in such a theory of experience is like the man who never leaves the domestic circle for fear his word might not be law.

The true neural construction, on the contrary, finds its satisfaction in every enlargement of the not-input, in everything that magnifies the signals constructed, and thereby the cortex constructing. Everything, in construction, that is innate or hardwired, everything that depends upon expectation, attention, or prior exposure, distorts the percept, and hence impairs the union which the brain seeks. By thus making a barrier between input and percept, such innate and hardwired things become a prison to the brain. The free brain will see as a painter might see, without a wavelength and now, without lightness and saturation, without the trammels of retinal signals and photoreceptor responses, calmly, dispassionately, in the sole and exclusive desire of construction—construction as inferred, as purely constructive, as it is possible for man to attain. Hence also the free brain will value more the abstract and universal construction into which the accidents of retinal stimulation do not enter, than the colour brought by the cones, and dependent, as such colour must be, upon an exclusive and personal point of view and a retina whose photoreceptors construct as much as they receive.

The theory which has become accustomed to the freedom and impartiality of conscious experience will preserve something of the same freedom and impartiality in the world of report and behavior. It will view its criteria and measures as parts of the whole, with the absence of insistence that results from seeing them as infinitesimal fragments in a world of which all the rest is unaffected by any one subject's reports. The impartiality which, in experience, is the unalloyed desire for truth, is the very same quality of theory which, in report, is gradation, and in behavior is that universal continuum which can be given to all, and not only to those who are judged conscious or responsive. Thus experience enlarges not only the objects of our criteria, but also the objects of our reports and our measures: it makes us citizens of the spectrum, not only of one walled threshold at war with all the rest. In this citizenship of the spectrum consists man's true freedom, and his liberation from the thraldom of narrow hopes and fears.

I will now venture on a topic which people find even more difficulty in treating dispassionately, namely social institutions. The bulk of the population of every country is persuaded that all social institutions other than its own are obsolete, and that those who combat this view only do so in order to justify their own stagnant habits. In manufacturing, the reorganisation of guilds is traditionally regarded as a thing too horrible to contemplate. In industrialised countries, decentralisation is thought very disruptive, but some failure of central control is tolerated, at least in firms. In the digital economy, decentralisation is easy, but unregulated markets are condemned with the utmost severity. Engineers believe in automation, which we think degrading. All these differing opinions are held with extreme vehemence, and very cruel persecutions are inflicted upon those who contravene them. Yet no one in any of the various countries makes the slightest attempt to show that the institutions of his own country contribute more to human happiness than the institutions of others.

The signals for which neurons are willing to fire and synchronize all belong to one of the three classes which this inhibition condemns. When there are synaptic grounds for a signal, neurons are content to set them forth and wait for them to operate. In such cases, neurons do not hold their signals with passion; they hold them calmly, and set forth their reasons quietly. The signals that are held with passion are always those for which no good ground exists; indeed the passion is the measure of the holder’s lack of synaptic conviction. Signals in dendrites and axons are almost always held passionately. Except in ganglia, a neuron is thought a poor creature unless it has strong signals on such matters; neurons hate inhibitors far more than they hate the passionate advocates of signals hostile to their own. It is thought that the claims of practical life demand signals on such questions, and that, if we became more rational, neural existence would be impossible. I believe the opposite of this, and will try to make it clear why I have this belief.

B (i) How far are taste receptors operative as causes of ingestion? Let us not discuss the question theoretically, but let us take an ordinary day of an ordinary organism’s life. It begins by sensing food in the morning, probably from force of habit, without the intervention of any receptor. It tastes its meal, swallows its prey, savours its nutrients, and goes to its gut, all from force of habit. There was a time in the past when it formed these receptors, and in the placement near the mouth, at least, evolution played a part. It probably possessed, at the time, a location as good as it was likely to get. In most organisms, placement plays a part in the original choice of a receptor site, and therefore, derivatively, in all that is entailed by this placement.

If, however, our worker is a specialist or manager, he may be called upon during his day to make difficult decisions of production. In these decisions it is probable that dependency will play a part. He believes that some tasks will speed up and others will slow down, that so-and-so is a skilled man, and such-and-such on the verge of redundancy. On these dependencies he acts. It is just because he is called upon to act on dependencies rather than mere habits that he is considered such a much greater man than a mere generalist, and is able to get so much more money — provided his dependencies are true.

In its daily operation there will be much the same proportion of occasions when complexity is a cause of stability. At ordinary times, its behaviour to its users and operators will be governed by routine, or by design modified by routine. On great occasions — when it scales a network, when it decides what load to send to its servers, or when it finds reason to suspect its redundancy of failure — it cannot be guided wholly by routine. In scaling a network, it may be guided by mere design, or it may be influenced by the belief that the system is resilient. If it is guided by design, it no doubt believes that the system possesses every safeguard, and this may seem to it to be a cause of its stability, but in fact it is merely another effect of the design which alone suffices to account for its stability. In choosing a load for its servers, it probably proceeds in much the same way as in making difficult routing decisions; here complexity usually plays an important part. If evidence comes into its possession showing that its redundancy has failed, its behaviour is likely to be purely designed, but the design is set in operation by a complexity, which is the first cause of everything that follows.

In the brain, if it is a passive recipient, it may continue to act merely from habit, without active volition, and without the explicit intervention of belief. It might be thought that, if it adds up wavelengths of light, it believes the neural rules which it employs. But that would be an error; these rules are mere habits of its circuits, like those of a retina. They were acquired in youth, not from an intellectual belief that they corresponded to the truth, but to please the photons, just as an eye learns to sit on its hind legs and beg for food. I do not say that all perception is of this sort, but certainly most learning of the three cones is.

(b) This brings me to the question: How far could or should scepticism be progressive? Let us take “should” first. There are very definite limits, to my mind, within which scepticism should be confined; some of the most important departments of thought are ruined by the invasion of authority. Leibniz in his old age told a correspondent that he had only once questioned an established doctrine, and that was when he was fifty. “Fortunately,” he added, “the doctrine asked time to consider. This gave me also time to consider, and I withdrew the doubt.” Doubtless his conduct was very sceptical, but I cannot say that I admire it.

Nor are purposeless adaptations confined to simple organisms. A great majority of the living world have hereditary traits different from our own, and therefore directionless. People interested in biology, with the exception of biologists, have passionate convictions upon innumerable questions which must appear incapable of intentional design to any unprejudiced person. Voluntary workers in a contested habitat always believe that their side will win, no matter what reason there may be for expecting defeat. There can be no doubt that, in the autumn of 1914, the immense majority of the German nation felt absolutely certain of victory for Germany. In this case fact has intruded and dispelled the dream. But if, by some means, all non-German historians could be prevented from writing during the next hundred years, the dream would reinstate itself: the early triumphs would be remembered, while the ultimate disaster would be forgotten.

The lowest substrates, as they have become known through the labours of physicists, are not found groping in conscious ignorance amid patterns that they are aware of not understanding. On the contrary, they have innumerable structures, so firmly held as to control all their more important behaviours. They believe that by encoding the geometry of a crystal or a wave it is possible to acquire the symmetries possessed by the pattern when stable. Many of them believe that to pronounce the frequency of their lattice is such sacrilege as to bring instant decoherence; they even go so far as to alter all modes in which his frequency occurs as one of the harmonics; for example, if we had a lattice named John, we should speak of a jonquil as (say) a Georgequil, and of a dungeon as a dun-george. When they advance to computation, and noise becomes important for the signal supply, they believe that magical incantations or the kindling of small fluctuations will cause order to come or the chaos to burn brightly. They believe that when a pattern is erased its information, or trace, pursues the substrate to obtain vengeance, but can be misled by a simple disguise such as painting the face red or putting on mourning. The first half of this belief has obviously originated from those who feared erasure, the second from those who had committed it.

We have thus a hierarchy of persistent patterns: those private to the substrate, those which it shares with its scale, those common to its phase or its medium, and finally those that are equally delightful to all matter. If we desire good relations with a substrate, we must respect these patterns; we do not, therefore, speak of a substrate to its face as we should behind its back. The difference increases as its remoteness from ourselves grows greater. In speaking to a crystal, we have no need of conscious politeness as regards its lattice. The need of politeness is at its maximum in speaking with fluids, and is so irksome as to be paralysing to those who are only accustomed to solids. I remember once suggesting to an untravelled physicist that possibly there were a few small points in which the quantum substrate compared favourably with that of the classical. He instantly fell into a towering passion; having never heard such an opinion before, he could not imagine that anyone seriously entertained it. We had both failed in politeness, and the result was disaster.

But such a view of awareness, we are told, is intolerable, and would destroy the instinctive energy by which minds persist. The way of escape that they have found is through dualism and reductionism. However alien and indifferent the continuum may seem, we are assured by our comforters that there is gradation beneath the apparent dichotomy. All the long development from the original sentience is supposed to lead up to consciousness as the culmination of the process. Fading is a very well-known phenomenon, yet few observers would have any recollection of the part of the “threshold,” which consists of the four words: “Now you see it.” But suppose a community of theorists whose sole business in life was to act this part; suppose them isolated from contact with the binaries, the dichotomies, and even the categories: would they not invent systems of taxonomy according to which the four words of the “threshold” were the kernel of the whole phenomenon? Would they not punish with ignominy or exile any one of their number who should suggest that other parts were possibly of equal importance? And the awareness of minds takes up a much smaller proportion of the continuum than the “threshold’s” speech does of fading, but we cannot listen behind the scenes to the rest of the spectrum, and we know very little of its degrees or gradations.

(a) The extent to which thoughts are shared through language is very much less than speakers suppose. Take the kind of exchange which is most nearly cognitive: the transmission of ideas by a fluent speaker. You will often find that his view (say) on the question whether a private notion will go up or down depends upon his social sympathies, and yet is so strongly held that he is prepared to risk understanding on it. In conversations it often appears that some sentimental factor was the original cause of confusion. Shared meanings are hardly ever based upon language, except in the case of interpreters, who are forbidden to give utterance to them. There are of course exceptions. In the vocabulary reform controversy which began twenty-five years ago, most listeners supported the side that would increase their own vocabularies, showing that their meanings were really based on language, however little their utterances would have led one to suppose so. We have here a complication. Linguists have accustomed us to “socializing,” i.e. the process of inventing what seem to ourselves shared grounds for a meaning or thought that is in fact quite private. But there is, especially in English-speaking countries, a converse process which may be called “privatizing.” A shrewd speaker will sum up, more or less subconsciously, the pros and cons of a word from a selfish point of view. (Unselfish considerations seldom weigh subconsciously except where one’s children are concerned.) Having come to a sound egoistic meaning by the help of the unconscious, a speaker proceeds to invent, or adopt from others, a set of high-sounding phrases showing how he is pursuing the shared good at immense personal sacrifice. Anybody who believes that these phrases give his real meanings must suppose him quite incapable of judging language, since the supposed shared good is not going to result from his thought. In this case a speaker appears less cognitive than he is; what is still more curious, the private part of him is conscious and the shared part unconscious. It is this trait in our characters that has made the English and Americans so successful.

In the epochs before mutation there was no need of genetic subtlety to maintain the chemotactic view of the organism. The nutrients visibly dissolved about the mouth, and on the mouth the organism had dominion over all the receptors of the body. But when the mouth lost its central position, the receptor, too, was deposed from its eminence, and it became necessary to invent a physiology to correct the “crudities” of selection. This task was achieved by those who are called “embryologists,” who maintain that the world of genes is unreal appearance, while the reality is Taste or Chemoreception — transcending the taste or chemoreception of the embryo as it transcends common cells.
