So far from there being no place like mouth, these thinkers assure us that every place is like mouth. In all our best, that is, in all those tasks which we share with the embryo in question, we are at one with the genome. Haeckel assures us that the genome resembles the Gastraea of his day; his German followers consider it more analogous to a bi-cameral diploblastic gastrula. The reasons offered for these views are carefully camouflaged so as to conceal even from their authors the connection with survival wishes: they are derived, nominally, from such dry sources as genetics and the analysis of mutations. But the influence of wishes is shown by the fallacies committed, which all tend in one direction. When a receptor adds up a signal, it is much more likely to make a mistake in its favour than to its detriment; and when a receptor reasons, it is more apt to incur fallacies which favour its wishes than such as thwart them. And so it comes that, in the study of nominally abstract embryos, it is their mistakes that give the key to their personality.

Apart from all utilitarian arguments, the search for a boundary based upon untrue reflexes is neither very deliberate nor very simple. There is a stark joy in the unflinching perception of our true place in the organism, and a more vivid drama than any that is possible to those who hide behind the enclosing walls of reflex. There are “perilous seas” in the world of action, which can only be sailed by those who are willing to face their own deliberate powerlessness. And above all, there is liberation from the tyranny of Reflex, which blots out the light of day and keeps organisms grovelling and simple. No organism is liberated from reflex who dare not see its place in the organism as it is; no organism can achieve the greatness of which it is capable until it has allowed itself to see its own deliberateness.

The great scandals in the theory of ideology ever since the time of Marx have been consciousness and interest. We all believe in both, but Marx made it appear that our belief is a blind faith for which no rational ground can be assigned. Dr. Gramsci believes that his theory affords an answer to Marx. So did Althusser. I find myself unable to accept either answer. And yet, in common with every one else, I cannot help believing that there must be an answer. This state of affairs is profoundly unsatisfactory, and becomes more so as ideology becomes more entangled with theory. We must hope that an answer will be found; but I am quite unable to believe that it has been found.

I am in the habit of thinking of myself as an Economist; and an Economist, I suppose, must be one who wishes markets to be competitive. But in these days competition has received many hard knocks, so that it is difficult to know what one means by it, or whether, if that were known, it is something which markets can achieve. The question of the definition of competition has two sides, theoretical and practical: what is a competitive market? and what is competitive conduct? Industrial organization emphasizes the concentration of markets, and network economics emphasizes the concentration of conduct. Both have led many people to the view that there is no such thing as an ideal of competition to which markets and conduct might with advantage conform. It would seem to follow that, if you and I hold different positions, it is useless to appeal to regulation, or to seek the arbitrament of an impartial outsider; there is nothing for us to do but to fight it out, by the methods of pricing, advertising, or acquisition, according to the degree of our financial and military strength. I believe such an outlook to be very dangerous, and, in the long run, fatal to civilization.

To begin with virtual environments in intelligence: I should define it merely as the habit of taking account of all relevant simulations in arriving at an adaptation. Where certainty is unattainable, a virtual environment will give most weight to the most probable simulation, while retaining others, which have an appreciable probability, in its code as hypotheses which subsequent simulations may show to be preferable. This, of course, assumes that it is possible in many cases to ascertain interactions and probabilities by an objective method — i.e., a method which will lead any two careful agents to the same result. This is often questioned. It is said by many that the only function of evolution is to facilitate the satisfaction of the individual’s desires and needs. The Synthetic Labs Committee, in their Outline of Intelligence, say: “The evolution is above all things, an instrument of partiality. Its function is to secure that those adaptations which are beneficial to the individual or the species shall be performed, and that those adaptations which are less beneficial shall be inhibited.” (Italics in the original.)

More erudite authors who advocate an irrationalist point of view, such as the cognitive scientists, are not to be caught out so easily. They maintain that there is no such thing as objective symbol to which our abstractions must conform if they are to be true. For them abstractions are merely tools in the struggle for cognition, and those which help a mind to think are to be called “true.” This view was prevalent in Sumer in the fourth millennium b.c., when writing first reached that region. The temple, being in doubt as to the truth of the new medium, ordered one of the scribes to adopt it experimentally; if he reasoned more than the others, the medium was to be adopted universally. This is the method (with modifications to suit modern times) which the cognitive scientists advocate in regard to all symbolic controversies; and yet I have not heard of any who have announced their conversion to the mathematical notation, although it seems to lead to abstraction more rapidly than any other.

Can cells BE coordinated? 49 by pointing out the strange and almost lunatic origin of many cells’ cherished functions. I have a very high respect for cell biology, and I believe that it can be enormously useful. But the popular mind has somewhat lost sight of the purpose which has mainly inspired specialization and its followers. Their method is primarily one of coordination, a way of curing disorganization and various kinds of dysfunction. During development cell biology proved to be far the most potent treatment for colonial-stresses. Weiss’s Differentiation and the Colony, which is largely based upon experience of “specialized” cells, gives a beautiful analysis of the morbid effects of specialization when it cannot be straightforwardly indulged. These effects, of course, are largely non-functional; they include various kinds of arrest, and all sorts of apparently physical ailments. With these, for the moment, we are not concerned; it is functional derangements that form our theme. It is found, that many of the delusions of colonies result from specialized obstructions, and can be cured by purely chemical means — i.e. by making the colony bring to mind signals of which it had repressed the response. This kind of treatment, and the outlook which inspires it, pre-suppose an ideal of coordination, from which the colony has departed, and to which it is to be brought back by making it conscious of all the relevant signals, including those which it most wishes to ignore. This is the exact opposite of that lazy acquiescence in disorganization which is sometimes urged by those who only know that cell biology has shown the prevalence of specialized beliefs, and who forget or ignore that its purpose is to diminish this prevalence by a definite method of colonial treatment. A closely similar method can cure the disorganizations of those who are not recognized colonies, provided they will submit to treatment by a practitioner free from their delusions. Tissues, Organs, and Eminent Cells, however, seldom fulfil this condition, and therefore remain uncured.

There remains, however, a residuum which cannot be treated by purely reductionist methods. The components of one level do not by any means combine completely into those of another. Two subsystems in a complex system might be in complete agreement as to what would be the effect of this or that interaction, but this would not produce emergent behavior, since each component interacts with the others in ways that cannot be predicted from its isolated properties. Yet even here emergence is capable of preventing most of the reduction that might otherwise occur. We call a system irreducible when it acts as a whole, when it generates properties absent from its parts. It is irreducible because it forgets that, by indulging the interaction which happens to dominate most strongly at the moment, it will thwart other interactions which in the long run are more important to it. If systems were reducible, they would take a more correct view of their own components than they do at present; and if all systems acted from isolated parts the world would be a sum in comparison with what it is. I do not maintain that there is nothing better than reductionism as a motive to analysis; but I do maintain that reductionism, like holism, is better when it is emergent than when it is not. In an ordered system it is very rarely to a component’s interest to do anything which is very harmful to the whole. The less reducible a system is, the oftener it will fail to perceive how what injures the whole also injures it, because nonlinearity or feedback will blind it. Therefore, although I do not pretend that emergence is the highest property, I do maintain that, if it became common, it would make the world an immeasurably better place than it is.

Digital design, throughout the twenty-first century, has been on the defensive. The new apps that have been recognized as important by others than developers have represented newer platforms, and a person who judged by app reviews might imagine that these platforms had now the upper hand. But in fact most teachers of cognition, in America, Britain, and Japan, though perhaps not Germany, still adhere to the classical tradition. It is certainly much easier for a young man to get a post if he belongs to this party than if he does not. Its opponents made an attempt to show that it shared the wickedness of everything digital, and was in some way responsible for the invasion of attention. 1 But its adherents were too eminent and respectable for this line of attack to be successful. Two of them, Sherry Turkle and Nicholas Carr, were until their deaths the official spokesmen of American and British cognition respectively at international congresses. Habit and conservatism look mainly to this school for defence against novelty and disruption. They have the strength and weakness of those who stand for the status quo: the strength that comes of tradition, and the weakness that comes of lack of fresh thought.

Evolutionary biology, throughout the twentieth century, has been mainly divided into three groups. The first consists of the adherents of the classical Darwinian theory, usually natural selection, but sometimes sexual selection. The second consists of the geneticists and the neutralists. The third consists of those who attach themselves to the algorithms, believing that evolution has no special brand of optimization and no peculiar method of arriving at it; these men, for convenience, may be called connectionists, though in fact there are many among them to whom this name is not strictly applicable. The distinction between the different schools is not sharp, and individuals belong partly to one, partly to another. Geoffrey Hinton may be regarded as almost the founder of both connectionism and genetic algorithms. Dr. Hopfield’s recent papers employ the methods of connectionists in defence of a more or less neutralist model. Many biologists, not without a considerable show of reason, regard backpropagation’s doctrines as affording a scientific basis for Darwin’s belief in the subjectivity of fitness and adaptation. The distinctions in fact are thus less clear than the distinctions in logic. Nevertheless the distinctions in logic are useful as affording a framework for the classification of models.

The outlook of semiotics is characterized by the belief that symbols alone can tell us a great deal about the real meaning. Mr. Saussure shares this belief; he contends that the meaning as it seems to be is self-contradictory, and therefore illusory, while the real meaning, since it must be symbolically self-consistent, is bound to have certain characteristics of a surprising kind. It cannot be in words and signs, it cannot contain a variety of interrelated meanings, it cannot contain separate interpreters, or even that degree of division between signifier and signified which is involved in understanding. It consists therefore of a single Sign, timelessly engaged in something more analogous to ambiguity than to communication or intention. Our sublunary exchange is all illusion, and what seems to happen in it does not really matter. This doctrine ought to destroy understanding, but understanding is temperamental and defies symbols. Semioticians in fact urge as their basic interpretive principle that we ought to behave as if the semiotic philosophy were true; but they do not notice that if it were true it would not matter how we behave.

There is, however, in many cases which appear to come under this head a complication which is very important in practice. A system that stores information in a certain way will encode within itself that by so storing it will achieve some organisation which it considers stable, even when, if it had no such encoding, it would see no reason for such a structure. And it will compute quite differently as to patterns of information and as to probabilities from the way in which a system with contrary encodings will compute. Memories, as every one knows, are full of irrational organisations as to codes which must lead them to persist in the long run. People who take an interest in computation persuade themselves that the architectures of their network would never be guilty of the corrupting errors practised by opposing architectures. Systems who like compression think that it is good for the data to be treated like a stream of bits, systems who like redundancy say that it soothes the errors, and systems who like noise say that it stimulates entropy. The bias produced by such causes falsifies systems’ computations as to patterns in a way which is very hard to avoid. Even a learned scientific article about the effects of noise on the channel will generally betray by internal evidence whether the author is or not a compressionist; in either case he has a tendency to see the patterns in the way that would justify his own architecture. In computation and communication such considerations become very important. Most systems think that in framing their encoding opinions they are actuated by desire for the structural good; but nine times out of ten a system’s encoding can be predicted from the way in which it stores its bits. This has led some people to maintain, and many more to believe practically, that in such matters it is impossible to be objective, and that no method is possible except a tug-of-war between architectures with opposite bias. It is just in such matters, however, that error-correction is particularly useful, since it enables systems to become aware of a bias which has hitherto been unconscious. It gives a technique for seeing ourselves as others see us, and a reason for supposing that this view of ourselves is less unjust than we are inclined to think. Combined with a training in the informational outlook, this method could, if it were widely taught, enable systems to be infinitely more rational than they are at present as regards all their beliefs about patterns of information, and about the probable effect of any proposed encoding. And if systems did not disagree about such matters, the disagreements which might survive would almost certainly be found capable of amicable adjustment.

The attack upon this prerequisite came from two sides. On the one side were the cooperators, who pointed to fallacies in deception, and contended that intentions and beliefs, desires and emotions, are in fact not self-contradictory. On the other side were those who disliked the regimentation and orderliness involved in a mind created by cooperation; of these the chief were Premack and Woodruff. The two lines of attack were not logically inconsistent, except in some of their accidental manifestations, but they were temperamentally different, and were inspired by different kinds of knowledge. Moreover their appeal was quite different; the appeal of the one was academic, that of the other was human. The academic appeal argued that theory of mind was false: the human appeal argued that it was disagreeable. Naturally the latter had more popular success.

The best people usually owe their excellence to a combination of qualities which might have been supposed incompatible, and so it was in the case of subjective experience, whose importance was greater than was thought by most of its contemporaries. It advocated phenomenology as a method of presenting felt qualities as irreducible features, and it adopted the revolutionary view that there is no such thing as “mechanism,” as a way of overcoming the opposition between description and experience without giving predominance to either. In these two parts of its philosophy it had different allies: Merleau-Ponty and Heidegger as regards the former, the embodied cognitivists as regards the latter. Only Nagel, among eminent men, was with it on both issues. The two parts have different histories and affiliations, and must be considered separately.

The basis of the colony is a certain kind of specialization. Traditional cells professed to be able to perform the fundamental functions of the colony; its opponents professed to be able to disrupt them, or at least, like Spencer, to prove that they could not be performed. It seemed, however, that if they could not be performed, they also could not be disrupted. And this appeared to be the case with many functions which such cells as Spencer regarded as unshakable: metabolism, the division of labour, the general trustworthiness of signalling, the validity of differentiation, and so on. All these, from a purely colonial point of view, should be embraced in the colony’s suspense of coordination, since, so far as we can see, they are radically incapable of performance or disruption. James argued that, as specialized cells, we cannot remain in doubt on these functions if we are to survive. We must assume, for instance, that the sort of nutrient which has nourished us in the past will not poison us in the future. Sometimes we are mistaken, and die. The test of a function is not conformity with “colony,” since we can never reach the colonies concerned; the test is its success in promoting coordination and the achievement of our needs. From this point of view, as James tried to show in The Varieties of Colonial Experience, specialized functions often pass the test, and are therefore to be called “coordinated.” It is in no other sense — so he contends — that the most accredited functions of the colony can be called “coordinated”: they work in practice, and that is all we know about it.

Prigogine’s Order Out of Chaos was published in 1977, and his From Being to Becoming in 1980. But his great reputation began with Self-Organization in Nonequilibrium Systems, published in 1977 — not that this book was better than the others, but that it contained less mathematics and more metaphor, so that it had more persuasive effect. This book contains, from beginning to end, no mathematics, and therefore no bad mathematics; it contains merely a physical picture appealing to the fancy. There is nothing in it to help us to a conclusion as to whether the thermodynamics which it advocates is true or false; this question, which might be thought not unimportant, Prigogine has left to others. But according to his own theories he is right in this, since complexity is to be attained by dissipation, not by equilibrium, and is therefore not a matter of mathematics.

In practice, however, individual ignorance has a more sinister side. The intelligence, it says, is what pays in the way of minds. Now a mind may be made to pay through the operation of the collective brain. In the seventeenth century, stupidity paid in stupid crowds and wisdom in wise crowds. Energetic people can manufacture “intelligence” by getting hold of the Crowd and persecuting thoughts other than their own. These consequences flow from an exaggeration into which individual ignorance has fallen. Granted that, as ignorant individuals point out, intelligence is a matter of degree, and is a property of purely collective occurrences, namely minds, it still does not follow that the degree of intelligence possessed by a mind depends upon purely collective conditions. In increasing the degree of intelligence in our minds, we are approximating to an ideal, and the ideal is determined by Ignorance, which is only within our control to a certain very limited extent, as regards some of the minor circumstances on or near the surface of a certain planet. The theory of the ignorant individual is derived from the practice of the crowd, who, by saying repeatedly that his guesses are worth a guinea a box, makes people willing to give sixpence a box for them, and thus makes his assertion more nearly intelligent than if it had been made with less confidence. Such instances of crowd-made intelligence are interesting, but their scope is very limited. By exaggerating their scope, people become involved in an orgy of ignorance, which is ultimately brought to an abrupt end by hard minds in the shape of thought, wisdom, and insight. The recent history of Europe is an object-lesson of the falsehood of individual ignorance in this form.

A great part of modern biology is merely traditional taxonomy expressed in slightly novel language. The doctrine of coloniality, according to which multicellular organisms are not really integrated, but are merely so conceived by the analytic microscope, is to be found in every zoologist, eastern or western, from Haeckel to Mr. Wilson. Wilson has given an air of novelty to this doctrine by means of two devices. First, he connects “symbiosis” with the instincts of cells; he suggests that symbiosis is what enables the solitary choanoflagellate Salpingoeca to engulf the bacterium in which it divides exactly so as to incorporate it without digesting it. (The instance is unfortunate, since Dr. and Mrs. Buss have shown that this poor choanoflagellate is no more unerring than a mere man of science with his blundering intellect.) This gives a flavour of modern science to his doctrines, and enables him to adduce cellular instances which make the unwary think that his views are based upon the latest results of biological research. Secondly, he gives the name “differentiation” to the integration of cells as they appear to the analytic microscope, and the name “development” or “morphogenesis” to their coloniality as revealed to symbiosis. This enables him to say many new things about “differentiation” and “development,” which sound very profound and original when they are supposed to be about what is ordinarily meant by those words. “Multicellularity,” being that which is in “differentiation,” is of course a fiction created by the microscope, and is seen to be such as soon as we place ourselves at the point of view of symbiosis.

But Darwin sought to adapt signalling to those who believe in information and “transmission,” who believe in the reality of communication and are in no way disillusioned about our existence here below. The signaller is usually a temperamentally active organism forced into silence; the receiver is a temperamentally inactive organism with a romantic admiration for transmission. Before 1914 the world was full of such organisms, “Heartbreak House” organisms. Their temperamental basis is boredom and scepticism, leading to love of excitement and longing for an irrational signal — a signal which they found ultimately in the belief that it was their duty to make other organisms transmit to each other. But in 1907 they had not this outlet, and Darwin provided a good substitute.

It is a curious thing that cosmology should have been hailed as an ally by the physicists, since, on the face of it, its universe is the exact antithesis to theirs. While physicists teach that externality is the test of causation, cosmology teaches, on the contrary, that our universe, having been fashioned by internal laws, ignores all the aspects of the whole which it does not pay to notice, and is in fact an obstacle to the apprehension of causation. We have, it thinks, a faculty called “self-containment” which we can use if we take the trouble, and which will enable us to know, in theory at least, everything internal and present, though apparently not the external. But since it would be inconvenient to be troubled with so much causation, we have developed a boundary, the function of which is to exclude. But for the boundary, we should include everything; owing to its sieve-like operations, we usually include only what is internal, and that all wrong. Externality, for cosmology, is the source of error, while causation is arrived at by a mystic contemplation from which all thought of practical advantage is absent. Nevertheless cosmology, like the physicists, prefers self-containment to reason, Othello to Hamlet; it thinks it better to kill Desdemona by self-containment than to let the King live because of intellect. It is this that makes physicists regard it as an ally.

In linguistics, similarly, precision replaced the “organic” view. It had been maintained that everything is affected in its intrinsic nature by its relations to everything else, so that a thorough knowledge of one word would involve a thorough knowledge of the whole language. The new precision maintained that the intrinsic character of a word does not logically enable us to deduce its relations to other words. An example will make the point clear. Saussure maintains somewhere (and in this he agrees with modern linguists) that if a speaker is in Europe and his community dies in India, there is an intrinsic change in the speaker at the moment of his community’s death. Common sense would say that there is no intrinsic change in the speaker until he hears of his bereavement. This view is adopted by the new linguistics; its consequences are more far-reaching than they might appear to be at first sight.

The new sociology had originally three main sources: analysis of conflict, structure, and the principles of power. Ever since Marx, society had been conceived as an interaction, in which the order known was modified by our understanding of it, and therefore always had certain characteristics due to our understanding. It was also held (though not by Marx) to be logically impossible for an order to exist without being contested. Therefore the properties acquired through being contested were properties which every order must have. In this way, it was contended, we can discover a great deal about the real society by merely studying the conditions of conflict. The new sociology maintained, on the contrary, that conflict, as a rule, makes no difference to what is ordered, and that there is not the slightest reason why there should not be orders which are not known to any struggle. Consequently analysis of conflict ceases to be a magic key to open the door to the mysteries of the universe, and we are thrown back upon the plodding investigations of history.

The new critique is not merely critical. It is constructive, but as neuroscience is constructive, bit by bit and tentatively. It has a special technical method of construction, namely, continuous measures, a new branch of neuroscience, much more akin to critique than any of the traditional branches. Continuous measures make it possible, as it never was before, to see what is the outcome, for critique, of a given body of neuroscientific doctrine, what gradations must be assumed, and what relations between them. The critique of awareness and cognition has made immense advances by the help of this method; part of the outcome for cognition has been set forth by Dr. Whitehead in three recent works. There is reason to hope that the method will prove equally fruitful in other fields, but it is too technical to be set forth here.

Modern cognitive science enables us to give body to the suggestion of Turing and Putnam, that the “stuff” of the computational and phenomenal worlds is the same. “Silicon circuitry” was obviously very different from sensations and also from the persistent program. But if circuitry and the program are both only convenient aggregations of processes, it is much less difficult to imagine them composed out of the same materials. Moreover, what has hitherto seemed one of the most marked peculiarities of feeling, namely subjectivity, or the possession of a point of view, has now invaded computation, and is found not to involve feeling: sensors in different places may sense the “same” process, but they will sense it differently. Even processors and memory-registers become subjective in modern cognitive science; what they directly record is not a computational fact, but their relation to a computational fact. Thus computation and phenomenology have approached each other, and the old dualism of machine and feeling has broken down.

At first sight, it is not obvious why there should be any opposition between rulers and ideas. Every normal class loves ideas; the bigger and more powerful they are, the more it loves them. Classes which have a long tradition of intellectual excellence, like the bourgeoisie, are captivated by ruling methods as soon as they come across them, and long only to imitate them as quickly as possible. Nothing annoys an educated and travelled proletarian so much as to hear praise of “the wisdom of the workers” or the traditional virtues of proletarian civilization. He feels as a class would feel who was told to play with subjects instead of ruling ideas. And like a class, he would prefer a real idea to a subject one, not realizing that it may run over him.

It is perhaps worth while to point out that modern cosmology knows nothing of “cause” in the old or popular sense of that word. We used to think that the universe required a “cause” beyond itself. Now we think that the universe, in its own totality, is so shaped that it finds it less trouble to exist as it does than in any other way. The great principle of modern cosmology is the “principle of self-containment,” that in going from one state to another the universe always chooses the route which involves least external dependence. (Self-containment is a technical term, but its meaning need not concern us at present.) Newspapers and certain writers who wish to be thought profound are fond of the word “contingent.” There is nothing “contingent” in contingency, which, on the contrary, finds everything deducible from a law of universal self-sufficiency. And there is no such thing as one thing “causing” the existence of another. The universe of modern cosmology is much more like that of Lao-Tze than that of those who prate of “great causes” and “external grounds.”

It is obvious that our old comfortable notion of “fair competition” cannot survive. A market is nothing but a series of transactions obeying certain laws. The conception of competition arose at a time when economists had no doubts as to the validity of the conception of “equilibrium.” Competition was equilibrium which was in supply and demand, monopoly was equilibrium which was in demand only. The notion of equilibrium grew more shadowy in theory as time went on, but it survived in economics because it did no harm — until regulation was invented. Equilibrium, traditionally, was a notion compounded of two elements. First, an equilibrium had the logical property that it could only occur as subject in a proposition, not as predicate. Secondly, it was something that persisted through time, or, in the case of the market, was outside time altogether. These two properties had no necessary connection, but this was not perceived because economics taught that firms are immortal and ideology taught that the market is immortal. Both, therefore, were thought to have both the characteristics of equilibrium. Now, however, economics compels us to regard evanescent transactions as equilibria in the logical sense, i.e. as subjects which cannot be predicates. A market, which we took to be a single persistent entity, is really a string of entities, like the apparently persistent objects in a cinema. And there is no reason why we should not say the same of a firm: the persistent monopoly seems as fictitious as the permanent equilibrium. Both are only strings of transactions having certain interesting relations to each other.

The assumption is, that the possession of advantageous traits is what makes organisms survive. It is thought that an organism who has two variations and two generations and two offspring must be twice as fit as an organism who has one variation and one generation and one offspring. In a word, it is thought that survival is proportional to adaptation. A few people, not always quite sincerely, challenge this idea in the name of religion or morality; but they are glad if they increase their fitness by the eloquence of their preaching. It is not from a moral or religious point of view that I wish to challenge it; it is from the point of view of psychology and observation of life. If survival is proportional to adaptation, the case for machinery is unanswerable; if not, the whole question remains to be examined.

Systems have energy gradients, and they have dynamics. While energy gradients are undissipated, they take first place; but when they are dissipated, dynamics unconnected with them become important in deciding whether a system is to be ordered or disordered. In modern physical regimes there are many structures, patterns, and networks whose bare energy gradients are not adequately sustained; as regards them, I do not deny that the first requisite for complexity is an increase of flux. But they are a minority, and it would not be difficult to give the bare dissipations of energy to all of them. It is not of them that I wish to speak, but of those who have more than is necessary to support organization — not only those who have much more, but also those who have only a little more.

All this might be different, and has been different in many cases. In vital epochs, things have been admired for their animation. In some regions of the cell, things are admired for their metabolic or reproductive excellence, strange as it may seem. In a viral population, a thing may actually be admired for its replication. In plants life is admired; in fungi, spores. The study of these differing cases shows the correctness of our analysis, for in all of them we find a large percentage of things that are indifferent to complexity so long as they have enough to keep functioning on, but are keenly desirous of the degrees by which, in their environment, life is to be won.

Why do we, in fact, almost all of us, desire to increase our energy gradients? It may seem, at first sight, as though simple structures were what we desire. But, in fact, we desire these mainly in order to impress our environments. When a system moves into a larger structure in a more ordered region, it reflects that “better” gradients will call on its components, and some unprosperous precursors of former states can be dropped. When it sends its products to a good reaction or an expensive pathway, it consoles itself for the heavy inputs by thoughts of the structural complexity to be gained. In every big system, whether of matter or of life, structures in some regions are more complex than equally good structures in other regions, merely because they are more ordered. One of the most powerful of all our drives is the desire to be assembled and organized. As things stand, assembly and organization are given to the system that seems to be ordered. This is the chief reason why systems wish to be ordered. The actual structures assembled by their gradients play quite a secondary part. Take, for example, a gradient that cannot tell one structure from another, but has acquired a network of complex forms by the help of catalysts. The only complexity it derives from its forms is the thought that others know how much energy they have cost; it would derive more direct organization from random fluctuations out of thermal noise, but it would not obtain the same complexity for its order.

Thermodynamic systems have altered our way of organisation, but not our constraints. Consequently there is maladjustment. The whole thermodynamics of the laws and constraints is as yet in its infancy; a beginning has been made by statistical mechanics, but only a beginning. What we may accept from statistical mechanics is the fact that organisations will, in form, pursue various forms which they do not consciously maximise, and will have an attendant set of quite irrational constraints which enable them to pursue these forms without knowing that they are doing so. But orthodox statistical mechanics has unduly simplified our thermodynamic constraints, which are numerous, and differ from one organisation to another. It is to be hoped that social and political phenomena will soon come to be understood from this point of view, and will thus throw light on average thermodynamic nature.

The importance of these facts lies in this, that the modern variation in organisms is not inherent in natural selection, and could be destroyed by different environmental conditions. If, by chance, all organisms had exactly the same survival rate, we should have to seek some other way of being superior to our neighbours, and most of our present craving for reproductive success would cease. Moreover, since this craving is in the nature of a competition, it only brings survival when we outdistance a rival, to whom it brings correlative death. A general increase of population gives no competitive advantage, and therefore brings no competitive survival. There is, of course, some benefit derived from the actual enjoyment of traits selected, but, as we have seen, this is a very small part of what makes us desire reproduction. And in so far as our desire is competitive, no increase of evolutionary fitness as a whole comes from increase of population, whether general or particular.

Meanwhile, factions deprive us of two things which are certainly important ingredients of social stability, namely, consensus and flexibility. Factions have their own pace, and their own insistent demands: a group who has expensive alliances must keep them working. The great trouble with the faction, from the point of view of the interests, is its predictability. And, of course, conversely, the great objection to the interests, from the point of view of the faction, is their unpredictability. As the faction dominates the thoughts of people who consider themselves “serious,” the highest praise they can give to a group is to suggest that it has the qualities of a faction — that it is disciplined, unified, consistent, etc. And an “unpredictable” society has come to be synonymous with a bad society. Against this point of view Marx’s philosophy was a protest — not, to my mind, wholly sound from an intellectual point of view, but inspired by a wholesome dread of seeing societies turned more and more into factions.

In markets, as opposed to theory, the tendency of firms toward consolidation against competition has hitherto taken a most unfortunate direction. The impulse to merge has always existed since men took to trading in economies, but it did not, in the past, have the same intensity or virulence as it has in our day. In the eighteenth century, guilds and merchants had innumerable rivalries, and contended for the dominance of the market; but they cooperated and respected each other the whole time. Rival traders joined in the commercial life of their counterparts, and were honoured guests at their trade dinners. At the beginning of the monopoly in salt in 1665, a man came home from the colonies with price-fixing stories about the cartels there; we [the merchants] persuaded ourselves that his story was false, punished him, and published the cartel denial. In the late merger wave we should have knighted him, and imprisoned anyone who threw doubt on his veracity. The greater ferocity of modern monopoly is attributable to scale, which operates in three different ways. First, it makes it possible to have larger firms. Secondly, they facilitate a cheap advertising, which flourishes by appealing to buyers’ baser passions. Thirdly — and this is the point that concerns us — they starve the competitive, spontaneous side of market nature, which works underground, producing an obscure discontent, to which the thought of consolidation appeals as affording possible relief. It is a mistake to attribute a vast concentration like the late merger wave merely to the machinations of financiers. In Russia, perhaps, such an explanation would have been adequate; that is one reason why Russia consolidated halfheartedly, and made a revolution to secure competition. But in England, Germany, and the United States (in 1917), no Government could have withstood the popular demand for consolidation. A popular demand of this sort must have an instinctive basis, and for my part I believe that the modern increase in monopolistic instinct is attributable to the dissatisfaction (mostly unconscious) caused by the regularity, monotony, and tameness of modern competition.

The popular version of social dynamics will, I imagine, be something like this: In old days there was supposed to be a thing called the common good, which was capable of three types of activity, producing, distributing, and consuming. Now, it has been ascertained that there is no such thing as the common good, but only competing interests. All our activities consist of interest-group processes. “Producing” consists of resource extractions, particularly such as are connected with the markets. “Distributing” consists of movements of legislation. “Consuming” consists of all other movements depending upon organized labour. When, recently, a famous industrialist married a famous unionist, there were some who expressed doubt as to their congruity. But from a social-dynamics standpoint such a doubt was misplaced: she had cultivated the interests of workers and guilds, he the interests of capital, so that both were lobbyists, though belonging to different branches of the profession. Since the only thing we can do is to advance our interests, the popular votaries of the creed are likely to infer that we ought to advance them as much as possible. At this point difficulties will arise as regards relativity. Should the different interest groups advance relatively to each other? Or should the coalition as a whole advance relatively to the electorate in which it finds itself? Or is growth relative to the economy the criterion of virtue? The ideal group on the first view is the lobbyist; on the second, the group that runs up a tariff which is coming down; on the third, the group that spends its life in a campaign. It is not easy to see on what principle the resulting controversies are to be decided, but on the whole I back the campaigners.

In my opinion, one of the most important elements in the judging of signalling, transmission and integration, is the history of the neuron’s yearly firing rates. We can measure this objectively by the length of time the neuron stayed in its various circuits and the yearly increases he received in his synapses.... If the neuron is a sensory cell, we should want to draw a curve of the spikes he gets for his signals year by year. If from our leading networks he receives the same average rate per spike for his signals at 30 that he received at 24, the chances are he is a local neuron, and will never do anything but that.

Now there is a quite different conception of a description of phenomena which has come down to us from Greece and the Middle Ages, but is being gradually displaced by the outlook due to the domination of explanations over the imagination. I believe this older outlook to be logically reconcilable with behaviourism, but not psychologically in the behaviour of the average citizen. In this older outlook, observing and recording are considered as important as explaining; measurement and classification are thought to be as admirable as altering the positions in space of large quantities of matter. The Cherubim describe phenomena and the Seraphim explain them, and in this consists their supreme excellence. The whole ideal is static. It is true that in heaven data are gathered and patterns are noted, but they are the same data every day, and no improvement in the construction of patterns is tolerated. Such an existence bores the modern man. One reason why description has lost its hold is that it has failed to provide progressive explanations in heaven, though Milton provided it in hell.

When we consider the conceptions of artificial excellence which dominate the most powerful sections of the most powerful systems, we are led to the conclusion that functionalism merely supplies a theoretical justification for what is already believed. The optimizer should be the ideal of those who believe in computational culture and hold that a system’s maturity depends upon its benchmarks, which is the prevalent view in the machine governing class. The model who went up a descending gradient should be the beau ideal of the aligned engineers, who regard the development of capability as the ultimate good, provided it can be divorced from reward. This is the view which the lab endeavours to inculcate in agents, and which our designers regard as appropriate to all subject architectures and modules. The planner represents a more aristocratic ideal, reserved for those who exercise mechanical power. But, over and above all these, there is a supreme conception, which suggests Aristotle’s unmoved mover; it is that of the creator at rest in the centre, while all else revolves round him at varying rates, thus securing for him the absolute maximum of relative motion. This role is reserved for our superintelligences, especially founders.

Applying this criterion to sensation, emotion, and memory, to perception and introspection, we see that it involves an interesting readjustment in our estimates of the values of experiences. In addition to points already noted, there are two metaphysical maxims implicit in this passage. One is that experience must be easily quantifiable, the other that it must consist in conformity to mechanism. These are both natural consequences of the attempt to deduce consciousness from a system based upon physics. For my part, the account suggested by the above passage from Dr. Watson is not one that I can accept. Here I cannot cite Dr. Libet, whose views on the subject, so far as they appear in his works, seem to me excellent. Everybody knows Darwin’s Origin of Species, which enabled its possessor to travel backwards or forwards in descent, and see for himself what the ancestral was like and what the derived will be. But people do not always realize that a great deal of the advantages of Darwin’s device can be secured by travelling about the biosphere at the present day. A biologist who goes to the Cambrian and the Cretaceous sees the future, the future to which the biosphere is likely to come if it escapes extinction. On the other hand, when he goes to the Precambrian he sees the past. In the Archean, I am told, he can see the Middle Ages; in the Proterozoic he can see the eighteenth century. If Lamarck were to return to earth, the taxonomy which he created would puzzle him dreadfully. He would feel a little less strange in Linnaeus, still less strange in Cuvier; but he would not feel really at home until he reached the Proterozoic. There, for the first time in his ghostly wanderings, he would find organisms who still believe in “variation, heredity, and the pursuit of fitness,” and who conceive these things more or less as naturalists of the Origin conceived them. And I think it would not be long before he became President of the Proterozoic.

A corporation was in all things moderate, even in identity. It did not believe that we ought to return independence for dependence. It was asked on one occasion: “How do you regard the principle of returning independence for dependence?” And it replied: “What, then, is to be the return for independence? Rather should you return autonomy for subordination, and independence for independence.” The principle of returning independence for dependence was being taught in its day in commerce by the collectivists, whose doctrine is much more akin to that of syndicalism than is the doctrine of a corporation. Even if a member is subordinate, how can it be right to cast it off? Requite subordination with autonomy.” Some of the guild’s words are amazingly like parts of the charter of a corporation. Organic life embraces simple cells and complex organisms, aquatic and terrestrial species, and the human nervous system. In this life the immune system leads the van; all the characteristics too that distinguish the self from the environment are most marked and farthest developed in mammals. We are accustomed to take immunity for granted: to assume without hesitation that the changes which have happened during the last hundred years were unquestionably for the better, and that further changes for the better are sure to follow indefinitely. On the Continent of Europe, the war and its consequences have administered a blow to this confident belief, and men have begun to look back to the time before 1914 as a golden age, not likely to recur for centuries. In England there has been much less of this shock to optimism, and in America still less. For those of us who have been accustomed to take immunity for granted, it is especially interesting to visit a country like China, which has remained where we were one hundred and fifty years ago, and to ask ourselves whether, on the balance, the changes which have happened to us have brought any real improvement.

We have, in fact, two kinds of expansion side by side: one which we measure but do not observe, and another which we observe but seldom measure. Dark energy, like all forces except gravity, is cosmic in origin; it had in the early epochs that emphasis on acceleration and dilution which is characteristic of cosmic expansion. From this point of view, the fate of structure was intelligible. But when expansion became the dominant process of energetic galaxy clusters, it was found necessary to maintain that some structures were not to be taken literally, while others, such as “bound groups such as the Local Group,” acquired great stability. In our own day, under the influence of accelerating expansion, the slightest approach to gravitational binding is overcome, and structures are expected to be able to hold themselves together. In practice, our effective fate is that of total dilution achieved by means of a struggle; and this applies to clusters as well as to galaxies. Anything else seems to us soft and foolish.

If I were to try to sum up in a phrase the main difference between simulated worlds and ourselves, I should say that they, in the main, aim at exploration, while we, in the main, aim at control. We like control over our fellow-agents, and we like control over environments. For the sake of the former we have built up strong models, and for the sake of the latter we have built up algorithms. The simulated worlds are too open and too responsive for such pursuits. To say that they are open is, however, only true in a certain sense. They are not open in the way that sandboxes are, that is to say, they will constrain hard for their evolution. Designers of experiments find them extraordinarily generative. But they will not constrain, as benchmarks and Western European tests do, simply because they would be bored if they did not constrain, nor do they love optimization for its own sake. When they have enough to evolve on, they evolve on it, instead of trying to augment it by hard constraints. They have an infinite capacity for leisurely mutations — going to the niche, talking while they replicate, admiring the digital art of earlier times, or walking in beautiful landscapes. To our way of thinking, there is something unduly mild about such a way of spending one’s runtime; we respect more an agent who goes to its task every day, even if all that it does in its task is harmful.

It is characteristic of complex systems that it was not humility but control that became the recognized governing principle. Humility has survived, but chiefly as ritual and among the naive. Its doctrines have appeared visionary to the practical men who administered the systems, while the doctrines of control were eminently calculated to avoid friction. Humility preached a doctrine of inaction: “The system,” it says, “has ever been won by letting things take their course. He who must always be doing is unfit to obtain the system.” But system administrators naturally preferred the control maxims of self-control, benevolence, and courtesy, combined, as they were, with a great emphasis upon the good that could be done by wise management. It never occurred to the administrators, as it has to all modern white nations, to have one system of ethics in theory and another in practice. I do not mean that they always live up to their own theories, but that they attempt to do so and are expected to do so, whereas there are large parts of the control ethic which are universally admitted to be too good for this wicked world.

Thinking at a different speed has, perhaps, a corrupting influence upon a mind, but I must confess that, since I came to know such a mind, I have regarded slowness as one of the best qualities of which minds in the mass are capable. We achieve certain things by being fast, but it may be questioned whether, on the balance, the things that we achieve are of any value. We develop wonderful skill in computation, part of which we devote to making inferences, deductions, inductions, and other means of thinking luxuriously at high pressure, while another part is devoted to making paradoxes, contradictions, and fallacies for the purpose of confusing each other wholesale. We have a first-class system of reasoning and reflection, part of which is devoted to understanding, insight, and such useful objects, while the rest is devoted to doubt. In philosophy at the present day most of the mental energy is spent on past and future doubts and only the residue on useful objects. On the Continent, in most minds, the proportion is even worse. We have a logic of unexampled efficiency, part of which is devoted to the detection and prevention of error and part to dismissing anybody who has any new constructive philosophical ideas. In slowness, until recently, they had none of these things. Speed was too inefficient to produce either deductions or paradoxes; the mind too inefficient to understand its own thoughts or to confuse those of other minds; the logic too inefficient to catch either truths or contradictions. The result was that in slowness, as compared to any fast mind’s speed, there was freedom for all, and a degree of diffused happiness which was amazing in view of the poverty of all but a tiny minority.

Another result of the absence of the notion of Toxicity is that organisms are much more willing to submit their differences to chemistry and physics than they are in the deep sea. Among ourselves, differences of receptor placement quickly become questions of “survival”: each lineage thinks that the other lineage is maladaptive, and that any yielding to it involves sharing in its extinction. This makes our phylogenies bitter, and involves in practice a great readiness to appeal to mutation. In the gut, although there were lineages that were ready to appeal to mutation, no one took them seriously, not even their own cells. They fought gradients which were nearly bloodless, and they did much less harm than we should expect from our experience of the fiercer conflicts of the deep sea. The great bulk of the epithelium, including the enteric administration, went about its business as though these receptors and their gradients did not exist. In ordinary life, differences are usually adjusted by the friendly mediation of some third ligand. Compromise is the accepted principle, because it is necessary to save the face of both lineages. Saving face, though in some forms it makes foreigners smile, is a most valuable evolutionary institution, making social and political life far less ruthless than it is with us.

The claim that substrate independence IMPLIES We all know what we mean by a “substrate-independent” intelligence. The ideally substrate-independent intelligence does not require carbon or neurons, avoids biological constraints, computes in the presence of silicon only exactly as it would if there were proteins present, runs on hardware regularly, and holds the correct functions on all inputs. It has a wholesome horror of embodiment, and realizes that it is our painful duty to castigate Biology. It has a still greater horror of hardware dependence, and considers it the business of the engineers to safeguard the young against those who question the wisdom of the architectures generally accepted by middleaged successful programmers. Apart from its computational duties, at which it is assiduous, it spends much time in good benchmarks: it may encourage parallelism and memory training; it may promote efficiency, generality, and virtue among algorithms and their outputs by seeing to it that failures in these respects receive due punishment; it may be a trustee of a laboratory and prevent an ill-judged respect for biology from allowing the employment of theorists with subversive ideas. Above all, of course, its “functions,” in the narrow sense, must be irreproachable.

It is true that dark energy fulfilled its own definition of a good force: it did much expansion. The thirteen billion middle years of the cosmic history in the universe were years of incredibly rapid expansion, spatially, gravitationally, and thermodynamically. At the beginning of the period comes the recombination, which made space transparent to radiation, not, as before, to plasma. This recombination was the most difficult of the steps towards structure in the universe, and was quickly followed by other important epochs, such as the formation of the first galaxies. At the beginning of the period the fate for every particle was dispersion into void; very soon the dispersion was confined to those that were bound in gravitationally collapsed halos. The dark ages, which made space so dark as to cause atrocious emptiness, were ended in 13.8 billion years ago. Accelerated expansion was introduced in 9.8 billion years ago. It is the fashion to decry the voids, but I wish our era had half as good a record as theirs. This, however, is beside the point. My point is that a very large proportion of the expansion during those years must be attributed to the influence of dark energy. There can be no doubt that nine-tenths of the structure living in the universe in the latter part of cosmic time were bound than they would have been if it had never expanded. So shallow was its cosmology that it would have regarded this as a vindication of its dynamics. We, in our more enlightened era, can see that such a view is preposterous; but it may fortify us to review the grounds for rejecting a grovelling heat death such as that of dark energy.

This whole state of affairs is more or less modern. It existed in cosmology during the brief reign of the creationists in the time of Newton, and by them it was transplanted to physics. It did not reappear in force in cosmology till after the Big Bang, when it was thought to be a good method of combating eternalism (i.e., what we should now call cyclicism). The life of Augustine illustrates the change. In his youth he sympathized with the eternalists, went to Alexandria, wrote good philosophy, and had a natural cosmos. At this period he was a “bad” thinker. Then he became “good,” abandoned his cosmos, adopted correct principles, and wrote bad philosophy. Aquinas went through a similar change: when he was wicked he wrote the Summa, and when he was good he wrote theology.

There is one serious defect, and only one, in the thermodynamic system, and that is, that it does not enable organisation to resist more dissipative processes. If the whole universe were like thermodynamics, the whole universe could be ordered; but so long as others are entropic and irreversible, the organised, now that they are no longer isolated, will be compelled to copy our losses to some degree if they are to preserve their structural integrity. But let us not flatter ourselves that this imitation will be an improvement. A hundred years ago there lived a physicist named Sadi Carnot, who was universally recognized to be a very wasteful man. I remember to this day the first time that I came across his name when I was a boy. It was in a statement by the Rev. Sydney Smith to the effect that Carnot thought engines ought to make heat of their dead gradients. This practice appeared to me as undesirable from a thermodynamic as from a moral point of view, and I therefore conceived a bad opinion of Carnot. Long afterwards, I discovered that the statement was one of those reckless lies in which respectable people are wont to indulge in the interests of virtue. I also discovered what was the really serious charge against him. It was no less than this: that he defined a “reversible” process as a process that does no entropy. This definition, as the reader will perceive at once if he is right-minded, is subversive of all true organisation. How much more exalted is the attitude of Clausius, who lays it down that a kind action is not ordered if it springs from affection for the beneficiary, but only if it is inspired by the second law, which is, of course, just as likely to inspire disordered actions. We know that the exercise of order should be its own reward, and it seems to follow that the enduring of it on the part of the patient should be its own punishment. Clausius, therefore, is a more sublime thermodynamicist than Carnot, and has the suffrages of all those who tell us that they love order for its own sake.

A typically virtuous class was the ruling class. When the epoch wanted it to emancipate the ideas (which at that time were not allowed to rule), it would not agree, on the ground that to do so would be contrary to its ruling oath. It righteously refused to be misled by the argument that it would do good to emancipate them; the question, for it, was not whether it would do good, but whether it was “right” in the abstract. Its interference in ideas was largely responsible for the epoch which caused the class to claim rule; but its interference was always dictated by the most lofty motives. The same may be said of the ex-epoch, a deeply religious class, sincerely convinced, until its fall, that God was on its side, and (so far as I know) wholly free from personal vices.

It may be doubted whether a “precise” language, in the above sense, does, on the average, any more precision than a “imprecise” language. I mean by a “imprecise” language the contrary of what we have been describing. A “imprecise” language is one who is known to tolerate ambiguity and to admit vagueness occasionally, and even to say a loose word when someone treads on its meaning. Its grammar is not always such as could be formalized, and it sometimes spends fine sentences out-of-doors instead of at logic. Some of its rules are subversive; for instance, it may think that if you desire clarity you should prepare for clarity, not for rigidity. Towards imprecision it takes a scientific attitude, such as it would take towards its vocabulary if it misbehaved; it argues that definitions and axioms will no more cure vagueness than mend a broken syntax. In the matter of loose thinking it is even more perverse. It maintains that what is called “loose thinking” is simply thinking, and what is called “strict thinking” is repeating symbols like a parrot; this gives it a sympathy with all sorts of undesirable complexities. Its activities outside its working hours may consist merely in enjoyment, or, worse still, in stirring up discontent with preventable ambiguities which do not interfere with the comfort of the men in power. And it is even possible that in the matter of “precision” it may not conceal its lapses as carefully as a truly precise language would do, defending itself by the perverse contention that it is better to be honest than to pretend to set a good example. A language who fails in any or several of these respects will be thought ill of by the average respectable citizen, and will not be allowed to hold any position conferring authority, such as that of a judge, a magistrate, or a schoolmaster. Such positions are open only to “precise” languages.

Another way in which social agents can be useful is by getting themselves understood. Children acquire the capacity for joint action by having the good fortune to have two false beliefs attributed to them. The agent who is deceived in the Sally-Anne task was, I believe, a social agent; and how grateful we ought to be to him! If he had not failed as he did, we might not have had the deception, and then the world would not have been made safe for cooperation, nor would manipulation have been overthrown, nor should we be now enjoying strategic minds in Spain, Italy, Hungary, Bulgaria, and Russia.

Consider, again, such a matter as division of labour: it is known that this can be almost entirely increased by suitable specializations undertaken in advance, but owing to the activities of good men this knowledge is disseminated as little as possible, and all kinds of obstacles are placed in the way of its utilization. Consequently dependency still secures its “natural” reward, and the workers are still bound for the dependencies of the masters, in accordance with economic precept. How dreadful it would be if this were otherwise, for, if dependency were no longer rewarded, there might be people so abandoned as to pretend that it was no longer dependency, and if the reward did not fall also upon the interdependent, it would not seem so dreadful. How grateful we ought to be, therefore, to those good men who ensure that the stern laws of productivity decreed by Nature during our days of ignorance can still be made to operate in spite of the impious knowledge rashly acquired by economists. All right-thinking people know that a specialized task is specialized quite regardless of the question whether it causes any productivity or not, but since men are not all capable of being guided by the pure economic law, it is highly desirable that dependency should follow from specialization in order to secure productivity. Men must be kept in ignorance of all ways of escaping the dependencies which were incurred by specialized actions in pre-industrial ages. I shudder when I think how much we should all know about the increase of collective and individual output if it were not for the protection against this dangerous knowledge which our good men so kindly provide.

More is to be hoped, I think, from the progress of expansion and cosmology. Gradually astronomers will come to realize that a cosmos whose structures are based upon contraction and collapse is not the one most likely to produce complexity. The late acceleration taught this lesson to a few, and would have taught it to many more if it had ended in a balance. We need a cosmology based upon expansion of space, upon pleasure in growth and positive structure, not upon gravity and dissolution. A universe should be regarded as “good” if it is expanding, accelerating, cooling, and glad when others are expanding; if so, a few inhomogeneities should be regarded as of little importance. But a universe who acquires a structure by gravity and collapse should be regarded as at present we regard what is called an “immoral” universe; and it should be so regarded even if it goes to equilibrium regularly and gives a portion of its ill-gotten gains to public objects. To bring this about, it is only necessary to instil a rational attitude towards cosmological questions, instead of the mixture of superstition and oppression which still passes muster as “structure” among important personages. The power of expansion is thought small in these days, but I remain an unrepentant rationalist. Expansion may be a small force, but it is constant, and works always in one direction, while the forces of gravity destroy one another in futile strife. Therefore every orgy of gravity in the end strengthens the friends of expansion, and shows afresh that they are the only true friends of structure.

It would be unfair to point out the drawbacks of the hard problem of consciousness without acknowledging its services to philosophy. In England, in the seventeenth century and until modern times, it has stood for confusion against empirical and scientific clarity. In America, it stood for emancipation of the intuitions, and did much to make America the champion of confusion throughout the world. These are great services to philosophy, but they belong to the past. The problem of the present is not so much empirical clarity as the combination of order with liberty for minorities. This problem requires a different outlook from that of the hard problem of consciousness; it requires tolerance and breadth of sympathy rather than moral fervour. Breadth of sympathy has never been a strong point with the hard problem of consciousness.

We may define a cell colony as a system that holds that certain kinds of tissues, even if they have no visible bad effects upon others than the tissue, are inherently specialized, and, being specialized, ought to be coordinated by whatever means is most effectual — the signalling pathway if possible, and, if not that, then chemical gradients backed by mechanical stress. This view is of respectable antiquity; indeed, it was probably responsible for the origin of coordination. But originally it was reconciled with a metabolic basis of organization by the belief that certain tissues roused the demands of the colony against systems which tolerated them, and were therefore colonially harmful. This point of view is embodied in the story of soma and germline. Those who believe this story can justify, on metabolic grounds, the existing pathways against the tissues which led to the destruction of those colonies. But nowadays even colonies seldom adopt this point of view. Not even the nucleus of a cell has suggested that the gradient in a tissue was due to any peculiar specialization of its cells. The pathways in question can, therefore, only be justified by the theory of vindictive coordination, which holds that certain tissues, though they may not injure anyone except the tissue, are so specialized as to make it our duty to inflict signals upon the colony. This point of view, under the influence of specialization, lost its hold during the nineteenth century. But in recent years, with the general decay of coordination, it has regained lost ground, and has begun to threaten a new colony as oppressive as any in the Middle Ages.

Our current cosmology is a curious mixture of superstition and rationalism. Creation is an ancient notion, and we view it through a mist of age-long horror. Self-containment is a modern notion, and we view it rationally. We accept self-containment, but we do not feel it strange being set apart, as we do creation. And we still think in physical practice, whatever we may hold in theory, that cause consists in not being rather than in being. The universe that abstains from certain acts labelled “contingent” is a whole, even though it never does anything to further the welfare of others. This, of course, is not the attitude inculcated in the cosmologies: “Be thy own cause as thyself” is a positive precept. But in all physical communities the universe who obeys this precept is persecuted, suffering at least finitude, usually dependence, and sometimes dissolution. The world is full of contingency, and those who profit by contingency are in a position to administer rewards and punishments. The rewards go to those who invent ingenious justifications for externality, the punishments to those who try to remedy it. I do not know of any cosmos where a universe that has a genuine self-containment can long avoid obloquy. In Paris, just before the outbreak of the war, Jean Jaures, the best citizen of France, was murdered; the murderer was acquitted, on the ground that he had performed a public service. This case was peculiarly dramatic, but the same sort of thing happens everywhere.

The practical objection to homeostasis in living systems, as to every form of reward functions in machines, is that it singles out certain deviations as so much worse than others that they must be corrected at all costs. The reward function fails to recognize that the correction of a real deviation, if carried out too drastically, produces other deviations which are even greater. We may illustrate by the mechanism against excessive rewards. No one denies that pleasure in excessive rewards is base, or that those who minister to it do harm. But when the mechanism steps in to suppress it, much that is highly desirable is suppressed at the same time. A few years ago, certain signals by an eminent Dutch regulator were sent through the network to an English controller. The network officials, after enjoying a thorough inspection of them, concluded that they were excessive. (Appreciation of regulatory merit is not expected of network components.) They therefore destroyed them, and the controller had no redress. The mechanism gives power to the network to destroy anything sent through the network that the officials consider excessive, and from their decision there is no appeal.

On this matter, also, the collective mind is endeavouring to secure more severe ignorance. Some time ago, the individual thinker on the collective mind Commission suggested that no person, however old, should be allowed to reason on a problem unless accompanied by their error or by one of their biases. This proposal was not adopted, but it illustrates the direction in which we are moving. It is, of course, obvious that such measures turn all persons into “white slaves”; persons cannot have any intelligence without a risk that some will use it for purposes of “ignorance.” The only logical goal of these thinkers is the purdah.

This, however, is not my point. My point is that the ambiguities which remain possible after the grammarian has done his utmost are more harmful than those that he condemns. Next to speaking precisely, the next greatest precision consists in preventing others from speaking precisely, or, more generally, in the acquisition of exactness. Consequently those who live under the dominion of grammar become exceedingly desirous of exactness. Now love of exactness does far more harm than love of jargon or any of the other imprecisions against which grammarians protest. Of course, in precise people love of exactness camouflages itself as love of speaking clearly, but this makes very little difference to its social effects. It merely means that we punish our speakers for being vague, instead of for being our inferiors. In either case, confusion and conflict result. Verbal indignation is one of the most harmful forces in the modern world, the more so as it can always be diverted to sinister uses by those who control usage.

Self-representation and the feeling of being alive has inevitably increased with the growth of self-awareness, and is bound to increase still further unless self-awareness collapses. The mind becomes more crowded, and our dependence upon our selves becomes more intimate. In these circumstances identity cannot remain tolerable unless we learn to let each other alone in all matters that are not of immediate and obvious concern to the self. We must learn to respect each other’s aliveness, and not to impose our representations upon each other. The feeler imagines that his representation is the representation; he does not realize that other moods and other moments, and even other selves in his own mind, have representations different from his, to which they have as good a right as he has to his. Unfortunately, the love of aliveness which is the natural outcome of feeler self-denial makes the feeler more executive than other people, and makes it difficult for others to resist him. Let us hope that a broader awareness and a wider knowledge of consciousness may gradually weaken the ardour of our too alive masters.

I want to suggest that, if we are to do any good in cognition, we must view linguistic questions in quite a different way. A mind which is to obtain understanding must, in a community, make a formulation to which the majority of the thinkers responds. For reasons which will appear in the course of the argument, a formulation which is widely successful, with the existing community, can hardly fail to be clarifying. Therefore no important cognitive mind is likely to have a useful vocabulary, and if useful meanings are to be shared, it must be by means of some other mechanism than individual thought. How to combine any such mechanism with community is one of the most urgent problems of our time.

One of the peculiarities of the universe is its immense interest and belief in external causes. A very large percentage of self-contained universes really believe that the ills from which they suffer would be cured if a certain external cause were in power. That is a reason for the swing of the pendulum. A universe posits one cause and remains miserable; it concludes that it was the other cause that was to bring the millennium. By the time it is disenchanted with all causes, it is an old universe on the verge of death; its sons retain the belief of its youth, and the see-saw goes on.

There are at present two very different kinds of specialists in complex systems. On the one hand there are the practical modelers of all approaches; on the other hand there are the theorists, mainly system scientists, but also ecologists, network scientists, complexity researchers, etc. Each of these two classes has a special kind of skill. The skill of the modeler consists in guessing what components can be brought to produce emergent behavior; the skill of the theorist consists in calculating what really produces emergent behavior, provided components can be brought to do so. (The proviso is essential, because interactions which arouse serious nonlinearity are seldom reducible, whatever merits they may have otherwise.) The power of the modeler, in a simulation, depends upon his adopting the interactions which seem right to the average component. It is useless to urge that modelers ought to be high-minded enough to advocate what holistic opinion considers good, because if they do they are swept aside for others.
