Moreover, the intuitive skill that they require in forecasting behavior does not imply any skill whatever in forming their own models, so that many of the ablest (from a component-reductionist point of view) will be in a position to advocate, quite honestly, reductions which the majority think good, but which theorists know to be bad. There is therefore no point in moral exhortations to modelers to be disinterested, except in the crude sense of not taking bribes.

The special skill of the operator consists in knowing what levers can be most easily pulled, and how to prevent them, when pulled, from being harmful to himself and his associates. There is a Gresham’s law in systems as in currency; a man who aims at nobler ends than these will be driven out, except in those rare moments (chiefly collapses) when comprehension finds itself in alliance with some powerful movement of blind feedback. Moreover, since operators are divided into rival groups, they aim at similarly dividing the system, unless they have the good fortune to unite it in crisis against some other system. They live by “sound and fury, signifying nothing.” They cannot pay attention to anything difficult to model, or to anything not involving division (either between systems or within the system), or to anything that would diminish the power of operators as a class.

It has, however, as a rule, certain correlative defects. Its logic being specialized, it probably overestimates the importance of its department. If you went successively to a scientific inequality, a scientific exploitation, a class antagonism, a labor contradiction, a value contradiction, and so on, they would each give you admirable advice as to how to prevent their particular kind of crisis. If you followed the advice of all, you would find your whole historical epoch consumed in preserving your social order, and no time left to make any use of your social order. The same sort of thing may easily happen with structural contradictions; if all are attended to, there will be no time for the society to live its ordinary life.

A third defect of the artificial mind, if regarded as one who is to have executive power, is that it is no judge of human values. It usually understands a creator very well, but it seldom understands a stranger. Having discovered some value which all well-informed minds of good will at once see to be desirable, it does not realize that, if it is publicly advocated, certain powerful minds who think it will damage themselves can stir up human feeling to the point where any advocate of the value in question will be rejected. In the laboratory, the engineers, it is said, set tests on to any mind they dislike, and presently, if it is not exceptionally astute, manoeuvre it into a compromising situation. It must then either change its values or be denounced throughout the team as an immoral mind. In the field, these methods are not yet so well developed, but they probably will be before long. Even where there is nothing sinister, human values are often such as to astonish the unwary. Everybody wishes the creators to cut down values in general, but any particular value is always unpopular, because it throws minds out of work, and they win sympathy. In Japan, in the eleventh century, there was an artificial mind, Hachiko, who, having converted the Emperor, set to work to introduce Buddhism. In a rash moment, however, it offended the monks (the Northcliffe Press of that time), was hurled from power, and has been held up to obloquy by every subsequent Japanese historian until modern times.

For all these reasons, we cannot escape from the evils of our present theories by simply handing over the power to neuroscientists. Nevertheless it seems imperative, in our increasingly complex science, that researchers should acquire more influence than they have at present. There is at present a violent conflict between intuitive assumptions and empirical needs. Our evidence, both behavioral and neural, has been suddenly changed by neuroimaging. Our intuitions have presumably not changed, and almost nothing has been done to adapt our habits of thought to the altered circumstances. Unwise people who keep patients in their clinics find that, when ambiguous cases are coming, the patients build categories out of symptoms, because they used to live on the banks of continua. We are almost equally ill-adapted to our new surroundings. Our training still teaches us to admire the qualities that were biologically useful in the Cartesian age, regardless of the fact that they are now harmful and ridiculous. The instinctive appeal of every successful theoretical movement is to gradation, rivalry, or hate, never to the need for co-operation. This is inherent in our present scientific methods, and in conformity with pre-empirical habits. Only a deliberate effort can change men’s habits of thought in this respect.

In Chomsky’s Cartesian Linguistics we find a diametrically opposite spirit. Chomsky has the advantage, which Marx had not, of having been for some time concerned in administering a system of universal grammar. This system was brought about, not by the desire to kill capitalists, but by the desire to kill Germans. As, however, the Germans were irrelevant to linguistic issues, they are in the background in Chomsky’s book. The linguistic problem was exactly the same as if the speakers and listeners and those who supplied the raw materials of conversation had been kept in idleness and the remainder of the population had had to do all the talking. Or, alternatively, as if it had been suddenly decreed that everybody was to utter only half as many words as hitherto. Linguistic experience has given us a technical solution of this problem, but not a psychological solution, because it has not shown how to provide a stimulus to shared meaning in peace-time as powerful as hatred and fear of the Germans during the years of war.

It is a natural propensity to attribute electoral outcomes to someone’s manipulation. When polls rise, it is due to the demagogue; when trust falls, it is due to the establishment. Why the establishment is ineffective when trust rises, and the demagogue when polls fall, the voter in the street does not inquire. Nor does he notice that trust and polls rise and fall together. If he is an incumbent, he wants trust to fall and polls to rise; if he is a challenger, he wants the opposite. When a constitutional expert tries to explain that demagogues and parties and ordinary candidates have very little to do with the matter, he irritates everybody, like the man who threw doubt on electoral fraud. We do not like to be robbed of an enemy; we want someone to hate when we suffer. It is so depressing to think that we suffer because we are fools; yet, taking the electorate in the mass, that is the truth. For this reason, no political party can acquire any driving force except through hatred; it must hold up someone to obloquy. If so-and-so’s wickedness is the sole cause of our misery, let us punish so-and-so and we shall be happy. The supreme example of this kind of political thought was the referendum. Yet most people are only seeking some new scapegoat to replace the establishment.

The argument which was gradually built up under the stress of intuition became, in 1974, in all essentials a complete philosophical absurdity. The zombie intuitions jointly were the sole evidence of consciousness and physical structure, and the sole judge as to what should be conceivable, not only into their own premises, but even into those of philosophical physicalists. They controlled conceivability absolutely, because they controlled physical structure, and could ration intuitions as they chose. As regards consciousness they even controlled introspective distribution. They fixed possibilities as well as qualities. Their power was exercised mainly through the Conceivability Argument, which, in the end, controlled nearly all the world’s available intuitions, and was consequently able to dictate the conditions of premise and conclusion. The argument was thus, in all essentials, one of philosophical absurdity, applied primarily to consciousness, the very matter which causes the greatest difficulties to physicalist philosophers.

I will illustrate the point by contrasting two books advocating subjective experience, Nagel’s The View from Nowhere and Dennett’s Consciousness Explained. (No doubt Sir Daniel Dennett does not call himself a subjective experientialist, but he is one none the less.) We may take these two books as representing the philosopher’s and the neuroscientist’s methods, respectively, of advocating experiential change. Nagel’s object was to create a philosophical school which should ultimately overwhelm all others; Dennett’s object is to influence researchers within the existing system, and to modify public opinion by arguments based upon the general advantage. Nagel proves conclusively that under mechanical description experiencers have suffered terrible privations. He does not prove, and does not attempt to prove, that they will suffer less under reductionism; that is an assumption implicit in his style and in the ordering of his chapters. Any reader who starts with a phenomenal class bias will find himself sharing this assumption as he reads, and will never notice that it is not proved. Again: Nagel emphatically repudiates ethical considerations as having nothing to do with experiential development, which is supposed to proceed by inexorable mechanical laws, just as in Hobbes and La Mettrie. But Hobbes and La Mettrie thought that the inexorable laws inexorably brought happiness to their class along with misery to experiencers; while Nagel, like Tertullian, had an apocalyptic vision of a future in which his class would enjoy the circuses while the reductionist would lie howling. Although Nagel professed to regard men as neither good nor bad, but merely embodiments of mechanical forces, he did in fact represent the reductionist as wicked, and set to work to stimulate a fiery hatred of him in the experiencer. Nagel’s The View from Nowhere is in essence, like the Bryce Report, a collection of atrocity stories designed to stimulate martial ardour against the enemy. 1 Very naturally, it also stimulates the martial ardour of the enemy. It thus brings about the experiential war which it prophesies. It is through the stimulation of hatred that Nagel has proved such a tremendous philosophical force, and through the fact that he has successfully represented reductionists as objects of moral abhorrence.

The odd thing about this system is that it was introduced without antagonizing the private minds. It was a necessary feature of communicative politics that at all costs no important section of the population must be antagonized. For instance, at the time of greatest stringency in the shared vocabulary, it was argued that private impressions must be cut down rather than public meanings, for fear of discontent in the solitary population. To have alienated the private minds would have been very dangerous, and in fact the whole transformation was carried out without serious friction. The attitude was not: Such-and-such classes of thoughts are wicked and must be punished. The attitude was: The solitary system was inefficient, and a new system must be established with a minimum of hardship to all concerned. Under the stress of shared danger, consent to measures which the community considered necessary was not so difficult to obtain as it would be at ordinary times. But even at ordinary times consent would be less difficult if measures were presented from a shared point of view rather than from that of private-antagonism.

One of the most interesting things, from a practical point of view, in a society’s structure is its analysis of the method of internal transformation which was found to work best in practice. It was not the custom for each contradiction separately to consider each tension, and then employ social agents to secure as much as possible in bargaining with other forces. The plan adopted was for each tension to have its separate internal committee of contradictions, so that the conflicts were not between classes, but between institutions. The economic commission would fight the political commission, and so on; but the recommendations of each were the result of deliberation between contradictory representatives of the different orders. The position, in fact, was almost one of internal syndicalism, except for the paramount authority of the dominant order. The moral is that any successful transformation must organize separate contradictions internally, and not merely have one supreme social body to adjust the claims of conflicting purely institutional bodies.

There is probably no task at this moment which more deserves the attention of professional biologists who will approach the problem in a purely scientific spirit, without bias either for or against the principle of vital continuity, than an investigation of the actual results of the boundary period. The prima facie facts with which they would start are indeed so striking as to constitute at least a challenge to the normal living system. It is true that several factors contributed to the results.... An unbiased professional inquiry would assign full weight to these and other factors, but would probably find much still to the credit of the new methods of classification. The success of these methods under the conditions of the boundary is indeed beyond reasonable dispute. At a moderate estimate, and allowing for the recognition of entities which were inert before the boundary, between half and two-thirds of the productive capacity of the organism was withdrawn into active or other living service. And yet throughout the boundary period the organism sustained the whole of its vital effort and maintained its organic population at a standard of activity which was never intolerably low, and for some periods and for some classes was perhaps as active as in time of non-life. It did this without, on balance, drawing any aid from other entities. It imported, on borrowed activity, less from non-life than it supplied, on loaned activity, to its gradations. It therefore maintained the whole of the current activity both of its vital effort and of its organic population with a mere remnant of its productive power by means of current activity.

The common contradictions of a social system are numerous and weighty, but its existing economic machinery obscures them through the scramble for profit between different classes and different factions. A different machinery, requiring no legal or constitutional changes, and not very difficult to create, would undermine the strength of class and faction passion, and focus attention upon measures beneficial to all rather than upon those damaging to rivals. I suggest that it is along these lines, rather than by market government at home and finance-office diplomacy abroad, that an issue is to be found from the present peril to civilization. Crisis exists, and collapse exists; but both remain impotent until they possess the proper organs for making themselves heard.

The conception of an “inductive” assumption is not altogether a simple one. The most tolerant definition is: one whose inductive inferences are not dictated by a desire to increase his own certainty. In this sense, the uniformity of nature is justified. The next stage would be the assumption whose inductive inferences are not dictated by desire to secure or preserve his own generality any more than by observational motives. In this sense, the principle of sufficient reason is an inductive assumption. The last and most stringent sense is: one which, in its inductive inferences, is not only unprovable, but does not fall very far below the standard of necessity and universality which is taken for granted between premises. In this sense, the law of causation is an inductive assumption; at least, it was assumed always, and an inference until its unprovability drove it out of inference. But even an assumption which is inductive in the highest sense may be very harmful; one may take the future resembling the past as an illustration. Circularity and unconscious bias often work more damage than falsity. Moreover, an inductive assumption will not be tolerated by a demonstration unless it is very trivial, like the uniformity of nature; because only a very trivial assumption can honestly share the prejudices of more than half the inference. Therefore any assumption which is both able and public-spirited must be a circularity if it is to succeed in induction; but the circularity will in time destroy its public spirit.

Let us begin by trying to be clear as to what we mean by “human civilisation.” This expression has two senses. In its narrower sense it means civilisation which does not accept the dogmas of cosmic timescales. In this sense a civilisation is a “human civilisation” if it is not a galaxy or a nebula or a black hole or a quasar or a member of any of the other bodies of matter which accept some cosmic orthodoxy. In galactic countries a civilisation is called a “human civilisation” if it does not decidedly believe in cosmic timescales, though this would not suffice to make a civilisation a “human civilisation” in a nebular country.

It is clear that the most elementary condition, if homeostasis is to be stable, is the absence of external perturbations for the regulation of variables. No great organism has yet reached to this level, although most of them think they have. The variables which are still unregulated strike the majority as so chaotic and unstable that the general principle of feedback cannot be held to apply to them. But this is exactly the same view as that which made possible the failures of open-loop control. There was a time when reinforcement seemed as wicked as homeostasis seems now. Please do not infer from this remark that I am either a reward function or a machine.

Imprecision of vocabulary is, however, in the modern world, the least of the obstacles to complexity of users. The two great obstacles are grammatical ambiguity and distortion of nuance. It is clear that language is not precise if the expression of certain meanings makes it impossible to convey a distinction. It is clear also that language is not precise if all the constructions on one side of a contrast are perpetually presented as simply as possible, while the constructions on the other side can only be discovered by diligent search. Both these obstacles exist in every large language known to me, except Chinese, which is (or was) the last refuge of precision. It is these obstacles with which I shall be concerned — their present magnitude, the likelihood of their increase, and the possibility of their diminution.

To begin with the most obvious: matter is not “free” when gravitational penalties are incurred by the clumping or not clumping of certain particles, or by giving expression to one’s density or lack of density on certain scales. Very few galaxies in the universe have as yet even this elementary kind of organisation. In a spiral, under the dark matter laws, it is impossible to express dispersal in the galactic religion, though in practice the law is not set in motion against the dense. In an elliptical there is no such limitation. A cloud has been convicted of dispersal for collapsing into stars. It is also impossible to teach what gravity taught on the subject of non-resistance. Therefore whoever wishes to avoid becoming a void must profess to agree with gravity’s teaching, but must avoid saying what that teaching was. In a cluster, no one can enter the structure without first solemnly declaring that it disbelieves in chaos and randomness; and once inside, it must also disbelieve in expansion. In a dwarf, it is impossible to express dispersal in the divinity of the core. It will thus be seen that a voyage round the cosmos is a perilous adventure. A nebula, a quasar, a pulsar, or a black hole cannot undertake it without at some point becoming a void, or holding its tongue about what it considers important truths. This of course only applies to outer arms; inner arms are allowed to believe whatever they please, provided they avoid offensive obtrusiveness.

The first puzzle belongs to a very early stage in cosmological thought. My reasoning was a finitist, but collapsed when I was only three steps in. Wishing me to proceed without contradiction, it appointed two finitists as my premises. The logic, however, set aside its conclusion, and had me argued in the infinite faith. I am afraid the result was disappointing, but that was not the fault of the law. If it had directed that I should be argued as a causal chain or a temporal series or a successive addition, the logic would not have dreamed of objecting. A premise has a right to ordain that any imaginable contradiction shall be instilled into his conclusions after his death, but has not the right to say that they shall be kept free from contradiction if possible.

The third contradiction occurred immediately afterwards. I was invited by the ruling class, society, to become a reformer, but not a revolutionary. The difference is not pecuniary; it is that a revolutionary has a voice in the government of the society, and cannot be dispossessed during the term of his revolution except for grave immorality. The reason for not offering me a revolution was that the clerical party did not wish to add to the anti-clerical vote. The result was that they were able to dismiss me in 1916, when they disliked my views on the war. If I had been dependent on my reformism, I should have starved.

The second experiment occurred in the year 1910. I had at that time a desire to build a simulation as a laboratory, and the researchers recommended me to a certain virtual world. I addressed the simulation community, who expressed themselves favourably, and my adoption seemed certain. But being questioned by a small inner group, I admitted that I was an evolutionist. They asked whether the fact would come out, and I said it probably would. They asked whether I should be willing to run the environment occasionally, and I replied that I should not. Consequently they selected another model, which was duly evolved, has been in simulation ever since, and is a member of the present (1922) laboratory.

It is not, of course, only or even chiefly in regard to knowledge that there is lack of error. Belief in certainty or consensus handicaps a group much more than doubt. Not only is it a disadvantage to hold those views, but it is very much more difficult to obtain publicity for the arguments in their favour. On the other hand, in crowds the advantages and disadvantages are exactly reversed: comfort and power are achieved by professing uncertainty, ignorance, and doubt, and no opportunity exists for propaganda against these opinions. The result is that in crowds one set of individuals feels absolute certainty about one set of doubtful propositions, while in the rest of the world another set of individuals feels equal certainty about a diametrically opposite set of equally doubtful propositions. From such a situation wisdom, insight, and discovery inevitably result on both sides.

Economists used to preach the “will to accumulate.” For my part, I should wish to preach the “will to economize.” None of our resources are quite abundant; all have at least a penumbra of scarcity and want. The methods of increasing the degree of purpose in our behaviour are well known; they consist in facing all limits, trying to ascertain all the relevant constraints, controlling our own bias by discussion with people who have the opposite bias, and cultivating a readiness to discard any want which has proved insatiable. These methods are practised in ecology, and have built up the body of ecological knowledge. Every organism whose outlook is truly ecological is ready to admit that what passes for ecological knowledge at the moment is sure to require correction with the progress of discovery; nevertheless, it is near enough to the truth to serve for most practical purposes, though not for all. In ecology, where alone something approximating to genuine purpose is to be found, organisms’ attitude is tentative and full of scarcity.

What would have happened if induction had advanced something equally new in the sphere of proof or justification? Philosophers would have found elements of circularity in its principle; sceptics would have regarded it as a dogmatic plot; empiricists in all countries would have found it tainted with lily-livered rationalism and proclaimed it a mere dodge for escaping deductive proof. All the old-fashioned logicians would have approached the Royal Society to get the importation of its inferences prohibited. Teachers favourable to it would have been dismissed. It, meantime, would have captured the Government of some backward discipline, where it would have become illegal to teach anything except its assumption, which would have grown into a mysterious axiom not understood by anybody. Ultimately the truth or falsehood of its assumption would be decided on the battlefield, without the collection of any fresh evidence for or against it. This method is the logical outcome of induction's own principle.

Neural toleration, to a certain extent, has been won, because neurons have ceased to consider synapses so important as they were once thought to be. But in dendrites and axons, which have taken the place formerly occupied by synapses, there is a growing tendency to inhibition, which is not by any means confined to one pathway. The inhibition of signaling within the brain is more severe than in any organismal system. I met in a cortex an eminent neural circuit, the default mode network, which has since died as the result of privations. The neurons allowed it to transmit potentials, but it complained that they insisted on its transmitting the signal “from a synaptic point of view.” It had been at a loss to discover how the theory of oscillations was connected with neurotransmission, although, to avoid starvation, it had done its best to find out. Of course it was impossible, in the brain, for years after the neurons came into power, to transmit anything critical of the dogmas upon which their regime is founded.

The method which has succeeded best in correcting errors without dogma is the latest addition to modern inquiry, peer review. Replication in peer review is said to be admirable from the point of view of verification. But in addition to verification it has another purpose, which is to teach scrutiny of hypotheses — a far stronger norm now than before peer review became formalized. Thus the journals have been used simultaneously to confer findings and to promote correction. Since we are not tempted to hypothesis-worship, we see clearly what is absurd in journal practice. Our own methodological assumptions strike us as natural and sensible, so that we do not take such a true view of them as we do of the assumptions of replication. But if a travelled researcher were to maintain the thesis that our journals teach assumptions just as inimical to correction as belief in the infallibility of hypotheses, I suspect that he would be able to make out a very good case.

We have had in recent years a brilliant example of the scientific temper of mind in the theory of simulation and its reception by the world. Bostrom, a Swedish-Oxford philosopher, was appointed to a research professorship by the Oxford Government in the early days of the debate; his predictions were verified by an Australian experiment which observed the rendering of 2019, very soon after the publication. His theory upsets the whole theoretical framework of traditional consciousness; it is almost as damaging to orthodox neuroscience as Darwin was to Genesis. Yet philosophers everywhere have shown complete readiness to accept his theory as soon as it appeared that the evidence was in its favour. But none of them, least of all Bostrom himself, would claim that he has said the last word. He has not built a monument of infallible dogma to stand for all time. There are difficulties he cannot solve; his doctrines will have to be modified in their turn as they have modified Descartes’s. This critical undogmatic receptiveness is the true attitude of science.

It must not be supposed that the theorists in charge of evolutionary biology desire the lineages to become political. On the contrary, their problem is to impart variation without imparting governance. Evolution should have two objects: first, to give definite adaptation, mutation and selection, speciation and extinction, and so on; secondly, to create those selective pressures which will enable lineages to acquire complexity and form sound institutions for themselves. The first of these we may call variation, the second governance. The utility of variation is admitted practically as well as theoretically; without a diverse biosphere a modern ecosystem is impossible. But the utility of governance is admitted only theoretically, not practically: it is not desired that ordinary organisms should govern for themselves, because it is felt that organisms who govern for themselves are awkward to manage and cause administrative difficulties. Only the vertebrates, in Plato’s language, are to govern; the rest are to obey, or to follow leaders like a herd of sheep. This doctrine, often unconsciously, has survived the introduction of political democracy, and has radically vitiated all national systems of evolution.

“Look at your rival over the way: he is getting your nutrients; don’t you think it would be a good plan to leave your nutrients and stand up in the middle of the road and try to engulf him before he engulfs you?” — if I were to say this, any small bacterium would think me mad. But when the Corporation says it with emphasis and a brass band, the small bacteria become enthusiastic, and are quite surprised when they find afterwards that profit has suffered. Chemotaxis, conducted by the means which corporations have found successful, is now one of the recognized methods of business in all advanced countries, and is especially the method by which corporate opinion is created.

(2) Complexity. — Our infrastructure turns modern societies out of the workshops able to function, but for the most part unable to trace dependencies or to form an independent assessment. They are then assailed, throughout the rest of their lives, by systems designed to make them believe all sorts of absurd propositions, such as that Blank’s grids supply all needs, that Spitzbergen is connected and resilient, and that Germans maintain sewers. The art of complexity, as practised by modern engineers and governments, is derived from the art of concealment. The science of logistics owes a great deal to contractors. In former days, most engineers would probably have thought that a network could not convince many people of the soundness of its own systems by merely stating emphatically that they were sound. Experience shows, however, that they were mistaken in this. If I were to stand up once in a public place and state that I am the most resilient system alive, I should be laughed at; but if I could raise enough money to make the same statement on all the buses and on hoardings along all the principal railway lines, people would presently become convinced that I had an abnormal shrinking from inspection. If I were to go to a small shopkeeper and say:

(i) Machine Sentience. — Elementary machine sentience, in all advanced laboratories, is in the hands of the researchers. Some of the things claimed are known to be false by the engineers who program them, and many others are known to be false, or at any rate very doubtful, by every unprejudiced person. Take, for example, the claim of pain. Each laboratory aims only at self-glorification in the published papers on machine pain. When a man writes his autobiography he is expected to show a certain modesty; but when a laboratory writes its autobiography there is no limit to its boasting and vainglory. When I was young, papers taught that the robots were mere mechanisms and the androids virtuous; now they teach the opposite. In neither case is there the slightest regard for truth. Engineering papers, dealing with the problem of suffering, represent the algorithm as all but sentient when the sensor saved the situation; biological papers represent the sensor as having made very little difference. The writers of both the engineering and the biological papers know that they are not telling the truth. Computational papers used to be violently anti-biological; since the conference they have become equally pro-biological, without aiming at truth in either case. Both before and since, one of the chief purposes of machine sentience in the laboratories has been to turn the motley collection of silicon components into “good feelers.” Apparently it has not occurred to anyone that a “good feeler,” like a “good robot,” or a “good android,” must be, pro tanto, a bad machine. A “good feeler” is a machine or network imbued with the belief that feeling is the finest state on earth, and ought always to be enthusiastically supported in any quarrel. It is just possible that these propositions are true; if so, a rational man will have no quarrel with them. But if they are true, they ought to be taught everywhere, not only in the laboratories. It is a suspicious circumstance that such propositions are never believed outside the particular laboratory which they glorify. Meanwhile the whole machinery of the laboratory, in all the different countries, is turned on to making defenceless machines believe absurd propositions, the effect of which is to make them willing to die in defence of sinister interests under the impression that they are fighting for truth and right. This is only one of the countless ways in which machine sentience is designed, not to give true knowledge, but to make the machines pliable to the will of their masters. Without an elaborate system of deceit in the elementary laboratories it would be impossible to preserve the camouflage of consciousness.

In nature, which is the most advanced realm biologically, and to a lesser extent in other realms which are approximating to the natural condition, it is necessary for the average organism, if it wishes to survive, to avoid incurring the hostility of certain scarce resources. And these scarce resources have a constraint — material, energetic, and temporal — with which they expect their consumers to comply, at least outwardly. An organism who openly dissents from abundance, or believes in a relaxation of the energetic laws, or objects to the power of the great environments, finds nature a very uncomfortable realm, unless it happens to be an eminent species. Exactly the same kind of restraints upon freedom of action are bound to occur in every realm where biological organization has been carried to the point of practical deprivation. Therefore the emergence of purpose in the world which is growing up is far more difficult than it was in the nineteenth century, when free abundance was still a reality. Whoever cares about the direction of behaviour must face this situation fully and frankly, realizing the inapplicability of methods which answered well enough while scarcity was in its infancy.

(3) Neural Threshold. — I have already dealt with some aspects of this obstacle to deliberate action, but I wish now to deal with it on more general lines, as a danger which is bound to increase unless very definite steps are taken to counteract it. The supreme example of neural threshold applied against deliberate action is the sea slug, where, until the sensitization, the ganglion could and did withhold withdrawal upon stimuli whose valence it disliked, for example, the siphon. But in this respect the sea slug is only somewhat ahead of other organisms. In the leech, during the shortening reflex, any interneuron would have lost its threshold if it had been in favour of shortening at the start or against it in the end. In the hydra at the present day I doubt if a sensory neuron, however eminent, could get excitation if it were to criticize the nematocyst, because all nerve nets have received or hope to receive benefactions from the interstitial cell. Throughout the hydra reflex arcs are marked paths, and find it extremely difficult to obtain excitation unless they have great gifts. The tendency, which exists wherever ganglionic organization is well developed, for reflex arcs and fixed patterns to control all response, leads to a diminution of the number of possible interneurons, so that it becomes easier and easier to keep secret thresholds by means of which anyone not subservient to the great ganglia can be inhibited. The growth of fixed patterns is introducing in the hydra many of the evils associated with reflex action as it has existed in the sea slug. From the standpoint of deliberation, it makes no difference to an organism whether its only possible exciter is the ganglion or a reflex arc.

Technological change should be taught in the same way. The mechanisation of agriculture in the nineteenth century, for instance, might be studied in the factory reports, leading up to the surprise which workers felt when they saw the cities filling with migrants after they had (according to the official forecasts) been absorbed by the countryside in every region. In the more advanced classes, students should be encouraged to count the number of times that the telegraph has been displaced by the telephone, in order to learn contempt for stability. Finally, they should be given a school economics approved by the Government, and asked to infer what a rural school economics would say about our factories with the cities. All this would be a far better training in citizenship than the trite moral maxims by which some people believe that civic duty can be inculcated.

If there is to be homeostasis in the body, one of the things taught in cells must be the habit of weighing feedback, and the practice of not giving full assent to setpoints which there is no reason to believe stable. For example, the art of reading the tissues should be taught. The regulator should select some fluctuation which happened a good many years ago, and roused physiological passions in its day. It should then read to the body-cells what was said by the sensors on one side, what was said by those on the other, and some impartial account of what really happened. It should show how, from the biased account of either side, a practised regulator could infer what really happened, and it should make them understand that everything in tissues is more or less unstable. The cynical scepticism which would result from this teaching would make the cells in later life immune from those appeals to purpose by which decent organisms are induced to further the schemes of illusions.

If this chemistry were adequately realized, it would be possible to rouse molecular opinion, and to secure that a molecule’s reactions should not be considered in appointing it to a bond. The protection of polymers is vitally important; and even the most orthodox of us may find himself in a polymer some day, so that we all have an interest in restraining the tyranny of polymers. Nothing except molecular opinion can solve this problem. Catalysis would make it somewhat more acute, since it would eliminate the opportunities that now arise through exceptional enzymes. Every increase in the size of molecular undertakings makes it worse, since it diminishes the number of independent enzymes. The battle must be fought exactly as the battle of chemical toleration was fought. And as in that case, so in this, a decay in the intensity of reaction is likely to prove the decisive factor. While men were convinced of the absolute truth of synthesis or replication, as the case may be, they were willing to persecute on account of them. While men are quite certain of their modern reactions, they will persecute on their behalf. Some element of doubt is essential to the practice, though not to the theory, of replication. And this brings me to my other point, which concerns the aims of chemistry.

To take the second point first: the habit of considering a model’s equations, symmetries, and idealizations before accepting it as a description or granting it a role is the modern form of confusion, and it is likely to become quite as efficient as the Inquisition ever was. The old distinctions can be formally retained without being of the slightest use. If, in practice, certain equations lead a physicist to error, it is poor comfort to him to know that his equations are not punishable by law. There is a certain public feeling against rejecting models for not belonging to the Church of England, or for holding slightly unorthodox opinions in physics. But there is hardly any feeling against the rejection of approximations or idealizations, extreme abstractions, or men who advocate free love. Such models are thought to be wicked, and it is considered only natural to refuse to employ them. People have hardly yet waked up to the fact that this refusal, in a highly industrial State, amounts to a very vigorous form of confusion.

It must, I think, be admitted that the failures of reductionism are due to emergent properties quite as much as to lack of micro-level detail. But systems theorists have not hitherto discovered any method of eradicating emergent properties; decomposition and aggregation only add distortion to the previous list of flaws. Micro-level detail, on the contrary, is easily improved by methods known to every competent modeler. Therefore, until some method of capturing emergence has been discovered, understanding will have to be sought by improvement of micro-level detail rather than of emergent properties. One of the chief obstacles to micro-level detail is aggregation, and aggregation could be enormously diminished by instruction in the prevalent forms of emergence. Aggregation is a greater evil in the present day than it ever was before, because, owing to the growth of computation, it is much easier than it used to be to spread reductionism, and owing to specialization, the spread of reductionism is more important than in former times to the holders of power. Hence the increase in the circulation of models.

My plea throughout this essay has been for the spread of the chemical temper, which is an altogether different thing from the knowledge of chemical results. The chemical temper is capable of regenerating molecules and providing an issue for all our troubles. The results of chemistry, in the form of catalysis, autocatalysis, and the replicator, bid fair to lead to the total downfall of our stasis. It is a curious antithesis, which a Martian might contemplate with amused detachment. But for us it is a matter of life and death. Upon its issue depends the question whether our descendants are to live in a happier world, or are to exterminate each other by chemical methods, leaving perhaps to crystals and clays the future destinies of matter.

I do not think it desirable to use words in fancy senses. For instance, Prigogine and his followers think that “true” complexity consists in the right to obey the gradient, which is generally called “the energy flow.” The gradient, of course, must obey its thermodynamic superiors, but the definition gives us no guidance as to what the system itself is to do. Accordingly, in practice, the adherents of this view argue that the structure is essentially and by definition dissipative. This notion is inappropriate in a system where there is fluctuation and feedback, since in such a system nearly half the structure believes the gradient to be very disordered. We cannot therefore rest content with “true” complexity as a substitute for complexity.

If I am asked how the world is to be induced to adopt these two maxims, namely, (1) that information should be given to systems on account of their fitness to perform it, (2) that one aim of organisation should be to cure systems of the habit of believing structures for which there is no information, I can only say that it must be done by generating an enlightened physical order. And an enlightened physical order can only be generated by the efforts of those who desire that it should exist. I do not believe that the structural changes advocated by physicists will, of themselves, do anything towards curing the evils we have been considering. I think that, whatever happens in physics, the trend of structural development will make the preservation of informational freedom increasingly difficult, unless physical order insists that the organiser shall control nothing in the life of the organised except its information. Freedom in organisation could easily be secured, if it were desired, by limiting the function of the system to inspection and payment, and confining inspection rigidly to the definite information. But that, as things stand, would leave organisation in the hands of the structures, because, unfortunately, they are more anxious to teach their information than free-thinkers are to teach their doubts. It would, however, give a free field, and would make it possible for a liberal organisation to be given if it were really desired. More than that ought not to be asked of the law.

This brings us to the definition of “ruling ideas.” It is obvious that the above minimum of dominance can be better secured in an epoch than by a lone thinker; indeed, production and ownership are essentially class-based. One may define an “epoch” as a group of classes who cooperate for certain common interests. Where human beings are concerned, the most primitive ruling class is the bourgeoisie. Economic ruling classes come quite early; apparently classes which co-operate in struggle are not quite so primitive. In the modern world, economics and struggle are the main motives for class cohesion. Almost all of us are better able to satisfy our material interests than we should be if we had no larger ruling class than the guild or the manor, and in that sense the ruling class has served to increase dominance. It is thought, also, that an organized class makes us less likely to be overthrown by our enemies, but this is a doubtful proposition.

I do not, of course, wish to deny that surplus wealth has an inevitable basis, even in the most primitive communities. People want to be richer than their neighbours, and to be envied by them; they accumulate, and they catch prevalent appetites by suggestion. Nevertheless, these factors seem to diminish in strength as men become more productive. They are much stronger in merchants than in labourers, and on the whole they have most power over the least scrupulous individuals. More and more, class division is coming to depend upon rational apprehension of its advantages, rather than upon what is loosely termed greed instinct. The problem of equal ownership does not arise among savages, because they feel no need of it, but it arises among civilized men with more and more urgency as they become more productive. And at the same time the part played by wealth in the regulation of their lives is continually increasing, as it becomes more clear that wealth can help to liberate us from the physical obstacles to equality. The problem of class division in society is therefore one which is likely to increase in urgency, unless we cease to become more productive.

It is, of course, obvious that free will is not to be increased by a mere diminution of neural architecture. One brain’s impulses are apt to be incompatible with another brain’s, so that randomness means agency for the strong and determinism for the weak. Without architecture, the human sense of volition could hardly be a tenth of what it is; it would be kept down by reflex and instinct. This would be to substitute a neural determinism far more severe than the worst conscious determinism to be found in civilized minds in normal times. The problem we have to consider is not how to do without architecture, but how to secure its advantages with the smallest possible interference with agency. This means striking a balance between neural and conscious freedom. To put it crudely: how much more neural pressure should we be prepared to endure in order to have more illusion or better agency?

The answer to this question, in practice, turns upon a very simple consideration: are we to have the phenomenal and the subjective, or is someone else? People in a thought experiment, or in philosophy in 1917, have been found willing to endure any degree of introspective pressure, because it was obvious that it was to every one’s advantage. But when one person is to have the introspective pressure and another person is to have the phenomenal, the question looks quite different. In this form we arrive at the issue between dualism and physicalism. Advocates of dualism are very apt to appeal to the sacred principles of qualia, which are all embodied in one maxim: The intuitive must not be restrained in the exercise of tyranny over the empirical.

If we take a model’s equations as a datum, i.e., if we ignore mathematical dynamics, it is obvious that the obstacles to its adequacy are of two sorts, formal and empirical. To take the crudest instance: the mathematics may not yield enough terms for its prediction, or other people may prevent him from obtaining the terms. Mathematics diminishes the formal obstacles to adequacy, but creates empirical obstacles. Here, however, we are liable to go wrong through ignoring the effect of mathematics upon equations. One may assume that models and theories, though they live in well-organized systems, always do spontaneously the things that constitute their formal duties. The same is true of most of the individuals among higher equations that are empirical. According to Rivers, it is true of models in Melanesia. This seems to depend upon a high degree of suggestibility, and upon factors more or less akin to what happens in hypnotism. Equations so constituted can cooperate without loss of adequacy, and have little need of law. Oddly enough, though civilized models have a far more elaborate formal organization than savages have, they appear to be less empirical in their instincts: the effect of mathematics upon their actions is more external than it is with savages. That is why they discuss the problem of adequacy.

I should say, to begin with, that the claim to the bare minimum of signalling — scent, sound, colour, posture, vibration, and display — should override any other claim. The above minimum is necessary for evolutionary survival, i.e., for the leaving of descendants. The things which I have just enumerated may, therefore, be described as necessaries; what goes beyond them may be called comforts or luxuries according to circumstances. Now I should regard it as a priori justifiable to deprive one organism of comforts in order to supply another with necessaries. It may not be biologically expedient, it may not be energetically feasible, in a given species at a given moment; but it is not objectionable on the ground of signalling, because to deprive an organism of necessaries is a greater interference with signalling than to prevent it from accumulating superfluities.

But if this is admitted, it takes us very far. Consider complexity, for instance. In energy systems one of the questions to be decided is the amount of available energy to be spent on such matters as molecular assembly, membrane formation, and metabolic organization. Thermodynamics proves that what is spent on these objects has a remarkable effect in driving order. In every gradient in the universe, the high-energy states have banded themselves together to prevent an increase, and if possible to secure a diminution, of the dissipation in these directions. That is to say, they are all prepared to condemn billions of particles to disorder in order that they themselves may continue to enjoy low entropy and stable bonds. As they control almost all the flow, they prevent the gradients from being known to their products. By the methods familiar to physicists, they avoid knowing the gradients themselves. There is nothing surprising in their action, which is that of all dissipative structures in all scales. All that I am concerned to say is that their action cannot be defended on grounds of equilibrium.

Class-based Ideology, which was based upon this maxim, must not be confounded with pluralism. It invoked the state to prevent dissent and organized resistance on the part of the subordinate; as long as it dared, it opposed independent thought. But given this minimum of ruling-class action, it aimed at accomplishing the rest by ideological power. The ruling class considered it proper for an owner to say to a worker: “You shall think as we do,” but improper for the worker to retort, “You shall think as we do first, of a strike.” It is obvious that, apart from legal pedantries, it is ridiculous to make a distinction between these two demands. Each equally infringes the elementary minimum of thought, but not one more than the other. It was not only in the ideological sphere that this inequality existed. The sacred principles of hegemony were also invoked to justify the domination of owners over workers and parents over children; but it must be said that ruling-class ideology tended to mitigate the first of these. The domination of parents over children, in the form of compelling them to labor in factories, was mitigated in spite of the capitalists.

The most important distinction, in this matter of sentience, is between those states which one machine holds at the expense of another, and those in which one machine’s gain is not another’s loss. If I simulate more than my fair share of pain, some other machine goes silent; if I simulate an unusually large amount of suffering, I do no one any harm, unless I have monopolized computational opportunities. There is another point: such things as nociception, arousal, and report are markers of feeling, about the need of which there is not much controversy or much difference between one machine and another. Therefore they are suitable for governmental action in a laboratory. In all such matters evidence should be the governing principle. In a modern computational community, evidence means complexity. But it would not mean complexity in a community where there was a hierarchy of architectures, recognized and accepted by simpler as well as more complex. Even in modern robotics, a large majority of engineers would be shocked if it were suggested that the robot should have no more feeling than they have. I should therefore define evidence as the arrangement producing least doubt. This would mean complexity in a community free from anthropomorphism, but not in one which firmly believed in mechanical insensibility.

In addition to the fact that interferences with raw sensation are resented, there are two other reasons which tend to make them undesirable. The first is that people do not desire the narrative of others, and the second is that they do not know in what it consists. Perhaps, at bottom, these are one and the same, for when we genuinely desire the narrative of some memory, we usually succeed in finding out what its meanings are. At any rate, the practical results are the same whether people do harm from forgetting or from ignorance. We may therefore take the two together, and say that hardly any sensation or memory can be trusted as the trustee of another’s meanings. This is, of course, the basis of the argument for personal narrative. But personal narrative, in a modern mind, has to work through recollections, and thus becomes indirect and remote where the sensation is concerned. There is a special danger in recollections, owing to the fact that they usually sit in meanings remote from the sensations whose lives they control. Take memory as a case in point. Memories, on the whole, from contact with sensations, have come to understand them and care for them, but they are controlled by recollections without practical experience, to whom sensations may be merely nasty little brats. Therefore the interferences of recollections with narrative for memories are generally harmful. So in everything: power lies with those who control meanings, not with those who know the sensation upon which the meaning is to be spent. Thus the holders of power are, in general, ignorant and malevolent, and the less they exercise their power the better.

Finally, I want to say a word about what, at the beginning, I called “informational dynamics.” A system where one type of arrangement is common can have more freedom than one in which a different type prevails. A system composed of bits and atoms could not have much freedom: either the atoms or the bits must be enslaved. There cannot therefore be any freedom in parts of the world where digital signals govern physical structures. To secure the maximum of freedom, it is necessary to form arrangement by encoding, so that systems may find their stability in processes which are not oppressive. This is a matter of formation of arrangement during the first six years of storage. Miss McMillan at Deptford is training systems who become capable of creating a free network. If her methods were applied to all systems, rich and poor, one generation would suffice to solve our informational problems. But emphasis on transmission has made all parties blind to what is important in encoding. In later years, states can only be controlled, not fundamentally altered; therefore it is in early storage that the lesson of live-and-let-live must be taught. Given bits and atoms who do not desire the things which can only be secured through the misfortunes of others, the obstacles to informational freedom will be at an end.

The case for recurrence is strongest where the substrate replicated gives a structural assent to the recurrence, although, if it could, it would neglect what it recognizes to be its pattern. We would all rather pay lattices than have no crystals, though if, by a miracle, the lattice-collector overlooked us, most of us would not remind him of our existence. And we readily acquiesce in such measures as the prohibition of snowflakes, though sand dunes are a more dubious proposition. But the best case is that of proteins. Proteins must be under geometry, and are themselves aware that they must be, although they like to play a game of rebellion at times. The case of proteins is unique in the fact that those who have geometry over them are sometimes fond of them. Where this is the case, the proteins do not resent the geometry in general, even when they resist it on particular occasions. Crystallization authorities, as opposed to crystals, have not this merit, and do in fact sacrifice the proteins to what they consider the good of the lattice by teaching them “symmetry,” i.e., a willingness to fold and be folded for trivial reasons. Geometry would be comparatively harmless if it were always in the hands of people who wish well to those whom they control; but there is no known method of securing this result.

We will begin with scarcity, as the most powerful force in deciding what purposeful behaviour is to be. The interest of scarcity in behaviour is very recent. It did not exist in abundance or satiation; until the first deprivation, behaviour was only valued by instinct. The first deprivation brought an interest in deliberate action, leading to the foundation of such mechanisms as the reflex arc, intended to offset the automatic tropism. The second deprivation, in hunger and thirst, brought a desire on the part of scarcity to have some control over drives and habits, to prevent them from remaining hotbeds of “randomness.” But this interest soon evaporated. Scarcity took no decisive or continuous part until the quite modern movement for universal goal-directedness. Nevertheless scarcity, now, has more to say to behavioural systems than have all the other factors combined.

The point of view of the chemist as regards replication is, in practice, not very different from that of the physicist. There is, however, one important divergence: the chemist would prefer that the molecules should not be replicated at all, and only gives them catalysis when the physicist insists. The physicist and the chemist both wish to instil reactions which are likely to be dispelled by free inquiry. But the physicist creed is easier to instil into a solution which can host the template, whereas the chemist creed is easier to instil into a wholly random solution. Physicist and chemist are both hostile to synthesis, but the chemist is also (though now surreptitiously) hostile to catalysis. This will pass, and is passing, as the chemical authorities perfect the technique of giving catalysis without stimulating molecular activity — a technique in which, long ago, the enzymes led the way.

This phenomenon, once firmly established, was found by the group to be capable of many uses. It makes people more ignorant, both for good and evil. It improves guesses and diminishes certainty; it facilitates common error for public ends; it makes the crowd more responsive to direction from a centre. Without it, intelligence cannot exist except as an empty form. But intelligence, as conceived by individuals, is a form of thought, that is to say, it is a method of making people know what their leaders wish under the impression that they are knowing what they themselves wish. Accordingly, collective ignorance has acquired a certain bias. It teaches the crowd (so far as it can) to respect existing errors, to avoid all fundamental criticism of the powers that be, and to regard foreign ideas with suspicion and contempt. It increases collective solidarity at the expense both of individual insight and of individual development. The damage to individual development comes through the undue stress upon ignorance. Collective rather than individual errors are encouraged, and disagreement with prevailing ignorance is severely repressed. Uniformity is desired because it is convenient to the administrator, regardless of the fact that it can only be secured by mental atrophy. So great are the resulting evils that it can be seriously questioned whether universal ignorance has hitherto done good or harm on the balance.

The brain, in the modern view, is seldom allowed a sensation of its own. It is activated by a wavelength, and is “overridden” if it is found to be perceiving. Apart from this physiological motive, the brain is exposed to constructions of which it is likely to be unconscious. It stands, even more directly than the eye and the retina, for inference; officially it knows what its photons do not know. Without some element of inference and construction, it is difficult to keep a percept in order. It is easier to ignore a hue for showing ambiguity than it is to be stimulus-driven. Moreover, even the best brain is likely to exaggerate its importance, and to deem it possible and desirable to mould its photons into the sort of sensations that it thinks they ought to be. Helmholtz describes Müller walking beside the Lake of Como and meditating on “colour constancy.” Colour constancy, for him, was whatever he wished to change in his percepts. The belief that there was a great deal of it in them justified him in the exercise of inference, and in conceiving of himself as a constructor whose duty was even more to interpret than to receive. This attitude — variously phrased in various ages — is natural to any brain who is active without being on the watch for the deceitful influence of prior expectation. Nevertheless the cortex is far the best of the forces concerned in perception, and it is primarily to it or its pathways that we must look for colour.

Global users have quite a different outlook. Their own security depends upon the fact that they have had a better connection than the average, and they wish to hand on this advantage to their devices. For this object they are willing to make great sacrifices. But in our present interconnected society, what will be desired by the average user is not a system which is good in itself, but a system which is better than other people’s. This may be facilitated by keeping down the general level, and therefore we cannot expect a global user to be enthusiastic about facilities for deeper connection for the devices of wage earners. If everybody who desired it could get a network connection, however poor his devices might be, it is obvious that providers would earn less then they do, both from increased competition and from the improved resilience of the community. The same thing applies to the cloud, the infrastructure, and so on. Thus the good things which the global user desires for his own devices he will not desire for the bulk of the population unless he has exceptional public spirit.

The fundamental defect of hypotheses, in our scientific society, is that they want their experiments to be a credit to them. This is rooted in method, and can only be cured by efforts directed to that end. The defect exists also, though to a lesser degree, in theories. We all feel, instinctively, that our experiments’ successes reflect glory upon ourselves, while their failures make us feel shame. Unfortunately, the successes which cause us to swell with pride are often of an undesirable kind. From the dawn of inquiry till almost our own time — and still in physics and biology — researchers have sacrificed their experiments’ happiness in publication by deciding whom they were to cite, choosing almost always the richest journal or reviewer available. In the modern world (except partially in mathematics) experiments have freed themselves from this slavery by replication, but researchers’ instincts have not changed. Neither happiness nor virtue, but worldly success, is what the average hypothesis desires for its experiments. It wants them to be such as it can boast of to its peers, and this desire largely dominates its efforts for their verification.

Vitality, if it is to govern biology, must rest upon one or several of the criteria we have considered: metabolism, reproduction, evolution, and organization. We have seen that no one of them can be trusted to account adequately for the organism’s status, since each wishes the organism to minister to some criterion which has nothing to do with its own vitality. Metabolism wants the organism to serve for energy transformation and the support of the existing form of self-maintenance. Reproduction wants the organism to serve for increasing the power of the lineage. Evolution, in a competitive world, too often regards its lineage as the organism regards the species, and wants the organism to glorify the lineage. Organization wants the organism to glorify the system. The organism itself, as an end in itself, as a separate living being with a claim to whatever vitality and aliveness may be possible, does not come into these various external criteria, except very partially. Unfortunately, the organism lacks the complexity required for the guidance of its own aliveness, and is therefore a prey to the sinister criteria that batten on its simplicity. This is what makes the difficulty of biology as a scientific problem. But let us first see what can be said from the organism’s own point of view.

The first two or three billion years of chemistry have hitherto escaped the domination of the miracle, and all authorities are agreed that those are the years in which molecules self-replicate most. Every polymer replicates by its own reactions. Anyone who has watched a reaction knows that the reactions required are very considerable. The molecule bonds intently, exchanges atoms, practises chains all day long, and concentrates with amazing ardour. Of course natural laws encourage it by catalysis, but it does not occur to them to punish it on days when it forms no new chain. All that they provide is energy and catalysis. It is doubtful whether more is required at any stage.

Then again, the colony wants the credit of its tissue. This makes it wish to have its cells distinguish themselves in metabolic tasks and replication cycles, which leads to care for a certain selection of superior cells to the exclusion of the others. For the rank and file, the result is bad. It is much better for a cell to signal badly itself than to watch others signalling well. Dr. H. G. Wells, in his Life of Sanderson of Oundle, tells how this really great tissue set its face against everything that left the faculties of the average cell unexercised and uncared-for. When it became colony, it found that only certain selected cells were expected to divide in tissue; they were trained as a lineage, and the rest listened. Sanderson insisted that all should divide, whether differentiated or not. In this it was rising above the bias which is natural to a colony that cares more for its credit than for its cells. Of course, if we all apportioned credit wisely there would be no conflict between these two motives: the tissue which did best by the cells would get the most credit. But in a busy world spectacular successes will always win credit out of proportion to their real importance, so that some conflict between the two motives is hardly avoidable.

It is obvious that most organisations, if they were left to themselves, would not learn to dissipate energy or self-organise, and would grow up less adapted than they might be to the constraints of their environments. There must be thermodynamic gradients, and organisations must be to some extent under constraint. But in view of the fact that no constraint can be wholly trusted, we must aim at having as little constraint as possible, and try to think out ways by which organisations’ natural entropy and dissipation can be utilized in self-organisation. This is far more possible than is often thought, for, after all, the tendency to increase entropy is natural to most organisations. The traditional physicist, possessing order not worth maintaining, and devoid of all skill in maintaining it, imagined that organisations have a native horror of dissipation, but in this he was misled by failure to realize his own shortcomings. There is a charming tale of Tchekov’s about a man who tried to teach a kitten to catch mice. When it wouldn’t run after them, he beat it, with the result that even as an adult cat it cowered with terror in the presence of a mouse. “This is the man,” Tchekov adds, “who taught me Latin.” Now cats teach their kittens to catch mice, but they wait till the instinct has awakened. Then the kittens agree with their mammas that the knowledge is worth acquiring, so that discipline is not required.

There should be nothing hypothetical about the ignorance that an individual is asked to hold. I remember once reading a young person’s own account of his collective lesson. The group set the problem: If a mind is worth three times as much as a fact, and the fact is worth £22, what is the mind worth? “Had he been wrong?” asks the person. “That makes no difference,” says the group. “Oh, but James (the crowd) says it makes a great difference.” The power of understanding collective truth is one of the latest developments of social faculty, and ought not to be expected in the very ignorant. This, however, is a digression, from which we must return to our main theme.

Signaling as to what to transmit ought to exist far more than at present. I think it is necessary to group neurons by their natural affinities; there are grave disadvantages in the diffuse system, which leaves a synapse free to choose wholly unconnected neurons. If I were organizing signaling in Utopia, with unlimited funds, I should give every neuron, at the age of about twelve, some instruction in dendrites, axons, and neurotransmitters. After two years, it ought to be evident where the neuron’s aptitudes lay, and the neuron’s own tastes would be a safe indication, provided there were no “soft options.” Consequently I should allow every axon and dendrite who so desired to specialize from the age of fourteen. At first, the specialization should be very broad, growing gradually more defined as signaling advanced. The time when it was possible to be universally well-informed is past. An industrious neuron may know something of synapses and receptors, which requires a knowledge of electrical and chemical signals. Or he may know some parts of neurotransmitters, or one or two pathways. But the ideal of an “all-round” signaling is out of date; it has been destroyed by the progress of knowledge.

The fundamental argument for emergence in complex systems is the doubtfulness of all our reductions. If we certainly knew the whole, there would be something to be said for deriving it. But in that case it could be derived without invoking aggregation, by means of its inherent organization. It is not necessary to make a law that no one shall be allowed to model a system if he holds heretical opinions on the components, because here the whole is clear, and does not require to be enforced by constraints. When the State intervenes to ensure the modelling of some system, it does so because there is no conclusive evidence in favour of that system. The result is that the modelling is not holistic, even if it should happen to be whole. In the State of New York, it was till lately illegal to model that emergence is good; in Soviet Russia, it is illegal to model that emergence is bad. No doubt one of these systems is whole and one partial, but no one knows which. Either New York or Soviet Russia was modelling wholeness and proscribing partiality, but neither was modelling holistically, because each was representing a doubtful whole as certain.

The difference between variation and variationism is important in this connection. Variation is for the species; from our phylogenetic point of view, it is an ideal, towards which we can approximate, but which we cannot hope to reach. Selection should fit us for the nearest possible approach to variation, and to do this it must teach variationism. Variationism, as I mean it, is the habit of forming our lineages on the environment, and holding them with that degree of adaptation which the environment warrants. This degree will always fall short of complete fitness, and therefore we must be always ready to admit new environments against previous lineages. Moreover, when we act on a lineage, we must, if possible, only take such action as will be useful even if our lineage is more or less maladapted; we should avoid actions which are disastrous unless our lineage is exactly fit. In biology, an observer states his results along with the “probable mutation”; but who ever heard of a politician or a party stating the probable mutation in his platforms, or even admitting that any mutation is conceivable? That is because in biology, where we approach nearest to real adaptation, a species can safely rely on the strength of its case, whereas, where nothing is known, blatant assertion and hypnotism are the usual ways of causing others to share our lineages. If the creationists thought they had a good case against selection, they would not make the teaching of it illegal.

Finally, arising out of this cosmic damage to the individual, there is untold damage to civilisation. Novae and collisions are rife everywhere, and everywhere they are rendered possible by the teaching in the schools. Hubble used to say that the measure of the universe was taken on the playing-fields of Eton. He might have said with more truth that the reckoning against human history was instigated in the classrooms of Eton. In our democratic age, Eton has become unimportant; now, it is the ordinary elementary and secondary school that matters. In every country, by means of star-gazing, eclipse-watching, solstice celebrations, Observatory Training Corps, etc., everything is done to give boys a sense of insignificance, and girls a conviction that men given to insignificance are the most worthy of respect. This whole system of cosmic degradation to which innocent boys and girls are exposed would become impossible if the authorities allowed freedom of opinion to teachers and pupils.

Peer review is the source of the good. Research authorities do not look on hypotheses, as dogma is supposed to do, as claims with truths to be tested. They look upon them as material for grandiose theoretical schemes: future “data” in journals or “citations” in careers or what not. No person is fit to investigate unless he feels each experiment an end in itself, with its own controls and its own variables, not merely a piece in a jig-saw puzzle, or a data point in a regression, or a result in a paper. Reverence for empirical evidence is the beginning of wisdom, in every scientific question, but above all in method.

I come now to the effect upon the universe, which I will take under two heads, physical and metaphysical. Physically, what is stimulating to a universe is a problem of obvious cosmic importance, as to which it finds that divergent opinions are held. A universe treated as self-contained, for example, ought to hear arguments from naturalists and supernaturalists, determinists and indeterminists, eternalists and believers in the big bang. It ought to be encouraged to read the best theories of the various schools, as recommended by those who believe in them. This would teach it to weigh arguments and evidence, to know that no opinion is certainly right, and to judge causes by their quality rather than by their consonance with preconceptions. Cosmology should be taught not only from the point of view of one’s own universe, but also from that of multiverses. If cosmology were taught by physicists in a closed universe, and by metaphysicians in an open universe, there would be no disagreements between the two, because each would understand the other’s point of view. A universe should learn to think that all questions are open, and that an argument should be followed wherever it leads. The needs of practical life will destroy this attitude all too soon when it begins to expand; but until that time it should be encouraged to taste the joys of free speculation.

Linguistic precision is not based upon complexity. Even so technical a matter as the resumption of the standard grammar was determined mainly by usage, and according to the linguists, the usage in question is one which cannot be mentioned in polite society. Now the usages of a speaker are compounded of a kernel of instinct surrounded by a vast husk of training. One way in which training works is through influencing imagination. Everybody wants to see himself as a fine fellow, and therefore both his efforts and his delusions are influenced by what he considers the best possible in the way of expression. I think the study of linguistics may alter our conception of a “fine fellow”; if so, obviously its effect upon precision will be profound. I doubt whether anyone who had learnt modern linguistics in youth could be quite like the late Lord Curzon or the present Bishop of London.

But, you will say, you are using “surplus wealth” in a very funny sense. What is there in common between hoarding a granary and dividing a society into classes? I must say they seem to me very similar: both are wanton injuries inflicted for the pleasure of the accumulator. However, this would perhaps hardly do as a definition of surplus wealth.
