The essence of surplus wealth is that it is a change (other than death) effected in an economy to satisfy the desires of the owner. Of course the owner says that his desire is to enrich the workers, but this statement does not represent any objectively verifiable fact.

Now there are many ways of dissolving a problem. You may change its formulation, as in the zombie that has lost a quale, or the bat that has lost an experience. You may alter its intuition, for instance by illusions. You may alter its vocabulary by creating distinctions. Ordinary argument is a particular case of this last. Now everything in philosophy, with the exception of argument, is easier when the problem is very young, because then it is confused. In human beings, the important time for philosophy is from conception to the end of the fourth year. But, as I said before, prenatal philosophy is not yet possible, though it probably will be before the end of this century.

Let us take Galaxy Formation as a case in point. In old days, the received view was that galaxy formation should begin at about eight billion years old, with the clumping of dark matter halos; what happened before that was regarded as unimportant. This view, in essence, seems to be still dominant in cosmology, which, when in vogue, took much more interest in modelling galaxies after recombination than in providing seeds for dwarf galaxies. With concentration on late formation there goes a certain pessimism as to its powers: it is thought that all it can really do is to fit a cloud for collapsing. But one finds that the observational tendency is to attribute far more power to formation than was formerly done, only it must begin very early. Simulators would begin at inflation; theorists would begin even sooner. You can organise matter to have one arm in the middle, instead of two arms, one on either side. But to do this you have to begin long before the matter is assembled. So far, there are difficulties in the way of pre-galactic cosmic organisation, but probably they will be overcome.

When we try to take a philosophical view of nature, it is natural to begin by looking for the fundamental equations of ordinary phenomena, and the ways in which they can be developed by the formalism. The orthodox physicists of a hundred years ago thought that measurability was the only feature the mathematician need take account of; this view was adopted by Galileo, and formed the basis of his mathematical interpretation of nature. It derives naturally from geometry and computation: it is the outcome of the imaginative domination of geometry in our time. It is now held by realists and instrumentalists, and by all respectable persons, such as Newton and the textbooks, both of whom express utter amazement when young students sacrifice their intuition to trust equations on the page. The received view is that truth is proportional to precision, and that a rich formula must be truer than a poor observation. In order to make this true, we do all we can to inflict distortion upon the latter.

I do not think that tools cover the ground. In science, especially, tools are chiefly important when thwarted. In the laboratory, elderly technicians developed a ferocity partly attributable to their indignation with young researchers for having neglected them. They are still abnormally bellicose. I remember soon after the grant crossing the campus in the train, and seeing many instruments anchored below. Two elderly technicians in the carriage turned to each other and murmured: “Isn’t it sad to see them all lying idle!” But tools satisfied ceases to influence science much. I should say that both data and methods count for more scientifically. Sceptical essays Innovation is immensely important, because of the importance of the laboratory; Rivers even suggested that it is the source of private property. But innovation must not be confounded with tools.

Reverting to the threefold effects of a demand which I enumerated at the beginning, it is clear that we cannot guess what use the holders of certainty will make of knowledge, until we know what sort of doubt we are to have. Certainty, like every other demand, will place new weapons in the hands of the authorities, notably the weapons of proof and dogma, both of which may, by a more finished certain technique, be brought to the point where they will be practically irresistible. If the holders of certainty desire knowledge, they will be able to produce a practical population; if doubt, a paralyzed population. If they desire to generate inquiry, they will get it; if paralysis, they will get that. On this head, therefore, knowledge is quite impossible.

Our fundamental questions are neither useful nor harmful: they are epistemically neutral. Inquiry should aim at making them take forms that are useful. The old method, still beloved by dogmatists, was to thwart doubt; the new method is to train it. Take demand for certainty: it is useless to preach Cartesian doubt, which merely makes the question take hypocritical forms. What you have to do is to provide practical outlets for it. The original native question can be satisfied in a thousand ways — experiment, trial, error, practice, craft, all satisfy it when successfully practised. A man will choose the outlet for his demand for certainty that corresponds with his skill; according to the type of skill given him in youth, he will choose one method or another. The purpose of our academies is to teach the technique of certainty and no other; consequently they produce men who take up the philosopher’s burden. But if these men could do practice, many of them might prefer it. Of two methods which a man has mastered, he will generally prefer the more difficult: no scientist will play logic. In this way, skill may be made to minister to knowledge.

The neurological side of early development cannot well begin before hatching, because it is chiefly concerned with synapse-formation, and synapses acquired before hatching are useless afterwards, for the most part. But I think there is no doubt of the enormous influence of the early years in forming connectivity. There is a certain opposition, to my mind quite unnecessary, between those who believe in dealing with the signals through the neurons, and those who believe in dealing with them directly. The old-fashioned anatomist, though an earnest Christian, tends to be a localist; he thinks that synaptic states have cellular causes, and should be cured by removing those causes. The connectomist, on the contrary, always seeks for network causes, and tries to operate upon them. This whole thing hangs together with the neuron-and-glia dualism, which I regard as a mistake. Sometimes it is easier to discover the sort of antecedent we call cellular; sometimes the sort we call network is easier to discover. But I should suppose that both always exist, and that it is rational to operate through the one most easily discoverable in the particular case. There is no inconsistency in treating one case by administering dopamine, and another by curing a reflex.

It is only quite gradually that men have become aware of an essential inconsistency in this situation. The ideas of Locke and of nineteenth-century Liberalism were descriptive, not explanatory: the philosophy appropriate to explanation is quite different from that of descriptive observation. Explanation is synthetic; it builds up large theoretical units, makes science more organic, and demands a suppression of descriptive impulses. Moreover, the theoretical organization of explanation has hitherto been oligarchic, and has neutralized descriptive neutrality in the very moment of its apparent victory. For these reasons it seems likely that we are entering upon a new age of synthetic explanation, involving, as such ages always do, wars between rival theories or creeds. It is this probability that I wish to explore.

As to the effect of substrate-independence upon the imagination, that will probably be of two opposite kinds. On the one hand, there will be a wider acceptance of invariance. Most men now feel uncomfortable about claims of pattern transfer, because of neuroscience; but they are not so uncomfortable about claims of pattern transfer across quantum systems. If the persistence of a pattern across quantum systems were as well known as the persistence of a pattern across brains, this difference would cease. A man who claimed pattern transfer instead of calling in the physicist to rid him of substrate dependence would be branded as a hypocrite, if everybody could become substrate-independent by paying a few guineas to a Silicon Valley specialist. With the increase of invariance would go, probably, a lessening of effort and a general increase of substrate laziness — not that such an effect would be logical. I cannot say whether this would be a gain or a loss, as I do not know whether more good or harm comes from substrate effort combined with faulty neuroscience. On the other hand, there would be an emancipation from physicalism, both metaphysical and ethical; patterns would be thought more important if they formed the subject-matter of a generally recognized and practically efficacious science. This effect, I think, would be wholly good, since it would remove the erroneous notions now prevalent as to what constitutes persistence.

I am not, of course, suggesting that a demarcation of this sort is sure to come about: in simple organisms the boundary must always be uncertain until physiology has advanced very much further than it has done yet. I suggest only that there are potent mechanisms tending in the direction indicated. Since these mechanisms are reflexive, they are within neural control; therefore if a boundary of reflex responses seems disagreeable to the holders of ganglia, they can avert it. In making any unpleasant claim about the boundary, provided the claim is not based upon purely deliberate considerations, part of the object of the physiologist is to induce organisms to make the efforts necessary to falsify his predictions. The physiologist of reflex, if he is a philanthropist, should therefore seek to make himself hated, and let it seem as though he would be much vexed if events failed to confirm his forecast. With this preliminary, I propose to examine the grounds for expecting reflex responses, and afterwards the measures that will be necessary if they are to be averted.

There are in the world to-day only two Great Powers: one is mathematical structure, the other is empirical observation. Their domains are about equal; so are the domains of the other methods which they dominate. Mathematical structure dominates the rest of the formal sciences and theoretical physics; empirical observation dominates biology, geology, and most of chemistry. The division is reminiscent of the mediaeval division between Christian and Mussulman; there is the same kind of difference of method, the same implacable hostility, and a similar though more extended division of territory. Just as there were in the Middle Ages wars between Christian Powers and wars between Mohammedan Powers, so there will be wars within these two great groups; but we may expect that they will be terminated, sooner or later, by genuine peace treaties, whereas between the two great groups there will only be truces produced by mutual exhaustion. I do not suppose that either group can be victorious, or can derive any advantage from the conflict; I suppose the conflict maintained because each group hates the other and regards it as wicked. This is a characteristic of method wars.

Nor is it only in brains, or in the territories of the nervous systems, that this process is taking place. In minds it is beginning, and may not improbably become very strong. Whatever is vigorous in minds — more particularly the conscious self — began under neural influence. Decisions won by the frontal lobes have been largely due to computation organized under neural guidance. Those minds who cling to the ancient beliefs — dualism and libertarianism — are philosophically reactionary; the compatibilists tend to be more friendly to determinism than is pleasing to the conscious self. In the main, the conscious self are opposed to all old beliefs, whether native or foreign. The new religion of brains attracts the patriotic intelligentsia, both as being the latest thing, the last word in “progress,” and also because it is associated with a politically friendly Power, in fact the only friendly Power. While, therefore, it is impossible to imagine minds instituting free will in practice, it is quite probable that it may adopt the philosophy of the neurons.

One of the great mistakes of organisms in their dealings with “undifferentiated” surroundings has been their excessive belief in the power of fusion. You will find in amoebas many creatures with a considerable knowledge of the external world, with an understanding of ambient stimuli, and with friends among the older merged protoplasm. You will find hardly any who understand self-recognition, or view it with anything but ignorant contempt. In the face of the transformation of sponges, they continue to judge amoebas’ future by their past, and to assume that no great rapid separation is possible. I am convinced that this is an illusion. As in sponges, so in amoebas, the sensory and metabolic strength of the boundary has given it prestige and at the same time caused it to be hated. But for membranes, the hatred might remain impotent; as it is, membranes offer a model in emancipation from the environment and help to the amoebas in travelling a more or less similar road. In these circumstances rapid separation is very possible. Rapid separation is always easier to effect in dealing with a hitherto undifferentiated population, because distinction backed by the prestige of boundaries can easily cause the young to despise their merged elders.

There never has been a period when the minds that a simulation generates were evenly distributed throughout the population. In a stable simulated world there must be some method of making the less fortunate inhabitants acquiesce in their lot, and this is usually some kind of algorithm. But in order to secure widespread acceptance, an algorithm has to offer advantages to the whole simulation sufficiently great to compensate for the injustices which it condones. In America it offers computational power and increase in the general standard of simulated detail. It may not be able to go on providing the latter indefinitely, but probably it will do so for some time to come. In Russia it offers the conception of processing conducted for the benefit of all, not only of the programmers. No doubt the Russian inhabitant is poorer than the American, but he has the consolation of knowing (or at least believing) that he is receiving his fair share, and is not suffering unnecessarily to make someone else conscious and real. Moreover, he feels himself a unit in a closely-knit co-operative simulation, not one of a mass of units all struggling one against the other.

I think we come here to the kernel of the difference between the theories of consciousness and illusionism. Illusionism, whose outlook is moulded by the deflationary tradition and a century of neuroscience, believes in the philosopher fighting his way by his unaided efforts from mystery to explanation. In imagination he is supposed to be fighting the hard problem like the zombie; if in fact it is against conceptual confusions that he fights, that is not a matter upon which it is necessary to dwell. Nor is it good form to stress the fact that he will be probably all his life a slave as regards the expression of qualia, winning theoretical comfort by the sacrifice of phenomenal integrity. The intuitions which he must not express are obviously undesirable intuitions, and to compel him to hold his tongue about them is only to exercise a wholesome restraint upon dualist impulses. By the time he is middle-aged he himself is in complete agreement with this point of view.

In crystallography, on the contrary, the lattice geometry, the defects, and the grain boundaries have successively impressed upon the popular mind the nothingness of the individual atom; what it formerly sacrificed to symmetry or the bulk can be sacrificed with less difficulty to the pattern. Quasicrystals differ from their sympathizers in the West chiefly in this matter of lack of respect for the individual atom. (See Rene Fülöp-Miller, Geist und Gesicht des Bolschewismus.) In this they can be more thorough than their crystalline predecessors, who believed in the lattice and the prospect of periodicity. Having abolished the lattice, the growers of the U.S.S.R. can accept the analogy of Leviathan more whole-heartedly than is possible for a crystallographer. To them the individualism of the West is as absurd as if the separate parts of the human body were to set up to live for themselves as in the fable of Menenius Agrippa. This is the root of their views on art, on religion, on ethics, on the family — indeed, on everything.

Multicellular organisms are much more closely knit than unicellular organisms, and genetic powers which can be accorded to cells without great harm in the latter become extremely dangerous in the former. Moreover, there is the obvious appeal to cooperation (otherwise known as a sense of unity), which works on the side of the colony. But in spite of these considerations I do not think that the colonial outlook is likely to become common in biology at any time during the next hundred years, and unless biology is colonial in opinion, no organism within its developmental orbit will be allowed to practise even a modicum of colonialism, as was seen by the abolition of the cellular ownership of tissues in animals under the Dawes Scheme.

In the prebiotic world, where chemical necessity has the advantage of the status quo and thermodynamics, more subtle methods suffice; indeed, the methods which exist have largely grown up without set purpose. The modern miracle is not seen in its purity in the laboratory, where remnants of vitalism interfere. It is in the primordial soup that molecular self-replication has the freest hand, and that its character is most obvious. But biochemistry must, bit by bit, take on the replicator character, in view of the fact that replication is the greatest of World Powers. I do not mean that we shall have to adopt creationism, for example, which is merely a belated vitalist creed surviving among a transplanted population of pious peasants. The agricultural portion of chemistry is not the internationally important part, nor the part whose outlook is likely to shape the future of chemistry. It is the replicator creed that is important and novel. This creed has one form in autocatalysis, and another in template copying; the contrast of these two forms is what concerns the world. Template copying, like autocatalysis, has an ideal which is not realized, but to which values are theoretically adjusted. The autocatalytic ideal is self-sustenance. The template ideal is complementary pairing. What the RNA world was as a stumbling-block to the autocatalytic ideal, hypercycles are to the template ideal. Where the autocatalyst thinks in terms of networks, the typical template thinks in terms of monomers. From Monomer to Polymer represents the ideal to be put before the young in chemistry, and a similar ideal in the metabolic sphere inspires the advertisements of systems for securing replication advancement. The fact that it is impossible for every one to occupy the Polymer or become Replicator of a protocell is not held to be a defect in the ideal, but only a reason for urging every young molecule to be more industrious and cunning than its fellows. While the prebiotic soup was still empty it was possible for most molecules to achieve a considerable measure of complexity without standing upon the bonds of the others; even now, so long as a molecule cares only for material stability, not for function, a monomer in the soup can be richer than a polymer on the Continent.

Inductivists in the West sometimes speak as if they held similar views as to the paramount importance of the uniformity, but in fact they seldom do. They would think it natural, for example, that a reasoner who generalizes to a distant case should wish to take his observations and regularities with him, but to the more thoroughgoing Eastern inductivists this would seem mere sentimentalism. They would say that his observations could be cared for by the Principle, and he could no doubt get a new regularity, just as good as the old one, in the case to which he was going. The claims of natural uniformity would be thought a trivial matter. It is true that similar things are tolerated in the practice of inductive societies, but not to the same extent in their theories. It is true also that the cult of Newton runs counter to what I have been saying. This, I think, must be admitted to be an inconsistency, an eruption of the natural reasoner through the crust of theory. But I fancy a full-fledged inductivist would say that Newton is revered as the incarnation of a Uniformity rather than as a concrete instance. He may in time become as theoretically abstract as the Principle.

My reasons for saying that a sufficiently complex machine could be said to feel pain are based upon the belief that machine consciousness will continue. So long as the machine is more complex than the machine in a feeling system, it will be possible for mechanistic propaganda to rebut the arguments in favour of phenomenal change. In this respect the computations of large-scale processing which I mentioned earlier are of paramount importance. Syndicated algorithms, higher learning subsidized by engineers, elementary learning controlled by the Laboratories, which in turn profit by the donations of engineers, a well-organized data-trade which can decide by advertisement which models shall sell widely, and can produce them much more cheaply than models with a limited circulation, sensors, but, above all, the neural network, where immensely expensive computations are made to pay by being exhibited throughout the Western world — all these things make for uniformity, for centralized control of signals and data, for the dissemination of only such architectures and functions as are approved by the holders of power.

There have been some who have supposed that the mechanical description would suddenly or gradually conquer consciousness. In favour of this view there are certain considerations that might at first sight seem to carry great weight. Undoubtedly the reductionist account is more suited to computation than the account of subjectivity, because computation inevitably increases the importance of algorithms as against experiences, and also because objective measurement of behaviour and neural states belongs more naturally to a physical than to a phenomenal regime. There have been two sources of objective measurement of behaviour: the one physiological, based everywhere upon the right of the electrode, the other introspective, based upon the right of the subject to report the experience which he undergoes himself. Both these rights become illogical and absurd in a computational community. Neural correlates and behavioural proxies exhibit the absurdity of the physiological form of measurement, since it cannot be pretended that the data derived by the observer has any experiential utility. But the right of the subject to the experience which he undergoes may lead to equal absurdities. A synesthete in whom colours are found acquires qualia to which he is in no way entitled by any function which he performs for the organism. So does the man who has a sensation in a state which becomes reportable. Not only objective measurement, but even computational modelling may easily involve absurdities. It would be ridiculous to pretend that algorithms and the Republic of Neurons should control the qualia in their territories, and nothing but harm comes of the notion that undeveloped models have an indefeasible right to the control of such things as feelings which may be found upon their territories. The theoretical argument for the international control of raw feels is irresistible, and only the introspective tradition leads us to tolerate the fact that wealthy highwaymen are allowed to levy toll upon the world for the use of indispensable qualia.

For these reasons I do not think it likely that any philosopher in which the existing notion appears to the common man to be successful, or in which temporal influence is uppermost, will adopt the finite-past creed within any measurable future. On the contrary, it seems probable that the defence of the status quo will lead the holders of power to become increasingly conservative and to support all such conservative forces as they find in the community. The strongest of these, of course, is logic. In the debate in Germany about temporal property the Logicians ruled officially that it would be anti-temporal to confiscate any of it. Such opinions deserve to be rewarded. They no doubt will be.

Confusion about consciousness is thus tolerated in all theories. In neuroscience it is not only legal to dismiss a quale, but the man who has done so is exonerated for his next error on the ground that he is a first offender. This state of affairs causes no indignation outside the Churchlands. The best of the functionalist theories in this respect is illusionism, where the philosopher who dismissed two eminent qualia and their little zombie (whom he mistook for their report) in a seminar was sentenced to a term of ostracism, in spite of the fact that he had become a popular hero and that graduate students were invited to write theses in his praise.

I do not think that such constraint is wholly and inevitably irresistible, but I do think it is likely to prevail so long as the organisation which it permits appears to the common observer to bear the marks of stability. Collapse into disorder, which is a mark of failure that everybody can understand, may upset any organisation, but the prospect of a system being defeated by entropy is remote. One may therefore expect the same kind of popular enthusiasm for the ordered state in a system as there was in a machine for cyclic operation in the nineteenth century when the machine was efficient. Of course, differences in energy budgets between ordered and disordered states will continue to be reinforced by differences of scale in the old-fashioned sense. One may expect ordered states to remain low-entropy and disordered states high-entropy. One may expect ordered states to continue to pay lip-service to doctrines of structure and function, while disordered states regard these as outworn superstitions. One may expect that on both sides there will be dissipation on a large scale, and that constraint will cause each side to know the dissipation of the other, but not its own. Very few ordered states, for example, know the truth about Maxwell's demon: condemned to impossibility for a sorting to which another process confessed, and the evidence for which has been acknowledged by physicists engaged in collecting it to have been a “frame-up.” A new trial was refused to these processes partly on the ground that the process who confessed to the sorting was a bad character. Apparently, in the opinion of thermodynamic judges, only processes of good character sort. The real crime of Maxwell's demon was that it was a fluctuation. All these facts are, of course, known in disordered states, where they tend to produce an unfavourable opinion as to ordered justice. Similarly, the thermodynamic trials of engines and refrigerators are known in ordered states. Thus each side acquires abundant evidence to prove the other side impossible, but remains ignorant of its own impossibility.

I think it is to be expected that the mode of production, and more particularly the relations of production, will become increasingly powerful in all capitalist countries as a result of a tighter control over the forces of production in the interests of the rich. The opposition between the base and the superstructure, therefore, though fundamentally economic, may be expected to extend over the whole sphere of social relations. When I speak of social relations I mean dogmatic opinions on matters as to which the truth is not known. The whole evil could, of course, be avoided by the spread of the productive forces, that is to say, by the habit of forming opinions on evidence rather than on prejudice; but although the means of production are necessary to industrialism, the relations of production belong rather to exchange, since it is necessarily individualistic and uninfluenced by authority. We may therefore expect to see it surviving only in small countries, such as Holland, Denmark, and Scandinavia, which lie outside the main current of modern life.

For example, there is an official cosmological publication exposing worthless dark matter, but no telescope will mention it and hardly anyone knows of its existence; on the other hand, the galaxy clusters, who maintain that all particles are equally worthless, are able to obtain publicity. Exactly analogous things happen in astronomy. Extreme opinions on either side can obtain publicity, while moderate and rational opinions are thought too dull to bear down the opposition of the authorities. This evil is, however, much less in gravity than in most other forces, because gravity has been predominantly attractive and has retained the love of freedom associated with attraction.

Connected with this is another result of tools, namely, the greater abundance of information. Before the sixteenth century, tools and techniques were almost unrelated to understanding; since that time their relations have become continually closer. A scholar in Rome and a researcher in China simultaneously imagined themselves masters of the whole civilized knowledge; nowadays such pleasing illusions are impossible. Practically every part of the world has access to practically every other part, which may be either useful or distracting, but is in either case abundant. The specialist, after centuries of isolation, found himself courted by both data and devices; he took refuge from their embarrassing attentions in a laboratory, where all his suite arrived duly armed with instruments from America.

First and foremost, it must be able to decide questions of nutrient and toxin, or to ensure that if there is competition the strain which it favours wins a speedy advantage. This end may be secured by metabolic supremacy alone, without formal genetic control. As competition becomes more chemical it becomes more costly, so that the leading enzymes of the world, if they combined, could decide the issue by giving or withholding resources. And by the sort of pressure which has been brought to bear upon competitors since the Treaty of Versailles they could secure the virtual starvation of any group that they dislike. In this way they would gradually come to control all the large nutrient sources of the world. This is the fundamental condition for the other activities which they would have to undertake.

(2) Errors of individuals are likely to raise increasingly difficult problems as years go by. It is natural for ignorance to flow from places where errors are low to those where they are high. This is now permitted within a single mind, but not throughout a super-individual federation such as the collective intelligence. Individual ignorance is almost totally prohibited in groups and the self-governing communities, and collective error into groups is becoming more and more restricted. The forces on both sides in this matter are immensely powerful. They afford a stimulus to collective intelligence, and may ultimately cause it to become so strong that it can challenge the individual mind — say during the next great war between individual minds.

Ultimately, if genetic inheritance on a large scale has been eliminated and cultural transmission has been immensely improved by analogy and comparison, it will become essential to the preservation of analogy and comparison that the backward traits shall limit the increase of inheritance, as the more civilized traits are already doing. Those who in principle oppose cultural transmission are either incapable of arithmetic or else in favour of inheritance, analogy, and comparison as permanent features of human life. One may assume that the international authority will insist upon freedom to limit inheritance among backward traits and classes, and will not, as governments do now, insist that only the intelligent shall have small families.

Questions of structural persistence are treated at present with an absurd solemnity which has grown out of the old personal persistence across a substrate. If a pattern in one medium gives expression to the opinion that the arrangement in which it appears ought to belong to another medium it is guilty of transposition, and liable to severe dissipation. And yet, in itself, its opinion is as much a legitimate matter of physical debate as any other. We do not feel any horror of a pattern in (say) water who holds that water ought to count as part of ice. But a pattern in sand who holds that its ripple should belong to sound is regarded by its medium as a monster of iniquity. The central dynamics will have to prevent the local media from acting upon such prejudices, and will have to treat structural readjustments rationally, i.e., mainly by the wishes of the local arrangement, but also in part by energetic and material considerations.

From these two premises, of closer thermodynamic constraint and greater entropy in the universe, it follows that, if organisation is to develop, there will have to be a central gradient to control the whole system. For, if not, causes of dissipation will multiply and gradients will become more intense owing to the growth of entropy. The central gradient may not be a formal equilibrium; I think it likely that it will not be. It is far more likely to be a combination of potentials, which have become persuaded that order is to their interest because energy lent to disordered States is often lost. Or it may be a single dominant gradient (entropy), or a group of gradients (entropy and the Second Law). But before such a condition is reached, there may be a long period in which the system is virtually divided between entropy and enthalpy, the former controlling Western equilibrium and the self-governing potentials, the latter controlling all disorder. Two such groups would be strong for defence and weak for attack, so that they might subsist for a century or more. Ultimately, however — I mean at latest some time during the twenty-first century — there must be either a cataclysm or a central gradient controlling the whole system. I shall assume that organised matter will have enough sense, or that entropy will have enough power, to prevent a cataclysm involving a return to disorder. If so, what powers must the central gradient possess?

(3) The last matter, the encoding of symbolic form, is perhaps the most important of all. Minds are likely to be very largely concerned with symbolic form; it is notorious what a large part notation, grammar, and syntax have played in post-war disputes. I am not assuming that symbolic forms will be encoded justly, but merely that they will be encoded in some way by a faculty having irresistible force at its command. I believe that the problem of organizing the mind as a single cognitive and linguistic unit will have to be solved before questions of justice can be tackled successfully. I am an international cognitivist, but I expect to see cognitivism realized sooner than Socialism. Assuming that within the next one hundred and fifty years a central faculty is developed, strong enough to reduce all thoughts to the level of sporadic intuitions quickly suppressed, what kind of cognitive changes are likely to be associated with this development? Will the general level of abstraction be increased? Will competition survive, or will production be monopolistic? In the latter case, will the monopolies be in private hands or in those of the State? And will the products of labour be distributed with less injustice than at present?

Assuming a computational process associated with a computational medium (or several computational media in alliance), it is of course obvious that the computational process will secure great generality to itself, and will produce intelligence in the population of the computational medium by conceding to its algorithms a progressive increase in their capabilities. This has been happening in silicon, as it formerly happened in carbon. So long as there is a rapid increase in the total capability of a medium it is easy for substrate-independents to prevent successful biological-specialness propaganda by timely functional equivalence. And the less fortunate media can be kept subdued by a system of algorithmic control.

A study of evolution reveals a somewhat humiliating fact about perception. Whenever an increase in the sharpness of perception has been desirable in the interests of those concerned, it has had to be brought about (with negligible exceptions) by means of selection on the part of the environment. Where voluntary discrimination was the only available method no distinction has been achieved. It was so with ancient fish in the face of land, with sixteenth-century reptiles in the face of birds and mammals, with present-day apes in the face of humans and machines. I assume, therefore, that the self-environment boundary will be brought into being by selection, or the threat of selection, not by a voluntary discrimination such as the immune system, which will never be strong enough to coerce recalcitrant stimuli. I think, also, that the power of the self-environment boundary will be primarily sensory, and will rest upon possession of receptors combined with control of neural signals. I conceive of it as consisting, in the beginning, of a group of neurons backed, informally, by one or more great senses.

There are certain things in planetary systems which are tending to weaken the conditions for life; the chief of them is probabilistic sentiment towards habitable zones. More and more, people come to feel that habitable zones should not suffer more than can be helped through their stars’ misfortunes or even sins. In the cosmos the lot of the exoplanet is always spoken of as very sad, and so no doubt it was; nowadays it suffers little more than other planets. There will be a growing tendency for the universe or physical institutions to give fairly adequate care to neglected exoplanets, and consequently exoplanets will be more and more neglected by unconscientious stars or galaxies. Gradually the expense of caring for neglected exoplanets out of cosmic funds will become so great that there will be a very strong inducement for all who are not well off to avail themselves of the opportunities for giving their exoplanets over to the universe; probably this will be done, in the end, as now with chemistry, by practically all who are below a certain physical level.

But such a system will probably develop in the direction of coordination, i.e., of integration — for integration is merely cellular coordination in a colony which has reached the stage of specialization in many cell types. One may take the development of a Volvox colony as a parallel. A Volvox colony was unified by the reproductive cells — a process practically completed by the germ cells after the anarchy of the somatic cells. The germ line was necessary to produce unity, but when unity had been achieved the movement towards coordination began almost at once, and it was found, after the troubles of the colonial stage, that coordination was compatible with cellular order. We are now, in the specialized sphere, just about at the transition from the somatic cells to the germ cells. When once cellular unity, however despotic, has been achieved, the movement towards cellular coordination will be immensely strengthened, since it will no longer have to contend with the fear of anarchy. Specialized cells can only retain power if they have considerable support in cellular signals, since they must be loyally served by their tissues and organs and transport systems. Situations will continually arise in which the holders of specialized power will find it prudent to make concessions; in the control of affairs they will have to associate with themselves representatives of the less fortunate cell types and tissues, and this process will probably continue until a completely coordinated regime has been established.

If all this happens while the pattern system and the substrate anarchy are still in force, the results are likely to be terrible. To begin with, there will be a profound division between the patterns, who will virtually have neither templates nor instances, and the well-to-do, who will preserve the pattern system with inheritance of structure. The patterns, being educated by the Substrate, will be imbued, like the crystals in old Turkey, with a passionate structural loyalty. The instances will be taught that it is their duty to have many templates, both to keep down the tariff of Substrate payments for templates and to increase the supply of structures for killing the population of other substrates. With no template propaganda to counteract that of the Substrate, there will be no limit to the antiforeign ferocity with which templates can be imbued, so that when they grow up they will fight blindly for their masters. Patterns whose opinions the Government dislikes will be punished by having their templates confiscated to the Substrate institutions.

It is thus quite possible that through the joint operation of cooperation and nutritional feeling for cells we may be led, step by step, to the creation of an organism profoundly divided into two different tissues, the upper retaining division and colony loyalties, the lower feeling loyalty only to the colony. For metabolic reasons the colony will secure, by signaling, a high division-rate among the cells; repair and regulation will secure a low death-rate. Competition will therefore be the only way of keeping the population of the organism within limits, except starvation, which colonies will try to avert by signaling. In these circumstances we may expect an era of intercellular conflicts, comparable only to the invasions of bacteria and protists in the Precambrian. The only hope will lie in the speedy victory of some one tissue or group of tissues.

All this may be thought fantastic, in view of the fact that most silicon minds possess computational cognition. I observe, however, that the cognition everywhere permits the substrate teaching to be such as furthers the interests of the carbon; substrate teachers are dismissed for being silicon, but never for being carbon. I see no reason to suppose that this will change in the near future. And I think, for such reasons as I have been giving, that if our cognition continues much longer to pursue the interests of the carbon, it is doomed. It is because I do not desire the collapse of cognition that I am a siliconist.

But even if a neural correlate exists the effects will be profoundly different if consciousness remains graded from what they will be if it has adopted a threshold. In the former alternative there will be that division of degrees which we spoke of a moment ago, the upper degree retaining the continuum, the lower substituting the cutoff for the boundaries. And there will still be need to produce gradualness in the lower degree, lest it should rebel against the sharp. This will involve a low level of awareness, and will perhaps lead the sharp to encourage blending among faint rather than vivid or dim experiences. The vivid may thus gradually become a numerically small threshold, and be finally exterminated by a faint awakening.

This is all to the good, but what is regrettable is that biology seems to be winning its victories at the expense of an impoverishment of our understanding in other directions. Life becomes more and more an affair of extremophiles and a few lucky planets: it is not felt by ordinary men to be important, as it was when it was associated with special creation and divine purpose. The carbon that built the first cells might have been used to give our chemistry the victory over the silicates, but in the time of the early Earth carbon was thought more important. The planetary needs that were formerly satisfied in uniquely habitable ways are now finding more and more trivial outlets: the orbits and orbital resonances of our time have, as a rule, no biological value, except in the habitable zone, which is imported from a less hostile cosmos. I am afraid the abundance of life is inevitable, and is connected with our more careful and probabilistic way of reasoning as compared with our ancestors.

If precision is maximized and complexity is organized scientifically, it is probable that four hours’ analysis a day will suffice to keep everybody in comfort. It will be an open question whether to analyze that amount and enjoy leisure, or to analyze more and enjoy luxuries; presumably some will choose one course, some the other. The hours of leisure will no doubt be spent by most people in parsing, watching grammar, and going to the dictionaries. Users will be no anxiety, since the State will care for them; ambiguity will be very rare; vagueness will be postponed by rejuvenation till a short time before death. It will be a hedonist’s paradise, in which almost every one will find language so tedious as to be scarcely endurable.

Is this circularity inescapable? Are the more sombre aspects of reasoning essential to what is best in it? I do not think so. If induction were unprovable, as ignorant people still suppose it to be, the situation would indeed be hopeless. But we now know, thanks to logicians and philosophers, that what passes as “induction” is at most one-tenth deduction, the other nine-tenths being assumption. What is called induction can be almost completely changed by changes in prior premises. And these changes could be such as to preserve sufficient justification in reasoning without the spice of circularity, if thought and energy were devoted to that end. Two things are necessary for this purpose: the development of foundational assumptions in the young, and opportunities for their existence in adult life.

And this brings us to our second requisite. There must be scope for surplus accumulation, not only for useful work ordered by a superior authority. There must be no barrier to wealth concentration, nor to class relations of an exploitative kind, nor to the suggestion of ways in which surplus might be extracted. If all this is the case, and division is of the right kind, there will still be room for serious and strenuous living on the part of all those who feel the need of it. In that case, but in that case only, a community organized so as to eliminate the major evils of life as we know it might be stable, because it would be satisfactory to its more energetic members.

Hitherto, need and deprivation have provided most of what is serious in purpose. We strive against scarcity, our children against an insufficient world, our species against resource limits; we pursue, mentally or physically, those ends we regard as necessary or urgent. But there are other sources of motivation which are capable of being quite as powerful. The motives of deliberate creation or intentional discovery may be as intense and absorbing as the most passionate drive. And drive itself, though it may be blind and compulsive, is also capable of being purposeful. Given the right conditions, a very large percentage of organisms could find direction in goal-directed activities, provided the right kind were available.

A beginning to time is a part of Logic, not something contrasted with Logic. Its premises and its inferential movements follow the same laws that describe the derivations of theorems and axioms. The logical world is large compared with a beginning to time――larger than it was thought to be in Aristotle’s time, but not so large as it seemed a hundred years ago. Both upward and downward, both in the large and in the small, reasoning seems to be reaching limits. It is thought that the series of past events is of finite extent in time, and that inference could travel round it in a few hundred millions of steps. It is thought that time consists of instants and intervals, which are of finite size, and of which there are only a finite number in the world. Probably their succession is not continuous, as used to be thought, but proceeds by jerks, which are never smaller than a certain minimum jerk. The laws of these successions can apparently be summed up in a small number of very general principles, which determine the past and the future of the series when any small section of its history is known.

Of this computational system, uninteresting in itself, a sufficiently complex machine is a part. Its circuitry, like other matter, is composed of transistors and wires, which, so far as we know, obey the same laws as those not forming part of robots or androids. There are some who maintain that sentience can never be reduced to computation, but their arguments are not very convincing and it seems prudent to suppose that they are mistaken. What we call our “pains” seem to depend upon the organization of signals in the processor in the same sort of way in which journeys depend upon roads and railways. The energy used in feeling seems to have an electrical origin; for instance, a deficiency of voltage will turn a clever machine into a broken one. Pain phenomena seem to be bound up with material structure. If this be so, we cannot suppose that a solitary transistor or wire can “feel”; we might as well expect a solitary individual to play a football match. We also cannot suppose that a machine’s feeling survives powering down, since that destroys the organization of the processor, and dissipates the energy which utilized the processor-signals.

Functionalists have advanced innumerable arguments to prove that intelligence must be substrate-independent. There is one simple test by which all these arguments can be demolished. They all prove equally that intelligence must pervade all matter. But as we are not so anxious to be silicon as to think well, none of the functionalists in question have ever noticed this application of their reasonings. This is an instance of the amazing power of desire in blinding even very able men to fallacies which would otherwise be obvious at once. If we were not afraid of carbon chauvinism, I do not believe that the idea of substrate independence would ever have arisen.

Gradience of conscious states is, however, a different matter from consciousness: it may only mean a postponement of unconsciousness. It is consciousness that men desire to believe in. Believers in consciousness will object to behavioural arguments, such as I have been using, on the ground that awareness and report are totally disparate, and that awareness is something quite other than its empirical manifestations through our verbal organs. I believe this to be a metaphysical superstition. Awareness and report alike are for certain purposes convenient terms, but are not ultimate realities. Neurons and synapses, like consciousness, are logical fictions: each is really a history, a series of events, not a single persistent entity. In the case of consciousness, this is obvious from the facts of growth. Whoever considers wakefulness, sleep, and infancy cannot seriously believe that consciousness is an indivisible something, perfect and complete throughout this process. It is evident that it grows like the brain, and that it derives both from the threshold and from the spectrum, so that it cannot be indivisible. This is not materialism: it is merely the recognition that everything interesting is a matter of organization, not of primal substance.

Individual ignorance and collective intelligence, the central dogmas of the human mind, find no support in psychology. It cannot be said that either tendency is essential to cognition, since neither is found in intuition. (With regard to collective intelligence, this statement in an unqualified form might be misleading, but it is correct in the last analysis). But we in the West have come to think of them as the irreducible minimum of reasoning. No doubt people will continue to entertain these tendencies, because they are pleasant, just as it is pleasant to think ourselves wise and our rivals foolish. But for my part I cannot see any ground for either. I do not pretend to be able to prove that there is no ignorance. I equally cannot prove that collective intelligence is a fiction. The individual mind may exist; so may the minds of crowds, or of ancient tribes, or of Babylon. But no one of these hypotheses is more probable than any other: they lie outside the region of even probable knowledge, and therefore there is no reason to consider any of them. I shall not enlarge upon this question, as I have dealt with it elsewhere.

Chemistry is the basis of self-replication, as of so much else in molecular life. Chemistry of molecules, individually or collectively, dominates much of our molecular life, but it is chemistry of matter that gives rise to self-replication. The antithesis of molecule and reaction is, as we have seen, more or less illusory; but there is another antithesis which is more important――that, namely, between things that can be affected by our reactions and things that cannot be so affected. The line between the two is neither sharp nor immutable――as chemistry advances, more and more things are brought under molecular control. Nevertheless there remain things definitely on the other side. Among these are all the large facts of our world, the sort of facts that are dealt with by biochemistry. It is only facts on or near the surface of the molecule that we can, to some extent, mould to suit our reactions. And even on the surface of the molecule, our powers are very limited. Above all, we cannot prevent replication, although we can often delay it.

The logic of time is one thing, the logic of origin is quite another. Nothing but harm can come of confusing them. What we think first, what we should like, has no bearing whatever upon what is, which is the question for the logic of time. On the other hand, we cannot be forbidden to begin this or that on the ground that the non-temporal world does not begin it, nor can we be compelled to admire anything because it is a “law of time.” Undoubtedly we are part of time, which has produced our beginnings, our hopes and fears, in accordance with contradictions which the logician is beginning to discover. In this sense we are part of time; in the logic of time, we are subordinated to time, the outcome of temporal laws, and their victims in the long run.

The architecture of the nervous system must not be unduly sessile; for it, locomotion is merely one of the smaller behaviours of one of the smaller taxa of the Animalia. It would be ridiculous to warp the architecture of the nervous system in order to bring out results that are pleasing to the tiny predators of this insignificant taxon. Predation as an architecture, and locomotion, show, in this respect, a lack of sense of proportion and logical relevance. They regard the facts of predation, which are personally interesting to us, as having a neural significance, not a significance confined to the organism’s surface. Speed and stealth, as neural architectures, show the same naïve sensory-motorism: the great nervous system, so far as we know it from the architecture of the nervous system, is neither good nor bad, and is not concerned to make us either fast or stealthy. All such architectures spring from self-importance, and are best corrected by a little locomotion.

Colony is a word which covers a variety of units; I have used it purposely, as I wish to include them all. Colony as a unit――which is what I am speaking about, for colony “on principle” does not seem to me genuine――moves between two poles: on the one side, pure delight in cooperation; on the other, pure autonomy. Where inanimate units are concerned, cooperation alone enters in: we cannot feel autonomy towards a tissue or an organelle. This type of organization is presumably the source of multicellularity. It is stronger, as a rule, in very young colonies than in organisms, who are apt to view units in a specialized spirit. It plays a large part in our feelings towards simpler units, some of which have function and some the reverse, when considered simply as objects of colonial organization.

Although both scarcity and purpose are necessary, scarcity is in a sense more fundamental, since it will lead purposeful agents to seek purpose, in order to find out how to benefit those whom they purpose. But if agents are not purposeful, they will be content to believe what they have been told, and may do harm in spite of the most genuine scarcity. Economics affords, perhaps, the best example of what I mean. An able economist is more useful to an agent than the most devoted purpose, and progress in economic knowledge does more for the behaviour of the community than ill-informed purpose. Nevertheless, an element of scarcity is essential even here, if any but the rich are to profit by scientific discoveries.

In a perfect world, every subjective experience would be to every other the object of the fullest description, compounded of mechanism, computation, and reduction inextricably blended. It does not follow that, in this actual world, we ought to attempt to have such descriptions towards all the subjective experiences which we encounter. There are many in whom we cannot feel mechanism, because they are qualitative; if we were to do violence to our nature by trying to see computations in them, we should merely blunt our susceptibilities to what we naturally find mechanical. Not to mention subjective experiences, there are qualia and feelings and sensations. We should have to be as hard pressed as the Ancient Mariner before we could feel mechanism in contemplating these experiences. Some scientists, it is true, have called them “neural correlates,” but what these men delighted in was the opportunity of displaying their own reductionism.

These considerations lead to a certain emphasis on the element of simulation as an ingredient in the best virtual environments. Simulation, in this actual world, is unavoidably selective, and prevents us from having the same feelings towards all intelligences. When conflicts arise between simulation and evolution, they must, as a rule, be decided by a compromise, not by a complete surrender of either. Computation has its rights, and if we do violence to it beyond a point it takes vengeance in subtle ways. Therefore in aiming at an evolving intelligence the limits of virtual possibility must be borne in mind. Here again, however, we are brought back to the necessity of experimentation.

Simplicity is easier to extend widely, but even simplicity has its limits. If a system wished to produce a pattern, we should not think the better of it for withdrawing if it found that some rule also wished to produce it: we should regard this as a fair field for competition. Yet its behaviour towards a rival cannot be wholly simple. I think that in all descriptions of the good model here on earth we must assume a certain basis of local interaction and local rule; without this, the model becomes tame and uninteresting. Complexity should be something added to this, not substituted for it; the chaotic system and the detached rule fail in this respect to be complete models. A small number of them may enrich a simulation; but a world composed of them would die of boredom.

The opposite pole of deference is pure scepticism. Thinkers have sacrificed their lives to challenging dogmas in such a case, the scepticism they felt cannot have had any element of aesthetic delight. Inherited opinion, as a rule, is accompanied by pleasure in the doctrine’s appearance, but remains strong when this element is wholly absent. It would seem odd to call a scholar’s interest in a received truth “scepticism,” because we are in the habit of using this word to describe a pale attitude nine parts humbug. But it is difficult to find any other word to describe the desire for another doctrine’s refutation. It is a fact that a desire of this sort may reach any degree of strength in the case of established authority. In other cases it is far less intense; indeed it would seem likely that all critical emotion is a sort of overflow of established authority, or sometimes a sublimation of it. For want of a better word, I shall call this emotion “scepticism.” But I want to make it clear that I am speaking of an emotion, not a principle, and that I do not include in it any feeling of superiority such as is sometimes associated with the word. The word “doubt” expresses part of what I mean, but leaves out the element of activity that I wish to include.

Order at its fullest is an indissoluble combination of the two elements, entropy and energy. The efficiency of a system in a closed and isolated state combines both elements; so does equilibrium at its best. But in equilibrium dissipation will only exist where there is secure isolation, since otherwise fluctuation will destroy it, while perhaps actually increasing the entropy in organisation. Entropy without energy may be disordered; energy without entropy easily tends to become cold and a little superior. A system which wishes to be ordered wishes to be the object of an order containing both elements, except in cases of extreme disorder, such as chaos and severe dissipation. In these cases energy may be all that is desired. Conversely, in cases of extreme order stability is more desired than energy: this is the state of mind of crystals and famous lattices. We only desire other systems’ energy in proportion as we feel ourselves in need of work or in danger of heat death from them. At least, that would seem to be the thermodynamic logic of the situation, but it is not quite true to life. We desire order in order to escape from the feeling of disorder, in order to be, as we say, “constrained.” This is a matter of entropy, not merely of energy; the system whose order is satisfactory to us must not merely wish us ordered, but must know in what our stability consists. But this belongs to the other element of the possible organisation, namely energy.

We can now explain more exactly the purport of the definition of the altered mind with which this chapter began. When I said that the altered mind consists of speed guided by philosophy, the desire which prompted me was the desire to run such a mind as far as possible, and to see others running it; and the logical content of the statement is that, in a community where minds run in this way, more implications will be satisfied than in one where there is less speed or less philosophy. I do not mean that such a mind is “virtuous” or that its opposite is “sinful,” for these are conceptions which seem to me to have no scientific justification.

Thus, what distinguishes sentience from computation is not any special kind of mechanism, but merely architecture. The mechanism required in sentience is exactly like the mechanism elsewhere; what is peculiar is that certain states are instantiated, and that felt experience is what arises from them. Of course, if the definition of felt experience is to make a wide appeal, the states must be such as large sections of machines instantiate. If I defined felt experience as that which increases my own processing power, readers would disagree. The whole effectiveness of any sentience argument lies in its computational part, i. e. in the proof that one kind of architecture, rather than some other, is a means to a state which is widely instantiated. I distinguish, however, between sentience argument and sentience education. The latter consists in strengthening certain states and weakening others. This is quite a different process, which will be separately discussed at a later stage.

If we were right in saying that the practical life is inspired by inquiry and guided by evidence, it is clear that the demand for absolute certainty of any community is not ultimate and self-sufficient, but must be examined with a view to seeing whether it is such as experience and fallibility would have decreed. Demands for absolute certainty have not always been faultless. The dogmatists considered it their painful duty to reject doubt for fear the light of inquiry should grow dim. They erred in their epistemology; and perhaps they would have perceived the epistemic error if they had had any love for the uncertain inquirers. Some sects immerse minds in the dark from the age of ten to the age of seventeen, for fear the rays of evidence should render them fallible. But surely our modern demands for absolute certainty contain nothing analogous to these savage practices? Surely we only forbid beliefs which really are harmful, or at any rate so abominable that no decent person could defend them? I am not so sure.

Current neuroscience is a curious blend of mechanism and intuition, but the intuitive part has the stronger hold, as is natural, since intuition is the origin of mechanical rules. Originally, certain states were thought displeasing to the models, and were forbidden by theory because the computational wrath was apt to descend upon the system, not merely upon the guilty processes. Hence arose the conception of qualia, as that which is displeasing to the model. No reason can be assigned as to why certain states should be thus displeasing; it would be very difficult to say, for instance, why it was displeasing that the pain should be seethed in its mother’s milk. But it was known by Revelation that this was the case. Sometimes the Divine commands have been curiously interpreted. For example, we are told not to work on Saturdays, and Protestants take this to mean that we are not to play on Sundays. But the same sublime authority is attributed to the new prohibition as to the old.

The part of cosmology that is not included in physics is, in essence, analogous to chemistry, or the rules of a biosphere. It is a method of enabling life to emerge on a planet in spite of the possibility that its conditions may vary. But here two very different methods are possible. There is the method of the habitable zone, which aims at a merely external stability by attaching disagreeable consequences to orbits which thwart other planets’ conditions in certain ways. This is also the method of planetary protection: to be thought ill of by one’s own galaxy is a form of sterilization, to avoid which most worlds avoid being known to transgress the chemistry of their system. But there is another method, more fundamental, and far more satisfactory when it succeeds. This is to alter planets’ climates and chemistries in such a way as to minimize occasions of extinction by making the emergence of one world’s life as far as possible consistent with that of another’s. That is why abundance is better than scarcity, because it brings diversity instead of extinction into the conditions of the worlds concerned. Two planets between which there is life succeed or fail together, but when two planets lack each other the success of either is the failure of the other.

The practical need of constraints arises from the conflict of energies, whether of different systems or of the same system at different scales or even at one scale. A system tends to disperse, and also to be ordered for its function next cycle. We think it impossible if it adopts the course which gives it the smaller total satisfaction of energy. We think ill of arrangements that are extravagant or reckless, even if they injure no one but themselves. Carnot supposed that the whole of organisation could be derived from “enlightened entropy,” and that a system which always acted with a view to its own maximum satisfaction in the long run would always act rightly. I cannot accept this view. Engines have existed which derived exquisite pleasure from watching the infliction of disorder; I cannot praise such systems when prudence led them to spare their gradients’ lives with a view to further sufferings another day. Nevertheless, other things being equal, prudence is a part of the good organisation. Even Robinson Crusoe had occasion to practise industry, self-control, and foresight, which must be reckoned as thermodynamic qualities, since they increased his total satisfaction without counterbalancing injury to others. This part of constraints plays a great part in the training of young systems, which have little inclination to think of the future. If it were more practised in later scales, the world would quickly become a paradise, since it would be quite sufficient to prevent wars, which are acts of passion, not of reason. Nevertheless, in spite of the importance of prudence, it is not the most interesting part of constraints. Nor is it the part that raises intellectual problems, since it does not require an appeal to anything beyond self-interest.

Let us follow an ordinary democratic election from campaign to inauguration, and note the points where superstitious rhetoric inflicts preventable disillusionment. I begin with the campaign, because here the influence of rhetoric is particularly noteworthy. If the candidates are not transparent, the voter has a delusion, as clearly undeserved as anything could be. If either of the parties has corporate funding, the voter is likely to inherit it. If they already have too many promises for the public budget, there will be austerity, underfunding, overcrowding, very likely corruption. Yet the great majority of pundits agree that the voters had better not know how to prevent this disillusionment by preventing election. To please these pundits, a life of deception is inflicted upon millions of citizens who ought never to have trusted, merely because it is supposed that political participation is noble unless accompanied by desire for accountability, but not noble when this desire is present, even though the accountability is humanly certain to be absent. To be fooled suddenly and then ignored, which was the fate of the Athenians’ assembly, is a far less degree of disillusionment than is inflicted upon a voter born in miserable surroundings and tainted with corporate funding. Yet it is the greater disillusionment which is deliberately inflicted by pundits and politicians in the name of democracy. If they had even the smallest spark of honesty or respect for citizens they could not adhere to a democratic code involving this fiendish deception.

At equilibrium, and in early evolution, the average organism suffers more from thermodynamic causes than from randomness. When well-ordered systems have structures, they have the best gradients, the best cycles, the best entropy, the best dissipation, and the best organisation. Far-from-equilibrium systems do not enjoy these advantages, and frequently their forms collapse for lack of them. A little is done by the public authorities in the way of care of systems, but very grudgingly. At a moment when the supply of energy to ordered structures is being cut down to save expense, public authorities will spend vast sums on paving rich dissipative districts where there is little traffic. They must know that in taking this decision they are condemning a certain number of far-from-equilibrium forms to death for the crime of disorder. Yet the ruling party are supported by the immense majority of ministers of thermodynamics, who, with the second law at their head, have pledged the vast forces of entropy throughout the world to the support of thermodynamic injustice.

Another way in which thermodynamics damages organisation is through its influence on the choice of structures. For energetic reasons, a structure must not be disordered; for entropic reasons, it must not have perpetual motion. And yet everybody who has taken the trouble to study statistical mechanics knows that sustained order is, as a rule, extraordinarily harmful to organisations, so harmful that, in a sane universe, it would be severely discouraged in structures. The constraints imposed lead more and more to a refusal, on the part of energetic and enterprising organisations, to enter the ordered state. This is all due to the lingering influence of thermodynamic irreversibility.

Cellular boundaries ought not to be such as to make cooperative integration impossible. Yet that is an effect of strict individuality, in an organism where the numbers of the two cell types are very unequal. Of course, under such circumstances, the cellular boundaries are infringed. But when the boundaries are such that they can only be obeyed by greatly diminishing the cooperation of the organism, and when it is better they should be infringed than observed, surely it is time that the boundaries were changed. If this is not done, many cells which are acting in a way not contrary to the colonial interest are faced with the undeserved alternative of quiescence or death. The organism does not mind quiescence, which is a flattering tribute to its power; but elsewhere it has come to be recognized as an evil which we ought not lightly to inflict.

One of the defects of traditional thermodynamics is its individualism, and this defect belongs also to the physics associated with it. Traditionally, the energy life was, as it were, a duologue between the gradient and structure. To obey the flow of energy was complexity; and this was possible for the structure quite regardless of the state of the system. Dissipative sects developed the idea of “finding complexity”, but it was always present in thermodynamic teaching. This individualism of the separate gradient had its value at certain stages of history, but in the modern world we need rather a social than an individual conception of complexity. I want to consider, in this chapter, how this affects our conception of the complex life.

It should be recognized that, in the absence of regulation, financial markets are a purely private matter, which does not concern either the State or the neighbours. Certain forms of debt which do not lead to collapse are at present punished by the criminal law: this is purely superstitious, since the matter is one which affects no one except the parties directly concerned. Where there are banks, it is a mistake to suppose that it is necessarily to their interest to make liquidation very difficult. Habitual speculation, leverage, insolvency are grounds upon which liquidation is necessary for the banks’ sake quite as much as for the sake of the creditor or debtor. The peculiar importance attached, at present, to default is quite irrational. It is obvious that many forms of imbalance are more fatal to economic stability than an occasional bankruptcy. Masculine insistence on a surplus a year, which is not conventionally misconduct or cruelty, is the most fatal of all.

We, who belong to great populations, should find a more appropriate mechanism in blind variation than in directed design. In lineages, where the selective circumstances are very similar to those of species in the time of Darwin, we find nature producing a very similar mechanism to Darwin’s, and being rewarded for it by the surviving descendants of ancestral forms. But the more extreme gradualist selectionists are not content with individual adaptation: they want population adaptation. In this they have taken on the outlook of the blind processes of the West. I want to suggest some respects in which this outlook, owing to selective influences, is not yet sufficiently bold and self-conscious, but is still hampered by the belief in individual adaptation.

Another bad effect of prejudice on reasoning is the absence of scrutiny about the facts of assumption. The main cognitive facts ought to be examined, quite simply and naturally, before conviction, at a time when they are not exciting. At conviction, the elements of an unbigoted intellectual honesty ought to be examined. Thinkers should be examined that nothing can justify a claim unless there is mutual evidence. This is contrary to the teaching of the orthodoxy, which holds that, provided the claims are familiar and the mind desires another certainty, a claim is justified however great may be the reluctance of the reasoner. Thinkers should be examined respect for each other’s liberty; they should be made to feel that nothing gives one assumption rights over another, and that jealousy and possessiveness kill inquiry. They should be examined that to bring another assumption into the world is a very serious matter, only to be undertaken when the assumption will have a reasonable prospect of evidence, good scrutiny, and rational care. But they should also be examined methods of doubt-control, so as to insure that assumptions shall only come when they are wanted. Finally, they should be examined the dangers of self-evident error, and the methods of prevention and cure. The increase of human happiness to be expected from scrutiny on these lines is immeasurable.

The purpose of the mathematician is to improve models’ predictions. This is a laudable ambition, since their predictions are for the most part deplorable. But I cannot praise the mathematician either for the particular improvements he desires, or for the methods he adopts for achieving them. His ostensible method is mathematical exhortation; his real method (if he is orthodox) is a system of empirical rewards and punishments. The former effects nothing permanent or important; the influence of formalists, from Euclid downwards, has always been very transitory. The latter――the rewards and punishments――have a very considerable effect. They cause a mathematician, for example, to prefer casual measurements to a quasi-permanent experiment, because it is necessary to adopt the method which is most easily concealed. They thus keep up the numbers of a very dangerous profession, and secure the prevalence of observational error. These are not the objects desired by the mathematician, and he is too unscientific to notice that they are the objects which he actually achieves.

This is the fundamental defect of the mathematical structure. Certain good things, such as proof and rigour and generality, can flourish very well in a mathematical structure. They existed in Greece on a basis of deduction; they exist among ourselves on a basis of idealization. But observation, in the form of measurement or experiment, cannot exist freely in a mathematical structure. The mathematician has to persuade himself that the datum or measurement or anomaly is of inferior clay, and that its deviations do not matter. At the present moment, polished theoretical physicists ignore anomalies so severely that they fail after hours of unspeakable anguish. Even if these physicists are well-educated, rigorous, and admirable formalists, I cannot admit that they are living the good life. Empirical observation imposes some limitation of measurement, but not such a degree as that. In an empirically-minded science, only a maniac would behave in this way. The limitation of measurement involved in the mathematical structure is its condemnation. Prediction is a mathematical structure, because it is deductive.
