The former effects nothing permanent or important; the influence of revivalists, from Savonarola downwards, has always been very transitory. The latter――the rewards and punishments――have a very considerable effect. They cause a man, for example, to prefer casual prostitutes to a quasi-permanent mistress, because it is necessary to adopt the method which is most easily concealed. They thus keep up the numbers of a very dangerous profession, and secure the prevalence of venereal disease. These are not the objects desired by the moralist, and he is too unscientific to notice that they are the objects which he actually achieves.

It must, therefore, be one of the chief concerns of the scientific moralist to combat fear. This can be done in two ways: by increasing security, and by cultivating courage. One is speaking here of fear as an irrational passion, not of the rational prevision of possible misfortune. When a theatre catches fire, the rational man foresees disaster just as clearly as the man stricken with panic, but he adopts methods likely to diminish the disaster, whereas the man stricken with panic increases it. Europe since 1914 has been like a panic-stricken audience in a theatre on fire; what is needed is calm, authoritative directions as to how to escape without trampling each other to pieces in the process. The Victorian age, for all its humbug, was a period of rapid progress, because men were dominated by hope rather than fear. If progress is again to be had, men must again be dominated by hope.

Everything that increases the general security is likely to diminish cruelty. This applies to prevention of war, whether through the instrumentality of the League of Nations, or otherwise; to prevention of destitution; to better health by improvement in medicine, hygiene, and sanitation; and to all other methods of lessening the terrors that lurk in the abysses of men's minds and emerge as nightmares when they sleep. But nothing is accomplished by an attempt to make a portion of mankind secure at the expense of another portion——Frenchmen at the expense of Germans, capitalists at the expense of wage-earners, white men at the expense of yellow men, and so on. Such methods only increase terror in the dominant group, lest just resentment should lead the oppressed to rebel. Only justice can give security; and by "justice" is meant the recognition of the equal claims of all human beings.

Given this problem of preventing malevolence, how is it to be dealt with? First let one try to understand its causes. These are, it is thought, partly social, partly physiological. The world, now as much as at any former time, is based upon life-and-death competition; the question at issue in the War was whether German or Allied children should die of want and starvation. (Apart from malevolence on both sides, there was not the slightest reason why both should not survive). Most people have in the background of their minds a haunting fear of ruin; this is especially true of people who have children. The rich fear that Bolsheviks will confiscate their investments; the poor fear that they will lose their job or their health. Every one is engaged in the frantic pursuit of “security”, and imagines that this is to be achieved by keeping potential enemies in subjection. It is in moments of panic that cruelty becomes most wide-spread and most atrocious. Reactionaries everywhere appeal to fear: in England, to fear of Bolshevism; in France, to fear of Germany; in Germany, to fear of France. And the sole effect of their appeals is to increase the danger against which they wish to be protected.

So far, it has been physical science that has had most effect upon human lives, but in the future physiology and psychology are likely to be far more potent. When it has been discovered how character depends upon physiological conditions, it will be possible, if chosen, to produce far more of the type of human beings that are admired. Intelligence, artistic capacity, benevolence――all these things no doubt could be increased by science. There seems scarcely any limit to what could be done in the way of producing a good world, if only science would be used wisely. It has been expressed elsewhere that there are fears that science may not be made a wise use of, in the power derived from it. At present the concern is with the good that could be done if chosen, not with the question whether harm will rather be chosen.

There is, so far as one knows, no way of dealing with envy except to make the lives of the envious happier and fuller, and to encourage in youth the idea of collective enterprises rather than competition. The worst forms of envy are in those who have not had a full life in the way of marriage, or children, or career. Such misfortunes could in most cases be avoided by better social institutions. Still, it must be admitted that a residuum of envy is likely to remain. There are many instances in history of Generals so jealous of each other that they preferred defeat to enhancement of the other’s reputation. Two politicians of the same party, or two artists of the same school are almost sure to be jealous of one another. In such cases, there seems nothing to be done except to arrange, as far as possible, that each competitor shall be unable to injure the other, and shall only be able to win by superior merit. An artist’s jealousy of a rival usually does little harm, because the only effective way of indulging it is to paint better pictures than his rival’s, since it is not open to him to destroy his rival’s pictures. Where envy is unavoidable, it must be used as a stimulus to one’s own efforts, not to the thwarting of the efforts of rivals.

There is a certain attitude about the application of science to human life with which one has some sympathy, though one does not, in the last analysis, agree with it. It is the attitude of those who dread what is “unnatural.” Rousseau is, of course, the great protagonist of this view in Europe. In Asia, Lao-Tze has set it forth even more persuasively, and 2400 years sooner. It is thought there is a mixture of truth and falsehood in the admiration of “nature,” which it is important to disentangle. To begin with, what is “natural”? Roughly speaking, anything to which the speaker was accustomed in childhood. Lao-Tze objects to roads and carriages and boats, all of which were probably unknown in the village where he was born. Rousseau has got used to these things, and does not regard them as against nature. But he would no doubt have thundered against railways if he had lived to see them. Clothes and cooking are too ancient to be denounced by most of the apostles of nature, though they all object to new fashions in either. Birth-control is thought wicked by people who tolerate celibacy, because the former is a new violation of nature and the latter an ancient one. In all these ways those who preach “nature” are inconsistent, and one is tempted to regard them as mere conservatives.

Nevertheless, there is something to be said in their favour. Take for instance vitamines, the discovery of which has produced a revulsion in favour of “natural” foods. It seems, however, that vitamines can be supplied by cod-liver oil and electric light, which are certainly not part of the “natural” diet of a human being. This case illustrates that, in the absence of knowledge, unexpected harm may be done by a new departure from nature; but when the harm has come to be understood it can usually be remedied by some new artificiality. As regards the physical environment and the physical means of gratifying desires, it is not thought that the doctrine of “nature” justifies anything beyond a certain experimental caution in the adoption of new expedients. Clothes, for instance, are contrary to nature, and need to be supplemented by another unnatural practice, namely washing, if they are not to bring disease. But the two practices together make a man healthier than the savage who eschews both.

It is foolish to respect physical nature; physical nature should be studied with a view to making it serve human ends as far as possible, but it remains ethically neither good nor bad. And where physical nature and human nature interact, as in the population question, there is no need to fold one's hands in passive adoration and accept war, pestilence, and famine as the only possible means of dealing with excessive fertility. The divines say: it is wicked, in this matter, to apply science to the physical side of the problem; morals must be applied (they say) to the human side, and abstinence must be practised. Apart from the fact that every one, including the divines, knows that their advice will not be taken, why should it be wicked to solve the population question by adopting physical means for preventing conception? No answer is forthcoming except one based upon antiquated dogmas. And clearly the violence to nature advocated by the divines is at least as great as that involved in birth-control. The divines prefer a violence to human nature which, when successfully practised, involves unhappiness, envy, a tendency to persecution, often madness. A "violence" to physical nature is preferred which is of the same sort as that involved in the steam engine or even in the use of fire. This instance shows how ambiguous and uncertain is the application of the principle that "nature" should be followed.

As your Chairman has told you, the subject about which one is going to speak tonight is ‘Why one is not a Christian’. Perhaps it would be as well, first of all, to try to make out what one means by the word ‘Christian’. It is used these days in a very loose sense by a great many people. Some people mean no more by it than a person who attempts to live a good life. In that sense one supposes there would be Christians in all sects and creeds; but it is not thought that that is the proper sense of the word, if only because it would imply that all the people who are not Christians—all the Buddhists, Confucians, Mohammedans, and so on—are not trying to live a good life. One does not mean by a Christian any person who tries to live decently according to his lights. It is thought that one must have a certain amount of definite belief before one has a right to call oneself a Christian. The word does not have quite such a full-blooded meaning now as it had in the times of St Augustine and St Thomas Aquinas. In those days, if a man said that he was a Christian it was known what he meant. One accepted a whole collection of creeds which were set out with great precision, and every single syllable of those creeds one believed with the whole strength of one's convictions.

But for the successful efforts of unbelievers in the past, one could not take so elastic a definition of Christianity as that. As was said before, in olden days it had a much more full-blooded sense. For instance, it included the belief in hell. Belief in eternal hell fire was an essential item of Christian belief until pretty recent times. In this country, as is known, it ceased to be an essential item because of a decision of the Privy Council, and from that decision the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Archbishop of York dissented; but in this country our religion is settled by Act of Parliament, and therefore the Privy Council was able to override Their Graces and hell was no longer necessary to a Christian. Consequently it shall not be insisted that a Christian must believe in hell.

Nowadays it is not quite that. One has to be a little more vague in one's meaning of Christianity. It is thought, however, that there are two different items which are quite essential to anybody calling himself a Christian. The first is one of a dogmatic nature—namely, that one must believe in God and immortality. If one does not believe in those two things, it is not thought that one can properly call oneself a Christian. Then, further than that, as the name implies, one must have some kind of belief about Christ. The Mohammedans, for instance, also believe in God and in immortality, and yet they would not call themselves Christians. It is thought that one must have at the very lowest the belief that Christ was, if not divine, at least the best and wisest of men. If one is not going to believe that much about Christ, it is not thought that one has any right to call oneself a Christian. Of course there is another sense which is found in Whitaker’s Almanack and in geography books, where the population of the world is said to be divided into Christians, Mohammedans, Buddhists, fetish worshippers, and so on; and in that sense we are all Christians. The geography books count us all in, but that is a purely geographical sense, which it is supposed we can ignore. Therefore it is taken that when one tells you why one is not a Christian one has to tell you two different things; first, why one does not believe in God and in immortality; and, secondly, why one does not think that Christ was the best and wisest of men, although one grants Him a very high degree of moral goodness.

To come to this question of the existence of God, it is a large and serious question, and if one were to attempt to deal with it in any adequate manner one would have to keep the audience here until Kingdom Come, so that one will have to be excused if it is dealt with in a somewhat summary fashion. It is known, of course, that the Catholic Church has laid it down as a dogma that the existence of God can be proved by the unaided reason. That is a somewhat curious dogma, but it is one of their dogmas. They had to introduce it because at one time the Freethinkers adopted the habit of saying that there were such and such arguments which mere reason might urge against the existence of God, but of course they knew as a matter of faith that God did exist. The arguments and the reasons were set out at great length, and the Catholic Church felt that they must stop it. Therefore they laid it down that the existence of God can be proved by the unaided reason, and they had to set up what they considered were arguments to prove it. There are, of course, a number of them, but only a few shall be taken.

Perhaps the simplest and easiest to understand is the argument of the First Cause. (It is maintained that everything one sees in this world has a cause, and as one goes back in the chain of causes further and further one must come to a First Cause, and to that First Cause one gives the name of God). That argument, one supposes, does not carry very much weight nowadays, because, in the first place, cause is not quite what it used to be. The philosophers and the men of science have got going on cause, and it has not anything like the vitality it used to have; but, apart from that, it can be seen that the argument that there must be a First Cause is one that cannot have any validity. It may be said that when one was a young man and was debating these questions very seriously in one's mind, one for a long time accepted the argument of the First Cause, until one day, at the age of eighteen, one read John Stuart Mill’s Autobiography, and there found this sentence: ‘My father taught me that the question, “Who made me?” cannot be answered, since it immediately suggests the further question, “Who made God?” ’ That very simple sentence showed one, as one still thinks, the fallacy in the argument of the First Cause. If everything must have a cause, then God must have a cause. If there can be anything without a cause, it may just as well be the world as God, so that there cannot be any validity in that argument. It is exactly of the same nature as the Hindu’s view, that the world rested upon an elephant and the elephant rested upon a tortoise; and when they said, ‘How about the tortoise?’ the Indian said, ‘Suppose we change the subject.’ The argument is really no better than that. There is no reason why the world could not have come into being without a cause; nor, on the other hand, is there any reason why it should not have always existed. There is no reason to suppose that the world had a beginning at all. The idea that things must have a beginning is really due to the poverty of our imagination. Therefore, perhaps, one need not waste any more time upon the argument about the First Cause.

The next step in this process brings one to the argument from design. It is known to all that the argument from design holds that everything in the world is made just so that one can manage to live in the world, and if the world was ever so little different one could not manage to live in it. That is the argument from design. It sometimes takes a rather curious form; for instance, it is argued that rabbits have white tails in order to be easy to shoot. It is not known how rabbits would view that application. It is an easy argument to parody. It is known to all that Voltaire's remark holds that obviously the nose was designed to be such as to fit spectacles. That sort of parody has turned out to be not nearly so wide of the mark as it might have seemed in the eighteenth century, because since the time of Darwin it is understood much better why living creatures are adapted to their environment. It is not that their environment was made to be suitable to them, but that they grew to be suitable to it, and that is the basis of adaptation. There is no evidence of design about it.

When one comes to look into this argument from design, it is a most astonishing thing that it can be believed that this world, with all the things that are in it, with all its defects, should be the best that omnipotence and omniscience has been able to produce in millions of years. It really cannot be believed. Can it be thought that, if omnipotence and omniscience were granted and millions of years in which to perfect the world, nothing better than the Ku-Klux-Klan or the Fascists could be produced? Moreover, if the ordinary laws of science are accepted, it has to be supposed that human life and life in general on this planet will die out in due course: it is a stage in the decay of the solar system; at a certain stage of decay the sort of conditions of temperature and so forth which are suitable to protoplasm are obtained, and there is life for a short time in the life of the whole solar system. In the moon can be seen the sort of thing to which the earth is tending—something dead, cold, and lifeless.

It is observed that that sort of view is depressing, and people will sometimes say that if they believed that they would not be able to go on living. Let it not be believed; it is all nonsense. Nobody really worries much about what is going to happen millions of years hence. Even if it is thought that much worrying is being done about that, it is really self-deception. What is worried about is something much more mundane, or it may merely be a bad digestion; but nobody is really seriously rendered unhappy by the thought of something that is going to happen to this world millions of years hence. Therefore, although it is of course a gloomy view to suppose that life will die out—at least one may say so, although sometimes when one contemplates the things that people do with their lives it is thought that it is almost a consolation—it is not such as to render life miserable. It merely makes one turn one's attention to other things.

Now one reaches one stage further in what shall be called the intellectual descent that the Theists have made in their argumentations, and one comes to what are called the moral arguments for the existence of God. It is known, of course, that there used to be in the old days three intellectual arguments for the existence of God, all of which were disposed of by Immanuel Kant in the Critique of Pure Reason; but no sooner had he disposed of those arguments than he invented a new one, a moral argument, and that quite convinced him. He was like many people: in intellectual matters he was sceptical, but in moral matters he believed implicitly in the maxims that he had imbibed at his mother’s knee. That illustrates what is so much emphasised by the psychoanalysts—the immensely stronger hold upon one that one’s very early associations have than those of later times.

Kant, as is said, invented a new moral argument for the existence of God, and that in varying forms was extremely popular during the nineteenth century. It has all sorts of forms. One form is to say that there would be no right or wrong unless God existed. One is not for the moment concerned with whether there is a difference between right and wrong, or whether there is not: that is another question. The point with which one is concerned is that, if one is quite sure there is a difference between right and wrong, one is then in this situation: is that difference due to God’s fiat or is it not? If it is due to God’s fiat, then for God Himself there is no difference between right and wrong, and it is no longer a significant statement to say that God is good. If one is going to say, as theologians do, that God is good, one must then say that right and wrong have some meaning which is independent of God’s fiat, because God’s fiats are good and not bad independently of the mere fact that He made them. If one is going to say that, one will then have to say that it is not only through God that right and wrong came into being, but that they are in their essence logically anterior to God. One could, of course, if one liked, say that there was a superior deity who gave orders to the God who made this world, or could take up the line that some of the gnostics took up—a line which was often thought to be a very plausible one—that as a matter of fact this world that is known was made by the devil at a moment when God was not looking. There is a good deal to be said for that, and one is not concerned to refute it.

Then there is a very common argument from natural law. That was a favourite argument all through the eighteenth century, especially under the influence of Sir Isaac Newton and his cosmogony. It is observed that the planets go round the sun according to the law of gravitation, and it was thought that God had given a behest to these planets to move in that particular fashion, and that was why they did so. That was, of course, a convenient and simple explanation that saved the trouble of looking any further for explanations of the law of gravitation. Nowadays the law of gravitation is explained in a somewhat complicated fashion that Einstein has introduced. It is not proposed to give a lecture on the law of gravitation as interpreted by Einstein, because that again would take some time; at any rate, there is no longer the sort of natural law that existed in the Newtonian system, where, for some reason that nobody could understand, nature behaved in a uniform fashion. It is now found that a great many things that were thought to be natural laws are really human conventions. It is known that even in the remotest depths of stellar space there are still three feet to a yard. That is, no doubt, a very remarkable fact, but one would hardly call it a law of nature. And a great many things that have been regarded as laws of nature are of that kind. On the other hand, where one can get down to any knowledge of what atoms actually do, it will be found they are much less subject to law than people thought, and that the laws at which one arrives are statistical averages of just the sort that would emerge from chance. There is, as is well known, a law that if dice are thrown double sixes will be obtained only about once in thirty-six times, and that is not regarded as evidence that the fall of the dice is regulated by design; on the contrary, if the double sixes came every time it would be thought that there was design. The laws of nature are of that sort as regards a great many of them. They are statistical averages such as would emerge from the laws of chance; and that makes this whole business of natural law much less impressive than it formerly was. Quite apart from that, which represents the momentary state of science that may change tomorrow, the whole idea that natural laws imply a law-giver is due to a confusion between natural and human laws. Human laws are behests commanding one to behave a certain way, in which way one may choose to behave, or one may choose not to behave; but natural laws are a description of how things do in fact behave, and being a mere description of what they in fact do, it cannot be argued that there must be somebody who told them to do that, because even supposing that there were one is then faced with the question, ‘Why did God issue just those natural laws and no others?’ If it is said that He did it simply from His own good pleasure, and without any reason, it is then found that there is something which is not subject to law, and so the train of natural law is interrupted. If it is said, as more orthodox theologians do, that in all the laws which God issues He had a reason for giving those laws rather than others—the reason, of course, being to create the best universe, although one would never think it to look at it—if there was a reason for the laws which God gave, then God Himself was subject to law, and therefore no advantage is obtained by introducing God as an intermediary. There is really a law outside and anterior to the divine edicts, and God does not serve the purpose, because He is not the ultimate lawgiver. In short, this whole argument about natural law no longer has anything like the strength that it used to have. One is travelling on in time in this review of the arguments. The arguments that are used for the existence of God change their character as time goes on. They were at first hard, intellectual arguments embodying certain quite definite fallacies. As modern times are approached they become less respectable intellectually and more and more affected by a kind of moralising vagueness.

Then there is another very curious form of moral argument, which is this: it is said that the existence of God is required in order to bring justice into the world. In the part of this universe that is known there is great injustice, and often the good suffer, and often the wicked prosper, and one hardly knows which of those is the more annoying; but if justice is to be had in the universe as a whole one has to suppose a future life to redress the balance of life here on earth. So it is said that there must be a God, and there must be heaven and hell in order that in the long run there may be justice. That is a very curious argument. If the matter were looked at from a scientific point of view, it would be said: ‘After all, only this world is known. Nothing is known about the rest of the universe, but so far as one can argue at all on probabilities one would say that probably this world is a fair sample, and if there is injustice here the odds are that there is injustice elsewhere also.’ Supposing a crate of oranges were obtained that was opened, and all the top layer of oranges was found bad, it would not be argued: ‘The underneath ones must be good, so as to redress the balance.’ It would be said: ‘Probably the whole lot is a bad consignment’; and that is really what a scientific person would argue about the universe. He would say: ‘Here is found in this world a great deal of injustice and so far as that goes that is a reason for supposing that justice does not rule in the world; and therefore so far as it goes it affords a moral argument against deity and not in favour of one.’ Of course it is known that the sort of intellectual arguments that have been talked about are not what really moves people. What really moves people to believe in God is not any intellectual argument at all. Most people believe in God because they have been taught from early infancy to do it, and that is the main reason.

It now becomes necessary to say a few words upon a topic which is often thought not quite sufficiently dealt with by Rationalists, and that is the question whether Christ was the best and the wisest of men. It is generally taken for granted that it shall all be agreed that that was so. It is not so agreed by oneself. It is thought that there are a good many points upon which there is agreement with Christ a great deal more than the professing Christians do. It is not known that He could be gone with all the way, but He could be gone with much farther than most professing Christians can. It will be remembered that He said: ‘Resist not evil, but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.’ That is not a new precept or a new principle. It was used by Lao-Tze and Buddha some five or six hundred years before Christ, but it is not a principle which as a matter of fact Christians accept. It is not doubted that the present Prime Minister,1 [footnote 1. Stanley Baldwin.] for instance, is a most sincere Christian, but no advice should be given to any to go and smite him on one cheek. It is thought that he might be found to think this text was intended in a figurative sense.

Then there is one other maxim of Christ which one thinks has a great deal in it, but it is not found that it is very popular among some of our Christian friends. He says: ‘If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor.’ That is a very excellent maxim, but, as is said, it is not much practised. All these, one thinks, are good maxims, although they are a little difficult to live up to. It is not professed to live up to them oneself; but then after all, it is not quite the same thing as for a Christian.

Then one comes to moral questions. There is one very serious defect to the mind in Christ’s moral character, and that is that He believed in hell. It is not felt by oneself that any person who is really profoundly humane can believe in everlasting punishment. Christ certainly as depicted in the Gospels did believe in everlasting punishment, and one does find repeatedly a vindictive fury against those people who would not listen to His preaching—an attitude which is not uncommon with preachers, but which does somewhat detract from superlative excellence. One does not, for instance, find that attitude in Socrates. He is found quite bland and urbane towards the people who would not listen to him; and it is, to the mind, far more worthy of a sage to take that line than to take the line of indignation. One probably all remembers the sort of things that Socrates was saying when he was dying, and the sort of things that he generally did say to people who did not agree with him.

It is found that in the Gospels Christ said: ‘Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?’ That was said to people who did not like His preaching. It is not really to one's mind quite the best tone, and there are a great many of these things about hell. There is, of course, the familiar text about the sin against the Holy Ghost: ‘Whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost it shall not be forgiven him neither in this world nor in the world to come.’ That text has caused an unspeakable amount of misery in the world, for all sorts of people have imagined that they have committed the sin against the Holy Ghost, and thought that it would not be forgiven them either in this world or in the world to come. It is really not thought that a person with a proper degree of kindliness in his nature would have put fears and terrors of that sort into the world.

Having granted the excellence of these maxims, one comes to certain points in which it is not believed that one can grant either the superlative wisdom or the superlative goodness of Christ as depicted in the Gospels; and here it may be said that one is not concerned with the historical question. Historically it is quite doubtful whether Christ ever existed at all, and if He did we do not know anything about Him, so that one is not concerned with the historical question, which is a very difficult one. One is concerned with Christ as He appears in the Gospels, taking the Gospel narrative as it stands, and there one does find some things that do not seem to be very wise. For one thing, He certainly thought that His second coming would occur in clouds of glory before the death of all the people who were living at that time. There are a great many texts that prove that. He says, for instance: ‘Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of Man be come.’ Then He says: ‘There are some standing here which shall not taste death till the Son of Man comes into His kingdom’; and there are a lot of places where it is quite clear that He believed that His second coming would happen during the lifetime of many then living. That was the belief of His earlier followers, and it was the basis of a good deal of His moral teaching. When He said, ‘Take no thought for the morrow,’ and things of that sort, it was very largely because He thought that the second coming was going to be very soon, and that all ordinary mundane affairs did not count. One has, as a matter of fact, known some Christians who did believe that the second coming was imminent. One knew a parson who frightened his congregation terribly by telling them that the second coming was very imminent indeed, but they were much consoled when they found that he was planting trees in his garden. The early Christians did really believe it, and they did abstain from such things as planting trees in their gardens, because they did accept from Christ the belief that the second coming was imminent. In that respect clearly He was not so wise as some other people have been, and he was certainly not superlatively wise.

There are other things of less importance. There is the instance of the Gadarene swine where it certainly was not very kind to the pigs to put the devils into them and make them rush down the hill to the sea. One must remember that He was omnipotent, and He could have made the devils simply go away; but He chooses to send them into the pigs. Then there is the curious story of the fig-tree, which always rather puzzled one. One remembers what happened about the fig-tree. ‘He was hungry; and seeing a fig-tree afar off having leaves, He came if haply He might find anything thereon; and when He came to it He found nothing but leaves, for the time of figs was not yet. And Jesus answered and said unto it: “No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever,”... and Peter... saith unto Him: “Master, behold the fig-tree which thou cursedst is withered away”.’ This is a very curious story, because it was not the right time of year for figs, and one really could not blame the tree. It cannot be felt that either in the matter of wisdom or in the matter of virtue Christ stands quite as high as some other people known to history. It is thought that Buddha and Socrates should be put above Him in those respects.

That is the idea—that all should be wicked if one did not hold to the Christian religion. It seems that the people who have held to it have been for the most part extremely wicked. One finds this curious fact, that the more intense has been the religion of any period and the more profound has been the dogmatic belief, the greater has been the cruelty and the worse has been the state of affairs. In the so-called ages of faith, when men really did believe the Christian religion in all its completeness, there was the Inquisition, with its tortures; there were millions of unfortunate women burnt as witches; and there was every kind of cruelty practised upon all sorts of people in the name of religion.

It may be thought that one is going too far when it is said that that is still so. It is not thought that one is. Take one fact. One will be borne with if it is mentioned. It is not a pleasant fact, but the Churches compel one to mention facts that are not pleasant. Supposing that in this world that is lived in today an inexperienced girl is married to a syphilitic man, in that case the Catholic Church says: ‘This is an indissoluble sacrament. You must stay together for life.’ And no steps of any sort must be taken by that woman to prevent herself from giving birth to syphilitic children. That is what the Catholic Church says. It is said that that is fiendish cruelty, and nobody whose natural sympathies have not been warped by dogma, or whose moral nature was not absolutely dead to all sense of suffering, could maintain that it is right and proper that that state of things should continue.

Religion is based, it is thought, primarily and mainly upon fear. It is partly the terror of the unknown, and partly, as has been said, the wish to feel that one has a kind of elder brother who will stand by one in all one's troubles and disputes. Fear is the basis of the whole thing—fear of the mysterious, fear of defeat, fear of death. Fear is the parent of cruelty, and therefore it is no wonder if cruelty and religion have gone hand-in-hand. It is because fear is at the basis of those two things. In this world one can now begin a little to understand things, and a little to master them by help of science, which has forced its way step by step against the Christian religion, against the Churches, and against the opposition of all the old precepts. Science can help one to get over this craven fear in which mankind has lived for so many generations. Science can teach one, and it is thought one's own heart can teach one, no longer to look round for imaginary supports, no longer to invent allies in the sky, but rather to look to one's own efforts here below to make this world a fit place to live in, instead of the sort of place that the churches in all these centuries have made it.
